To be honest, I can't really find much wrong with the PC port of Chaos Theory. As a long fan of the series who has completed all games on their hardest difficulty, I can safely say that I know what I'm talking about.
The controls are a lot better than what people seem to think, having the mouse wheel to control your speed is extremely helpful as it allows you to maintain speed, whereas on console you would have to keep the analog stick in the same place and try not to either flick to far forward by accident or not go fast enough. The mouse aiming is extremely handy when using gadgets such as the airfoil rounds and the pistol's OCP, as those rely on extreme accuracy. Lockpicking has become a lot easier as you don't have to rely on getting the precise location on the analog stick to lockpick, all you have to do is spam the crap out of the correct WASD key. The game also allows you to bind keys (To an extent) so that you can get most of your gadgets around a confortable area. Notice however that I said to an extent. Some keys cannot be changed such as Ctrl, Shift and Enter which is quite unfortunate given that I need to take my hand off of my mouse to try and grab a guard. However, on a lighter note, the controls are compact (Excluding interacting and viewing the OPSAT), and all it takes to get used to them is a bit of muscle memory. In short, the main controls are built around WASD, goggles are keys 1-5, aiming your gun is E, crouching is C and jumping is Space (Surprise surprise).
Controls aside, let's talk gameplay. For those unfortunate few who never got to play the original Splinter Cell games, back in the day when Micheal Ironsides voiced our sneaky beaky spy friend, I'll give you a rundown of the plot. You're tasked with rescuing a Bruce Morgenholt from some Spanish fort in Peru. He's a computer programmer who with the help of some other dude finds out about these 'Masse Kernels' which can be used for all kinds of dodgy stuff, and when I say dodgy I'm not talking about herion dealing behind a Netto. Essentially they can be used to hack into things once thought unhackable and could be used to spark World War III (This time with North Korea, so you know it's gonna be good). So your job as our tall 'murican friend is to stop that. Now we've got the plot aside we can actually talk about the game itself. Chaos Theory does an amazing job of making stealth seem realistic and it has to be the most punishing for it out of all that I have played. The game encourages you to take your time and find alternate paths, or wait for them to appear if you wish to go stealth. Or if you don't even Splinter Cell, you can go in all guns blazing and kill everyone like a peasant. Even though the game gives you three options of loudout (Stealth, Assault and a balenced one) the game will prefer you go stealth, and I would too as it not only makes the game more rewarding and fun, but also eavesdropping on certain conversations or interrogating certain guards or civilians (In some cases) will reward you with door codes, medkit locations and other handy information that could even reveal the identity of one of the main antagonists later in the game.
On the subject of level design, nothing has been changed and that's not a bad thing. Chaos Theory's levels were certainly some of the best designed and rivial Pandora Tomorrow's in my opinion. The ideas were unique such as sneaking around on a cargo ship, breaking into a penthosue during a blackout or infiltrating a retrofitted North Korean missile battery. But all of these levels still allow for all styles of play and each have their own set of side objectives that will help you completionist legends out there, but this may require you to go stealthy you Call of Duty scrubs.
Some levels even make stealth harder by adding flooring that will make noise when walked on in a certain place, having broken glass or other obsticles that may make sneaking around harder. What's that? Sound matters in a stealth game? Yes. On your HUD you will find two meters, one representing light (Or your visibility in the current light you're in) as well as a sound meter. This is where Chaos Theory becomes one of the more superior stealth games as sound is key to sneaking around. You gain the ability to move around louder when there's a radio on nearby or a generator is active as it masks your sound. Making the stealth in Chaos Theory more enjoyable and realistic at the same time.
All in all, I still think to this day that Chaos Theory sets an example of what stealth games should be like and is very well deserving of its 92 rating on Metacritic. Well worth the £7.99 on Steam. 9.8/10 IGN - Not enough water.

Well, there you have it, old Sam Fisher's peak, in this reviewer's opinion. This is probably one of the best stealth games ever made, for various reasons (though, like anything else, it is not without fault).
Let's talk presentation. The graphics are insanely good, especially considering this game came out in 2005; the character models are a bit blocky and basic by today's standards, the pre-rendered cutscenes haven't aged very well, and Sam's face is... weird, but for the most part, the environments, the lighting, Sam's animations, it's all top-notch stuff. I remember reading on a forum that someone complained later titles included a Sam Fisher that was way too "nimble" or not "heavy" enough. This game excells at making you feel like a very competent spy that is still reasonably limited by his human physical ability. In other words, your movements feel like they have weight to it; you feel like a badass, but not a superhero.
Sound is also amazing, the music changes according to how (un)subtle your approach is and how alert the enemies are, the gunfire is piercing and dangerous-sounding, the various environmental sound effects are stunning. I'd love to see a making-of just for the sound design of this game, that must have been some interesting foley work. The music deserves a separate mention, it does its job and there are some instantly catchy tunes, but it's never intrusive and it doesn't steal the spotlight. The only thing I'd raise my eyebrow at is the voice acting of some of the non-English-speaking characters (admiral Otomo and most enemy soldiers... *shudder*), it's just plain awful (I hate to sound overly PC but it's sadly pretty racist/stereotypical) and it's a shame, because this entry has some of the best voice-acting (here I mean Fisher and crew) and writing I've ever seen in a "spy"/stealth title. The tone balances on that fine line between serious and tongue-in-cheek (dark) humor so well it's like eating the best sweet&sour sauce on Earth. I was going for a 100% non-lethal, non-knockout playthrough and I actually saved, interrogated soldiers and re-loaded just to hear Sam's endlessly creative and witty threats and other dialogue.
On to the gameplay. The levels (and by extension, the missions) are flat-out amazing, varied, detailed and vibrant. The cool thing about Chaos Theory is that it has a number of different ways to complete your objectives and many different paths to take in the process. There's always a hidden vent or crawlspace to help you out, a ledge to shimmy along, a zip-line, a janitor's closet, a scaffolding, you name it. The bank, Displace and Hokkaido levels stand out in particular in this respect.
The actual objectives themselves also don't necessarily have one way of completion: for example, there is an objective in one mission that has you find out the identity of one of the antagonists. You can eavesdrop on a conversation in that mission and if you fail, you can find the intel on a PC in the next mission. Another example would be interrogating a soldier to gain some information vs. hacking a PC or searching a file cabinet - all three things will complete the same objective. One of my favourite features are the "opportunity" objectives: those occur only when (and if) you stumble upon an object or an event in the map which triggers it (like noticing the guerilla guards have expensive weapons - opportunity objective: find out where they got them). In short, rich, deep and engaging gameplay with just enough freedom to be fun and just enough linearity to keep you from scratching your head.
Since this is a game about a man and his gadgets, let me just list quickly what I mean: you've got a light meter (as in SC1) and a sound meter, your trusty SC20k launcher with a shotgun/sniper attachment, the good ol' SC20 pistol with OCP, a few new cool gadgets (EMF vision for one, lets you see electro-magnetic fields generated by electronic equipment) in addition to the standard night-vision and thermal vision, lock-picks, different types of grenades, shocker rounds, airfoil rounds, sticky cameras and so on. Suffice to say the arsenal is enough to complete your objectives and then some. The only issue is that if you're going for a 100% non-lethal/stealth approach, you won't really have much need for these amazing weapons because you can rely on good ol'-fashioned diversion and sneaking tactics; that said, I've completed the game on 100% stealth and I will definitely complete the game again, this time going all out and not caring about the mission rating because these weapons are SO fun to use and mess around with. The only gadget I think is a bit overpowered is the EEV hacking, which I think makes the game a bit easy because you can literally hack computers while standing 10m away. Oh, by the way, since I mentioned mission rating: the game rates your completion by deducting percentage for kills, alarms, being spotted and completing objectives. The most awesome feature IMO is that you can complete this game with 0 knockouts (other than those required for mission completion, I think there are about two or three). Not 0 kills, 0 KNOCKOUTS. That means you can ghost through the entire game without any of the guards having a clue you were even there. If that's not awesome, I don't know what is.
One last thing I have to mention is the AI. This is both a strength and weakness. Let me explain.
For the most part, the AI is good and when they start to get suspicious is where they really shine. They'll notice broken lights, even turned off lights, open doors, all that kind of stuff, and they won't stop investigating until they're sure there was "nothing here but ghosts and shadows", they'll even talk to their buddies about it and try and get their help ("What was that?!" "What?" "I don't KNOW what, that's why I'm worried!"). The problem is their behaviour *before* they notice something's off. If you know the ropes well enough, you can get away with stuff that is completely unrealistic and makes the AI look dumber than a moldy doughnut, even without gadgets. It tends to stretch your suspension of disbelief a lot: for instance, you can (in certain situations) literally walk right in front of a guard's face in not-entirely-pitch-darkness, or slip by him by hugging a corridor wall. Then again, if the AI was TOO relentless, the game wouldn't be fun. What I'm saying is, this game's AI is like a magic show - you either buy it or you don't. I tend to treat the guards and other elements in Splinter Cell as a game of chess, so to speak, and I don't pay much attention to what I'm doing as long as I get the objective done and they get to live another day. Is the AI realistic? No, not really. Is it done in a way that makes the game fun to play and the difficulty doesn't suffer in any extreme way? Yes. I guess another way to put it would be: they behave like stupid humans, but they still behave like good video game NPCs.
In conclusion, this title is worthy of a place in the Stealth Hall of Fame. If you're a fan of stealth games, you've probably played it already and if you haven't, well... get to it, and if you're new to stealth games, this is a great one to win you over. I know, because it did just that for me. And Fisher didn't need to press a knife against my throat to convince me.

Dragon quest was a game I thought was exclusive to ps4 but it did so hit pc and I am glad I waited being a huge DQ fan myself. The game has elements of DQ it from the charctersto the music, sound effects and even DQ element such as mixing pot and Tension mode. The art itself from Akira Toriyama (creator of Dragon Ball) is always superb.
The game however is a beat em up Musou genre game( I.e Dynasty warrior, One piece warriors etc) so not your typical DQ RPG. Fans of DQ and supporters or those that collect games will want to pick this one up.  The gameplay however can be quite repetitive and more of a novelty.

+ Japanese and English choice with text language options (English, French, German, Italian, Korean, Spanish, and Japanese)
+ Bindable keys, controller configurations etc.
+ Great art and graphics
+ Game is locked at 1080p 60fps (Gotta do some manual workaround to get the best you can from your cards to push AA etc, game cannot go above 1080 res)
+ Dragon Quest Music, Sounds and characters galore along with mixing pot crafting and tension mode.
+ Hundreds of monsters being on screen at once seeing them heading your way is quite impressive
+ Tension mode is very flashy and the cutscenes looks great
+ Plenty of characters in the game with thier own strength and weakness and also weapon style switch around 4 characters at the end of every round at the hub.
+ Lots of contents such as quests, sidequests, items, trophies, and even recipes to collect.
+ Rather than focused on just beating countless armies up, The game focus on a tower defense type of gameplay at times and boss fights.
- Not being able to go above 1080 res
- Gameplay can get sort of repetitive after a while
- Difficulty scaling choice, Game wasn't as hard and I couldn't pick a choice in difficulty. As you progress the enemy get strong but you get much stronger.
- Menu can be a bit tedious at times, Buying an item one at a time, Putting it on characters, accepting etc. Kills alot of time just spamming the Accept button

Starseed Pilgrim is a very unique game. Most of the fun comes from experimenting with the different colored blocks and figuring out what everything in the game world means. Nothing is explained when you first start, but the game doesn't penalize you at all and lets you explore the mechanics as you teach yourself how to play and develop your own strategies for succeeding. In the simplest explanation, you place differently colored blocks to try to get more differently colored blocks and grow your tower while escaping the spreading darkness. Each colored block behaves differently, so the engagement comes from figuring out how to optimize your block placement to get as far as you can.
I don't think Starseed Pilgrim will keep you coming back for too long, but it's the kind of unique game you should try for a little while to see what works and what doesn't. I would recommend if you're interested in abstract indie titles or if you're a game designer looking for more unique study material.

Match 3, Marvel, but.... Microtransactions.
The game's mechanics of a match-3 to initiate fights is far from new anymore - but its complicated by the need to "heal" injured combatants either by waiting or buying health packs.
That's the first clue.
The next is leveling up the characters. You do gain some of the upgrade materials and items from missions, certain ones earned at certain stages - but to make your team strong you need to further upgrade the skills, then upgrade the character, and repeat. There is a relative cap, but the distance from what the free to play model gives you and the time it would take to get there is absurd compared to just paying for it. It scales up the higher you go. Pay for more to get less and so on.
Hence the microtransactions. Lots and lots of microtransactions.
I wouldn't have an issue if it was possible to gain a decent team of your favorite heroes easily, just to enjoy the story, or possible to upgrade them relatively well without spending a fortune... but this game takes it to a whole new level.
Be wary, this is a Pay to Win game, and boy you could pay in spades with the level of microtransactions here.
Players beware. The lure to pay to win here is way too much for it to be worth it.
Other than that, its a standard Marvel-oriented game following the mainstream stories on their own minor twist with the ISO-8 junk I first saw years ago with the Facebook varaint. The story is alright, the game itself is okay. The over-abundance of microtransactions to make you pay a fortune is not really making this game worth it.

In concept, I really wanted to like this game. It's a cool idea and it has a lot of potential to be a really neat game that would be super fun to play, but it has a few glaring problems that mean I just can't recommend it at all.
First and most visibly, there is no manual, or instructions, and people seem to think it's cute that you have to figure this game out yourself. That'd be fine if it were less complicated, but it's actually a pretty intricate game with complex mechanics to it that are VERY frustrating not to know at first. I put this game down for a long time, having given up on it or just assuming it was broken, then only recently found some kind soul had written up a very good description of the game's mechanics. I ended up still disliking it, for the reasons below, but I felt I needed to mention up front that if people can't figure out how to play your game, THAT IS A PROBLEM WITH YOUR GAME. It just is. The cutesy mystery crap around how to play this game is just obnoxious. If all your game has to offer is the mystery of how to play it, that's pretty pathetic.
Moving on. The lack of gamepad support makes this game awkward to play, to say the least. There are no settings, so you can't adjust the key bindings, so basically unless you happen to love the key bindings it comes with (arrow keys with "up" as jump), you're just screwed. Gamepad support isn't hard to implement these days, and this game feels like an incomplete project without it.
Speaking of the lack of settings, there is only one supported resolution in this game: too damn low if you have anything approaching a modern computer. It's not as big of a deal as the other problems I had, but this is definitely an issue when the window is utterly lilliputian in size. So the playfield size is infinite, but your window into it is non-negotiably small, and there's no full-screen setting.
I can't ever get back the minutes I've wasted trying to play this game. Don't waste yours too.

Yeah the controls are a little different, but to all the reviewers who are flaming that the controls are clunky and uncontrollable, hogwash.  I got used to the controls in the prologue, and while there's no dedicated "jump" button I've never had an issue with getting where I wanted or picking up objects etc so forth.  As for people flaming the story, all I have to say is CoD got higher reviews and CoD can hardly be considered a game at all.
I personally believe it should be a mid to low 80's game, score wise.  Nothing will ever stand up to Thief 2: The Metal Age, that game was just pure platinium awesome and I really wish people would review the game for itself and not that it's not 100% true to what you remember.  If you're looking for a sneaky steal everything fun game, Thief might be for you.  Just don't expect it to be Dishonored.

This game had potential to be something great, but it sadly fell short.
As someone who has been playing fighting games for a majority of my life, this game seemed like it would be a trip to play. In the end, it's a very basic 'fighter' with an interesting cast, a handful of modes, and only a few maps.
The combat is centered around timing your attacks and trying to chain them until your oppoenent KOs. Everyone has an Armor Meter, which shields your health. When this is gone, your HP is next. There is no way to replenish your Armor meter, regardless of how much you have left. There is some strategy to the fighting, as landing Back Attacks will net you extra damage. However, this is completely moot since a vast majority of the cast has attacks that register as Back Attacks if you're close enough.
You have two main attacking buttons: Light and Heavy. By mixing them, you form your combos. However, the combos are almost universal for everyone, with only slight variations. You also have two Rage Skills, which can be activated with a Rage meter that builds up as you attack and are attacked. These can range from nearly useless to nearly game-breaking.
When you start, you are given enough in-game currency to purchase any character you wish. This concept seems odd, but interesting. It essentially forces you to get good at your selected character. Fortunately, there is a training mode which will let you try out every character before you go make your choice.
As for the game modes, you have Team Battle, Defense, and Free For All. Each mode has maybe two maps. You earn Rank Points, which will allow you to purchase gear from the shop, and Meseta, the ingame currency, based on your performance. The better you do, the more you get. What irritates me is the lack of modes and diversity of maps. You'll easilly get bored of the same thing and seeing the same layout after a few hours.
Personally, there are several other Free to Play games that are much more fleshed out and have way more content to indulge yourself with. Don't waste your time with Archeblade.

GRID Autosport is a perfect mix of arcade and simulation racing which has only been this well executed before by the SHIFT series, it's a huge step in the right direction after the disaster that GRID 2 was.
The graphics are really good and the game is well optimized (I'm playing it in a macbook air without trouble), the gameplay is fun and allows for different kinds of players, if you are not a hardcore racing gamer, you can just play in 3rd person with traction and stability control activated and you are gonna have fun, in the other hand, you can play in 1st person with assistants off, tune your vehicle settings for each track and try to get the most out of it as well.
The multiplayer is very good, lag is not a problem since the cars become ghosts when the connection is problematic, avoiding unexpected collisions. The single player is also a lot of fun and a good start to make you prepared for the online.
There's a good variety of cars, but the lack of more classical GPs is problematic, there are many fun city races, but regarding the classics you will only find in the standard game Hockenheim, Sepang and Spa Francochamps, not even Nurburgring is available, which is a shame.
The AI is a complicated matter, for one thing they are very competitive and entertaining, they fight between themselves, even crash between themselves, they try to overtake you constantly and it's a good competition, in the other hand, sometimes they can be too agressive and crash you out of the race in a situation that is clearly not legal by the FIA standards, when this happens it will make you VERY mad.
GRID Autosport has a few problems regarding AI and lack of tracks, but overall its a great racing game, the best I've played since SHIFT 2 (I haven't played PCars yet, chill out), and it's certainly worth your money.

tl;dr - All in all, good game. You either like it or you don't imo. Has a mobile game fatigue system, but each individual character you make has their own fatigue bar, so it's not like you only get 30 minutes. You get roughly 2~ ish hours per character before fatigue kicks you out to another character. Combat mechanics are some of the best, especially in a free to play game. It's like mixing a beat 'em up, a fighting game, and an mmo all in one. Very fluid, fast, and fun game. Everything is streamlined to be as fast and efficient as possible. Crafting gets kind of ignored by most new players because it's just so ignorable for the longest time. Very frequent events and love from the developers. Constant rebalancing so there's never really a bad class, at least not forever. Monthly-ish updates. I like it. Gets a bit repetitive after a while. Has raids, two. An old one and a newish one that got added in the middle/end of this past fall I think. Company is small but puts good effort into making their game better. I respect them, and their work, and I can see a lot of people doing the same too.
Most people probably won't give this game a chance simply because of the fatigue system, I assume. Whether or not that's true, idk, but most people see that as a sort of issue and compare it to the fatigue systems of mobile games. Each individual character you make has a fatigue bar, so you can actually play this game all day. If you're not into that, it's fine. I wasn't either and still kind of am not, but I think it's a good thing. I'll go into depth as to why I think that in the gameply section.
Graphics - 9/10
Gameplay 7.5/10
Music 7/10
Story ???/10 (From what I've seen it's kind of anime-esque but also not. Am kind of intrigued but still haven't seen much)
Graphics - Good spritework with good animation. Art is actually very good and well detailed. Character designs look dope AF.
Gameplay - Okay here's the thing. The combat is super fluid and fun, and each individual subclass (of which I think there are over 50?) feels different with maybe like 6 ones that are clones from the old days when the old devs didn't want to put effort into making different gendered classes. Those same classes have also gotten updates, but I haven't gone to look and see if they're not clones anymore. Regardless, only the male/female fighter and male/female gunner subclasses were clones. Everything else shares, at most, a thematic similarity. An example of this is the male and female mages. Both have classes that use elemental magic, though the classes have very different abilities. It's just that they both use fire/water/light/dark magics. Even then, not each subclass from both of those base classes share thematic differences, giving you a very wide variety of classes in the game. Combat is very straightforward, and depending on the class you pick, can be experienced very differently from person to person. Take the time to try and find a class you actually like. You get your subclass at level 15 and can rearrange skill points whenever at any time. Up to level 50, you can also change your subclass.
Gameplay gets really repetitive very quickly, but the fairly constant progression where you gain new skills helps a decent amount. Still, it gets kind of annoying, but not so much that it's a direct turn off (at least for me).
Music - It's not absolutely amazing but it's pretty good. Instrumentation could use work but otherwise it's fine.
Story - There's a god who was fractured due to something, I can't remember. When he refused with one of his parts, it fused these two worlds together, creating the one you play in throughout the game. There's a giant flying whale with an inverted waterfall on its back, and also has some massive ruins that houses a cult? It's weird. Also there's 13 apostles that are referred to as apostles simply because they're just that powerful/cool. Idk, seems pretty cool. I'm thinking of finally going and making a new character just to experience this in full. Seems neat.

It's like mixing a beat 'em up, a fighting game, and an mmo all in one. Very fluid, fast, and fun game. Everything is streamlined to be as fast and efficient as possible. Crafting gets kind of ignored by most new players because it's just so ignorable for the longest time. Very frequent events too, and love from the developers. Constant rebalancing so there's never really a bad class, at least not forever. Monthly-ish updates. I like it.

Chaos Theory is a good stealth game, but inferior to others I've played.
The main problem with it is that most levels are a fairly linear progression of small-medium sized rooms, and not a lot of them as levels aren't really huge (♥♥♥♥ing consoles). The light and sound systems are pretty much ripped from Thief, which is good, and it even goes further by negating the sounds you make depending on ambient noise. There's also night and thermal vision which are used by some foes and cameras, and tricks to get around it. Sound design is nothing groundbreaking, and usually you can't use sound to figure out enemy positions (this is a third person game, though so it's fairly easier to do so without sound) but the music is amazing breakbeat with some jazz thrown in (I really like Amon Tobin's work so I'm kinda biased here).
There's an average amount of tools you can use to sneak around, from sticky cameras to flashbangs and smoke grenades, you can get creative, especially since you can grab ledges and hang on to ceiling pipes, allowing some more interesting methods of evasion. You can also mostly play the game as a full-on shooter if you're... dumb, or something, as the game provides three layouts each mission (stealth, combat and a balanced one). Unfortunately you can't customise the layouts, though. And some missions have a fail state for killing people, so sometimes you can't do combat.
You play as a field agent for the NSA, investigating a cybernetic superweapon, and later trying to avoid starting a war between Koreas. If you really enjoy playing as that sort of character I'd really recommend this game as it does get you very into the role. Given bigger and more open levels I'd really love this game to be honest, but the level design is most of what keeps it from greatness.

Going into this game, I was expecting it to be very similar to the Dynasty Warrior franchise that I've grown acustomed to.
I must say, I'm a bit taken aback by the fact that the dev's thought that mindlessly killing loveable looking creatures that really don't seem to have any intent to harm you whatsoever would be a good idea for a videogame.
I get the concept, it's really cool sounding in theory. Admittedly I don't know very much about the Dragon Quest Franchine, I was hoping this would get me into it, maybe make me want to find a DragonQuest game i could get my hands on, I don't know if this will deter me, but it certainly wouldn't give me MORE of a reason to get into it.
It sounded like a cool idea, but really it doesn't feel like any sort of challenge. The enemies are just monotonous to kill, within less than two hours it felt like I was just doing chores.

When I was 11, I bought a racing game called Gran Turismo for my Playstation Portable. Back then I couldn't tell the difference between a pickup truck and a Lamborghini (I'm exaggerating, but when it came to cars, I really did lack knowledge). I didn't have any interest of cars back then, just like every other kid, I liked Grand Theft Auto and Minecraft. Yeah that's right, I'm not afraid to tell the world that I used to like it! But after I bought that game, that one little racing game with over 800 cars, it changed my life, my perspective on how I saw the world around me. In no time, I became a car enthusiast, and switched to PC gaming. But I lost my Gran Turismo... and for 3 years I've never had a legitimate racing game. But then I bought this game. It took me a whole week to decide on buying this game. I had to break everything down, such as seeing the requirements, reading online reviews, and looking at gameplays. At first I thought to myself, "I should probably save this game for an H1Z1 sale." But then I thought back to Gran Tursimo days. After that, there was no stopping me from buying it. And then, after 2 hours of waiting for 6 GB to go through, while watching episodes of How I Met Your Mother... I launched it. I clicked on career mode and then I started my first race with the Ford Mustang Match 1. It was an amazing race and brought back so many memories of 11 year old me... Plus I had all the DLC for the game and had a lot of fun. Everything about this game is amazing! The graphics, the physics, the handling of the cars, it's all just so realistic! Despite the fact that this game only has a limited amount of cars everything else is amazing! And it has split-screen mode so if you want to challenge your friend to a race, you can! If you are a car enthusiast, I encourage you to get this game!

The game has an interesting idea for a puzzle and interesting variations on tsaid puzzles. BUT the game is too random for it to be fun or completable. Completing a "level" to bring seeds back to the "overworld" to explore is fine.
Getting to the challenges in each level is bloody impossible.
Here's why:
- After the first 1-3 seeds, the seeds you get are entirely random. Only restriction to this keeps you from getting the same seed twice in a row.
- How 2 of the 6 seeds grow is semi random. That's a third of what you have to work with and PLENTY enough to mess up your best laid plans.
- Where the keys AND THE ALTERNATE EXIT FOR THE CHALLENGES spawn is completely random. This is the clincher. We haven't had a chance to review this yet, but we did write an article about the PAX demo. Here are some key quotes from the article.
"Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! is perhaps one of my most anticipated games of this year. I loved the first game and its unique combination of restaurant management and time management gameplay. It constantly challenged players to assemble orders quickly using a large number of ingredients, testing both speed and memorization skills. It is a great game and, somehow, Vertigo Gaming has managed to create a sequel that appears to improve upon the original game in nearly every way. I was recently given a chance to take a look at the PAX preview build of the game and share my thoughts on it.
[...]
Beyond the largely superior graphics and larger number of dishes that you can cook, gameplay is largely the same as the first game. There are a few nice details that have been added, such as customers that sit in the background, the customers that are sitting there changing as time passes, but it will feel very familiar to those who have played the first game. You will still manage a restaurant, earning money over the course of each day that will be spent upgrading your restaurant, and play through dozens of levels of time management-style gameplay, choosing which orders to complete and completing them through intricate processes that are meant to emulate the actual preparation of the dishes that you are preparing.
One of the larger changes to the game is that you can now play a true cooperative mode in which both players are able to complete any task. No longer is one player stuck simply expediting while the other gets to cook; now, each player can pick and choose which order they want to work on and complete the order independently of the other or even prepare foods to be used . This greatly enhances the cooperative experience, as it makes it feel as if both players really get to play the game. The one issue is that, in part due to the colors that the developers chose, it can be difficult to tell whose selector is on which space when you first start playing, which can lead to some frustration early on, but, in my experience, you will adapt fairly quickly if you keep at it.
[...]
While I’ve yet to be able to experience Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!!’s deeper, progression-based systems, I’ve enjoyed the PAX preview build quite a bit and have already sunk two hours into it. The game improves on its predecessor in almost every way, offering improved graphics, more detailed environments, and a better control scheme. The dishes that were included in the preview build were both fun and, at times, a bit terrifying due to the number of ingredients that you had to manage. I’m looking forward to seeing more of the game and its alleged 60+ hour campaign, especially when it comes to dishes like sushi that I’ve yet to be able to experience."

I played this several times on 'free play weekends' and actually won a game. While I had some fun, I feel like I saw everything the game had to offer in a weekend or two. After winning, I didn't really have any burning desire to play again. That's hardly the kind of replay value I expect from games of this genre. I never got past the feeling that Beyond Earth was just a reskin of Civ V.
Everything looks great, but I never really felt a connection with my faction nor did I really feel any antipathy towards my rivals. I actually disliked the indigenous creatures more than I disliked the other factions. While that's fine (the mind worms in Alpha Centauri were equally troublesome early on) the critters appear to be nothing but irritants and can't be used/captured/developed in any way that I can tell. I liked the quests, but they didn't really add as much to the gameplay as they could have. The units are very generic and are the same for every faction, which makes them uninteresting, uninspired, and ultimately, pretty damned boring.
In conclusion, I honestly don't think there have been any significant improvements to the original Civ recipe since Civ II and Alpha Centauri were made. Others have made games that took the Civ recipe to greatness (particularly Master of Magic and Age of Wonders: Shadow Magic) but Firaxis seems to have forgotten long ago what made Civ I, Civ II, and Alpha Centauri fun to play. The wonderful thing about science fiction is that you can imagine some really cool things based on sound scientific principles. However, I didn't find anything in Beyond Earth that was particularly imaginative outside of the environment itself (the artists really did a great job). Since Alpha Centauri is still playable on current gen systems, I'd recommend playing that over Beyond Earth.

This game is an incredibly good horror game that has a good combination of creepy atmosphere and jump scares. It actually reminded me a lot of a different horror game I've played called I See You. It's the kind of game that makes you think you're playing the role of a character, but the game actually makes it feel like it's trying to interact directly with you, the player behind the screen.
And it's exactly for that reason that the game manages to be so disturbing. I won't spoil the actual mechanics the game uses to interact with the player, but I can say it'll catch a lot of people by surprise - and often. It constantly tricks the player into thinking he/she has accomplished something or that they've finished the game, only to then reveal something new.
The only flaw I've found in the game is movement. While the actual controls work as intended, it's easy to get stuck at walls, which can be a problem when you're trying to run from something. Also, for some reason, you can't strafe when crouching. It's not actually a problem, but it feels weird.
Overall, if I had to compile a list of must-play horror games, IMSCARED would definitely be included.

This game is simply fantastic. Switch 'N' Shoot is a small, simple, but incredibly well-polished game with extremely good attention to detail: the sound, the visuals, the writing (cute little thematic blurbs on starting a game, game-over, and advancing to next sector), the controls (you may laugh but it's true), the personal color palette settings, the gameplay experience itself. There is absolutely zero friction between the game-over screen and starting a new round; you can get back into the action almost immediately. It is easy to tell that the game was made as a true labour of love -- even the "Made with Unity Personal Edition" splash screen on starting up the game isn't enough to detract from this. The game is surprisingly entertaining and challenging the further you pogress. I had or rather still have a good time with it, though I have to say, I enjoy the android-version (not sure if there is an IOS-version) more than the PC-one, but one thing at a time...
--- The good stuff ---
- The game is very accessible (obviously)
- Actually challenging in later sectors
- No mindless button smashing. Quick and careful consideration when pressing the button
- Every button on the keyboard or gamepad works (I think)
- Really addictive (most definitely on phones)
- Nice artwork in full screen
- Amusing dialouge
- Cool soundtrack
--- The not so good stuff ---
- Only two enemy types (as far as I've seen)
- Lacks variety ind design for sectors
- Maybe a little bit pricey for some people
- Certainly a little bit pricey for the ad-free upgrade on phones!
- It seems to be better suited for smart devices rather than a PC
- No means of pausing the game (quiet a problem on phones)
- If you got to the boss, you saw everything (probably)
- Not really for people who aren't interested in beating the global Highscore
--- OVERALL ---
It's a cool little game, no doubt about it. But if you not here for the Highscore, personal or global, you might not get your money's worth. In fact if you look past that, you find a game that's perfectly functional, but lacks variety aside from getting the best score in one run. This game tries to emulate an old acrade shooter with it's style which is perfectly fine, but I'm sure a few more enemy types or diffrent looking sectors wouldn't have hurt the experience. I still belive that the game was originally meant only for smartphones or tablets if you actually think about the control scheme or the choice in screen sizes. Even so the game is still entertaining and good for short sessions. If you have a littl bit of money to spare and look for a game with the emphasis on getting a Highscore, you might want to check this out.
This game is both available on Steam and smartphone devices, but the latter might be a little expensive for a smartphone app of this caliber (even though it is the same price like on steam) unless you're fine with having ads popping up. I still gets the thumps up for me, because I enjoy the android-version so much. But please! Add a proper pause function (at least for smartphones)!

This War of Mine receives my recommendation.
Such a beautiful looking game with quite a unique and grim art style it instantly drew me in aesthetically. Sound and music are well done and fitting for the scenes around you. All of this geared up to create a certain atmosphere which is amplified by the gameplay.
You start off with a number of people unable to escape a city gripped in civil war. Short on basics like food and water or luxuries such as coffee and cigarettes, threatened by neighbours who are equally as desperate and will resort to raiding former friends for anything to survive and facing certain doom should they run into rebels or the military forces besieging the city.
Split into two main phases, you will spend the day doing the best you can to ensure that your people are kept fed, watered and rested. Keep them informed of local events by constructing a radio, allow them to relax in an armchair with a good book and a heater stocked up with wood to survive the harsh winters, construct your own little herb garden and distillery to keep the liquor and cigarettes flowing... can you hold out until someone comes around with the antibiotics you need to save your friend or will their infection spread?
And by night, you'll become the raider or the raided. Take a fast runner or a someone that can carry a load of stuff into the elderly neighbours house and steal their food, break into a bombed out old house that's been abandoned for weeks or perhaps that old construction site down the road still has some electronic parts so you can grow your own food. Will the old man attack you when you steal his last morsel of food? Will there be a gang hanging around the old supermarket, raiding the last bits of salvageable material and will they point their guns in your direction? Will you have to kill to obtain those necessities?
Moral implications of your actions impact the individuals in the game. Some people can rationalise the stealing from a vulnerable person to ensure the survival of the group, other people will kill anyone that gets in the way of them obtaining what they need to survive... some people cannot cope with anyone in the group committing atrocities and will begin the deep, dark spiral into depression and mania...
The atmosphere generated by the cumination of mechanics and gameplay aspects wraps you up into the experience and you certainly care what happens to your people, and to others that are suffering in similar circumstances. The choices are yours to make and you benefit from or pay for them in measured amounts.
Each game isn't all that long but will provide you with a fair amount of gameplay. If it stopped there then you'll be pleasantly happy with your purchase and content for the outlay but you can create your own basic custom games and the Steam Workshop provides user made content which further expands the gameplay.
I encountered no obvious bugs during my time but did wish that there was a little more depth in some areas such as the night time or different starting houses (as there's only the one).
Buy it, enjoy it... It's worth it.

The game uses a first person view and extremely low resolution visuals and sounds to build a really eerie experience that only very old 90' Dos games managed to. Its strong point lies in the puzzles: they mostly consist of riddles you have to solve outside the program, looking inside files and folders it will create for you on your desktop. This concept, while not by any means new or original, is still very refreshing to see used in these days. The difficulty is not excessive and if you read carefully the instructions/tips provided and commit to it you will find it all around pretty fair, but to fully complete it you may need to look around for help on a couple things.
The controls are very simple and the game plays smoothly without evident technical problems, just the collisions may prove a bit finicky but overall are not crucial to the experience. The graphic is again very simple and can be compared to the likes of Doom with a Silent Hill feel, same goes for the sound and background effects, and the absence of a musical soundtrack only increases the uneasy feel it tries to convey. The render distance is very short, a questionable choice that anyways does not get in the way of the gameplay. The game does not abuse cheap jump-scares and instead maintains a constant spooky atmosphere from start to finish. It does not last too long, probably around 2 to 3 hours, but may prompt you to play it more than once to better understand what everything is about.
All in all I would say a great work especially considering the developer is only one man. I encourage you to give this game a try and commit to it, you will have a nice experience.

I've been a fan of the Thief games since Deadly Shadows. Not a hardcore fan, but I do love my stealth games. Thief is exactly what it says on the tin, a thief game set in a medieval'ish setting with some magic.
The Good: The graphics are pretty good. Some dialogue sync errors, but I'm not too picky. The sound is rather nice as well, but it's mostly quiet. I'm not quite far enough to comment on how well rounded the equipment/upgrades are.
The Bad: The ai is kinda iffy, but what game aren't they. They'll be some people who say they love the ai and some who nitpick it. Load screens...everywhere. The city feels really closeted. Lots of alleys and it's easy to get lost despite there being a map. Also, the only way I was able to make my way around was the little hud icons for where you needed to go. There's an option in the custom difficulty level to turn this off too. What the crap? It's hard enough to navigate the game with it let alone without it. I'm not one who needs a gps to get from my car to my front door either.
The Ugly: The story, oh god the story. This has to be the most unoriginal story ever conceived by mankind. The plot could pretty much be summed up as Robin Hood with magic and amnesia. It's just so boring. It doesn't help that Garret has all the personality of a bag of rocks and so does about every other character. I just couldn't find myself getting into the story or characters at all, which really breaks a game like this for me. Some games, Loadout for instance, aren't meant to have a story. But, for a game like this to have a horrible story, it ruins it.
I want to like this game, but I honestly feel like I'm going to play it and skip every cutscene. I love the gameplay (most of the time), but just despise how blah they made the story.

This war of mine, (starvation simulator 2014) is a war game where you don't play as an elite soldier who can't sprint for more than 10 seconds, you play as a group of survivors trying to live in a war torn city. This war of mine is loosely based off "The Siege of Sarajevo" During the Bosnian war.
The gameplay is a point and click, resource management, meaning you have to click your characters and get them to do tasks such as make tools, cook food, sleep, and bandage any injuries. The game is divided into day and night cycles, during the day you manage your characters, )feeding them and making them sleep) build necessities, and manage resources. Nighttime consists of scavenging for supplies, with a singular character in a variety of locations. These could be bombed out homes, abandoned schools, or other survivors shelters. Sometimes the player might come across other survivors, sometimes friendly, sometimes violent. During night time the player must collect as many resources as possible in order to maintain their shelter and their characters needs. Occasionally your shelter may be raided during the night. This can be prevented by patching holes in the walls, and having weapons accessible for whoever is still in your shelter.
The shelter the player starts with is locked to that play-through. Although, this isn't necessarily a bad thing. There are only 2 home bases available (acquired randomly) both approximately the same size with the same starting materials. The player will start building things. This includes metalworking benches, herb/vegetable gardens, animal traps, and makeshifts stoves. These all make surviving significantly easier.
Depending on the scenario you were playing, different locations available on the map (to loot and explore) unlock at different times, usually after a few days. Each location is different, with randomly generated supplies to be found. Sometimes location can have different scenarios, such as one play through the grocery store might have the military in it, and in another play through there might just be some scavengers. This adds immense replayability.
The sound in the game is over all well done. It adds a feeling of stress or concern. The art direction in the game, although basic, is a perfect match for the 2D side Scroller. The charcoal effects ingame add a feeling of darkness and dread, with almost 0 colour to be seen. Overall the art direction and sound are extremely well done, and fifth the game well.
Depending on the scenario you playing, you'll be given certain starting characters. Each with their own abilities, backpack size, and potentially addictions. These characters need to be fed, rested, and kept in a good mood. They also need to be in good health. Your characters may get injured from raiders or scavengers, or sick from lack of heat in the shelter. They can also fall into a depression if the player controls them and a negative fashion. An example of this would be having your character steal from other survivors, or kill other survivors. This can be counterbalanced by doing maintaining them/entertaining them  or helping other survivors. The counter side to this, is in the event that someone asks for your help, and you refuse, your characters feel sad, potentially falling into a deep depression, preventing them from doing basic tasks, like eating, or defending the shelter. The same can happen if you let your characters get to hurt, too sick, or not take care of them properly. This adds more difficult to the game, becoming less about keeping them healthy but also about keeping them happy.
The ingame combat system is minimal. Most situations you will engage in melee combat with a melee weapon. Guns and ammunition are extremely hard to come by. In most situations, The player will save weapons for defending their shelter at night. The game overall doesn't want you to fight other survivors, it's not good for the characters sanity, or health. However if you decide to go down a path of stealing at The game overall doesn't want you to fight other survivors, it's not good for the characters sanity, or health. However if you decide to go down a path of stealing of and murdering,  be prepared to deal with depressed characters.

My experience with Autosport has been mixed, but mostly positive. On one hand, I enjoy the game. It's different than grid one and two being that it lacks customization and a sense of progression as a racing team. Rather, you're a driver for hire racing for multiple different teams. You don't buy your own cars, you don't customize them, you simply choose a contract and race a series for them. I can see how this would turn fans of the series off.
However, the racing itself I found to be very well done and, despite some flaws, fun to play. It feels more like a racing sim such as project cars (albeit with assists and the signature rewind feature of Grid), yet still playable for casual fans of the genre and those looking for more of a easy-going racer. The thing I like about the racing is the ai. Whether you think it's good or bad ai, i still found it fun to play against. The reason being that the ai is more aggressive than a typical racing sim and thus leads to a more interesting experience. You find yourself dodging pile-ups, trying to powerslide around corners, and trying to avoid being taken out by opponents that are set on winning. That's a turn-off for some, so it's up to you whether you like that hectic style of racing.
The game works great with my cheapo thrustmaster wheel, so I assume if you have a racing wheel it won't have much problem calibrating with it. The game is also optimized very well, and being that it's made for intel cards I assume it'll be perfectly playable on a standard computer without a dedicated GPU like Nvidia or Radeon. However, my particular model of GPU (Nvidia gtx 860m) gave me some issues with the game, which I suspect were from the windows 10 upgrade since it worked fine on windows 8. The game would crash after 15 minutes of gameplay on the nose with no error message. Apparently this is a somewhat common issue among Nvidia users. This problem never resolved itself until eventually I got a new computer with a 960m. If you have an 860m and run windows 10, be careful.
If I were to rate this game out of 10, I'd say it deserves 7/10. It leaves a lot to be desired for hardcore Grid fans, yet might be exactly what you want for others. I for one enjoyed it for what it was.

Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! Is an amazing game. I did recieve this game for free as I am a beta tester, but that does not influence my decision on the game whatsoever.
The main mode in the game is cooking. You get orders, and need to work your best to fill these orders. Even when it gets more hectic, but that's the fun of the game. The different types of foods are the main draw.
The foods are all very detailed, and if you eat the game when hungry, it will make you even more hungry. Even foods I don't like in real life when on my menu in the game make me very hungry, as they are beautiful to look at when ready to serve to a customer in the game.
There are two main modes. Cook for Hire, which has you go through preset restaraunts and menus to attempt to gain a gold medal in each of those places, as well as the main draw for me, Cook, Serve, Delicious Mode.
CSD Mode has you manage the menu of your own place, and in the most recent 1.1 update, reintroduced Classic Mode from the original title, with some changes that are in place due to the changes in the overall gameplay structure. You can of course ignore the entire booster and detractor setting, or chill out with zen mode, or even push yourself with Stress Kitchen. All of these modes do utilize the new equipment upgrade option, which lets you purchase upgrades to make specific chores pop up less frequently.
The game is immensely fun. If you like cooking shows on TV, this game will be a fit for you.

Cook, Serve, Delicious 2 is a hectic cooking/restaurant manager game, and seems to be a step up from the first game in every way.
Let's start by saying that the food looks so damn delicious. Almost as if they were drawn after photos of real food. (I wouldn't be surprised if that was the case). On top of that, the first game had 30 foods, where as this 2nd game has 180. That is a HUGE increase. Some fans of the 1st game might feel a bit overwhelmed, since you could memorize all the recipes in the first game. Now, that is a lot harder.
I'll give a quick explanation to how the game works for people who have not played the 1st game yet. Customers will come up to the desk and order some food. Once you take their order, you need to press the corresponding buttons to add the right ingredients. For example, if they order a beef burger, you need to press M (for meat) to add the meat patty, then K for ketchup, M for mustard. Sometimes customers vary it up by asking for extra or fewer ingredients, so you need to be careful when making each meal. Most ingredients' hotkeys make sense, like C for cucumber. However, occasionally you will need to add an ingredient like Chili sauce, which uses "H". This is because the game tries to keep letters universal, and a lot of ingredients are shared between recipes. You get used to it after a while.
Now onto the new stuff in this sequel.
The game has added Holding stations that allow you to serve a lot more customers in a more efficient way. This allows you to, for example, prepare 6 German pretzels. They will stop cooking automatically as soon as they are done, and whenever a customer comes by asking for a pretzel, you can instantly give it to them. The only downfall is over the day those pretzels will become a bit less fresh. You can trash them whenever you want though, and prepare some new ones.
Holding stations also allow you to prepare side meals. Things like salads, which will increase the patience meter of waiting customers.
All of this does a really nice job at making you feel like you really own the restaurant. The game can be incredibly hectic, but it feels so rewarding when you do well.
More chores have been added to the game now. Things like throwing away trash, washing dishes, setting up roach traps are all small distractions in between serving food, but very important if you don't want people to be disgusted by your restaurant.
As you play through the game you will gain the ability to unlock more foods and decorations for your restaurant.
In the first game, your restaurant automatically upgraded its looks as you went through. In this game, you unlock parts and have free reign over where you want to play everything, which is great. You can even place the same painting on the wall multiple times. It might look ridiculous, but you have choice. The only problem here is currently the restaurant customizer is clunky. Deleting objects is a separate menu that takes a few seconds to get to, and there is no mouse support so you need to move things slowly around. Hopefully that'll become more fluent with future patches.
This time around, you can also play a mode called "Chef for hire" that allows you to work for other restaurants. Places that specialize in things like pizza, or Japanese food. This is a nice bonus way to just stick to a certain category of food if you feel like just making that stuff.
On the other hand, you can just work for your own restaurant, choose your available foods in the menu, etc.
Co-op is way better in this game. In the first game, only player 1 could cook, and player 2 served the food, which was very boring for the 2nd player. In this game, you can both cook and serve at the same time. It feels quite rewarding to work side by side and complete multiple meals at once.
Currently, the game is missing the funny story and emails that the first game had, but the dev has said they plan to add it in asap.
Overall, it's just more of the first game, with a few new improvements here and there. That's not a bad thing at all, because the first game didn't really have any problems, in my opinion. The music is lovely, the visuals look great, and the gameplay is as frantic and fun as ever. I strongly recommend the game to anyone that is interested in it.

Oof. I love this game. Slamming keys while scrambling around, trying to serve your customers and not missing any chores has never been so much fun. The music is amazing. The sounds are so spot on and so satisfying when you throw grapes in a bowl and tenderise your chicken breast. The art will make you hungry.
It is like Cook, Serve, Delicious, with incredibly more content. The Chef for Hire mode, where you breeze through different levels of different restaurants and unlock a lot of fun objects for your own restaurant is an amazing addition. Decorating and customising your own restaurant is a welcome change from the first game, also. I can hang fourteen cat pictures on the wall without consequences.
As of writing this review some minor things are missing, such as the email system, which is a feature from CSD I've grown to love also, and I hope that the spam mails we'll be receiving now are going to be as amazing as the last ones.
Really, the art is going to make you so hungry.
I don't recommend playing this on an empty stomach. I really don't.
EDIT;
The CSD Classic made is bumping this game up for me to a solid nine out of ten. The emails are also ridiculously fun; there are your regular spam emails, but there are also emails that bring you lighthearted stories to the table. All in all a wonderful update.

So, after the absolute mess of a launch, which included the developer patching literally gamebreaking bugs the day after the game was *meant* to be launched, this is still not worth your money. 2 significant delays later (Fun fact, this was meant to come out in early Q4 2016). This should be an early access release.
Controlling menus with your mouse has been a given for the past 20 years. Not here - It's an upcoming "feature"! I might have generously forgiven this as an afterthought, if the menus were actually functional when using the keyboard. They're awkward, clunky, and not great to navigate.
The challenge from CSD1 is gone. Gone are the days of frantically washing dishes and chucking out trash in the hopes that you can get it done before your lasagne burns. Chores in this are boring and unwelcome. Yes, there's finally some variation to them, but they're way too easy. No mashing arrow keys, just the same two (or, if you're lucky, three) letters over and over, down from 4-5 in CSD1. One of the joys of the first game was the hardcore aspect of it - If you knew the letters for ingredients off by heart you didn't have to switch recipe pages, you could literally just input them and they'd go on the meal. Now you're forced to switch pages regardless of if you know the key you need to press.
The game is way too forgiving. Timers go on a green -> orange -> red -> burnt scale, but there's no actual penalty if you go into orange or red zones, you can still make it a perfect order! Why introduce such a convoluted mechanic then not bother to implement it properly or even explain it?
The orders presented to you are bland and not at all appealing. The people coming to your restaurant don't feel like people like they did in CSD1. This is tricky to explain but if you've played both games you'll understand what I mean. There's just no kind of variety to the dialogue when they place their orders.
To say the game's tutorials and introduction are lacking would be an understatement. There's no story whatsoever other than "HERE's A RESTAURANT AND SOME OTHER UNEXPLAINED RESTAURANTS, GO COOK", and half of the tutorials aren't even finished. They're literally just text. I got most of my information on how to play from the game's Discord channel, which was mercifully helpful.
Customers are meant to take sides/drinks in order for you to get a "Delicious" order, but they don't. They literally just sit there until someone comes in an orders *specifically that*. It could have been a good mechanic if it were something manual you had to do, but if it's going to be automated, at least make sure it works.
Speaking of sides, there's no penalty whatsoever for items in your holding station "decaying" or going off. No cash penalty, no loss of your perfect streak, nothing apart from *maybe* some extra trash to take out, which, as I mentioned before, is now pointless and dull.
Another lacking feature is emails from the previous game - There are none here, despite a writer having been employed specifically to write quite literally thousands of words (Citation: them). Maybe they'll be added in a future update like a good 80% of the game should be, but it's something that should have been in there from the start.
The new Chef For Hire section could be a good addition - IF IT HAD EVER BEEN EXPLAINED TO ME! The levels have been awkwardly forced in with no explanation as to how they work or how they benefit you. Do you get money for playing them? Do you unlock things?
Daily missions could also have been neat - If they made any sense. Are they real day objectives or game day objectives? If it's the latter, some of them are impossible. What do I get for completing them? IT'S NOT EXPLAINED.
This might seem like a lot of complaints - It is. And it's exacerbated by the fact that they're all flaws I've noticed in less than an hour of playing.
All in all this should have been an early access release, and even then I'd have been hesitant to recommend it. I hoped to be streaming this on my Twitch channel but as it stands I won't be touching this with a bargepole. It feels very much like a cash-in on the success of its predecessor, but it's not at all well done. One day I might be able to recommend this, but without a doubt AVOID FOR NOW.

Alright; it shouldn't need to be said, but I'll still go ahead and say it: this is not a direct sequel to the previous Thief trilogy! It's a reboot (such an icky word) or rather a re-imagining of the franchise. Hence dropping the '4' bit from the title early on in development. It's also been more than 15 years since the last game was made; games have come a long way since then. So, really, it shouldn't surprise
that this game doesn't play
like those previous titles. That being said, Thief does an amazing job at what it aims to do.
It's got some of the most impressive AI that I've seen in recent  stealth games (which sadly isn't saying alot I know) that actually behaves in a relatively believable manner. Basically, this isn't a cheap knock-off that will let you get away with crouching at someone's feet in direct light and not be seen simply because you're in 'stealth' mode. Patrolling guards will actually react to sound (from knocking over a broom to sprinting across rickety boards) as well as sight. They also won't simply stroll right past a fallen comrade.
Garret still has his trademark arsenal of fancy arrows that aid him in his master thievery, made all the more fantastic by the game's underlying steampunk theme; this is a Victorian-inspired city on the verge of an industrial revolution. Blunt arrows are specifically designed to be weaker and break upon impact and will allow you to knock switches or levers from a distance without sacrificing precious ammo. Water arrows will let you douse torches and a variety of other light/fire sources, creating a shadowy environment for you to 'get your thief on' in. Rope arrows will help you ascend (or descend) to otherwise inaccessible areas.
You've also got an upgradeable blackjack for knocking out unsuspecting city guards, a handheld claw (think grappling hook minus the rope) that lets you scale certain surfaces to reach higher ledges, a modified socket wrench, a wire cutter and other equally nifty little tools to help you get the job done. Basically, Garret and Batman have a heckuva lot in common.
The only thing this game is really lacking, in my opinion, is a strong narrative. The gameplay, however, is solid and thus I suppose I can forgive it - I won't lie though, this would usually be a deal breaker for me. The gameplay is just
good. Plus, it's not completely devoid of a plot; it's just not anything particularly special and at times can come across as slightly convoluted or overly trope-y.

IMSCARED is one of those games that messes with you. It's one of those games that can be repetitive, but, in the end, it was worth it. There are some things I need to go over, however.
If you haven't played the game yet, and you want to in the future, DO NOT READ THIS. IT CONTAINS SPOILERS.
IMSCARED starts off where the Gamejolt verions also starts off. You have a folder thats created on the desktop, and that is where the documents are created when you are playing. I had no problems with the first section of the game. It was all familiar, and, so far, I was happy with the remake of IMSCARED. Although, some parts are different, such as the new sounds, better frames, and the video that pops up, I was still happy with the outcome.
The second part, HER, is scary, to an extent. The start of this section is confusing, but, it plays just like the first part of the game. Once you go into the cellar, however, is when the game gets quite difficult. You have to figure out the code to unlock the gate so you can get the rope. After that, the entity HER begins to chase you. This part I found frustrating because you had to exit the game at a certain point, but the entity was very fast, but, at my 2nd try, I did it, but it may be frustrating to others. After you quit the game, you are able to use the rope to climb down the balcony. You are then greeted to a hedge maze. This part was VERY frustrating because of the "mirror code". You had to find pieces of a mirror to find the code, but, like all first person mazes, this one was confusing. I eventually found all pieces and the code, and exited the maze. After that, the train station. You have to destroy 3 gramaphones to get the metro key. I found this next part cool because you have to change the time to get the metro ticket instead of waiting. After you enter the metro, you have to "face the truth". This part was amazing.
WARNING: MEGA SPOILER
You have to face against HER. You have to kill HER. But, the game won't let you have bullets for your gun. "Six will do."
The next part was clever. After you enter the name, you are in the grocery store. You have to complete the to-do list. But, as you quit the game, you appear outside of the grocery store. After all of that, you have to get 3 valves in order to reveal a door. You need all achivements to enter this door, however. Once you enter the door, you have two options. Take the flower or end the game.
In conclusion, IMSCARED is a good game, but can be repetitive. Some people may find this annoying, others won't. For me, I was okay with it. But, some of the jumpscares in the game are cheap, and that somewhat annoys me. I won't tell you where they are. ;)
In the end, IMSCARED is a truly fascinating game, and you should give it a try.

You control a spaceship that has to destroy incoming alien spacecraft. Your single button controls both the ship's navigation as well as weapon firing. Every time a button is pressed it fires a single shot but it also switches the way your ship is traveling. For example, if you're traveling right and press a button you'll fire a shot and begin traveling left. You can go through your screen, similar to Pac-Man, so you don't have to avoid hitting the sides of your screen.
It's a simple enough concept and one that may sound less than intriguing. However, it is addictive. Why? Because you're always concentrating on killing enemies but also making sure you're getting from A to B quickly enough to do so. Therefore, what this means is that there will be a great number of times in each game that you will fire just to switch without having any intention of attacking an enemy. This takes a high level of concentration.
New players will die quick and fast - this is to be expected - and here they will find something that I find a combination of humorous and addictive. Players do not input a name into the game. The game gives you funny little names. Each time you die you'll get a funny quote such as "This was expected of Schloot" (or whatever that round's character's name was). You'll also get assigned a character name at the beginning of each game generally with a word of luck.
There is a high score table that for whatever reason begins out of order. I'm not sure if something is supposed to be implied by this but it may be something for a future update. This yet another challenge. I'm not close to getting top spot but it's certainly not impossible.
The presentation is as simple as the concept. While I understand that this will deter some players I would urge you that it shouldn't. The game doesn't need a fantastic art presentation and it's much more than suitable. If the game did have fancy artwork - aside from the arcade cabinet stylings on each side of the screen - it would have a detrimental effect on the game. The simple presentation is fantastic game design in my opinion.
No. Unfortunately, it hasn't been Steamified as of yet. Of course, I'd like to see trading cards and Steam achievements added to the game as I do every game. However, this is a game that would do very well in having a global leaderboard system implemented into it. I don't see this as being a game that would encourage friends to compete locally against one another (though it might be fun) so using the Steam leaderboards would give the game a competitive edge.
Switch 'N' Shoot is US$1.99. I believe that most players will get much more than their monies worth within the first time that they play the game. It's a cheap price to pay for a game with a simple concept yet highly addictive fun.

What is
?
You play some sort of astronaut jumping from planet to planet, trying to collect the items floating between them.
That sums up the whole game, basically.
You may have already noticed that
is a 2D game, so the "planets" are more or less just rotating disks.
The "planets" vary in size and angular velocity. The description of the game mentions it is "procedurally generated", I guess that is what they meant.
As you progress through the game, the "planets" get smaller, they rotate faster and the distance between them increases. To deal with the growing difficulty, you can spend the picked up items to buy some upgrades. Now you can do multiple jumps in the air (space?), jump faster, pick up items at a greater distance, but nothing that changes the fundamental mechanics of the game. Additionally, the price for the upgrades is quite high, so you need to play again and again until you can afford to buy some upgrades, resulting in a gameplay that feels repetitive really quick (read: grindfest).
Again, what is
?
Long story short: it is a simple flash game.
The kind of game you can play on the web. I have no idea what the first flash games were, but they have been around for 15 years, easily. The more sophisticated ones, at least.
So, the thing is, there are dozens of flash games out there that are better than
. And they are free.
On the plus side,
has nice animations, and the visual style is pretty cute. And it has one distinct advantage over flash games on the web: achievements.
For the genre (flash games):
58 / 100
For the grand scheme of gaming things:
5 / 100
