DISCLAIMER: I have not played any of the previous Thief games so my review is from the viewpoint of this game being the first in the series. I will not be able to make distinctions like "Well blah blah mechanic worked like this/better than in the last game" I'm judging this game based on other AAA titles, not previous installments in the franchise
If I had to try to explain Thief i'd say its like a mix of Deus Ex: Human Revolution, Dishonored, and a teensy tiny tad of Assassin's Creed.
I feel like the supernatural powers you get in thief make you a "super thief" but not inhumanly powerful. In Dishonored the supernatural powers and comparatively increased offensive capabilities essentially make you a inhumanly powerful "wizard-assassin" you teleport around and stick to the shadows for no reason other than points or playstyle because even on the highest difficulty you'll likley have little problems helplessly slaughtering everything in your path, or escaping with the teleport move that essentially much makes you uncatachable by NPCs. In Dishonored you're pretty much a god. It would take a serious crowd of enemies to kill a skilled Dishonored player, even on the highest difficulty.
The powers you get in Thief seem realistic, like something that someone who is very skilled in sleight of hand could actually be capable of doing if they were focusing. The game has a mechanic called Focus which the mana-like resource for it recharges with "potions" or over time. When you "focus" in game you can do things a little quicker, and more efficently. It also makes important interactable objects stand out. I find this mechanic useful because viewing a game enviornment on screen is totally different than in real life in therms of things you can interact with. I feel like on screens I miss things that would have been much more obvious had I been there in real life either because the screen's clarity will never match that of my own eyes or I simply see the items and assume they are a non-interactable decoration. FOCUS IS NOT A CORE MECHANIC OF THE GAME! YOU DO NOT NEED TO USE FOCUS! I uasually only use focus for a couple seconds every now and then to view and make decisions on which route to my objective I will take and make sure I have not left any loot behind. Thief isn't as much about combat as Dishonored. In thief the main character states hes not the type to kill without reason so it feels like you're supposed to either avoid the gaurds entirley or sneak up behind em to knock em out.
You're also much less "combat-effective". In thief you have no sword, just a bow (the mechanics of firing the bow feel like they have been designed to prevent faced paced bow combat, after all you play a master thief not a master bowman), and your blackjack which does terrible damage (6 or so hits to kill a light armor gaurd, i havent even tried to pull it out on a heavy yet) and seems to have an RNG chance (maybe like 30%) to cause the enemy to fall down to their hands and knees  for a 1 button takedown. The Takedown takes a couple seconds to activate so if theres a 2nd gaurd attacking you the gaurd will likley be able to defend his downed ally until hes back on his feet. In Thief you really feel like the enemies are stronger than you (rightfully so, theyre trained, armored gaurds with swords!) and and adding more gaurds exponentially increases their combat effectivness against you. The gaurds in Thief are ruthless. They will not stand around and wait for you to be ready like in Assassins Creed and the dodge mechanic in thief is not as useful as in Assassin's Creed or Dishonored. They just run up and if you attack them they block, if youre not attacking them theyll spam attack you in the sides and back LIKE ANY PERSON WITH MORE BRAINCELLS THAN A JELLYFIGH WOULD DO. The best way to deal with them is definetely to avoid them entirely or sneak up behind em and knock em out Deus Ex style.
In Dishonored the supernatural powers and comparatively increased offensive capabilities essentially make you a inhumanly powerful "wizard-assassin" you teleport around and stick to the shadows for no reason other than points or playstyle because even on the highest difficulty you'll likley have little problems helplessly slaughtering everything in your path, or escaping with the teleport move that essentially much makes you uncatachable by NPCs. In Dishonored you're pretty much a god. It would take a serious crowd of enemies to kill a skilled Dishonored player, even on the highest difficulty. THIEF IS NOT LIKE THIS! One gaurd may be easy enough to hand in 1v1 combat should you want to but 2 gaurds is a tough fight and 3 gaurds dosent really seem to be possible without doing something unrealistic and gimmicky like kiting. (AI's have their boundries and I feel like it can be immersion breaking to exploit them so for the most part I choose not to.)
Thief seems to be about exploiting your enviornment and honed abilities to take advantage of the situation. Where as Dishonored is more about controlling the situation entirely, Deus Ex is about discovering the situation, and Assassins Creed is more about "PARKOUR AND KILLING HALF THE CITY GAURD IF FUN!!!" Thief definetly has a strong story though. Dishonored is very cartoony with a lot of jokes and such. You never get a true "plague in the city, crorruption at an all time high" feeling in dishonored when you commpared to the powerful atmosphwere created in Thief. Thief's storyline is on the level of Deus Ex. It pulls you in to a realistic, gritty, totally immersive world thet really makes you feel like YOU'RE the main character and YOU'RE making decisions in the game.
Thief has a great video settings menu with all the bells and whistles, the game also has a benchmarking option which automatically navigates your screen through a short in-game series of events designed to test your graphics settings so you can get things as fancy as possible and still get solid FPS. This VERY useful and innovative feature should be included in all games!

This game has been on Steam since 2012 I believe. Since then, Nexon has gone through countless updates, time and time again, breaking Steam MS. I was forced to play MS through the website most of the time. This was not the issue. I have been playing MS since a month out of Beta. It was the best thing to happen to me, to date. However, what really got me down was when my friends quit, or I got hacked, or if I was being ks'ed, etc. I remember when Victoria Island was the only continent and there were only 4 Adventurers and HPQ was the only pq. Everything changed after the BB patch. It became SO much easier to level up that anyone could get 120 levels within 24 hours, without 2x EXP. The game changed from being too hard to too easy, it was ridiculous. Now, though, Nexon has finally caught up to all of the demands of the Veterans and have made the game harder to level up from level 30-60 and 170-200, which are the prime levels. After many updates to nerf the OP grind fest and 24 hours max leveling, the veterans are now complaining that the game is too hard. Ha! Too easy now too hard? Pick a side and stick with it, I thought. I'm starting to agree with them though, the game has become harder than it was after the BB patch, but it's still easier than before. The major updates, like Chaos, Legends, and Jump were all very exciting, especially if you play with friends. This game is hugely based on friends. It is SO boring without friends to play with. The game actually rewards you for playing with your friends now, apparently. I used to have MS open 24 hours per day for 7 days a week, even though I wasn't there to play myself - I just wanted to have it open for when I got home. (That's kind of exaggerated; My longest time on MS was only 77 hours, after which I had dc'd).
If you were to ask me what MS is about, I couldn't tell you. There is just so much to it, you have to experience it yourself. But let me warn you. The game doesn't like new players. It feeds on the old ones, like me, who have characters over level 150 (the max being 250). I really like it though. if I were to start all over, I'd only be willing to do it with friends (and if I had the time. I basically have no time for MS anymore because of school).
Back to Steam MS though. This Steam version is weird. It sometimes works and it sometimes doesn't work. Many people experience trouble with the Steam version for a variety of issues: someone typed in the wrong email address, and so you can't change it; someone forgot their pin; the game doesn't load for some people; and the list goes on. My suggestion would to just play MS through the website if it doesn't work on Steam.
Please disregard the amount of hours I have played MS on Steam. 80% hours are just from me afk'ing A LOT. The other 20% of those hours are me enjoying the game with my (now-dead) friends.

You dropped the ball with Grid 2. You took a great series and watered it down into homogenized irrelevancy. That perfect balance between sim and arcade is now weighted heavily as an arcade racer. As a longtime fan of Grid 1, putting probably 100 hours collectively into the PC and Xbox 360 versions, I am insulted.Well lets start with why its bad, shall we?
Every car handles like it has weights in the trunk. You could drift any car by just tapping on the brakes lightly, regardless of what the car is. I can drift an old comaro just the same as a Nissan Silvia. Every car handles the same. You licensed all these cars so you can make them all handle badly or sell them off as DLC.
The whole experience just seems to have bumped its head a few times. Sleek, easy to navigate menus are replaced by ugly menus that try too hard to look like a youtube page. On these menus there is unoriginal "taunts" by your rivals that are more annoying than intimidating. After each event, your team leader will make some stupid comment and you will be forced to watch a cutscene with licensed ESPN logos and real ♥♥♥♥ing ESPN commentators. Yes, they spent the majority of their budget on unskippable ESPN branding.
In the first Grid, there were many disciplines spanning over three regions. Across the US, EU, and JP regions there was some diversity. Each region had its own identity and unique experiences. In the second grid, every place feels the same and every discipline feels the same. Demolition derby was added as an afterthought.
I really did give this game a try. I wanted to stick it out and believe it was good. I couldn't make it past 8 hours though. In that 8 hours, I drove samey cars around samey tracks in unmemorable disciplines. When is the fun going to kick in? When is this game going to give itself a reason to carry the Grid name?
It is simple fun. Honestly worth the 50 cents it is going up for right now.

The Good:
The graphics are great, the voice acting is passable, and it's nice to see an old franchise trying something new!
The Bad:
Wow, where do I start?
First, it's barely ported to the PC, which can be a royal pain.  If a company can't even be bothered to make the button prompts for a PC appear as something other than X-Box controller prompts, then they really shouldn't be allowed to call it a 'port'.  I know it's a little nitpicking, but the only place to see what button controls what is through the main menu that you have to exit the game to find.  And then it only tells you things like 'Jump - Space'.  Which is fine, right?  Because you know that you need to press Space to jump.  But run up to a treasure chest and it says 'Press A'.  Well... which button is 'A'!?  Turns out its your jump button.  There is a SECOND key binding menu, this one only accessible WHILE PLAYING the game (that is, not at the title screen) that tells you 'A - Spacebar' and such.  But doesn't tell you that Space Bar is your jump button.  So if you didn't bother to read the menu keybindings before playing the game, then you get the privelege of hitting every button on your keyboard and mouse until you figure out what they all do.  And good luck if they tell you to hit 'X' or 'RT' or some nonsense during actual gameplay.
Seriously, KOEI, Square, how hard is it to do a proper port?  All that would need changing are some graphical icons inside the game.
Now we get to the gameplay.  If you had watched the trailer, you might have been seriously mislead into believing you were buying a free-roaming adventure game, possibly FF XIII-like in combat, I hear it compared to 'Dynasty Warriors' a lot, or any number of open-world hack n' slash games.  Not true!
You will have been duped into buying a Tower Defense game.
If that's your thing, then this isn't a con by any means.  You can revisit maps later and just fight wave after wave after wave of endlessly-spawning monsters, but 'run up to monsters and smash or hold X' isn't what I would call the height of entertainment.  But pretty much all of the 'story missions' break down to 'fight boss', 'clear enemies', or 'defend location'.  They even use a monster-spawn mechanic so you can set up gaurdians along the routes the monsters will take to the objective you have to defend.  Don't be fooled.  This IS a Tower Defense game, not Dynasty Warriors.
The DLC they promise you makes it sound like they're going to give you some weapons and maps.  They are not.  That Digital Slime Edition they put out as bait just means these items are added to all the other items in the game you have to find and obtain.  Okay, it's not bad that they added some new items, but I would barely call some reskinned weapons inserted into the game a free DLC.
Overall, this game seems horribly simplified, misrepresented, rushed to PC, and generally not meant for anyone over the age of 10.
Oh... and Healix.  STFU Healix.  Forever.

This should have been good.
Puzzle Quest is a solid concept, Marvel has a huge stable of interesting characters spanning decades of comics.
But... this fails on both sides.
The game is divided into chapters, each of them involves chasing after a new random villain. There is an overarching story about the Green Goblin being the leader of a new organization that replaces Shield which COULD have been interesting... but several chapters in that still hasn't gone anywhere and is more a convenient framing device to wheel various heroes and villains on and off stage.
In levels you're either picking your set of 3 heroes from your own stable or get backup from the fitting hero (e.g. Spiderman coming to your aid against Venom), but the selection of available heroes is limited in two ways.
Firstly, you can have a total of FOUR heroes to start out and the only way to increase this limit is to spend premium premium hero tokens which are hard to acquire without paying money. It's reasonable that within a chapter or two you're up to six hero slots, maybe eight if you only buy the slots. This means you have a very limited roster of heroes at the ready to develop and to be called into action if you need to change up your tactics.
The other problem is that the character roster seems very limited. You get the obvious main characters from recent Marvel films , the big-name mutants, the fantastic four and some random villains from what seems to be mostly the Dark Avengers. Ooh, Squirrel Girl too, which gives it some bonus points. However, there are plenty of characters that did not make the cut. I haven't seen Rogue or Phoenix yet, for example. Did we really need five different Storm, Black Widow, Iron Man and Thor variants instead of a more diverse roster? Don't get me wrong, I LIKE that I can pick which Storm I like best (both her look and skillset, though it would have been even better to pick these separately...), I'd just wished that there had been a few more lesser known characters.
Combined with the absolutely secondary and forgettable story it's just a total waste of the Marvel license.
At least this side should be easy to get right, right? Puzzle Quest 'inspired' games are plentiful and it's clear by now what works in free to play titles and what doesn't... turns out it apparently wasn't that easy.
The very core of the Puzzle Quest gameplay is still there. You take turns manipulating a match-3 square board in an attempt to gather resources and defeat the enemy. Puzzle Quest was strictly a one versus one system, but in this game each side can consist of up to 3 characters.
Each character has up to three skills, each tied to a colour on the board, and an attack value for each colour that determines the damage it does to the targeted enemy when making a match with it. Fortunately there is no need to switch an 'active character' or anything to maximize your damage. So if you brought Lady Thor and Gamora and match yellow tiles then the game just looks up which character would deal the most damage (in this case Thor) and have that character attack. Which character attacks based on the various colours is also indicated on the stones in case this is relevant for any of the active skills in the battle (which rarely happens).
This bit is solid. It suffers from some of the same randomness that plagues this type of game in almost every iteration, where the enemy just happens to luck into a huge combo that drops into place from the top of the screen as tiles get destroyed, but it's hard to fault this particular game for that.
What it DOES do wrong is that there are way too many different colours on the board. There are SIX different colours of mana to gather and use for skills and a seventh block type with the team up tokens (that allow for one-shot special attacks that aren't as impressive as they sound). The original puzzle quest had 4 mana colours, damage tiles, experience tiles and coin tiles for a total of seven as well, so you'd think that'd be okay but it tends to fall flat. Going back to the Thor example (she was the rarest character I managed to get and is awesome), she has a cool skill that deals damage to the entire enemy team but it needs 12 yellow mana (or AP as the game calls it). The problem is that there are so many different colours that it's hard to specifically try to gather a single colour (or even two colours to focus on...). It seems more about just making matches than gathering specific mana types.
The above would be an okay if imperfect implementation of the puzzle quest side of things... but of course we have to remember that this is a free to play game, so there have to be things in place to limit what you can do so that you either grind for it cough up some money.
Prospective players will be happy to hear that there is no energy mechanic in this game... then immediately disappointed again when I explain that damage the heroes receive in a game is persistent and then needs time to heal (my Thor needed several hours after being knocked out). You can start games with injured heroes, but it obviously sets you at a disadvantage. Medkits can be used to instantly heal a hero (outside of battle), but they are in short supply. Beyond the 10 you start the game with I've found ONE from a one-time mission reward. Of course a solution is to just switch to other heroes until your preferred ones are healed, but as I mentioned above, you have very limited roster space available so the game really wants you to focus on single heroes.
Which brings me to the next big point, which is hero progression. Remember how in Puzzle Quest you got experience points from fights like in an RPG? Well, this isn't like that at all. Winning a game gets your heroes nothing, but you as the player receive some ISO-8, a mutation drug that might have a justification for being there in the later part of the plot, it's just sort of explained and then dropped entirely at the start. The idea is that you spend this ISO-8 to power up your heroes, and it's easy to see this as a communal experience point pool... except that it doesn't get filled very often.
Every mission you play gives you a few hundred ISO-8 for the first time you complete it and might also have another batch in its drop table of random one-time rewards, which means that the total amount of ISO-8 is LIMITED. Sure, you can buy more with real money or by selling off some of your spare heroes, but that kind of goes against the point.
Using ISO-8 to level up your hero increases its life and the damage dealt by matching specific tiles, but only up to the hero's current level cap. This limit can be extended 12 times by sacrificing a duplicate card, or almost duplicate anyway. You see, each of the heroes you receive or buy will only have one of its three skills randomly assigned to it. So Thor can either hit the enemy with his hammer, gather a storm cloud (spawning a bunch of yellow tiles on the field) or call the lightning down (using up that yellow AP the previous skill got you), but only ONE of those things until you find another copy of that hero.
And before you get your hopes up, there are no places to farm this stuff. You'll be stuck spending ISO-8 or hero tokens (you know, those hard-limited currencies I was complaining about earlier?) to get a random hero. A duplicate hero that has a skill you already have unlocked can be used to develop that skill, making it more effective and sometimes making it do slightly more things (e.g. more tiles when gathering storm clouds). Upgrading skills can also be done directly with hero tokens, getting new skills can not. To have a 'perfect' character you'll need 3 cards with 3 different skill slots and a ton of money OR 13 cards, divided in groups of 3-5 over the 3 skills.
Which means that even if you pay, you'll need a ton of luck to get what you want which is just frustrating.

Starseed Pilgrim is about discovery, to an extent which I have never seen before.  It is a masterpiece.
The game does not tell you what its mechanics are, what your goal is, or what the narrative is - at least, not directly.  Instead, it sets you free to discover whatever you can.  Fortunately, you cannot lose, so every step, every success, and every failure, lets you learn something new that will bring you closer to answering the questions you have.  If the idea of iteratively poking at an arcane puzzle appeals to you, you will likely love this game.
However, if you consider yourself impatient, it may not be for you.  Starseed Pilgrim requires patience, as its discoveries take time to unravel bit by bit.  If you don't like failing, that also might mean it's not for you.  While the game isn't brutally difficult, you will definitely "fail" many times.  Failing is an important part of its learning, as is being able to pick yourself up and try again.
There's not much more I can say about the game, as going deeper into the mechanics would spoil some of the discovery - the very crux of the experience!  If you've read this and aren't put off, I heartily recommend that you give Starseed Pilgrim a try.  You may fall in love with it as I have.  But even if you don't, I can guarantee that it will be unlike anything you've ever played before; that in itself might be worth the price of admission. :)

Otherwise, if you tire of grinding quickly or just want to play with top tier real life decks, you should try Magic Online.

The patriarchy hurts everyone-- even the Men (and women) of Yoshiwara.
I could've gone either way, but since I've gotten a fair few hours of solid entertainment from both this and its successor, Ohgiya, I'll go with recommending purchase-- on sale. Here's the thing, though: it's not for everyone, and the enjoyment I've gotten from it isn't remotely the enjoyment promised at face value. What has me coming back to Yoshiwara isn't the "churning" tongue kisses (really), nor the inhabitants with eyes that wander like a chameleon's, but instead is the soapy, magnificiently unpredictable mess that forms the narrative. Anything can happen in Yoshiwara, and like a dream, that anything remains blithely untethered to the constraints of reality or logic.
The first leap of faith demanded by your potential imaginary lovers is the concept that on an island (mostly) devoid of men, a cursed world requiring all women visit the red light district once they come of age for the purpose of procreation and (one imagines in some cases) sexual fulfillment, the player character is somehow a bafflingly innocent virgin, stranger to desire and independent thought alike. This, combined with a sweet face, constitutes the entirety of her charm. However, it's enough to attract the attention of all the power players in the primo pleasure palace, Kikuya. Do you think this leads to a sex-positive story of self-fulfillment? Do you think a young woman from a female-driven society will be assured of her value and joyful in exploring the uncharted depths of her desire? Do you wonder how the game will thoughtfully address the troubling notion that many of these characters are sex workers against their will?
Summer child, no. Does it trouble you to have a charater's sexual awakening consist of repeating, "That's embarrassing!", along with the aforementioned churning tongues? Go read some D.H. Lawrence or something. However, stick with Kikuya, and as a consolation prize, there will be elopements, midnight rescues, unpredictable mothers, deus ex machinas abounding, and an ogre or demon or some such. No will mean yes, consent will be irrelevant, plot will be the gymnastics required to leap from one obstacle's resolution to the next obstacle's mad presentation. Don't worry, though: there are only Happy Endings, and Super Happy Endings in Yoshiwara.

Switch 'N' Shoot is a brillintly simple throwback that works flawlessly. One button shoots AND moves your spaceship, movement is only side to side. Aliens drop down from the top and all you need to do is shoot and avoid them or DIE. One life is all you have and most players will score a whopping ZERO points as they come to grips with how challenging this is. You'll soon see that lateral movement lets you go off-screen, which is a handy tactic until you slam into an alien when trying to nab that gold power-up. OOPS.
It took me about 20 minutes to make the leaderboard with a whopping 9 points that turned into 13 a few frantic games later. I'm currently at 17, but needed to stop because it's a stupidly busy day here and I need to catch up on work. Anyway, go beat my score and bug me about it with a screenshot. I'm going to be dipping back into this for a long time.
Oh, and ABSOLUTELY mess around with the game options. You'll get some good laughs reading as you tweak stuff.

Magic, as a card game, has always struggled against its blatant cash grab design, the randomness of lands, and temptation of overpowered cards. The various PC versions over the past few years took the basic formula and heavily restricted the cards available so as not to compete with the physical version. Overall, this worked surprisingly well as a semi-casual game.
This new free to play version takes the same form as the previous entries and basically throws in tons more cards enabling actual creative deck building. Sadly, the problems pop up right away, a crappy ui, no two headed giant ai, and a glacial card unlocking pace. Play is especially painful early on, as unlike in earlier iterations where you unlocked cards for a particular deck, here you unlock a few cards from the huge pool available, resulting in decks that are a comical hodge podge of random cards. This is probably par for the course for free-to-play, but the prices mimic the physical version, in other words, more than I care to spend.
If Magic weren't a popular, long running game, this game wouldn't be worth mentioning.
As for the current card designs, Magic has slowly improved over the years. The new cards play much smoother than older iterations. The transforming creatures, in particular, add a solid choice element to the game. It's all constrained by the core outdated design of the original game, but Magic is popular for a reason and it has improved over time.
The game keeps me busy on my freetime. If you give this game a chance you might like it.

THIEF. You probably expect the oldschool THIEF, you go through the reviews, they say "IT'S NO OLD THIEF, WHY."..
It was probably the last time i listened to any reviewsites, except the game has an overall of <35. However.
You are Garrett, the masterthief and you start with a girl named Erin, going through the city, moving on many roofs, but already arguing. The objective was, to get something. It wasn't really clear. They were on the roof of a cathedral and looked down to people summoning something. Well, THIEF is obviously not a straightup middleage game without any fantasyelements. To keep it short. They start a fight because Garrett doesn't like how it works, she is loosing her claw and she tries to catch it, falls down and you have absoluetly no idea what happened. Except that you were one year unconscious. Enough of that.
The game is welldetailed, every building is different so far, well some are just for some letters or documents, but still exciting.
The atmosphere is awesome in a dark city with a terrible plague that keeps everyone small, except for guards and the rich ones and has great soundeffects, steps (blood, glass, books, leaves, etc.)
There is tons of small loot to pick up, so you can buy different arrows that can help you through the game or upgrading your armor and different goodies which are permanent, like 25% lesser to pay for arrows. Also collectives, from a picture with a naked female body and a goathead. Rings, necklaces, signs and so on.
The most important thing is the gameplay. You can play in different ways. Go full stealthy. Go and knock everyone out. Or go  aggressive and kill everyone. Focus is your friend of bluemarking loot, which can be very helpful, use it. But you don't have permanent focus, and it doesn't refill, unless you use flowers. The enemies aren't that smart sometimes, but smart enough to recognize steps if you are too loud or if they see you in the light. Even if you hide in the dark, they can see you if they're near enough. The controls are flawless, i actually expected a terrible port.
The only annoying thing is to press [E] for pressing a bar or to open windows.
Like it or not, it might be no oldschool THIEF, but it's still a pretty nice game and i didn't regret to spend my time on it.

I am an old school thief fan having bought the original thief when it was first released.  It holds a special place in my memory and was one of my favorite franchises.  Thief 1 and 2 where great I didn't care as much for deadly shadows on the xbox.  The console versions I believe held the game back and loading screens throughout the city broke up the immersion.  That is one of the issues I have with the new thief.  Even though we have new consoles out they are still underpowered when compared to a good gaming pc which i'm playing on.  The city is once again broken into sections that must load. The load screen is only 2 seconds tops for me but it still kind of breaks the immersion.  Besides that I am very impressed so far with the game, in comparison to the older games everything has been improved, besides not having garrets voice actor back. Gameplay wise Garret moves smoothly through the city and climbs and jumps with ease.  Some people have said the game is very linear but I've mainly been getting lost exploring the city, there are all kinds of paths and tunnels to travel through.  So far I have played the first main mission and have been going at the side missions, the side missions are a good way to explore the city.  I am playing on master difficulty with everything turned off.  The game is a true stealth game which I am very pleased that they kept it this way. Once again if you are seen by a gaurd you will have a tough time fighting them off, two gaurd and your as good as dead.  The atmosphere is great and like old thief games you have to really search for some loot.  The first mission its easy to find but after that its more challenging.  There is much to find for those who like to explore something like 200 documents, 84 unique loot items among other challenges to find.  I'm disappointed that people are bashing this game because it really is a good time.  In a world where irrational games closes, and where tomb raider selling 4 millions copies is considered not worth thier time making it I am worried about thief and other unique titles.  So many people will look at a review by someone who doesn't understand the genre and then not buy a game.  If you are a gamer that is sick of call of duty then buy this game.  This will be a good example to other publishers, they will be watching to see if this genre can make money, if it doesn't sell well then you can bet that this is the last thief game we will see again and other publishers won't want to take the risk making anything other than shooters.  Gamers need to show that they will buy other experiences besides shooters.  Titan fall was a blast and will sell well but gamers really need to buy other kinds of games such as thief.  True thief fans should really like the game unless they are the kind that go into this with a poor attitute to begin with.  I will update this when I finish the game but so far I'm getting my monies worth as I've played over 6 hours and only done 1 main mission and 4 side missions.

Timing is everything in this simple-concept platformer. The object is to jump from one spinning planet to the next, while picking up as much junk as you can in between. You can spend your junk (screws and stuff) on upgrades to make the jumps a little easier and more effective at picking up more junk.
The graphics are cute, the music is bubbly, and the gameplay is really excellent. You'll catch on right away but mastering the jump angles and timing between planets, which are different sizes and rotate at different speeds and often in different directions, is a bit trickier and what makes Beyond Gravity worth playing.
Addictive and really fun. This is the perfect casual game to steal quick little breaks in between other stuff you need to be doing instead.

However, what really got me down was when my friends quit, or I got hacked, or if I was being ks'ed, etc. I remember when Victoria Island was the only continent and there were only 4 Adventurers and HPQ was the only pq. Everything changed after the BB patch. It became SO much easier to level up that anyone could get 120 levels within 24 hours, without 2x EXP. The game changed from being too hard to too easy, it was ridiculous. Now, though, Nexon has finally caught up to all of the demands of the Veterans and have made the game harder to level up from level 30-60 and 170-200, which are the prime levels. After many updates to nerf the OP grind fest and 24 hours max leveling, the veterans are now complaining that the game is too hard. Ha! Too easy now too hard? Pick a side and stick with it, I thought. I'm starting to agree with them though, the game has become harder than it was after the BB patch, but it's still easier than before. The major updates, like Chaos, Legends, and Jump were all very exciting, especially if you play with friends. This game is hugely based on friends. It is SO boring without friends to play with. The game actually rewards you for playing with your friends now, apparently. I used to have MS open 24 hours per day for 7 days a week, even though I wasn't there to play myself - I just wanted to have it open for when I got home. (That's kind of exaggerated; My longest time on MS was only 77 hours, after which I had dc'd).
If you were to ask me what MS is about, I couldn't tell you. There is just so much to it, you have to experience it yourself. But let me warn you. The game doesn't like new players. It feeds on the old ones, like me, who have characters over level 150 (the max being 250). I really like it though. if I were to start all over, I'd only be willing to do it with friends (and if I had the time. I basically have no time for MS anymore because of school).
Back to Steam MS though. This Steam version is weird. It sometimes works and it sometimes doesn't work. Many people experience trouble with the Steam version for a variety of issues: someone typed in the wrong email address, and so you can't change it; someone forgot their pin; the game doesn't load for some people; and the list goes on. My suggestion would to just play MS through the website if it doesn't work on Steam.
Please disregard the amount of hours I have played MS on Steam. 80% hours are just from me afk'ing A LOT. The other 20% of those hours are me enjoying the game with my (now-dead) friends.

Writing this review, I'm 7 hours into the game. So, what can I say about it ? Is it possible to review GRID2 without mentionning GRID ?
I don't think so.
So, let's kick it off with the new things. The things they added.
- The LiveTrack. 100% unrealistic, painful if you like to know the tracks you are racing on, the LiveTrack is used for classic races or Endurance... Speaking of which:
- Endurance mode. Basically, it's a fancy name to try and make you believe it's also brand new, when it's really just a race that ends at a specific time rather than a specific line.
- Story. Let's face it, the first GRID was minimalist, story speaking. But it also didn't need it, and the lack of it - or the small presence of it - didn't bother me. This time, however, there is a scenario. This time, you are building the WSR, the World Series Racing. Some cinematics, some (fake) coverage by ESPN... It definitely feels more alive.
Now, for the things they modified or deleted.
- Cameras. No more interior camera - which is a shame, we'll admit it - and, more importantly, totally trashed up TV cameras - taking away all the value of the replays. No really, replaying your best drifts on GRID was like watching 2 Fast 2 Furious, in GRID2 it feels like the cameraman browses /r/trees on a daily basis.
- Teammate. It was fun, knowing your fellow crew member was out there, helping you out on the track, pushing opponents out of the track, stealing the first place and apologizing deeply when he finished last. Now, all you have is the guy talking to you since day 1 (but you still don't know who it is) and complaining he'll have to mend your car when you wreck it.
- The Drifting. It's hard to explain. But the drifting in GRID felt a hundred times better. Firstly, you were
on the track, without stupid people pushing you out of the way because they forgot which race category they were in. Secondly, the vibe was astonishing - the japanse speakerman going crazy over your moves, the crowd... And lastly, it just felt more responsive. The combo system was nice and clear, the way the car drifted was purely arcade but so enjoyable...
- No more rep/money system. GRID2 brings in the "fan system", already seen in Blur, for example.
- Aaaaaand the way the sponsors work changed too. And this time, it clearly is below what GRID offered.
That's not all, these are just the things that pop out first when I think about it. Now, the graphics are really nice, there are plenty of cars to choose from, and the tracks are still interesting. So ?
1) Stay away
2) Only recommended when on sale
4) Highly recommended
5) This is a must play
It's probably still better to grab it while it's on sale - hint: it's really cheap - but if you like arcade racing, and/or the first GRID, well, go for it.

While the art style and the work on the sprites and animation shows some ambition and cohesion I can't say the same for the rest. For a game that was meant to be taken as a joke I find the character roster totally uninteresting (infantry man, officer, pilot, sailor, nurse, cabaret lady, etc) and find the presentation to be somehow silly.
The worst part of the game is the combat itself which is broken because of the horrible hit detection. Also, there is just no way to counter a combo meaning you have no choice but to block until the whole thing has been performed. Even worse, you don't even need to learn the silly combo and special moves to be good at this game even when playing on the hardest difficulty. You can just use the same tactic over and over until you reach the end of the Tournament mode, which takes only 10 minutes to complete.
Also, let's not forget its technical limitations : the game doesn't feature any fullscreen or widescreen mode! And it doesn't support gamepad neither which is a shame for a fighting game.
Basically, what you see on the store page is what you get. Veteran Combat is nothing else but a silly game that was meant to be played as a joke. It might entertain you during the first 10 minutes but not beyond.

Let me start by saying that the artwork is beautiful, but that's about all the positive I can say about this game. The plot is paper thin with holes large enough to throw a mule through. An island where no men are born. Ok. Keep in mind that this story  takes place in a modern era, where on the "mainland" (where traders and travelers go freely back and forth, mind you) has electricity, modern houses, shopping malls and, presumably, no red light district where pretty men are held hostage as sex slaves until they pay off...something? But we don't send our daughters to the mainland to find a man, no, that would be weird. We encourage them to visit a professional sex worker and have his baby. And everyone's fine with this. Ok.
Each story revolves around a similar arc: Inexperienced Girl somehow wanders into Kikuya (house of ill-repute in the red light district) and for some reason is provided a free banquet and the attention of her choice of courtesans.  After much blushing and stuttering she spends the night with the courtesan of her choice, only to surprise him with the news she doesn't want to "sleep" sleep with him. They get to know each other better, she falls in love, vacilates back and forth about whether she can trust that he actually loves her/can live with him sleeping with a different woman every night, (hello! he's a male ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!) She decides for any of a variety of reasons that she can't and stays away, until he comes looking for her either via post or in person. She falls back into his arms, they declare their undying love for each other, a wedding happens, they live happily ever after. The end.
Even taking into account the generic nature of the romance, this is a very, VERY poorly written and translated story. The love scenes are laughable, and the heroine's response to every situation is some combination of blushing, stuttering, crying and the inelegant "Ngh!" But even with the terrible heroine and the awful sex scenes and the plot holes, I could stand it if the story itself didn't just SUCK. No depth whatsoever. No real conflict. DEFINITELY not work $30. Firstly, I'm giving a Not Recommended since it's not at all a "good" game, but read on for a more in-depth explanation.  For what it's worth, I'm enjoying it in a certain way.
Men of Yoshiwara: Kikuya has really nice art, but the writing/translation is really rough and makes for some unintentionally hilarious moments (a guy parts the chick's legs and says "it's the fist time", lmao), and the story is extremely typical and very disjointed at times.  I only really played Iroha's route, but I'd be shocked if his is the only route with these issues.  Like, there was a part where the MC didn't even finish the sentence she was saying, and it was suddenly several hours later at an entire different location, and they were talking about something completely different.  The MC herself is the naive pushover archetype, and all the dudes are man-hos, so expect a lot of the "jaded sex fiend falls in love with the pure innocent maiden whose body responds to lewd" thing.
If you're a sucker for nice art and you can enjoy something while simultaneously laughing at how bad it can be, then by all means, get this game.  If you're looking for a serious, solid otome with good writing, then you really shouldn't, especially at the regular price.  I fall into the first camp (and I got it on sale), but if the art wasn't good, this game would be absolutely terrible.

Even though I actively play the game and like it, I give it negative review due to unfixed bugs and developer's attitude.
Sure, all games have bugs, and sometimes they are pretty fatal, but we all live in the belief that they are unintentional and that the devs are working hard to provide us the patch as soon as possible.
This is not the case with this game. They release scheduled patches, nothing bad or uncommon in that itself. They have scheduled an update once per three months. There are no hotfixes, even if the bugs are fatal. And sometimes they skip updates, because they could not meet the deadlines. Skip, not defer. "Sorry, we could not get Oath of the Planeswalkers work, we'll just release it with the next set. Oh, and we just invalidated all your decks. And broke the priority system."
We are still waiting for the Dev to fix these two fatal bugs (I'm not going to rebuild my decks with the deck builder, it's awful).
I know for a fact that patching competetive online free-to-play game on multiple platforms is a great effort. This is why you need to be as flexible about it as possible. You need to ditch your rigid waterfall model and scheduled updates, and start being responsive.
I'll change this review to positive once they fix the known bugs and announce that they start doing hotfixes.
UPDATE: With the latest update, the fatal bugs got fixed (priority works again and old decks are again playable). I still strongly object to their updating model, so the review stays negative until they announce new model. Otherwise, the game works quite nicely (minor bugs exists, but you'll get over them).

While all in all, not a bad game, true Thief fans from the original games will find themselves dissappointed. I was sad to see that Thief does not have the same feel as the old games. The humor that you receive from listening to the guards talk is also gone. Citizens wandering around the city do not acknowledge you, giving them a lifeless feel. The story is not as good as the stories in the previous games as it feels less compelling than the Dark Project, the Metal Age and even Dark Prophecy. The new game is also missing some of its most dynamic parts. What happened to the Hammers? The Pagans? Not to mention the unique enemies you encountered in all the previous games (mechanist robots, pagan creatures, keeper statues, etc). You also have to watch Garrett steal and interact with everything as opposed to just taking things, this wouldn't be a problem except that it slows down your ability to stay out of sight of guards. The combat in this game is an improvement, but as the old Thief games were the birthplace of stealth games, combat never was a big focus in Thief, if you're being seen by guards then you're doing it wrong. Overall, the new Thief lacks the dynamic story and gameplay of the original. I give it a 6/10. If you didn't play the original games then you likely will enjoy the game for what it is.

I was really looking forward to this game, since I LOVED the past ones so much.  The plots in the previous games were so good, and the atmosphere was stellar.  How could they go wrong?  Well, let me break it down:
1) Easy Maps.  The paths through the level are similar to Half-Life, where there is only one possible solution, but without the creativity or size.  You can't mess up, go the wrong way, or explore the levels at all.  I really wish they would have looked harder at Assassin's Creed and Oblivion for how to make maps open and fun.
2) Easy Guards.  Again, you can sneak by things so easily.  They are also idiots with a very easy pathing system.  Please make them more unpredicatable and smarter about how they are being manipulated.
3) Overall Easy Game.  Why is it that game developers today are making games so damn easy?  Look at games like BioShock that had an excellent story, but if you died you could respawn 10' away and just keep going.  Seriously, make a game with a real difficulty that requires use of your brain.  Don't just make the dumb guards god-like and call that difficulty.  Go play Demon Souls for a while and you will see a game with a true difficulty.
As much as it pains me to say it, skip this game.  They really made it for people that want little to no challenge.

You have a limited amont of actions per day -  1 before work and 3 after, and 6 actions on Saturday/Sunday. Writing one message or SpaceBook post, requesting one friend, REJECTING a friend/relationship request etc takes up one action. Oh, and you have to make sure you eat or your health starts declining, so eating will take at least one action per day. Of course, you can organize events to restaurants and be social, but some events take more than 3 actions. It feels a bit silly that grabbing a burger and pressing one "Thumbs Up" to someone posting a bunch of random lyrics takes the same amount of actions.
The most efficient way to achieve your goals seems to be simply locking in on one person to brown-nose (hint: the person hiring for the next position you're shooting for) , developing your skillset enough that you'll just barely qualify and ensure that the hiring person just adores you. Rinse and repeat. And it does feel very repetitive, in spite of there being multiple potential ways of escaping the station.
The interface involves clicking through a lot of menus, and makes me wish for a "favorite actions" shortcut bar where I could for example drag the S.H.O.P. meal I intend to buy most days to optimize my health.  Clicking on a skill in the career tree does give suggestions on how to improve that skill, which is a helpful feature, but for a lot of skills the options are rather few and mostly involves going through weeks of work shifts on a certain job.
The game has its funny moments and chuckles, but there's also a lot of tedious repetition for the XP just to get to the next stage.

At first glance I loved this expansion but sadly, it is still not even close to Civ V. It's missing key components that break the game for any strategy but a war based empire.
1. Warscore broken: You can pound a nation into the dirt for several turns, but without a land unit near their city to threaten taking it, they will never surrender. This means naval nations built on trade are rendered useless. Wars will start you can never finish.
2. Diplomacy: While there are some neat improvements since the original, the new system lacks key components.... such as defensive alliances. Ally with a small power and they will use your power to declare war on a big guy. Not a broken issue, makes sense, but the lack of options for pacts and agreements make the diplomacy system not even half what earlier Civ games were.
Do NOT recommend this game. Wait till they come out with more expansions to fix the broken issues, then wait till it's on sale in a gold bundle so you aren't ripped off for each individual release.
Sorry Sid Meiers, you've lost a fan.
EDIT: SInce the expansion, massive improvements to diplomacy. Not sure if I like what is done, but definately less broken. Warscore still an issue...

I started this match-3 free-to-play game without putting any money into it, and while the time limitations of such f2p games is in place, it still allowed me to play for stretches of about an hour a few times a day.  I got a nice puzzle fix, and I have to say that, compared to other f2p match-3 puzzle games, I found the reward system for this one giving me that extra little incentive to actually keep coming back to this one.
By doing the quest lines I was able to acquire some character covers to upgrade my characters, and earn the Iso-8 which is used to level them up after upgrading, and even some gold which I proceeded to use to pick up a few more cover slots allowing more heroes.  With about 6-9 heroes available in various stages of upgrade, I was able to start in on some phases of the Deadpool dailies, earning Iso-8 more quickly and continuing to upgrade.
Joining a random active alliance I began to get meager rewards from the weekly events and start giving it a shot myself.  I obviously did not get very far or do very well, but I did succeed in getting just that little more gold or Iso-8 or hero cover, and the prospect of earning just a little more kept me coming back, as did the continually expanding daily login bonus. (up to day 105 and still going, including a three star hero cover and heroic level random covers to boot.)
Once I reached over 200 hours played, I decided to go ahead and support the game itself by spending $50 on it.  I have picked up AAA titles for my consoles for $50 and not spent nearly as much time, both hours-wise or days in a row played, as I have this game.  I have to say that, had I put that money in sooner, I don't believe it would have boosted my performance much in the beginning, but at the point I was at, having finished the story quests for all their repeated rewards and filled my f2p expanded roster, being able to add a dozen more heroes suddenly made my capabilities at this stage much more effective, and the game has just renewed itself in making me want to return to it each day just to see how much I can accomplish this time.

I preordered quite a while ago as I have been following this game since it was revealed as Thi4f (Thief 4) many years ago. Myself like others were quite skeptical of this game following the game play videos released. After playing the first mission, I am pleasantly surprised - especially after seeing some of the recent reviews on Metacritic/IGN and the likes – the thing is, I really don’t think they have been playing it correctly.
Now, there are a few things to do if you want to enjoy this game. First - turn off focus. Play on master difficulty or custom difficulty, and turn off pretty much everything you think will break your immersion. The light crystal isn't necessary as you can tell when you are in the light or not - I mean seriously..
Same goes for guard alerts. When they see you - do you REALLY need lightning spiking around their heads? No, if they see you, you'll know - we aren't stupid. Jeeze these modern gaming trends do get on my nerves. The point of this game is to be as immersed in it as possible.
With these things set you are guaranteed to have an enjoyable experience. This is a first-person only Thief title unlike the previous installment (Thief Deadly Shadows) - which had the option for either or.
So this is a reboot - Garret doesn't have his mechanical eye (at least not yet - maybe that happens eventually) and the city is well ... kind of like it was in previous games. Guards are still overly violent and rude. There is some kind of disease they keep talking about called the gloom – which really reminds me of Dishonored.
As for the gameplay – with everything set like I said above (thank god they put these options in). This can be one of the most heart beating experiences in gaming you can have.
Lurking in the shadows trying to frantically pick a lock in time before the guard does his sweep near you.
You WILL get caught, you CAN get away. And you can retry.
The feeling you get when you successfully strip a house clean of all its valuables without anyone even realizing (even though you are right there) is just an experience that you will not find in any other games except … well, the previous Thief games. And maybe Dishonored. But all HUDS and crap really got in my way. With stealth games – you want it to be as minimalist as possible. All you want is Garret.
As for what I’ve seen, it is quite linear, this is a narrow corridor city you will be making your way through. Yet, I still felt like I had options. I could still go off and explore, take the rooftops, sneak past guards and pick the lock of the front door before anyone noticed. This is where Thief shines.
Now for some negatives. I am going to ignore focus mode and everything of the likes as I have already stated my opinions on it.
The loading. For a 2014 game, it isn’t very impressive when every section of the city is barred off with a load screen. This is how it was in Deadly Shadows as well. But well... I guess I expected more. Thankfully these aren’t very long.
And the thing that really irks me; is the quick time events. Spamming ‘E’ to open a frekin window. NO THANKS. THAT’S NOT A GOOD IDEA. Just open the Window for us, spamming ‘E’ really doesn’t make anything better. This is something I really think should be removed in a later patch.
The cinematics are OK. But gosh darn it the ones that aren’t rendered in game are very chopping and often the sound falls out of sync. Again, this will be fixed in a patch.
I am very early in the game, but based on my first impression. I am happy with my purchase. I will update this review as I progress..

I should point out I'm the kind of guy who has immense dislike for the entirety of social media and doesn't use any of them seriously except to enter site giveaways and such. Hell, I don't even have a proper private Facebook account. With that in mind it's not really a stretch to see how I would have little tolerance for a game like Redshirt. And it does pain me to say so because Redshirt was developed solely by one person so credit where credit is due.
Problem lies in the premise as far as I'm concerned – this is the kind of game that could've been spun off into a more established RPG, and god knows we can always use more science fiction RPGs when you tally their number versus fantasy RPGs, but is instead at its core a a social network simulator with all the tediousness that apparently implies. What do I mean by that?
Well, it's the constant minutia.
You see, you get to create a character from couple of races and some cosmetic choices, none of which really matters that much aside from some disposition and your sex for relationship preferences later on, after which you promptly start at the bottom of the hierarchy on a station Megalodon-9. Along the way you have to navigate through Spacebook, making friends along the way as well as organizing various events, maintaining relationships both real and online, advance in your career, etc. It's actually quite a decent offering when I think about it, to be honest. One major issues that arises is that you're navigating with all of this just through menus. That may have been a great asset and cost cutting design choice, but in practical terms it means you better get used to staring at lists to fill, bars to grind and repeated faces.
In structural terms you get a predetermined number of ACTIONS each day which you can then use to choose what you want to do. For example, in the morning you get one action before going to work and then you get more when you're done with said work. Needless to say, you also get free weekends with a lot more action points which means you can do a lot more. Speaking of work you do get daily results based on a lot of factors such as you adeptness, quality/attitudes of co-workers, pure random chance with events, etc. Doing certain type of jobs will net you experience in specific skills and interests. If anything, job market itself is rather extensive and you have a thorny path set out for you if that's how you want to win the game. Oh, I didn't talk about that yet, did I?
Basically, early on a timer pops up with X number of days until... something, happens and you're expected to get off the station by then. How you go about it is really the best part of Redshirt because there's quite a few options. You can get to the top of the job ladder, bribe your way out, romance or be BFF with the right person to secure a way out or simply pay for an exorbitantly priced ticket. None of these is really simple and will take a while whether you're playing the Spacebook game 24/7 or saving up money. As tempting as it would be to getting tunnel vision and focus on getting out you can't really do that because you still need to exist on day-to-day basis aka handling your happiness and health meters, and also dealing with others. This is where EVENTS you use action points to initiate come into play with all their variety and consequences they can incur. I'm not talking CYOA approach here because that's not it, but let me give you an example: you spend two action points to throw together a holo-sculpture viewing for you and your friends, contact them on Spacebook and they agree only for one guy to bail out – in the end you get some art appreciation experience and happiness goes up. This is just one example.
Getting down to the nitty-gritty and past just bland descriptions my problem with this one is something I've already mentioned and it's something Redshir shares with Daily Chthonicle in a sense that the game simply isn't engaging to play. You're stuck to menu navigation and no, not even occasional away missions change that up, and the entire ordeal gets repetitive real fast because you end up in a cycle of monotonous daily life until something interesting pops up. Which strikes too close to home for comfort.
Joking aside if you actually have a thing for social networks and religiously checking what people are doing every waking moment of their lives you might find this quite engaging. Fortunately, I prefer my sanity intact so I'll give it a wide berth.

After 500+ hours of gameplay, 4 lvl 90 characters and 7 under-leveled ones, I think it's safe to say that this game is actually pretty good for a very old game. It reminds me of my days playing maplestory (RIP) and is a refreshing change from all the visual eye-candy games that I play. The combat is very smooth and fluid as long as you know your character's skills and skill flow (battlemage FTW). Lots of characters and subclasses to choose from, each catering to every gamer's play-style. Not P2W, but rather more Farm-to-win. The only bad thing I found out about this game is that it is running on P2P connection. Meaning, if you have good internet but one of your party members are lagging, then you lag too. Which is kind of a bummer. But overall, this game got me really hooked. 9.5/10
Pros/Cons: +/-
+Wide array of characters to choose from, and each character has at least 2-5 subclasses each.
+Each character has different storylines and different interactions with some NPCs.
+Fluid combos (smooth transition from auto-attack to skill)
+Flashy skill animations
+Easy to max out your character levels just from scenario quests (and a little bit of grinding on the side)
+GM's give free stuff sometimes and are very approachable.
+The community is very helpful to newbies (like me)
+Farm to win. None of that microtransactions BS.
-P2P connection :/
-No character customization (Either buy avatar pieces in auction hall, purchase time-restricted av's with mileage, or buy av pieces in the cera shop)
-PVP is kind of broken (because P2P connection)
-Some characters can be hard to play and require thorough gearing for it to be effective

DFO is now more accessible than ever, and that's a good thing.
PROS:
-Leveling has been simplified, Main quests are the ones that net the most EXP. Watch some guides to know the absolute
most optimal route of getting quests done.
-Free Skill re-allocation. No more pay gold to modify your skill tree. Now you're able to experiment as you please with any build in any character.
-A LOT of Character slots.
-Great events to help you catch up with the endgame.
-If you didn't like the class you're currently playing, you can change your sub class for free until lvl 49(or 59, I don't remember well)
-Most classes are extremely fun to play
-99% of your skills can also be used by inputting a combination move, giving a feel of really doing a combo.
-The Stamina sistem is not as prohibitive as other Korean MMOs. Allowing you to pick and drop DFO easily.
-Gorgeus art style that only gets better once you see the ultimates and combos in action.
CONS;
-Endgame is still unforgiving, and raiding with others can be a bother if you don't have a class that benefits the entire team.
-The later part of the game becomes One touch kill. Either you kill everything in the screen or you get combo'ed to death.
-Farming for legendaries can be a HUGE pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ as well as extremely time consuming.
-Not every class is equally efective in speedrunning the dungeons, and some will struggle a lot with clearing.
-Item shop is usually overpriced.
-Trying to buy CERA through steam is akin to asking for a RIfle Licence.
Overall, the game is a solid 7/10 and it's easy to avoid the burn.

I used to play a ton of this game a few years ago, it was a great game. Excellent design and progression, ruined a little bit by the start of an infestation of in game purchases. Even looking at the game now the only thing wrong is how the purchases were structured: not skins or flashy effects that have no actual impact on game balance, but outright power you can add to your character by spending real cash.
EDIT: after about an extra hour, I've gotten everything to work and played this game for two full fatigue bars.
Before I comment on the actual game, there appears to be an issue with DFO informing steam upon exit. I now have to forcibly close steam every time I log out of DFO because steam thinks DFO is still running and insists on me closing that first.
On to the gameplay: I first played this game in china, on and off ever since its release, racking up several high level characters, but always end up quitting due to latency issues. The latency was of course expected as I live literally across the globe. The reason why I mention this is because of the amount of difference I felt between what is essentially different translations of the same game.
In the Chinese version, all voice actors were Chinese, and the dialogues, prompts, etc were translated with equal high standards. There was still overwhelming number of hotkeys to get used to, and the cluttered user interface. However all the in game instructions, tutorials, events were worded perfectly and organized extremely well. I never felt overwhelmed and knew where to get easy to digest extra information if necessary.
In this version, the voice actors were what I guess the original Koreans, which is fine. But the clutter of user interface is actually worse than before, and somehow if I were to click on one of the million events going on, there is little info actually given, sometimes to the point of unhelpfulness.
It's not completely unreadable or anything, but it just takes a little extra effort to understand something that could've been presented a lot better.
When this game came out in NA I couldn't believe it was a flop, it is such a glorious game, but now playing the English version for the first time, I understand. For the same game, it is amazing how rushed the conversion felt, same with the launcher. The whole thing just feels like low maintenance cash grab, I feel actually a little heartbroken at how awkward this game feels, not in terms of gameplay, but simply intuitiveness and interactivity.

I have no idea why I got this game, maybe because of the whole male courtesan thing, or maybe because the guys looked cute. I thought the premise was kinda interesting although the background setup about how the whole male courtesans thing came to be felt a bit iffy to me but whatever, give me my male courtesans.
My favorite is Hayabusa, because he's such a cutie. Initially, based on first impressions, I wasn't really that sold on the rest of the guys other than Hayabusa and Iroha but reading their stories changed my mind about them. Now I've got a soft spot for Takao and maybe even Tokiwa. I like how they all have their own stories to tell, and despite all that bling bling and glamour they have their own insecurities and maybe even aspirations.
Since this is a game about male courtesans, it's inevitable that there would be some "steamy" moments, but I didn't find it that smutty or overwhelming, maybe because of all those "flowery" language they used to describe the scenes LOL, but mostly I was glad that there's actually a story to read. Granted, the stories aren't what I would call intense or deep (no pun intended), but I think they are decent enough for some quick casual reading. I'm okay most of them except for Iroha S2 where I really wanted to throttle the MC lol. I generally don't mind the stereotypical "pure/clueless/innocent" MC trope but I can't stand stupid. Luckily Iroha made up for it so it's all good.
And speaking of Iroha S2, I spotted quite a few grammatical and spelling typos like you're vs your (grammar nazi alert!) compared to the other stories where the translation was quite decent. I could deal with those though, but it seemed to me like some rather rushed work or careless mistakes with his S2. I wonder why the other guys doesn't have a S2 though.
Story aside, the quality of art is quite good, as are the the range of expressions for the sprites and backgrounds. There were a couple of CGs/sprite I thought looked a bit weird but the majority are generally good. One thing I want to mention is that Kagerou looks pretty much your typical shota in sprite form so initially I wasn't that keen but damn, he looks good in his CGs. And need I mention those gorgeous outfits? I never get tired at looking at those!
The music  isn't too bad but it's a tad repetitive. The lack of voice acting though, is a shame. Considering the story premise, I would have love to hear them trying to sweet talk me LOL!
Overall, I think this is a pretty decent game for some casual reading although I'd recommend waiting for a sale if you plan to get it. There are also about 16 short sub stories in additional to the sequel and date scenario, so it isn't that bad of a deal especially if you got it during a sale!

Starseed Pilgrim is a tough game to review.
On one hand, it's handling and execution is absolutely superb. The art is fantastic, the mechanics sound, and the sound design flawless. The game is without a doubt a wonderful experience.
But on the other, it's not an experience for everyone. With very little introduction, the game can be jarring. The game's centered around a planting mechanic, where you gather individual seeds from heartblocks, and plant them to make larger formations. There are two worlds: home, where you can grow plants at your leisure, and the other worlds, where you collect more seeds and escape darkness while attempting to create a safe path home.
I don't wish to give anything more away, but the game never goes beyond this. Like the game Proteus, there is no actual end goal, outside of exploration, but given your ability to fail and back yourself in a corner, the game can lose its charm quickly if you're not the patient or contemplative type.
This being said, the game never ceased to intrigue and surprise me. I've enjoyed my time with it, and while it might be a while til I play it again, I have every intention to come back and continue exploring.
This journey may not be for everyone, but it is a journey well worth taking.

I want more visual novels in general, especially otomes, to come to the west for me to read and enjoy.  That said, I hope that the ones come over are ones I can actually truly enjoy and love.  I have mixed feelings about The Men of Yoshiwara: Kikuya.  I originally bought it in 2015 going, "lol, otome game that needs my support, but...male ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, lol."
I enjoyed the Japanese architecture, the attire, and the character designs - a lot of the men truly are that flashy; or are deliberately attempting to look so to catch the eye of potential customers.  That much is fine.
The setting, however - the world building - was absolutely horrendous.  I grew up hating the convenient excuse of female-only races that had to lure men (and upon luring them, the men could enjoy themselves); so why would I suddenly appreciate the reverse?  Or something similar.  The idea that MEN ARE RARELY BORN ON THE ISLAND, SO WE DECIDED TO CREATE ♥♥♥♥♥HOUSES OF IMPORTED MEN is just a stupid, convenient excuse that annoys the heck out of me.  I certainly wouldn't appreciate the reverse concept either.
However, simply having a house of male courtesans / ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s  to appeal to a clientele not so commonly targeted...that's fine, in theory, if they'd just gone that route.  And I do appreciate the realism that most of the men, under all the flair and presentation and glamor, do not actually want to live their lives there.  They were sold, traded, or otherwise dragged into a situation that they have to adapt to and deal with.
The female character is "true" to the culture of the world the game has built and does not think of how unwilling they might be until it comes up in each route itself, but then, she also never intended to deliberately seek the attention of male courtesans, either.  She's caught up in that world accidentally and is shown to have a sympathetic perspective from the start when encountering a couple that has to escape the island since one of them is, in fact, a male courtesan that has not yet paid his debt to the house that took him in.
There's parts of this game I like.  There really are.  I especially liked the CGs; the art was tasteful when it was sexual (heck, I actually really liked some of those scenes overall) and I really like how soft everyone's hair looked.  I also love that the female character wasn't generally faceless - she was extremely cute, and the most attractive character in the entire game to me.  My tastes revealed, I guess?  Whoops.
That said, certain routes feel like a chore to complete, and I end up feeling like this world setting would have been better as a bigger budget game instead of a port from a mobile game.  For what it is, it isn't that bad - most mobile otomes in my experience are extremely worthless to play - but this one didn't feel like that.  It just felt like it really missed the mark on potential, for me.
A setting like this with a lot more world buildup and less direct focus on romance routes (while still maintaining the romance later on) would have been extremely intriguing, but that's not what was created.  This game, and its setting, might have been able to convince or trick me into enjoying the worldbuilding a lot more if there was a much longer prologue, with a lot of character interaction and circumstance to force the female protagonist into these characters' lives.  Something that took much longer to read, with more intricately detailed routes once the paths really branched.
Instead, I have to say that this isn't an otome I'd recommend unless you're wanting something that is a step up from most mobile otome games, but isn't as good as Nameless, Sweet Fuse, or Hakuoki.

I wish I could give this game a 'mediocre' rating, because 'mediocre' sums it up pretty nicely. It's not terribly bad for an Otome game (there are far worse games out there) but it's also not particularly good. That's why I can't recommend it.
First of all, if you are a hardcore Otome fan, then you'll probably buy this game regardless of what I'm about to write, so feel free to stop reading here and buy it.
Still with me? Alright. I haven't played all of the routes yet (one route took me about 1.5~2 hours), so what I'm criticising might not be applicable for those remaining 3 routes (although I don't have much hope for that).  I'll elaborate a bit on what I disliked/liked in the routes that I did play:
CONS:
- The writing is simply not good. For the most part, the conflicts are artificially created and very predictable and/or cheap.
Almost all of the routes can be summarized by
I mean I didn't go in expecting some huge plot twists, but I still felt that the problems resolved themselves pretty quickly. Most of the drama seemed very artificial and forced, as the reader could easily predict how it was going to be solved without much trouble (and without the need of Protag-chan doing something meaningful other than throwing money around and/or happening to know someone).
- The main character is the epitome of a Mary Sue. I already hinted at that when I talked about the writing, but I thought it deserved its own bullet point. I mean most Otome protagonists are bland, but that doesn't make it not worth mentioning. I was particularly annoyed with the protagonist here because she doesn't actually do anything other than being innocent/naive. Those traits are basically her whole characterization.
As a result, the 'choices' that you need to make are pretty awful. Not in the sense that they were unfair, but rather they were... cringey (I don't like using that word, but I can't find a better one to describe it). I found myself face-palming at every other choice or so because it was just that bad. Many of them were basically something like:
Bishie-san: "I LOVE YOU PROTAG-CHAN AND I'M NOT SAYING THIS BECAUSE YOU PAID ME!!"
Yeah, I think you get what I'm talking about (and if you thought that was cute, then by all means, get this game. There's lot of choices like that). Speaking of choices...
- There aren't any real choices. The game plays like a kinetic novel in that your choices affect nothing other than two to three sentences after it and your "likeability" meter, which you can check anytime. So if you wind up choosing the wrong choice, you'll realise immediately and can just load back to the choice selection screen. That's not really necessary for most choices though, since they're pretty predictable. There's two endings (happy and super happy) depending on your likeability meter at the end, but you can just select to start from the last chapter with 0% likeability and you'll get the happy ending instead of the super happy one.
- The game looks very unpolished. There are quite a lot of typos, awkward translations, wrong pronouns used or even a wrong speaker attributed. It's still definitely readable but breaks immersion very quickly.
Also, the interface is ugly. You can really see that it's a mobile port.
Additionally, the game itself feels very clunky because of missing screen transitions, badly looped (and repetitive) music, which also changes frequently and abruptly.
These things all contribute to a lack of immersion (which in my opinion is very important in an Otome game). The game wasn't completely bad, though.
PROS:
+ The art is super pretty. This was the main reason for me to buy this game and one of its few redeeming qualities.
+ Most of the negative aspects I mentioned above apply to many Otome games, particularly the mobile ones. If you compare this game to those, I'd even say it's one of the better ones (I'm not talking Mystic Messenger mobile game though, more like the typical ones like 'Be My Princess' or 'Midnight Cinderella' or 'Kissed by the baddest bidder' and stuff like that). If enjoy Otome games like that, then you might like this one as well.
All in all it was mildly enjoyable. I didn't hate it, but it also didn't particularly impress me. I think if you don't have high expectations on this game and just see it as 'another Otome with a passive protagonist and the same stereotypes as bachelors', then you won't be let down.
I think this game had a lot potential in its premise, but unfortunately fell short in the execution.
However, I tried the other game that plays in the same world as this one, "The Men of Yoshiwara: Ohgiya", and I have to say, from the little bits that I have played, it is MUCH better than Yoshiwara. The protagonist is much more bearable (you get the option to slap your bachelor across the face) and the available bachelors were in my opinion more appealing.
If after reading this, you're unsure whether you should get this game, I'd suggest trying "Ohgiya" instead, since it's basically an improved "Yoshiwara".
