UPDATE: In time I see what a strong impression Starseed Pilgrim has left on me, recalling it now and again. Mechanically it's brilliant. I originally gave this game a negative review, but I've since come to reevaluate what the notion of a worthy game playing experience is. My initial reaction, after 6 hours played, was that I had wasted most of those hours on repetition, with no further revelations after those of the initial couple hours playtime. New players should take up Starseed Pilgrim without the expectation of the great puzzle leading anywhere special. Instead, solve the puzzle, play with the mechanics for a couple of hours, explore and enjoy the lonely ambience. Then put the game aside. It doesn't have to be any more than that, not at this price. Enjoy the experience.
----
Exploration, discovery, mystery, wonder, suprise. Just some of the brand of adjectives that seemingly every review of this game coos. And true enough, the game does have that. For the first couple of hours I was glued to the screen while I solved the metapuzzle that is Starseed Pilgrim. The puzzle is to understand the game's mechanics, and wonderful and clever mechanics they are.  The problem: the game does nothing afterwards. In the solving of the mechanics, you've already seen all of what the game has to offer. Those nouns above comprise about 10% of your playtime, The rest: repetition. With its involving atmosphere and great use of sound, as well as said mechanics, I was expecting Starseed Pilgrim to evolve into a masterpiece. What a shame.

A lot of folk dislike this game and a lot of people love it, all with valid reasoning. I played all the older titles thouroughly before picking this one up so I suppose I have a good frame of reference. Easily the worst Hitman game but NOT a bad game.
Reasons I dislike it:
-It is very linear in terms of completeing tasks or missions, which in the previous titles allowed a lot more freedom to complete objectives, despite being older styled games.
-The disguises, oh god the disguise “system” never worked. Before if you could get a disguise without being noticed, you can get around certain areas and as long as you don’t run or get too close to the guards you’d be fine. But the disguises in this game don’t work AT ALL, you have a limited time before inevitbly being spotted, and the only way to avoid that is to tip your hat or rub your bald head, aka use your instinct. So the main way to get through majority of the missions is by rolling around like an autist and hiding behind things.
-It seemed to go for more action than stealth, they stripped a lot of the stealth aspects that made the previous games fun. I don’t want to be that person that keeps referring to the old games as superior, but seriously, they could’ve changed the mechanics around without taking away so much.
-I feel as if it were too easy, a lot of the missions just felt like they had no challenge at all and I could easily just roll through without having to think about how I was going to compete each section(s).
-The checkpoint system instead of the manual save slots. I hate this in ANY game. Nothing infuriates me more than checkpoint spots instead of being able to manually save yourself. If you usually played the hitman games on pro then this probably wouldn’t even be an issue, but I usually like to go through my first run on normal or one above just to get a feel for each mission.
-Majority of the kills are in cutscenes.
-No dance floors where 47 can dance

Reasons I love it:
-It’s a game (plus a book) focused more around agent 47 than any other game, and it wasn’t just about professional contracts. I know some didn’t like this, but I really loved that it was a story driven on him going out of his way, and betray the agency he had worked with for many years, to actually save someone that he had no obligation to save. I really love that it had him kind of break out of the professional-killing mode and instead do something that most wouldn’t imagine him doing. I think it gave a lot of insight on him as a person, not just some killing machine.
-47’s look was very nice and improved. I much prefer this look over the new Hitman (tmtmtm) look of his. Aboslution has to be the peak of his rendered looks, in my opinion.
-Cutscenes and general graphics look very nice, even to this day, I think they have aged pretty well and it’s still quite a beautiful game to play.
-Throwing objects and distracts actually worked. This was a problem I had in Blood Money, sometimes dropping items (coins, syringes) as distractions worked, and sometimes (most of the time) it didn’t, even like 2.5 ft away from whoever you were trying to distract and you’re hidden. I like that it was more reliable than the previous title for distractions.
-He actually RUNS faster. In all the previous title he just jogged. I mean, it makes sense considering he’s on professional contracts, but it’s nice to have a speedier pace than a jog.
-The NPCs actually have more dialogue with you. Even small things like “howdy” or “how ya doin”, etc when you go near npcs adds to the immersion of the world, in the previous title NPCs did have dialogue but were more commonly quiet unless you stood by them for like 30 seconds.
-The wrestling outfit

Overall while I found some things in this game infuriating I also found it really enjoyable. I think it’s worth getting, maybe on sale, if you’re really into the series.

Reviewed this ages ago (see ORIGINAL REVIEW at the bottom), but the new Amonkhet update has prompted me to revisit this -- I love this game, and have put countless hours into it already, but this latest release seems to have broken the game entirely with ridiculously powerful card effects.
Amonkhet turns the focus onto tokens and building them up, which in itself is fine, but the way they've gone about it has made it nigh-impossible to beat the AI decks. I'm all for promoting weenie decks and the like, but the game is twatting me for 15+ damage within just 4-5 turns regularly due to cards like Aven Wind Guide (gives all tokens flying and vigilance), and Temmet, Vizier of Naktamun (+1/+1 for token and unblockable).
The new Trial of Solidarity card also gives +2/+1 and Vigilance to everything for example, and then the Exert mechanic goes and adds another +1/+1 to everything, etc.
Regal Caracal is another OTT card - gives you 2 x 2/2 Cat Tokens with Lifelink (gain life), tag this with one of the many Indestructables and the game is over before you know it - 20 Life doesn't go very far when you're being attacked by 5+ flying creatures, all with 6/5, Flying and Vigilance, meaning game over basically -- I'm talking by turn 6 or 7 btw, if I even last that long...
And to top it off, because of the Embalm ability, cards that are really powerful need to be defeated twice, and even three times when the 'double token' Enchantment is in play. Given there are many cards that return stuff from the graveyard, everything needs killing several times over...?
I am regularly getting not just beaten but entirely demolished, often with the computer AI still having 30+ Life points. This isn't just Dark Souls level of difficulty we're talking, it's an issue which will force players to play similar decks to the computer just to be in with a chance of competing against it...
Unfortunately, because the release is already 'out there', I'm not sure what Wizards can do about it, but I suspect that Pro-Tour and other professional players will 'break' this set very easily -- it's going to be interesting to see the fallout, because I genuinely think it spells trouble for Wizards and MTG going forward... and the Pro-Tour games are going to be over that much quicker, too - a fact that Wizards won't be able to 'hide' due to Pro-Tours now having such a massive online presence/audience, etc.
It saddens me to say it, but I cannot recommend this title on any level at the moment. A bad state of affairs given that it's been my 'comfort game' for a few years now...
Not impressed, guys -- please do something about it
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Okay... mixed feelings about this game -- at the end of the day I've played 350+ hours of it, so there's obv something about it that keeps drawing me back. It's also a very good rendition and introduction to the current MTG 'world'  (and visually better than the Online Magic game on Wizards' own website), but not without its issues and/or bugs. And somewhat annoyingly, I get the impression that fixing these bugs doesn't seem to be any kind of priority for the games developers...
I appreciate the many connotations of the game and card interactions must make compiling the software a logistical nightmare, but these are still game-breaking bugs that can lead to unintentional harm being delivered to the keyboard and/or screen by one's fist... Grrr...
My biggest issue is with certain cards that provide additional mana when sacrificed (Crumbling Vestige and Vessel of Volatility being notable examples) -- this mana often disappears if there are no creatures to spend it on, even when there are other spells (Sorcery, Instant, etc) you could have conceivably used it for further along during your (or opponent's) turn. Surely this mana should be sticking around at least until the end of the turn and/or untap phase if it's not used, instead of just disappearing when the Timer has swooped round?
My other gripe would be with the annoying "Player has been replaced by computer AI" when the only option provided is "Continue Playing?" (or quit out of the game and forfeit the match and a rank level). Note this is NOT the same as the "Player has left the game, Continue Playing AI or Leave Game" textbox...
Other than the above, there is no better introduction to the game if you're not fortunate enough to live near a hobby shop and/or local players group (and/or especially not prepared to spend real money on MTG Booster Packs or a Deckbuilders Box for 'real' cards, etc).
It would be nice to think the new Eldritch Moon set(s) will be incorporated into the game at some point, but as it stands there are already a shed-load of bugs that need fixing first (if you read the forums, etc), and evidently there are already loads of cards missed out anyway...
Finally, some form of Random Draft mechanism would be a fabulous bonus if they developed an online version of 40-card Limited, but am guessing it's not the sort of thing that'll be provided as a free service. That said, I'd pay 1000-1200 coins (hard-earned ones at that!) to join in such a game when I could, especially if they allowed you to keep the cards you'd drafted in this way from your boosters...?
Overall, a great FREE intro/primer to the world of MTG imho...

Thief is a great instalment to the series and as kind of a reboot it's does a great job paving the way for what will hopefully be the first of many more 'next-gen' Thief games.
The game it's self is aestically very pleasing, the graphics are second to few and overall gameplay is smooth and relatively uninterrupted. The mechanics are well enough for sneaking around and looting etc, but don't expect to be going toe-toe with more than 1 enemy at a time. Basically, if you're discovered by more than one guard, it's a death sentence and you will learn how quickly you can load last save. Whilst I wasn't expecting much of a combat system from the game, I was hoping for sneak damage perk when using the bow and perhaps some minor melee combat, or the ability to counter (non-lethal) attacks so I could make my escape route with a sense of panic and urgency. That said, you can purchase/find poison cloud arrows that incapacitate the enemy – just don’t miss as the game is more unforgiving than getting the drunken wrong end of a cigarette. I would have like to have seen more of an awareness indication on guards and enemies – this would aid the swooping between shadows and give better aid to timing of attacks/takedowns as well as increasing the difference between similar games, cough, Dishonored, cough. It’s awfully frustrating drawing an arrow on your bow to maximum tension only to have it stick in a guards head and then him be fully aware and alert of his assailant.
What the game does do well is the stealth and sneak ability, far superior to the likes of dishonoured and much less clunky than say for instance Skyrim. It’s impossible not to compare the game to Dishonoured with all the similarities but Thief is not smothered by the steampunk, futuristic, often hard to follow alternative universe. Instead, the immersion is founded on a gritty late 1800’s era where plague (the gloom) is run rampant through the city streets. You’re free to run the streets and break into houses via rooftops plundering all the fancy cutlery and golden microscopes you can fit in your endless wizard pockets. The game turns these delightful items immediately into an equivalent gold value you can spend on tools for more felonies. There’s an unmistakable satisfaction gathering up all the collectables to a set of rare items and where the game falls short of combat more than makes up for it with blatant burglary and theft.
Thief doesn’t benefit from a completely free roam environment (like Assassins Creed series) unfortunately. This really brought the points down for me as Garett can easily scale most things then be completely unable climb or jump others that seem remedial in comparison. Perhaps if there was more of an assassins agenda going on in the game this could have been a reality for the game but ultimately it comes off as laziness or lowered expectations for the game. Fortunately, it doesn’t ruin the game but would have given it that additional dimension that could have made it a triple A title or worthy of a higher RRP. That said, I think the game is worth the money and is a good bang for the buck.
I recommend this game if you get a kick out of sneaking around, outwitting your opponents and solving puzzles to progress the story. The story it’s self-unravels as you play through the game and combined with the incentive of stealing some fancy pants items, well makes the game worth playing. If you are looking for more of a brawling experience though, I cannot recommend it, you will be sorely disappointed and likely frustrated that your kick♥♥♥♥♥reflexes and ability to strike multiple keys in quick succession will do you no good here. On top of requiring a decent spec machine this game will also require patience, attention to detail i.e. don’t knock over cups, tread on broken glass etc and an appreciation for stealth & thievery.
So far, I can’t really knock the game given what I spent on it. It has been worth every dollar and I’m sure it will continue to be so while I uncover more loot and more story.

After I have experienced SO much about Maplestory, from playing it since 9 years ago plus on various private servers, I think it is time to hit delete key and post a caveat for curious 12-year-old like you to see. This game does not hurt if you play with some friends. Honestly, being playing with friends is the only good way to play this game since they serve as a reminder that you still have a real life. Without such link to the reality, it is too easy to be sucked into the scheme of Maplestory that is deliberately, fundamentally created to exhaust both your mind and wallet
Because remember: the philosophy of any MMORPG is to encourage competition between players strictly on the level of vanity and facile values, being how beautiful you look, how much money you have, how high damage can you hit...... Especially when you are lonely in the game, this emotion is easily ellicited because the game encourages so in any aspect. But the trick is, we all understand there is no ending to beautiful cash shop items and the amount of currency you possess, why can't we/I keep from not coming back to torture ourselves in the grinding and trading that ultimately lead to no real satisfaction?
Because those game developers(e.g. Nexon) understand how pleasure works in us. What human desires is not a specific, final object, but a differential value through a growing experience. That is to say, pleasure is only gained through change; and after you arrive at a threshold, being it posed by the game or your brain, you are only left with emptiness. And this is when you want to start the loop again, again, and again. This is precisely why we only want to make MORE money, why we want to spend MORE cash items, and get MORE levels/damage without it ending at a specific number. This is why Nexon created so many new types of characters and jobs: they want to give you the pseudo-novel feeling each time you restart the experience, while in fact, nothing has changed about how your pleasure works. It's an everlasting loop.
So instead of clicking the "Play Game" button. Why not think about something more valuable in your life? Whether or not you are willing to participate in this collective subconscious hell of pleasure looping is your own choice. If you really want to play, play it with friends. I am lonely, I don't have friends. Since I understand all these, I decide to quit.

As someone who has spent 2k+ hours on this game, I can honestly say I can't recommend the game...not anymore. While the progression of the game is amazing, the characters and skillsets they possess beautiful, its when it truly matters that everything you work for seems to just become useless, obselete, and you get thrown to the side like trash.
When you reach the endgame, and reach the grinds and raids it comes with it, THAT is when the game goes downhill. Most raid groups seek only the strongest geared characters, those who possess full sets of Epic tier equipment and accessories to be their comrades in the battle against some of the most intense boss fights devised by team Neople.
Seems ok, as item levels are important in any raid based mmos. The problem, then, becomes the acquisition of said gear. Grind for Epic Sets is HELL (haha, hell party farm.) With a mobile-gacha-game-tier probablity of drops, it becomes neigh impossible to get entire sets in a reasonable amount of time (compared to other mmos). Couple this with a entry fee to enter hell mode, and you have a recipe for brain anuerysms.
You can't even get into said raid parties if your equipment is one tier lower, the legendary tier (that is, unless you are a supporting class, and even then, most just ditch you to find a better geared support unless your gear is +12).
All in all, the grind just feels like chinese gold farm level, and I can't enjoy myself as I watch my teammates melt boss' health with sparkling gold gear, all the while I sit on the sidelines occasionally buffing and debuffing. It just feels like the challenge of the game becomes how long will it take to get my Epic set, and will I rage quit before I do (in my case, I ragequit.)

---I will change my review for this game if an update changes things.---
Lengthy introduction...
In an otome game, the interest is in the storyline and the writing. The writing is well done (while not the best) and the storyline is interesting; the poor translations and errors in the game are not appreciated. I regret paying $30 for this game.
Overall if you are someone who is able to ignore grammatical errors and just general porting mishaps...while still paying thirty dollars (USD) for it; you will be able to play this game. The characters are pretty stereotypical for an otome...you have the arrogant a-hole, the foreigner guy, tsundere, and even mysterious boss...so you aren't going to be disappointed. There's a character for everyone and the heroine is pretty "heroine-like"; she is very idiotic and pure. Also a virgin.
I would have given this game a thumbs up if there was only one detraction. However, there are many. I have found various errors in a single route (Kagerou) and I am disappointed. The poor English translation really detracts from the work as it gives me the vibe of a young child doing the editing. (Actually, if I had to be honest, I think a small child might be able to do a little better.) I understand this may not be the fault of the editors if they are not native English speakers, but if Dogenzaka Lab expects an audience to purchase a $30 game, it better be in tip top shape.
So far what I've found is...(for grammar/bugs)
- Several homophones are found throughout the story; however the translators chose to use the incorrect word. It is "waste of time" not "waist of time".
- In chapter 8, Kagerou's name changes from English to Japanese characters...when he says '...!' Even though that is a minor error, it shows how this game was not carefully looked over before ported.
In general...
- The characters aren't really unique, like I said. When you're in a red-light district, you'd expect a little spice in your boys...not your "Ouran High School Host Club" gone bad kind of deal.
- "Screen change" is terrible. It doesn't even let me full screen properly and everything becomes pixelated.
- I have discovered, through intensive Googling, there is a voice-acted version from the PS Vita. Why not port that instead, instead of the sh♥tty mobile version?
On the bright side, I really like the way you can just play through the prologue once, and not suffer through it in games like Amnesia. Unfortunately I can't accept all of these faults and just "f♥ck it" while giving a thumbs up. I would like the game to be re-ported or at least updated to match the price the audience pays. This is worth more like $10 over $30 at this quality. I've probably ranted too long, so I'm just going to end this here.  A solid 4/10. It could be a 6-7/10.

If you are new to civ beyond earth but played civ 5 then my advice is to
Use Social Policies Differently
as in pick and choose do not go down one singular path. the number of trees is reduced to the equivalents of honor, tradition/liberty, aesthetics/rationalism and then an extra tree for production mixed with commerce.
Treat affinities as ideologies/religion
stick with one (unless using rising tide due to mixed affinities) it is a levelling up system unlike anything seen in civ 5, istead of using culture you need to complete quests and reaserch to gain points. this gives you benefits such as:
Harmony-benefits from the planet and alien units.
Purity-anti alien benefits and tank like armour units.
Supremacy-human/cyborg augmentation and mech/walker units.
Do not treat aliens as barbarians
if you stay away from them they will not go straight for your cities like in civ 5, but if you do go straight out an attack them throughout the game, go purity or expect to fail at first, it will be like in a civ game but the barbarians only attack your civ.
Pay attention to quests
being able to compete early game quests can give a significant advantage to almost anything.
Build wonders
make sure if you are building wonders, this can provide massive bonuses like the stellar codex, gives you tons of sattelite coverage so you can put some planet carvers next to your neigbors capitol tis is just one of the many amazing wonders

This is another game that makes me wish Steam had a middle option instead of just thumbs up or down. At its core, and i mean it's very basic core, it's a perfect way to play magic. It's everything else that make it bad. I really honestly believe you dont earn tokens fast enough to buy booster packs. So not only are you at a disadvantage from the start with meanial somewhat useless cards, but if you really want to get a boost in your colection and actually be able to compete against other players, your going to have to throw some cash at this. Now for $10 you can get 1200 tokens(coins/ingamecurrency) out of which you can get 8 booster packs. 6 cards per pack thats 48 cards. Problem is, the likelyhood of you getting enough of the same cards to use in a deck is slim to none. There is no player trading so your again, stuck using a near useless deck with near useless cards either playing the AI for a smaller token award if you win, or taking your chances against another player. Ive opted to spend about $30 to see how well i could farm cards with cash. Ive yet to pull a set of 3 cards that are the same to use in any type of deck. Now im sure with another investment of $30 or $50 I could definately cet a set to use, but frankly who wants to spend $80 for an online game when you can go to the local comic stole and spend the same to take the cards home with you.
Not to mention no chat during games which is not a big deal to me but to some it could be. Again NO PLAYER TRADING.....kinda lame and screams "We dont want you to trade because we want you to get your cards through the cash store." and also kinda defeats the heart of MTG in the first place.
So thumbs down for me. Its fun to play if your patient and dont mind grinding games with lame decks to earn coins for more packs, but please, dont give these people your money. It wont do you much good and they will simply laugh all the way to the bank.

Starseed Pilgrim is the kind of game where I can't give it a negative review, because it means I don't, "get it," and at the same time, I can't give it a positive review, because its author(s) were so pre-occupied tripping over itself in attempts to be thought-provoking, they seem to have forgotten to include... content. There's symbolism and artistic metaphor, but they're so vague and caved-in under so much repeatition that few, if any, players can actually give them even a minimal identity. There's straightforward gameplay with puzzles to be solved and rewards to be had, but the biggest puzzle is solved the instant the player has planted a seed of each color for the first time and collected a key. The rewards for success are nebulous and consist mostly of being faced with the same puzzle again, while the penalty for failure is also being faced with the same puzzle again. It's essentially entertainment for art-game snobs, who want a reason to laugh at the riff-raff that don't appreciate it the "right" way, and for defeatists who are only comfortable playing in a world where all their actions are doomed to begin with. Certainly, people other than the above mentioned types can enjoy Starseed Pilgrim, but the intentional kind of enjoyment this game produces isn't about trial and error puzzle-play (like House of Dead Ninjas), exploration of a metaphor-strewn environment (like The Path), or even some combination of the two (such as Limbo). Basically, this goes into the same category as "Vinnie Vole's Existentialist Nightmare."

As a fan of games like Toss the Turtle, a "see how far you can get and slowly build up upgrades" kind of game on Steam seemed right up my alley. Unfortunately, Beyond Gravity was not that game.
I guess I'll start with the good points. The art and sound assets are nice, and the port is competent, if bare-bones. The goals the game gives you are also a nice change of pace, giving you something to look forward to beyond just playing the game. The game is also extremely cheap, only a dollar on sale at the moment. Unfortunately, that's about all the nice things I can say about this game.
The gameplay is fun at first, but then you quickly realize that not only is there very little variety, the upgrade curve is all wrong. You can keep going and going and going, but it really doesn't provide you any benefit unless you manage to perfectly hit each and every screw to get the multiplier going up. In fact, several of the goals incentivize you to simply jump into the void at the very start of the game over and over again simply to get the deaths required to unlock the next one. And if you want to build that multiplier up, you're probably going to need to pick up some upgrades, which are frankly hideously expensive at the start. It should be the other way around: give you cheaper upgrades at the beginning to give you a feeling of progress as you move through through the unlock system. Instead, you'll be grinding out screws over and over and over again before you even get one. In about two hours of play, I unlocked two things. It's almost like it was built to sell in-app purchases in a mobile game. There are no such purchases, either on Steam or in the mobile version, which makes it only more bizarre.
Hard-to-acquire upgrades and little variety in gameplay make this hard to recommend. At a dollar I'd say you're right about getting your money's worth. The game has a fair amount of visual polish, but it's a shame there's not so much game behind it to encourage you to keep playing.

Within the Skills & Inventory screen, if you go through each of the available Skills one at a time, then click on each of the "EVENTs" listed for them, it brings up the chosen event on the left hand side pane.  Many of these events are buggy however and the actual event that shows up on the left, does not match the name of the event you clicked on on the event list.

These bugs make the game frustrating and make various paths through the game impossible because you are unable to advance certain skills properly because the events to do so bring up the wrong actual event, so you do not gain the correct skill points.

Before playing this game, I listened to the audio version of the Redshirts novel by John Scalzi in case there was a connection between the two.  As it turned out, they aren't related, but both have the same trope-filled sci-fi spoofery and misanthropic humor. And the book is a fun listen, anyway.
I'm noob to social media and Redshirt is basically a Facebook simulator, so there was a bit of a learning curve for me. Once I got past that, I became quite addicted. It's fun to broaden one's network on the space station, set up social events, apply for higher-paying jobs, keep a romance going, and try to reach a successful ending.
The game often feels like a grind when you arrange the same social events again and again to make your stats increase. Also, Spacebook friends sometimes act so capriciously that there is no way to win with them (like real-life Facebook friends I suppose). For example, you might arrange for a social outing but not invite a particular person because he's busy. Then you're told that he got a little upset about not being invited, even though he wouldn't have been able to come. But if you had invited him, you would have lost happiness points since he would have turned down the invitation.
The game is enlivened by witty flavor text, animations, and good music. It's pretty well made but there are occasional bugs. At one point, the game was completely stuck because some flavor text wouldn't appear; I had to terminate the program and reload the save until this problem resolved itself.
Redshirt asks what if online social networking really does end up running our lives.  It observes how social networking makes relationships broader but shallower, communication easier yet less effective. It reminds me of some of the work that Christine Love has done.

Crime Secrets: Crimson Lily is an exceptionally good hidden object adventure game made by One More Level and is very similar to the 9 Clues series (the developers might be the same just working under a different name) where the player has to investigate crime scenes and gather clues to figure out solve a serial murder case. I'm quite surprised by the mixed ratings the game has currently, since the quality of the plot exceeds other HOGs and its serious tone (several people get killed) is quite uncommon in the genre.
When the usual female detective (the protagonist in most Artifex Mundi games) goes on a vacation to a beautiful snowy mountain resort to relax, she suffers a car accident. By following the police officer, who was also present at the crash and reaching the hotel eventually, she must use all her wits (and sixth sense) to track down a serial killer and uncover a case, in which many of the locals seem to be involved.
The game's unique feature is the segments where we have to search for clues at the crime scene and arrange them in chronological order to reconstruct an event (a murder most of the time), that happened there. It then replays before our eyes and helps us locating another clue, evidence or useful item, that'll get us one step closer to finding out the identity of the murderer (there'll be a twist, even if we have suspicions about who he is).
There's a variety of puzzles providing enough challenge and the hidden object scenes aren't overused (which is a good thing). The charm of the game lies in its story and the wonderful scenery it takes place in: the beautiful snow-covered mountain landscape, the vivid coloured interior of the antique hotel are all great to look at. The chilly wind blowing improves the already perfect atmosphere further. The attention to the little details is also something to be appraised: we find little notes and photos, recordings that link the participants together and our diary proves to be handy (besides being interesting to read) as well. There are collectibles in the form of snowflakes and origamis that can be fairly easy to miss, so keep your eyes peeled.
As for problems I could mention some strange/illogical item uses (the occasion for example where we have to use a shovel to pull something off a shelf, or cut a pillow open to burn the stuffing) plus the strange appearance of angel statues made of ice and traps towards the ending. I also encountered a description error where a hula dancer doll's flower necklace was wrongfully described as a 'fishing rod' (I did have to use it as a fishing rod though, so as a hint it was pretty good ;))
As mentioned before I was completely satisfied with the graphical presentation: it is as beautiful as a HOG should be with excellent scenery. I really liked the artwork, it has a classic stylized feel about it, at the expense of realism a bit. The suspenseful music and the superb environmental sounds with the wind blowing and wolf howling (yes there are wolves as well) are truly impressive. The voice actress, Amy Robinson did a very good job providing her voice to our detective.
I was absolutely fascinated with Crime Secrets: Crimson Lily and I would recommend it to everyone, even to players who normlly don't play casual adventure games. The story and the wonderful landscape both make it a memorable, outstanding (for me, one of the best) example of its genre. It is one of those rare HOGs which I'd definitely play through again in time.
PROS
+ amazing, atmospheric locations
+ exciting plot with twists
+ crime scene investigation and reconstruction
+ a good variety of puzzles
+ great sound effects, voiceover and music
CONS
- some illogical item uses
- a bit surreal towards the end (ice angels?)
RATING
8.5/10

A really amateur barebones sidescrolling shooter that you would expect to find on a 2006 flash game site for free.
You move left over a panoramic image while occasionally shooting at some creatures. You do this until you inevitably get chomped in half by a creature that will spawn under you before you have enough time to kill it.
There are no other movement options besides walking left or right, creating a very uninteresting playing field. Enemies spawn on both sides of you, eventually forcing you into an inescapable sandwich that will kill you in a matter of seconds. Of course, that's assuming you make it past the first minute without getting one-shotted by the lanky monochrome zombies.
There's a "challenge mode" as well where you pick from 5 different challenges that start you with weapon/equipment presets, but nothing changes. You still shoot at some plain creatures with a plain background with plain weaponry.
Some of the weapon and character sprites are done decently for being created in what looks like MS Paint, but other than that, there is not much to look at.
As for the soundtrack, you have a lyrical rock track or an instrumental industrial track. Both of them achieve the "2006 flash game" theme very well.
Unless you want to spend money on something you'll regret sooner or later, there is no reason to buy this.

Crime Secrets: Crimson Lily is a Hidden Object Game where you play a detective who stumbles upon a murder spree in a remote hotel.
The visuals are above average, and the story is interesting enough to keep playing. There is a diary I never once looked at, a map that I also didn't need to use. There's almost no backtracking and for a HOG, there are very few HO scenes. The puzzles are on the easy side and the voice acting is terrible.
There are couple of different mechanics such as analysing a scene and trying to piece together what happened. There are also a couple of blue light scenes where you try to find clues, but they are used very little and most of the game plays out like a standard run of the mill HOG.
For it's time, Crime Secrets: Crimson Lily would have been very good, but it's starting to show it's age, and there are better games out there. If you enjoy HOGs and want to kill time with an easy one, then Crime Secrets: Crimson Lily isn't hard and will keep you entertained.

My experience with the Dragon Quest Heroes
----------Positives----------
Well, for starters, I really had my doubts about purchasing this on Steam. Since it could've turn out to be yet another clunky PC port like many others we got throughout the years, I wasnt so sure whether to buy it for ps4 or PC. In the end, I got encouraged by the holy refund option Lord Gaben has provided us, so I decided to buy it from Steam. I'm glad and relieved to say; WE GOT A VERY GOOD PERFORMER PC PORT HERE! Maybe some AA issues but nothing that your gfx control panel cant handle, pop that FXAA from nvidia/amd control panel and enjoy the smoothness.
My second biggest doubt was its being a musou game. I really dont like musou games, although, a musou infused action rpg game within the Dragon Quest universe? That didnt sound bad at all so it managed to pique my interest, and im quite glad it did, because game is great so far.
Combat is fluid, intense (maybe a little bit too easy at the beginning but im sure it'll pick up the pace as I make my way further into the game), monster summoning is a nice touch and adds a small strategic depth to the game, plenty of characters to play with to catch the spirit of musou genre and its done successfuly, story and dialogues are fun and lil bit of cheesy just like they're supposed to be in a spinoff title. And I dont even feel much of a need for talking about the amazing art style the game has; still the beloved Dragon Quest concept, yet its redefined with Pixarish cartoon lines, just perfect. Soundtracks are also pretty sweet to listen and has the classic Dragon Quest tunes to them.
----------Negatives----------
Although, there are some down sides. They tried to sprinkle some rpg elements here and there, but it feels quite half *ssed! Like character development for example. At the beginning of the game, you get few level ups by playin the prologue. When you hit the camp, you distribute the skill points, unlock few of the unlockable active skills, and thats that. All the other unlockable skills are just some minor passive effects and stats, which are almost the same with every single playable character, and doesnt really add much of a change to the characters.
Also the game's UI is so frigging big! I mean, if we werent gonna get higher resolution than 1080p (yes max res is 1080p) developers could've included some UI Scaling option. I sure as hell dont like a minimap which takes 3/10 of my whole screen.
There's also an issue of, how do I put it, trying way too hard for being old school. Like certain menus, for example the side quest panel; grabbing quests shouldnt take this long. We didnt need to hear 5 seconds of music after accepting every single quest and you cant even skip this! Same with the event dialogues, camera focuses a certain event, characters talk about that event -all is good so far-, but why am I not allowed to skip these dialogues after I finish reading them!? Why in the hell you make me for like 10 seconds for each dialogue to disappear, which takes almost around a half minute in certain cases when more than few characters decided to talk. There are many other annoyances like these, every single interface activity takes way too long and feels clunky with forced, non skippable dialogue windows and lame♥♥♥♥♥jingles.
And finally,there's also the problem of pre-order bonus DLCs. By the time I wrote this review, we didnt had the promised slime edition dlcs, they added them one and a half day after the release, and those slime weapons are just starter weapons. So anyone who pre-ordered the game was already way too past the starting point, therefore couldnt use those dlc weapons. Yeah, false marketing at its best here, almost feels like a scam.
I did hope in this case, that the developers would make these weapons to adjust to your characters' levels when you grab them from mailbox,  since that was the only way to make up for this false marketing, but that didnt happen either.
There are also no badge crafting and steam trading cards for you collectors as well, and this might be a downside for some.
----------Conclusion----------
All and all tho, im quite happy with the Dragon Quest Heroes. Game's addictive formula really makes up for it's downsides. If you are an old fan of the series, lots of beloved characters will make you feel nostalgic and you will love this complete new touch both the gameplay wise and concept wise. If you are a newcomer to the series, you'll still enjoy a good ARPG and will be making your entry to one of the most beloved jrpg series. So, a win for everyone. Great buy, great port,great fun.
----------SCORE: 8,5/10----------

--Initial look/Hype--
I have always been a big fan over the civilisation series, all the way from the original on the Commodore 64 to Civ 5(which is currently my favorite in the series). So when i heard that a new game taking place after Civ 5 with influences from Alpha centuri was about to come out, i was understandably excited.
--Graphics--
It's basically what you would expect from a Civ style top down strategy, the graphics would be the same, if not better than the last. Unfortunately this was not the case, they obviously took the time to put some detail into the animation of the units and aliens but the finish was more reminiscent of Civ 4.
With the small file size of the game and the lackluster graphics, it still managed pushed my duel graphics card and CPU to the max. So much in fact that the game was lagging heavily and i could not figure out why.
--In game world--
The world kept true to it's promise, a Civ game on another plannet. If you choose to create a game instead of doing a quick start, you can choose the plannet, your sponsors, factions and colony type.
--Game-play/Controls--
Again fairly standard and what you would expect from a Civ game, point click interface in a turn based setup. The strength of units also felt unbalanced but not nearly as much as the city progression did.
I found the tech tree and culture tree to be a little too involved and complicated. So far as to not have a great progression of tech, instead it was haphazard and some tech seemed to be in the incorrect category, all of this made it abit hard to try and plan out the colonies progression.
--Story--
I'm not going to rate this, the Civ games have never had a story beyond you start with nothing and build up to something.
--Overall--
Again being a huge fan of the series, I was greatly disappointed. Badly rendered graphics, maxes out hardware for no reason and an expansion that just adds more crap to the game without really fixing any of the problems.
If you want to play a great strategy, play Civ 5, don't waste your money on a rushed and in my opinion, unfinished game. This will be the first time I have ever requested a refund from steam.

This is a devious little puzzle game.  You are trapped and must find your way home.  But to do so, you must plant and harvest seeds to grow different types of paths.  And if that isn't tricky enough, you must also collect keys to open doors when the world inverts, shifting from light and color to dark and filled with stars.
The clues to what you need to do are subtle.  So subtle that some people might not get them at first.  They appear as poems written on the walls of the level.  But even without the poems, the longer you play the more you figure out.
There are two types of seeds that are very important.  Pink seeds grow pink paths and when you harvest the pink blocks, you gain more seeds to grow more paths.  However, the pink seeds grow very slowly.  Green grass seeds sprout areas that have hearts in them.  When the world inverts those hearts will turn into stars, which you can harvest to use for seeds back in the main world.  Each type of seed creates a different type of path with different properties.
Getting to the first two levels is easy.  The third level requires collecting three keys and going through a door locked by three keys - which aren't all that easy to find.
The music is interesting, as each seed grows with a different tune, making for changing sounds throughout the game.
If you like devious spacial-awareness puzzles, I recommend spending time to try to figure this one out.

This is an absolutely incredible, touching game. I'd honestly tag it as horror, and here's why -
because when you play it, you won't have fun. It's not meant to be fun. It's meant to be realistic, and that's exactly what it is.
I remember looting one place out of desperation, only to realize that an elderly couple lived there. My actions indirectly caused their deaths. There were many times when I'd witness something absolutely awful, but I couldn't step in and make things better. Doing so would, without a doubt, get me killed. Playing this, I was insignificant. Just some ordinary, unnotable noone who was trying to survive.
This game will ♥♥♥♥ with your feelings. This game will leave you haunted by your actions - both what you did and did not do. There are no heroes. The game is, in more than one sense of the word hillarious. In this game you are one of the countless "Red-Shirts", that were often used as - alien trap discharge - units in the TOS and TNG Series. Work yourself up, from the security standard issue "Mop the Warp Conduits" - Worker up to high levels of social ranks on a large spaceship on a long term tour.
Oh, and don't forget the merrits of programming the replicators with 999 cat-food recipes, or learning how to use alien melee weaponry as meditative art form. Yes, the game is funny, it has a strong connection to Star Trek, and some other space opera. But I am quite torn if I should give the game a recommendation at all. To a hardcore, blood and grit Science Fiction fan the game can be an outright insult.
Acutally sometimes the game reminds me in one way or another of a "How to die a gruesome death in an entertaining way"-Simulator... Because of the god damn title... not because it is one... and I am always reminded on the "Redshirt Blues"... and some other rather derogative terms used to describe the actual use of sacrificial lambs in modern media.
Yeah, the game is funny - but it's also getting quite boring after a while, and you always think, "Ok, it's in my library now, but I don't have the nerve playing it at the moment..." and you will find at last a dozen of reasons why to let it rot like a lead duck in a swampy pond... mostly because it is as entertaining as the same duck down there.
The game has it's humorous silver linings - but there is too much low humor in the game to make it really a worthwhile addition to any collection. The price is too high for a casual game that might give you only a limited time of fun, and the time of wearing it out can come very, very suddenly... Oh, and yeah, it has also some dating sim qualities... which - well, darn it - I think I dive for the lead duck, it's more fun!

My Claim: Redshirt is quite possibly the best "Real Life Simulator" ever concieved.  Move over "The Sims," because this game gets it right.  This is how the real, modern world works so pay attention!
Careers: No one cares about your skills, you education, or your talents.  No one is going to read your resumé or give two farts about what you studied in college.  All your potential bosses are ever going to do is immediately look you up on Facebook and look at your profile.  Do you share thier hobbies?  Their political views?  Dress the way they approve of?  Most importantly, do you know someone that they do?  Because these are things that decide if you get hired, fired, promoted or passed over.
Relationships: Are you handsome?  Beautiful?  Rich?  Smart?  Athletic?  No one gives a crap.  Your Facebook page is your relationship application form.  How many friends do you have?  Do you follow the latest trends?  Do you watch the right shows, listen to the right music, misquote the right famous people?  Do you effect an air of false depth by shamelessly cutting & pasting mopey song lyrics without any semblence of context?  Ohmygosh, you are, like, so
, then!  Relationship request accepted.
Finance: In the future no one will ever truly own anything ever again.  The future is all subscription based, where "ownership" simply means that you'll be paying weekly and monthly upkeep fees on stuff until the sun burns out and the Universe freezes over.  Well guess what, kids?  The Future is Now!  Watch as every week your pitiful paycheck is immediately consumed just trying to keep the garbage that you bought four months ago from breaking down for another few days!  Get sucked into the competetive ego drive that is created by your lame, shallow friends constantly braggging about
personal treasure troves.  Piddle away your financial future on a pointless treadmill just to keep up with everyone else in a vain quest for popularity.
Life: In the end whether you succede or fail, prosper or rot in misery, literally live or die all boils down to your dedication to sacrifice all your personal goals & aspirations upon the blood soaked altar of ephemeral on-line popularity.  Your own thoughts, opinions, ideals and very personality shall all be slowly morphed over time to match that of those that you need to suck up to and impress in order to get ahead.
Summary: If ever there was a game that perfectly, unabashedly and honestly summed up this shallow, sick, cruel, twisted world we live in today... it is Redshirt.  No other game is so forthright about telling it like it is.  It's not what you know, it's who you know.  It's not what you think, it's what your boss thinks.  Relationships are just lateral career maneuvers.  Friends are just rungs on a ladder, aquired when above you and discarded once below.  I highly recomend buying this game (along with the complete DVD set of Geroge Carlin) to every naive, gullible middle-school student in America.  Because it's never too soon to start sharpening the knives.

It is amazing how a 12 year old game can hold up for this long.
For many including myself. Chaos Theory has been the defining chapter in this franchise. The one that all other chapters are compaired to. For me, Chaos Theory improved upon the concept from the first two titles and made a defining atmosphere in which we the player actually feel like a super spy when we play. Much like Theif and Metal Gear and how those franchises defined the genre, Chaos Theory added new elements that would help define future stealth gameplay.
I think the reason why so many hold this title to be the best Splinter Cell is because it was followed by Double Agent which forked off into a more casual style of stealth. Which continued further up the line with Conviction. Blacklist, while still holding the causal aspect introduced with Double Agent. Did try to re-focus on the core of the franchise and what made it great.
I remeber getting the demo disk in an issue of Xbox Magazine which consisted of the Lighthouse mission. I was so captivated by it that by the time the game actually released. I had played that mission hundreds of times. What really made this game for me though was the introduction of co-op. Something that I had always wanted to do in Splinter Cell.
I enjoyed Chaos Theory so much that it was a staple in LAN parties with my group for several years.
I bought this on Steam a few years ago and never got around to playing it. Having just recently garnered an interest in going back and playing all the old titles, I remembered that I had this in my library. While the game itself is 12 years old, I do like how it looks on PC. It's no Witcher 3, but for a 2005 title. It looks damn good in my opinion.
Controls took some getting used to for me. I was so used to playing this game on a controller that it felt alien for me to play on mouse & keyboard. But I quickly got comfortable after 30 or so minutes. The story is the only thing that I feel to be dated. It's no masterpeice but it gets the job done in getting you hooked. Then again, the story wasn't really Chaos Theory's main driving point either in what made it popular.
So far I have been enjoying it. That rush of nostalgia that I get with every favorable spot and event puts a smile on my face. The gameplay is something that I wish the following titles kept. I hope the next instalment goes back to the franchise's roots and brings back the Splinter Cell we all know and love.
I highly recommend this game for anyone looking to get a feel on what Splinter Cell has been about. What once was a defining title in the stealth genre. It still looks, sounds, plays, and feels like a fun and enjoyable game even after all these years. It also has a good degree of difficulty if you want to achieve 100% Ghost statistics on the missions. So it will offer a nice challenge too if that's what you're looking for.
You are also still able to play the co-op and Spy vs Merc MP by using Hamachi or Tunggle. So that's a plus as well.

When I first saw this game, I thought it had a unique take on the “Bullet Hell” genre and I couldn’t wait to play it. However, after playing it, it felt rushed and unfinished and here’s why:
Pros:
♦ Sound/Music you can use is decent enough (It fits the genre well enough)
♦ Graphics are great for the time, art-style and genre of the game (I say this as the game was released in 2010 and the graphics, even though they are not spectacular seem to fit the time the game was released and the art-style the Devs were seemingly going for. Even though they are not eyegasmic or spectacular, they are still decent enough for what the game is)
♦ Unique take on the "Bullet Hell" genre (This is great as it isn't just another "Bullet Hell" game. However, it is unique, it could've been executed better)
♦ Fun whilst it lasts (The game seems to only be fun whilst the unique concept lasts)
Cons:
♦ Opening Cinematic looks more decent than the actual game (This says a lot for the game and if the game looked and played like the opening cinematic I’d thumbs it up in no time)
♦ The unique concept of the game was executed poorly (I say this even though I said it had a Unique take on the "Bullet Hell" genre in the pros section, the game seems as though it was rushed in more ways than one and that the Devs could have spent a little more time perfecting the uniqueness of their concept they added to the "Bullet Hell" genre to make the overall game better)
♦ Difficulty goes from “None” to “Hard” (This is annoying as it starts on "None" then immediately goes to "Hard", "Harder", "Hardest" etc. Not sure why it doesn't start on easy)
♦ No Tutorial (This is annoying as when I first started I had no idea what I was collecting, shooting or how to play, little own what the controls did)
♦ Free Play mode difficulty selection glitch (This is weird as when you go to select a difficulty the line goes under multiple difficulties and you can even select a difficulty where there is no text telling you what difficulty it is. This is bad as you have no idea what difficulty you are selecting)
♦ Game feels rushed due to multiple typos (This is terrible as every game should have zero typos. Typos such as get's instead of gets, resuem instead of resume and genera instead of genre etc)
♦ Hard to know which control each weapon corresponds to (This is annoying as you'd think your Z, the one you can spam, would be your main weapon but apparently it's not. Therefore, setting up your character/weapons for the first few times is immensely confusing)
♦ No in-game options menu (This is terrible as you can't seemingly change resolution, sound, graphics etc)
♦ "Music Room" option on "Main" Menu is pointless (This is because if you select a song from the "Music Room" you can't use it on any menu or even in-game. This makes it pointless)
♦ Movement controls seem a weird concept (To me personally when you are trying to dodge/shoot things, having to zoom in and out with multiple buttons on the keyboard seems way annoying and ruins some of the game for me as it's hard to move and zoom at the same time. This means if you are zooming in to dodge something from behind you, you are most likely still going to hit something in front of you)
♦ Auto Aim (Depending on the weapon, it tends to auto aim. For example, if you have "Bullet" selected for the "Cannon" then you can hold "Z" and just auto fire killing everything because it auto aims and has no ammo. This makes the game way too easy and way less fun)
♦ No way to tell when you're nearing a boss, about to kill a boss or nearing the end of a level (This is annoying as there is no indicator and things seem to just come out of nowhere at random times)
♦ Hiscores don't register unless you win the game (This is weird as I'd expect when you die for your score if it's higher than a score on the score board to register it)
♦ The hiscores have random scores in them even though I haven't registered any (This is weird as there is a random number in the "Hardest" HighScores column and no numbers in any of the other difficulties columns)
♦ Controls can't be changed beyond the two pre-sets (This is annoying for those who want to change controls for whatever reason)
♦ Pricey (For the price there are better "Bullet Hell" games you could pick up for free or even cheaper on Steam)
♦ Hitbox seems a bit off at times (I find this is the case because sometimes when you think you're not going to get hit you get hit and when you think you're going to get hit you don't)
♦ Repetitive (Seemingly the only difference between each playthrough is the difficulty which only increases/changes the number of things spawned in that you must shoot and dodge and doesn't change much else. This means each playthrough will virtually be the same each time with a slightly increased number of enemies and harder boss. Also, level variants don't seem to be unique or change much from the previous level, only the bosses seemingly change between levels)
♦ Clicking the “X” in windowed mode on Windows doesn’t close the game, you must scroll down to exit on the main menu to close the game (This is annoying as you should be able to close the game whenever you want by clicking the “X” in windowed mode)
♦ No Steam Trading Cards or Achievements (This gives you no incentive to keep playing beyond beating the game once)
Overall, even though the game had a unique take on the “Bullet-Hell” genre, there are way too many cons than pros to even considering recommending this. Also, I can’t recommend buying a game when it has obvious typos, is rushed and when its price is higher than other better “Bullet-Hell” games.

Crime Secrets: Crimson Lily is an exceptionally good hidden object adventure game made by One More Level and is very similar to the 9 Clues series (the developers might be the same just working under a different name) where the player has to investigate crime scenes and gather clues to figure out solve a serial murder case. I'm quite surprised by the mixed ratings the game has currently, since the quality of the plot exceeds other HOGs and its serious tone (several people get killed) is quite uncommon in the genre.
When the usual female detective (the protagonist in most Artifex Mundi games) goes on a vacation to a beautiful snowy mountain resort to relax, she suffers a car accident. By following the police officer, who was also present at the crash and reaching the hotel eventually, she must use all her wits (and sixth sense) to track down a serial killer and uncover a case, in which many of the locals seem to be involved.
The game's unique feature is the segments where we have to search for clues at the crime scene and arrange them in chronological order to reconstruct an event (a murder most of the time), that happened there. It then replays before our eyes and helps us locating another clue, evidence or useful item, that'll get us one step closer to finding out the identity of the murderer (there'll be a twist, even if we have suspicions about who he is).
There's a variety of puzzles providing enough challenge and the hidden object scenes aren't overused (which is a good thing). The charm of the game lies in its story and the wonderful scenery it takes place in: the beautiful snow-covered mountain landscape, the vivid coloured interior of the antique hotel are all great to look at. The chilly wind blowing improves the already perfect atmosphere further. The attention to the little details is also something to be appraised: we find little notes and photos, recordings that link the participants together and our diary proves to be handy (besides being interesting to read) as well. There are collectibles in the form of snowflakes and origamis that can be fairly easy to miss, so keep your eyes peeled.
As for problems I could mention some strange/illogical item uses (the occasion for example where we have to use a shovel to pull something off a shelf, or cut a pillow open to burn the stuffing) plus the strange appearance of angel statues made of ice and traps towards the ending. I also encountered a description error where a hula dancer doll's flower necklace was wrongfully described as a 'fishing rod' (I did have to use it as a fishing rod though, so as a hint it was pretty good ;))
As mentioned before I was completely satisfied with the graphical presentation: it is as beautiful as a HOG should be with excellent scenery. I really liked the artwork, it has a classic stylized feel about it, at the expense of realism a bit. The suspenseful music and the superb environmental sounds with the wind blowing and wolf howling (yes there are wolves as well) are truly impressive. The voice actress, Amy Robinson did a very good job providing her voice to our detective.
I was absolutely fascinated with Crime Secrets: Crimson Lily and I would recommend it to everyone, even to players who normally don't play casual adventure games. The story and the wonderful landscape both make it a memorable, outstanding (for me, one of the best) example of its genre. It is one of those rare HOGs which I'd definitely play through again in time.
PROS
+ amazing, atmospheric locations
+ exciting plot with twists
+ crime scene investigation and reconstruction
+ a good variety of puzzles
+ great sound effects, voiceover and music
CONS
- some illogical item uses
- a bit surreal towards the end (ice angels?)
RATING
8.5/10

Access the options via the 'More' button on the main menu.  Options include separate sliders for Music, Sound and Voice overs, plus Custom Cursor, Full-screen and HD Mode.
There are four difficulties to choose from: Casual, Advanced, Expert and Custom, plus we have a jump-to MAP and a totally useless diary.
Let me say right off the bat to keep an eye out for snowflakes and origami.  They're easy to miss, and - as there is very little backtracking - if you progress too far, you won't be able to go back for them!
The gameplay is more adventure-lite than anything else.  There are hidden object scenes, but not a lot of them. Some scenes are recycled, but the second time you visit them, you'll be looking for items via picture - Fragmented Object-style - rather than having a written list.
There is minimal light interaction on most of the HOS... Things like lighting a candle or putting batteries in something before you can select them.  If you prefer not to do the scenes at all (or if you're stuck and don't want to use a hint), you can switch to a
mini-game instead.
There is a second kind of "hidden object scene" where you are searching for clues to figure out what happened in an area.  There are nine clues to find, each of which is listed below, only the writing is covered in snow... You won't be able to see what the listed clues are until you find them.  It's definitely different and it's also not as difficult as it sounds.  Simply hover your cursor over anything on the scene that looks odd or out-of-place, and if a "?" appears, click on that area to reveal the clue.  Once you find all nine, you'll have to do a mini game, which works like this:
Nine pictures, each representing a clue, will need to be put into chronological order.  It would be incredibly difficult to find the correct order, except that the sequence can be discerned by matching up the swirls that run through each picture.  Once you find the correct order, you'll see a recreation of what happened on the scene, all narrated by our lovely heroine detective.
The voice overs aren't amazing, but they're not as bad as some of the ones  I've heard in casual games, believe me!  The English is just fine during narrated portions, but there are a few localization errors in some of the
hidden object scenes (and during the "Search for Clues" sections, but I didn't pay attention to what those said, just what I was seeing on the screen.)  Here are the mis-listings I saw, and what they actually want you to find:
Puzzles in the game are pretty simplistic, and most of them require no brainpower whatsoever.
Most achievements are obtained via natural game progression, the exception being not using a hint during HOS, not skipping puzzles, and one each for finding all of the collectibles.  As I mentioned at the beginning of this review, the Snowflakes and Origami are VERY easy to miss, especially if you forget that you're supposed to be looking for them like I did... D'oh!
For all of you achievement-hunters out there, there's a handy Steam Guide Walkthrough
that will give you all of the collectible locations ;)
Crime Secrets is not the best IHOG I've ever played, but I certainly do not feel that it deserves all of the negative reviews it's been getting.  I enjoyed this title far more than the last IHOG I reviewed, and will eventually go back to get those two missing achievements.  Despite the general consensus (on Steam), I enjoyed and recommend this game.

Looking at the steam port, there are features lacking that I would like to see added: voices, the 7th love interest, the animated sprites.
The mobile version is pay per route/story which costs FAR more than the asking price on steam for the full game.
If I assume the sequel and date stories are $0.99, the price for 1 route = $5.97 x 7 = $41.79
Therefore I think the steam version is the better one to buy if you want to experience the full game. The vita version is not available in English, but is the only version with voices.
+ Art is very nice. I quite like the painterly, soft colors with sketchy lineart. Sometimes the MC has eyes, sometimes she's drawn in an angle that purposefully hides them.
+ There are 2 endings for each guy, super happy ending and happy ending. Both endings are HAPPY in the full sense of the word, which I'm A-OK with. I've been playing a lot of games with bad/unfulfilling endings so these felt refreshing to me.
+ There is bonus content. You can unlock a few short stories as well as short epilogues.
+/- Romance is the main focus of the plot (forbidden love). Lightly to moderately smutty, ranging from descriptions of kissing and touching to metaphorical descriptions of sex. Brief scenes of softcore porn is the most accurate way to describe it.
+/- Quite a few grammar errors here and there on each route. This did not bother me much as I play a lot of mobile otome games where the translation is almost always poorly done.
+/- The story explores the world it set up, but does not focus on the truly dark themes it presents. Forbidden romance is the main theme of D3 Publishers's/Dogenzaka Lab's otome game titles. I enjoyed reading the stories for the most part.
- The MC is super naive and reckless. I should be tolerant of this, since these traits are so common for otome protagonists, but it doesn't stop it from being infuriating at times.
- BGM is monotonous, I found myself muting it after 2 playthroughs.
- Unvoiced. There is a voiced Vita version that also has a 7th guy, not to mention the mobile version has sprite animations that were removed from this port as well.
- Chapters end abruptly, which makes them feel short. The only exception is Iroha's sequel, which has less chapters, but are lengthy and are divided appropriately. The extra stories are also short.
- The choices don't really seem to matter, as you can easily achieve the super happy ending with less than 50% likeability (except Hayabusa and Iroha's sequel route).
I would recommend this because the steam version has all of the story content available for a reasonable price (versus the mobile version). I prefer stories that have a lot of romance (I'm pretty tolerant with sleazy, cheesy romances), so this game definitely fills that spot for me.
The steam version has gone on sale (about twice now) for about $10 which is a must buy price if you ask me. I bought the game on release which was $18 and I felt it was worth the value.

You will probably see negative reviews for this game for one of two reasons. The first being that it takes too long to download, thats a very silly complaint considering the initial install is legitimately just the launcher. The actual game download is around 9GB in size, which isn't bad for a ten year old game. The second reason you will see a lot of negative reviews and complaints is because this game has a fatigue system, which thanks to all those crappy freemium appstore games we know from our phones sets off a massive red flag for most people. The fatigue system bothers some people but I personally don't see it as the glaring issue new players think it is. The fatigue system allowed me to play my first character for a solid three and a half hours before running out of energy. Once I was out of energy I simply made a second character and continued to play until I decided that I had played enough and logged out of that character and stopped playing for the day. With the 30+ classes available I see no reason why you should be upset that you have to switch characters after your fatigue on one character runs out. The fatigue system encourages players both new and old to experiment with new classes.
I'm a new player to this game and I find the amount of hate this game gets for its fatigue system to be rather surprising given how linear it is. If you think you can tolerate the very generous fatigue system this game has then I would highly recommend giving this game a try as I belive it is a great beat 'em up rpg. Not only is the combat satisfying but the soundtrack in this game just gives me old arcade style vibes that beat me over the head with nostalgia. From calm classical scores in the citys to the electric guitar filled battle anthems this game does it perfectly.
As I'm quite new to this game I may come back at some point to update my review should my views of it change, and so I may comment on the end game and things of that nature. As of now though I whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone who thinks this game looks interesting.

IMSCARED has a few original ideas, but really fell flat in the end. There are different environments that you traipse through, each with a different atmosphere, but nothing felt intuitive or exciting. Sometimes there's a hidden key you haven't found, and sometimes you have to go check out files that the game is creating on your desktop. Sometimes you even have to close and restart the game yourself to continue. The fact that the game never communicates what you have to do to advance can sometimes create situations in which you're not sure if you should be looking around harder because you missed something, or if you should write a five page essay and submit it to the game. The fourth wall bits are interesting but poorly implemented for a cohesive horror experience.
The story is weak and vague, the graphics have a nice style but make text illegible, and the jumpscares were mostly unnecessary. Some parts of the game rely on sound within a 3D soundscape, and sound seems to originate in one position but does not change relative to your movement. Certain actions like climbing a ladder or printing tickets have a gratingly loud volume for no reason.
Many achievements were very arbitrary, and ended up being necessary to finish the game. Oh, and if you want to go back to get the achievements, have fun figuring out the ridiculous hallway hub. 2 doors go to 2 areas, one door with a pickup is needed to access a password screen to get to 2 other areas. It's as dumb as it sounds.
IMGLAD that I didn't pay more than $4, which still seems too steep for the overall quality of this "game,"  or waste more than 2 hours getting achievements to see the loud, lame ending. It's an experience, but one that I could have lived just fine without.

I very much wish I could give this game more than a YES or a NO, because there are things I love about it and I will continue to play it but the caveats are starting to outweigh the positives.
Good
- It's Magic and it's not horrifically expensive.
- You really don't need to put real money into this, although that's way less true than it is for, say, Hearthstone. Building a decent collection is sloooooow with just play.
- I actually like this format. I know other people are clamoring for the power level to be more like paper Standard, but part of the reason I play is because of the absurd variety of decks you can build. It's a very weak format for Constructed, almost like Sealed if you had a ton of boosters to pull from. If you don't already know, most (all?) of the cards from Magic Origins, BFZ, OGW and Shadows (currently, I don't know how long they will update) are in the game, BUT you can only have one of each Mythic, two of each Rare, or three of each Uncommon. This makes building a deck a veeeeeery different affair.
- I don't have anything else, but some of these positives are a Big Deal for me. Being able to play Magic without buying every single card or trying to open them in packs is great. If Cockatrice were less of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to use, I'd be all over it. But this is what we have.
NOT VERY @#$%ING GOOD AT ALL
- This is an issue I hadn't put much thought into because I learned how to play in 1998, but seriously, if this is your intro to Magic, you're sort of screwed. The tutorial teaches you just the absolute basics and I can't evaluate the learning curve of the solo game as if I were a novice, of course, but it does not seem like a tool I would use to teach people. It's like learning how to play poker solely by consulting a list of hands by rank.
- I have logged SEVENTY HOURS of this game and my card pool is laughable. I have the mobile version of Duels 2015 and it took me half that to get every card in the game. I've been buying exclusively packs of Origins (which I recommend, because this is a game of synergy and those cards are designed to work together) and I'm not even done with the set yet. The change to a full F2P model is really showing. There's also a cap on how much you can earn in one day, although I mostly just play each day until my quests are done, so I haven't had that problem.
- This is the real issue: this game has been "streamlined" much the way you could make a person more aerodynamic by cutting their head and limbs off. Anybody who plays Magic Online will tell you that "stops" are a vital part of the game. It's a hard thing to explain briefly, but advanced Magic is a game of timing. This game is set up in such a way that there are a number of plays that are legal, advantageous and even perfectly commonplace in paper Magic that cannot be replicated here. If you don't have anything you can do at the moment that you can't do at "instant speed," and your Main Phase comes up, the game skips it. If your hand is full of Instants or you have nothing you can cast in your hand but you do have effects on the board, you don't get Main Phases, period. You go straight into combat, straight to the End Step, or both. A skilled Magic player will understand the kind of havoc this wreaks on strategy. If the only card in your hand is an Instant draw spell, you might finish combat only to find yourself playing it during the End Step, drawing a Creature or a Sorcery, and having no chance of playing it until your next turn, not because of the rules of Magic but because the makers of this game assume nobody who understands the intricacies of Magic will bother playing it. They literally built this game from the ground up to cater specifically to new players and idiots. And while you will quickly learn a way around it, don't even get me started on auto-tapping your lands.
- There are bugs, plenty of them (you WILL lose games you should have won for no reason), but I have more problem with things in this game that were done on purpose than things they did accidentally. Damn, that is a sad sentence.
- One bug worth pointing out specifically: there is a way, I won't tell you how, to disconnect in such a way that your opponent has to take a loss. It is incredibly easy to do. I can't believe I haven't been scammed even more than I have. The game goes into a state where you can only concede. I don't know how it affects their score, but yours does go down. Unbelievable.

And that statement would hold true even for the precursor to this game, a free indie title released more than a year ago. IMSCARED has been a long time coming into its current incarnation into a full game,
It's hard to explain how good this game is without spoiling any of the experience, but here goes.
The horror game genre is undoubtedly gimmicky and saturated like the film one, it's hard to find something that truly suprises a die-hard participant in the genre.
Some may argue over the pixelated art style, the cliche "meta" gameplay, or even just the length of the title. But I disagree, it's these things and how well they're done that make this game truly shine.
Where others have simply copied and combined aspects of previous works, Ivan (the developer of IMSCARED) has outdone himself to the point where this game simply excels at being, well, horrific. There is a moment in this game to scare everyone and give them the chills, not a single opportunity is wasted to let you know the situation you have gotten yourself into.
IMSCARED doesn't get old, not in the sense that it has replay value, but it is true:
What this title does is excite you while unsettling the hell out of you for the entirety of the experience, from the start to the very end (oh, and I do mean very end, this game while technically short, feels like a lifetime to complete in the very best way possible).
Oh and just one last thing.
Forgive me.
