I have changed my review since the most recent update, and I am enjoying the game much more now. There are still some problems, but it is much better. This is currently the best free-to-play card game on the market in my opinion (way better than Hearthstone). If you can tolerate the free-to-play, pay-to-win model of this game and the steep learning curve, you will have a lot of fun.
Cons:
1. Controls have also been over-simplified, especially if you play with controller. There are no 'last played' or 'graveyard browser' buttons like there were in previous Duels games, and these buttons were essential for playing with controller.
2. Can't rebind controller buttons.
3. The layout/ui needs an overhaul, as it doesn't fully utilize the amount of screen space. Cards and icons are small, and the camera zooms out even more when there are a bunch of cards in play. Basically you have to constantly zoom in on cards to see what they do.
Pros:
1. Learn & play Magic for free.
2. You can freely build your own decks however you want, after unlocking or buying card packs. The deck builder is good and has decent filters/options.
3. Fun singleplayer campaign, challenging yet not unfair or annoying. Completing campaign gives you a decent amount of coins to start buying boosters with.
4. Manual mana tapping is handled well (this was a problem with previous Duels games).
5. You get to play with the most recent Magic sets.
Other Info: This iteration of Duels is “free-to-play”, and pay-to-win. This makes sense since it is a collectible card game, so the more cards you buy, the more powerful your deck will be. Previous Duels games only had pre-built decks, this game does not. You
unlock boosters with in-game currency, but it is slow. It costs 150 coins to unlock a booster pack containing 6 cards, but you only get 30 coins from winning an online game. You can also get coins from single player and daily challenges.

Pretty fun racing game!
I expected it to be more realistic when it comes to car handling, but it is in fact quite arcady and a bit loose. I am playing with a Xbox controller and the controls are not super responsive and direct when it comes to the steering with the L joystick, but it's acceptable. You might need to get used to it a bit in the beginning, after that it's fine.
The game has a ton of cups and challenges to keep you busy for many many hours (enough content). Even with the arcady feel it is actually quite chalenging to drive against the AI! So far as I have played the amount of different tracks is quite low, I played for 7 hours and only driven half a dozen different tracks (and reversed), also the amount of different cars and classes is quite low.
One really noticable quality gap in the game is the cockpit view. It is really low detailed in most/all cars and they made the cockpit on the lower part of your screen blurry to camouflage it. It is extra noticable, because basically everything else in the game is pretty solid and good quality.
As for realism I think this game falls far below the racing sims on the market. Even Gran Turismo feels more real (direct/responsive) when it comes to car handling, but the AI in GRID is way more fun to race against and the races are more custimizable then in Gran Turismo. I also don't think that this game tries or was intended to be a realistic racing sim, but an enjoyable not over complicated racing experience. And that it does quite well.
Overall I think this is a pretty solid and fun racing game and worthy to pick up during a sale.

: Koei Tecmo Games LTD
: Square-Enix
==========
Finally, we get a Dragon Quest title on Steam! I got the PS4 version when they put it up for pre-order, and have since sunk dozens of hours into it. Even if it is a Mosou-styled game (think Dynasty Warriors or even Hyrule Warriors) it's still a great game all its own and just oozes the usual Dragon Quest charm. If you were on the fence about purchasing the game because it was coming from Koei Tecmo, fear not! They surprisingly did a fantastic job with their port of this title, and YES, they ported the PS4 version and not the Japan-only PS3 version. The game has a lot to offer, and is a lot of fun to play!
The Steam version includes all of the special Slime Weapons from the various special editions released for consoles. You have to reach a certain point early on in the game to access them though.
==========
Monsters and humans have lived alongside each other in perfect harmony for as long as anyone can remember. But one day, every monster in the world (save for one) suddenly turn on their human friends and begin attacking towns and cities around the world. Luceus and Aurora, captains of the Arba Royal Guard, serve as your playable "main" characters. Together with Healix, Luceus' slimy companion is the one monster who remains unchanged, and King Doric, King of Arba, Luceus and Aurora set off on a quest to discover the secret behind the monsters turning, and put a stop to it. The game plays like your typical Dynasty Warriors title. That is to say, you control a character and hack/slash/jump your way through literally hordes of enemies, which are all iconic monsters from the beloved Dragon Quest series. Skeletons, Slimes, Drackies, etc are all here and look amazing.
Early on, the player gets access to an invention called the Stonecloud, which is essentially a giant flying fortress or airship. The Stonecloud will serve as the player's base of operations in their campaign to combat whatever plot has befallen Arba. Housing all the amenities the player will ever need, the Stonecloud is an indispensable tool in your quest. Shops, a Chapel, and other locations are found on the Stonecloud, and is where your characters will return after each successful battle to recuperate and prepare for the next skirmish.
Along the way, you will encounter and recruit many heroes from past Dragon Quest titles. Players will recognize many faces, such as Terry, Yangus, Alena, and Isla. All of them are controllable on the battlefield, as your party consist of 4 characters which can freely be swapped between. Each one has a certain play style and unique abilities that can be used to clear waves after wave of monsters in each area. Dragon Quest Heroes also features the Tension system that originated from Dragon Quest VIII. As you take and deal damage, a meter fills up. Once full, you can enter a state of High Tension, which boosts your speed and attack power, and grants access to devastating Coup de Grace attacks!
In addition to all of the playable characters, Dragon Quest Heroes introduces the Monster Medals mechanic. As you defeat monsters they each have a small chance to drop a medal which bears their image. When picked up, these allow the player to summon these monsters to the field to aid them in battle. Monster Medals come in 2 varieties: Sentry and Saviour. Sentry monsters stay in the general area they are deployed in and defend the area from all attacks. Saviour monsters are 1 time use monsters than provide HP or SP recovery, or other beneficial effects. Using these Monster Medals can often prove to be quite a boon in many different combat scenarios, which can range from defeating all monsters or defending a certain point or character on the field. Each Monster Medal takes up one, two, or even three of the six available medal slots you have, with more powerful monsters taking up the most slots. Picking up medals for monsters you already have summoned will heal them. Monsters are best used to hold strategic points on the battlefield while the player takes care of others, or providing buffs to your party that they otherwise do not have access to.
A lot of other features are present in Dragon Quest Heroes. The Alchemy Pot from Dragon Quest VIII makes a return, utilizing the materials you find during battle to create accessories. You can use the gold you earn each stage to buy weapons, shield, accessories, and orbs. Orbs act as your armor, bestowing upon your characters the benefits of the armors they represent. Mini Medals are earned by completing quests, found on the battlefield, or earned from defeating large numbers of specific enemies; These are then used to buy materials, Alchemy Pot recipes, and special weapons. Accolades act as achievement markers, rewarding you with Mini Medals as you complete certain milestones.
==========
Being a port of the PS4 version, the Steam version looks amazing. The AA is a little rough around the edges, but there are workarounds for that for the time being. The game capitalizes on the unique art style that Dragon Quest has had throughout the years, and Akira Toriyama's artwork is front and center throughout the game. There's enough eye candy here to satisfy any newcomer to the series.
==========
Remember all the classic Dragon Quest sounds, songs, and jingles from yesteryear? Heroes has it all! It's such a nice touch to hearken back to the good old days with the music and sound effects. Many of them you'll recognize from Dragon Quest VIII, honestly. Picking up items, sword slashes, etc. All sound amazing and just instill a great sense of nostalgia. The soundtrack fits the game near perfectly, even if it is a bit light-hearted. Fans will recognize a lot of the tunes present, and even come to love some new ones.
A thing that alot of people like to see is the option to have Japanese voiceovers. Those are available here! I have no issues with the English voiceovers, but some people do, so it's nice to have the option to toggle between them for those players.
==========
60 FPS? Check!
Multiple graphics options, including resolution? Check!
Controller support? Check!
In-game button prompts that match your controller? Check!
Multiple control schemes? Check!
No issues here! The game runs very smoothly on my rig (specs on my profile) and I have yet to experience any problems with framerate, stuttering, lag, or anything of that nature. I don't expect to either!
I have public screenshots of all the options on my profile if you are curious.
==========
This is an amazing Dragon Quest title, even if it doesn't follow the usual Dragon Quest formula. If you ever want more Dragon Quest titles to come to Steam, buying this game is the best way to vote for more. A solid experience, Dragon Quest Heroes definitely deserves a spot in your Steam Library. Fans of the series will certainly find a lot to offer them, with tons of content and replayability. Nostalgia abounds, and the game is just a complete and utter joy to pick up and play.

Crime Secrets has a good enough crime story for a casual game, but it struggles to provide meaningful content beyond some hidden object scenes and the most simplistic point ‘n’ click mechanics.
I’ll be honest: if a hidden object game made in 2016 starts with a scene where a private investigator’s car crashes at a remote location, I cannot help but start being rather sceptical towards it. Even if we are talking about the quasi-sequel of the 9 Clues games, where our detective heroine bumps into yet another murder case, this time at a snowy mountain resort.
This scepticism is only partly justified, because while the story is predictable and pretty self-repeating (count how many times you have to find an item used as a knife, screwdriver, or lockpick, or the number of ambushes against the detective), it is still plenty enjoyable for a casual game murder mystery.
A HOG needs actual gameplay content though, and this is where Crime Secrets lacks. Most of it is spent with simplistic item hunting with barely a handful of hidden object scenes or puzzles along the way. Those few are fun, but that cannot excuse their low number.

I got this game on sale, and I wanted to like this game, I really did. I loved the first GRID. The graphics are really nice, among the best for a racing game when it came out. The single-player story mode is cheesy, but it does okay to fill the gaps between races. The engine sounds are mostly accurate, far more so than the first GRID game. It's really unfortunate that this is where the good parts of the game end.
The driving physics are awful. Literally some of the worst I've ever played. I understand they wanted to focus on drifting and making it a key component of racing, but it is so poorly implemented that certain vehicles are essentially unplayable. Driving the Koenigsegg Agera R is a nightmare... it feels exactly like driving on ice, which I have actual experience with, living in a place that gets really cold during the winter with tons of snow. It's really a shame that ALL of the cars drift. All of the vehicles, regardless of being described as "Balanced" and / or "Grip" when you select them, will drift, no matter how perfect you try to take a corner. As soon as you hit the brakes, you can feel the vehicle start to fishtail. Some cars are okay, but I've found at least 50% of the time, racing is just not an enjoyable experience.
Even worse is the computer AI. They drive their line and regardless of if they hit a wall, if you bump them, and even if you try to spin them out, it's nearly impossible, they do not make mistakes. It feels exactly like a crappy simulation, minus actually simulating anything.
I did enjoy the first 18 hours or so in the single-player game. Really the coolest part of the game was my second race when I drove up the side of a mountain, fell back down on top of the opponent's car, and still won the race. However, after over 21 hours, I've finally put my controller down in frustration, and most likely will not pick it back up for this game.

You will probably see negative reviews for this game for one of two reasons. The first being that it takes too long to download, thats a very silly complaint considering the initial install is legitimately just the launcher. The actual game download is around 9GB in size, which isn't bad for a ten year old game. The second reason you will see a lot of negative reviews and complaints is because this game has a fatigue system, which thanks to all those crappy freemium appstore games we know from our phones sets off a massive red flag for most people. The fatigue system bothers some people but I personally don't see it as the glaring issue new players think it is. The fatigue system allowed me to play my first character for a solid three and a half hours before running out of energy. Once I was out of energy I simply made a second character and continued to play until I decided that I had played enough and logged out of that character and stopped playing for the day. With the 30+ classes available I see no reason why you should be upset that you have to switch characters after your fatigue on one character runs out. The fatigue system encourages players both new and old to experiment with new classes.
I'm a new player to this game and I find the amount of hate this game gets for its fatigue system to be rather surprising given how linear it is. If you think you can tolerate the very generous fatigue system this game has then I would highly recommend giving this game a try as I belive it is a great beat 'em up rpg. Not only is the combat satisfying but the soundtrack in this game just gives me old arcade style vibes that beat me over the head with nostalgia. From calm classical scores in the citys to the electric guitar filled battle anthems this game does it perfectly.
As I'm quite new to this game I may come back at some point to update my review should my views of it change, and so I may comment on the end game and things of that nature. As of now though I whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone who thinks this game looks interesting.

Do you like open, detailed maps? Do you like being able to choose creative ways to eliminate your targets? Do you like maps that aren't full of copy-paste linearity? You're not going to like this game.
It's been said that this game is a good game, but not a good HITMAN game, which is accurate.
The graphics, voice acting, gunplay, and dark humor in this game are all great, but at the end of the day, these are things that a normal HITMAN game would have and more.
The levels in this game aren't that replayable. Only 20% of the levels are replayable in this game, versus 100% in the likes of Blood Money and HITMAN 2016. This is due in part to the fact that the levels are very linear, excluding the Hope, South Dakota map. Instead of big, open maps, you'll get little mini maps. 75% of these maps don't involve you assassinating a target, and rather move from point A to point B.
The story isn't good. Unless you're one of the 2% of players that are in it for the story, you'll likely not care.
Gunplay is amazing. Best in the series. However, this is a HITMAN game, not Grand Theft Auto. Instead of refining the gunplay, they should've focused on including more ways to kill your targets.
Is it a bad game? No. Do I recommend it as a HITMAN game? Certainly not. That does not mean you should ignore it. This is a GOOD game, but I can't recommend it for you if you're new to the series or a diehard HITMAN fan. I've dumped a few hours into this game, and no, it's not utter garbage as some people will say.
Just play the likes of Blood Money and HITMAN 2016 before picking this up.

Let me be honest, I wanted to enjoy this game. I really did. I wanted it to be good, because as a fan of dating sim and otome games, I am painfully aware of the fact there is not a lot of varity in those kinds of games available outside of Japan. It's mostly indies or ported games so the attitude towards these games is mostly, "Take what you can get and be grateful."
This game though, I'm not impressed with. I played for two straight hours and I just feel dirty because of it. To be fair though, the music and art design are very impressive. It looks and sounds very well done and I'd give it top marks on that alone if it weren't for my beef with it.
The writing and the characters are awful. I mean, completely awful. The lowdown is this. There's a redlight district on an island you're tasked with making a delivery to and on the way you help a couple trying to escape because men on this island are effectively slaves. Uh... okay, and I'm going to try to be romanced by one? Way to make me feel creeped out right off the bat. Anyway, you help them escape so he can get married and in return you come into some money and fancy clothing. You're actually there to make a delivery and so when you go to the place in question, you immediately meet (most of) your romance options.
These guys are creeps, like almost every single one of them. Playing this I got grabbed, felt up, talked down to and forced to drink alcohol AGAINST MY WILL MIND YOU! I was compared to a piece of meat, and the owner, the OWNER himself told me I needed to be pretty and more receptive in order to "earn a man's seed". Seriously, what in the world?
Now, I'm not going to pretend I'm some expert on courtesans or this time period. While I've studied a little I'm sure there are plenty of people who know way more than me, but I know there is a difference between hooker and courtesans. You go to the nice places to be entertained, romanced and bedded. You go see a hooker to sleep with and be on your way in twenty minutes and probably treated poorly because they couldn't care less about entertaining you.
That's how I felt here. I felt like I'd stepped into a place where no one knew the first thing about how to treat a lady. More than that, of course the female character has to be this shy little waif who will just take this appalling treatment. The, "Uh... ah... I... um..." responces to everything happening to here was so cliche, along with the, "Even though I'm shy and uncomfortable with this, he's too alluring for me to fight against it." Why did this have to be done? Why can't I just play a girl who WANTS to go to this place instead of being forced to stay by the owner? Why can't I pick a guy and make it rain for him? Why does this essentially have to be a story about a girl romanced against her will by a guy who is, again, a slave? Why when I do get a choice on how to act, (By the way I basically told the owner I didn't want to hear his vulgar bs about seed recieving. Seriously, what?) only to get laughed at and dismissed? Guys? Uh... I'm a customer here, both in and out of this game world. Is a little respect for the customer that much to ask for?
So in the end you play a girl who despite saying multiple times she doesn't want to be there and wants to leave, is forced to stay and pick one of the men there that insulted and grabbed at her without even knowing so much as her name, and she is too weak willed not to do anything but go along with it. Pick someone wrong and you get yelled at by the other workers there and made fun of, pick someone else and basically the exact same thing happens, and it all goes down hill from there. It all has this forced feeling to it, and honestly that's not what I want. I didn't get forced to buy this game. I bought it, sat down and played it because I wanted to.
Yet here's the intro. "Your heart, body and womanhood are all on the line. You will never be able to escape. Not from the seductive wiles of the courtesans. No, let's be more accurate: From the pure love of the courtesans." No... no I think the first statement was correct. It's wiles and it's not even seductive wiles at that. This whole thing of there being no men on the island feels cheap, as if this is the only reason the men can get away with acting like such jerks. "Oh... well, women can't get the D anywhere else so they put up with these guys." "What about the men on the mainland who can get married and be happy with you and give you children and a family life? Clearly the rich women could afford it at least." "SHUSH! PLAY THE GAME, SCUM! DON'T YOU DARE BRING LOGIC IN HERE!" Except, yeah. Let's bring in logic because the second I stop to think all these things, the game isn't fun. It's lame, and more than that, it's insultive.
"You will never be able to escape." Yeah, game. I can escape. I can get away from your  jerk men and I can get away from your bs writing. It's called turning the game off and playing something else. Didn't think of that one, did you?
I know I'm in the minority here. I bought this game because it had such great reviews, but if you're one of the fans like me who actually wants the story to be somewhat decent, don't bother. This game will insult you, treat you awful and keep pounding home that garbage of you can't get away. Doesn't bother you, play it. It does bother you? Walk away and save your money.

It comes as advertised. A 2D Retro Arcade-Style beat-em-up RPG.
You pick a character class and almost immediately start by killing things in one dungeon or another. In a short while, you get to pick your sub-class that will truly define what your character is best at (Spoiler Alert: They are all good at killing baddies; so, it just boils down to a preference of style more than anything else, really).
No reason to pay at all unless you feel like supporting the devs and you want to customize your avatar to set yourself apart from the free player crowd.
Takes a little effort to level up, but the system is very casual about it. You only get to run through so many dungeons a day per character you've made before you reach your daily limit on that character. And that's what really helps set it apart from other dungeon running games. The fact that it forces its players to pace themselves, which may not appeal to all, but it does appeal to me. Plus, if you want to play longer, you can always just make more characters and play with them.

The Hidden Object scenarios are very simple, as if it was meant for those who have very short attention spans. This isn't that bad, but offer little fun. Solving puzzles that show a result lag a bit at the end, as if there is a slight pause. Immersion is slightly taken away here.
Also, the detective you're playing is a goof ball. How is an experienced detective so often so careless in what she does? "YES, PLEASE lock me in here because I left the lights on and the door wide opened!" "Please knock me out because I just love rushing into scenes without a care in the world!" O__O
The 'acting' of the various characters is nothing to write home to. The act of most of the characters act like robots wearing human skin. The voice of the antagonist sounds forced and deliberate.
However, on the more positive aspects of the game, the art work is pretty vibrant and makes the ambiance believable. The idea of the puzzles are pretty interesting, though ultimately quite simple in design.
I think the overall idea of the game is nice, but the flow feels broken and the main character is a very dumb person.

I have changed my review since the most recent update, and I am enjoying the game much more now. There are still some problems, but it is much better. This is currently the best free-to-play card game on the market in my opinion (way better than Hearthstone). If you can tolerate the free-to-play, pay-to-win model of this game and the steep learning curve, you will have a lot of fun.
Cons:
1. Controls have also been over-simplified, especially if you play with controller. There are no 'last played' or 'graveyard browser' buttons like there were in previous Duels games, and these buttons were essential for playing with controller.
2. Can't rebind controller buttons.
3. The layout/ui needs an overhaul, as it doesn't fully utilize the amount of screen space. Cards and icons are small, and the camera zooms out even more when there are a bunch of cards in play. Basically you have to constantly zoom in on cards to see what they do.
Pros:
1. Learn & play Magic for free.
2. You can freely build your own decks however you want, after unlocking or buying card packs. The deck builder is good and has decent filters/options.
3. Fun singleplayer campaign, challenging yet not unfair or annoying. Completing campaign gives you a decent amount of coins to start buying boosters with.
4. Manual mana tapping is handled well (this was a problem with previous Duels games).
5. You get to play with the most recent Magic sets.
Other Info: This iteration of Duels is “free-to-play”, and pay-to-win. This makes sense since it is a collectible card game, so the more cards you buy, the more powerful your deck will be. Previous Duels games only had pre-built decks, this game does not. You
unlock boosters with in-game currency, but it is slow. It costs 150 coins to unlock a booster pack containing 6 cards, but you only get 30 coins from winning an online game. You can also get coins from single player and daily challenges.

I bought this game at launch and could never get it to run. Went through all the bug fixes etc etc checked my system a million times (yes it was compatible). After doing everything I could I found threads with many people in the same position who simply could not get the game to work. This was before steam refunds and I had already used the code thus I am unable to sell/gift etc this game. The conclusion the screwed of us came to was "this will eventually be patched". So I put the game away, and now much much later, here I am, on a new system trying to get this game to run and failing.
This game has been and will continue to be a bug-ridden pox on the good name of Civilization. From reading many many reviews it is clear this game was an unimaginative mod sold at full price as a new game. They kept the single-unit-to-a-tile system, which makes the AI unable to mount defensive or offensive war - a problem I am very familiar with from civilization V. Because of this I recommend going back to Civ 4 beyond the sword and playing mods like Rhyse and Fall if you can. Playing Civ V and BE (I am made to understand) is like playing chess against a person without their mental faculties. A futile exercise where you win regardless of your actions and strategy.
BE also suffers from a severe lack of personality, a problem shared to a lesser extent with Civ V.
Overall don't buy this game or its expansions. One developer who wanted to innovate/get a credit to his name changed Civ to a one unit to a tile system that for some reason Firaxis is still commited to (guess they don't want to switch horses in the middle of a race eg george w bush) and kills the game.
I can't get my money or wasted time back, but at least I can impart you with the wisdom to skip this poorly made and unsupported mod until they do a total overhaul (probably not until civ 7 or 8 at this rate), thus saving someone the torment.
I prefer more customizable arsenal like Hitman Blood Money.

I played Magic: The Gathering in high school many years ago, very casually, and recently was given a deck to use at a local comic shop - again, very casually. My gaming interest in Magic is, thus, quite casual. I enjoy playing but will never aspire to be competitive. That said, Magic Duels is a lovely game for someone like me. There are a few caveats though. Here's my rundown:
PROS
-It's free.
-Not only is the base game free, it comes with a decent selection of starter cards and you earn 'coins' as you play the Story Mode or Battle Mode (against AI opponents) with which you can purchase boosters and unlock more cards. Given that M:tG can be quite expensive, this is a *huge* feature in its favor.
-There are myriad other ways to earn additional coins like community goals and winning the first Versus Battle of the day.
-Great for newcomers or casual folks who aren't heavy on the rules - the tutorial features are fairly helpful.
CONS
-I see the complaints about turn phases getting skipped. There's a Stop Timer button and I haven't felt like I've missed an entire phase but I did have a card that was supposed to bring a counter in when it entered the battlefield and that never happened. I'm not certain it wasn't my fault somehow. The Stop Timer button only gives you a couple seconds in which to actually click it though, so you have to be ready to pause.
-I'm not sure if it's just my newness or the community or what but when I play a Versus it says it's trying to match me up with someone. I think that's literally what it means, since I've played against someone with Rank 9 while I was Rank 1 and just Conceded a game (when that happens it subs an AI in to finish the match so the other person can still win and get coins) where my opponent was using nothing by Rares or better. My deck had none. I would not consider the two decks 'matched' as in 'balanced'.
-There's no chat or communication available between players. I know this can be a difficult thing to integrate and support but it's so essential to the experience that I really feel it's the biggest lack in the entire game.
Overall, Magic Duels is a nice way to get into M:tG or play casually but for those wanting the full experience of face-to-face opponents, the feel and sound of cards shuffling and being played, and the impending debt that accompany the game the way it was meant to be played it does fall a little short. I still recommend it though - it's free!

Half-formed in ideas and at the same time feels unfinished even in the small amount of content that it is providing. The idea of figuring out how to accomplish tasks with no direction just using the tools of the game itself is actually cool but it really is lost in the random nature and poor implementation of this game.
First off the game has no options for video, audio, or controls. I don't expect it to be scalable to large screens but an ability to map controls would've been nice but the fact that you can't mute the audio is very annoying for a puzzle title that is largely based on multiple retrials. I had to turn it down in the system settings to be able to listen to my own music/podcasts. That's one of the main reasons it feels like an unfinished game. Most flash games let you at least mute the volume. Anyway, let's delve into the game itself.
(this gives away the tricks) You are some kind of spaceman-person in this game who gets seeds when you enter a level outside of the hub. The seeds do different things that always end up building blocks to extend the ground and reach a star block. Both a block at the beginning and the star block contaminate the other blocks, blackening them and that spreads, if a black block is touched you go to an opposite world where the everything but the blocks you walk on are solid and the star turns into a key that unlocks a "door" at the black block back at the beginning so you go through at the star block and exit back at the beginning.
(this gives away more) The bright green seed makes bright green blocks that have hearts in them, when you go back to the minus world after getting the key the hearts are collectible and turn into seeds when you go back to the hub. You plant the seeds at the hub and go up to find spaceman-holograms that have cryptic sayings above them and more levels.
That's all I've found that this is. Which is not enough of a game to me and progression is largely based on the random nature of the seeds you're given and the way the seeds grow the ground blocks, both of these things can make an entire entry into a level pointless because you might get a bunch of good seeds at the beginning and then at the end you only get the dark green seeds that in later levels mean you lose because you can't dig them up in later levels to allow yourself to progress.
Also, you can complete a level and not get to the exit or collect a heart in time and then it just quits out the level and you lose because it's always good to make you randomly lose for no forseeable reason and again wasted time. It's also possible to enter at the star and completely miss contact with the key because it doesn't take up a whole block and then the entire time spent is wasted because the hitbox of the key is small for some unknown reason.
If it was easier I wouldn't have liked the game better but I wouldn't have disliked it enough to write this review in the negative. It was a small cheap game that became more unlikable the more I played because there was nothing there but more of the same except with even more limited options to arbitrarily make it harder instead of having variable gameplay.
I don't like feeling like my time is wasted. When the only thing I did wrong was miss the hitbox of a key when dropping into the minus world and I lose 5 minutes of my time for no real reason other than the key's hitbox is small or I got a bad order of seeds then it's not a game I would recommend to anyone and would, in this case, actively discourage it for that feeling of loss that comes coupling puzzles with random chance.

What an incredible and truly unique experience. The atmosphere is menacing, the scares are terrifying, the music is creepy and fitting, and the ending is unforgettable.
The antagonist messes with your head psychologically, then emotionally. You will feel very uncomfortable as you are forced to make heartless and horrible decisions, but this leads to one of the most bittersweet moments in gaming I have ever experienced.
Some of the puzzles were very clever and fun, forcing you to think outside of the box in order to solve them in ways no other game has thought of. However, they aren't perfect. A couple puzzles were very tedious: the hedgemaze and the grammophone puzzles specifically. Without spoiling anything, these were a pain to get through and were the only sections that are actually detrimental to full experience.
The game could use some more graphics options. Forcing the player to play in a lower resolution is archaic and creates a delay when having to alt+tab to the folder. There are also no FOV options or checkbox to turn off headbob. These two options would prevent a lot of simulation sickness for those that can get a little light-headed from first person view video games.
That all being said, any fan of horror should definitely check this out. It is beatable in 2-3 hours, and fully worth the price of $4.

PROS:
CONS:
A great game, which goes back to times, where you had to spend hours just to figure out what you have to do next.

Cons:
~ Monetized, and not well. Darn near everything costs and you will never have enough of whatever to do the job.
~ Rewards you cannot use until you pay or earn premium currency for the space to claim it.
~ Time-Based System would be acceptable if it were shorter.
Pros:
~ Puzzle Quest Series' infamous "Stacking the Deck against you in place of intelligent opponents" difficulty system seems to have been abandoned. You get lucky drops of new gems just as often as the CPU does. Defeat is not decided for you in advance.
~ Interesting improvement system, despite monetization angle.
~ Guild system and game modes that reward you for acting together, though apart (sharing powers, guild-wide rewards in their special events). Makes many good things you get into benefits you can share (such as your great high-level card being sent out as a backup to allies).
Play it. Cautiously.

If you keep those rules, they payout is much like a subscription:   You win a couple of new characters every month and you pay a little to expand your roster.  Very reasonable.

If you buy a 42 pack which features him (3.2% chance per card draw of getting one of his three abilities) then there is about a 25% chance you don't get him in the draw of 42 cards.  ((1.0-0.032)^42)   What's the chance of getting all three abilities in a 42 pack?  Haven't done the math, but it must be around 5% or worse.
So how much is a 42 pack?  15800 gold points.  You buy gold points for about 20000 for $100.   Therefore if you want a solid chance at getting all three abilities, you might pay about $400-$500.   You could get luckier.
Knowing all this, I still bought a 42 pack this week and got two of the three abilities.   I was very lucky and I can barely resist buying another 42 pack.  That is the hook.
Playing with the low level characters is very fun, there'se nothing wrong with it.  It's the desire and excitment about playing with a new one which makes you break your rules.
BTW, the endpoint for cost of a slot for a character seems to be about 850 gold per slot.  That's about $4.25 per character once you have a fullish roster.   If you win a character, you pay $4.25 to keep it.  Fine.   But then you want the other 2 abilities that you didn't win.   Keep that under control and you will find this game reasonably priced.
Oh, BTW, you do get all of the 1 and 2 star characters essentially for free over time and the cost of the extra slots is cheap at first.  It's the 3 and 4 stars that tempt you into paying.   You'll be happy in the moment and kind of sick in the long run.
I saw a comment on a review which pointed out that any free to play game that you play for more than a couple of hours should have a massive thumbs-up.  OK, so thumbs up for that.  You'll love it for 5 or 10 hours, then you have to start resisting the temptation to pay.
Having said all this, I can't argue with the thumbs-down reviews.  They're not bull####.  Watch your wallet if you start playing this, especially if you love it.

I have to say, if you are a very competetive player you will NOT enjoy this game (or you'll spend a ton of time and money on it).  To this day, I have spent a wopping $5 on it, and that was more than enough for me. I got lucky and recieved a level 70 character.
At any rate, to the heart of the game:
It's a puzzle game. Your characters (3 per group) have skills that are powered by having so many of a specific color gem(s). So, you want to mix and match characters that will compliment the others. An example of this would be that some characters power is to change the colors of the gems. So if you have someone who changes gem colors to yellow and you have another character who does a power attack after getting so many yellow gems, have them on the same team.
In the game, there is a single story line you can go through and collect items: money for more character slots, tokens to get characters/skills, characters/skills, crystals to level your characters after equipping said skills, etc. The story mode does jump in difficulty, don't expect to sit down and hammer through it in an hour or two; it takes days, if not weeks (still not through them all).
In the meantime, there are daily events that link into I believe an almost two week long (if not longer -I came in to a season in progress so I'm not sure about the length) that you can do as well. The main seaon lasts a while, but there are dailies or longer events that come up.
The thing I lika about them, is they are not all versus other players (though those are available as well), some of them are solo events, and have a mix of using your current characters, or having some of your characters beefed up (some have your levels jump into the 100s), or even characters you don't have but are pretty beefed up that you can use as well.
I do need to point out though, that when your character runs out of health, you will either have to use a helath pack (one  returns in 35 minutes if you used them all) or just wait for them to heal over time.  As I have stated (and noticed from a lot of the negative comments), you really don't lose much over this if you aren't playing to be the best.
Patience, tactics, with a bit of luck, and you'll be fine.

Redshirt is a Facebook simulator with Sci Fi window dressing. Your mission is to social engineer your way to the top of the space station hierarchy. Along the way, you can make friends, start (and end) relationships, and arrange events with your cohabitants.
The gameplay involves making a limited number of moves per day on "Spacebook". This includes liking posts, sending messages and friend invites, and inviting friends to events. These events not only bring you closer to your friends, but will also change your interests. You must balance your interests to make friends with whoever your desired target is (either a goal given to you by the game, or the hiring manager at the next job you want). During the day you will also have to work, which will give you money and have an effect on your relationships.
Redshirt is one of those games where it's fun to tool around in for a few minutes, but after a bit you feel like you have seen everything that the game has to offer. I managed to get a really good promotion by dating the hiring manager, but the only reward I really got was that I could do the process all over again for an even better job. For those that enjoy that type of manipulation, maybe the fun can last for a few cycles. For me, I got bored rather quickly. The main feedback you get from your actions is your changing relationship status with other inhabitants of the space station. It comes in the form of the green and red bar that will be familiar to anyone that has played the Sims. The real issue I had with it was that there is not much separating one character from the next, besides a cartoon portait that looks a little bit the same from one character to the next. besides alien race of course. You never really feel like you are interacting with separate characters, like you would in the Sims for instance.
I do not recommend playing Redshirt. I felt like I was just playing Facebook with generic robots, which I guess in the end was what I was really doing. From my time with it, I didn't feel the motivation needed to keep advancing.

Beyond Gravity is a fun, simple little game. It's an obvious mobile port: it only has one button and the intro video even says "Tap to continue" instead of "click." While it may seem a little rushed or lazy, that doesn't deter from the game.
First, it's cheap. Lists for $2, but whenever it goes on sale it's an easy decision to buy. The point of the game is to jump from planet to planet, collecting as many screws as you can. There are 40 goals/ achievements, all of which can be obtained fairly reasonably.
PROS
+ The game is fun and has a good balance between being simple and challenging.
+ The game is inexpensive.
+ It is really easy to get 100% of the achievements in a short amount of time.
CONS
- The game is short. I got everything in just over three hours, you could do it in less.
- Limited replayablity. Once you've gotten all the tasks/ achievements, there's not a ton of incentive to play more. There are skins and additional skills, but you can do everything without them, leaving little incentive to push to collect them.
- Some of the tasks are more of a grind than anything else. They don't involve any skill per se, just jumping or dying over and over until you hit the number.
All in all, I would most certainly recommend the game. It's simple, it's fun, it's something those of you with small children can play with your kids. I would suggest you get it on sale, although $2 is far from unreasonable. I would give it a 7/10.

This is a terrible game, even compared to other (mobile) game with similar gameplay mechanics.
The core mechanics are basically identical to those of Gravity Guy and several similar mobile games:
Play a simple game (hop from planet to planet in this case) collect items and complete goals (up to three at a time) in the process and buy "upgrades" that make the core gameplay a bit easier and allow the faster collection of said items to buy more upgrades etc.
For a game like this the core mechanics need to be at least a tiny bit engaging and the carrot and stick that are the upgrades need to be well balanced - none of that is the case here:
Upgrades are way too few, way too expensive and have minimal impact on the gameplay which isn't all that terribly strong to begin with. It feels like a Freemium grindfest that forgot the in-game store without adjusting the prices accordingly.
In addition, this may very well be one of the laziest mobile to PC ports I have ever seen. The PC version is identical to the Android version, it doesn't even have an exit button, nor does it react to the ESC key. There is, currently, no way to cleanly end this game - as a result (perhaps) resolution and graphic quality settings are never saved and one has to adjust them each time upon launch.
Even at 99 cents, this is a waste of money.

Not a very good hidden object game.
- The story is a mess:
* many people get killed but you never get hurt even though you face the murderer every 10 minutes, just because...
* Some freezing device is used during all the story and no one questions how it works or consider making a lot of money from it
* There are hints about relationships between many characters that never seem to play an important part so I stopped caring about them
* You ask one guy to wait for you outside in the cold and actually never come back to him :D (although he leaves that place by himself MUCH later)
- The deductions sequences from found clues are non-sense (fortunatly, you don't have to figure the order by logic, there's a pattern on the pictures to find it)
- The finding object sequences are not very interesting:
* there a not a lot of them
* most objects are right in your face (you have at most
object that's actually hidden)
* some descriptions are badly translated
- Several "puzzles" are pointless:
* some require only clicking 4-5 times on the object until it rotates in the right position
* Some others consist of clicking a random sequence of 3 buttons: you don't need luck or logic, that's only 6 possibilities and that's how you're supposed to solve it since there's no clue
* One of the final puzzles that involves mixing potions is completely broken and can be solved while skipping 90% of the steps.
- Some dialogs seem to have bugs: there's no voice and some don't even make sense for the situation
- Some graphics and animations look really good, while some others are ridiculously bad
- The voice acting is ok, but the tone of the voice can be annoying sometimes
- Even with a good computer and the game being installed on an SSD, the game slowed down after playing for some time, mostly the loading times between sequences were getting longer and longer. At some point, I had to quit and relaunch the game, which fixed the problem. It happened after a few hours though, so it's not so bad.
- It's still a hidden object game and I enjoy even the bad ones.

Normally a genre I enjoy, this one broke just about every one of my cardinal rules for being likable. My extended play time is largely due to it being so engaging I actually dozed off while playing.
So I think a list is in order this time....
1. Badly or completely mistranslated names for hidden objects
2. I actually broke the game very early on by using two items together in the wrong location and it then refused to let me have a mouse cursor
3. Backgrounds do not update to reflect story based changes. See that area over there? the one with the giant multicoloured object? Zoom in over there and pick up the object. Now zoom out and hey presto it's reappeared!
4. Collectibles also do not always ...collect? I mean they are counted but they don't always diappear so you are unsure if they are counted. Whilst there is a somewhat saving grace in that collectibles are counted across multiple playthroughs (so you can spot the ones you missed) since they all appear in every playthrough even that becomes a little difficult to keep track of.
5. Some of the animations look like they really couldn't be bothered.
6. Some of the interative areas, likewise, are missing any text/voice decriptions - oooh a question mark cursor? *click* *nothing*
7. The puzzles, which are normally pitched somewhere between "easy" and "mildly irritating" are instead pitched at "I'm a three year old" level. I thought perhaps I'd missed an option in the difficulty settings... but sadly no.
8. The story, which actually had a reasonable amount of promise as a murder mystery, is garbled to the point where it can be hard to work out exactly who is who and makes only a little sense. It also means the addition of a "look for clues" minigame where you click on random items in the hope that they will be clues and then rearrange them, jigsaw style, into an entirely nonsensical narrative.
9. If you don't want to hunt for hidden objects you can switch to a mahjong game that requires zero skill and shuffles all the pieces remaining should you ever happen to get stuck. If you are achievement hunting this is pointless, since there are no achievements associated with it but if you're just looking for a clear this may save you from getting stuck in mistranslation hell.
10. No free play/bonus chapter/extended content of any sort once you complete the game. Hitting play at that point will just start you over at the beginning. There is a "more" section on the menu but this is just a catch all for settings/help/achievements.
11. As with most artifex mundi games if you run it for an extended period of time it gets slower and slower. However where I have previously only usually found the slowdown noticable if i was doing multiple play throughs in this case it was very obvious after only a relatively short playtime. Additionally quitting the game often didn't seem to actually close it, requiring a force kill via task manager before it could be restarted.
(and of course if I could just have persuaded the protagonist to keep hold of the penknife and lighter that are in the very first area just imagine how much simpler everything could have been!)
There are many, many better examples of this genre out there if this is your thing.

I was about to try MTGO out, but while setting up an account, the WotC site asked if I'd ever played MTG before, I said no, and it took me straight here. Magic: The Hearthstone is fantastic for first time players. It spells out the rules very clearly, & gives 1-2 turn mini battles to explain some abilities, mechanics, etc.
The deck build wizard - er, helper. This is still MTG. Deck Build Wizard might actually be a thing, idk - gives you just enough autonomy to let you feel like you have some control, all the while giving you a specific build & explaining why it should be the way it is.An d of course you can avoid the wizard and build your own from scratch.
I like that there are weekly community quests, where as long as you contribute to the total in some way, you get a bit of gold. I only started playing ther other day & am not confident enough to play against real people just yet, so I can't speak for the matchmaking.
Now the negatives: Note that these are all nitpicks. That's because this really is Magic: The Hearthstone. It's Magic, which is a very old card game that has stood the test of time for many players, in a Hearthstone format, which is very welcoming to casuals while encouraging people to keep playing and trying new things. It's solid. Anyway:
This is clearly a mobile port. The UI should've gone through at least
kind of changes for a mouse/keyboard. Apparently there's controller support, and I'm willing to bet even that feels better.
The deck builder/card search is severely lacking in that it doestn't even have a keyword filter. In a game like Magic, where creature subtypes sometimes seriously matter especially for deck building, this is an appalling oversite.
If there is a way to concede a match, someone please tell me. It's torture to have to play 3 more rounds when you already know there's nothing you can do but watch yourself get stomped on for a bit. Even if you do get that extra land, it's too late. Just let me bow out and move on, please.
If you've never played Magic before, but are curious, this is a great place to start. Maybe you'll move on to MTGO or paper Magic, maybe you'll stick with this (again, no idea how robust the community is yet), maybe you'll think it's stupid and move on. Either way, it's the best starting place. No pressure. Just play.

I play a lot of HO games when I'm not in the mood for a 30-hour RPG or the intensity of a first person shooter, but this game makes me wish I put that time into one of those other types of games.  Don't get me wrong. I've played worse HO games than this; but for me the negatives outweigh the positives.
The art is up to the normal standards for HO games, which is fine, although the animations - particularly the facial animations - border on creepy. The puzzles are relatively easy, which is welcome considering that some puzzles in HO games can be rage-inducing. And you can get all achievements in one play-through if that's important to you. There are a few sections that are basically a reverse HO where you have to "investigate" a crime scene and find the locations of interest without knowing what those are, which is an intersting change of pace.
However, the story and premise are laughably bad even for an HO game, and that's saying something. Characters are uninteresting and have no depth at all. And the voice acting.... oh, dear god. "Ear bleeding" might describe how bad it is. Mute the audio for your own sake. And some of the items during the HO segments are misspelled for that item but are still legitimate words, which obviously is really frustrating.
Again, I actually have played a few HO games that are worse than this (but not by much); however, there are a LOT of HO games that are significantly better. Spend your time and money on those.

They actually gave me gold, which can only be used to buy boosters, as a response to me being unable to buy boosters. It's just silly. If you are a fan of Sid Meier's games, you will enjoy Beyond Earth.  The spirit of Alpha Centauri is channeled into a Civ V feel, but there are enough differences to distinguish this from Civ V.  If you enjoy turn-based strategy games and want to colonize an alien world inhabited by alien flora and fauna, this is a good game for you.  However, I think additional expansions will be necessary to realize the full potential of this game.  The webwork tech progression provides for a variety of strategies, but unit type and progression are more restricted than Civ V.  This makes sense if one understands the influence of Alpha Centauri, but Beyond Earth lacks the unit customization its predecessor enjoyed.  Although because each faction 'evolves' as you advance, some unit customization occurs, but Beyond Earth compensates with interesting city developments which offer orbital capabilities, for example.  Sound interesting?  I recommend it.

I remember this game coming out back in 2009. Back when I went to SDCC with my friends. Those of us that visited the Nexon booth or whatever the booth was that gave out a free demo key or disc or something, got to play DFO before it hit the uh, free to play market.

After finishing the story mode and logging in once in a while to do quests I find this game to be very dry and lacking compared to the old Duels of the Planeswalker games. That's not to say that the older games weren't dry and lacking in the first place; Magic Duels takes what was missing in the old games and hams them up but also completely missing what the old game excelled in. You are able to 'create' your own deck in a limited format. As of this writing, only Magic Origins, Zendikar, Gatewatch and Innistrad. It's kind of standard but not really? Did I mention that you only have 6 cards per booster and that you can buy coins to purchase more boosters. You can theoretically get all the cards without paying but... that's is a long, long process.  You're still missing a lot of fun modes from previous games like Archenemy and a more comprehensive 2HG mode. Also, let's not get into the glitches that Stainless Games has maintained over the years.
Unless you're okay with grinding to get new packs to hopefully brew a half decent deck and want to get your free MTG fix, I wouldn't recommend this game.

This game desperately needs some Mobile SAM equivalents. Your units are sitting ducks and there's nothing to counter flying units.
The submarines are also a bit OP as they can attack cities, land units and other ships when they could only even attack other sea based units in the previous Civ game. A good balance would be for them to attack only cities and other ships, not land units.
Beyond Earth is overall a fair follow-up to Civilization's V success. The base game was nothing spectacular and incredibly vanilla. But after Rising Tide and subsequent patches, it's overhalled Diplomacy and added more depth and identity to the game. Communiques show more dialogue and adds more identity to the Civs, movable ocean cities add a new dynamic, artifacts are fun to look for and combine, more art and aesthetic has added identity and lore to the game,and the Spoils of War feature allows for more control over ending wars and negotiation.
With Rising Tide, i rate this game 7/10. The base game I rate 6/10. It's a good game if you basically just one "Civ in Space" that's not just copy and paste. By the next DLC, if it's done right, this game should have a true mythos, lore and identity of it's own with adequate replay value. Which I think this game should focus more on.

But man. The art. It's so stunning and wonderful, a huge part of my gameplay was staring at cgs or sprites in pure awe. As a fellow artist, i felt that artworks in this game were totally my art goals. I'd recommend the game for that alone, and yet it has a very well done story with it. Amazing!
Music isn't really outstanding, although there's one track (which i fondly call Takao's Theme, since it plays for the first time when he shows up) that i love wholeheartedly. What's good it's that common music doesn't get annoying even after playing all the routes.
I liked how gentle and not very vulgar nsfw scenes were. As for someone who doesn't really enjoy nsfw things, it was a huge relief, since i was afraid i'd just have to skip some scenes while sighing annoyed.
What might be not everyone's cup of tea is that the game is ultimately sweet, happy, and cute. It tries really hard to show some drama and action, but the sugar and love overwhelm everything. It is not essentialy a bad thing, and is perfectly enjoyable, just be aware that it's that kind of game where love always wins and is the most important. After money.
As for downsides, it's kinda sad not everything from the vita port of the game was brought to steam. I also felt sad that there's no equal amount of side stories per character. It kinda feels like something is lacking, but i have no idea whether original japanese game has more stories. If it does, i hope they will be implemented eventually.
As the game is now, i don't think i can recommend it for the full price. But when it's discounted, go for it. I spent some quality time playing this game.
Oh yeah, and heroine's mother is the best character in the game. Just sayin'.

This War of Mine is brilliant! This War of Mine had me captivated and wanting more, until things started to get rough. I was unable to finish my first campaign due to one of my characters dieing. - The graphics set the mood of the game.
- Gameplay mechanics (The fact that you have to constantly have to make harsh decisions)
- Making your own story
My Cons

- More options in making your own story (Limit of traps, farms, etc.)

All in all, this game is a beauty. 20$ (roughly) for this game, but man is it worth it, When on sale, you shouldn't even think twice on buying it and giving this game a shot. Like I previously said, this game is 10/10.
Would kill and rob a priest again.

Thank you Square Enix for ruining the last good Stealth game, and turning it into a Dishonored/Bioshock Clone.
With that mess out of the way, I'm a huge fan of the Thief series. Played & loved them all. If you take the whole "nostalgia" thing out of this reboot, it's not a bad game. Gameplay is pretty good. Difficulty settings are unique in that you can customize the difficulty multiple ways however you wish.
It looks very Dishonorish to me though. Im having a hard time getting over that hump because of the nostalgia I hold for the previous games.
The Voice overs are well done, including the new guy doing Garret. He's does the mannerisms well that I can look passed that.
However, I miss the campy NPC voice overs. I want the horrible British accents back! Come on now. The Bear Pits? Remember the Bear Pits?
Well the Bear Pits are sadly not in this game folks. Instead we have decent voice acting for the NPCS... but they're missing the old Thief NPC charm. It's more Bioshock NPC realism... very disappointing for me.
Gameplay feels like Dishonored... sorry it does. The fact that Jump was replaced with "Swoop" eh.. It's not a bad mechanic. I mean it works well for what it does in many situations.  But Jumping is kind of always been in the Thief games. I don't understand why it was taken out for this one.
The UI is a blessing. Very customizable. It doesn't get in the way. It's pretty easy to pick up early on. No steep learning curve here.
Another gripe I have is no sword or attacks of any kind beyond the new & improve Take Down.... again very Dishonorish.. but it works I guess.
Overall I can't really not recommend this game, based on nostalgia woes. It's a reboot after all. But apart from that, it's a decent game. If you get around it NOT being like the original Thief games, you have enjoy this one.

Although it is a good racing game with decent physics and good wheel support, there were some extremely frustrating oversights.  Not allowing car selection in career mode was terrible.  Not being given specifications on the car forced upon you is even worse.  You literally need to either Google the car to see if it's RWD, FWD, or 4WD, or test it on the road prior to every event just you know what the hell you're dealing with.  Pretty substantial oversight for casual players who don't know these car specs off by heart.  I also find it immensely irritating that if your rear wheel, not even just the point of contact, touches a single blade of grass, your entire back end loses all traction.  There is a reason this game includes a rewind feature.  The developers likely knew that practice just wasn't enough and that people were going to find themselves in situations they needed to undo based on major bugs.
If you're into racing games and enjoy cruising through decently high-res well-made scenery.  You should at least have this title in your collection.  If you're looking for a more realistic and less frustrating racing sim, I'd save your money for Project Cars or Assetto Corsa.
If you want a Game that ruins the Fun Factor right of the bat, by throwing you into your very first Match against high experienced players .. go ahead and play it.

This isn't a bad way to burn some time, and players *can* get a good experience out of the game without spending money.  Free players may not be able to compete with the top players (which may or may not be all right as far as some players are concerned),  but they can still enjoy themselves if inability to compete at top tier doesn't trouble them too much.
There is a pattern of finish a timed quest, use the rewards to do the next timed quest, use the rewards from that to help the next timed quest, etc. etc. that is very relentless.  If you're a completionist, be aware you can never "complete" things.  There's always something else to do.  (This is a plus for some players, though.)
If you've played other "freemium" games and haven't felt compelled to spend a lot of money, and are completely fine with letting rewards from limited time quests slip by, then this game is one you should pick up.
I left the game for a time because I was tired of grinding for rewards.  The game can be played enjoyably without feeling the compulsion to grind if you can ignore the rewards system, but I'm not that sort of player.
Though I can't recommend this game for *myself*, I feel that's more a reflection of my preferences as a player than any shortcomings of the game itself, so I am generally positively recommending the game for other players.
Additional comment for money players - I did spend money on the game, and I did have an interaction with customer service, which though a bit on the slow side (still quite reasonable by my standards though) I personally found to be professional, polite, and that resolved my concerns 100% to my satisfaction in the end.  Of course, individual experiences may vary, and I heard there were changes with the company that publishes the game after I stopped playing, but my experience in other freemium games has not nearly been as satisfactory.  I recommend reading up on other recent reviews to see if other players had satisfactory customer service resolutions.

Beyond Gravity's store page does not LIE, per se, but it makes some real stretching-the-truth claims. Calling this a "one button procedurally generated platformer" is sort of stretching a few of those: when you boot it for the first time, it will become clear you're playing a touchscreen mobile title thrown onto Steam haphazardly*, and the entire purpose of the game is "collect space debris to upgrade yourself with powerups", as you leap between constantly-revolving planets, trying to dodge obstacles and leap at just the right time to continue your chain of screw-grabbing without breaking the combo (so you get more parts per cog).
The problem is, claiming this "doesn't get repetitive" is a lie. It's just "click, click, wait, click, click in midair because you have a double jump and need to adjust course, wait, click, wait, wait, click, click..." ad nauseum. As well, you're going to be playing A LOT of abortive runs to get the first powerup. I did about 8 rounds and was only at ~3500 of the minimum-10k currency you need for your first powerup. They get more expensive. If you want something to just zone out with and relax here and there, that's great, this is a great game at the price. I was hoping for something a little more challenging, not just a time-killer.
* I don't care if a game comes from mobile, but I do care when you do it so, so poorly. Menus have no scrollbar and barely respond to a scrollwheel. You're going to be dragging the menu if you want to do anything, always a fun time when you use a mouse.

I've been playing Maplestory since I started Middle School (I'm a second year at High School) and I know that because I'm young I can make a few biases, but Maplestory is not a super, terrible, never-play game. It's a game that's only likeable to people who can make an honest judgement after putting a good few to several hours into the game and get to the in-game point and not just be an ignorant angry reviewer that makes a judgement after the tutorial (seriously, why do people do that xD).
I will not lie, the game has it's pros and cons, some pros would be that the game is really fun to play with friends (especially for boss fights and Party Quests). There are a lot of unique quests, questlines (there is a difference xD), dungeons, and PQs (Party Quests) (These quests usually have stories that can be a little cliche, but, in my opinion, are still good). There is a vast amount of unique playable jobs (Somewhere around twenty to thirty). Each with a playstyle that fits almost any MMORPG player (I will admit, the jobs are really unbalanced but the game is 99% PvE so I tend to disregard that fact but it's out there)
Some cons I will name are what take people away from the game (they're both good and bad reasons). One con that really takes people away is long-leveling (Really, let's be honest, can you name an MMORPG (that's pretty popular) that has a fast leveling system that doesn't get you to max level within 100hrs of gameplay?). Another bothersome (even for me) con is the amount of grinding (Ok haters, you got me there, grinding is a pain, but it's as well popular in a lot of MMORPGs). I know I'm real late with this review but if I can save someone a buck or two...then it's worth the time to write it.  Now, if your style of play is "run and gun" and you really don't care about achievments and/or challenges then stop reading this review because you might actually like this game.
However, if you are like me and love to play to complete challenges and/or acheivements; you need to read this whole review before you purchase the game.  If I saw a review like I'm writing prior to me buying this game...I would NOT have purchased it.
This like a many other games I've commented on in the past; has the potential to be pretty good but sadly falls desparately short of even being decent (again for accomplishing challenges and achievements).
Here are some of my problems with this game.
1.  There is no consistency in how the game plays:
- I've been spotted by enemies who've had their backs to me and I've had enemies look right at me and not see me.  This really affects how you are able to play the game as you never know when your challenge run is going to be blown because the AI did something they weren't scripted to do and this is going to frustrate the crap out of you.
2.  It is clumsy:
- The game is easily glitched (in the AI movement) if you step outside of what the game developers wanted you to do to complete the level/mission.  I've seen guards remain locked into their programmed route regardless of what I try to do to influence it and I've seen guards change their programed route and start doing something different (usually when I want them to stay locked in) .  I've actually seen many instances where the AI have glitched in front of an exit because I tried to get them to deviate from their route so i could escape.  Even seen instances where no matter what I did the guard WOULD NOT go and investigate a noise I was creating....they would turn yellow as if they were going to go investigate and then would turn back white.
- The action indicators ARE HORRIBLE (E for Enter, Q for subdue, etc).  You have to be right on top of these to get them to actually activate and sometimes that don't even work.  Many times I've attempted to "activate" something in the game and had to turn 47 in one specific position just to get the activate to work.  I have had numerous challenge runs ruined because 47 just would not get out a friggen window when I wanted him to; or could not get into a box to hide because "E" just did not want to work or he would not subdue or garotte when I wanted him to which would get me spotted.  Oh, and sometimes you go to garotte someone but instead you engage in hand to hand combat which everyone hears...that is unbelievably frustrating!
3.  It is glitchy:
- Some of the challenges don't pop until you leave the game. I played one level 10-15 times trying to get a challenge to pop.  It was the level where you have to subdue scientists and hide their bodies without being detected.  I believe the number was 15 (you get credit for the take down and for hiding the body so you are supposed to be able to do this with 7 1/2 scientists).  Well I can only get the game to give me credit for 14 and never did see the 15 out of 15 (15/15) indicator actually pop but noticed the next day when I went to try again that the challenge was done.
4.  It's overly frustrating:
- Some of the challenges are just ridiculous.  I'm playing one now where you have to kill everyone in the 3 areas of the level (level with the "Saints") without being spotted; it is so hard to do when take into account all the issues I pointed out above.
5.  It is annoying:
-  I hate games where they put in acheivements that depend on others.  Hitman has one achievement that requires you to have a "friend" create a contract which you have to play.  If you got no one in your friends list that likes this game; you will not be able to complete the achievement.  So I'm going to have to beg one of the friends to suffer through this crappy game just one more time and create a contract for me and if they don't want to...I'm screwed and won't be able to get 100% completion and that is unacceptable!
Now, I will continue to press on until I have completed all the challenges and all the achievements (I hope) because I've become a slave to achievements but I would not recommend this game to anyone that is like me...it is clumsy, the graphics aren't that good, it is not well thought out, it is glitchy as hell, and it has made me want to push my $5,000 computer onto the floor; and that upsets me.  This will probably be the last time I play anything in the Hitman Series.

ArcheBlade blends very attractive, eye-catching character art with extremely lopsided gameplay and an aggressively sharp learning curve into an unappealing result that's pretty hard to swallow. I can't reccomend it to frequent players of what traditionally would be called, "fighting" games, because the format is something extraordinarily different. While gameplay resembles Monday Night Combat in many respects, the total lack of balance between different characters and the need to buy each new one a la carte as they're released won't generate much appeal to players of that variety of game, either. Controlling some of the characters is a clunky and frustrating experience, and getting better at playing is far less about mastering strategy than it is finding something to exploit; something which is a mainstay of retro platformers, but not something that's going to do anyone too many favors in an environment where balance across opposing teams is a make-or-break factor. And, in a nutshell, you can only offset so many flaws with extremely nice Korean comic-style artwork.

For claification sake, I've played this game since Beta and I love the overall animation and playstyle imaged as a 2D platformer. And while I hate to bash something I fell in love with, this is no longer the game that I use to know.
Back in the early days of MapleStory, you had your 4 standard classes: Mage, Warrior, Archer, Thief. Mage and Warrior had 3 subsets each; Archer and Thief had 2 subsets. Finding equipment and hanging out with friends was easy because there was just a few servers and not that many maps. The level cap was set as a crazy 200, but the mindless grinding wasn't so bad, cause you could easily be with your friends and if you found an equip you couldn't use, one of them could and vice versa.
But Maplestory grew. On the surface, you would think this is a good thing; more people = more friends = more equips. True, but Nexon saw this as an excellent opportunity to milk its players through microtransactions.
As the game grew, Nexon built more servers and maps, creating virtual spacial rifts between players. It became more and more difficult to get to the same map as a friend without using a teleport rock (a microtransaction item) or wasting a bunch of time. Nexon created pets, vanity items, world transfers, shops; all for real money. When that wasn't enough, they created more character types, those who couldn't share the cash shop items with the original characters, essentially urging players to rebuy cash items. The new characters also lead to the nerfing of some of the original characters under the guise of "improved" for rebalancing issues. Nexon raised the level cap to 250, milking players for even longer. They created a lottery system called gachapon for in-game items using real money, not to mention special event "lotteries".
Don't play Maplestory. It's not what it use to be. The fun is sucked out of it. Don't waste tons of time and money on it like I did.

This is one of the very rare games that asks the player to first find the problem that he then has to solve.  There are very few of these games that simply drop the player in a box and respect his intelligence enough to allow him to teach himself the rules.
It's all about discovery through creative thinking and a lot of trial and error.
I'm 15 hours in to this game and the revelations haven't stopped coming.  There are seemingly unachievable goals -- tasks that are nearly equal in difficulty to Spelunkys challenges.  And meanwhile, there are deepening mysteries that the game doesn't confront me with but allows to sneak in to my mind.
I can't get enough.  The perfect discovery game.
Many people will be put off.  This game is hard.  It uses something very rarely seen in games of any kind, and that's inductive reasoning.
Deduction is a common mechanic, but successfully pulling off induction is a very rare and special thing.
