In sum: Actually a fun Civ game, but needs some improvement, and patching may cause problems.
(Base game, no DLC)
CivBE is in a sense, Civ V in space.  But it really feels like a prototype of game concepts, not a completely polished game.  A lot of time was spent on the visuals and sound, and the core Civ gameplay is intact.  If you understand Civ V, you can jump right in, the new concepts will start to make sense.
Some of it is brilliant.  Some should have been obvious and ought to be backported to Civ V, such as auto-renew trade routes.  It's still exciting to see battles with the equivalent of Civ V end game units, still satisfying to crush your enemies.  There is something very satisfying about the first time you kill a siege worm, and I rather like the quest concept in the game.
But this gets to the problems.  The AI is passive compared to the bloodthirsty Civ V AI.  No improvements to AI strategy are here (I had an enemy put a rover unit in a lake next to a city for no reason at all).
The affinities are a great concept, and a offshoot of the ideologies in Civ V BNW, but instead of committing to a single course, you research determines your affinity, letting you move up in whatever affinities you wish.  But affinities have a major flaw: there is no progression.  Only leaps and bounds.  The affinities have replaced unit upgrades, meaning a single tech could push you up 3 affinity levels, giving you massive instant unit upgrades.  This can be done right in the middle of a war, turning the tide sort of randomly.  The victories are also heavily affinity  based, meaning if you choose the wrong affinity, you might not be able to get the win you want.
The tech web is a good concept, just needs a bit of revision.  I rather like the not-so-linear approach to technology, and I hope with the expansion and later patches this improves.
The ability to customize your country is also a nice idea, letting you choose your own bonuses rather than presets like in Civ V.
A serious problem, however, with all of Firaxis's latest games is present here: patching and support.  Like the worst moments of Civ V, CivBE patches are known to introduce problems, and at this moment, there is a game-breaking bug introduced last week that is pretty much only solved by buying the expansion.  Firaxis has a tendency to release unannounced forced patches, and does not properly test them before release.  If Civ V is any indicator, bugs have remained in that game for five years without being addressed, and I hope in the long-term that they do not repeat this behavior for this game.  So there is no guarantee that if this game works one day, that it will continue to function properly the next day.
For all of the negative, which there is no shortage of complaints on this game, however, I very much enjoy it and I am looking forward to losing a lot of time with it.  Do not expect Alpha Centauri II, and don't expect a revolutionary new game.  This is a descendant of Civ V, different enough that it could not be reasonably called a mod, but similiar enough.  It is just a different take on the concept of Civ, and hopefully with a little time and effort from Firaxis, will get better.

When I bought this game, I hadn't expected it to have SO much content. I have a little over eight hours in and there's still much more for me to enjoy.
When your mother asks you to run an errand for her, you end up in the Yoshiwara pleasure district, where the men of the island you live on offer their bodies to women in exchange for money. At one of the more famous brothels, they mistake you for the daughter of a wealthy merchant, and invite you to pick out one of their courtesans for the night. And purely by accident, you happen to have a lot of money on you; enough to buy a dreamy night of pleasure...
Depending on who you pick for the night, the story diverges from there as you explore your romance with this beautiful courtesan. There are six guys to choose from, all with different and distinct personalities, and playing their route will give you background information on them. They all have dreams they wish to achieve, despite their situation, and maybe you can help them with that...
+ Lots and lots of content! Sequel stories, date scenes, etc
+ Many romance options to choose from, not all with stereotype personalities
+ Intimate, steamy scenes; definitely 18+ (though the art is not explicit)
+ All characters get a bit of depth
+ Gorgeous artwork
+ Almost impossible to get a bad ending with the man of your choice
- Horrendous editing for the English version, including but not limited to: homophones, bad translations, messed-up character names, weird punctuation, typos, etc.
- Only two or maybe three background songs
- Rushed art here and there
- A weird focus on the main protagonist being a pure & innocent virgin
- The protagonist in general is very passive and weepy
- Some creepy sexual behaviour, but not in all routes
- If you put the game on full-screen, it becomes terribly pixelated
In the end, I would recommend this game if you're into visual novel/otome/romance games but ONLY if you wouldn't be bothered by the terrible editing. For me, that's the worst part of the game. Unlike many of the other reviewers here, I never played other versions of this game but the PC version, so I was not bothered by the lack of animation in the character art, for example.
At its core, this game is a romantic & steamy adventure. All the romance options get some manner of depth when you play through their route, and not all of them turn out to be the stereotypical man you had expected them to be. Of course, I fell head over heels for the stoic intellectual, Kagura, though the manager of the store (Iroha) also has one heck of a story.
Just... maybe don't buy this game at full price. Content-wise, it might be worth it, but in terms of editing for the English version and lack of animated character art & voice acting, it's not. Oh well. I did end up buying it at full price myself anyway

I've never left a review for a game on here (that I can remember), but after playing through every route the steam version has to offer I feel compelled to. This game was a happy accident, and is now one of my favorite otome games ever. If you enjoy visual novels and are willing to read something more mature then this game will definitely be the better buy than the mobile version.
-Great storylines per route. They all tend to interact with each other well without being too repetitive.
-Great characters. I honestly don't dislike any of the cast. Yet they're each unique.
-Music is great. I wish I just had the soundtrack.
-Artwork is beautiful (even if some expressions can get a tad wonky)
-In terms of content, you actually get a lot in this package. Keep in mind on mobile platforms each route costs roughly $3.00, plus different price tags for most of the other bonus content.
-Fun and cheesy writing (also a con XD )
-The backdrop of the story is actually really friggin' dark when you think about it.
-Promotes a proactive heroine. The men are trapped in Kikuya and can't see you. If you want the man, YOU have to chase after them.
-Doesn't shame sexuality and actually promotes it.
-Little details from character designs, to the rules of how service in Kikuya takes place, are decently accurate mirrors of Oiran life back during the Edo period (with some creative liberties, of course).
-No voiceovers, which is a CRYING SHAME. This game was originally made for the PSP or PS Vita which sported voice acting from a top-notch cast, including the giant known as Kosuke Toriumi. Those who also have a basic knowledge of Japanese will miss out on furthur understanding since we have to rely only on the translated text.
-Despite this being a port of the mobile version, we don't get the sprite animations the movile versions have. So basically we got cheated in terms of ports.
-Cheesy writing in some of the scenes. Also some relatively odd choices in editing.
-Choices don't really change the actual story. You might get a different reaction but the plot doesn't really diverge.
-PSVita version has another character that we don't: Keiji.
-Price, despite the content you get with it, isn't very competitive. I bought this on sale for $19.99 or something like that, and I felt that price was much more fair. You can buy the infamous Hakuouki and Sweet Fuse for much cheaper than this and both games offer easily twice the content. Unless you have extra money hanging around I'd wait for a sale.
The Men of Yoshiwara immediately caught my attention because of the unique premise. During the Edo period of Japan (the period of isolation before the Meiji restoration), there were segregated pleasure quarters in designated "Flower Towns" where prostitution was legalized with very strict rules. Yoshiwara was one of those towns. Here
(NOT Geisha. There are differences), or courtesans as the game calls them entertain clients with similar skill sets to Geisha but also sell their bodies for a night of pleasure and companionship. Basically ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a heart of gold story.
Usually in stories revolving around the Floating World the women are the center piece, but this game turns the idea on its head by putting men in the role of the Oiran. In this game's case it also comes with a bit of a tragic story: men are apparently very rarely born. As such, all men born on your island are automatically sold to the pleasure district in order to help women have babies. Yeah...these guys are basically breeding tools. Hence my point about a dark backdrop.
This also shows us male characters in a more vulnerable light. Usually in otome games men are much more...powerful. More overwhelming. After all they're the stars so they should stand out. But here they're Oiran, and it's illegal for them to freely chase the heroine. So we get to see males still exhibit their masculinity but also be vulnerable. Some of their stories are actually pretty heartbreaking. You still get the scenes where they take the lead and teach the heroine about "love" and dominate, but for the most part this vulnerability of them being trapped and exploring typically "feminine" tropes is a side to these characters we don't see often. And it's a very enjoyable change of pace!
That being said every game has its hang ups. Certain portions of the game do read like a cheesy (badly written) romance novel. Which can make this HYSTERICAL to play with friends reading aloud. However sometimes it does drive you out of the immersion (those who played Iroha's route will know what I mean: "His whitefish fingers."
Or even "I accepted his wedge." Wedge? Really? ). On top of this the player's choices really don't change how the story plays out much. You only gain points towards one of two possible outcomes.I'm actually a little bumed there's no bad ending possibility because in this scenario there's PLENTY abound that could have happened.
That said, the story's unique and the characters are just downright adorable. Iroha and Kagerou won me over, but my heart ached for each guy. The Heroine is also surprisingly progressive! She's usually the one who makes the first step in initiating actions in the storyline. It's one of the few games that made me want to play through every possible outcome.
Huge thank you to the developers for localizing the game in English! And thank you for giving us a complete package on Steam. I HATE the nickel and dime method mobile otome games enforce. Definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun otome game to get lost in. Just beware: it's rated M for a reason ;D

Today I played through my favorite game from last year, Starseed Pilgram. I've been meaning to replay this for a while, but when the game's developer, Droqen, was a guest on one of my favorite gaming podcasts the other day (Video Games Hot Dog), I knew that now was the time…
What makes this game so great? Primarily, it's the lack of tutorial, or any instruction beyond the very basic controls. That's it—no explanation of your objective (or if there even IS an objective), or how to achieve it. But if you can resist the temptation to look up an explanation on the web, the experience of figuring out the game's systems for yourself is irreplaceable, and it is forever YOURS.
That being said, this is still a fun and challenging game to replay, even without that initial experience of discovery. The music is procedural and relaxing, and the game's mechanics change enough as you play so that you are required to keep changing your strategy. This will probably not be the last time I play this game, which is quite rare.

Before I start, I'm abit of a stealth game nut.  It's one of my favorite genres to play.  The Thief series has been one of my favorites.  When a game gives a stealth approach toward playing it, I almost always choose it.
This new iteration of Thief is not nearly as bad as all the review sites will have you believe;  It's actually pretty good entertainment.  Is it better than The Dark Project or The Metal Age?  Of course not, but frankly we're never going to get amazing games like those ever again.  It's time to move on.  Or don't.  That's fine.  You can still acquire those games through Good Old Games or Steam.  This is just as good as Deadly Shadows, maybe even alittle better (I literally played through Thief 3 the week before this came out, so it's still very fresh in my mind)
Is the story good?  Meh.  It's ok at best.  I do like all the hints at the factions we were so use to seeing before.
How about the level design?  It's abit linear, yes.  Very pretty though.  There is an asylum level halfway through that is just as creepy and atmospheric as Shalebridge Cradle ever was, and is much more terrifying, imo.
Is the immersion good?  I think so, yes.  I love how much you see of him using his hands.  I think it really helps draw you in to First Person games.
Is the sound quality as good as the other Thiefs?  Kinda varies.  For the most part its great, but sometimes certain lines are spoken really quietly or the audio and animations aren't synched up.  Currently there is a bug where dialogue between npcs simply repeats over and over.  Also nobody says taffer.  :(  Disappointing.
My one major gripe with it would have to be Garret's visual appearance.  I HATE THAT MASK/SCARF THING he wears.  He looks like a gothic frog.  I would pay money for a dlc skin that made him look more like a classic version.  I would also pay money for a dlc that used Stephen Russel as a voice-over.  The new guy (Romano Orzari) doesn't do a bad job though.  He just doesn't feel as emotive as Russel did.
You really connected to Russel's Garret; probably what helped was because he narrated the story inbetween levels.  You don't get that in this new Thief.  He just seems like he's brooding a lot.
That being said, I am enjoying myself by playing on Master with waypoint markers turned off.  I only use focus to check for traps since it drains so fast on this difficulty.  I really like the toggle mini-map.  I really like the side-missions.  Love all the different arrows, even if some of them are just one-use tools.  Visually, the game is gorgeous.
There seems to be ALOT of fanboy hate for this game, and I can understand it.  Just look at all the positive reviews people are giving for it and the amount of people voting down on them.  Sorry guys, I've learned to appreciate games for what they are, for their own merits, not for what I wanted them to be or wished they played more like.
Is the new Thief a worthy tribute to the series? Yes.
Could it have been better?  Of course.
Is it worth playing?  I think so.  I'm enjoying it.

Thoughts (after playing through four routes):
If you're to buy this game, don't expect an intricate plot or more depth and development to the romances like the romances found originally on console/PC. This PC version (and the Vita version) was based off the original otome game on IOS and Android which like many mobile otome games, were designed for playing during the trips to school/work on public transport - so it was made to be brief. Despite this, I still enjoyed playing the routes, they were a lighthearted from other heartbreaking/heartwrenching otome games I have played and it was interesting seeing the different motivations and reasons for being in Kikuya from the different courtesans.
Art usually plays a large amount in persuading me to purchase an otome game and this game has really pretty art in the character sprites (though it is a shame that they have removed the emofuri animations found in the original version of the game), CGS (especially Hanabusa's ones--being the newest) and trading cards. But to be honest, what else can you expect from a big otome game company.
There were a handful of times I have smiled/chuckled whilst playing the game especially during banter between the courtesans but they can't hold anything against some of the 'iffy' translations in the game.....e.g referring to a male's p**is as a 'wedge' xD
Unfortunately i'm currently grinding through Hayabusa's route - 'unfortunate' mostly due to personal preferences against the childhood friend route in otome games^^; However, overall I quite enjoy this game though I do wish that there was a 'skip read' option just to make replaying routes to get the alternate ending easier (though to be honest, it would only affect the last chapter) and an 'Autoplay' option like most otome games but once more, these are mostly due to personal preference.
I hope they'll introduce more characters (such as Kenji Ito currently not on this version) as well as sequels. The former probably having little chance of happening with the upcoming release of The Men of the Yoshiwara: Ohgiya (fingers crossed it'll be released on Steam! ^-^)

Picked this game up on a sale $2.49, and just got around to playing it. I started two playthroughs - one to get a "feel" for the game, the other I actually got around to finishing. Did I enjoy it? Yes. Will I be replaying it? Not going to be my first choice.
For the TL;DR: interesting little game if you want a distraction, but definitely wait for a sale to come along to buy this. Otherwise... no.
Basically the game places you in a Facebook-like interface where you make friends, post statuses, organize events, and go to work. It's a juggling act to keep your stats up to get yourself off the spaceship before the "days" are up. There are some interesting concepts, like making friends, messaging the right people, the "etiquette" of making and meeting new friends, and at first there are a few stories to be told. In my playthroughs my character even had their significant other "stolen" from them by another "friend". The concept is a very novel one, and does a fairly good job parodying how social networking works.
However, it gets very tedious by the time you start hitting the "endgame", and once you have secured yourself a way off the shuttle there really isn't a motivation to play anymore as the stories are limited and the jokes begin to wear thin, nor is there much new content. At the price right now ($9.99), it's not worth picking up, so be patient if you want to give this game a go.

is a collaboration between One More Level and Artifex Mundi. Many of the mechanics, sound effects, and puzzles are borrowed from the 9 Clues series, and I'm sorry to say it's in a way that just isn't as well done.
The game has an unfinished quality at times due to places where the vocals and text don't match up, don't make sense, and/or have timing issues. Even worse there are places where the text for items doesn't match the actual item, such as a bowl that is actually a bow, a pen that is actually a pencil, and a glasses case that is actually just the glasses. The story also lacks cohesion and is sloppy in a way that's often confusing. These flaws end up making the places where the gameplay has the typical hidden object puzzle adventure game idiosyncrasies more apparent and annoying. For example, fire extinguishers are useless if you can't get to them. A crowbar would totally be the best tool to open a stuck can of paint. Music and sound effects that don't fit – for example, using sounds that are clearly dogs for wolves – round off the unfinished feel.
I still am giving this game a recommend for those who are devoted Artifex Mundi fans like myself. For those new to the genre, there are many better titles to choose from.

Every good detective needs a vacation every once and awhile, however criminals are always around to ruin the day. In
you play a detective who just wants some time off but finds herself entangled in a murder mystery at the hotel where she’s staying. This hidden object game offers fun gameplay mixed with an intriguing mystery. Cut off from outside help, can our heroine solve the mystery without ending up the next in a body bag? She can with our help!
On her way to a nice vacation, the protagonist finds herself run off the road near the hotel where she is staying. A blizzard is also rolling in and as she finds herself in the shelter of the hotel she also finds a murderer on the loose. It’s time to question witnesses and dig deep into the case which leads our detective down the slippery slope of gambling and corruption as not everyone is as nice as they seem. Overall I enjoyed the story, it had a few plot twists which I enjoyed. My only issue was how people were dying or getting hurt but the main character was always fine. Sure, she got kidnapped or knocked out a couple of times but it was odd that the murderer who is fine with killing people never just killed the detective to get her out of the way. Also, the main character herself was smart but never had a weapon or protected herself very well, but that’s a minor peeve.
This title is a hidden object game, meaning it’ll have hidden object scenes and puzzles mixed in. A unique feature that this game has is a detective mode, you’re given a scene where a crime happened and you have to find the clues. Once you do, you piece together a timeline on what happened at the scene to figure things out. Some might not like this feature but I personally love it, I find it fresh and a nice change of pace. This isn’t the first time this has been in an Artifex Mundi game either, so I personally hope it’s used more often. My only issue with the gameplay is that it’s very easy, I found myself solving a few puzzles by accident even. I could have also used with more hidden object scenes as well.
The graphics are great in this game. All of the hidden object scenes were easy on my eyes and the resolution was great. The only flaw would be the character animations, there wasn’t a lot of blinking and they looked somewhat lifeless. But the backgrounds were great and the animation on items was fine. The audio was good as well, fitting background music and sound effects. The voice acting left a lot to be desired, while they weren’t bad actors they could have probably used better direction. But I do appreciate a hidden object game with full voice acting.

I would say that Crime Secrets: Crimson Lily is an independent sequel of the 9 Clues series. Indeed, the game feature also a female detective that will make her investigation in order to solve a case. And independent because 9 Clues series and Crime Secrets series? are not made by the same developer and are each unique.
As I warned you previously there isn’t any additional story: only one short main story.
For the story : you are a female detective on vacation at the mountains but as soon as she arrived her vacation are shortened by a grim murder. She will then lead an investigation and try to stop that insane murderer that freeze its victims to death. She will slowly discover that the city wasn’t a peaceful place at it seems.
The game has two graphics issue that I’ll talk in the (*) point at the end. And you need to know that the game is set in a surrealistic story as well as some puzzles are a little surrealistic.
As every Artifex Mundi game you can move freely in different area (the surrounding area of the hotel) and need to solve some puzzles and find all objects in hidden objects scenes. The game has (different difficulties? and) a guest feature: every one of the family can play an independent save and resume the game where they left it. When you first play the game you’ll have a notebook where you have all your objectives as well as all your notes. You also have a map to not get lost and you may be able to fast travel with it too. Adding to that you’ll have a hint button that will help you in many ways but be warned that you may not use it in any puzzle or hidden object scene (HOS) or investigation scene (IS). Hints can be used to know where you need to go, where is the next interaction or to show an object or clue in an HOS or IS or to skip a puzzle. To conclude this part, you’ll also have an inventory to store useful items through your journey.
Puzzles are fine, different and perhaps short. There is only the classical Hidden objects scene (HOS) as far as I remember. The one where you need to find objects hidden with the help of their name. Colored names mean that you have to interact directly with the scene or use an item in the scene.
As some other Artifex Mundi game : you’ll have to find collectibles scattered across the game. (Origamis and snowflakes) The only bad thing is you can’t track them (how many you’ve found) and can’t see them after (like a showcase) …
One of the very good thing of this game is that there are 2 unique features you won’t find in any other Artifex Mundi game (except some games) :
•	You’ll have several Investigation Scene (IS) to solve in two steps. (a remastered version of the IS of 9 clues series)
•	And a smart combine or interact feature for some specific items (same as Grim Legends 3)
The first step of an Investigation scene is to find every evidence hidden in the scenery. After that your second step is to place the evidence in the right order: that’s a linear puzzle where you need to order each tile to have the correct shape. After that you unlock a cut scene where you see how the events have happened.
As I said earlier you’ll find several items where you’ll be able to interact with in your inventory. They are marked by a white plus. When you click at them you zoom in the item. They always need to be interacted and combined with another or several items to have the final item.
(*) :
The game has a few pixelated cut scenes. (one or two?) And have an annoying issue that occurs in some parts of the game: when you pick an item or a collectible the scene doesn’t change. (you got the item or collectible but you can still see it in the scene)
(#) :
First there is an issue with an achievement: “Hidden Object Master” may be granted long before you finish the story!
Now let’s get back to the missable achievements :
In addition to no skip or use any hint while playing every puzzles and Hidden objects scenes, there are a few more missable achievements. One ask you to not skip any cut scene during the whole story.
Finally, the last two one require you to find every snowflake and origami of the game.

I remember waking up as a kid, excited and eager to start up my dad's computer, hopping into the world of Maplestory, ready to take on whatever the game was going to throw at me that day. Needless to say, I was hooked. The cartoony yet oddly satisfying visuals, the huge world that was set before me, the deceptively simple class system, all things that I adored about it. For a while, I couldn't get enough of this game. It was my first MMO ever, and, to this day, probably still my favorite. Nothing comes close to the fun I had while killing mushrooms in the starting zone, slaying Balrogs on airships, destroying robots in Ludi, and finally, conquering Zakum. I made many friends, joined a slew of guilds, and mostly, just had fun. That's what videogames were about back when I played Maplestory, and in a sense, it seems like they've kind of lost that recently, although that's a different topic entirely. Maplestory now seems to be much more oversaturated in terms of classes and things to do, actually making it an overwhemingly experience rather than an extremely enjoyable one, one that I had when I played. Needless to say however, I still had a HUGE amount of fun with this game, and is hands-down one of the best experiences, if not THE best, I've had in gaming. I cannot speak to the community now, but when I was playing, it was a bunch of generous and fun loving people, one's that were willing to help others when they needed it. I miss Maplestory, specifically old Maplestory, even more specifically v.066, when things were simpler and I had a bunch of NX to spend on a different hairstyle.
I miss you Maplestory.

My decks keep disappearing, just happened for the 9th time in a few days.  Really, this entire product is not properly implemented.)
2)  Loads of players already have played a lot, so they're running around in multiplayer, even deranking to kill new players for easy gold.  You can't really win in multiplayer unless you spend a lot on cards, and == multiplayer is where the gold is at ==.   (If you do want utility commons, that still means buying loads of packs until you can fill out your commons collection.  So really no escape from buying packs.)
3)  Limited card library.  There are not a lot of viable decks, and you can't craft specific cards, so A) play gets repetitive after a while, B) it takes a while (or money) to build your collection to the point you can build one of those viable decks.  So you really do have a pay-to-win / grind-to-win for what's a rather limited game.
4) Mods ban people on forums that don't like what they've done, and delete critical posts (even polite ones).  Source - looked at Magic: 2015 to see how people reacted to Magic: Duels as a successor, looked on Magic: Duels forums and noticed certain posts had been deleted.  Well, really.
==
Although there are a load of things holding this game back (no second main phase, really?), even though the developers are pretty unresponsive (not responding to lack of second main phase, really?), mods apparently act shady, loads of iffy things - if you're a dyed-in-the-wool Magic fan, or just sick of Hearthstone or whatever, go ahead and pick this game up.  Why choose the lesser of two evils (Hearthstone) when you can choose the greater of two evils (Magic: the Gathering).  You can have some fun, etc.
But if you start thinking about spending money, take a good hard look at the developers' lack of support for the game, the limited meta, overbearing mod actions - it's just really not good.
Note - there ARE some nice things for new players, like you start off with a load of cards and lands that produce multiple mana types.  Still leaves you dead against anyone with any kind of bank (whether money or time invested) but enough to play around some, anyways.

It's pretty rare to see two Artifex Mundi in the upcoming list and to see a game released two weeks before the Steam scheduled one. However, I was waiting for Crime Secrets as it was previewed on All About Casual Game. And you're used to me being a huge fan of Artifex Mundi's catalogue, so I'm buying these games pretty quickly, as the studio is also doing interesting discounts.
In Crime Secrets, you're a private investigator, ready for snowy vacations, when you discover a sheriff being frozen to death at the gate of your hotel, when you just saw him a few minutes ago very much alive. Given the fact that the police will not come before a lot of time (because someone is clearly setting a trap), you began your investigation.... Between Susan, the hotel owner and recently widowed, Peter, a young man, David, one of the workers and John, the armed reporter, which is a friend, a future victim and the enemy?
The story is well-written, as you didn't expect the twist in the end. However, it's just disappointing also to see many efforts rewarded by nothing (or in other words, the story is taking the direction you don't want). But I've really enjoyed the game.
The gameplay is quite the standard one: items to find and to use, to modify and to combine, puzzles to solve and hidden objects scenes to clear. The latter come under two forms: the traditional list of words and the classic list of shapes (though here, you see clearly what you need and not a silhouette). Before describing the feature already present in 9 Clues 2, I just wanted to point that the puzzles are too easy. I don't mind some casual difficulty but I was under the impression that in two clicks, you was the king of the puzzles. I understand better why I didn't see a Solve all puzzles without skipping achievements.
You have also the detective mode: you arrive on a scene and you have to click on points of interests (revealed in a list the bottom of the screen once discovered). Then, you have to put each event in their correct timing (with one or two colored lines on the tiles helping that task). Once solved, the main character will explain what happened while the game is showing it, with characters being black silhouettes. It's a feature that I've liked since I've played it but it's just a shame that it's not used more in the game.
Add to that the hunt for hidden snowflakes and origamis and you'll have a complete game (apart that it's not a CE but I'm not missing this specifity). Besides, you will see that a origami isn't in the same scene as a snowflake and that despite the beginning of the game having these in each scene, it's not like that at the end of the game. It made me sweat a little when I couldn't see any of them (some origamis are hard to spot), so you bet that I was relieved when I saw the achievements for finding all of them unlock.
The graphics are also very nice, as usual. Contrasting to the murder context, everything is very bright and colorful. The soundtrack is also great, very fitting. And as usual, the voice acting is quite nice.

I've just read a few reviews and there seems to be quite the back and forth between the people who think this is minimalist indie wank and those who are lauding it for similar reasons that this game caught me. I would simply approach this game in the same way you approach a game like Tetris or Bejewelled (but the game's not easy! The Bad: Awkward, unneeded 3rd person moments of climbing. The story feels flat and the characters aren't fleshed out at all.  When exploring the open world hub called "The City" there are loading screens everywhere. That being said, they go by pretty quickly or are hidden via a QTE event. Audio problems ranging from guards repeating their lines immediately after speaking, being able to hear them from a great distance away as if they are right next to you, or absolutely no audio at all during cut scenes (each of these things happened randomly at some point).  Removal of the dagger is a turn off for some but as I normally ghost anyway it was not a problem. The size of the levels vary from linear to nonlinear at times.
The Good: The stealth is amazing and it's exhilarating to dash from one shadow to the next as you sneak around. The game itself looks beautiful and, in my opinion, really captures a steam punk Victorian London feel. The game mechanics steer you towards the stealth route (as it should) by removing the dagger (though really you can still use arrows if you wish to kill). The guards are not stupid and while you can take one on no problem, alerting several generally results in a death. That being said, an extremely patient player can take down all guards or slip past them entirely. The light and shadows look fantastic and work wonderfully as a stealth mechanic, though don't expect to be invisible in the shadows on harder difficulties when a guard walks right up to where you are. Speaking of difficulties, there are a ton of customizable options for tailoring your game to your desired difficulty. The game itself has a solid length and lasts even longer if you do all the side missions, which are probably the best part of the game. A ton of loot is hidden in the hub world as well as every story and side mission, including special collectables like paintings, rings, and plaques (can you complete all the sets?). The new focus mechanic is a welcome addition allowing you to view interactable objects such as loot, traps, and things that can be opened. That being said this new mechanic is not necessary to complete the game and can be turned off entirely. While the levels are not as big as in previous Thief games they still offer multiple ways of reaching objectives. Lastly there are upgrades you can purchase throughout the game for your focus abilities and trinkets that increase things like max health or decrease resource costs.
While this may not be the classic Thief game many were hoping for, it is still a great game in it's own right. Aside from the audio problems (which may be fixed with future patches) the game gave me no problems and was enjoyable from start to finish. Though it may not be a perfect game, any fan of the stealth genre should enjoy Thief. I personally give it a 7/10. If you are on the fence I hope this helps!

Disclaimer: My very large 388 hours was mainly me leaving my PC running after getting bored and wandering off to read books or whatever. I've actually "played" the game for a fraction of that time.
I have always loved the Civ's, which is why it's very difficult to vote this one down.
With a £25 price tag on top of the base game, it's difficult to justify this purely because of it's complete lack of replayability.
The good:
New factions. This is mainly just because it's something different to try out. I used to play a lot of the SMAC and alternative history faction mods so this was right up my alley.
New biomes. The unique world quests were a nice touch, and the biome-specific alien behaviours were exciting to sink my teeth in to. It really changes how you play each game and that lends to replayability.
The bad:
The diplomacy system, even with the recent patch, was a sad failure at correcting the initial system. It's better, but it didn't quite "get there". Yes, there more buttons to press, more things to do... but it's still just as irrelevant as the old system was. Simply put: you work to please your neighboring AI, raising respect and fear... and they declare war anyway? Might aswell go full military build from turn 1.
The dev's have done difficulty... wrong. In my view, handicaps != difficulty level. Difficulty level, for civ should equate to smarter, more agressive, less compromising AI. The AI shouldn't simply have "better stuff" than you. Yes, people have said that they've beaten this game on top difficulty. No, they didn't say it was fun. Just look at SC2's AI for a good example. The AI there executes unit build orders and issues battlefield commands to ultra tight timing and precision, but crucially, never actually cheats. It's more fun and rewarding, win or lose, to compete on a level playing field against a better opponent. It's never fun to beat an opponent with inbuilt advantages over you - all this shows is that the game is too easy to exploit/AI is dumb.
No diplomatic victory conditions. Remember Alpha Centauri, with the UN victory? Bribing players for votes? If you wanted to win diplomatically, you had to play a really cleaver game of plate-balancing to keep all the AI's on your side, while not upsetting any of their rivals too much, and it was really fun. In Rising Tide, there is little reward for keeping the AI happy, since it's far far easier (and safer) to build up a strong military and just crush them.
The ugly:
Hybrid affinities. They just aren't very useful. Sure, they look cool, but strategicially they don't seem to have any personality of their own despite what the dev's claim. I think that the hybrid affinities should instead have been "more" affinities, with more strategic resources to support them.
Ocean cities. It's fun at first, but after the initial buzz you begin to realise that sea cities are just... strategically weak, and boring, all at once. It's too hard to expand your territory to get at the resources you need, and there are no defensive terrain features to exploit (mountains, etc...). My game with the NSA was me in the middle of the sea all by myself (save the occasional AI unit wandering by) with almost zero interaction with the other AI's who were all land based. Forever alone.
Conclusion:
It appears that the dev's do not place any value in good AI for this game, and I feel that this was a grave mistake. With a bit of personality - faction agendas, personal feuds, political backstabbing, secret alliances, taboo strategies (where are the atrocities?) - the game could be a vibrant breeding ground for creative play, and I would be coming back to it again and again. Sadly however, it's effectively a selection of small, shiny-looking and well marketed mods created for a quick cash-in on the fans for little return.

If you're interested in "metahorror" - the fourth-wall breaking, game-is-alive bag of tricks found in other games like Pony Island, Undertale and Eternal Darkness, IMSCARED is worth a look.
The full release version of a free game that surfaced on the internet in 2012 called "ImScared: A Pixelated Nightmare", IMSCARED's Steam version contains 2-3 hours of start-stop gameplay in which it repeatedly crashes, "ends", or cheats in some way to force you out of the game and restart it.
While the stop-and-go gameplay is jarring at first, it's eventually desensitizing. Thankfully, IMSCARED adjusts itself with this in mind, and drops the shock-seeking act in favor of unique puzzle solving that intertwines what you do inside the game with what you do outside of it. You'll transition from being a victim of IMSCARED's shenanigans to learning how to use them to your advantage, but despite gaining control you'll still feel uncomfortable not knowing what's going to happen next.
The implementation isn't flawless by any means - the uphill climb to the game's ending may prove more frustrating than frightening for some, and certain sequences may result in death desensitization. In certain places, IMSCARED is a little too particular about what you have to do in order to progress, and there is potentially a great deal of backtracking required to collect everything required to complete the game.
Even so, the feeling of playing a game that's actively plotting against you is done to a T in IMSCARED, and if that's a feeling you'd like to chase - especially if Pony Island/Undertale whet your appetite - then IMSCARED delivers.
(A word of warning, currently Windows 10 users are reporting rampant problems with the game's file-creation mechanic - which is required to progress and ultimately complete the game. Avoid if you're a Win10 user, until/unless that functionality is patched.)

Custom difficulty is ABSOLUTELY the way to play this game. Put it on the Master setting, turn off focus, and set options that make it a 0 kill, 0 knockout, 0 detection scenario. This may sound like it would be too hard, frustrating, or even boring, but it's far from the truth. THIS is why Thief has been getting less-than-good reviews: the reviewers are ploughing through on the normal difficulty setting to get their ♥♥♥♥ing review out the door, and with all the helpful options enabled, a lot of what makes this game great gets screwed up.
What you quickly realize playing a Custom setting of over 700 (there is an achievement for this) is that the maps were expertly crafted to accommodate this play style. There is always a solution that does not require any sort of confrontation, and it is this type of solution, whether it be quick-dashing from small shadow to small shadow, putting out lights, or creating distractions, that keeps the game thrilling in every engagement. In this way, every piece of loot is a challenge, whether it be attempting a quick lockpick while a patrolling guard is approaching or stealing a jewel from a tabletop right underneath somebody's nose.
Meticulously blackjacking enemies and reducing the level's population one-by-one is much easier and robs the game of that constant sense of tension that works so well. When the enemies are a CONSTANT threat and you give yourself no ways to engage them, Thief is pure gold.
It may be harder this way, and it will certainly be a longer game, but Thief is meant to be taken slowly, one area at a time, each room like a puzzle to be worked out.
Perhaps Eidos Montreal's biggest mistake was not having enough confidence in their own gameplay and dumbing Thief down for the masses, hoping for a universal appeal. A hardcore, old-school type game might have gotten more attention in the press and more praise from the people who devoted some time to it.

This is the 2nd best game I've played in 2015, behind Life is Strange.
I just have to bring this up, good job 11 bit for not making it another stupid survival zombie game.
Pros:
+ The crafting system is awesome.
+ The looting system is awesome.
+ The many different ways of playing the game, do you want to make moral choices and not kill people for supplies or do you want to murder and plunder because war is hell?
+ The combat system is great.
+ Different characters have different traits and things they enjoy, for example 1 character is a coffee drinker and is good at trading(Good at trading=able to get more and give less in trades) and 1 character likes smoking and is a good cook, so you keep cigarettes at the ready and have them make the food etc...
+ Not 30FPS locked, making this a pro because of the idiotic amount of developers that say "Meh.. it's 2.5D, LETS LOCK IT AT 30!"
+ Great sound effects and music.
+ Again, great variety of how you want to play the game.
+ Tons and tons of replay-ability.
+ Great graphics for it's genre, and the actual art style is awesome.
+ Can do several play throughs with different sets of characters, great for completionists to survive the game with all the different sets of characters.
+ Different items gets their value changed throughout your game based on their availability, for 5 days maybe the price of meat sky rockets up in price and another time maybe the price of cigarettes or wood sky rockets up in price for a few days, making them great to trade with.
+ The fact that you need to bring items with you when you scavenge at night is good, you can't just blaze through a house or something, sometimes you need to bring equipment to break a chain on a door, sometimes you need a lockpick etc...
+ Sometimes people will knock on your door for help, so you can chose to not help them or give them one of your valuable bandages(just an example) in hopes of them maybe returning one day with a gift as a thank you.
+ 100% of their DLC's proceeds goes to a charity helping war victims.
Cons:
- The mood mechanic of the game is not that great in my opinion. Yes I understand that these are normal humans like you and me who are thrown in the middle of a war, they are not soldiers, they are normal everyday people, so yes, I understand that if you chose to kill another person for loot or steal from an old man that you get sad, but the fact that it matters so much annoys me, war is hell, it doesn't make sense for the characters to get depressed and constantly bring up the fact that you stole from someone. But I understand that they get sad after killing another person, of course.
- Trading(bartering as it's called in-game) system is not... that good. I almost everytime feel like I got ripped off unless I traded with Katia, the character that has a trait so she can get more out of trades and give less than others but... as I've explained in this review, you can play with different sets of characters, most of them do not have Katia in them, just a few.
9/10. Must buy. Consider the DLC as well to help out some people.
Edit:
3 years later and the developers are still adding content to this game, quite good content infact.
Still an amazing game that I play all the time.

I first played IMSCARED back in 2012, when the GameJolt edition was just out.
Being italian myself, I was - sadly - skeptic about its value, because we're notoriously bad at making games. I'll admit I was blown away. The low-fi visuals and audio, the fourth-wall breaking, the Yume Nikki vibe. All in all, a well-thought, hand-crafted piece of eeriness. I liked it so much I kept that version for years and gave it a play every now and then, showing it to some of my friends as well.
Then, February 2016 came and on twitter I saw my friend benzoin-gum re-tweeting Ivan's announcement about the Steam release - that was a really nice surprise, and I thought I owed Ivan a beer for the entertaining he's granted me years before, free of charge. Hence I bought it, and that was it, I didn't even
to play it again initially, but shortly after I caved in and gave it a go.
Lo and behold, there were a bunch of new areas to explore, new stuff to see and hear. New chapters, and secrets. I didn't know that, it was a very welcomed surprise. Yes, the game still lives to its old expectations and surpasses itself in this expanded version. I'm one achievement short from completion, but I reckon it won't be long due.
For the price of a pint of beer, I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes Yume Nikki, or had at least one dream in their lifetime where everything was bright yet the sky lied still, and black.
The last chapter was very intensive and frightening. This game is worth your money.

IMSCARED is a pixelated indie horror game originally released for free on Gamejolt some odd years ago. The steam version includes the free version plus another 2.5 times that content. So essentially 3.5x the free game. It is a defining game of the indie horror genre, and breaks the fourth wall in a way that I have never seen any other game do. These fourth-wall mechanics are incorporated into the gameplay, making it an even more unique experience. I believe that IMSCARED is the #1 indie horror game out there, and an absolute must-play for anyone interested in the genre.
The only con of this game, to me, is the labrynth portion that occurs ~1/4 of the way through the game. It was honestly a huge stalling point and not very fun to me at all, making me frustrated to the point of almost quitting. After getting over this though, the rest of the game was amazing. I had expected it to be the original game plus more thrown together content to make it 'long enough' to justify the (incredibly low) price, but that's not what this game is at all. Every part of it- save the labrynth- is a wonderful, unique terrifying experience.
9.5/10

Social network simulator.
Ever feel like social networks like Facebook and Twitter take up a ridiculous amount of your time. Ever wanted to stop the addiction but don't know how. Well look no further because now you can play the social network game.
Story
There is minimal story. You play as a new arrival to a space station.
Gameplay
As a social network simulator, majority of the game composes of developing connections with various other characters on the station. The aim of the game is to try to get off the station ASAP, but in order to do that you need to move up in 'status'. You do this by making friends, getting new jobs and promotions. To improve relationships with other characters you may invite them to eat, watch a movie, play sport or a wide variety of other activities or simply liking their posts and sending messages. Each character likes and dislikes certain activities. As your relationships with characters improve, so do their messages towards you, even going so far as flirting. The same can be said the other way round, if you offend them, in which they may un-friend you. Besides managing your connections you also have to go to work, which earns you money which you can spend to buy new items or to go to events. You also have to manage your health and happiness by spending time eating at restaurants and doing relaxing activities. Some people may find the game boring with the limited activity. I however found it amazingling addictive putting in several hours into it before calling it quits.
Audio
Music isn't anything special. The sound effects serve their purpose. there is not voice acting, with all dialogue spoken via text.
Graphics
The graphics are all presented via 2D pictures. They aren't amazingly detailed, but aren't an eye-sore either.
I recommend this game to people who want to reap the benefits of social media, on steam or who have never experienced social media in their lives.

I'm not at all compelled. The difference in abilities between all the characters I tried seemed shockingly minimal. Basically everything is a skill shot or an aoe, and it will either do damage, do damage and slow, heal, or do damage and heal. Most characters have a mobility skill that works nearly identically. The only variation seems to be in healers and tanks, but it's still just healing or applying a shield to yourself or your teammates.
Having all the abilities at the start feels weird. I know there's no way around that in this format, and I've even enjoyed other games that do this such as Heroes of the Storm. The difference is that you have 6 abilities (8 if you count heal and revive). This makes the basic control of your character much less approachable than other arena combat games. It's not the number of abilities that is the problem here -- I'm completely comfortable playing DotA with 6 active items for a total of 10 abilities -- it's the fact that you start with all of them, and again, how similar they all are. I think the characters would be much more compelling if they had fewer skills and more specialization.
That's my main problem with the game. The characters are very generic, and this is likely necessary to the format of the game. Keeping 3v3 blind draft balanced requires giving every character a certain variety of skills, which made it feel far too homogeneous for my liking. I could get used to the keyboard controls and mouse aiming. I could get used to having 8 abilities out of the gate and learn how they all work. But, after 2 or 3 games of it, I'm not at all interested in trying.

I really liked this game. I use the past tense here because I'm not sure how replayable it is, but my first playthrough was a good time. And since I purchased the game on sale for 75% off, I'd say $2.49 is money well-spent for 8 1/2 hours of play. Especially as this game is pretty unique, as it combines a lot of my favorite genres and has a distinct flavor/atmosphere/personality (I'm not sure of the word to use here, but that's the idea.)
Things I Really Enjoyed:
1. Humor / writing: Sometimes absurd, sometimes satirical, sometimes cheesy. Probably where that "personality" comes from
2. Combination of genres that I like, which are rarely combined in this way.
3. Intuitive / Easy to get the hang of the interface
I think you'll like this if you enjoy turn-based games, life sim games, space games, and social and/or time management games, but probably only if you do NOT hate using Facebook in real life, as this has a heavy Facebook-like simulation component.
Overall it needs to be more challenging. And there are a number of things that I wish had been more fleshed out.  But I applaud its uniqueness and its wit.

I was hoping this would be a funny game about balancing your space career and your space social life, but I was horribly disappointed. The career part is pathetic, because you don't get meaningful choices. You just click the "Do Job" button when it tells you to and slowly build stats. I guess you can try to befriend a hiring officer to get promoted faster, but that's part of the social game. Even the away missions are just another glorified stats screen, just like any other day of work, except you get sadder because a random person died.
The social aspect is really all there is in the game, but it isn't fun. It's a game about building relationships, except those relationships have no value, and the only way to build them is to invite them to dinner, basically. Being in a romantic relationship increases your happiness stat, but it feels empty. You don't know anything about the randomly generated name and avater you're "In a relationship" with, they have no character, you don't care about them. It's the same with all the other friends, non-friends, coworkers, bosses etc that you have potential relationships with. They're just numbers with no compelling reason to care about them. The player's feelings and the avatar's stats are so disconnected that it's actually kind of insulting when the game tells you how happy or sad you are.
One might say that that's all just part of the satire of social networking, but it fails to be good satire because it doesn't feel like the thing it's mocking, because in real life, it's implied that other people actually exist. And besides, being satire doesn't excuse a game for being boring.
The game isn't funny, which is disappointing. I got a few chuckles from flavor text here an there, but nothing stood out. It was all cheap referential stuff, the kind of humor that forms the broth of a good parody, but there was no meat to it. Nothing actually funny ever took center stage, because the game was too focused on simulating a high-schooler's idea of self-worth, which would be dull even if I didn't have to enable it.
The UI is mucky. Lines of stats are overrepresented and none of your potential actions are organized in a way that does a good job of conveying what your options are or what their effects are. The art is low quality, and the sound design is shoddy. Beeps and voiceovers and loud music overlap without any real design. The potential system, to those who have not played this game yet, is basically an extra 2-3 stats tagged onto almost any peice of equipment. These stats account for the majority of a player's strength/damage, much more so than the stats you regularly get through upgrading items by in game means. These stats start out very poorly, and are rolled randomly by using what is called a cube. Occassionally, the tier of the potential will go up when you roll (This is quite rare, maybe 1 in 30 rolls give or take. Some people need around 100 if they're unlucky), giving access to better potentials. Note that these potentials are RNG, so as a warrior, you may very well get DEX, INT, LUK, M.ATK or any other useless stat 95% of rolls.
To get a single cube through in game means takes up to a week, more or less. Crafting them is ludicrously expensive and trying to obtain them from killing bosses is pointless due to the ludicrously low drop rate ( To get one cube, you'd have to do a twice daily boss each day for on average a month, give or take. I say this from personal experience ).
Of course, you could always BUY cubes. They're $1-$2 each (The $2 one is necessary for upgrading the final tier ), or they come in $10 and $20 bundles. Note that it's ONE DOLLAR TO BUY A SINGLE CUBE. Making a single end game tier item can take HUNDREDS OF CUBES, and that will get you almost NOWHERE progress wise. You need a FULL SET of these types of items to have a CHANCE at one of the end game bosses. This, coupled with the fact that group play is extremely discouraged in boss fights makes these end game bosses impossible (The HP on these bosses is in the hundred billions. Consider that I, a long time player who doesn't spend money can't shave even a fraction of their HP bars in 10 minutes. Now consider that most bosses have a 20 - 30 minute time limit).
It is also impossible to make money in the game from 'end game' activities, because unless you have an extremely high damage range, all the bosses you will be able to fight have useless drops.
I didn't even mention the fact that a lot of boss drops are trade locked unless you pay $2-$3 to untrade lock it for one trade.

If there's one word I could use to describe Dungeon Fighter Online (or DFO, as it's usually shortened to), it would be "unique." While it does have many of the things you'd expect in an MMO, this is nothing like any other MMO you've played before.
The biggest standout feature is, by far, the combat. Taking inspiration from old-school fighting games and beat-'em-ups, you proceed through instanced dungeons, beating the crap out of anything that gets in your way. You can use skills either with twelve hotkeys, or with command strings like in traditional fighting games. Using skills and comboing is simple enough that it won't overwhelm new players, but has enough depth that it remains fun even after thousands of hours of gameplay.
DFO also stays true to its old-school roots in the aesthetic departments. Graphics are primarly gorgeous pixel art, with some more anime-style art for character and NPC portraits. Skills look absolutely fantastic, and animations in general flow very well, making combat look seamless and awe-inspiring. The soundtrack is excellent as well, with some very memorable themes (Final Pursuit comes to mind).
The place where the word "unique" comes in most though is with your options for your character. The game's description says there are 14 classes, but this is a bit misleading, as there are actually 14
most of which have four sub-classes you can choose from. There are currently 51 classes on DFO, with two more having recently released on the mother Korean server, and another two coming soon. What makes that number truly incredible is that every single one of those classes feels completely different to play. Even the male and female variants of each class can be wildly different. From traditional fist-fighters, to gunslingers, mages, swordsmen, holy warriors, elves, and the ever-infamous lancers, there's a huge variety in class options.
The game's first stumble comes with the story. You mainly progress through the story by doing special "Scenario" dungeons, where you experience the events of said story and read some NPC dialogue after each dungeon. While the story was interesting enough that I read it, it's really nothing too special. The actual world of Arad, and the lore related to each class, is much more interesting than the main story, which is a shame. I wouldn't necessarily call this a massive downside though, since MMOs have to be designed to last long past when you've finished the main story, and I'll get into that later.
First, I want to tackle a few things that could drive people away from the game, with the first being the FP system. Yes, this game has Fatigue Points, which limit the number of dungeons you can enter daily. However, if you take some time to actually play the game, you'll quickly discover that it's an incredibly trivial limitation that can easily be bypassed. Potions to restore fatigue are readily available, and fatigue isn't shared among characters, so you can simply swap over to another character and keep playing when one's fatigue runs out.
The second thing to tackle is the cash shop. Yes, this is a free-to-play MMO, so there's gotta be microtransactions somewhere in there. As someone who's played other F2P MMOs before though, I'm glad to say that DFO has one of the best-handled cash shops I've ever seen. Absolutely nothing in the cash shop is game-breaking enough to make paying players have an insurmountable advantage over free players, and almost everything in the cash shop can be traded, meaning it's going to show up on the auction house, where free players can buy it with gold. My only gripe with the cash shop is that I wish costume packages didn't disappear after a few months, it makes the selection of costumes a bit sparser than I'd like.
Somewhat related, it's also worth mentioning that the events range from great to amazing. It's pretty normal for endgame gear and cash items to be handed out for very little effort, which makes it even easier for free players to keep up. I've never once bought the premium service available in the cash shop, and I have nearly half a year of it from nothing but events. I've also gotten multiple rare clone avatar sets (the highest tier of costumes) without ever using the cash items normally needed to get them. There's nothing even remotely pay2win about this game.
There are only a few things I could put as true negatives. Like a lot of Korean MMOs, endgame is
grindy, with a lot of progress being gated by RNG, the most notorious example being Hell Mode, where the best gear in the game is found. The community can be pretty toxic at times, especially in Raid, so it's best to find a guild of decent people and stick with them. Also, if you're here for PvP, look elsewhere. The PvP scene is completely dead due to connections being handled by p2p, which just doesn't work that well for an international server.
In summary, DFO is a fantastic and unique MMO with incredibly fun combat, tons of classes to try, and no pay2win crap. If you can handle a bit of grinding, and enjoyed the fighting games of old, then I highly recommend giving this game a shot.

I've played enough of this game to have figured out the core mechanics, and therefore (for this game at least) its core concept. Let's start with that this game doesn't explain itself, except by telling you the controls. The rest is up to you, as the player, to figure out for yourself. If you don't like burrowing into a game, experimenting in trial-and-error, than do not get this game. You'll probably be left bewildred, confused or frustrated.
If on the other hand, you don't mind this at all (or don't mind grabbing to 'cheat' by looking up the core mechanics in a guide or something), than figuring out the game's mechanics is going the be the primary pleasure for the first hours of so. You'll learn about planting seeds, the growing black squares in the screen shots and about the characteristics of each individual 'plant' (the collored blocks). You'll have to be observant. But once you have figured out all the characteristics, you've gotten the first achievement for this game.
The second part of this game, is using that knowledge to further explore the world. I did this a bit, and i got bored with it. I didn't have the feeling that there was an actual point to this "Starseed Pilgrim Part 2". I just couldn't find a proper goal. Nor am I able to find on the internet with some quick searches if there even is any. Maybe it's proceduraly generated to be of infinite size and therefore cannot be 'completed' or won? As such, I've lost my will to continue spending precious time on this game, as I've started to perceive it as a time sink.
As such, I cannot automatically endorse this game, nor immediately recommend it. If you are a very curious person, and like the figure out game mechanics, than you can at least play the game for "Part 1" and feel good about yourself once you did. And maybe you are curious to find out if the game is more than, that it appeared to be to me, a game-concept... euhmm.... game?

In my opinion, the Thief reboot did a good job of achieving the goals it set and even though it fell short of some people's ever climbing epectations, overall I am thoroughly enjoying this game. I woudn't compare it to the other thief games beyond "same character" and "same basic skillset" ie lockpicking, bludgeon them til they pass out, bow, ect. And please, please stop comparing it to Dishonored. Let it be it's own game. But I digress.
--------Points of interest-----------
The Mechanics:
Whenever it came to feeling like i was immersed into the game and pulling items off of shelves, out of desks, picking locks, ect, I felt Thief was incrediblly accurate. Everthing about the mechanics that they promised us (as far as I can recall) has been met.
NO. You cannot jump like mario at will but you aren't playing morrowind leveling your atheletics either. You want to stay quiet and out of sight and for better or worse you now climb up crates or walls when neccessary, instead of jumping around like  buffoon. Does this take away from the game? Not in the sleightest. There are many, MANY games where you cannot jump and iv'e never heard an outcry as big as this for them.
Customization and the like:
As far as customizing your gameplay goes a feature i enjoyes was the custom difficulty to add more bonuses. I immediately got rid of most my arrows with that. However, whenever it comes to predator or ghost for missions, oftentimes id end up inbetween even if you only knock out a few people. Thus being The "predator" would mean you'd obviously have to downright kill more and for ghost you couldnt even knock out a few to grab loot which makes it exceedingly difficult in some cases.
Story: Ill edit this in once I finish but I'm a completionist to the bitter end so it might take a while
Sound:
I don't quite see what people think is wrong with Garrett's voice although you're friend you meet up with end chapter one, his voice sounds quite dull. However my computer isnt exactly up to speed to play this game to sound wise I'm missing out on cut-scenes.
I listened to the soundtrack and a few that stood out to me was the library music and the "uprising" song part of which i recognized from the trailer, although have yet to hear in game. Most scenes and music match accordingly the only times I was sleightly miffed was during the rooftop chase and end chapter 1 in Watch Alley. Hopefully there aren't more but those soundtracks in the given area where too sudden of a change for a scene where (in the case of watch alley) i was sneakin around behind some crates.
Option menu:
This is downright beautiful. There are so many options to customize that most games don't really put out there, but as the gamer i LOVE to see them. nuff said.
OVERALL I think thief was (and is I'm still working on it, I'm a completionist) a fairly good game. The mechanics are great. The sound/music matched up 90% of the time save for a few off scenes and the options menu was just fantastic. Oh and the menu itself had a great layout, very clean.
As a fangirl of the Thief franchise: 9/10 even if they screw over the story
As your average avid gamer 7/10 purely from the technical standpoint. Once I finish the main story it could go up or down.

I felt compelled to write a review mainly because I didn't like or hate the game first starting out, and I really wish there was an option to make a review "Conditional", because your liking or hating of this game will depend greatly on your appreciation of the genre and aesthetic, along with the price attached.
To start, if you don't like puzzle platformers or obscure indie games, don't even bother with this.
Avoiding any descriptions that'll sound like an art gamer's musings, the narrative of the game bounces between vague and understated. The mechanics are simple, though the overall objective is one that will require guesswork to figure out, and even when you've passed the first level, it's still unclear exactly what you're building towards. Success is rewarding, and failure seems often. The feeling of being cheated by game mechanics can sometimes happen early on, but once you start understanding how different seeds work and what things get you "killed", this feeling diminishes. The uniqueness of the game is intriguing enough that I've returned to it a few times since owning it, picking away at the game's shell in short bursts. It's an easy game to start, toy around with, and leave alone for a while.
This leads me to my final point, and a reason why I lean towards not recommending buying Starseed Pilgrim.
Put simply, the price.
Though six dollars is a modest amount compared to most indie games on Steam, this price just doesn't feel justified to me. I aquired the game from a recent Humble Bundle, where I received numerous other games for about the same price as this game by itself. Knowing that there are other games of equal or lesser price that have a more apparent value-yield going in, I can't recommend this as a safe buy. As said before, the game's narrative is obscure and doesn't offer direction, much less a sense of depth that would make you compelled to dig deeper for greater lengths of time. It's a unique and clever way to spend a few minutes casually teasing your brain with ways to accomplish the game's simple objective, but that's an experience that's worth less than six dollars. If you can pick the game up for half that, I'd say it's definitely worth the gamble, but only if you're one to enjoy puzzle platformers.

I'm going to review on a general level and avoid huge spoilers here.
The first thing that stood out to me was the artwork. It's what drew me to this game in the first place. I think it's very nice and I like the style.  I have no complaints about the art itself, but it's more about me pointing out inconsistencies: (1) Regarding the CG's, sometimes the heroine's eyes would show, and in others they don't. I know that it's a thing in visual novels, but usually games would have already decided with showing the main character's eyes most of the time or not in CG's. (2) The clothes of the person the heroine is talking to would change from time to time, but the dialogue makes no note of him changing clothes. Aside from that, the art seems soft, much like the heroine's personality.
Regarding the story, some routes were more interesting than others. Some routes showed more character development and relationship progression than others. It was a bit unrealistic to fall in love after a couple of days, but I did enjoy the stories for what they were. Personally, my favorite route was when I pursued a certain manager. It's nice that the game included a second story for him. On the other hand, the heroine's childhood friend does not appear in other routes, does not have any substories, and is not mentioned in any other route. I happen to like the childhood friend trope, so I was a bit disappointed with that. There were also some spelling errors (homophones) and awkward use of some words throughout the game. Like the use of "comfit" in the game... I think it was referring to konpeito? Not a big deal, but the dialogue was a bit confusing at times.
Anyway, by the time I finished all the stories and the routes, I still wanted to read more. I don't regret the purchase, despite the things I pointed out. I fully enjoyed it and I liked all the characters.

This may not be the number one otome game on Steam (I would give that title to Amnesia: Memories for now), but it is worth your time and money and definitely makes me feel good to play!  If you have ever played any mobile otome games, you know what you are in for.  You choose your guy right from the start, there are distinct chapters and side stories, and the story is VERY ADDICTIVE!  Unlike mobile offerings, however, you pay one price to own the game and have everything right from the start.  No distracting microtransactions, in-app purchases, energy, etc.  The game is perfect to play in very small bursts, but if I had more time I could definitely see myself enjoying just going through a whole route all at once!  I am always eager to find out what happens next.
The short prologue followed by a screen where you "choose your guy" reeks of a mobile game money-making setup, but surprisingly, it actually works in this game's favor.  (No spoilers, this is all "first few minutes" info here)  Basically, your protag walks into a brothel, briefly meets each guy, and is asked to pick which one she wants to spend the evening with.  This setup seems contrived for most games, but actually makes sense for the situation at hand (given my not-first-hand experience with host clubs and like that I've gained from Japanese popular culture)!  Also, the protag has the stereotypical "I'm such a pure, innocent, naive virgin" vibe which is another otome game trope, but even that makes sense for this game.  In the first few minutes we find out that since men are almost never born on her island, she has hardly even seen any other young men in her life.  No wonder she has never learned about the "birds and the bees"...she has never had any reason or motivation to!
My major gripes with this game would be some grammar, spelling, language errors, which you have probably seen before if you have played mobile otome games, or even any of mangagamer's very early releases, etc.  It didn't bother me that much but it is worth noting.  Also, the default screen resolution looks fine, but is too small on my 32-inch TV that I game on, so I turned on fullscreen and the graphics took a noticeable nosedive, worse than nearly every other visual novel I have played.  Despite this, the guys are still very attractive so I don't let that hinder my enjoyment of the game either...but still worth noting.
