This review contains spoilers.
I tried really hard to like IMSCARED. A game that has the player interacting with an entity that communicates with them by creating text files on the player's desktop is intriguing. The visual style, while not entirely original, feels dated, a commonly overlooked way to create unease with the player. The game's price point is also low and suitable for a game with this level of content. However, IMSCARED stumbles in a lot of areas and left me frustrated with it. I'll break down what I didn't like about the game.
1. I said in my introductory paragraph that I found the interaction between the player and the game to be intriguing. While it is, it's also a bit awkwardly implemented. There are several points in the game where you need to be reading a text file while playing the game. During these segments, you can put the game in windowed mode, but the window is incredibly tiny and the controls sometimes glitch out while you're trying to go back and forth between the text file and game.
2. The game "crashes" and closes itself on several occasions. This harkens back to Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem and the original Metal Gear Solid, where the game attempts to fool the player into thinking that the game is actually interacting with something in the real world. I initially didn't mind this, but the game began to abuse it. If you get caught by the monster at certain points in the game, the game will close and you'll be brought back to your desktop. There were points where you're required to solve puzzles with little to no conveyance as the monster chases you around the environment. If you get caught, you're brought back to your desktop, losing your progress up until the start of the puzzle. I actually took breaks from this fairly short game because I was so frustrated with my constant failures. I also imagine my Steam friends were getting annoyed, constantly seeing me start and stop playing the game. If the game maybe brought you back to the menu screen when you died rather than completely closing out, this wouldn't be so much of an issue.
3. Jump scares, jump scares, jump scares. I see a lot of reviews praising this game for being "truly scary", but I see very little criticism of its over-reliance on jump scares. While I'll admit that the game made me feel uneasy at times with its retro atmosphere and creepy ambience, there were way more occasions where something would pop out and make a loud noise at me for a cheap scare. There are points where an overlay will flash on the screen with a loud noise and the game will close, something entirely jumpy and even more forgettable. The worst offender, however, is a puzzle about 3/4 of the way through the game where the player is tasked with finding record players in a maze and destroying them. You're being chased by the monster during this segment, but weird figures will come down from the ceiling and screech at you for absolutely no reason. They add nothing to the experience at all and don't play into the puzzle in any way, just being added as cheap scares to make the situation less scary than it would have been if you were simply being chased.
4. The game is somewhat fragmented. There isn't really a hub location until the very end of the game, and the areas you're going through have little to nothing to do with one another. You go to a supermarket, a train station, a basement area and a hedgemaze throughout the course of the game. These areas aren't really connected to each other until the very end, and even then the game only connects them through a series of doors that teleport you to them. Some of the areas even require you to input different things into a text prompt, something that is vital near the end of the game if you didn't get all of the achievements (I'll expand on this later). Overall, you find yourself teleporting from area to area. The game will close, and you'll find yourself in an entirely new location without any explanation as to why. As a result, nothing feels familiar and the game feels stitched together, like a collection of different ideas.
5. Movement is awkard and actually somewhat buggy. It's fairly simple, being mapped to the WASD keys for moving, the Shift key for sprinting, and the Ctrl key for crouching. However, it's easy to get "caught" on objects, requiring you to reposition the camera in order to move again. If you want to try this, you simply need to walk along a wall and rotate the camera towards it. You'll eventually get stuck and won't be able to move unless you rotate the camera away from the wall. This wouldn't be so bad if there weren't actual segments where you need to get through cramped spaces and you're constantly getting stuck on both sides of the wall. There's also a segment where you're being chased through a hallway, and while I only got caught on a bookshelf once, it still exemplified how buggy the movement is. It's also worth noting that if you crouch next to certain objects, you can clip through them, which looks very awkward and allows you to peer inside some things.
6. Near the end of the game, the player is about to go through the last door when the game prompts them that they need to get all of the achievements in order to proceed. At first I thought this was a trick, but it's serious. Closing the game will bring you back to the start of the game, which has opened up some new doors to previous parts of the game where you can obtain these achievements. When I started this game, it was less than a week old. The achievement list gives absolutely no clues as to how the achievements are obtained and the discussion board was barren of help. This left me stumbling about, trying to figure out how to get the last few achievements so that I could actually finish the game. Some of these achievements are incredibly obscure, requiring you to do things like knock on a wall and set your system clock to certain times in order to get some items. Achievements are meant to entertain completionists, not frustrate people who just want to experience the game.
I truly, dearly wanted to enjoy IMSCARED. It does some really interesting things and has a very low price point. However, the times where I was wowed were undermined by the amount of times I was frustrated or disappointed. In the end, this is just a short indie horror game with lots of jump scares and a somewhat entertaining fourth-wall mechanic. It's not incredibly noteworthy and I can think of other games that do fourth-wall breaking better with less frustrations and more polish.

This is the 2nd best game I've played in 2015, behind Life is Strange.
I just have to bring this up, good job 11 bit for not making it another stupid survival zombie game.
Pros:
+ The crafting system is awesome.
+ The looting system is awesome.
+ The many different ways of playing the game, do you want to make moral choices and not kill people for supplies or do you want to murder and plunder because war is hell?
+ The combat system is great.
+ Different characters have different traits and things they enjoy, for example 1 character is a coffee drinker and is good at trading(Good at trading=able to get more and give less in trades) and 1 character likes smoking and is a good cook, so you keep cigarettes at the ready and have them make the food etc...
+ Not 30FPS locked, making this a pro because of the idiotic amount of developers that say "Meh.. it's 2.5D, LETS LOCK IT AT 30!"
+ Great sound effects and music.
+ Again, great variety of how you want to play the game.
+ Tons and tons of replay-ability.
+ Great graphics for it's genre, and the actual art style is awesome.
+ Can do several play throughs with different sets of characters, great for completionists to survive the game with all the different sets of characters.
+ Different items gets their value changed throughout your game based on their availability, for 5 days maybe the price of meat sky rockets up in price and another time maybe the price of cigarettes or wood sky rockets up in price for a few days, making them great to trade with.
+ The fact that you need to bring items with you when you scavenge at night is good, you can't just blaze through a house or something, sometimes you need to bring equipment to break a chain on a door, sometimes you need a lockpick etc...
+ Sometimes people will knock on your door for help, so you can chose to not help them or give them one of your valuable bandages(just an example) in hopes of them maybe returning one day with a gift as a thank you.
+ 100% of their DLC's proceeds goes to a charity helping war victims.
Cons:
- The mood mechanic of the game is not that great in my opinion. Yes I understand that these are normal humans like you and me who are thrown in the middle of a war, they are not soldiers, they are normal everyday people, so yes, I understand that if you chose to kill another person for loot or steal from an old man that you get sad, but the fact that it matters so much annoys me, war is hell, it doesn't make sense for the characters to get depressed and constantly bring up the fact that you stole from someone. But I understand that they get sad after killing another person, of course.
- Trading(bartering as it's called in-game) system is not... that good. I almost everytime feel like I got ripped off unless I traded with Katia, the character that has a trait so she can get more out of trades and give less than others but... as I've explained in this review, you can play with different sets of characters, most of them do not have Katia in them, just a few.
9/10. Must buy. Consider the DLC as well to help out some people.
Edit:
3 years later and the developers are still adding content to this game, quite good content infact.
Still an amazing game that I play all the time.

I played the game from start to finish with very few hiccups, and I genuinely enjoyed my time with it. It does have long loading times, and the performance isn't always great - but these things are not so much up to the developer as to the engine and its limitations (in its current state). Still, it doesn't keep you from experiencing what the game has to offer, and it certainly has qualities. It's a fairly simple game, but not in a negative way - you explore the levels, read notes, find keys and kill any enemies you encounter. The atmosphere is very good, and the levels are well-designed and filled with details that makes the world feel quite realistic and "lived in". There is also a fairly well-developed background story, which is conveyed through the afore-mentioned notes that you find scattered about the levels. I definitely look forward to the next chapter of the game.
In the end, though, it comes down to expectations - if you're expecting anything close to an AAA-title, you'll certainly be disappointed. But for a low-budget, "made by one person" game? You can do
worse than this. If the latter description is something you can appreciate I can quite happily recommend picking this up - especially considering how dedicated the developer seem to be to this project.

I was going to wait to play this on the new engine and when the Indie Developer had added his usual tweaks and improvements,  but I thought I'd just have a look at it and ended up an hour and a half into the game. So it's quite playable and hooks you in.
The Dev has a good record with an earlier RPG maker game, Waste Walkers so you can expect a lot of improvements and updates and community involvement as time goes on.  Brave choice of game engine too.
+ It has a story. The storyline keeps you playing to see how it all unfolds.  It's the storyline that keeps you playing Affliction, and it takes the first couple of levels for it to start to unfold, but after that you want to play on to see where it's going.
+ Frequent updates and improvements since release and involvement with the community
+ Video cut scenes mostly made in the game engine itself. A lot of work has gone into these for an indie dev.

+ The many levels, more like "scenes" suit story driven side of the game very well.
+ For a game using the GG engine he's managed to keep a very good framerate going, mine's ranged from over 170fps  down to 50 fps on a 4 year old machine which isn't even entry level today (i7, 16gb ram, gtx 750 ti)
+ Very good use of sounds gives the game a great atmosphere.
+ cell-shaded is a nice look. It can be changed but I left it on.
+ you have to figure stuff out, it's not handed to you on a plate, and where there are hints they are mostly just that, hints.
- Loading times between levels are very long (due to the GG engine), but this is the current engine version, so that ought to be fixed while the game is still in early access. I do hope so because after a while you start being very careful not to die because the loading time is more than punishment enough for a mistake or forgetting to save.
The game is not yet complete, but given the dev's proven track record with Waste Walkers and that game's great reviews and feedback, this early access is going to turn out a real gem.  The developer does see through his projects until they are properly finished, and always puts a lot of work into them, no reason why this should turn out any different.  A lot of work and thought has gone into Affliction, the story, the cut scenes, wringing every last FPS out of the engine, voice acting, custom scripts, and it is only going to get better and more polished.

The developer is using a game engine that's basically a fun way to learn Lua scripting and or create basic games for your kids, or simplistic 3D maps for your DnD sessions, it's certainly not, at least for the most part, intended to be used to create games you are going to charge money for, but that's been the way Steam has been going for a couple of years now so it's no suprise to see this in Early Access and asking for your cash. But, for now, let's ignore the engine used and look at the game itself:
There are 0 options for changing settings or rebinding controls, the control screen (and every other menu screen) is nothing but a blurred image with even blurrier text. The intro video is the same, just a bunch of super blurry images and text with "old film" overlays on top.
I played the first 5 levels or so, if you can call them that, they're so small that "scene" would probably be more accurate than level. Each one took longer to load than it did to comlpete, seriously. This is certainly not open world as the store page says.
The AI is laughable, it should honestly be renamed ALOI, if you cant work out what the LO stands for then maybe this game is right up your alley ;) . Often times you will walk around a corner to see the ai walking into a wall, all other times they'll just stand on the spot and shoot in your general direction, not posing any kind of challenge.
The crouch button only works properly on the first press on a level, only letting you stand back up if you jump and then only working if you hold the c button down afterwards, very sloppy.
All the in game sound effects and animations are terrible, clearly stock assets or out of cheap asset packs, just like every other asset in the game such as buildings, characters, vehicles etc etc. Some of these assets, such as the brick walls dont even have tile-able textures, so you get horrid seams down the middle of walls.
The overall quality of the assets, as well as the heavy limitations of the engine itself honestly make this game feel and look like a 3D game from the early 90's, except they tended to have decent size levels and fun gameplay.
The game then crashed when entering the police station level, which was level 5 or 6, after 12 minutes of gameplay, with about 60% of that being loading times between levels.
Yes, it is in Early Access, and at this point it can only improve (if you are at rock bottom then the only way is up), but this is also something most developers should/would be embarrased about asking money for, whether it's in EA or not, and I cant see that improving as long as GameGuru is the engine that's being used. And again, yes, I acknowledge it's in Early Access, but you can't polish a turd, no matter how much you buff it.
Definitely not worth your's or anyone else's money, and here's a tip, if Jim Sterling plays your game on his "Spray and Play" series (which he did with this) and you still cant see that what you have "made" is utter rubbish then you may be dillusional, seek medical attention!
Also in the 2 weeks since release the developer has only put in a maximum of 20 minutes dev time into the game, but according to him, this equates to "a ton of changes and improvements, requested by the community", what requests? what community? 2 lies in 1 there.....

*EDIT*
I couldn't post this as a comment since it was too long, so I'd like to post it here for the developer to view. It'll provide more insight on why I disliked the game:
Before I write anything else, I'd like to thank you for responding to my criticism and appearing to be open to it. I appreciate a person who is open to hearing another's opinion, especially in a case such as this, where it is a developer hearing from a consumer. It's a very rare thing, as most developers, especailly indie devs who are relatively new to releasing games, are quick to ignore or quash differing opinions regarding their games in favor of valuing their own thoughts or preconceived vision above all others. Since you've taken the time to outline your thoughts, out of respect, I'd like to respond to you in kind.
I think you're absolutely right on a few points. I certainly should have focused more on your game as a whole rather than the engine itself. I have a very bad track record with games made in this engine, and by bad I mean all duds and not a single passable game among them. To this day I've played about a dozen if not more games designed in GameGuru itself, and most of them are guilty of the sins I listed in the review above. However, I will give you credit in that I did notice that the characters were not from any of the asset packs that I have come across before. I commend you on taking that extra step and working on your own, since I feel that way too many people have become too comfortable (especially on steam) with buying and reusing the same standard, tired npcs and character models found on asset stores or that were packaged with the software itself.
I also think it's great that you're tackling neglected engines in order to challenge yourself. I genuinely believe that is a very interesting means of expanding your creative horizons and promoting your own growth as a game developer. Having graduated from RPG Maker, I can see that you're no stranger to adversity, and I can't help but find it a little amusing that you decided to try your hand at this particular engine, since it will no doubt lead you into familiar territory as far as reputation goes.
Finally, after some thinking on the issue, I'd like to also agree, to a certain extent, about your views regarding Early Access. If I were to look at your game again and omit my feelings regarding the engine and other games associated with it, I'd say that I can see where you're coming from. Early Access is designated for games that want to take their audience along for the development cycle, and if what you say is true, and you intend on listening to user feedback and ironing out the quirks and bugs that may arise as a result, then you're using it the way it was intended, and I applaud you for that. Unfortunately, countless games have abused the EA system in halfhearted attempts at easy cash. So sometimes it's difficult not to judge a game, especially an indie one, based on that brading alone. In your case though, it does seem like you genuinely have an interest in improving your game, which is refreshing.
Now then, here's what I don't agree with. And I'll do my best to be constructive.
This is a little nitpicky, but I don't agree with you framing this game as an RPG. Absolutely no part of this game can fall into that category. Believe it or not, I bought this game (judging by the screenshots, tags, and your own description of the game), believing that I'd get an experience similar to a game I played awhile back called Brigand: Oaxaca. This is 100% a shooter. There are no other elements to this game other than shooting, unless you consider finding keys or moving a box RPG elements. It'd probably be best to remove the tag and reword your description a bit in order to frame it a bit better.
Your level structure is far too short. I realize that GameGuru is a difficult program to work with when it comes to realizing your vision for the game, since it's pretty limited, but when it takes me more time to load a level than to clear it, you have a problem. One of the areas took less than 10 seconds to clear before I reached the next loading screen, and I'm not exaggerating. Expanding your areas in order to provide more gameplay before having to wait to load the next would be a huge improvement. And just to be clear, I don't blame you for the loading times. That's all GameGuru's fault. EVERY game I've played that uses the engine, no matter how small, takes the same amount of time to load each new area.
I did not approach this game with a predetermined, bitter mindset. Quite the contrary. I wasn't expecting anything stellar, but I was expecting something slightly entertaining and possibly funny. Since 2015 I've made a kind of ritual of streaming what I deem bad or unknown games on Twitch. As of today, I've played well over 400 bad games alone, and I'm very good at sniffing ones out that fall into one of these categories. Every once in awhile I find a hidden gem that actually turns out to be an enjoyable experience, either because of how hilarious it is, or because it's legitimately fun. Your game falls into the bad category. The story and environments are bland and forgettable. The enemies are dull and do not pose a threat unless you run directly into them (this again is the engine's fault, not yours). Nothing that transpires draws me in or begs me to invest myself in theworld or what's going on despite what you claim in your description of the game. So, while I agree with you that my ranting about the engine should have been left out of the review, my opinions regarding your game were determined by nothing other than the game itself.
You and I are similar. We both love video games. We both are passionate in different ways about video games. I wasn't expecting a AAA title. I wasn't expecting something that would blow me away. I was just expecting an enjoyable experience, nothing more than what you claimed you would offer. And this wasn't enjoyable.
So, I'd like to ask you something. If you were to remove yourself from the mindset of a developer, and if you were to play this game as a consumer, could you call this game, as it is now, enjoyable?
Thank you for your time, and for taking the time to respond. I really appreciate it.

I grew up playing this game as soon as it was out in North America, all the way back in 2005. I was just a kid then, not even a middle schooler. I spent most of my free time on the computer playing the game with my brother and his friends. Back then, leveling was SLOW; it would take a week just to get to Lv.30. The only way to level at all in your 2nd job was to PQ the same quests over and over half a dozen times just to level up once, and even once you did, you didn't find much content at the next level.
Because of this, most of the original game was extremely social. The goal to getting anywhere was cooperating with other players, as interaction was key to success. Because of the snail-leveling, you would spend most of your time in one of the 6 towns, listening to gossip and learning important information, getting into Parties and Guilds, and making friends. This game was key to my survival, as I live in a hellish redneck ghetto town. My online friends helped me see the light through dark times, and I owe them everything; even a decade later.
I stopped being very active after 2008, but did check on the game after BB. My original draft of this review was negative, but the modern maple is loaded with new content and 5x as many classes as the original game. Leveling is fast now; I could get 10 characters to level 30 in a day. Even then, there's still a lot of grinding. The EXP you need is a fraction of what it used to be originally. Money is still an issue, and the economy makes no sense to me.
The cash shop is still a waste of money, and you are forced to spend real $ on skillbooks, or else your characters will be stunted in their later growth. The modern community is very antisocial because of the soloing aspects. It's not the same game I remember as a child, but this could still provide you hundreds of hours of content, and it's been free for a decade!
If you're bored and want a free mmo to try, this would be one of your destinations for many years, and for good reason.

Playing IMSCARED was an interesting experience. Although the game is very short (3 hours at best if you're looking to find all the secrets) it's filled with nice and never seen before ideas. Here I can just say that it's truly something unique and worth to try, even if you're not the kind of person who enjoys the so-called "walking simulators". I am not, just to say.
The only real flaw that I can find in this title considering the fact that has been developed by a single person resides in its graphics: I understand that the pixelated style is intentional, but a 256x144 resolution is really ridicolous. 480p should be considered the minimum for decency in this kind of games, going lower than that just makes everything look worse than it should. Aside of this, I think that IMSCARED is a little gem that delivers an experience that requires thinking without being pretentious or excessively cryptic, and that keeps a substancial coherence with its premises. Which alone is, in these times, something more valuable than everything else.

TL;DR:  If you can ignore terrible typos and homophones and the storyline/setting appeals to you, I recommend it. If you have concerns about the content, please scroll down to the "Content" section of my review.
---
: If you've read mobile otome games before, I'd say it's "about what you'd expect", though I enjoyed this one better than any of the other mobile otome games I've played before. (Granted - I haven't played any mobile otome game past about a dozen chapters. I get too annoyed with the way the story is doled out and would rather pay for all of it at once.) I find their editing rather appallingly bad and I wish they'd put more effort into correcting at least that much, but I don't regret the money I spent (I purchased the game when it was 40% off, or about 15 dollars USD).
: Please keep in mind if you didn't already get the impression from the age confirmation that there is "H"/adult writing. The CGs themselves are PG-13-ish level at the most racy, but the writing can be quite... direct. Some of it is nicely steamy, some of it verges a little on the vulgar side (most likely due to the editing/translation). If you prefer "sweet" romance, this is really not right for you, even though the heroine is herself quite "sweet".
As another warning - if forced seduction/assault is something that upsets you, this is also a title you'll want to avoid. It happens in multiple routes, though I will "spoiler" that the worst I can remember it getting is groping and partial nudity. To put it in context, I think a lot of it is the man in question misunderstanding the situation and some of it is pure desperation. Please consider your own comfort levels.
: Overall, the translation was decent. I understood most of what was being said and I think I picked up most of the subtext. (Certainly, I understood the subtext far better than the heroine...) There were a few areas where I wasn't certain what was going on, but that is probably because of...
: The editing on this is appalling. Extremely shoddy work. It's very embarrassing. Typos everywhere, terrible formatting of the text, mixed up homophones, and text errors like a hyphen being a square or character names turning into squares. They even mix up names from time to time! I have a lot of experience reading and communicating with people who know English as a second language, so I was able to understand, but for other people, it might be more difficult to get past.
: Mixed bag. Some of it is very lovely. Some of it is clearly rushed. Overall, I did like it, but there aren't a ton of CGs or poses/sprites for each gentleman, so if art is the main reason you're getting the game, you'll probably be disappointed.
: Good. Each character is pretty distinctive and their character sprites clearly show their personalities using costuming and body language.
: Please understand that this game was originally a mobile game. Mobile otome games typically have very linear plots, generally broken down into tiny chapters, and generally do not have bad endings. They also typically give you a short, rushed, contrived way to meet all of the available bachelors and throw you headlong into picking out one without really knowing much about them.
In short, I'm not a huge fan of the way it opens. The story tries to have it's cake and eat it too - they want to stress how virginal and pure the heroine is, but also stress that it's perfectly normal for a woman her age to visit the red light district. You're not given a choice to demure - you have to pick out a courtesan on your first meeting. It's really rather a strange thing for me to gripe about since I knew I was buying a game that focused on male courtesans, I just felt a lot of the heroine's pressure and embarrassment and it made me feel uncomfortable because of the heroine's "purity" (which they stress extremely heavily throughout the game).
The routes and their related hero are all nicely melodramatic (there's really not much subtle about any of the stories since anything that starts out being subtle is hammered home hard). I enjoyed all of the heroes, though they were painted so broadly, it did end up feeling a little unsatisfying for me. They were never as I expected, even after meeting them in other routes and I did enjoy that. But most of them fell in love so quickly, most of the tension came from external forces, rather than internal.
: Your typical "pure-hearted idiot" + "forever virgin". Neither are particularly tropes I like, and when paired together, it makes me slightly uncomfortable. I understand
the men were drawn to her, considering because of their profession, they rarely met anyone like her, but I wish she and the player weren't treated like idiot children. It's particularly annoying when you're presented with options that either make you tone-deaf or leave you open to being called stupid. For all my complaints, though, the Heroine did have something of a personality and didn't provoke me to want to shake her until her head rattled, so that's an improvement over most mobile otome heroines!
I know I've ranted quite a bit, but most of it is minor concerns. I'm just expressing my own openly in case anything I've said is a deal breaker for someone else! Most of the offenses were things I either have a high tolerance for (melodrama), took in stride considering the context (the forced seductions), or am willing to ignore just to have another amusing otome game translated into English (the embarrassing editing). I hope the review helped you!

You know games like Rogue Legacy or One-Way Heroics or other (usually procedurally-generated) titles where you lose but make progress to assist you in making it to "the end"? Okay, this is that, but incredibly abstract and with no explanations given.
A lot of people recommend going into this blind. I'm gonna break this down into two tiers of review: one that's incredibly minimalist and gives away as little as possible, and one that'll be more detailed for the curious who give no heed about spoilers.
THE BRIEF REVIEW: Game only uses a few keys total. Plant seeds which grow in different ways/have seperate effects based on their color (or shape, if you have colorblind mode on). Your enjoyment will greatly hinge upon how much you want to experiment with this process until you figure basics out. Hint: grow upwards, grow outwards, and remember you can delete blocks beside/below you.
THE SPOILING REVIEW: Seriously, stop reading probably.
Okay anyway.
The game gets a little repetitive as you try to 'grow' Green blocks because they have block seeds in them. Your journeys into the resetting world(s - plural, you need to explore to find new ones) will be based on reaching a black speck in the void to get a key, so you can get inside the structure you've grown, grab the seeds, and use the gate at the bottom to make it 'home' with your haul. Use those to grow out the permanent structure, and find new places/some worldbuilding text.
Do this for a while, blindly seeking out the next area with whatever construction you create. That's the game, and as far as I can tell, it does not change. I cheated and looked around to see if I had anything new coming and went "I think I'm good here" a few worlds in. Not bad, but decide for yourself if this seems like your bag, spoiler-haver.

--REVIEW IN PROGRESS--
For the record, I've already played through this game multiple times (smartphone and PS Vita). This version seems to be a direct port of the game from the smartphone app. I'm putting my review as recommended based on my previous experience, however, as I play this version I will update the review accordingly.
First off, I really love this game. I like the characters, and each route feels interesting, as well as the setting this takes place in. Finding out the reasons or motivations for characters to why they're in Kikuya is an interesting mystery, though I admit some scenarios are just frustrating. Certainly not for everybody, as things can get very intimate (there's, um, R18+ stuff described), but it's something that I think is enjoyable to some. It's probably D3Publisher's best otome game, or at least, it's most popular if it's getting a Steam release. That said, this version has a lot of flaws.
Being that this is a direct port, all the routes of all the guys available in the smartphone version so far are here. I played the entirety of the prologue, and for the most part there were few changes in the text, if at all. What I noticed is that they took out character animations, and they improved the GUI for players in the main game. However, it still retains a very "smartphone" feel, and inputs often feel sluggish. Furthermore, the way they ported it gives you no options to change your resolution. You're given a measly "Screen change" to go to fullscreen mode, but if you do that the ENTIRE GAME becomes blurry and pixelated. Save slots are limited, something I hated about the original as well, but route exploration is not that difficult.
The font is strange and there seem to be white artifacts floating around in it. They also didn't clean it up as much as I would have hoped for, so many lines will seem very awkward. If I recall correctly, Hayabusa's routes have much cleaner and better translated dialogue.
They used the opening from the PS Vita version, though, which makes me wonder why they didn't just port that version and included Hayabusa. The PS Vita versions (Otoko Yukaku) is superior to the smartphone version and this version combined. That version has improved art (fixing awkward character portraits), more backgrounds, more music, an extra character (Keiji Ito) and voice acting from famous Japanese seiyuus. Furthermore, it has extra endings and new scenarios and CGs. To top it off, the main routes of the main five guys (Takao, Tokiwa, Kagura, Kagerou, and Iroha) play relatively the same with a few differences. They really should have just ported Otoko Yukaku for Steam, because this version is inferior to the PS Vita one.
I was also just told the event CGs from the Vita version are in this one. I'll have to see them in the routes.
I'm hoping things get cleaned up, though! If it did, I will gladly keep that recommendation for otome players.

I bought this back when it first came out because I thought the premise was intriguing. I've always been a fan of Star Trek, and I thought a game about how those poor, unfortunate redshirts and other nameless, unimportant crew members survived the insane situations that inevitably befell the crew would be neat. I thought a game about being an underapprciated but vital part of a team would be fun.
This game is not that game.
Let's go through each of the claims this game makes any why I think most, if not all of them, are bogus.
1: "Satirical, tongue-in-cheek social simulation, filled with humour and political intrigue." If by "political intrigue" you mean "boring, petty interpersonal drama that I get enough of in my daily life," then yes. This game has political intrigue coming out of its nostrils. I will say that it is at least mildly satirical, as the implication that social media is a poor substitute for actual interaction is a perfectly valid one. I will admit, though, that I didn't find too much about this game to be funny.
2: "Detailed character creation: choose from 5 different species, from human to tentacled squid creature!" It isn't that detailed, I'm afraid. Additionally, it actually makes very little difference what species or even sexual orientation that you choose, except in very rare circumstances (such as being depressed because you don't have a significant other and everyone you can date is not interested in people of your gender, and the one person who is hates your guts; I don't need a repeat of my everyday life, thank you).
3: "Each game is unique: Megalodon-9 is full of procedurally generated AI-driven characters, each with their own random personalities and profile pictures." Each game is unique, but the NPCs aren't sure the names and species and personalities might change, but they're all the same, vapid, uninteresting characters.
4: "Customise station settings: define the kinds of personalities you'll encounter, from friendly chatterboxes to self-obsessed bigots." This bit is accurate, at least.
5: "Update your Spacebook, strategically 'like' statuses, and send private messages to your fellow station citizens." This is also an accurate feature.
6: "Arrange Spacebook 'events' with your friends, frenemies, and even higher-ranking officers, to influence your relationships and skills." Despite being accurate, I'm not sure how this and the prior item are even features.
7: "Multiple routes to success through turn-based gameplay, from skills-based diligence, to romance, to charismatic schmoozing." This is accurate, to a degree. You cannot rely on just one to succeed, however; the best route always involves using everything at your disposal. And you'll need to: without romance, for example, your morale may drop .And if you're in a bad mood, your work will suffer. If your work suffers, say good-bye to that promotion. And before you know it, you're another soulless drone lamenting your lack of a love-life and your boring, dead-end job, anxiously awaiting the weekend so you can go to wine-tastings to get your mood back up for the coming week, only to repeat the cycle ad infinitum.
8: "Navigate an extensive, non-linear career tree, by gaining the right skills... or just by making the right friends.
Make friends and manage romantic relationships -- if you can handle the drama!" On a personal note, this is something I dislike about this game, especially when paired with the above item. Don't get me wrong, I love playing games where I get to be a manipulative schemer. But when the best run I ever had involved buddying up to my supervisors and discarding them when I'd gotten a promotion, that may say something about how viable a skill-based playthrough is.
9: "Strategically manage your interests and skills." See the aforementioned bit about wine-tastings.
10: "Buy items in the Self-Help Object Purveyor (S.H.O.P.) to increase your stats and skills, from RoboCats to illegal hoverbikes!" True, and also a requirement.
11: "Away missions!" Also known as "which one of my friends is going to die miserably and send me into a self-destructive spiral?"
12: "Humorous parody of social networking culture." A parody, perhaps. But I wouldn't say it's a particularly humorous one. I found most of the jokes to fall flat.
13: "Puns! So many puns." Yes, but they're not particularly funny puns.
Now that that's done with, here's my final conclusion. Redshirt was fun, for about 10 minutes. Then it became very, very tedious and very, very boring. And while that's fine to a degree, especially if your game is parodying something as boring as social media, the game itself has to be fun. Quite simply? Redshirt is not fun. I cannot suggest that anyone buy this game for anything more than $3.00.
Seriously, wait for it to go on sale if you have to buy it.

I grew up playing this game as soon as it was out in North America, all the way back in 2005. I was just a kid then, not even a middle schooler. I spent most of my free time on the computer playing the game with my brother and his friends. Back then, leveling was SLOW; it would take a week just to get to Lv.30. The only way to level at all in your 2nd job was to PQ the same quests over and over half a dozen times just to level up once, and even once you did, you didn't find much content at the next level.
Because of this, most of the original game was extremely social. The goal to getting anywhere was cooperating with other players, as interaction was key to success. Because of the snail-leveling, you would spend most of your time in one of the 6 towns, listening to gossip and learning important information, getting into Parties and Guilds, and making friends. This game was key to my survival, as I live in a hellish redneck ghetto town. My online friends helped me see the light through dark times, and I owe them everything; even a decade later.
I stopped being very active after 2008, but did check on the game after BB. My original draft of this review was negative, but the modern maple is loaded with new content and 5x as many classes as the original game. Leveling is fast now; I could get 10 characters to level 30 in a day. Even then, there's still a lot of grinding. The EXP you need is a fraction of what it used to be originally. Money is still an issue, and the economy makes no sense to me.
The cash shop is still a waste of money, and you are forced to spend real $ on skillbooks, or else your characters will be stunted in their later growth. The modern community is very antisocial because of the soloing aspects. It's not the same game I remember as a child, but this could still provide you hundreds of hours of content, and it's been free for a decade!
If you're bored and want a free mmo to try, this would be one of your destinations for many years, and for good reason.

Very interesting game.. You start with 3 players and try to survive for a long as possible.  Each day someone comes to your door to barter, ask for help, or to provide various supplies.  Each day at exactly 8pm, night starts when you must assign tasks. Use your survivors skill for task they are best suited for to better their outcomes.  After dying a few...several times, I figured out a few secrets to surviving.  Build a stove to cook and always barter for meat and veggies because they're not always available and you can make multiple dishes to stretch the ingredients. make or barter for a weapon. It's easier to fend off looters at night even with the smallest weapon.  Build a couple of beds and a radio. Rested survivors do better than tired ones  and a radio will help you know when it's time to build a heater for winter.  If the cold catches you, your survisors could freeze to death in one night. Upgrade your work benchs to build more items like saws, and crow bars to opmitize your scavaging missions, as well as patches to board up your hideout to better protecxt against looters.  Keep your survivors content by paying attention to what they ask for.. it'll keep them upbeat and more productive. Dont steal or kill unless you have too.. your survivors will get demoralized and sad.   All in all, this is a pretty fun game to play. Happy surviving

This game first came over as an appealing game. It was free, and consisted all standard decks with good lore in the tutorial, very easy to get a hang of. In fact, contrary to the other Magic games, this one actually gave you a vanilla liberty to create your own deck.
But as I grew accustomed to this game, I noticed how AWFUL this game is. Here are some points that you, as Magic player, really need to be aware of:
- You are not granted full deck-creating liberty. The developpers have excluded many cards from the sets (like Stasis Snare or Stone Haven Outfitter).
- On top of the point above, they are disallowing you from using more than 3 uncommons, 2 rares or one mythic each type of card. That's absolute BS.
- They will not add any cards Pre-Origins. Even cards from high-demanded sets like Modern Masters, Tarkir or Ravnica, are not going to be in there.
- The start for experienced Magic players is extremely frustrating. It takes a lot of time (-or money) before you finally get a good card for your deck.
- The matchmaking in a game is horrible. Here you come with a few matches played, with your 90% starter deck, expecting to be able to fight a rank 18 player with a full custom deck.
This game is absolutely broken. It's either grind- or pay-to-win, the game is horribly easy to abuse/exploit in terms of making the other person instantly lose by letting their game freeze/crash, this game has SO many no-go's in what a game should be like.
I had my time done on this game. Time to head back to my local game store and play some real MtG there.

I was always a big hardcore fan of the Splinter Cell Series. To this day, I still lowkey enjoy the games whenever I feel like binging on a "James Bond" induced spy thriller. This is the passion that I felt like when playing this game at first. Sneaking through enemy guards through crevasses and navigating in the dark. It really does give the player a unique spy experience. But, however it falls off in a lot of categories which really doesn't match up to modern day expectations. And, you can't really blame the game just because it's a little outdated by at least a decade.
First of all, the most recognizable control problem when going into the game for the first time is the SNEAKING. It's kinda hard to figure out at first but, you have to scroll with your mouse to control the intensity of the sneak. and whenever you f*ck up just because you forgot to sneak softer totally blows and you have to start back from save. (not even auto save, so yeap you gotta remember to save). The sneaking controls are more preferably for the console controller due to the analog stick requirement of ease for lockpicking and sneaking.
Another problem is the level design. Pretty much it's linear. Point A to Point B, while also filling out objectives.
This one sometimes get's on my nerves, but sometimes you just start calling the guards f*ken blind for not spotting you like 2 meters away. Like, I know it's a game and stuff, but it should at least simulate realism.
A good aspect I liked was the storytelling, always loved it, and Fisher's comments are pretty hilarious at times.
Overall, in the end you either finish the game by looking for a walkthrough of the game because it get's very hard to locate objectives some times. OR, you just rage quit and save time.

Dungeon Fighter Online is many things. MMO Beat-em up gameplay with skill trees would be the quickest way to describe the game. There's plenty to love and some things to hate. Some great things are that the combat is fluid, engaging and never really gets very boring. Starting out it may feel otherwise due ot limited available skills, but the further you get, the less you'll be spamming the "X" button (unless your subclass has a specialized standard attack). Skills start out pretty normal, but as you unlock stronger skills later they become very flashy and very damaging to enemies.
The music and artwork are incredible and despite the art being pixelated, it's some of the best I've seen.
There is a LARGE selection of classes and subclasses so it's pretty easy to find a playstyle that suits you and they give you plenty of alt character slots and an unlockable account stash.
The game is pretty F2P friendly. I've been playing since before any US release and have not had any difficulty with gear progression, though it is very RNG dependant and grindy, so if you don't enjoy grinding (it's a Korean game, what did you expect?) then that could be a bit of a turn off.
There is a system that limits how much you can play per character daily called "fatigue points" (FP) which is replenishable with items to a degree, however with how many character slots they give you it can be hard to exhaust your FP account-wide. This is really my biggest gripe with the game as I enjoy focusing on a single character, however it will take the average player about 2 hours to exhaust the FP on a single character once you hit mid-end game (again, you can replenish your FP once you run out to extend your playtime).
The game has significantly more good than bad, and anything that I feel is bad is mostly about something that I don't like in general, not really anything specific to the game itself. The current company handling the game (Neople, who are also the devs) are handling it much better than the previous company (Nexon NA) and is definitely worth a try. I've dumped thousands of hours and $ into several iterations of the game and it definitely has been worth it.

I am a huge fan of the original Thief games which are in my top 10 favorite games of all time. So I was worried this new game would not live up to the original. I am about half way thru it and I think it does it justice. In many respects they improved things, such as the graphics, which is to be expected. The voice actors aren't the same but are OK. A problem with this game that the older game did not have is the characters have limited sound bytes so you hear the same dialog a lot. The old games were good about not doing that. The writing isn't as good, but its not bad. It's just that the original games were top notch. As good as Half Life games. This is solid but not quite as powerful. The original games had a creepy feel to them that was actually very effective. You always felt danger was around every corner.

So I would say it's well worth the money and I want more. Thief is an awesome series.

It's funny, before I even knew about his praise for the game I was thinking, "this has gotta be a Jonathan Blow darling". A puzzle platformer with airs of cryptic profundity and abstract poems on the wall, a spacey soundtrack, simple art, and exploration of an unusual game mechanic.
And sure enough, I find he's waxing poetic about it, continuing his narrative about how morally and intellectually bankrupt the games industry is, and by inference, how smart and morally superior he and his inner circle of indie freedom fighters are.
I'm personally not crazy about the game. Spoilers ahead. Discovering the function of the seeds is fun, and using them to explore, but once you gain that skill, its application becomes repetitive. There aren't many new surprises ahead - different colored "suits" offer only minor changes in your abilities and don't alter the gameplay much. Finding "special stars" with a triple lock behind them is something of a crap shoot, with random placement each time, and that plus randomization of the seed growth means you'll be dying a lot and repeating the same strategies over and over until the randomness works in your favor.
The unique challenges at the end of the triple locks are fun, but you have to do a lot of grinding to get to them, and if you die you lose - to the point that it wasn't worth the time for me.
The game feels a bit unfinished - I wish it had explored these mechanics further and introduced new surprises more often. Perhaps new seed types, or more and varied challenge levels without such a grind to get to them.
I also found the poetry and tone a little (hate to say it) pretentious, and deliberately cryptic. Obfuscating things verbally doesn't automatically mean there's a profound message underneath, though people seem to think it does. To me the best art / poetry expresses something clearly - if everyone who sees it has a contradictory interpretation, it's probably just random noise. The game seems to take itself very seriously - and I found myself yearning for a little humor and lightheartedness.

I enjoy match-3 games, and this comes with all of the benefits and drawbacks that come with competitive versions. (Matches aren't timed, but opponents take alternating turns against you, with possibilities for long strings of watching the computer play when it gets a lucky combo.) The game makes full use of 4- and 5-matches, giving each a different bonus, and recognizing T-shaped and L-shaped 5-matches. (Games that don't do this drive me crazy.)
As a free-to-play game, I like that everything in-game is still accessible without purchase. Progression is a bit slower, of course, but it is possible to win "hero points" (in-game gold) and expand the slots available for heroes.
The unique elements of this game are two-fold:
1) A collectable card-game like element of choosing which heroes to keep and level up, and which combinations to use in each battle.
2) A chance for gamers not already steeped in superhero lore to get to know Marvel characters and interactions a bit better. It's quickly turning me into a fan!
There are two modes of play: "story mode" and "versus".
* Story mode has in-character intro and outro dialog, pulling you into a comic storyline. It's a fun way to immerse yourself in the lore of the Marvel universe.
* Versus mode pits your selection of heroes against heroes from another player's roster. It is worth noting that you are not actually playing the other person, but rather the AI using their heroes and abilities. This is a huge positive for me, because I don't have to deal with connection lags, people who afk for long periods, or trolling in a chat window. But if you're looking to match wits against a human opponent, this might leaving you wanting for more.
Over 40 hours in, this continues to be a deeply engaging game!

Do you enjoy Marvel superheroes?  Do you enjoy matching threes?  Do you enjoy not paying for games?  Well, then, perhaps you should try Marvel Puzzle Quest, a free-to-play match three game featuring Marvel superheroes.
Conceptually, MPQ is quite simple.  You pit your team of three superheroes against another team of three superheroes or villains and take turns rearranging coloured tiles to match lines of three or more in classic Bejeweled fashion.  The twist here is each superhero has at least one (and up to three) super powers they can use to affect the tide of the battle.  Each tile you match on the board adds coloured "action points" to your reserve, which in turn fuel your heroes' powers.  So after you've banked 9 blue action points, you can use Black Widow's ability to stun her opponent, giving you a couple free moves, 10 green action points will let you use Storm's lightning ability to smash a bunch of random tiles, and so on.  While some powers can really turn the tide of the battle if used effectively, many are just lame.   Would you rather have an ability that changes the colour of a few tiles, or simply clobbers your opponent for 1000 points of damage?  Yeah, me too.
The game is split into two basic modes, Story mode and Versus mode.  In the former, you're following a sort of simplistic campaign, punctuated by a series of really lame cutscenes involving no animation,  a single background, and some cringe-inducing dialogue.  In the latter, you're sort of going head-to-head with another player's team, except not really, because the computer is actually controlling their moves.  The AI is generally not very strategic, and will often make mistakes such as creating a tile that benefits itself, then immediately destroying it.
Two "currencies" fuel your efforts; Hero Points and ISO-88, used to both buy new heroes and upgrade their powers.  Unsurprisingly, you can buy either of them by ponying up some real life cash.  I'm not sure why anyone would do this.  The real fun of MPQ – at least for me – was earning points to buy new heroes and then upgrading their powers.  So the option to simply buy as many points as I want would pretty much nullify most of my enjoyment of the game.  Unfortunately, even if you do spend some big bucks on the game, you still can't just buy whichever hero you want; you're just paying for random card drops and hoping the card you want is somewhere out there.  Even worse, if you finally DO get one of the more rare heroes, you won't even be able to use all their powers unless you find more rare cards to upgrade them.  You can theoretically earn more Hero Points and ISO-88 by replaying old missions, but quite often you'll get some lame 20 point reward instead of the juicy rewards you were promised.
Marvel Puzzle Quest has fine production values.  The art is bright, colourful and well-done but the animation is very minimal.  This is most noticeable when using the superheroes' powers, some of which look nice, but many of which look really lame.  Likewise, the music is great, but repeats constantly.  Voice overs would've added some more personality to the proceedings, but it's pretty clear this was not a big budget game.
So why would anyone want to play this game?  Well, for starters, it's free.  And the classic match three gameplay has timeless appeal.  Unfortunately, for all its trappings, MPQ really is just a match three game.  So no matter how much strategy or tactics you attempt to throw at it, you're still at the mercy of whatever coloured tiles drop from the sky.  And you'll still lose matches because the AI somehow managed to get an unstoppable chain reaction of matches, with devastating results.   Even without spending a dime on the game, I managed to beat all the story missions and place fairly well in the versus events.  And for some of the many hours I spent, I was actually having a blast.  Marvel Puzzle Quest has the sort of gameplay that's strategic enough to be engaging, but not complex enough to keep you up all night. As long as you keep winning, it keeps doling out a steady stream of upgrade points and "recruit tokens" you might be able to turn into a new hero for your roster.  It's not a game anyone should spend money on, but if you like matching threes... hey, did I mention it's free?

The best competitive PvP game that was ever made!      10/10  if it had a playerbase and still 2s/3s/etc. team-modes
LoL, WoW, CS, Dota and what not can't compete with BLC at all.
Sadly BLC never gained much recognition, because it's not a casual game where you can do "chill" PvE and farm all the time like in LoL and also because of bad marketing resulting in a small awareness level. The average player who did hear about BLC or whom I tried to convince to play it actively deemed it as too difficult and stopped shortly after.
You actually have to be good yourself in BLC and the skillcap and teamplay possibilitys are way higher than in LoL or other games. The solo carry potential is way higher and the chance that you disappear in the mass, making your actions insignificant, resulting in you losing the game, although you personally really deserve a win is way less likely than in other games, if it had a player base that is.

Hitman Absolution is stealth assassination game done wrong.
The game hardly takes itself seriously. Or tries to take itself way too seriously at times.
The levels, missions, set piece battles, and challenges along the way are designed in a super annoying, quite restricting, overly frustrating and ultra-scripted ways.
Retry a checkpoint and be sure that the same thing will happen. Trail and error, rinse and repeat a bunch of time until you make it "right" in a way that's somewhat "smooth" and acceptable for you.
Combat isn't fun. It's messy.
Enemy AI feels dumb, and sneaking feels off.
Some corridors in the game feel like the most linear and annoying thing ever. Especially during action scenes.
There are a 101 ways to kill your main target - and it feels too easy and too ridiculous. It depends on these super-scripted events and windows of opportunity - that present themselves - often several times in an infinite loop:The smart deadly killer walks near a fuel station which fuel pump you can tear for a leak - and lights his cigarette before tossing it to the ground. KILL CHANCE. He then walks over a ledge with deadly man eating pigs. KILL CHANCE. He then walks out in the open for sniper fire directly in front a building his man are watching where a high caliber sniper rifles conveniently awaits. KILL CHANCE. Finally he will lean near a generator in a  place quite wet where...KILL CHANCE!!
Now to be honest - I mixed several KILL CHANCES from memory here. Because the game is just super- UN-MEMORABLE. But the fact is - you will have more or less these kinds of funny/silly/embargoing/gory/stupid kill opportunities throughout each level - that you can get the general idea!
The problem is-  it makes enemies feel like they were born to die, live to die, destined to die and placed neatly in deadly death spots.
Another example is railing over a fall into a bile pile of blood/corpses or something (can't remember) - the enemy will walk over there, wait a bit and continue his cycle patrol like path. OVER and OVER and OVER again - repeating the same spot and doing the same thing - in case you missed the chance to drop the piano on him the 1st, 3rd and 99th time - you get another!
The only thing making gameplay "difficult" is the clunky movement, clunky awkward and irritating / frustrating stealth system and stealth based part. Chunkiness that prevents you to kill the guy by pressing the red button of death - when you can just shoot him with a rocket launcher.
Yes you can kill him and all his minions easily if you just dumb some bullets or shoot some red barrels - but if you want to do the super-scripted special kill chances- you are going to have to work and wait in a SUPER-TEDIOUS and unrewarding way. None of that gameplay ever felt satisfying or fun to me.

The graphics are good, but they world isn't very impressive to look at. It feels small and closed in.
The story was just not clicking, it wasn't doing it for me. It felt random, and lacked any drive, meaning or reason. Just a dumbed down revenge tale of sort. With a poor ending too. It was extremely forgettable.
Its iconic character lacks more character than ever. Replace it with a man killing robot and you will have the same experience and results, mabe even better.
Sadly I cannot recommend this game.
Sure, I had my fun with it for a while. I finished the game at a high/est difficulty. I done most of the little tasks in-missions if not all. But the game constantly and repeatedly leaves you with this sour unpleasant taste, it's unmemorable, unrewarding, unsatisfying, and unexciting.
If you are a Hitman fan - then maybe that's a game for you. I played Hitman 1 and this one. The lasting appeal was non-existent and overall I wouldn't want to replay this game, and probably wouldn't have got it if I knew how it would be.

I haven't played Hitman 2016, yet. Blood Money was the best Hitman game I've played, so I'll judge Absolution in comparison to that. And it turns out to be a very unfavorable comparison.
Let's get the good out of the way: this game looks pretty good. Game mechanics are more polished. The instinct and blending-in mechanics are interesting. ...And now, time to dig into everything that's bad about Absolution, or at least worse than Blood Money.
The levels are chopped up into really small, mostly linear segments. Probably because the consoles couldn't have handled them otherwise. Gone are the large, sprawling levels of BM where you could execute the whole thing in a variety of different ways. Everything feels cramped and claustrophobic.
The devs apparently want us to play every level over and over again to increase our score, and even displays top scores from other people on your friends list in the menu. But I don't care about increasing my e-peen. And that's literally the only motivation, far as I can see. If the game doesn't care about me gunning down every civillian on the level, why should I? BM at least motivated you with reckless killing directly impacting your bottom line.
In the same vein, "evidence" is now just a collectible. Again, for the sole purpose of increasing your score. In BM evidence was actually, you know, evidence that you left behind. Such as a security camera recording of 47, or living witnesses that saw you do bad stuff. Such things impacted your notoriety, making subsequent missions more difficult. It was a cool and logical way to motivate the player to play like a professional. But logic and lasting consecuence don't exist in Absolution.
You cannot drop firearms to the ground. This tells me I'm never going to walk through a metal detector, I'm never going to get frisked while trying to enter a restricted area. Oh well, there goes that game mechanic, to be replaced with nothing at all. Also, you can hide any kind of firearms in your bottomless butt, including sniper rifles and assault rifles. No need to think about Agency drops or how to smuggle in a gun. Less complexity, less challenge, less things to hold my interest.
No more manual saving where and when it is most convenient for your chosen route. Most levels don't have mid-level saving at all. The larger ones have player activated one-time save points in static locations. Useless garbage. Get ready to play every difficult segment from the beginning every time you mess up.
There are several cinematic sequences. You know, the ones that plague triple-A gaming, where the game desperately tries to be a movie instead of a game. I don't count that in Absolution's favor. That's not what Hitman is about.
The difficulty to stealth a level bounces between insultingly easy and frustratingly, teeth-gnashingly difficult. Where in BM I fibrewired my way through the entire game and loved every second of it, in Absolution I've more than once just gave up on stealth and shot my way through the rest of the level. Mostly because no manual saves means I have to do the entire thing all over again at the slightest mistake. And since the levels are so small and linear, more often than not you can't even go somewhere else and try a different route. Straight out combat is too easy, but then Hitman was never about combat.
Contracts mode allows you to grind the same levels in a slightly different way. This is the only way to earn money, for which the only use is upgrading your weapons for increased combat effectiveness. This completely misses what Hitman is about. Anyway, it's already too easy to shoot your way through any and every level, if you so choose. No upgrades are necessary, making Contracts mode completely superfluous.
Absolution is not a bad game, it's just a bad Hitman game. All the wasted potential makes me a very sad panda. If you wanted to play a pretty looking but shallow triple-A amusement park ride of a game, you have plenty to choose from. But if you want to play a modern Hitman game, your list of options is thin indeed. Hitman games are not like most other games out there, and they shouldn't try to be.

Overview:
StockUp is a gambling game masquerading as a stock market game.  You buy stocks, and the prices may go up or down.  Contrary to what is said on the store page, this game is neither "fun" nor a "simulation."
Graphics and Sound:
I knew what I was getting when I got this bundle. (Which I only got for the sake of buying Make That Money.) So what if it's 2017 and the game is text driven?  There's quite a few text-based games that date back to the Reagan administration that are good fun.  Obviously a stock market game doesn't need graphics to make it interesting or fun, but I expect the text to be clear and concise!
The sound on the other hand, is actually far more positive. The soundtrack may be the most positive aspect of the game.  None of the songs help set the mood for a high stakes financial setting, but at least the songs are pleasing to hear.
Positives:
The intro to the game is amusing.
Negatives:
This is the worst game I've ever played involving something masquerading a the stock market, and I've played just about everything except for Black Monday.  (And I'm sure Black Monday is better on account of it's craptastic CGA pictures.)
Conclusion:
Now I see why publishers bundle games together:  Because you wouldn't buy stuff like this as a standalone game.  If only I had a physical copy of this game, I could have thrown it in the air and shot at it with my Glock, but alas, stuff like this shows you just how good the NES bomb Wall Street Kid really was, and as bad of a game Wall Street Kid turned out to be, I'll even go back to it every so often.
But if you want a stock market video game, get Rags To Riches.  It's F2P outside of Steam, and despite being nearly twenty-five years old, no other stock market game comes close.  If you want to spend money on Steam, buy trading cards for your favorite game instead.

I've been playing Magic: the Gathering for 19 years. This is a fun game for both experienced players, and those who are new to the game. You can play against other people, or you can play against an AI opponent.
If you're experienced, there is an advanced deck-building mode, but if you're new to the game, it has a deck wizard (no pun intended!) to help you as you build your decks. As you play the game, helpful tips guide you along, which you can choose not to reappear as you learn. The game tempts you to spend real money to obtain  "coins", which you can use to obtain booster packs in this game, so that you can get better cards to add to your decks. If you don't want to spend real money, you have the option to complete "quests", such as casting certain types of spells enough times, which give you the coins you otherwise would spend real money on to purchase the digital booster packs.
The only complaint I have is that there is a timer, which lasts for about two seconds. It activates in response to everything you do. From my experience and perspective, the timer is useless, and it's annoying. I see no advantage to it, and it actually hinders your gameplay if you forget about it, or if you don't click on it in time to stop it so that you can cast another spell, or use one of your cards' abilities in response to something.
You can customize avatars, backgrounds, and the names of your decks. The music is exciting, relaxing, and entertaining as well.
This game is fun! I love it! I just wish there was a button you could click to proceed to the next step instead of the timer. For keyboard commandos who like to do things quickly, keyboard shortcuts would have been the perfect finishing touch. I really don't see any reason why everybody wouldn't love this game.

Trying to remain brief at describing why I liked it "...a LOT", I made a list of stand-out features:
For me this was one of the first factors that pulled me towards that game. More specifically I would like to compliment the level design and architecture. The game takes place in various locations but one of the main locations, Chicaco, especially let the developers show their amazing design skills. Nice graphics only helped amplify all that and all that combined got me immersed more than in any game before.
Since I had played Blood Money before Absolution, I could immediately appreciate the greatly improved controls and the general control over the movements of 47. Besides the improved looks and graphics, the animations in this game also look very nice and make the game much more fluent.
Another very important factor is how well written the characters are. Combine that with proper Hollywood voice cast and you end up with characters that you can properly relate to. I would especially like to stress the amazing portrayal of the main antagonist,
, by Keith Carradine. Easily one of the best antagonists that I have seen.
Many people criticize this part but this game is more story driven than other Hitman games. How this reflects in gameplay is that the player progresses through smaller sandbox levels, varying in sizes, as opposed to other Hitman games where one level is usually one big sandbox. This limits the player's options and choices at times but really adds to the cinematic feel of the game which was something that the developers were knowingly going for. I quite liked it in that sense as I feel they managed to create this effect pretty well.

Thief is one of those games for you stealth purists out there. If you enjoyed Dishonored, DO NOT think this is the same game. Yes, they were both first person stealth games, BUT Dishonored lets you choose whether to be chaotic or not. In Thief, the game is centered on being a shadow. You don't want to be seen or confronted in Thief. On normal difficulty, you have to be skilled at the barebones combat system to survive a fight with two guards. The game doesn't WANT you to kill or knock anyone out. The way the game is meant to be played is to stick to the shadows and leave without a trace left that you were there. The game even has a CUSTOM DIFFICULTY that lets you change several settings. Over all, this game is amazing IF you enjoy stealth.
*To the people saying that you CAN play Thief chaotically, I know that, I was trying to get the point across that it is generally not advised and is not the original way the game was meant to be played. Also, many of the comments here comparing Dishonored to Thief are extremely biased towards one game or the other, I love and appreciate both games, and I think they are both amazing in their own ways.

It's kind of weird for me to review this game. I'll start with the cons. My major "complaint" is how hard it was for me to get used to the mechanics, three dash-jumps from start + slowmo was a lot to get used to, and if you're like me and decide to start the game on hard you're probably not gonna have a great time on the first level... And that first level is 1/7 of the game, which takes me to the next point: the game is really short, like, 40 minutes short, it ends when you're finally getting the hang of the controls.
Now, the reason I find hard to review this is cause those cons are also pros. The game is short, but no two parts are the same and every section in every level is filled up with new content and mechanics. The controls feel weird at first but HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥it's awesome to use the slow-mo to dodge two bullets, change weapon in mid air to hit that third one with the katana, make a few wall jumps get height and dash above those enemies, change to rocket launcher again without even touching the ground once and... You get it, it's fun.
To me, what makes the game is its replayability, and I'm sad cause I know not many people are into that. Each level has 4 difficulties with actual variations in them (different boss patterns, enemy placement, etc), and if you think finishing a level is fun, try finishing a level on v. hard without dying. It feels so rewarding when you know the layout and just how to use your abilities properly.
This review is already a mess and I haven't mentioned most of the stuff, so: graphics look cool, music is fine, story is almost non existent (still charming and the two dialogues are... good, I guess?) and everything feels made up with so much love. When you die, for example, Wryn says different stuff in different stages, that alone shows you how much attention they put into this little game.
Currently I have just a few hours, but I *WILL* finish everything on v. hard.
TL;DR: the game gets its awesomeness from replaying and learning the stages, so if that's not your thing, it's probably just gonna have twenty minutes of gameplay.

I have over 1000 hours into Civilization 5.. I played it from classic and bought all the dlcs. Civ 5 was an extremely fun game with almost every game starting out differently, and even though I played against all these civilizations multiple times, I found myself meeting new challenges and having to overcome different obstacles. "Oh I barely have a standing army after the last war? Here comes Arabia who owns half of the continent. Oh I am 5 techs behind almost everyone else? Let in invest heavily in science. 30 turns later I find myself ahead of everybody. Mongolia is invading within 100 turns? Let me position my troops in this narrow passage and hope for the best" I have a lot of memorable games that I cherish from Civ 5. Which is why I was so excited for Beyond Earth. Not only does it fufill my love of the civ games, but I'm also a fanatic for sci-fi/fantasy games. To be able to build up a civilization.. on a foreign planet? Two birds one stone.. Civ 5 wasnt perfect. Honestly religion was OP and, although, they made new ways of becoming allies with city states it didnt really have any depth to it at all. That, and the fact some civilizations had weak♥♥♥♥♥passives (ie. China/ America).. But it was all still fun. Not to mention some starting points you get lucky with. "oh I have cannons at 1000 CE(AD) while you still have long swordsmen? Tough." So when I finally hop into Beyond Earth, I'm excited... The lack of civilizations was a major turn off but it's fine. I'll just play Space America. I get in.. See the enivronment.. and it's all the same just colored differently. No real innovation.. The tech tree I was excited for was all honestly just bland and stupid. Especially if you are going for a specific way of life (i forgot what it's called ingame) and its getting to the mid-late game. No joke I beat my first campagin in 5 hours. That's all it took. Warfare isnt even fun in this game. I only built up a big army to deter others. I had no intention of using it.. It was♥♥♥♥♥♥to say the least. In my next game, which i play months later, I build up this huge army early game.. I planned on capturing a few cities from a close neighbor to solidify my hold in the region and pick up some extra resources.. I built 15 troops. Infantry, combat rovers, missle units, rangers what have you... None could make a dent in his weakest city. It's impossible to take a city early game. There is no point in having troops(except for against aliens) in the early game because none of them are going to have anything that will take your cities. Early aggression is pointless so you are forced to hash it out late game, and by then, they probably expanded into 5-10 other cities(in my experience maps are typically narrow and small even when set on huge). In short, there is honestly not a lot of counterplay. Again, warfare is boring. No fun at all. If warfare and diplomacy already dont put you off in the first place the visuals and the environment will. It's a pretty game yeah, but no innovation whatsoever. Such a shame too.
