I have played this game over 350 hours, and I have only put $1 into this game, which was when I first started playing. Personaly, I do not recommend that anyone put money into this game because a lot of people have already done that, so the outcome would be rather disapointing, but that is left to your discretion.
This game has very interesting machanics for a puzzle game and the fact that it is Marvel is very cool. I also enjoy the animations for the character abilities. Additionally, the story content is usually humorous and fun to follow.
The game has changed in a few ways over the last year.
First, when I started playing this game it was almost imposible to win in PvP or random events because people that put lots of money into the game had better characters at much higher levels. However, I continued to play and found ways to deal with it. But there is better news for new players. The game has been switched so that players are paired with other players around thier average level. So basically add all your character levels and divide by the number of characters. This machanic also tries to push people away from the idea of getting one high level character because it would offset your team average and put you at a disadvantage in a higher tier.
Originally, there were certain lower level characters with overpowered abilities, which have since been nerfed or changed to even out lower tiers because earning certain characters is a chance of luck and not everyone is lucky enough to get those characters early on.
I think the game has overall changed for the better, eventhough there were a few changes I didn't like.
As a new player it would be much advised to play through most of the STORY content in order to build a decent team and obtain COIN to purchase more character slots (I would advise that you use COIN ONLY to purchase character slots because you dont get a lot and it costs more and more for ever 3rd or 4th slot obtained).
I hope this was insightful. If so please rate it as helpful.

I don't recommend this game for three reasons. One, not enough variety; two, the shop prices feel too high; three, there's little sense of risk.
The gameplay involves jumping from planet to planet while collecting screws and dodging fireballs that travel up and down. That's a nice foundation, but it's all there is. If you can line yourself up and time your jumps properly, you can go on for dozens of minutes in a single run and not see anything new besides planets, screws, and the occasional group of fireballs. It would have been nice to see different types of obstacles, planets, or powerups, especially once you survive past the first few minutes.
My first run lasted around twenty minutes, and I managed to collect around 10,000 screws. Not bad, right? Actually, that was barely enough to buy the cheapest item at the shop, and all it did was increase my jump speed slightly. Most items cost at least 40,000 screws, which equates to over an hour of playtime at my speed. When you consider how repetitive the gameplay can be, that feels way too long.
There are optional challenges you can complete, but I've gone through around 50% of them, and so far the payouts don't seem to exceed 1,000 - 2,000 screws. Maybe the later ones are better, but some of them are rather tedious (play 30 games), and you can only pursue three at a time. Keep in mind that most of the shop items themselves- jump faster, attract screws from father away, increase your score multiplier- aren't anything exciting, in my opinion.
You press the left mouse button to set your angle, then release to jump. You can cancel a jump by holding down the left mouse button long enough, so there's no sense of commitment when you pick an angle. As the speed of the planets and fireballs increases, you can repeatedly cancel angles that look bad without any apparent penalty (unless I'm missing something). It makes me wonder what will kill patient, precise players first: the fireballs, or boredom?
Now, I bought this for $1, so you could argue I'm being awfully nitpicky at that price point, and I don't entirely disagree. Still, I think Beyond Gravity really lacks a sense of longevity. If more gameplay elements- planet types, obstacle types, powerups- were added, I'd consider changing my stance, but as of this writing I don't recommend it.

I've been play MapleStory for many years so I have bias towards it but regardless I'll try to be honest about it.
MapleStory is unlike many MMOs by the fact that it is a 2D sidescroller. Apart from maybe GunBound, there
aren't many 2DMMORPGs around and Nexon has done an incredible job over the years developing this game.
Although it's quite different now from when I first played it, I still find myself being drawn back in by the seasonal
events they put on annually. I've never truly stopped playing MapleStory for this reason. I can go months and even
years without play it but still find myself logging in to see what's been changed and updated.
CLASSES!
so MapleStory has an insane amount of classes. Although there are the 6 base classes (or jobs as they call it) of Thief, Magician, Warrrior, Archer, Pirate and Beginner (yes, some people play the game as the starting character and don't choose a job). There are seperate job groups that change the standard formula. This means there are a total
of 28 unique classes (not including the different Beginner or starter classes). And they are constantly balancing and
adding more each year.
F2P
The game is free to play with mirco transactions, however it's not pay to win. You can buy EXP boosts but only up to a certain level meaning high level characters have attained it without forking out money to boost there. There is plethora
of cosmetic item and more are constantly added.
Downsides
Now like most MMORPGs you will eventually find yourself stuck doing fetchquests and grinding for hours. It's for this reason I often stop playing during the main chunk of the year. My advice is to play during holidays such as Christmas, Easter, Halloween, Thanksgiving and New Years. That's where the most fun is.

No. Just no.
Translation issues aside--and there are many—an ability to chain dialogue events and map assets in RPGMaker does not a storyteller make. I appreciate that the developers are trying to build a short-story experience within a very simple choose-your-own adventure plot flowchart, and it’s a promising use of the platform. But Dear Red is sadly incoherent, not fun *at all*, and does not credibly integrate the fairy tale morality it touches on—and fails to provide anything approaching human motivations for the terrible decisions made by its sociopathic protagonist or the “murderer” father, despite its intermittent navel gazing.
The gameplay is also dreadful. Make a choice, end the story, and go back to the last save state to try the next option with a misplaced hope that the fragmentary and ludicrous scenario will start to make some sense. Two of the decision paths you must take to unlock “the full story” require you to sit in one place after dialogue events without interacting with anything—not that there are any real interactions or inventory choices to make. Bad architecture (demanding walkthroughs for completion), worse scenario.
I’ve played more than a half dozen RPGMaker games, and I would only recommend one of these titles despite its flaws: Waste Walkers, which generates a believably tense and messy dystopian environment through inventory management and a foggy, largely unknowable world map. Dear Red exists in three small environments and a baker’s dozen of choices you don’t really want to make and can’t empathize with… and the “real ending” payoff is insultingly ridiculous.
TL;DR are BundleStars dollar bundles ever worth the backlog?

The James Bond series focuses on a fictional British Secret Service agent created in 1953 by writer Ian Fleming, who featured him in twelve novels and two short-story collections. Since Fleming's death in 1964, eight other authors have written authorised Bond novels or novelizations: Kingsley Amis, Christopher Wood, John Gardner, Raymond Benson, Sebastian Faulks, Jeffery Deaver, William Boyd and Anthony Horowitz. The latest novel is Trigger Mortis by Anthony Horowitz, published in September 2015. Additionally Charlie Higson wrote a series on a young James Bond, and Kate Westbrook wrote three novels based on the diaries of a recurring series character, Moneypenny.
The character has also been adapted for television, radio, comic strip, video games and film. The films are the longest continually running film series of all time and have grossed over $7.040 billion in total, making it the fourth-highest-grossing film series to date, which started in 1962 with Dr. No, starring Sean Connery as Bond. As of 2017, there have been twenty-four films in the Eon Productions series. The most recent Bond film, Spectre (2015), stars Daniel Craig in his fourth portrayal of Bond; he is the sixth actor to play Bond in the Eon series. There have also been two independent productions of Bond films: Casino Royale (a 1967 spoof) and Never Say Never Again (a 1983 remake of an earlier Eon-produced film, Thunderball). In 2015, the franchise was estimated to be worth $19.9 billion,[1] making James Bond one of the highest-grossing media franchises of all time.
The Bond films are renowned for a number of features, including the musical accompaniment, with the theme songs having received Academy Award nominations on several occasions, and two wins. Other important elements which run through most of the films include Bond's cars, his guns, and the gadgets with which he is supplied by Q Branch. The films are also noted for Bond's relationships with various women, who are sometimes referred to as "Bond girls".

Publication history
Creation and inspiration
Main articles: James Bond (literary character) and Inspirations for James Bond
Ian Fleming created the fictional character of James Bond as the central figure for his works. Bond is an intelligence officer in the Secret Intelligence Service, commonly known as MI6. Bond is known by his code number, 007 (pronounced "double-oh-seven"), and was a Royal Naval Reserve Commander.
Fleming based his fictional creation on a number of individuals he came across during his time in the Naval Intelligence Division during World War II, admitting that Bond "was a compound of all the secret agents and commando types I met during the war".[2] Among those types were his brother, Peter, who had been involved in behind-the-lines operations in Norway and Greece during the war.[3] Aside from Fleming's brother, a number of others also provided some aspects of Bond's make up, including Conrad O'Brien-ffrench, Patrick Dalzel-Job and Bill "Biffy" Dunderdale.[2]
The name James Bond came from that of the American ornithologist James Bond, a Caribbean bird expert and author of the definitive field guide Birds of the West Indies[4]. Fleming, a keen birdwatcher himself, had a copy of Bond's guide and he later explained to the ornithologist's wife that "It struck me that this brief, unromantic, Anglo-Saxon and yet very masculine name was just what I needed, and so a second James Bond was born".[5] He further explained that:
When I wrote the first one in 1953, I wanted Bond to be an extremely dull, uninteresting man to whom things happened; I wanted him to be a blunt instrument ... when I was casting around for a name for my protagonist I thought by God, [James Bond] is the dullest name I ever heard.
— Ian Fleming, The New Yorker, 21 April 1962[6]
On another occasion, Fleming said: "I wanted the simplest, dullest, plainest-sounding name I could find, 'James Bond' was much better than something more interesting, like 'Peregrine Carruthers'. Exotic things would happen to and around him, but he would be a neutral figure—an anonymous, blunt instrument wielded by a government department."[7]
Hoagy Carmichael—Fleming's view of James Bond
Fleming decided that Bond should resemble both American singer Hoagy Carmichael and himself[8] and in Casino Royale, Vesper Lynd remarks, "Bond reminds me rather of Hoagy Carmichael, but there is something cold and ruthless." Likewise, in Moonraker, Special Branch Officer Gala Brand thinks that Bond is "certainly good-looking ... Rather like Hoagy Carmichael in a way. That black hair falling down over the right eyebrow. Much the same bones. But there was something a bit cruel in the mouth, and the eyes were cold."[8]
Fleming endowed Bond with many of his own traits, including sharing the same golf handicap, the taste for scrambled eggs and using the same brand of toiletries.[9] Bond's tastes are also often taken from Fleming's own as was his behaviour,[10] with Bond's love of golf and gambling mirroring Fleming's own. Fleming used his experiences of his espionage career and all other aspects of his life as inspiration when writing, including using names of school friends, acquaintances, relatives and lovers throughout his books.[2]
It was not until the penultimate novel, You Only Live Twice, that Fleming gave Bond a sense of family background. The book was the first to be written after the release of Dr. No in cinemas and Sean Connery's depiction of Bond affected Fleming's interpretation of the character, to give Bond both a sense of humour and Scottish antecedents that were not present in the previous stories.[11] In a fictional obituary, purportedly published in The Times, Bond's parents were given as Andrew Bond, from the village of Glencoe, Scotland, and Monique Delacroix, from the canton of Vaud, Switzerland.[12] Fleming did not provide Bond's date of birth, but John Pearson's fictional biography of Bond, James Bond: The Authorized Biography of 007, gives Bond a birth date on 11 November 1920,[13] while a study by John Griswold puts the date at 11 November 1921.[14]

Between games like Undertale, Pony Island, and IMSCARED, the idea of breaking the fourth wall of the game to terrify the player directly is quickly becoming one of my new favorite tricks.
IMSCARED is the full retail version of the original, much smaller game of the same name released back in 2012. If you've heard of it or seen any gameplay videos or Let's Plays, chances are you're already aware of the game's central "gimmick". If you'd prefer to go into the game blind (which I recommend) then don't read any further. IMSCARED is a good game for a very cheap price. Worth the play.
If you're curious, then read on: IMSCARED's main idea is that the game will mess with your computer itself to deceive, attack, and scare you. Essentially created a horror game acting like a malicious, haunted virus. Right off the bat the game automatically creates a folder on your desktop where it will send you messages, sometimes to aid you, and other times to taunt you. The ways the game requires you to think outside the box and the ways it uses your computer become more creative and more clever as the game goes on. For a gimmick, it's a well implemented gimmick.
It should be noted that when I say the game's tricks get more clever as you go along, the entire game really is the same way. The first gameplay section of IMSCARED (past the short tutorial) is the original 2012 game in it's entirety with one or two very minor changes. Compared to the rest of the game afterwards, the beginning segment feels amateur, and it's not a great testament to what the game had up it's sleeve. It feels very much like the developer took the original game and has been building and improving on it since 2012, leaving the segment feeling a tad uneventful and slow (not that the segment is bad, mind you, but the rest of the game just feels a lot better).
You're probably going to either tolerate or hate the graphics. It's VERY low-res and can make finding small object sprites hard. On the flipside, it does help push the idea that "this is a video game that's acting very wrong". Movement can be annoying, as the game has a tendency of having you get stuck on objects or even in narrow corridors, especially when running.
The game's no Silent Hill 2, but it has some fun, creative scares and incredibly creepy atmospheres, especially when it incorperates the gimmick of a haunted video game. Even the least subtle parts are still better than many cheap indie horror games.
Much of the gameplay consists of puzzles, which get better as the game goes on and it fully utilizes the central idea to it's potential, even if there's a bit overreliance on keyhunting, usually there's more than just backtracking to keep it interesting.
Overall, for four dollars, IMSCARED is a good game to check out. Maybe it won't for your style if you can't suspend some disbelief at times, but if you can, then I believe you're in for an enjoyable and scary ride.

The core gameplay is very very good, I'm not going to try to go in depth with why its good but its basically the only relevant 2D side scrolling retro beat them up and it works very very well in turning that genre into a functional combat system for an mmo. If you are looking for that alone then this game fills that niche very well.
However I have quite a few gripes with the MMO aspect of this game. When nexon owned it, leveling up was a lot slower, but the slow grind allowed you to enjoy each of the dungeons in each area with strangers and the social aspect was a lot stronger due to more players playing back then. In this current version of the game, leveling up is primarily single player and is a very streamlined process where you do scenario quests one after another. You are systematically rushed through each area to get levels and finish the epic quests to reach level cap asap where the "real game" begins.
Late game is pretty much where I had to stop playing because the game simply became a chore. My character platued in power and the only way for me to get stronger was do 3 daily quests a day for a whopping 30 days straight, the game has a huge amount of "daily quests" where it basically forces you to commit to doing those missions every day for up to a month, then funnle you into a new area where you grind something else for a month. Then theres hell mode, which is a very expensive way to get the ultimate late game items, imagine gachpond systems in other games, except every time you roll for an item you have to do a mission for 5 minutes for less than 1% chance of getting something good and that something good might not even be an item your character can use.
I still recommend this game, but only play it as long as you are having fun with the combat and all the cool classes. If you ever feel like the grind is becomming too repetitive or too big of a commitment for marginal gains, just drop it like a rock because its just an abusive relationship at that point with no real pay off besides wasting your precious time.

A once-great game with a rather unique style, ruined by balance changes homogenizing all the classes, pay-to-win power creep, and no customer support.
Aside from the graphics of skills being different and some classes requiring ammunition to use theirs, it's all a matter of using the fastest skill that hits multiple times so you can hit the damage cap twelve times in a single attack. With the occasional buff to prevent the bosses from instagibbing you with one of their attacks.
The only challenge most bosses in this game have come from one of two factors:
1, Attacks that reduce your health and mana to 1, dispel your buffs, or take control away from your character.
2. Having HP totals somewhere in the billions, and a short time limit to bring that to zero. Not a problem for people who hit the damage cap with every attack (50,000,000), but for people too self-aware to spend loads of dosh on cash items to upgrade in-game equipment they're impossible.
Getting away from the game mechanics, the servers are infested with hackers and botters. How infested? There are more botters in the game than actual players. There's a "Report to GM" function, but if a GM actually responds to it, you should probably either buy a lottery ticket, or more likely slap yourself in the face because you are in a dream world where the impossible is possible. GMs only show up to host godawful events and spam emoticons while spouting lies.
On that note, the game has an autoban function built into it, which 90% of the time bans nonhackers doing something mundane for no reason. On the off chance a hacker/botter actually
banned, they'll eventually be unbanned because Nexon likes giving people "second chances" and unbanning everyone who was ever banned up to that point. Why? Because hackers spend money too ya know! Gotta keep profits up!
I said there is no customer support, but I was lying. There
a customer support ticket system, but it would probably better if it didn't exist at all. Tickets can go without a response for literally
. Nexon also has this opinion that having your account hacked into is the player's fault and refuses to compensate. One of the Global exclusive areas even has a quest line that mocks this, giving the middle finger to everyone who had their account broken into and laughing at them.
Long story short, Unique art-style Platformer-MMORPG that crashed and burned and then was grinded into the dirt. Cause of death? Power creep, pay-to-win, and apathy and malice from the company that runs it. Avoid it like the plague if the plague were also on fire and making rude gestures at you.

One of the best stealth games.
Certainly a classic, and the strongest entry in the Splinter Cell series imho.
Also runs on a potato.
Which is what I used when I first played it on release, ya know, back in the day with those high falutin cd rom devices.
You can tackle most of the missions all guns blazing if you want, or opt for the classier stealth method - but with all the different weapons, tools, distractions, and environmental opportunities available to you both paths are generally viable.
When using stealth, you will find that patience, observation of the enemy and exploration are rewarded. Taking the time to learn patrol routes, and finding convenient ways to dispose of corpses or making a mental note of sneaky exits for when the mission goes wrong all go a long way here.
Fortunately the levels are very well designed and encourage this whilst still giving you other options.
The soundtrack is generally awesome, being composed by the legendary composer Jesper Kyd and the ambience of all the environments really helps to draw you in.
And the lighting. While the graphics still hold up well today, this was one of the first games that allowed destruction of lights.
Yes it is possible to shoot them out entirely - strangely satisfying with a "pffft" from the silenced pistol.
That being said the accurate yet cool default pistol is also posessed of a better function that temporarily disables them (and cctv cameras) - it can shoot emp waves at short range.
How cool is that?
Its an even quieter method than the silenced pistol, does not waste ammo, and draws less attention if people decide to investigate. The light, or camera in question will soon reactivate and be perceived as a power fluctuation or some glitch which doesnt bother guards apparently. Just long enough for you to sneak past though or silently slit someones throat...

I really want to love this game. It's one of the best stealth driven games ever made. The other positive reviews can explain all the good points about this game.
But there's just one problem: This game was designed for consoles, and the keyboard + mouse controls are ridiculously awkward. Where console players just need to tilt their analog sticks, you need to manually adjust your movement speed with the mouse wheel. Where console players can have context senstitive controls, you can only designate each key to one action. It's frustrating when the game can't be enjoyed due to technical problems like this, which begs the question: Why not enable full controller support to fix all this?
Well, the lack of full controller support for this game really hurts, because now you have to go and install a bunch of other programs just to get the game to recognize controller input as if it was coming from a keyboard and mouse. It's a massive headache, especially when it doesn't work or requires programs that aren't free...
To be clear, this negative review is NOT concerning the game itself. It is criticizing the fact that this is a very lazy port of a console game. No controller support and super awkward controls make an otherwise excellent game VERY frustrating.
The day Ubisoft actually gives a damn about their games and enables controller support for this one I will change my review to positive.
Sadly, knowing how Ubisoft operates, that day won't likely ever come.
Edit: It seems the Xbox 360/One controller, as well as the PS4 controller (which is recognized as a 360 controller by programs such as DS4Windows) may give you more success than I did with a PS3 controller. Unfortunately I can no longer test that because I refunded the game after my initial review to avoid the hassle.
I still believe full controller support would improve this game, but it seems that you may be able to get it to work with those controllers. I definitely recommend testing it before you keep this game to make sure it works as intended (because if you can get it to work, you will be treated to one of the best stealth games of all time :D )

tl;dr A free, "light" version of Magic, great for a casual game to kill some time, but with some bugs.
So what are my thoughts on this? Well this is Magic the Gathering. It is clearly designed (like the previous Magic games) to hold you by the hand, probably to help new players through the complexity of the game. Unfortunately it can be hard for a new player to understand important things about the game, like the phases of a turn, when the game hurriedly skips through them. Sure, you can stop the timer by pressing space, but often I find myself forgetting to press it and missing important plays.
So what are the pros?
- Nice looking visually.
- Nice music.
- Story mode contains some lore about the iconic planeswalkers.
- Good for a quick casual game when you're lacking time or friends.
- Free to play.
- Magic the Gathering.
And the cons...
- Somewhat stupid AI.
- A bit too high randomness because of badly built decks in some story mode games.
- The game crashes occasionally, which coupled with the previous con will annoy you when you finally have a good hand are about to beat an opponent.
Personally I am not against microtransactions per se. It all depends on how it's done, and I do not expect anyone to make a game for free. So when it's done in a good way, I will even chip in to show the developers my appreciation. In this case however I am not going to invest anything until the game crashes are fixed.
I see some people complaining that it skips past phases in the turn even though you have a valid play. This is incorrect. It might seem like it, because when playing MtG at a table you will be doing things in a slightly different order. However, you can do these things in this game as well. It's just not as intuitive.

This has always been and will always be my personal favorite in the Splinter Cell series. The stealth gameplay here is phenomenal, challenging, and has a greater sense of believability than later entries. If you have played Conviction and/or Blacklist, be warned: those games are much faster paced than Chaos Theory. Chaos Theory requires a great deal more patience and the action is less flashy, but you feel like a genuine badass picking off enemies from the shadows. This is only accented by the game's difficulty level; it is a challenging game, especially on harder difficulties, but I never found it to be unfair.
The level design is very well done here across the board (single player, co-op, and versus modes all taken into consideration) and offer a variety of paths to complete your mission. There is also plenty of variety in the settings for these levels, from lighthouses to cruise ships to banks. The graphics for this game were phenomenal for the time and still hold up surprisingly well (particularly shadows and lighting effects), although character models can tend to look very "blah" compared to today's standards. The audio is honestly one of my favorite parts of the game. The music is great and fits the in-game tension perfectly, the voice actors  did a great job and have some funny dialogue, and Michael Ironside will ALWAYS be the true voice of Sam Fisher. Good lord, that voice.
The multiplayer in this game is phenomenal too. The versus mode is a fun "Spies vs. Mercenaries" mode where spies, who sneak around in third-person, attempt to hack information from terminals while the more lethally equipped mercenaries (who are controlled like a first-person shooter) attempt to stop them. It's an entertaining game of cat and mouse. The co-op mode also has it's own completely separate campaign from the single player version; however, it upholds the same standards of level design, challenge, and fun. I'm a big fan of co-op games and this is among the very best, in my opinion.
**An important note on the multiplayer: The Ubisoft servers for this game are down and you will be unable to play if you attempt to log in directly online through the game. There is a VERY easy workaround for this, however. I am currently using software called Evolve that allows you to create a virtual LAN connection with other friends, which allows you to play this game online through the LAN menu. I am mentioning this  because it's free and I truly think it is worth the time.**
Honestly, there's a lot to love here. Over the years this quickly became one of my all-time favorite games and still is to this day. If you are a fan of stealth games or you're simply looking for a challenge, I am certain you will adore this game.

Tom Clancy's: Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory: Featuring Tom Clancy is pretty cool, I guess.
You play as Sam Fisher, the world's sneakiest dad. Sam works for an organization called Third Echelon, who's entire purpose is to spook the enemies of America and take their things. Over the course of a few missions, Sam discovers a conspiracy to do bad things to somebody or something and has to use all of his sneaky tricks to stop it.
To be fair, I really like this game. Like, REALLY like this game. If I were to have to give a gold star to any game, it would probably be this one. Hurray, you did it! Mr. Clancy!
Oh no, Mr. Clancy is dead!
Bom Stancy's Stink Cell is one of those stealth games that actually focuses on stealth. Although you can go in loud and make a big scene, you are treated like a stinky idiot and penalized for it. In old games, if you got caught three times, the mission would end. The alarms are still there, but the missions don't end anymore, instead the enemies just get progressively more resistant to your presence. One alarm goes off and they know something is wrong, two alarms go off and they know something is definitely wrong and start packing heat, and on the third alarm they actually come looking for you.
It's a pleasant difficulty spike that actually punishes you and spanks your bottom for playing like a Sally.
Luckily, the stealth part of the game is the best part. You have two meters, the spook meter, and the loud noises meter. Stealth is based on line of sight and darkness, the darker it is, the harder you are to see, the spook meter actually shows how concealed you are in the dark, with the darkest meaning you can basically brush a guards beard sensually and whisper sweet nothings into his ear and he won't notice you, while if the meter is all the way to the light side you may as well be buying travel insurance and live in palm beach.
Sound is also a big thing that can either aid or hinder your success. There is a cap that moves depending on how noisy your environments are. Like a thunderstorm or a loud engine can conceal the noise you make while a room with someone sleeping or a hollow cave will make you easier to hear.
Your adversaries are usually guards, which is expected. The guards react to sound and when they think they saw something, but usually just bumble around until they realize something is amiss. What is pleasantly surprising is how the guards actually interact with one another. Outside of scripted conversations, they also coordinate with one another when they're looking around for something strange. While they're working together they usually have some kind of worried conversation about hoping not to find anything as well as mumbling to themselves if there's nobody looking with them.
It really gives life to the guards in a genre that is usually void of any kind of personality for your opponents.
You have a few ways of dispatching your foes. Outside of 007 style gadgets like the sticky camera and
the shock shooty, you can also choose to either knock them out, whack em, or just bypass them all together. There really isn't a better feeling than getting into a area and out without anyone even knowing you were there to begin with.
I am not going to continue to gush about this game.
Back in the day, there was a big scene for Chaos Theory's multiplayer, and rightly so. There were two multiplayer modes, one where you yelled at your friend for alerting the guards in co-op mode. And one where you yelled at other people because they somehow saw you while you were across the hall in the dark behind a box in the competitive mode.
Co-op mode was actually it's own game, where you and a friend took control of two freshly trained Splinter Cells as they went on missions that sometimes went on at the same time as Sam's outings. Each mission was built with team work in mind since the two agents had a set of moves they could perform like boosting each other on to high ledges, roping your partner down a deep pit, disrupting cameras with your microwave emitter while the other sneaks through the dark, and thinking about monster trucks and manly things while you climb your partner like a ladder and sensually rub against him.
While Co-op was really cool, competitive was a beast all on it's own. The game was a two on two affair where a duo of spies part of an organization known as SHADOWNET infiltrated into facilities protected by a mercenary group known as ARGUS.
When you play as Shadownet you play like a usual Splinter Cell with some extra moves and gadgets added in. But when you play as ARGUS, you play from a first person perspective and mostly rely on brute force and fire power. ARGUS patrols the map and guards the objectives while Shadownet has to sneak past them and steal the goodies without being spotted.
Competitive is tense, like, poop in pants tense. You have very little offensive options as Shadownet and are forced to either run or get filled with new breathing holes when you get caught while ARGUS has no idea if a Shadownet agent is near unless he has his flashlight pointed directly at him, or his noise detector goes off.
It's hide and seek but with more fire power. Both sides have enough options and gadgets to dispatch one another, like how Shadownet can break the necks of the ARGUS mercenaries they can sneak up on and how ARGUS can set up tripwires and mines to catch Shadownet spies off guard.
It's an amazing mode and sadly has whittled over the years due to just how old the game is.
But should you play Tem Sensy's Sneaky Guy: Math stuff?
Its still one of my favorite games ever. Even though the multiplayer glory days are over, the single player is still top notch stuff. You can get your money's worth on single player alone, but if you can get a few friends together to spook one another, I would recommend that as well.

Yet another indie game where the developer had a single barely fleshed out idea for a gameplay mechanic and then couldn't be bothered to create any actual meaningful gameplay or narrative or anything compelling at all, then just filled the rest of the game with minimal effort "artsy" aesthetics and vague, nauseatingly pretentious statements that mean nothing at all.

The core gameplay is very very good, I'm not going to try to go in depth with why its good but its basically the only relevant 2D side scrolling retro beat them up and it works very very well in turning that genre into a functional combat system for an mmo. If you are looking for that alone then this game fills that niche very well.
However I have quite a few gripes with the MMO aspect of this game. When nexon owned it, leveling up was a lot slower, but the slow grind allowed you to enjoy each of the dungeons in each area with strangers and the social aspect was a lot stronger due to more players playing back then. In this current version of the game, leveling up is primarily single player and is a very streamlined process where you do scenario quests one after another. You are systematically rushed through each area to get levels and finish the epic quests to reach level cap asap where the "real game" begins.
Late game is pretty much where I had to stop playing because the game simply became a chore. My character platued in power and the only way for me to get stronger was do 3 daily quests a day for a whopping 30 days straight, the game has a huge amount of "daily quests" where it basically forces you to commit to doing those missions every day for up to a month, then funnle you into a new area where you grind something else for a month. Then theres hell mode, which is a very expensive way to get the ultimate late game items, imagine gachpond systems in other games, except every time you roll for an item you have to do a mission for 5 minutes for less than 1% chance of getting something good and that something good might not even be an item your character can use.
I still recommend this game, but only play it as long as you are having fun with the combat and all the cool classes. If you ever feel like the grind is becomming too repetitive or too big of a commitment for marginal gains, just drop it like a rock because its just an abusive relationship at that point with no real pay off besides wasting your precious time.

I am going to recommend this game, just because I was a fan of this game since the Korean DnF first started.
And I think it's worth trying for an experience.
However, DFO right now is not the same one I enjoyed long time ago.
Neople made some questionable decisions, and that made the game quite boring.
1. More and more dungeons are becoming linear. Please stop. I think we call it "dungeon" for a reason.
2. The quests, dungeons give so much exp, that once you clear the quest, you never have to go back to the dungeon.
3. The quests are brainlessly simple, that gives abnormal amount of rewards. Why?
4. Too much events that keep spoon-feeding the player beyond necessary.
5. Growth weapons/armors. This eliminates the reason why people collect things until max level.
6. Minor: There are too much buttons that distract me. It's about time to clean up the GUI. It's simply messy.
Overall, the game is too geared towards people who played DFO for a long time with multiple maxed characters.
The end game stuff is definitely abundant, but getting there is so painful and boring.
And no, the solution is to not make lvl 1 ~ 89 easier.
No, you don't just give out lvl up coupons so people can skip that part easily.
DFO, when it first started, was a game of adventure, struggling against hard bosses, and getting that sweet reward when you finally beat the boss in highest difficulty (there were normal, expert, master, king difficulty for every dungeon) made everything worth it.
Now, all are given, you are already a hero, and you just gotta walk the same boring path every time you make a new character, barely being able to continue playing because of pretty skills that your new character has.
Sigh, but it's not like I don't understand what's really going on.
The true fun of DFO was always in MULTIPLAYER.
The co-op plays and PVP are the core foundations of this game.
This made you want to get other chars (as you either get jealous or feel the need of certain char in a party)
This also made it okay for dungeons to have very high difficulty (overcome with the power of friendship! *cringe*)
Now, try looking up DFO gamplay footage on youtube.
Unless it is in Korean, you'll have hard time finding co-op plays of DFO.
It's because the ping (internet connectivity) in US is not good enough for DFO's fast paced, combo based action.
This is the devs fault for making this game using P2P connection, as it naturally assumes all players have good internet connection; but hey, they probably never imagined that this game would be exported outside of South Korea in the future.
My rant was too long, but in the end, I just want to say that DFO is slowly but surely turning into a max level character collection game.
The original spirit of DFO was this: Adventure and challenging boss fights! And rewards that make all worth it.

In Starseed Pilgrim, the first thing you learn is that you can break blocks and plant seeds. You are then set upon a large, earthy block suspended in white void and expected to use your fresh and limited knowledge of this universe so far to explore away from your starting point. Different seeds grow at different speeds, shapes, directions, and wonderful sounds. You plant away and start to climb, sure without being sure that there must be something else in this vast emptiness besides yourself.
There is a challenge to the exploration, discovery, and successful return home – enough that even with the game's insistence on minimal to absent guidance, you'll want to make it at least once.
However, it is after surmounting this first hurdle that I no longer felt compelled to play, because the more I saw of Starseed Pilgrim, the more I recognized it as a solid proof of concept rather than a complete and satisfying game. Allow me to explain.
The blocks, the seeds, and the void are simple components: easily understood with some trial and error. These same elements, however, are also samey to a fault and become bland with overexposure. While the simplicity of the core mechanic is both visually and sonically polished, the simplicity of the game that contains it is lonely and boring; it feels incomplete. You will make your way from base block to base block with practiced efficiency, but there is less and less of a reason for you to do so. Exploration continues to reveal more of the same, as if the game had something against variety in design.
I have heard that, with some doing, you can indeed find the novel experiences that I expected as the rewards for my progress. I'm afraid that I just don't have the patience. I enjoy exploration for exploration's sake, but when a game tells me nothing and shows me even less, should I really be expected to keep at it?

I really did enjoy this version of the long running Civ franchise. Though I do prefer Civ 5 to BE, this is still a good game.
With a UI and gameplay similar to older Civ games, it's easy to dive straight in without needing to reacquaint yourself everything. The new research tree fits really thematically well with the ideas of the game, allowing you to spread your research across wide fields and specialising within specific areas. In addition the Affinity's add some new flavour to the game, giving each a unique look and feel (there are a few problems with this system though, I'll get to that). The introduction of the Orbital layer and satellites adds a new strategic layer to city planning and tile management and combat. However it is possible for one player to monopolise orbital control (I had one game where I could launch a satellite anywhere on the entire map). The satellites let you improve production, energy, science or provide military support. Allowing them to fit to your individual play style.
Now to issues with the game.
Whilst the Affinty automatically upgrades your units, it forces you to upgrade them the moment you have the minimum experience in any affinity level. Meaning you may end up with soldiers who are outside of the affinity plans you had. Whilst careful selection of research can combat this, it can become tedious. The rate at which aliens spawn and become hostile/peaceful can range from absurdly fast to never (world creation does come into play). Many of the environments become boring and bland with very little diversity of terrain across an entire planet. Whilst trivial, these can become annoying.
Overall though, it's a great game.
Loving it so far, would recommend.

You know there are two kinds of review you should take into consideration when you have a reboot for an oldschool game like Thief. There are the the people who are hardcore fans and are looking for the game they know and love, then there are the new players who are looking for a good game in general. I am new player, I have never played a Thief game before this so obviously I speak for the 2nd group of players. So far this game is very fun and unique among my game library. I am glad to see this game sticks to its guns and focuses on actual thievery and isnt combat such as Assassins Creed or Dishonored, fighting multiple enemys is suicide and stealth is always the best option. There is also the ability to customize the difficulty in any way that suits your playstyle to make it harder or easier, by chooseing harder settings boosts your score and rewards you for playing hardcore. Another feature I like seems to be similar to Splinter Cell, after a mission you receive a score based on three catagorys (Ghost, Predator, Opportunist). My only beef with this game so far is that its a little linear and the maps seem small compared to a game like Dishonored. Its just my preference, its nothing against the game. As long as a game maintains a strong story and good mechanics then being linear is fine, being a linear game seems like a bad thing these days and to me its just one method to telling a story.
On to the second part of this review.
When I was reading reviews on metacritic today I noticed that about 90% of the negative reviews were about how "modern" it was or how it was a crappy addition to the series. Now I can understand why people might be disapointed in the direction a game might take but it doesnt make it right to give it a 0/10. Fact is that this is a quality game and plenty of effort was put into developing it, thats all I can ask for.

This game is a pure example of what is wrong in the "Steam Greenlight" independent game industry. And mostly, what kind of trivial mistakes, the dervelopers, are doing in the process of developing an "indie game".
First, about this "game". It's suppose to be a MOBA type FPS but the "game" is in this stage practically from the beginning with no actual or visable updates. The only visable change was the changing of the name of this "game" from RiP to AXYOS. Yes, I know that the "game" is in "Early Access" but it's not, even, in an Alpha stage. I keep saying "game" with quotation marks because there is no game at all. Yes, the "game" looks like in the screen shots but that's it. Only nice characters models, some weapons and some textures made with the UnReal DevKit. And that's it!
No gameplay at all. There are 3 maps, one of them is in two variations : day and night. The layout of the maps is flat. And I mean really flat - very basic path layout.  There are some weapons but with no notisable difference, like damage or reload time, between them. There are some items/buffs and the idea of item/buff usage. But with no meaning how to be implemented into the gameplay. There is some basic AI maybe from the DevKit. These models just sits there with no connection and meaning between them. No backstory, also. Nothing, except the basic idea that this suppose to be a MOBA type FPS and you must to shoot people. There are achievements. But most of them are broken maybe because of the lack of gameplay or some other reason, I don't know, and can't be obtained. There are only 2 servers, the last time I checked but there is an "option" to create your own servers. Looks like "Make your own game" starter pack.
Now, about the mistakes. The dervelopers are making some of the most trivial and basic mistakes that I'm wondering if they have the abilities to start any kind of business. Obviously, they don't have a clear assessment about their abilities and concept. Can they handle the development of a FPS multiplayer game? But the most biggest mistake is the misunderstanding of the Steam "Easly Access". The main idea behind "Easly Access" is to cut the cost and time of Beta testing and the feedback to Q&A for bug and glitch removing. Not to funding your game like the dervelopers are doing with this one. Several times in the game's forums the developers are saying that they are using the money from the sells to fund the development, maybe that's why we have a DLC on not completed game, here. But if this is thue why the game is always on huge discounts( above 70%) on sales. And there is another thing. The dervelopers said, again, several times in the game's forums that they are temporary stopping the devopment of this game and changing to other project called "Neon Arena". And if the game is successful they will continue the development of their previous game. But again we got a surprise. We have not just one game but two games in a few months "Crispy Chicken" and "Neon Arena" which are actually one game just reskinned. This is a very suspicious behaviour: If we don't support the new game we will never get the old one!?  Another "misleading tactics" from the dervelopers side is the existence of achievements and Steam Trading Cards. I already said about the broken achievements but I must to mention that they are getting a fee for every traded card.  And to not forget to mention that the Col. Jack O'Neill SG-1 in his review is describing a problem with acrivation keys for this game. Here's the
Now, that kind of "business practices" shows not just misunderstanding of the Steam "Easly Access" or any basic business rules. But a very suspicious behaviour similar to the infamous "Digital Homicide".
This is a Early Access review and I may change it if I see any futute development. Until then, I highly recommend to everyone to stay away and don't buy this game, not even on high -90% or above sales. I bought it on sale with -78% discound and I regret of giving my 1,24EU to it. This "game" don't deserve to be accepted even as a gift.

Sorry to say but after playing the Forza games on console you realise how terribly mediocre this game is.
Deathly dull career mode, badly ill-conceived multiplayer system which requires you to laboriously level up each car before you can upgrade it to become competitive with other players.  Unintuitive menu and lobby systems.
You can buy your own cars, but each time you buy one, you have to level it up which is tedious and time consuming, and even then, there is NO guarantee you will ever actually get to race it.  Because there are so many different categories of car, WITHIN say the street class.  So you go to a street class race, but you still cannot use YOUR street class car because it's not in the correct sub category which you CANNOT choose, you just get what you're given.  It's a dreadfully designed system.
The track minimap doesn't show you anywhere near enough of the track, it is too zoomed in and cannot be changed.  Also the edges are faded which makes it even worse.  You get like half a second advance warning of where the next corner is.  It is almost useless.  By the time you can see the corner on the minimap you can see it in front of you on the road anyway.  Why not copy how other games do it, like Gran Turismo or Forza? Or NFS Shift, where the minimap automatically zooms outwards as you go faster?
Overall a very lacklustre and unrewarding game.

This game disappointed me. Mostly because it failed to live up to promises that it would return to the roots of the Grid franchise. I LOVE the original Grid. Despite being more arcade style than Forza or Asetto Corsa or any of the other various sims on the market the original Grid managed to make you feel like you were really racing. From team, teammate, and sponsor management to the way the different types of races ran, to the 24 hours of le mans being the highlight and marking point of every season, you really felt like you were running a team and that you were working towards a goal. Racing for something. Grid: Autosport promised a return to that original feeling but failed to deliver. After just a few hours of dull, meaningless, and slow gameplay I found myself returning to the original just to get the feel of a decent race in. Autosport does well in some ways.... The audio is amazing. Wind noise when in open wheel cars is awesome and imersive. Everything else is just lackluster. Like it didn't know where it wanted to go. One part Forza, one part Need For Speed, One Part Grid. All added together equals a mediocre experience that would be better played out in the original or in other games.

A few years ago I was going through an old footlocker and realized I had the box to this game (disc lost long ago) and plunked the key into Steam.
I was a PC gamer when Metal Gear was entering the 3D polygon era and while I did enjoy the VR Missions entry, I never had much interest in that series because while I owned the consoles for every generation, there were very few games I absolutely had to have.
The original Splinter Cell came out and I was amazed with how the stealth elements translated so well from games like Tenchu to the world of guns and electronic gadgets.  Pandora Tomorrow followed it up sort of well, but not many people loved it (including myself).  Chaos Theory is what I consider to be the final entry in the series- it took everything that made the first two games great and gave it a gorgeous graphics and mechanics update, and took the story in a direction that was compelling and interesting.  Every level has hundreds of different ways to play out, and you have 100% control over most of how that's decided.
They lost me after this game, and it's sad.  I tried every game in the series after Chaos Theory but nobody really understands that it might be OK to stick with what works anymore.  A followup to any of the first 3 Splinter Cell games, even HD remasters, would be freakin amazing but sadly, I seriously doubt they'd be handled with care.
Chaos Theory is probably the only game that I'd compare to the same enjoyment I got out of the first Tenchu.  It's a shame nobody picked up the core mechanics of this game with more than a haphazard spin of the wheel.

If you're not accustomed to 3rd person action game, you will not like this game at first.  You will die many times.  But don't give up.  Once you get used to the control scheme, combos, and so on, you will get addicted.  This is actually one of a few games that I played recently that I got really addicted.
One thing you have to keep in mind is that this is a very competitive game.  It's all about Player versus Player.  Expect to meet numerous rude players who will keep killing you, but don't just assume that you're just bad at this kind of game.  Believe I wasn't PvP type of guy either but I stuck with the game, and now I guess I can hold my own pretty well.
When you first start the game, be sure to check out all characters in training so that you know which one suits you the best.  You will be able to buy two characters at the beginning so be careful not to buy the rather difficult to control characters. (like Elika, Renny, DanMei and so on.)
Anyhow, once you get addicted to this game's competitive nature, you will be playing this game for hours without know the time flies.  I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who's looking for a non-stop pvp fighting action game.

This is a solid example of the tower defense genre. It's not genre-defining, or even particularly innovative, but if you enjoy tower defense games, then you should like this one. I like the art style, and the gameplay is simple and pretty balanced, with a variety of towers and lots of upgrades to help you keep up with the waves of dinosaurs.
I do wish that the little story blurbs and/or new tower explanations didn't come up every single time I replayed a level. Clicking to open up a tower's upgrade menu sometimes opens up a nearby tower's menu instead when they are too close, which isn't usually a big problem, except when the speed is at the highest setting. It seems like you have to click the base of the tower. If the top of the front tower overlaps the bottom of the back tower, clicking on the top of the front tower opens up the back one.
It would also be nice if the game had a little more "extra" content. The story is pretty bare-bones, which is fine for a tower defense, but even so, it's a bit hard to understand what is there. The opening shows you some kind of explosion, leaving you and your robot trapped in the past. It's not clear why you were going to the past in the first place nor how you're progressing toward fixing your time machine between each tower defense level. Also, it would be cool to have a bestiary where you could look up all the dinosaurs you've encountered so far in the story with their speed and health, and a similar listing of the towers you've unlocked, with their base range and damage.
I've had a good time playing it, and don't feel bad recommending it, despite the shortcomings. That said, if you're on the fence about getting this one, I also don't feel bad about saying you should probably wait till it goes on sale.

Day D Tower Rush is not a game that is jammed full of extra content like PixelJunk Monsters Ultimate HD is by any stretch of the imagination. Unlike the aforementioned title, Day D Tower Rush lacks any multiplayer, medal challenges, or ad-hoc play. That said, it is also less than half the cost of the that game, so if you don't care about those features then you could in theory get a competent tower defense game on the cheap.
As much as I enjoy this, the game unfortunately has its issues that could be quite annoying to some people and make the extra cost to avoid or the simple savings of not getting involved the better choice.

Ahh I have been waiting for this game for years to come out and finally it has, and it has met all of the expectations that I was assuming, so i'm gonna go over what's good and bad.  1st of all, ignore the meta review, it's kind of lieing, atleast I think so, 2nd of all, don't listen to IGN or any of those stupid reviewers, those people only review crap they like, plus they just get paid to badmouth anything good.
PROS:
Garrett!: Garrett has had a new voice actor, and some clothing changes, which fit him pretty good, he actually looks like a true thief now instead of the weird clothes in the 3rd game.  Oh, and the new voice actor looks JUST like Garrett...it's creepy.
First Person: It's back to it's original first person, and i'm glad, 3rd person was good in Deadly Shadows but it kind of killed some of the atmosphere, it only goes into third person if you are climbing along pipes or in a cutscene.
No more knife!: I'm glad they took this out, it felt way too overused in the others, you are a thief, not some killer, but don't fret, the blackjack is much better, you do damage and can still knock out targets, and even kill them if you want, but don't be a p*%#y, stealth it for gods sake, that's the whole point.
Upgrade system: There was a level up system at one point but they trashed it, and i'm glad that they did, now at the merchant you can buy item upgrades, increase health, take more damage, etc.
The Watch: The Watch is now a bigger pain than before, instead of just running away and hiding you have to go in houses and hide up on roofs if you don't want to get killed now.
Atmosphere!: It feels really nice, not just thrown together, even in levels that weren't supposed to be scary there was still a creepy feel to it all, and it was just like the last games.
Another scary level!: This I was glad to see...they put another scary level in the game, and I am only about 15 minutes in and i'm still terrified, if Eidos knows one thing, it's to make a good atmosphere.  And if you are one of those people that doesn't immerse themselves in a game, then you don't consider everything scary, if a scary level sucks even if you immerse yourself, that's different, but I played this level in the DAYLIGHT and got terrified of it, you're probably one of those idiots that just sprints through it ain't ya?
Alerting animals: There are birds and dogs in this game now, and they can be alerted if you make to much noise, birds don't seem to care if you are near them, as long as you don't make noise to disturb them, but dogs? The dogs are a$$holes, I didn't even go near the cage and the little c*%t started barking at me so I had to slide away.
Dash: You can dash now! As well as sprint, the dash isn't overpowered either, which is good, you basically dash in a short range from one place to another, but guards can still see you, it's nice in some cases, one time I was hiding behind boxes with a street light next to them, and if I walked out the guards would have seen me, so I dashed over and they did notice, but they didn't realy pay attention.
Freeroam: I am glad this is still in the game, the one thing I hated about the first and second games is that the maps were so bloody huge I got lost, I'M TALKING TO YOU GAMBLING DEN FROM THIEF 1.  Plus there are more opportunities to loot from windows, people, etc.
Sidequests: Basso has side quests you can do for some cash if you need it, some are short and some are long I believe, haven't really done them all that much except for 1, and it took about 10 minutes.
You're Eye!: The eye on Garrett has changed, and it's much better, now instead of zooming in with a GOD AWFUL brown effect that didn't really light up a area, you can now see secrets on walls and stuff, and even lights up the whole area if you can't see, it costs energy though, and the only way to get it back is with Poppy flowers.
Tools!: You can buy tools later on from the merchants, there is a alarm box tool (kills the traps that can set off alarms), the screwdriver/wrenchwhateverit'ssupposedtobe, it can unlock bolts from sewer grates and even plates on the walls for your collection, and the scalpel, which cuts off pictures from walls, all useful in some way.
CONS:
Characters: Some of the characters just kind of feel thrown in there, I don't remember "Basso." Although he might have been in the first game or something, as for Erin she is part of the story, so she gets a excuse.
No jumping, instead free running: I don't mind free running AT ALL, but it feels good, and weird in this game, you can't jump, incase you didn't read the title, you lazy f*%k, but you can vault over obsticles, jump up on ledges, glide over chest-high walls, etc, it feels a little wonky at times though, like it doesn't do what you want to do.
Iventory: I didn't know where to put this so I just put it here, the inventory is perfectly fine if you were wondering, but there is no more holy water/holy arrows, and you get a limit on flashbangs, which is good honestly, means be more stealth you p%$ck, don't run and gun, or you will die.
Frame issues: I noticed while I was playing that the framerate started being a total♥♥♥♥♥♥and lagged out a few times, but other than that it worked fine, one cutscene it got so laggy the animation and words sped up just to catch up, and I even turned a few things down lower to get more frame rate.
AI: Some of the Ai is stupid at times and will just wig out, one of those zombies started spinning around in circles in it's place, and some of the Watch got stuck on stairs, but other than that it's fine.
Map linearity: I don't mind having some linear maps or maybe something a little big, but I honestly didn't like how linear some of the maps can be, but some are just huge and they are fun to explore, that's one of the things I hated over the 1st and 2nd thief games, the maps got so huge it got annoying to run around trying to hide from everyone.
AND WHATEVER IS IN THE MIDDLE:
The story: I'm kind of in the middle between the story being good and bad, it's more towards good so far, I am a little lost, something about- oh yeah, SPOILER- something about Erin dying in a place where these people where chanting and she disrupted it and pretty much killed herself, even though Garrett attempted to help.
The Gloom: This is basically the Plauge from Dishonered, although I kind of didn't really care all that much, instead of you helping the citizens out by "Not killing" you basically just kind of wave it by like it's nothing, but everyone seems to be getting sick as you go, so I don't know where i'm at with it.
WHAT I THINK:
I think the game is pretty damn good despite a few things i've noticed and didn't seem to enjoy all that much, the game to me gets a good 8-9/10, I think if they were to take a little longer on it it might have done better, but who knows, some things you can't make any better, hint hint Castlevania 2 hint hint.

==Pluck Feedback==
-The sin-wave on the title screen logo looks a bit goofy. I like to reserve sin-waviness for stuff like collectables. Seeing the logo move back and forth kind of deprives it of any sense of weight / epicness.
-You might prefer “Press Start” to “Press Key”. The former is a general convention that means “Press anything”. The latter confused me, when all I had in my hand was an xbox controller.
-Gotta have analog stick support for traversing menus.
-The menu selection cursor moves vertically, then appears to update its position horizontally on the following frame. It gives me a bit of a headache, and looks jarring.
-Toggling to fullscreen softlocked my game. I can’t see anything anymore, but I can hear my cursor moving back and forth.
-The deadzone on the thumbsticks is non-existant, which is really unfortunate. Most xbox controllers experience some amount of thumbstick drift as they get older, so deadzones are a necessity. As soon as I began the game. I my character was already shooting!
-The help menu told me I could move with the thumbstick, but apparently we’re stuck with dpad movement. Dpads aren’t great for this kind of thing.
-I really wish the music changed going from the title screen to the gameplay. It feels a bit cheap, and by the time the player enters gameplay, they’ve already been exposed to the same music loop for some time, which sours them on it.
-Notice that, if you shoot in the direction you’re running, the bullets actually start behind the player (visible via their tail), and they don’t travel as far in front of the player. You should add the velocity of the player to the velocity of the bullet at the time the bullet it spawned. This should make it feel a bit better to shoot.
-The “wall-fall” effect is very pretty!
-The little ball of magic that the player avatar holds switches sides depending on where the analog stick is, but this can look really jarring when I’m aiming up or down. When I’m aiming straight northward, the ball freaks out, moving from side to side quickly.
-Hopping animation is cute, and an efficient way of animating.
-The game has a framerate hitch ever second or so. This isn’t game breaking, but it makes the game’s movement feel a bit choppy.
-Destroying crates is fun, and could use just a bit more juice. Maybe a slight bit of screen shake?
-Hits on enemies is indicated by a soundeffect, but not a great deal else it seems. You might experiment with making the enemies flash, or using some other aesthetic indicator of pain.
-I tend to die alot, and very suddenly. It’s usually a nasty surprise, because it’d somewhat difficult to know your health in this game. When people are looking at the center of the screen (because that’s where all the action is), they’re not looking at the bottom of the screen (where the health bar is). Find a way to show the player’s health at the center of the screen, so players don’t have to divert their eyes from combat to get that information.
-The dash mechanic has potential, but it doesn’t get you very far. I would really like some Smash-Bros-Style Pikachu functionality, where you can chain dashes to go around corners, dive around attacks, etc.
-Please consider zooming the camera in a bit. The sprites are pretty tiny, and there’s really no need for the player to be able to see into 9 rooms at any given time.
-I want to love coins, but I’m not sure what they’re for yet.
The game has a number of accessibility issues, and combat isn’t particularly satisfying, but there are some real elements of polish here, and I like the concept for some of the attacks (the swords are pretty nifty). Please take 494 so we can chat about it :D

I'll begin by stating that I understand what hardcore Thief fans are saying about this game. It's mostly true, but to deny that this game is fun if you enjoy the stealth genre, and has plenty of missions, side quests, and other activities to partake in, then you'd be lying.
The first portion of the game holds your hand some, and is linear. This is the tutorial mostly, and the 'showing you the ropes' part. After you get to the city hub, you have a decent degree of freedom to progress how you wish from there.
Whether you play with all the features enabled, or go hardcore, the customization of settings will help you choose what kind of challenge you get out of Thief. There is mystery, suspense, action, and drama lurking in the shadows, and as more secrets are revealed to you those shadows will suck you in. Thief is fairly addictive, whether you are a klepto trying to score all the loot or the big heist, or you like to feel like a real badass and complete the game as a ghost.
I love it so far, and recommend it to anyone that enjoys stealth games.

MOST OF THIS REVIEW IS CRITICISM EVEN THOUGH IT IS A POSITIVE RECOMMENDATION FOR THE GAME.
Before you read this review I would like to mention I have been a Civilzation series fan since I was 8.
________
The Raw Review (the one you most likely want):
Although I do recommend this game for alot of people, I do not recommend it for people who like real-time strategy AND (AND) do not enjoy sci-fi because those people would find this game boring and uneventful, as well as very similar to Civ V (Sid Meier's Civilization V). If you do enjoy sci-fi as well as I do, (time travel, warp engines, transparent titanium, etc.) then I do recommend this game for you. The more you like sci-fi the more you will enjoy the game.
________
The Detailed Review (the one you will want if you are borderline going to buy or not):
As many other people have mentioned in their reviews, the Rising Tide of Sid Meiers Civilization Beyond Earth has brought people back to multiplayer. The problem is though, you basically need to buy the game AND the expansion so the cost of the game is in reality 20-30$ more if you want to play multiplayer because no one seems to want to play vanilla Beyond Earth anymore.
Summary: Multiplayer (in a way) needs to be purchased because it is hard to find players who don't play the Rising Tide Expansion Pack
Aside from the Rising Tide Expansion, Single Player is too easy (AI vs. you). You get used to the easy difficulty (Mercury) and learn the strategies of the game, and you find that all the sudden you're so good at the game after only 90-160 hours that the Gemini difficulty (meant to be the medium-hard difficulty) is insufficient for your need for hard opponents.
Summary: The hard difficulty more easily than it should becomes the medium difficulty.
I hear other people talking about how the game is too unreal, and the reason why they feel that way is because that floatstone (a major resource of the game) is just a rediculous idea. They are right, but everything in the game can be at least vaguely (correctly) scientifically explained except floatstone and stationary "orbital" units. However, Orbital units are one of the things make the game unique and different from others.
Summary: (Aside from that un-realistic-ality) The game itself not affected very much by the not-very-realistic/possible things, but how you feel about the game is affected.
(Aside to creators of the game):
In the real world, landscaping exists. In this game, there should be floatstone workers (or named Drone Workers) added to rising tide as a unit that can move mountains or seal up canyons. (Or maybe add and remove ice at certain lattitudes...?)

So I have very mixed feelings about this game.  I have to say, it's worth avoiding so-called "Free to Play" games, as they intentionally abuse game design and put it not in the service of telling a story or making a compelling experience or whatever, but rather in the service of getting microtransactions out of the player.  It don't think it's possible to avoid that, save for doing a shareware model where you're playing an extended demo for free.
I assumed the above before playing any "free to play" games, and I'm more certain of it after sinking time in to quite a few over the past year or two.
All that said, Marvel Puzzle Quest is the best of them I've yet seen, and there's a lot of fun to be had from it...but at the same time, it would be a better game were it designed like the mainline Puzzle Quest games that you just purchase and play.  There doesn't appear to ever be an endgame here...it's basically just repeating story elements that ultimately are trying to get you to pay money, but never really lead anywhere.  I've seen stories in this repeated a half dozen times now, sometimes slightly mixed up, sometimes the same storyline/quest has repeated literally twice in a row.
And it's a shame, because a lot of what's here is actually great.  I played Puzzle Quest 2 while playing this, and I actually like the basic "puzzle combat" gameplay here better.  The art is generally fantastic too (and looks better and the screen layout is much better on PC than on iOS/Android).  This is the most fun I've ever had with the basic mechanics of a single screen action puzzle game.
The adaptation of characters' powers to the gameplay is well thought out-they're clearly trying and mostly succeeding in making it work.
I won't lie, it's a lot of fun to collect and power up your favorite characters and have them beat down your opponent.  But it gets frustrating when you realize it’s really towards no end…there’s no endpoint, just that endless repetition of mostly identical story elements recycled again and again.
The most egregious way they try to get you to spend (a lot) of money on it is for slots to hold characters.  They give you a very small number at the start, and since both for gameplay reasons and because it’s cool to have them, you’ll quickly want/need vastly more slots than they give you.  You technically earn the resources to buy slots within the game, but that’s a VERY slow process that’s not very practical-I think since I started playing they’ve made that worse too.  You’re pretty much forced into paying real-world money to be able to have the slots you’d want and need to actually continue playing.
So would I recommend this?  There’s so much fun in it, and it’s so well done in many ways…and yet at the same time, there’s no ending.  There’s no resolution to the story.  It’s just a fancy treadmill to get you to pay more, and it’s a shame that this same effort wasn’t put towards making this a “real” game.  Even an MMO model might make more sense for it (as it is actually an MMO in many respects).

I've marked this as a positive review. But please, read on:)
While I didn't play this game on steam, I did play it the millisecond it was available to play, several years ago.
Within literally hours of game being released, lvl10 people started bashing on, like, lvl6 people. It was fascinating, to say the least. I have never seen a game brought down in such a quick manner by its own community and with such efficacy. I played bunch of hardcore, "unwelcoming" games, but BLC is the only game that managed to develop a ridiculously antisocial atmosphere within mere hours and to totally devolve into a complete toxic mess in the matter of days. I have yet to see a game that has a player base near BLC's when it came out.
It usually takes a relatively long time for a game to develop the unwelcoming atmosphere and some don't develop that at all. Usually, the more skill-based game is, the more divisive and aggressive the community will be. But that won't happen until at least a few months after the game's release.
Technically and mechanically, the game is a masterpiece. I will dare and say that's an objective assessment. The feel of the game, the gameplay, the champions, it's all executed responsively and flawlessly. This game had an unfair fate, because of the bad economic approach and also bad marketing, but nothing rivals the absolutely attrocious player base it somehow managed to acquire in like two days since it was released.
Hearing some time ago that the game will come to steam, I hoped that it would finally receive the recognition it deserved. I have yet to install it, but sadly, it seems that the situation is even worse and that its player base will singlehandedly murder it for the second time. I can't understand the notion behind it, but if a game you love and play gets a second chance on a new, popular platform such as steam, it is very counterproductive for you to get defensive and not let people in "your game". For a multiplayer-based game, the ONLY chance is for it to have a healthy and relatively large player base, especially if there's a MM necessary, to provide even matchups.
But now, browsing through the comments, I see a pattern: unwelcoming community. Regardless of whether the review is positive or negative, this seems to be the only constant new players perceive and isolate in their reviews.
If this changes, though with the player base fiercely opposing the idea of the game getting new players it certainly doesn't seem it would (but one could hope), I would recommend this game possibly more than any game ever made. This might be an overstatement, but all things considered, BLC is a masterpiece in every way.
That said, remembering how it was only hours after the game's release, I actually don't know whether I'll install it or not. It seems that today's situation is only worse, which is hard to imagine.
All in all - game is superb. Player base, well, isn't - and don't take this lightly. It's not your standard dota, lol, wot etc. notion. We are all used to that. This is something very extraordinary.
So, basically, I will mark this as a "yes", because the game is fantastic. Would I advise people to play it though? Not really, but you are free to try and see for yourself. This might seem paradoxical, but it's not - if we talk about the game per se, it's wonderful, but it's the only game I've ever played out of thousands of multiplayer games I've played, that can effectively sour the gaming experience of even a full-fledged rhino-skinned lobotomized psychopath.
