I thought this game was cute, and I saw an episode of the cartoon once and though it was cute. I saw a lot of reviews comparing this game to the classic collectathon era of platformers on the N64, many reviews specifically citing Super Mario 64 and Banjo-Kazooie as games they felt were similar.
Importantly, if you are a fan of these games, do not believe these reviews. This game is nothing like those games at all. The stages are completely linear. There is no exploring to do. There are no hidden items. There are a few tiny branches in the path sometimes that will lead to a few extra items, but you can get those same items without taking the branch, so it doesn't matter. It's simply a waste of time. You can easily collect everything without even bothering with those branches.
Items are not unique. You could just play the first stage over and over without taking the branching paths and you'd collect everything in the game. So there's no real "collecting" to do. Everything is just laid along the straight path you take to get to the end, so there's no effort or discovery in collecting it.
You never have to figure out what you're supposed to do to continue in the game. It's always either walk forward or hop, or use your special ability as one of Pac-Man's many forms. You're always turned into the form at the moment you need to use it. There's never more than one solution to move forward.
When I heard the game was "easy," I was expecting this to mean there was low difficulty. Something like Hello Kitty Roller Rescue; however, what people mean when they say "easy" is that the game literally does not have difficulty. Often there are no obstacles or challenges at all, just a path to walk forward on. This has the same difficulty level as watching a TV show, except you have to hold down a button to allow the TV to continue to play. There's nothing to jump over or avoid. Just move forward. Sometimes turn. Sometimes hop up a ledge. There are no fail conditions. There's only a small handful of enemy types in the entire game (you'll be encountering pretty much the same few enemies all over every stage) and the solution to defeating all of them is just to mash the attack button. The enemies are slow and stupid enough, though, that you can just walk right past them without ever having to think about them.
Bosses are slow and dull. The way damage words in the game, Pac-Man will not get hurt if he is hit while in a special form. If the boss requires you to be in a special form, you can usually just stand over the transformation berry, so when you get hit, you just eat the berry again, so you never take damage. So then you pretty much are just waiting for the boss to the do the attack you can retaliate to, and then you respond, so the boss is pretty much nothing but waiting.
In fact, the entire game just felt like waiting. I never felt like I ever got to actually play anything. I felt like I was always walking through the filler section of a level -- the part where you just walk through a hallway before you actually get to some action or challenge. And bosses were pretty much just watching a bunch of animations until they died.
Of the 8 or so hours it took me to clear the game and collect all the achievements (which requires you play every stage twice), I'd say maybe about 30 minutes actually felt like I was really playing a platformer. The rest was just filler content with no difficulty or challenge in any way. The game may as well have just been an eight-hour cutscene.
The game's final world felt like it was thrown together at the last minute. It's extremely short and somehow even easier than the rest of the game. It almost plays itself. Stages are about 1/4 the length of other stages. The final boss I defeated in about 30 seconds without effort. Then the game just sort of... ended? There wasn't any kind of big animation or special cutscene or anything. Just a tiny joke scene where the characters basically said that everything you just did was pointless and nothing was gained from the whole ordeal. Pretty much a summary of the actual gameplay, I guess. Then the credits just... show up. And it takes you back to the stage select menu. It was really shockingly underwhelming, considering otherwise, the game was aesthetically very nice. There were lots of cute animations and lots of little voice clips and stuff. When Pac would transition to other areas or eat a fruit or something, there was a really cute animation to go along with it, and a lot of different ones, too. Each fruit had a unique animation, and almost all of the warp tunnels and stuff had unique animations, too. Overall, the game was very nice from a graphical standpoint.
But as far as being a game is concerned, it hardly ever feels like you're even playing a game. The "difficulty" is about on part with walking around the castle in Super Mario 64, or playing a fighting game against another player... but the other player is just a controller sitting on your couch with no one actually controlling it.
Even for children, this game would probably not be entertaining, unless they REALLY liked the characters and graphics and didn't mind that they really weren't doing anything. Children can handle the difficulty of games like Mario and Sonic, which are leagues above this game. I've never played a game with less difficulty than this. Even educational games for preschoolers have harder platforming than this. I would not recommend this to children.
I was really expecting to like this game, and I tend to be pretty open and like all kinds of games, even easy ones. I did enjoy Hello Kitty Roller Rescue quite a bit. I love Mega Man X7. I like lots of "bad" games and can find what is good about them. But this game has no redeeming qualities aside from some cute characters and nice graphics, and like maybe one stage that was fun to play, and only barely (the dragon stage!). The rest is tedious and painfully boring to get through. I don't like to judge a game without finishing it, but getting through this game was a struggle, even with it only having about 8 hours of total content even doing everything extra, and I'm pretty slow with games.

this is by far the best pvp oriented game I have ever played. It has a few short commings that I will address as well.
Pros.
-fast paced games ( most complete games last 5-6 minutes total)
-highly based on personal and overall team skill ( stats do not prove who wins)
-no meta ( you don't "have to have a healer" or tank or w.e pick what you want)
- no chat filter
cons.
-poor and or lack of management
- win traders
-long matchmaking times....
- lack of updates or content
-lack of players
-lack of players who are willing to practice and quit
-complainers....
That out of the way lets touch on the pros. This game will not have you sitting down for hours just for one match bored out of your mind. Even when lossing it just shows you what you have to work on. As stated this game soley works on your skill. You can litterally miss (or dodge) melee attacks making your skill level determine how good you are. There are prefered team comps however you can pick whatever champions you want as long as you kill their team before they can kill yours. In this game with no chat filter they do not overly babysit you and "force you to behave." If someone is being annoying just mute them and be on your way.
Now for the cons. The poor management is probably what gets under the remaining players skins the most. You will often see people typing in channels saying " if only this game had advertising etc. etc.
Lack of updates show the blatant fact that this game is running on autopilot. Even community driven events would have a highly positive impact on the game. Win traders are a plague in this community, I will not point fingers but it gets under everyones skins when you worked hard to get your rank and someone else got they highest ranks by cheating the system.
This game has a lack of players however I would like to note that many veteran players will re download the game to see the current state. If you were to look at the total amount of people who played just for one season the number is quite high even though the quene times are long...
Tagging along with lack of players is the bigger problem. New players have a huge learning curve as well as having to deal with smurfs and wintraders. It is not easy to begin this game and deal with long quene times so many quit.
And finnally people who whine all day about the game. Some people would probably stick around longer if everyone didn't whine in the public channels.
My conclusion is this game is a very good game however it is an unpolised gem. If you pick this game up and manage to get past the long learning curve you can very well spend a lot of time playing.

'PAC-MAN™ and the Ghostly Adventures' is an action-platformer port of the Xbox 360 version, and is based on the cartoon sharing the same name. As with many PC ports the game is limited to 30FPS, which was found to be acceptable and cooperative during my gameplay at all times. But is this new Pac-Man who enjoys burping in your face, talks in an annoying voice, and being a meme worth your time?
The game features 4 different worlds (2 are reused for a total of 6) with around 5 levels per world. Pac-Man has 7 different upgrades that provide new abilities used in both exploring the environment and dealing with enemies. Aside from the main game, the game also features 4 minigames which resemble classic games of the past such as Atari Tanks, Silver Surfer, Defender and the emerald minigame from Sonic 2. The game is short, with my first playthrough done in 4 hours, and replaying the game to get all of the achievements took a total of 9 hours. Although you might consider this to be too short for the average platformer, the levels provide a good balance of length and difficulty to remain enjoyable throughout the entirety of the game. The story, on the other hand, is directed towards fans of the show and will not spark interest amongst the majority gamers. The story involves saving Pac-Mans friends and tracking down the final boss Betrayus, which serves its purpose by being as simple as possible. The graphics in the game are passable as the character models look almost identical to the source material, although within each world there is a distinct lack of variety. Many of the assets are repeated over and over, which is complemented by the short level length to keep the game fresh. The game features professional voice acting from the show, which can be considered good or bad depending on how annoying you find the new Pac-Man.
PAC-MAN™ and the Ghostly Adventures provides a mediocore platforming game that shows a commendable amount of care and polish, which is rare considering that the game is based on a TV show. While I would jump to reccomend higher quality platformers such as 'Tembo the Badass Elephant' or 'Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams', those games provide longer levels with increased difficulty that may not be suitable for everyone. For those who want an enjoyable, short, and forgiving platformer, then I can definitely reccomend this game.
Unless you find Pac-Man terribly annoying, and for that I apologize.

The question is whether or not you can overcome those flaws and start to face the real challenges which are set before you in this game. I have some things to say about Pac-Man and the Ghostly Adventures. The sort of things you’d expect to be discussed about a 3D platformer, be that on the topic of level designs or how every 3D platformer is essentially Super Mario 64 redubbed. I promise we’ll get to those things, but first there is something more important I need to touch on, and that is: what the bloody hell is going on with Pac-Man’s lore?
I know what you’re thinking. “Pac-Man has lore?” At some point what was once a sparsely animated, power-orb munching arcade game would appear to have been wholly transformed into all manner of mass merchandise, chief among them now an animated kids show bearing the same name as this new entry in Pac-Man’s gaming catalog. What exactly goes on in this show remains a mystery to me, as the game itself offers not so much as a cursory explanation for some of the most bizarre developments. At some point Pac-Man appears to have made peace with his age-old ghost antagonists and is now…attending high school with them? Whatever truce was made though only seems to apply to the four most recognizable ghosts of the series, as Pac-Man is more than ready to devour each and every other ghost he encounters on his journey to do “something”.
The plot is of Ghostly Adventures remains entirely unclear to me, but it would seem to involve ravaging ancient temples for anything not nailed down, to then be immediately consumed by Pac-Man. For however altruistic Pac-Man would profess himself to be (proclaiming himself at times to be a super-hero), his entire purpose for being seems to solely revolve around gorging himself. On fruits, on ghosts, on historic artifacts, Pac-Man doesn’t care! The only thing more present than ghosts in this adventure are burger dispensing vending machines, though if need be Pac-Man seems just as happy to rummage through a trashcan for a bite to eat. His insatiable appetite is perhaps on the surface innocuous, but there is something deeply disturbing about a world that seems to exist solely to appease the hunger of its most famous resident.
So too is Pac-Man’s relationship with the ghosts that for some reason are both accepted and outlawed, simultaneous friend and foe, or more accurately, food. At one point it is revealed that collecting the eyes of ghosts will allow Pac-Man to generate more lives, calling into question just what exactly pac-people are. Were ghosts once pac-people too, or did the pacs evolve by devouring and multiplying through the consumption of ghost eyes? Is the real reason for the eternal war between Pac-Man and ghosts actually the result of pac-people enacting genocide upon the already dead for the sake of some disturbing means of reproduction? How many thinkpieces will it take before we arrive at the conclusion that Pac-Man was the monster all along?
There is a layer of Ghostly Adventures that I would love to believe is inexplicably aiming for subversive surrealism. So much of this kids show spin-off feels odd and unnerving compared to the Pac-Man games before it, that to have it finally reveal itself as some deeper commentary on an industry that refuses to let old icons die would be incredible. But the truth, as is so often the case, is far more mundane and expected. Ghostly Adventures ultimately isn’t the abstract arthouse Pac-Man game I never knew I wanted (and probably do not actually want to play, but only to exist), but merely the inevitable result of a series that has long since fallen out of relevance. Aside from perhaps Sonic there are few greater gaming has-beens than Pac-Man, a character who never really got to be one, but was almost immediately repurposed into a brand icon. At this point it seems fair to say Pac-Man is more popular within the realm of phone cases than videogames, and Ghostly Adventures isn’t going to change that. It’s a feeble attempt at regaining interest in an outdated mascot, breed from an even more misguided ploy to appeal to an audience that is likely too young to have ever even had an affinity for Pac-Man as anything more than a recognizable face of gaming.
Ghostly Adventures exists in the realm of so many TV and movie spin-off 3D platformers, which are at once entirely inoffensive and unremarkable. Remove Pac-Man and the ghosts and this could just as easily be any N64-era inspired platformer, replete with the requisite abundance of meaningless collectibles, and a camera that is often nauseating even when it’s working as intended. Levels are standard fair straight shots, relying mostly on an abundance of ghosts to slow you down than anything approaching clever platforming. Ghostly Adventures would almost be obnoxiously easy and trivial if it were not for how easy it is to die from slipping off a ledge or clipping on the edge of a platformer you ought to have been able to make. I never died so often as to have anything less than an unreasonable amount of extra lives, but each death brought with it enough repetition to still be an absolute chore to deal with.
Every platforming standard is accounted for in Ghostly Adventure, but it somehow manages to make genre conventions even more dull than they already were. There are ice levels and fire levels, spooky levels and colorful levels full of interconnecting tubes (the exit animations for which are probably the most variety to be found in the whole game), but it’s all so astoundingly boring. And maybe it’s my fault for hoping this game would be even slightly more than it appeared to be. It’s possible I am simply, as a friend put it, “kicking a kids game in the shins,” but even then I have to wonder what kid is going to play this over the likes of Mario or Minecraft. Perhaps judged solely against other games likely to confuse grandparents and disappoint their grandchildren on Christmas, Ghostly Adventures is far from the worst you could do, but calling it acceptable mediocrity hardly seems much of a compliment.
Ghostly Adventures is so utterly typical that it is too mundane to be legitimately upsetting. It falls perfectly in what seems to have become an established trajectory for videogame mascots (pioneered primarily by Sonic), where upon reaching peek obscurity developers then resort of inserting their iconic hero into games they were never designed for and which in turn do little to regain the status these characters once held. Ghostly Adventures isn’t bad, per say, it is just exceptionally uninteresting. It is not unreasonable to say you might enjoy parts of it, but even in its normality Ghostly Adventures finds a way to grate on you. Maybe it’s the way Pac-Man ends every level with an enormous burp which sees a swarm of ghost eyes escape from the bottom of whatever is inside his spherical body. Or it’s the realization that you’re playing a Pac-Man game that is in no way Pac-Man, but is rather the cold, inevitable result of a game designed for the sake of marketing potential. Or maybe it’s just that Pac-Man was always more cultural icon than game character, and that’s probably for the best.

I fired the game up and was met with an advertisement saying it recommends I play it with an Intel HD GPU so you can already guess just how excited I was to sink my teeth in to this.
As far as the game goes, it's a very beautiful arcade racer (as opposed to simulation. Whether this is good or bad depends on your personal tastes). The models, the lighting, the sound effects are all on point and they start you off with a half decent vehicle and have you work your way up in to much nicer stuff. There's a fairly basic yet still interesting story that makes you feel like you yourself are working your way up the ranks rather than simply "YOU BEAT LEVEL ONE. NOW BEAT LEVEL TWO."
Another thing I should mention is the game has a "replay" function mid race. If you wipe out, you can simply hit a button and rewind the race about 8 seconds or so and try that part again. Is this very helpful to new players? Yes. Is this a great thing to have on a practice course where you're just trying to work on your cornering and fish-tailing? Very yes. Is this a good thing to have in the actual races? No. Look at it any way you want, it's hand holding and cheating. It's no different from gutter guards at the bowling alley and by having this function, it reenforces that you don't need to actually be good because your mistakes don't matter. It isn't simply "You screwed up, oh well. I'll let you retry but don't do it again." You have 3+ rewinds per race. You could argue that your mistakes actually don't matter because it's single player, who cares what you do? Let me come back at this with saying that Single Player should be readying you for competitive play, be it online or when a buddy comes over, or whatever. Maybe I'm just set in my old ways of racing where if you screw up, you start over from the beginning and you keep starting over until you get it right. Your opponents will be waiting for you to slip up so they can over take you and you keep running that track until you have it perfect so that you don't give them that opportunity.
However, everything I mentioned above is rendered null by one thing: stability. I cannot play this game for more than 12 minutes. I have timed it, it's 12 minutes and 14 seconds exactly, every time my screen goes black. I have since found out it has something to do with compatability issues with DirectX 11 but this is a 2013 game, DX 11 had been out for four years before this game's release. Why are we still having these issues? More over, why was this game designed for Intel GPU's? I have since found a workaround but I'm still beyond salty about how I've lost races not because I took a turn to sharp, not because someone else over took me, not because of anything I as a player have done, but simply a black screen.

I have to say, it's been a while since a game captured my attention like this one. While it's somewhat easy to pick up, it takes a lot of time to master.
The gameplay, controls, are simple on the surface, but to really learn the ins and outs of how to actually play the game takes a lot of time and experience. So, if you are not willing to spend that time, you're going to get pummelled by those who have spent the time...
...because the combat in this game is, for the most part, all about timing. Yes, there's some relatively simple combos which you can learn fairly easily, and there's not a whole lot of depth to that part. No, the challenge is in learning when each character's vulnerability periods are in their moves, and learning when you should or should not use a move, and when you can take advantage of another character's vulnerable periods.
As mentioned, the controls are relatively simple. Standard FPS-style WASD+mouse type movement, jump, two attack buttons (being mouse L and mouse R), guard, dash, reload (which only is used in a few characters), two special skills, and a power attack modifier. Your basic attacks are made with your attack buttons, and hitting an attack button during the animation of a previous attack can chain an additional attack to it... the concept behind most basic combos. What will/will not chain depends on the character, though there are some which are universal, eg. L mouse attack followed by R mouse attack, which follows up the first hit with a knock-up move, allowing further comboing subsequently.
Aside from that, there's a rage bar that builds up from hitting/being hit, which after having a sufficient amount, you can use to execute your special skills. There's also the stamina bar, which is used up when you dash, but slowly regenerates over time. Using the power attack modifier (which is allowed at certain points in certain combos) allows you to enhance specific moves, such as a guard breaker or adding a knockup to a regular non-knockup move, but consumes stamina (though once upon a time it used to be rage).
Each attack animation though, has its own wind-up and wind-down delays, which leave you vulnerable to being hit yourself since you cannot interrupt the animation while it's in progress. Hence, the key to winning fights in this game is taking advantage of the opponent's vulnerable timings while avoiding leaving yourself vulnerable. And this is what takes time and experience to learn, and it's not something that you're going to pick up your first hour in the game. It will take a lot of lost battles while you learn, "Okay, if I do this move, it leaves me open to being hit if it doesn't connect or they block it," etc.
My first few hours in the game during the beta period, I was often up against people who had played hundreds of hours in the beta before, and it was a struggle to get a hit in at all against many of these players, and every opening I left was exploited. So, you learn not to leave the openings, and where the openings are that you can take advantage of. And when you're up against multiple opponents, you not only have to worry about the one person you're up against at the time, but that someone else might hit you from behind while you're trying to execute a particular combo.
Which brings me to what some consider a flaw in the combo system, that the combos are not particularly intricate or varied. If Archeblade was solely a 1 vs 1 game, I would agree. However, Archeblade is a team game for the most part, and the idea of combos being a focus is sort of a hard thing to implement in such an environment, because multiple players participating in a battle means that you're not likely to be free to finish off a big combo chain in any case. So while the fighting game enthusiast in me bemoans the lack of combos as such, the nature of the game sort of means that you can't really do a whole lot of them to begin with... I honestly don't know if there is a way to make the two integrate.
About character balance... quite frankly, it reminds me of fighting games, where some characters are easy to pick up, may have 'cheap'er tactics they can use, and certain characters will have certain advantages over other characters. But in my limited experience with barely 90 hours in the game, it seems to me that given that the nature of winning a 1 vs 1 fight is more about play/counterplay and mindgames, it's still pretty good for balance. Throw that all into a team play environment though, and such arguments should honestly become moot, since the goal then becomes to help the team win, and diverse roles where characters can complement each other become an advantage. Then again, true to the state of many multiplayer team games, you always have (too many) people who are focusing on getting kills rather than helping the team win, so they complain about the little imbalances...
Okay, enough about the gameplay.
Graphics: Nothing special, modelling and texturing are decent. Effects are not too flashy so that they are overwhelming, which I appreciate, because too much flash can become distracting and take away from awareness in a battle. Animations are well done, smooth and natural looking. Art design's well done overall and has some decent variation, but not completely to my tastes... more on that later.
Audio: Some of the one-liners from the characters are cheesy. Sound effects are fitting, and do their job well. Music is well done, but may or may not be to everyone's stylistic preferences, being a bit of a mix between a contemporary orchestral style with rock and electronic, mostly up-tempo as tends to be found in fighting games. The amount and variety of music though is sadly limited though, so while I had the music playing for the first 20 or 30 hours of the game, after that I turned it off and played whatever I felt like in the background instead, though every now and then I'd turn it on just to hear it, since the music isn't bad, just too short.
Network: This game seems to lack retroactive hit detection or any kind of latency compensation. So, it plays much like games in the early days of internet gaming in that you have to lead your
swing in the place that your target will be, rather than where they are currently on your screen at the moment. This is not a deal-breaker for me, having learned long ago how to play with this kind of lag, but I know some players have been quite vocal about the game being too hard to play without a sub-100ms ping. Nevermind that from where I am, most servers end up ~200-300ms, and I still think it's playable with some learning to adjust.
Issues with packet loss over the network or possibly server-side slowdown are likely responsible for some of the 'rubber-banding' issues which you sometimes run into, but I cannot confirm the technical issues with that, only that it makes sense logically from past experience with networking and online games.
Complaints: No deal breakers for me, but definitely some annoyances.
1. Minimum player limit for a map to start. And while you're waiting, you're stuck in the lobby... you can do nothing but chat. A more polished solution would be to let people run around inside the map, practice movements or fights, but not have the actual game/scoring active. Switch teams (if applicable), autobalancing, etc. during this time as well. Once the minimum requirements for the game to start are met, everyone is killed so they all respawn at the same time, and then the match can begin.
2. Outfits, specifically the gals. Renoah's the only one that comes with a default outfit that's got decent coverage. Ended up getting the alternate skin for Valle just so she could wear a proper dress! Well, at least they don't limit skin showing to the females exclusively.
Overall: Fun game, have enjoyed playing it a lot, and hope to continue to playing it for some time still. Too bad Codebrush didn't succeed financially with it.

MapleStory is a 2D, side-scrolling MMO with a lot of different fun classes to play as, those of which are highly customizable through their skills and their appearance. The world is based on free-roaming, and you can go basically wherever you want and choose to do whatever tasks you'd like. The community is nice, or at least as nice as your average MMO community. There's, of course, some hackers, but besides that, most of the people are kind and are just playing to have a good time.
I never really played this through Steam, as there's an outside launcher from Nexon's website that works better with my computer, but I've invested way too many hours into this game over a course of quite a few years (which definitely isn't a bad thing). It's a really cute game with an even cuter art style, but some of the quests you choose to go on can be a little challenging, so it's definitely not like it's just for babbies or people who aren't 1337 proz at MMO's. The gameplay itself can be a little bit tedious, though, as some of the quests require you to grind, and in order to grind, you basically press the same button a whole bunch and then go press another button a whole bunch of times to collect the items you needed to grind for in the first place. Another thing that I don't enjoy is that it started out as a simple game with the basics for classes to play as, but has expanded a teensy bit too much for my tastes.
TL;DR:
Pros:
-Cute
-Really great art style
-Can be challenging
-Enjoyed it for years
-Free-to-play
-Customizable characters
-Nice community (average)
-Addicting
Cons:
-Expanded too much from original game
-Quests can be time-consuming/tedious
-Some hackers (as expected for an MMO)
Scores:
Gameplay: 7/10
Free world: 9/10
Style: 10/10
Graphics: 9/10
Addictiveness: 11/10
Overall: 8/10

is a turn-based 4X strategy game. Fleeing Earth after the Great Mistake that ruined it, you land on a distant planet to establish a new world, building cities, dealing with rival factions and determining the ideological path you want humanity to take for its future to come. This review takes into account the
expansion set.
: After picking from one of twelve sponsors and customizing your faction, you start off with a single colony, building units, researching technologies (through an improved tech-web) and expanding your borders. You also manage (or automate) trade routes between your cities, other factions and neutral outposts. You can now build floating cities that behave differently from land cities: land cities expand their borders through Culture points, while floating cities claim territory by moving around. Also, while land has plains, grasslands, hills and forests, the sea bed will have coasts, reefs and oceans floors with its own lot of strategic resources and unique bonus resources. The five biomes are more than land/alien color palettes, they determine the map generator's algorithm, defines alien strength, speed and behavior (much more varied than the barbarians from
), and each biome has a unique Marvel quest. The reimagined diplomatic system is a breath of fresh air from former games of the franchise: gone are the resource trading and tribute paying, you now accumulate Diplomatic Capital points from buildings and agreements others buy from you, which you then spend in purchasing agreements from others and picking personality traits (each unlocks bonuses and unique agreements). Peace treaties are now negotiated with the new Spoils of War system, comparing scores from both sides' war accomplishments, the difference is then used to determine the "payment" (technologies, cities, resources) the loosing faction grants the war's victor. Furthermore, A.I. behavior is now defined in fear and respect levels: fear being your military strength compared to theirs, while respect rises and falls over time based on how well your faction is performing (ex: production rate, health, land improvement, each rival caring about different things) and actions you take (ex: build wonders, attack common enemy's city, sign agreement with common friend). Through science and a few mini-quests, you accumulate points in one of three different human evolution paths: human purity, cybernetics or gene tempering, eventually settling into either of six paths (the three affinities and three half/half hybrids), giving a much needed variety to factions' tactics and appearance. Archaeology comes around with its own twist, as you dig up artifacts that can be consumed for an immediate bonus, or collected for a larger bonus (including unlocking unique wonders). The game looks awesome graphically, and the soundtrack is worthy of a space opera epic.
: As was case with previous games of the franchise, it's an incredible resource hog, each passing turns getting slower as the game progresses no manner how powerful your PC is. The performance issues also cause textures to occasionally load wrong, and the game is constantly re-applying textures as you move around the map. The fact that each factions are randomly customized for each playthrough removed a lot of the individual personality rival civilizations had in past games. You get so many bonuses (affinities bonuses, building bonuses, sponsor bonuses, diplomatic agreement bonuses, Wonder bonuses, etc) that they become meaningless as they aren't as fun to get anymore. Even with all the biomes, planets, and customization, the game still feels somewhat repetitive from one playthrough to another and I can't put my finger on exactly why.
: ★★★★☆ - Next on your list!
This is not Alpha Centauri 2, but it's still a pretty good game (just as long as you get the
expansion set. Seriously, it's required). The re-thought diplomacy, its twist on water-cities and archaeology, and all the flexibility for buildings, units and factions, are enough to make it its own thing. It might not live up to everyone's expectations, but I'll nevertheless be getting a few hundred hours of gameplay by the time my focus turns to
, which in my book is plenty of bang for my buck. For all its flaws, it's still a game I recommend.

The final BIT.TRIP game (in the timeline atleast) returns to BEAT's style of gameplay playing like Pong, except reversed horizontally and more obstacles and patterns to keep you on the edge of your seat. Although, it never gets as difficult as BIT.TRIP BEAT's final level, which still haunts me to this day, since if you miss enough beats or run into enough circles you will be sent back to a checkpoint and not have to restart the entire level again.
The soundtrack (which I still go back to listen to every now and then, Catharsis being my favorite BIT.TRIP track and level) combined with the visuals in the levels are beautiful, and while there are only three levels they are all incredibly fun and a blast to play through. This is definitely my favorite BIT.TRIP game and one of my favorite games period, (I include it with BIT.TRIP COMPLETE when talking about my favorite games) and I reccommend playing through all the other games in order before this one to get the full BIT.TRIP experience!
Now regarding the problems with this port, while I haven't had problems that were with this port recently, I think I did have them when I first played the PC port, but recently and getting a new laptop I haven't encountered much problems, except for this one part where a timing of a power-up causes me to never fully complete one of the challenges.
Although there is one glaring problem that you might encounter, where the first boss is literally impossible to beat. I've played the Wii and 3DS versions many times before the PC port and never had a problem with that boss. As far as I know the bug is still in the game by the time of this review, so you might have to go find a save file that lets you past this boss. Or you could get the BIT.TRIP compliations, BIT.TRIP COMPLETE for the Wii, and BIT.TRIP SAGA for the 3DS, COMPLETE being my favorite since it has tons of bonus content including 20 challenge missions in each BIT.TRIP game and a soundtrack CD. Though get the 3DS one if you're like me and are terrible with the motion controls in the Wii versions of BEAT and FLUX.
So in the end, BIT.TRIP FLUX is a perfect game, that I'd highly recommend if you are fan of rhythm/music games or are a BIT.TRIP fan and you haven't bought this one for some reason.

Redshirt is a virtual "life" sim that you control by using a Spacebook app. The game lampoons Facebook and our always-online lives, and it's fun to appreciate if you are interested in game design and gamification, or hipster enough to enjoy the irony. In the first thirty minutes of playing Redshirt, you will be enchanted by the humour and the design of the game. But by pointing out the shallowness of the 'always-on' Facebook existence, Redshirt quickly shoots itself in the foot by making it impossible to care about any of the shallowly-presented characters - and the allure begins to pale. No cohesively directed story evolves, only the one that you've made with your Spacebook actions. While this makes the game replayable by using randomness, it also reduces meaning of what you're doing. There are no day-to-day challenges of Redshirt, the only way to lose the game is to play it out and hope you gain enough skills, relationships, or money to survive, after selecting where to spend your time.
Redshirt could have been an amazing game with a deeper level of gameplay or daily tasks that engaged and challenged the player. As it is, it's a nice game for those who enjoy the genre.

The concept is good, but the execution is shallow enough to wear thin within an hour or two... which is well before the end of the game. The game offers up multiple ways to 'win', which would seem to encourage replay, but the initial playthrough stretches into tedium and wears out its welcome well before the game completes. Each ending seems to be based on a slight variation in focus, but the game will be essentially the same each time, so it's impossible to work up the motivation to play again after the end credits roll.
The game has a lot of great ideas, but the shallow implementation holds it back. It's too obviously gamey, with obvious player-controlled victory, to have the pointlessness make a bigger statement about disempowerment. But the game itself is shallow enough that you'll have it all figured out early on, and spend most of the actual gameplay performing boring, predictable actions to move counters and progress timers. Things would have worked better with faster progression over a shorter timeframe, and more to make different victory routes distinct.

This isn't your game.
I know you, sitting there on your Steam Machines, casually parsing petabytes of review data to justify your purchasing habits. I know what you want from me. I know what you want from this game. You remember, back when you were a child, your first episode of Star Trek; you remember that feeling of wonder, of familiarity, that someone finally gets it. Maybe, if you look deep into the charred cavity your soul used to inhabit, you might recognize that it was the last time you felt wonder at all. But it is just as likely, more than likely, that these feelings will get swept aside. You want numbers. Metrics. Achievements. Scores.
This isn't your game. I am not your reviewer. This is not a computer. You are not alive.
Redshirt is about disempowerment and distraction. It is about being surrounded by all the fantastic wonder and adventure of the cosmos, and then working nine to five in a job that ruins your mind and body. It is about seducing an abhorrent tentacle monster because they can get you a promotion. It is about leaving your old friends behind because they post gross stuff on your social media. It is about working around your superiors' irrational racial biases, all for a chance to be a richer nobody than you were before. All the while, the story goes on - and all you see are updates. Newsflashes. Then it's time for drinks, and maybe an hour alone on your computer at home, because they don't pay you enough to be a hero.
Do you recognize anything?
I do.
I'm going to have a shower.
I'm going to go outside.

Fun, fast paced Online Arena Battle game. It's got a weekly rotation of playable Bloodlines (read: Characters) so you'll be able to play all the characters without having to buy them.
Really balanced game, don't have the idea that some characters are really much more OP than others.
It has quite a learning curve where you'll need to learn how to aim your hits and dodge the opponent's, but also knowing when to go for the kill and when to back off or you'll be killed because of your over-extending.
Little bit newbie unfriendly because it has medallions (like trinkets in WoW) that only unlock on certain levels.. And a trait-line which opens up even slower than the medallions. The traits will be able to buff your hp or damage by 20% if you're at the max level.
The queue system doesn't seem to take levels as a regard when you're queue'ing, so you might end up with a lot of high level players in your matches and you WILL feel inferior.. Not only because they will out-skill you hard, but also because their damage, armour and cooldowns are much more beneficial for them than yours.
It does have a very small playerbase, though.. Kind of unfortunate.
Oh, and of course, since this is a PvP-based game.. The playerbase WILL be horrible. The playerbase WILL try to insult you, no matter if you're sucking at the game or actually beating the enemy all by yourself. The game does have a chat censor though.. So prepare yourself for a whole lot of " **** you go home *** player " and broken English. There are a lot of Russian and otherwise Slavic (really, what's the difference though?) people playing this game.
The game also has a daily system. Every day you'll get a double Bloodcoins (ingame coins, not buyable with RL cash) bonus worth of 600 Bloodcoins (about 5 games or so.. Which is like 20 minutes).. So it's worth coming back for every day.
You can even buy sexy clothes for your unlocked Bloodlines (characters), most of which will however cost you Real Life Dosh.. It doesn't give you any stat bonuses or anything.
There is no Pay to Win aspect in this game, even though you can buy Bloodlines with RL dosh, you can also buy them with bloodcoins which you earn through playing games (+ the daily bonus, which will help quite a lot).. Or just wait for your favourite character to return in the weekly routine.. All the shop items which you can only buy for RL cash, are purely cosmetic.
Surely worth giving this game a go. It's free to play after all. The game is easy to learn, but a bit hard to master.

Wow, I cannot believe how overpriced this game is, even on sale.  I'm a big fan of the life sim genre and I own most of Positech's games. When I heard they had a new one out that looked like a satirical version of Kudos, I ignored all the bad reviews and jumped at the chance to buy it. What a mistake. This game is basically Kudos 2 with a space skin. But though it's lifted most of its gameplay mechanics from Kudos 2, it's a huge step backward. The interface is clunky and hard to manage (and for a game that is ALL interface that's a crying shame), the gameplay is a lot less fun, it's riddled with bugs, and the 'humour' is repetitive and gets wearing after just an hour of gameplay. And though it's been, what, six years since Kudos 2 was released, nothing has been improved - the gameplay is meandering with no meaningful objectives, there's no feeling of real characters to connect to, and there is endless, endless grinding. I am usually very patient with indie life sims, and will put up with bad writing, poor artwork and lots of grinding, but there has to be SOMETHING at the heart of it. But this life sim is absolutely lifeless. It's an amateur piece of garbage that's worth $5 at best. Do yourself a favour and pick up Positech's Democracy 3 instead - or if you're desperate for a life sim, try something by Hanako Games, or go to Abandonia and download Princess Maker 2.

After 100% and playing through the whole game twice I think I can finally review it.
It’s a decent and simple 3D platformer that you should probably pick up on sale, but maybe not on the PC mainly because if you do like the game and want to play the sequel then you’ll have to get it on a console since it probably won’t be released on PC. Although this only if you can ignore the ‘new’ Pac-Man.
Ah what can be said about Pac-Man. A legend to the video game industry? Or maybe one of the most recognizable video game character next to Mario? Well how about a new hip memester? Eh doesn’t sound that great and honestly that is probably the weakest part about this game. It’s just this ‘new’ Pac-Man himself it might just be with my age and not understanding why he burps at the end of each level, but maybe the kids these day will enjoy who he is. If you can ignore the ‘new’ Pac-Man, like I did then you’re in for a treat with this game. 3D platformers are a dying breed in the modern video game industry (2016). So when one comes out I’m always into checking it out and giving a chance mainly because unlike the 90s where 3D platformers were just in for the $$$ sorta like fps these days, 3D platformers create these days seem to be much more polished than ever before. Getting the story out of the way mainly because it’s very simple and I’d expect it from 3D platformer and especially a Pac-Man game. It’s the ‘get the important item before the villain gets it and takes over the world!’ It’s there and each cutscene can be skipped so if you have no care about that then you can easily ignore it. Control wise I should of probably tested how the keyboard and mouse handles, but I didn’t and played through this game with a Xbox 360 controller, controls are great overall. Gameplay is just like any other 3D platformer where you start at point A and try to get to point B. There's a enemies in the way and some type of ability mechanics in there. Ah yes Pac-Man can get abilities examples like fire, ice, metal, meme etc. They’re all fine and control well for the most part although very generic. The worlds also have the same problem as the abilities. They’re all just generic and 1 of them is even repeated. You guy the city, temple, volcano, iceland in the volcano, city again, and sorta volcano again it’s more in the area of hell though. They’re just there and some are longer than others mainly the later worlds where there’s only some a few levels in the world probably the game being rushed, but who knows. The game does bring some challenge which is nice I mean it can’t just be some cake walk. Graphics are acceptable and the music isn’t the most memorable soundtrack out there also if you’re a nazi about ‘muh 60fps’ then you’ll gas this game because it’s locked at 30fps. Now finally to the important question is the game actually fun? Yes it is, there isn’t some type of collect a ton aspect to this game, unless you’re going for all the achievements (which I do plan on making a guide for). All the levels aren’t that long and the boss fights aren’t overly frustrating. Like I said before buy this game on sale for <$10. It’s fun and won’t take you that long to finish. Have fun with the ‘new’ Pac-Man!

There's not a lot to say about this game. The main point to highlight is that it gets the job done as a simcade (perhaps a little more on the arcade side) racing game. I'll start with the good. One thing that is truly remarkable about this game is that the graphics are pretty impressive given the fact that it can run on Intel HD graphics. It looks and feels good, with good menu layouts and organization. Campaign is a good length, although it can get repetitive if you're not a super fan of racing. The variety of tracks is good enough and the amount of cars they have is ridiculous. Especially if you get the DLC, you might not get around to trying out all of them. The game modes are also pretty entertaining; there's a range of styles from a simple race, to overtake, to endurance, to touge (basically 1v1). You'll encounter all of them in the campaign mode if you decide to play your way through it. With all this being said, it's easy to see this is an all around good game that will keep you busy for a little while if you enjoy racing games.
Now it's time to talk about the bad. Thankfully, there's nothing terrible or broken about the game. The issues I see are really just areas where they could have improved. First, the AI doesn't seem very skilled in my opinion. Even when I set the difficulty to hard on a custom event, I find it easy to just pass everyone and claim a podium spot. It might just be that I'm a good driver, but as far as competition goes, there's not much of a challenge. I do however notice a difference between the beginning of the campaign and the end. It does get harder as you get better vehicles. Towards the end it becomes harder to obtain that 1st place victory on your first try, but it's nothing stressful. Another thing that bugged me was a good atmosphere that has been slightly tainted with the lack of a true soundtrack. For this simcade, I could tell it would be good to have some music that intesifies the race and makes an effort to make things interesting, even when you're leading by 10 seconds. There's only music for the eliminator events, which is a good idea, but the whole scheme feels unbalanced given that's the only time you'll get to listen to some tunes. Lastly, the biggest issue is that this game is really just single-player. The multiplayer portion is pretty much useless at this point since no one is on. It's a big shame because I don't feel like I can write a complete review without trying out the online gameplay, but it doesn't seem like I'll be getting a chance anytime soon. My guess would be people just got bored, so maybe all that's needed is a more engaging online mode, but it is what it is.
For $8.99, this is a great deal for a "single-player" racing game. It does what it does well and keeps you entertained for a significant amount of time. Great campaign, graphics, and car selection. One thing I forgot to mention is that I really like the customization options for your vehicles. A huge variety of liveries and designs is available to suit your style, and even with all the vehicles in the game, it's still possible to have a different design on each and have thousands of combinations left over. There's little to complain about the game, so it's worth it to grab it when it's on sale. Since there's really no multiplayer, if I were to see it listed at full price, I'd pass.
Final verdict: 8.1/10

I haven't played this game a huge amount since I got it, only really getting into it yesterday, actually. Anyway, this game is very good. It isn't great, and certainly isn't perfect, but it is definitely worth your time if you enjoy Magic.
PROS:
- This game contains a whole LOAD of cards. I'm not sure if every card in MTG is in it, seeing as I have never played the physical card game and therefore don't know too much about it, but if you're worried about this game being as limited as the 2013/14/15 iterations, then trust me, it isn't.
- The game runs smoothly and looks good in terms of artwork. The arena sets a good atmosphere and playing the game is overall an enjoyable experience.
- Possibly the biggest pro is the gameplay itself. If you haven't played MTG before then this game is very beginner friendly. I had never played properly before downloading this and picked it up quickly enough thanks to in-game tutorials etc. As for experienced players, I can't give such an insightful viewpoint, but the game is the same as the physical version so what's not to like I guess?
CONS:
- One problem is that this game simply doesn't feel professional and polished. It feels like it is in alpha development, or has been made by an indie developer. The art is great, but some of the animations and menu buttons simply don't quite mesh together as well as you would expect. This is only very minor though, and the overall game still feels great.
- The deck builder is pretty bad. This is possibly the low point of the whole game. The main problem is filtering through cards, which is not exactly very easy to do. There are filtering options, e.g you can filter by card colour or spell type etc., however there is no search bar for you to search for specific cards or abilities. In my opinion this i a design flaw, and makes deck building feel a lot more overcomplicated than it needs to be.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So, overall this game is definitely worth your time if you enjoy MTG or if you are looking to get into it and learn more about it.

From the same developers and publishers as Civilization 5 and 6, Firaxis and 2k bring us a sci-fi version of Sid Meier's Civilization as Civilization: Beyond Earth!  If you haven’t played Civilization games in the past: in short, they’re top-down, turn based simulation games, based on historical events, people, and more.  In past iterations of the game, players would have to become a successful civilization in some manner: by domination, science, religion, or score.  The same kind of thinking went into Beyond Earth, but for some reason, in addition to taking the setting of the game to a new place, they also changed timeless mechanics that worked well in previous games.  Keep in mind, this is being written after Rising Tides but I will omit any content that came with that DLC.
I'm glad to report that while playing on a higher end PC, I experienced no hitching.  Frame rate ran at 60 even in busier scenes.  Beyond Earth does a good job putting the user into the setting of humans landing on an alien.  All the vegetation, terrain, and resources look downright odd(odd is good in this case) in all biomes while still being beautifully designed.
While the unit upgrades are super sci-fi looking and match the art style of the game in general (unit upgrades are in simplest terms, stat improvements that are rewarded for reaching new “Affinity levels” via completing missions and come with visually different art to distinguish that new unit from others), unit upgrades are not easily recognizable.  The reasoning, in Civilization games before, it’s very easy to tell apart an Archer from it’s next upgrade, Crossbowman.  This is in-part because it’s common knowledge what an Archer or Crossbowman is.  Due to this being a sci-fi game, the designers obviously had to, at no fault to them, use imagination and fantasy to design these futuristic ground units.  Luckily selecting of your units and hovering over another unit or city will quickly provide a tooltip on the likelihood of that matchup and if it’s worth the fight.  Nevertheless, this is just the cherry on the top of the problematic gameplay of the game.
In my testing, besides the multiplayer aspect of the game losing contact with one client and skipping turns without stopping in 2015(I did not verify if that’s still occurring), I didn’t run into any game breaking bugs.
Gameplay on the other hand, provided a large obstacle.  For any that don’t know, reaching max Affinity and completing the mission tied to that max Affinity level is required to win a game.  The design decision to tie in upgrades with Affinity progression was a gamebreaker in my opinion.  This creates a snowball effect, and I’d go as far to mention the chicken and the egg.  To progress with a majority of missions, it’d be a lot easier with upgraded units that have more moves per turn, have higher strength, and higher defense.  Unfortunately, if any civilization progresses past you in Affinity, there isn’t more than one route to take.  Research trees don’t provide upgrades, but they do at times have new units, which ultimately need to be upgraded with Affinity too.
Generally the issue mentioned above overshadows any compliments I can give about the game (and I have more compliments, but not worth mentioning at this time).  Beyond Earth isn’t necessarily a bad game.  The developers seemed to try and make something really intricate and new with something that could have used something fresh.  I can see the hard work put into the game, but alas, recommending the game is

-You want many hours of new content for your money

Big Pharma is a surprisingly deep and engaging tycoon/sim type game, concealed underneath a drab and dull presentation.  It is also a game that requies a love of engineering and economics, and at times, it veers dangerously close to spreadsheet simulator territory.  Nevertheless, I have put dozens of hours into this game now, and I have enjoyed almost every minute of it -- even the times when my drug development has gotten screwed up.
If you have played a tycoon game before, then you should understand most of the basics of Big Pharma, but there will be additional concepts to understand as well.  Your job, as the CEO of your company, is to discover ingredients, research improvements, and then build assembly lines that refine and mix ingredients into drugs.  Some of your formulations can be incredibly complicated, especially as you develop more expensive cures.  You also have to develop these cures economically, using as little equipment and space as possible.  And, finally, you have to minimize the negative side effects whenever possible, a tough task at times.  The game requires so much forethought and planning that, at times, it almost acts like a corporate chemical engineeing simulator, which is a good thing for people who love to mix building, problem solving, and economics together.
Big Pharma does not have a ton of unique content, but it manages to stay fresh by throwing a whopping 35 scenarios at you, each with their own challenges and goals.  As a result, no two playthroughs will ever end up the same (although the early parts of the scenarios frequently play out the same).  Some of the goals that the game requires of you, especially after you get through the first twelve scenarios or so, become exceedingly difficult.  On many occasions, I have constructed what I thought was going to be the perfect assembly line, only to end up one square short of being able to place my final piece of equipment.  The game can be frustrating at these times, and it is definitely not for everyone.
As I mentioned in the opening sentence, the game's presentation is rather disappointing.  The machines and how they process the equipment looks pretty cool, but there are only a couple of music tracks that repeat themselves, ad nauseum.  The game otherwise looks quite plain and lacking in style.  At the beinning of each scenarior, you choose your avatar from a list of seven characters, but these characters have no personality and there is no perceivable difference in the gameplay between them.  Even a little bit of animation and emoting like what you find in a Sid Meier's Civilization game would have gone a long way to giving the characters some personality.  In addition, the game's marketing campaign suggests that it will provide some dark humor or satire on the questionable business practices of the pharmaceutical industry, but it never touches on this territory.
There is a certain audience for whom Big Pharma is going to hit the mark perfectly.  Fortunately, I was one of those people.  If you have a scientific or business background and you would love to play a fun game that puts engineering and business principles to work, then this game gets a strong thumbs up from me.

I have very much enjoyed this game.  It is half logistical puzzle and half management.  Trying to figure out how to make some of the more complex cures with the machines you have and in the space you have can be a challenge.  Think your doing well with millions in the bank? Well lets try to develop that cure for HIV.  Watch your millions burn up quickly as you spend it on new research and equipment grinding away at it for months if not years in the game constantly tweaking the line and then one day finally the first drug to cure HIV is sold.  Then you can jack up the price as you are the only one selling it!  It is very rewarding.  And then you have a light bulb moment and realized you can produce it for half the cost with no negative effects.  Time to rebuild the production line!
The AI is not great, but they can become a real threat undercutting your bottom line always forcing you innovate and develop new tech and higher teer drugsif you want to survive.
There are several different disease trees that you work through, the first drugs in the tree treating the simplest of things like soughing a cough, but as you discover more ingredients and develop better tech you can keep running that solution through higher and higher processes all the way up to creating a wonder drug that sells for thousands curing tuberculosis.  You may not always want to keep the raw formula from one to the other though as side effects and cost and become problems making you rethink everything from scratch.
If you like solving problems, tinkering and trying to figure out how to make things always more efficient and better this is the game for you.

Bleed is a short but highly replayable and entertaining shooty gun game.
You play as a girl named Wryn who is the default hero and you must go through 7 stages to kill the heroes to prove you're the best hero in the land. You start with Dual Pistols and a Rocket Launcher for the early stages but you can acquire 10 more from the shop or by beating the game on a certain difficulty.
You can dash in the air up to 3 times which allows for rapid movement, positioning and general movement which makes getting through every stage a blast, you also have an action meter, which when used can activate bullet time to precisely land bullets or dodge and wave through theirs.
You have 4 difficulties to choose from (Easy, Medium, Hard and Very Hard) which all change enemy positions, boss attacks etc.
It took me around 70-80 minutes to complete the story campaign on Normal difficulty the first time, so don't expect a super long campaign.
There are 2 other variants on gameplay though besides characters, you can play challenge mode which lets you choose/ random from any 3 bosses in the game and fight them all at the same time for fun, or you can attempt to go through Arcade Mode, which is every stage back to back with no health refills or anything, it can get pretty damn hard when it wants to as well, especially in the later difficulties.
Soundtrack is pretty good too.
Although short, it's a fantastic game, if you're into Score Attacking or overcoming some pretty difficult challenges you'll probably get your money's worth there.
Also goes on sale real cheap sometimes so definitely pick it up then, you won't regret it!

I played this on the ps2 a year or so after it was released. It was my first Splinter Cell title. I spent months only playing up until finding the man in the first mission, until I realized there was a door to load the next section. Once I got past that, it opened the door to loving Splinter Cell, and other stealth genre games.
I've heard plenty say this is the center piece of the series, and I somewhat agree. Of course it would be best to start at the first one, but playing this certainly gave a wonderful feel for the rest, Pre-Conviction.
-Graphically, it was great for its time of 2006 I believe, and to this day, I still marvel at some of the maps, and the atmosphere they can put off. It of course looks dated by today's standards, but it doesn't bother me much, which makes sense given the impact in my gaming life it had. I liked it still, and for those who don't mind older looks, this is certainly something then, but as I said, some spots still look quite good for today.
-Gameplay/mechanics wise, I also enjoyed it. Mostly. You actually had a JUMP button. You got to experiment with what you can climb on. If you can make that jump and grab hold. Your only shimmy technique was hands only and no legs, but it was still fine for what it was. Climbing over objects felt right. A little jump, bracing your feet, then vaulting over that railway. It felt so good, as did doing that then dragging a guy over the edge.
~Guards were, a bit dumb in some places. But still pretty good. They remembered stuff... they were made to notice things. Lights off, doors opened, locks broken, or dead bodies in a chair. You know. simple things. Being able to hide in a dark corner inches from them as they occasionally clip through you was ridiculous however, but that's permitted I'd think. No stealth game has perfected itself, especially not a decade ago.
~Combat was interesting. Each game does it different, but in this, it was before regeneration, and where the game really meant for you to not be a panther and wreck everyone. Doesn't mean I never tried, but it's rewarding when you played like the silent ghost you were meant to be. shooting could end you in seconds, forcing you to ensure you knew what you were planning. A draw back of decade old game is you can't shoot that guy, knife another, then grab the third in a span of two seconds like you can now. Fisher is totally capable of doing it in this, but it just wasn't able to be done, or wasn't thought to be implemented yet. Dunno.
~Sneaking was actually necessary. It's what gave you the ability to hear that extra dialog, whether it be for a secondary objective, or for a funny. It was also just.. necessary. It is a damn stealth game after all. Not saying running around with a shotgun, ragdolling people wasn't fun when bored. But, it was nice to take your time, look for that extra path, get that silent interrogation. Or, not touch a single person, and evesdrop. ( Touching someone lowers your score, yo. )

-The plot wasn't anything special, but it was just fine for this little family of people. Good guy go finds thing, discovers news about another thing, goes to find thing, travels to other places about thing, finds out info about guy involving thing, Good Guy looks and finds guy involved with bad thing, emotional moment ensues, and you press on to save the day in a climatic ending. After navigating an annoying as sh*t base. Only finished that last mission once. It's been a while. for the average player, it isn't something new. but for avid lovers of the franchise, it means the world.
-The characters. Oh, the characters. We have the smooth, bald, head rubbing leader Lambert. We have the computer wiz Grimsdottir. We have our tech man Reading. And a few others along the way that give you a briefing. Charming U.S. captain, an old friend or two, and a few other folk I can't recall, along with a whole set of guards and civilians you come across in each mission. Then we have Fisher, pride and true man of Third Echelon. The man you play as. The best of the best. And a great interrogater, with a big knife, and sharp humor. Words are exchangable. Lambert, Reeding, and Grim are with you always through voice comunication. And the group that you grow to love from 1 to double agent. They all have plenty of bits of humor too. This is meant to be a serious game, but every mission, there is at least a couple lines of quick humor, jabs at each other, along with other things you'd hear along the way. Not a day goes by where I don't get giddy hearing dialog bits from Sam, to random baddies in the mission, or to your team. It is certainly something to look forward to cherishing. One of the bigger reasons why I like questioning everyone in new areas, is to find these little nuggets of gold humor. Oh, and did I mention Spy Blue and Spy Red? Cooperative Splinter Cells for the win!
-I really don't think this will come to a close naturally, so I'll end it by force. I could go on and on, describing things, telling you all what I loved and .. not so much loved about this game. But honestly I think I've strayed from 'review' enough. It has it's quirks, like bad jumps and loud landings that make no sense, and loud search music from delayed take downs, but it has so much more great moments of comedy, gameplay and just overall enjoyment rolling around and ( optionally) stabbing folk in the back.
-As a nostalgic Chaos Theory player, I fully give this a 10/10.
-As a somewhat objective person, I give this an 8/10.
-As someone with too many bad jokes and a skill of wasting time, I give this an 11/10, and would certainly play again. Have been for 10 years now or so.

PAC-MAN and the Ghostly Adventures is a platformer for all ages. At least that's what Namco-Bandai wants you to think. Truth is, when I played this game i constantly asked myself: "Who is this for?" The level of difficulty is too low for someone with even a minimal talent for gaming, but the controls (specifically the need to rotate the camera) might be too much for small children. No...wait...I take that back. Kids today can handle complicated control schemes. I've gotten my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by enough toddlers in Call of Duty to figure that out. Hell, one of the levels in this game is actually called "
ning". So maybe the developer knows their audience, but they were just too busy coming up with hilarious puns to design a thoroughly enjoyable game.
This is one of those games where there's nothing distinctly PAC-MAN about it. The main character could have been Super Jump Kid. He explores traditionally-designed levels based on "City World", "Ice World", and "Ruins World". Along the way he jumps around, collects coins, and punches ghouls. Occasionally he'll get powers that let him use different attacks or solve problems. But nobody would buy
would they? So we get a tie-in game based on a cartoon.
Mainly what I'm getting at is that there isn't enough PAC-MAN in this game about PAC-MAN. The original arcade game has a simple concept. Pac has to eat all of the pellets, but he can't touch the ghosts or else he'll die. If he eats a power-pellet, then the ghosts will get scared, and then Pac can eat them. In Ghostly Adventures, Pacster simply eats the ghosts. I guess it's an improvement over the other 3D platformer Pacs, because in those games he smashes enemies with his butt, like nearly every other platformer hero. Also, I can see how having Pacster being vulnerable to ghosts could be frustrating in this kind of game. The problem is, allowing Pacster to circumvent the need for power pellets, gives the developer an excuse to load the levels with padding.
Each stage is filled with ghosts, and they tend to spawn in wide-open areas. This is a recipe for boring game-design. To defeat a ghost all you have to do is get close and press the "X" button, Pacster takes care of the rest. While each ghost is capable of performing various attacks, they aren't a threat in the slightest. This is due to the constant presence of ability-pellets. As I mentioned before, Super Jump Kid aka Pacster utilizes various powers to reach the end of each level. He loses these powers whenever he takes damage, but since ability-pellets disappearing could make for un-winnable situations, they simply respawn immediately. Also, even when you lose your power, you don't lose any health. This is how you game-design yourself into a corner. If that wasn't enough, Pacster can scare all nearby ghosts by making a goofy face. Using this ability requires a meter to recharge, but if you grab an ability-pellet, then you'll have a full-charge the next time you lose said ability. To sum it all up: When you walk into an area filled with ghosts, your first instinct will be to bump into an enemy, lose your ability, scare the ghosts, then mash away until the area is clear.
This is exactly why I suggest the alternative. By not putting forth the effort and creativity to design thoughtful ghost encounters, the developers behind this game end up trivializing the entire concept. Pacster is just way too good at ghost-eating. His poor old man had to carefully ration those precious power-pellets, just to survive the increasingly adept ghosts. The platforming isn't anymore difficult, due to the very generous jumps and prevalence of extra lives & checkpoints. In the rare cases that you die, it's most likely due to dropped inputs. A 30 fps lock is one thing, but when the game starts at 30, chugs to 10-15 fps, then slingshots to 60 for a millisecond, your double-jump might not register.
But this game is for kids right? It's not supposed to matter if it's too easy. However, if children today are capable of figuring out games like GTA, Call of Duty, and so on; Wouldn't PAC-MAN and the Ghostly adventures be an insult to their intelligence? Let's take M-Rated games out of the discussion. If kids today can play games like Mario 64, Sonic Generations, and so on. What's the point of giving them this? It might draw their attention for a few hours, but they'll realize how mind-numbing it really is. That's not to mention the awful writing. This game has some of the worst jokes in the world. If your son or daughter plays through it, I guarantee that they'll grow up to be a few cans short of a six-pac.

I haven't played this game a huge amount since I got it, only really getting into it yesterday, actually. Anyway, this game is very good. It isn't great, and certainly isn't perfect, but it is definitely worth your time if you enjoy Magic.
PROS:
- This game contains a whole LOAD of cards. I'm not sure if every card in MTG is in it, seeing as I have never played the physical card game and therefore don't know too much about it, but if you're worried about this game being as limited as the 2013/14/15 iterations, then trust me, it isn't.
- The game runs smoothly and looks good in terms of artwork. The arena sets a good atmosphere and playing the game is overall an enjoyable experience.
- Possibly the biggest pro is the gameplay itself. If you haven't played MTG before then this game is very beginner friendly. I had never played properly before downloading this and picked it up quickly enough thanks to in-game tutorials etc. As for experienced players, I can't give such an insightful viewpoint, but the game is the same as the physical version so what's not to like I guess?
CONS:
- One problem is that this game simply doesn't feel professional and polished. It feels like it is in alpha development, or has been made by an indie developer. The art is great, but some of the animations and menu buttons simply don't quite mesh together as well as you would expect. This is only very minor though, and the overall game still feels great.
- The deck builder is pretty bad. This is possibly the low point of the whole game. The main problem is filtering through cards, which is not exactly very easy to do. There are filtering options, e.g you can filter by card colour or spell type etc., however there is no search bar for you to search for specific cards or abilities. In my opinion this i a design flaw, and makes deck building feel a lot more overcomplicated than it needs to be.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So, overall this game is definitely worth your time if you enjoy MTG or if you are looking to get into it and learn more about it.
