Beyond Earth started out as a game with much to learn. Keeping the format of Civilization V, but a different idea in victories and social aspects, the story advances through a number of challenges, three specfically. Obviously, you are settling on an alien planet, you're not gonna be the only sentient one there. The first challenge you encounter is learning about the aliens on your planet, and what it takes to make them not a problem. Three affinities are available to choose from to lead your civilization in a certain manner of belief and social aspect.
, the affinity of peace and alliance. If you think you can find a way to co-exist or to "bond" with the aliens on your planet, and think your civilization would best prosper with the help of the neighbors near you, then you're someone meant for Harmony.
, the affinity of technological bondage and neutrality. Look back on yourself, and your past life or current interests. Were you that one guy who knew almost everything about technology, were you the one always called "computer geek" or tech-guru? Supremacy is the belief of bonding technology with humanity, literally bonding, no we're not gonna talk Borg or whatever hivemind thing Star-Trek has going on there, we're talking about mixing technology with the human body and discovering what and how technology benefits the human body and what enhancements comes with it. May be lacking in few aspects, but otherwise... a pleasant surprise.
Bleed reminds me about Noitu Love 2. Fact-paced action, 16-bit esthetic, high frequency of bosses per minute... It's all my cup of tea and I can happy report that pure gameplay is here really strong, worth checking out if you are someone who loves high-octane 2D platforming mayhem. Bullet-time mechanic is a catalyst that allows bosses to be seemingly more dangerous with their patterns and makes you feel like a total badass dodging bullets.
Game's goodness is unfortunately warped in not-so-stellar presentation and few other problems. What problems? Controls are great, but they require getting used to and gamepad is almost required to handle the challenge. Game also loves to kill you really fast if you don't know what to do. Fortunately, deaths don't feel cheap and checkpoints are plenty, You are never punished too much, but still better to get in good terms with Game Over screen.
Presentation and plot? Those are the lowest points of the game. Music unfortunately is really generic and not entertaining at all, barring some rare
of tunes. Plot is completely off-the-rails stupid, even operating on cartoon logic... and don't let me start on how out-of-place are your enemies: "World Greatest Heroes" consisting of blob monster, pair of worms and alien morphing goo balls and few more... What? Simply, it doesn't make a lot of sense and you hardly can "tune-in" into world. Missed opportunity.
While game is also extremely short, it's replay value is high and amount of generated enjoyment is good enough for me to give a solid recommendation. Price is also nice, so you should probably keep Bleed in mind if you have some leftover funds.

This game falls into a very niche realm of the strategy genre. It blends elements of business sims, puzzle games, and even a little RTS making for a very unique experience. There are a few problems though:
-Although it has many different scenarios, they all essentially boil down to either "make money" or "make a certain type of drug"
-It is NOT worth 25 USD. I got it for around $7.50 during the summer sale and frankly that should be close to the asking price
-Since there is only one real basic principle in the game (diluting and concentrating) there isn't that much room for strategy making it a little too easy
-Unlike most games along this line, it doesn't really feel like it has the customization features that most strategy games have. Almost all of the games will feel very similar despite having different opponents/ingredients/layouts.
With all of the bad, there is a lot of good that comes with it as well:
-The game is not all that taxing on your computer. I'm able to play this on a laptop with no graphics card and I haven't experienced any lag, even with the biggest factories
-The tutorial does a fantastic job. Granted, it isn't one of those tutorials that really immerses you into the game (there's a lot of reading) but it does teach and it teaches well. I have found no problems understanding what to do and how to do it.
-The gameplay is very solid as well. Once you get the hang of the basics, it is fun to utilize the puzzle aspect of the game to make a factory that is as compact and efficient as possible
-The UI works great. It isn't customizable, but I don't care, everything is very simple and it's exactly where I expect it to be.
All in all, I would reccommend this game to anyone who loves business sims and efficiency. If you are willing to delve into its interesting mechanics, you will be rewarded with a lot of control over your factory and some great challenges when it comes to efficiency. Just be warned that the game can get a little repetitive.

After your soul-crushing first run where you'll have to do some horrible stuff and where most of your charaters will have likely been killed or died from hunger, illness, bleeding out, or by their own hand, this is a fantastic survival game. Managing your resourses is a matter of life or death for your whole party and with the ability to play different scenarios -- you can even create your own story! -- you'll always be faced with a new, exciting challenge. At least once you get the hang of it and know exactly how to save your party without comprimising *all* of your morals.
The only critisism I have is sort of a nitpick, really. Every day, you have a random event happen. This can be whether or not your house was raided the night before, if someone fell ill or was wounded while you were away, or if someone comes up to your door for one reason or another. Since these are all random events, which means that if you stop in the middle of your game and restart it, you have a chance of creating a new set of random events happen.
I'd be lying if I said I didn't exploit this sometimes, usually if I didn't want a particular character to be hurt from a raid (Marin and Katia are treasures). However, there would be times where I didn't want to quit out of my game and risk all the possible events from being reset. This caused me to pause the game a lot and resulted in me having a crazy amount of hours recorded playing, when in actuality it's less. There've been days where I completely forgot it was running and would add a complete 24 hours to my recorded time.
However, like I said before, this is a nitpick and I acknowledge that it's not the game's fault for my own actions and forgetfulness. If anything I think it's great for having added a layer of difficulty by only allowing an automatic save at the very beginning of the day. Though I do think $19.99 is a little steep, I definitely would recommend this to anyone who enjoys resourse managing, light strategy and TONS of replayability.

Civilization Beyond Earth Rising Tide more than expansion
In the vastness of the universe and the shadow of the unknown, "Civilization Beyond Earth: Rising Tide" brings together new game mechanics and more reasons to explore to create something that feels new rather than just another Civ expansion.
Rather than adding a new scenario or tweaking a few mechanics, lead game designers Will Miller and David McDonough decided to take some very bold steps with some familiar gameplay to take advantage of the future concept of other worlds and Civilization. They started with the planets.
Instead of make the worlds more solid, the designers decided to embrace a more aquatic adventure. Given that more than 70 percent of our own planet’s surface is covered by water and how much is still being discovered in those briny areas, future and far-flung planets of “Beyond Earth” didn’t let the players explore as much of those worlds as they could have.

Did you know that when I first attempted to play this game as a child, I was too scared to play it because of the ghost character?
I bet you didn't, you smug sons of b****es.
Freddi Fish 2 is the continuation of the rich world of the titular character and his psychologically complex detective fish friend, Luther. While they are attending school one day, a mob from the Squidfather hits up the school, stealing supplies from it and frightening childrend, while disguised as a ghost. So Freddi and Luther must follow a trail deep into the bowels of Hell itself in order to uncover the dastardly truth of this sinister plot.
I might be making fun of the game, but to be completely fair, I did enjoy it far more than the original Freddi Fish.
The game centers around you catching the alleged ghost haunting the school by getting supplies for a trap. It seems a little a**-backwards, since Freddi and Luther have no literal idea when the ghost might come back, even if it does. I think their efforts would have been better spent actually tracking down the ghost. Hell, I even tried to at first but the b****** just up and disappeared after I chased him for a bit.
While you hunt down these various items, you get to explore are far more enjoyable and colorful world, and while the characters don't exactly fit in it like the last installment, it still looks more friendly than the ominous backgrounds of Missing Kelp Seeds. I was actually surprised with how much there is to do in the world this time around as well. Many characters will break into song (most of them not that great), there's a Space Invaders minigame (which is watered down, but still fun... no pun intended), and even movies you can watch (all of which center on dumb puns, not unlike my last pun).
While I can say that just throwing more sh** into a game doesn't make it better (A lesson that could be sorely learned by the Call of Duty franchise), it'll give the little snots a little something extra if they ever play this game. Which I assumed they won't. The only people that do these days are greasy f***s that are far too old to be playing a kids game.
Like... me...
A final point that I'd like to make, is that for this being a "Case of a Haunted Schoolhouse", there isn't a lot of mystery to it. All you're doing is collecting items for the trap. I mean, it is obvious to anyone who's older than 5 to tell that the ghost is f***ing fake, but the game goes out of its way to explain who the ghost really is before you even get a chance to start suspecting the various characters in the game world. And it's the same two damn punks from Missing Kelp Seeds and that cliche pun on The Godfather. When I saw those two tumors appear on screen again, I just sighed and rested my hand on my forehead, and promised myself it'll all be over soon.
Luckily enough, it was. This game, while larger than Freddi Fish Uno, is still pretty easy on the run-time, but also low on the relpy value. It definitely fits into most of the Humongous game tropes, with gathering items, talking to zany characters, and playing minigames along the way... but it all feels disconnected in the large world. It doesn't feel as creative as Humongous' later efforts to make fun kids games like Pajama Sam or Spy Fox 3. But it's still and improvement from the first game, and that's definitely a plus in my book. For all that, I'm giving Freddi Fish 2: The Case of the Haunted Schoolhouse a 5/10.

Like any of the other Puzzle Quest games, this is a match 3 score puzzle game with the theme of Marvel Heroes. It has a story mode competeting off against the AI in various story scenarios, now with weekly special events allowing players a variety of PvE puzzle games to choose from. And there is also PvP arena, while also simulated by the AI, you'll face off against other player's team, composed of three of their heroes and/or villians. Competeting in these events (PvE and PvP) will place you upon a ranking system in brackets of other players around the world. In these brackets, there are milestones providing various bonuses as incentives to duel creating an addictive puzzle grind for glorious rewards.
Generating in-game currency named, "ISO" you'll use this to level up your heroes and villians once you've unlocked (recruited) them either by purchasing the booster cards or earning them from playing the game. It's quite exciting earning cards, as each time you'll have a random chance - while some higher %'s than others - of obtaining that elusive hero or villian you've been after.
It's a fantastic Puzzle Quest game, and I am a fan of the previous PQ games as well... so perhaps I'm biased, but it's definitely a fantastic match 3 puzzle game and highly reccommended by me.

Magic Duels is set to be the format for the Duels of the Planeswalkers series going on into perpetuity, so we'd better get used to it! It's got some ups and downs, notably:
+ A fair free-to-play approach. Casual players should be able to obtain about a booster pack a day without spending any real-world cash, which in combination with the starter sets you're given, is sufficient to build and tune a respectable variety of viable decks.
+ The latest cards and game mechanics from the cardboard version of the game. No longer does Duels lag years behind the state of the game elsewhere.
- Some noticeable bugs and exploits. "Only when you could cast a sorcery" effects often work at instant speed; blockers can sometimes be left assigned illegally via shenanigans with the play timer.
- Dubious network code. Expect lots of odd timeouts and errors if you try Two-Headed Giant, in particular.
- Poor UI decisions. Screen real estate is used poorly, some options from past Duels games have vanished (the "zoom in on last played card" button; option not to automatically advance phases), and the deckbuilding screens could sorely use a more planning-friendly layout.
Despite the minor irritations, though, I recommend the game overall. It's some of the most engaging gameplay you'll find in the free-to-play space! It's also a great introduction to Magic if you might someday want to play Magic Online or the dead-tree game. I've sunk dozens of hours into it already, and will likely spend many more. Not bad for $0!
(Re the "Product received for free" tag--it's a free-to-play game, so of course I did? I didn't get any free coins, if that's what it'd mean in this case.)

Rocking Pilot:
~~~~~~~~~~

Good evening Ladies and Gents, and welcome to the Global Conflict broadcast. Today we have an exciting show for you! An anonymous chopper pilot reckons he can stop these silly wars and defeat Colonel Zarkoff! WYNC studio 1 audience is laughing out loud.  I must admit being the announcer of this realty show for so long, I think it’s funny, too! Let’s go live with this Rocking Pilot!
Rocking pilot is a retro arcade shoot’ em up (bullet hell) game were you control a chopper through forty-two missions across four worlds.
The first few missions are basically a quick and easy tutorial; when you pass those, you’ll be up for some intense challenges. Each of the stages has three phases to clear and others have an additional set of phases called the score mode. Each of the phases (three per stage) has a specific icon and it might be a key, a trophy or a skull (two trophies and a key, for example). When you successfully pass these phases, you will pick up those items which will go towards their respective gauges. Every time you collect three keys, three trophies or two skulls a reward appears, either as a case (new abilities or chopper skins) or it unlocks another level. In the score mode you have to reach a specific score to receive a crown and you have a total of six crowns to grab in this mode. Every four crowns, you’ll receive either a case or a chopper skins.
The pace of this game is truly frantic, which is what you would expect in an arcade game, and let me tell you, I was not disappointed. It has been a while since I was hooked on game like Rocking Pilot. When I stuffed up a phase and died (well, exploded) I had to do it again until I succeeded. I must admit to occasionally swearing at the screen! Oh well, it happens to everybody!
The gameplay is just brilliant; the area where all the action occurs is smaller than other games of the genre and I absolutely loved it. It is just fast, tough and if you are an arcade fan you’ll have a ball! Essentially, you’ll shoot at tanks, plans and soldiers and avoid their large numbers of bullets. Hover over the soldier quickly and use your propellers to dispatch them swiftly or use teh overdrive and smash away tanks, planes and repeal bullets. Hold on, the overdrive can only be active for a few seconds each time. Pick up abilities to inflict extra damage to the enemies . . . a hell of a game!
Another part I really enjoyed is the variety of phases. For example, you might need to save friendlies without shooting once or without using your overdrive. Another tough one; no friendlies can die or you’re back to square one - just brilliant!
Graphically the game is alright and the soundtrack is the hard rock style which is exactly what you want! Control-wise I still prefer to play with the mouse and keyboard rather than the gamepad.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Brilliant arcade game
-	42 missions and 4 worlds
-	Varieties of levels
-	Fun, fast and furious gameplay
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
One of the best arcade shoot’ em up I have played for a while!
9/10

Game: Agent Awesome
Developer: Chaos Industries
Publisher: Chaos Industries
Platform: PC
Agent Awesome is an isometric turn-based strategy game developed by Chaos Industries.
You play as Agent Awesome, the biggest bad♥♥♥♥♥ever. You must storm the building of your former employer, Engineering Vicious Ideas Labs.
The gameplay is harder to explain than to understand. You have two modes, that we'll call Strategy Mode and Real-Time Mode. When in Strategy Mode, time stops and you must select where to send your character, who to attack and which weapon to use. In Real-Time Mode, you see how everything works out. You can complete the levels by either killing everyone or avoiding detection. There are bonuses for both of the strategies.
There are a total of twelve weapons and gadgets. Unfortunately, most of them you will never use, and you will stick most of the game using only the Pistol and the Garrotte. There are a total of 12 levels, with an overall playthrough of two to three hours, depending on how many times you die.
There are multiple graphical glitches, including character models that skate through the floors and disappearing corpses, as well as really hard to control camera movements.
The dialogues are funny for the most part, while the soundtrack and sound effects are really forgettable and weak-sounding.
Overall, this is an interesting concept that can be improved over time. I recommend it to fans of strategy games.

In addition, there's reason to play the smallish number of levels over and over again when you earn points that can be spent on health and bullet time upgrades as well as new weapons. So what are you waiting for? Go get yourself a copy... or borrow some playtime with Bleed from a friend's account. It's time and money worth spending.

After your soul-crushing first run where you'll have to do some horrible stuff and where most of your charaters will have likely been killed or died from hunger, illness, bleeding out, or by their own hand, this is a fantastic survival game. Managing your resourses is a matter of life or death for your whole party and with the ability to play different scenarios -- you can even create your own story! -- you'll always be faced with a new, exciting challenge. At least once you get the hang of it and know exactly how to save your party without comprimising *all* of your morals.
The only critisism I have is sort of a nitpick, really. Every day, you have a random event happen. This can be whether or not your house was raided the night before, if someone fell ill or was wounded while you were away, or if someone comes up to your door for one reason or another. Since these are all random events, which means that if you stop in the middle of your game and restart it, you have a chance of creating a new set of random events happen.
I'd be lying if I said I didn't exploit this sometimes, usually if I didn't want a particular character to be hurt from a raid (Marin and Katia are treasures). However, there would be times where I didn't want to quit out of my game and risk all the possible events from being reset. This caused me to pause the game a lot and resulted in me having a crazy amount of hours recorded playing, when in actuality it's less. There've been days where I completely forgot it was running and would add a complete 24 hours to my recorded time.
However, like I said before, this is a nitpick and I acknowledge that it's not the game's fault for my own actions and forgetfulness. If anything I think it's great for having added a layer of difficulty by only allowing an automatic save at the very beginning of the day. Though I do think $19.99 is a little steep, I definitely would recommend this to anyone who enjoys resourse managing, light strategy and TONS of replayability.

For anybody considering getting this game... this is a hidden gem.
This War of Mine focuses on what other war games simply do not. The lives of regular people who are affected by the war, civilians. The thing to think about is, what would -you- do if war broke out around you, and you had to struggle to survive? Would you be willing to turn your back on neighbors and friends? Would you risk your own health and safety by sharing supplies with strangers, or leaving your shelter to help others?
This is one of those games that I figured, even if I like it, it won't take long to beat and I won't put a lot of hours into it, but I was wrong. I am over 60 hours right now and still playing it, and the only part of the game I even considered remotely boring was doing a solo Marko run and "playing the squirrel." The Anton and Cveta scenario was just downright frustrating, but I imagine that two older people trying to survive with only eachother in the middle of a war would probably have a hard time making it.
+Varied morality based on each citizen's life/lifestyle.
+Scavenging and combat system is well rounded and not entirely unrealistic.
+Excellent crafting system that compliments the games trading system.
+The survival aspect of the game forces you to manage resources and prioritize crafting.
+Addictions require you to consider an added level of comfort for those who have them, as well as an additional way to cope.
+Excellent personal stories and biographies give you an emotional connection to the civilians in your charge.
+Random events that add flavor to the everyday struggle in your shelter.
+Artistic style and game atmosphere.
+Varied survivor personalities and skills.
+Survivors with skills that are useful in real-life, but not-so-useful during a war, gives perspective to how war affects everyone.
+Alcohol can be used to help sad people feel better, but also as a trading item.
-A few minor bugs, most pertaining to the morality system. (Example: Citizens getting sad from "stealing" in a location where there used to be armed thugs. Everyone there is dead, it's not technically stealing anymore, and even if it was, it was from bad guys that one of your civilians already killed. (and were happy about it)
-Some aspects of the game are particularly easy to exploit. (Examples: You can change the random event of that day, or someone getting sick, or a few other aspects, just by leaving the game and restarting that day. Another example is that you can prevent resources from being stolen during a raid by starting a building project, and then canceling the project the next day to get your resources back.)
-Sometimes during the day you wish you could speed it up a bit while waiting for your civilians to dig through rubble or catch up on sleep, but you can only "end day" which is often more time than you wish to skip. A speed-up/slow-down feature would be nice. Also a "pause" feature that allows you to issue commands to your people at once, without having to try to flip between them as quickly as possible.
-It gets fairly repetitive after a few games, luckily there is an alternative shelter you can play in that helps to combat the repitition a little.
-Could definitely use more survivor options, base options, and customization of both of these things in both the regular game, as well as creating your own story.
-Could do with much more crafting possibilities and game items. Even the couch that you can sit on in some scavenging areas but can't craft for your own shelter is a good example.
-Depending on the length of the game, the construction space of your shelter can be very limited.
-Something like a craftable safe to keep select items more secure during raids would be a helpful concept.
UPDATE: -I almost forgot the most annoying con. "Alt+Tab" or basically any minimizing from full-screen mode will crash the game. The only "fix" I have found for this, is to switch to Windowed mode at the title screen, and then switch back to full-screen. For some reason, "Alt+Tab" works after that!
+/-Save Intervals. It would be nice if it saved it at the start of every night, as well as every day, but it also forces you to re-do an entire day, if you decide to exit out of the game when something goes wrong at night.
+/-The rainwater collector can be placed pretty much anywhere. It doesn't make sense to place it anywhere.
Without a doubt. Even if this game costed twice as much, knowing what I do from having played it, I would buy it.

USEFUL INFO FIRST: in order to activate Steam interface, add a shortcut in Steam to splintercell3.exe and play from it. You won't track the time spend on it, but who cares about that?
Now my review about Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell Chaos Theory... That's a long♥♥♥♥♥name for a video game!
When you think about stealth games, a few names come to mind: Hitman, Thief, Splinter Cell and MGS to an extent.
Hailed as the best games in the series most of the time, this review is based on a game I consider to be the pinnacle in that genre, along with Hitman Blood Money.
First of all, don't let the release date fool you. Chaos Theory hasn't aged one bit. It still looks good today, the mechanics are still top notch and mostly, it has tons of features you'd expect from a modern game, without all the flaws you can guess.
I don't know if it's just me, but stealth in FPS view always felt awkward and unpractical to me. Good thing this one has a third person view, have fun looking behind walls! It also features various ways to kill/knock out: whether you'd rather do it in close-combat, shoot them from a distance, pull them from a platform or even jumping onto them.
The environments are a bit varied, going from a jungle-like maze to the top of a lighthouse, cracking down the vault of the bank or retrieve information in city full of people not knowing any better... or even a god damn submarine if that's what you like. Granted, it's mostly close-quarters.
Storywise, it's nothing revolutionnary but it fits well. You follow a linear line up to the bad guys and get em down one by one up until the end. Politicals, bureaucrats, bankers... they all wanted a piece of that cake.
The OST ranges from forgettable to annoying, especially when you do a quick takedown and have to stand a minute or so of "ACTION MUSIC" for no reason. If there's one downside to the game, this may as well be the one. Nothing too irritating but it certainly ain't the soundtrack of Hitman: Blood Money.
Though the game is a rather serious one (shouldn't come up as a surprise considering the protagonist is named Sam), I can garantee you a handful of chuckles to be had. Whether it comes from a stupid mistake you did and alerted all the guards, or one of those on the verge of wetting his pants while being interrogated with a huge knife up his throat.
SO DO I RECOMMEND THIS GAME? YOU BET YOUR♥♥♥♥♥I DO! Did I mention it also features a COOP CAMPAIGN?
It lacks one thing though. Uplay isn't there. Oh wait that's a good thing!

Like any of the other Puzzle Quest games, this is a match 3 score puzzle game with the theme of Marvel Heroes. It has a story mode competeting off against the AI in various story scenarios, now with weekly special events allowing players a variety of PvE puzzle games to choose from. And there is also PvP arena, while also simulated by the AI, you'll face off against other player's team, composed of three of their heroes and/or villians. Generating in-game currency named, "ISO" you'll use this to level up your heroes and villians once you've unlocked (recruited) them either by purchasing the booster cards or earning them from playing the game. It's quite exciting earning cards, as each time you'll have a random chance - while some higher %'s than others - of obtaining that elusive hero or villian you've been after.
It's a fantastic Puzzle Quest game, and I am a fan of the previous PQ games as well... so perhaps I'm biased, but it's definitely a fantastic match 3 puzzle game and highly reccommended by me.

Freddi Fish 2 is one of the very first PC games I ever played. I played it off a CD I got in a cereal box on my dad's ancient Windows 95 computer, which I had for about 10 years.
This is a game I have this strange nostalgic fondness for despite fundamentally being a simple kids game. The plot centers on the two characters, Freddi and Luther, who have to discover the identity of a mysterious ghost who steals the toys of all of the other children. And they have to gather various objects inorder to build a trap to capture the ghost. Like I said it is fundamentally a children's game so the humor is a bit predictable, the puzzles are very simple and you're frequently told what to do and what to get. (IE: Freddi says you need scissors to cut some kelp, you need a wrench to remove a wheel, you need to ask a character for a combination to a lock. Etc.)
Something the game does have much like other Humungous games is random elements. When you start the game up, certain elements are removed wheras others appear. For instance, all of the trap items you need to locate are randomized during every playthrough. While this isn't that big of a difference it does make the second or third playthrough feel different. When I was a kid this blew me away at the time but nowadays it just feels like a way to pad out the game time. Since it is a very short game.
Going through it on the first try you can beat the game in maybe 30 minutes. This is a common aspect of Humungous games compared to other SCUMM games like the ones by Lucasarts. So it might not hold your attention as an adult, but it will return you back to a day when you were a kid, and every game was a treasure to behold.

Having played Puzzle Quest on my PS3 I was familiear with the RPG/Match 3 hybrid mechanic.  If not, you soon will be, because the game is free, so there is no excuse to not try it out.
That being said, I'm sure the largest criticism will be that it is pay to win, which is not  *entirely* true.  If you play daily, participate in tournaments, join an alliance that is active and stay active....you will naturally earn gold coins (premium currency) and the ISO that is required for leveling characters.  You will end up selling premium covers (2 stars +), because roster slots cost gold coins, and you don't want to pay.  However, if you stick it out, keep playing, you will get those slots and then you just have to pray for good drops from cover pulls.
The top players clearly pay or they have more hours in the day than God to play.  The game is meant to be casual, but can be cutthroat, give it a try, its the perfect game when you only have 15 minutes here and there.
EDIT 9/10/14
So being a player with 33 roster slots, Ive had some more time to reflect.  Clearly, as you progress without spending money, you are easily trumped in most high level encounters in tournaments, but success is not impossible with a little strategy and luck.
Most notably, I've noticed that as the developers continue to add new characters (covers or powers) to the possible roster, the chances that you will draw the same 3 star character necessary to level the one you already have becomes lower and lower.  For example, I've had a level 69 Hulk forever, because I have not drawn another cover due to the low 1% chance in most instances.  In the meantime I've accrued 5 or 6 other three star characters that are basically useless with only one cover outside of special circumstances during rare tournament opportunities.
What this means simply is, if you can't afford new roster space to increase room for new characters, you will almost never level those three star characters necessary for higher level challenges.  The devs clearly use this to milk more money and stiff the consumer.  They need to add more two star characters and make three star character opporunities more plentiful.
I still play, but with little opporunity for progression at this point, it is getting tedious and boring to play.

Rocking Pilot, developed by GunGrounds is a retro arcade SHMUP/bullet hell title that I just happen to completely suck at. Or at least I did at first. Then I gradually improved. This doesn’t matter, however, as the game has addictive gameplay and is a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton amount of fun to play. If there was ever a game that you could love and suck at the same time then this is it.
I miss the days where my mother would take me to the pizza shop and order dinner after work. It only happened occasionally but it was always a treat. That’s because the pizza parlors always had the arcade machines. She’d give me a few dollars and I’d play whatever games they had. A lot of the time it was SHMUPs like Raiden and Pacific 1941.
As a result, this is what I am immediately reminded of when I first started playing Rocking Pilot. It was a highly pleasurable blast from the past. Of course, instead of screens that are constantly rolling forward, Rocking Pilot is set in small arenas.
This is what fills the game with so much charm. It’s what the Americans would call a classic quarters eater. The idea of going to an arcade armed with pockets full of quarters. The expectation that you would inevitably walk home penniless. But it would all be worth it if only you could complete the damn game.
Sad but true. Gone are the days of quarter eaters. Replaced by Steam and the consoles in a world where achievements and trophies substitute the exhilaration of beating a game in a cabinet with friends surrounding you. It’s good in some ways and a net negative in others. However, Rocking Pilot has done a very good job of maintaining that vibe past the first impressions stage. The game is still difficult as I wade through the games multiple hours into my experience.
Yet, I appreciate this difficulty. Every level that I successfully navigate feels thoroughly rewarding. I have several aha moments. The mission briefings are clear yet there are times where I am so consumed in staying alive that I find myself ignoring them or forgetting about them. A quick glimpse at discussions about the game reminds me that I’m not alone in finding the game difficult. This is a glorious sensation. We are all becoming addicted to a game that is kicking our♥♥♥♥♥ This is what gaming was like back in the day. Unfortunately, very few games can elicit this type of response nowadays. The fear of never being able to complete the game is strong but the allure of doing so even stronger. This is why I became a gamer.
The mechanics of the game are quite simple. Using keyboard and mouse I zip around the small arena with the WASD keys. I use the right mouse button as a shield that couples as a device of destruction. The amount of usage the player gets out of this is limited but it enables the player to shield and to destroy some of the enemies. Not all, however. But just enough to give the player the impression that he is more than a pure weakling. There are enemies that you can just fly through and your propellers will obliterate them for you. In such cramped maps that the player is presented with you must be careful not to run into an enemy you can’t insta-gib. Finally, you have your basic firing weapon which will eliminate the enemy.
Of course, the game has a myriad of power-ups that assist the player for short bursts. I’d recommend that the player learns how to make the best use of these weapons quickly given their very limited ammunition. They can clear a map very quickly but they can also be wasted with very poor results. This, I feel, is half of the strategy in the game. These power-ups are earned by collecting the shiny jewels left for the player to collect when you kill an enemy. Thankfully, these drop regularly and powerups are plentiful but not to the point of an embarrassing amount of riches.
There is one criticism of the game that I want to get off my chest immediately. That is that I don’t like how small the actual playing arena is. I feel that the game would improve significantly by making use of more of the space. This, however, has been pointed out to the developer on the Steam forums. Thankfully, the community manager – I believe the lead developer himself – has responded kindly to the feedback. He has suggested that he can and will be improving this in a future update. Therefore, kudos to the dev team on listening to the community. That is how good games become great, memorable, titles.
Graphically speaking the game uses a lot of contrasting colors. These design choices were used to aid the atmosphere of the game. Audibly, the game is everything that you would expect from a retro-styled arcade game. There’s been enough love put into the game for both to shine without either ever being standout features of the game.
My personal highlight of the game presentation-wise is in the small cut scenes that occur between each mission. I like the story that is constantly being told. It does a delightful job in tying the levels together and to provide the game meaning. Although the game would have been fine without it, those who aren’t in it for the story can feel free to click through it, I thought that it was an intelligent game design decision.
The game has come shipped with Steam Trading Cards and Steam Achievements. What the Steam store page doesn’t tell you is that it has implemented some type of global leaderboard system. Whether this is utilizing Steam’s leaderboards I am uncertain but I believe it is. If so, I’d recommend that the developer or the publisher make the addition to the store page. It’s all in the details and I believe that this would help spur some sales.
Rocking Pilot is everything that I had hoped it would be and more. It’s a very difficult, retro-inspired arcade game that reminds me of the quarter eaters from yesteryear. As such, its difficulty will scare off some fans. However, I would thoroughly recommend that potential players use the difficulty status to improve your gameplay abilities. Rounds can prove to be short enough that it provides the ‘one more turn’ sensation and you’ll see gradual improvement the longer you play. It has been priced at $5.99 which is an entirely fair price to pay for such a quality product.

Rocking Pilot is a bullet hell game where you fight the enemy waves on your helicopter. It is inspired by the classic arcade games, but tries to introduce new features to the genre. Without spoiling the ending, the setting of the game itself takes place in “reality show” that shows wars and armed conflicts across the world. During every mission, your helicopter stays on screen and tries to perform the task given.
-	Each game zone brings its own interaction: hostages to be rescued, gas that blocks enemy and your bullets, mutant growth that can be killed only by rotors, etc. It feels like developers really spent a lot of time developing the enemies.
-	The graphics are bright and very polished: player’s action receive a good visual feedback. Picking up hostages, dealing damage and picking power-ups – all of this is clear and pretty.
-	Challenging and difficult. You can turn invulnerability/bullet deflection for some time, but not for long. It’s up to you when to turn this one, which direction to face, where to go and what enemies to shoot. Overall, the gameplay feels very skill-based.
-	The game by itself is not that long (probably the base storyline can be completed within 2 hours), but there’s a lot more stuff to do if you want to perfect it. There are also bonus levels with much higher difficulties. As it often is with shmup games, each stage offers extra milestones that can be completed for additional rewards / pickable bonus unlocks.
-	Collisions: bounding boxes are utterly confusing. You often have to kill the enemies using your helicopters rotors, that means you have to approach them, and it is not always clear how far you can go into the enemies without exploding. To sum it up, the death from collisions in this particular game felt like it was hurting the gameplay instead of helping it.
-	The UI is obviously meant for consoles: you have to pick language every time you launch the game. The game keeps launching on your display #1 no matter which one you set as a main one. No way to tune that in the settings. My monitors have different resolution and so I could not set it to run on the one I wanted to. You can turn on the windowed mode, but you don’t seem to be able to resize the window.
Overall, it’s a really decent bullet-hell game when it comes to the gameplay. If you enjoy bullet hell games – the game will be a good addition to your library.

Don't be fooled by my play time, I've played Maple long before it came to steam.
Maple is one of those games you can play for a bit, and then you take one of two paths, you either leave of boredom after a few weeks, or you lose a lot of money and spend months on this game, and then realize this game sucks and quit until you come back wanting more.
Maplestory is a 2D mmorpg with classes that represent characters that you will explore the world as. An idea of what classes are offered range from explorers that can advance into a warrior, mage, bowman, or thief to the master of dragons, or the elf queen of elluel, to more extreme things like magical girls or an animal girl with the power to fight with beasts.
To put it straight, you can make a new character, explore the world, level up, go through job advances and have more flashy skills, but eventually that magic dies.
You realize how much time you wasted on this game, how boring and tedious it was to sit down in one spot for ten levels, holding one button down, level up, and move on to the next spot. Then you repeat the process all over again on a different character.
This game sucks with ease of access. You want the best equips? You gotta work for it in the free market. A full set of the best and optimized equips has the potential to cost billions of mesos depending on how popular the class subset is. You can barely get ten million by normal play. So to make more mesos you have to learn the ins and outs of maple's economy, this has the potential to take weeks. Then you need to scavenge whats good and in high demand to sell in the market, and then, merchanting, buy low sell high. Even when you get to the point of learning the market, results are not immiediate. You can't begin with 5m and end the day with 5b.
The game is pay to win, but you can get nx buy gambling with other players and paying your hard earned mesos at a certain rate per 1k nx. The cash shop has many things you may want. All the items purchased in the cash shop can not be earned in normal play, you need real money for certain things like changing your character's appearance, pets, stat changing and stat enhancing items.
But don't get me started about hackers. This game is poorly managed by nexon. The market time and time again has been dominated by hackers. Tales of people losing everything they worked for due to hackers, with no compensation. There is no escape, and no salvation for the hacker situation in Maple.
This game is tedious, money siphoning, poorly managed, boring and not worth your time,but go ahead, play for a week or two, but don't take it too far. I lost thousands of dollars on this game, and I don't think you would want to do the same.

Let's start off by saying that I would recommend you try this game. It's fun, intense and is just generally a great game. But by no means is it perfect.
My biggest issue with the game is the length. It is literally 6 levels
and they are all very short. They can probably be completed in about 10 minutes on your first try, on easy mode, if you aren't used to this sort of game. But once you have finished them, there are a bunch of upgrades to unlock. However, you can only unlock them by replaying the levels over and over. The different difficulties don't  change the way the enemies behave so not even that will increase the replayability. So that is the biggest issue with the game, and it can put a lot of people off if a game is too short.
The second issue I have with the game is that the controls are weird. On controller, it's very difficult to aim since it's a twin stick shooter platformer but on keyboard it is more difficult to actually aim in all directions at once, and you will need to aim in all directions at once with the amount of enemies that spawn. The triple jump mechanic is interesting and if you pull off cool dodges with it then it feels satisfying but it does have its downsides that make it a little unresponsive sometimes.
The story is pretty lame so don't come to this game for a story and the artstyle is typical pixel art and doesn't detract from the game for me but it doesn't do anything special. The same goes for the music in the game.
Those were my main issues with the game. If you can get past those then you should try this game. It is really fun and intense. The harder difficulties can provide a great challenge and the bosses are also all very unique and some of them are quite challenging when you start the game.

TLDR: I wasn't sure about this game, but it was on sale and it had a cute name so I spent the money.
I do not regret this purchase - in fact, if I had to, I would happily pay the full price.
The tutorials inducts you into the game mechanics without being a chore to complete, and each scenario has goals but still provides you flexibility in how you choose to accomplish them.
Being based on "real-life" illnesses, you feel a bit of connection to the products you create. You expend time analysing the  recent hypertension compound your company's explorers discovered in the desert; using the machines at your disposal you upgrade it to diabetes medication that isn't on the market yet - you make a tidy profit for being the only supplier and you're sure there's some sufferer out there whose health has improved thanks to your work.
The difficulty level ratchets up as you play: it is never too hard but time restrictions keep you focused on your goals.
Mechanically, there is a lot to do to keep you from getting bored: research new technology, send explorers out to gather new compounds, analyse the market for drugs, compare yourself to your competitors (and aim to keep ahead of them), respond to market/consumption changes, and (most importantly) create and develop pharmaceuticals.
There are also a lot of decisions to make and the "right choice" is not always clear. Do you spend capital and reduce profits to remove a negative side-effect from a new medication? The answer to that question changes based on your unique situation. How much will it cost? Is the market competitive or do you have a monopoly? How much less will people pay for their cough medicine if there's a small chance they will get a rash from it?
The only improvement I would make to this game is adding more variable challenges. This exists somewhat in the Global Events mechanism - random policy changes outside your control which alters in-game values. For example, a new mental health policy might increase demand for antidepressants. Additionally, competitors sometimes patent a product you're already producing which can be a big shock to your profit margins and production lines. However, there could be more challenges in this sense.

Pay an additional $30 now to receive a mostly* finished product!
*Note: True finished status will require also purchasing our next $30 DLC.
Seriously, I was willing to put up with paying for DLC that fixed Civ 5, and in the end it became one of the greatest strategy games I've ever played. Now it looks like releasing unfinished products and charging $30 (and I'm sure there will be another $30 DLC further down the line) to finish it is the way that Firaxis and 2K want to conduct business.
I can't recommend that you purchase this game at full price, especially because you'll probably be forced to pay for $60 worth of DLC to receive what it should have been at launch. It's still a decent game, so go ahead and pick it up when they release the Complete Edition or when the base game and DLC go on sale for ~50% off or more. The game isn't necessarily bad (see the other detailed reviews people have made, most of them are pretty accurate), but it definitely isn't worth the current $40 price tag. To be fair, Rising Tide also looks like it's a decent DLC.
I've been a long time Civ player (since ~2, so not the longest by any means) but if this is how the games are going to be marketed from now on then I'm just going to jump ship now. If the next Civilization game has actual effort put behind its release and doesn't require that I end up paying $120 for the final finished product then maybe I'll come back. Until then, I'll try not to let the door hit me on the way out.

This War of Mine is a game that portrays the lives of the true victims of war. Instead of donning military equipment and gunning down enemy troops as soldiers, you play as civilians with daily struggles such as lack of food, medicine, and a shelter over their heads. Each character was an unique individual with occupations ranging from a news reporter to a professional football player to a school principal, but somehow each one is equal in the eyes of war, fighting to survive.
The gameplay focuses on the day/ night cycle whereby during the day,you control your survivors in a previously bombarded house and attempt to make it a proper shelter. In the first few days, you clear the litters of rubble, scavenge for materials in cabinets and start building comfort items such as beds. Thereafter, you build up the defences of your new home to fend off hostile raiders, while not forgetting to stock up on resources for the bitter winter. During the night, you can choose to send a survivor to scavenge in abandoned houses, ransacked supermarket/ school, or in desperate times bandit camps or military strongholds which have stockpiles of resources, but highly risky and hard to tell if the scavenger can survive the night.
However, it was the decision-making that made the game good. When you are low of food supplies, do you feed the scavenger who spent the whole night in a dangerzone, the guard who got injured defending the base from a bandit raid, or the sick who needs it for any chance of recovery, while knowing there is no guarantee he could even last one more night? Do you help when someone comes knocking on your door? Do you have to resort to stealing from others so that your friends at home can survive? Do you kill when you're caught? Is there even a difference between stealing and killing in such times?
Personally, the first playthrough was brutally hard as there was pretty much to learn. I was raided every night and I didn't understand why. Second playthrough was much more manageable and got repetitive quick, but I got owned in winter, when many unvisited places became unaccessible. I only managed to beat the game when I created a custom story, as I could alter the game difficulty from there. I would also like to note that you can create your own characters by importing photos from your library. This is also found in the Custom Story tab.
All in all, I started playing the game with high expectations and was not disappointed. It was a necessary game in an era with big AAA titles seeming to promote the 'shoot first, ask never' attitude with little to no consequences. Highly recommended!

Splinter Cell - Chaos Theory is stealth genre gold. It's the third title of the Splinter Cell franchise and is simply the best stealth game of the series. Ubisoft Montreal did great work on this. The character, Sam Fisher, is a veteraned soldier of the United States working in secret for the government's NSA. The game provides well written and voiced dialogues for Sam and most of the characters in the game that can be quite humorous at points.
The core stealth mechanics of the game are extremely well done and fun to play once learned. The actions and controls of the gameplay are pratical and fluid. The shadow and lighting systems are easy to use and provide clear feedback to the player at all times. The takedown system is fun to use and capturing an enemy is challenging at times. The stealth gadgets and weapons are fun to use and have some creative examples like sticky cameras, shock bullets, pistol emp, and more.
Level design is extremely creative and the game contains some very cool setpieces and level design.
The environmental sound is an aspect of gameplay as well. Game sounds can be heard by your opponents and even microphone talk in Coop can be heard by guards. Guards are well voiced and some have some creative writing that can be pretty entertaining at times. Gunfire sounds fine. Most of your weapons are silenced but it makes sense. Environmental sound effects are great. The music is done by Amon Tobin, a braziallian electronic music artist, and it fits perfect with the stealth mood of the genre. Its a fantastic soundtrack for a game

This game is scary good. It's a show of what happens when a developer is in sync with what is happening in video games.
Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory was released in 2005 for the Xbox, PS2 and GameCube - development for PC was sort of an afterthought. It served to hold as the best stealth game of all time. You control Sam Fisher (or other characters, in CoOP or Spies vs. Mercenaries), playing as a true spy throughout various secret missions, which eventually take you across the sea to Asia.
The controls, for PC version, after tricky to get used to at first but serve the player very well in having complete control over Sam Fisher. It's not hard for the player to learn how to be running full speed, execute a combat roll, and be sneaking up against a wall. The interface is extremely clear about what the player has equipped and what is going on around them. Overall, the presentation is extremely clean cut and minimalistic, immersing the player as much as they can in their role of sneaking around and interrogating and executing/knocking out baddies.
Multiplayer is an option as well, consisting of a CoOp game mode and Spies vs. Mercenaries. Both modes are tweaked to better reflect the player having a fun experience, with CoOp having tweaks that require and encourage cooperation with things like a change of the electronic-jamming pistol, cooperation-exclusive moves like boosting each other up and a martial arts toss, and an interweaving campaign with the single player mode. Spies vs Mercenaries pits spies against mercenaries, giving the mercenaries more lethal means of dispatching the spies while stripping spies of most lethal means to kill someone, instead settling for crowd control methods.
Chaos Theory is a timeless game. It truly is, and for whatever price is available on Steam, ranging from $9.99 to $2.50, is worth it. My only word of advice is to be cautious that Ubisoft does not force this game onto their horrid DRM system, uPlay - we don't want to purchase a game on Steam and have to be told to sign up for YET ANOTHER ACCOUNT like the Assassin's Creed series.

So, Blacklist turned out to be pretty good and a huge improvement over Conviction which was a detraction from the core SC formula. However, the definitive SC experience will always be Chaos Theory, which largely corrected the flaws of the previous games while further improving the strengths.
When this game released in 2005, it was a graphical masterpiece that pushed the consoles to their limits, and also put strain on the most powerful PC GPUs of the time. Ten years later, the graphics still hold up pretty well, especially the lighting effects which are essential to the stealth gameplay.
The freedom of choice you get in this game is incredible, and sadly absent in the later titles. In previous games, it was difficult to do things more than one way. That guard HAD to be KOed/killed. That door's lock HAD to be picked. There was rarely more than one path. In Chaos Theory, the levels are more sandbox-like, with multiple possible routes for you to discover. You can break locks or you can spend time picking them.. You can wait for a guard to come walking up to a door, and then slam it into his face with all your strength, or you can wait for him to turn away, and do a standard stealth KO. You can open a door slowly, pushing it a little more forward with each press of the W key, or you can fling it open and exposing yourself. You can hack electronic locks or retinal scanners or you can force guards to cooperate. You can hack PCs to disable lasers and cameras or you can play a dodging minigame. It's also much easier to carve your own 100% avoidance path this time because you get a lot of room to breathe.
Every single enemy could be interrogated which expanded gameplay possibilities and also made for amusing easter eggs.
The alarm system was much more forgiving without making the game too easy. Gone are the days of instant-failure because some dude saw you even if he didn't get a chance to radio for backup.
The story was quite engaging, and made Sam Fisher more involved in the plot rather than just an everyday cleanup guy.
AI was significantly improved from older games. Enemies would start using flashlights, lighting flares, and calling backup instead of just walking blindly towards the sight of a broken light.
Melee attacks, a serious letdown in the past, are now my favourite way to deal with trouble. Sam Fisher now gets a knife that can do one-hit kills. If he wants to go non-lethal, he throws a fast punch to the head - a LOT more effective and realistic than the stupid elbow move in the previous games.
Chaos Theory isn't a shooter, and it's difficult to play it like one without dying within seconds. Nevertheless, should the♥♥♥♥♥♥hit the fan, the guns are more effective than before, giving you choices of attachments (gadget launcher or shotgun or sniper attachment?) and making ammo more readily available (you can now carry more than 2 mags per gun at a time). The pistol is more accurate so you don't waste so many rounds to take out one light. The rifle with its attachments can make for many interesting possibilities (long range stealth kills, sticky shocker KOs, etc).
Co-op mode was the first of its kind, allowing two players to play as Splinter Cells and boost each other over walls and work in tandem to do coordinated kills. It was even more fun than the campaign, but sadly a bit short.
I've never tried Spies vs Mercenaries so no comment there.

Bleed, the fast paced shoot em up! And is it good? Well, yeah! Just read this review to find out exactly why!
This game is good, there's no denying it. And I'm not just gonna sit here and say "yeah the game's good, get it". Because that would be scummy of me. I'm going to start with the basics of the game and then move on to talk about the art and controls. Each will have quite a bit to talk about, so be prepared for that.
So, as for the basics of this game, Bleed is a fast-paced, frantic platformer. As you run around the levels you will encounter many beasts and ghouls, all of which unique to the level. When I say unique, I mean that each enemy is never really shown again in the same level. To put it simply, the sprites are never lazily thrown around as if the game doesn't matter, it's obvious that the devs of this game have put a lot of thought and effort into the actual design of the levels and the enemies, which pays off in the end.
In terms of gameplay it's, as I've said before, fast-paced and frantic. This is further enforced by the side-scrolling element which is tossed in. You advance in each level by either scaling upwards or downwards and running from place to place. As to be expected in a side-scroller, I suppose. Whilst also talking about gameplay, I think I should talk about the biggest mechanic in the game. Time slowing. How it works is, you hold down your RMB (Right Mouse Button) and it slows down time. This is extremely helpful and in most situations extremely vital to your safety and ability to live.
One thing that I ADORE in this game is the amount of weapons. From a Shotgun to even a Katana, each weapon is unique and will help you in it's own way. Some enemies are best tailored to certain weapons and some can be destroyed with all types. This shows a sign of a good game when the player has multiple choices as to what they want to use to defeat certain enemies, meanwhile challenging themself to try it with harder or lesser used weapons.
Feeling like the game could just a little bit of "OOMPH"? How about you ramp up the difficulty with the different difficulty options! Each option is still hard in it's own right, so you don't have to worry about picking a difficulty and thinking that you're forced to play it for the rest of the game, whilst steamrolling the game.
If anything, I could say that this game is honestly one of the hardest games I've ever played. And I would be telling the truth 100%. This game is tough as nails, but I still find myself yearning to play it just knowing that I could beat the game in a harder difficulty, or even just play with a whole different weapon choice. Even once you've beaten the main game, Arcade Mode will have you coming back for more. Arcade Mode is honestly harder than Campaign mode for one simple reason; You have to beat the game with one life. Yeah, I know, hell. It's amazing fun all the same, and if you make a mistake you can remember it for the next time you play!
Enough about my undying, adoring love of the gameplay itself and onto my undying love of the art of this game. Yeah, okay the game is pixelated and that's totally fine! There's nothing wrong with pixel art when done RIGHT. And boy oh boy did this game do it right.
Firstly, you should note how gorgeous the sceneary is in this game. The backdrops are so well done and show an obvious amount of time and detail which has been poured into it. Each character and enemy alike are so well done that you can find yourself staring at how brilliant the sprites actually are.
Weapon art is done incredibly well, each weapon differing from the other and allowing you to actually see how different the weapons are from one another.
Alright, onto the final stretch, trust me.
The music in this game is brillant. It's amazingly upbeat and cheerful and can make you just want to buy the OST for friends upon friends.
Now, for the bit I've been waiting to talk about for quite a while. The places where this game kinda falls short.
Okay, look. This game isn't perfect but that doesn't take away from how good the game actually is, so take these little nitpicks with a grain of salt.
The controls:
- There's a damn good reason I didn't put the controls in something that I enjoy. It's because I don't really like the controls with this game when using keyboard. Controller, as recommended by many, many other reviewers, is totally agreed with by me. I mean, don't get me wrong, the game is 100% playable with mouse and keyboard, but it's just a bit rough. For me, at least.
Achievements:
- Some achievements feel super, super, hard to get. I'm all for a tough achievement but I don't like games that have achievements which make me curse the game itself.
Apart from that, everything else in this game is pretty great!

TL;DR: A fast-paced action platformer of 16-bit retro looks,
is one of those games that anyone who likes platformers should play.
In
, a girl named Wryn wants to become the ultimate videogame hero. She sets out to beat all the previous heroes of the old times. Her super powers? Bullet time and excessive amounts of fire power.
Retro in looks, the game is set in the vague year 21XX and the graphics are reminiscent of 16-bit era. It works in
's favour as the silly and colourful enemies and bosses have a refreshingly distinctive look to them. The soundtrack is plainly awesome. I love how the tracks have been carefully chosen to fit all scenarios; especially the last level's soundtrack was simply intense.
With colourful artwork come the silly looking enemies. Cats and flying ooze blops litter the levels. The bosses include worms, a slug and a dragon among other silly things. While the common enemies are simple and predictable, all bosses have at least three special attack patterns that get faster and more intensive the higher the difficulty setting becomes.
The fast-paced gameplay of gunslinging and attacks coming from all directions at once is alleviated by Wryn's super power: she can slow down time at will (or at the click of a button). Bullet time renders many impossible looking situations manageable, even easy, but the twist is that the bullet time energy is limited and replenishes only when not used. Wryn can do three consequential dives in the air (like double jumps but better), a feat that becomes really useful when dodging attacks while using bullet time.
There are nine different weapons to try, two to start with and the rest to unlock through experience (gained by winning levels or challenges) and beating levels. You start with dual pistols and rocket launcher, and since there are no reloads it's rather common to just run through a level with the fire button down all the way.
One can buy e.g. a flamethrower, a sniper laser rifle and a sword that can be used to ricochet bullets back at enemies. All weapons are unique and useful in their own way but some require more practice than others. You can only equip two weapons at a time, which is a bummer since often you'd like to use 3 different ones in a given boss fight. Though weapons can be changed by going to escape menu, it's still a break in the flow that is bad in a fast-paced game like this.
I played
without problems using keyboard and mouse but controller is recommended (I have one but I still preferred K+M). Controller enables more accurate dodges and movement while mouse allows more accurate targeting so both are totally viable settings. At least one controller is required to play local co-op, which I sadly didn't get to try out.
Mastering bullet time, dodging and useful weapon combinations are the key to winning the boss battles and especially when playing through the Arcade Mode where you also have to manage the combometer (for highscores and for certain weapons), done by hitting enemies and not getting hit yourself.
has seven levels that can in principle be beaten in an hour or so but the four difficulty levels add a lot to replayability unless you just started out to torture yourself through it with the Very Hard mode.
While in Story Mode there are check points and you can play any section as often as you wish, the Arcade Mode makes you play through the game without a single death. As your health bar does not get replenished between levels this puts
into the category for extremely difficult games to complete 100%. Nevertheless it is almost completely fair, so you know every mistake is your own.
I needed tens of tries to survive through Hard and Very Hard difficulties in Arcade Mode but it felt very satisfactory once I did it. As such take my 21 hours to 100% completion with a grain of salt - it could take you a bit less time if you were good or very much more to 100%
depending on your skills. You might even find it to be nearly impossible. That said,
is a very good action platformer, and if you like the genre it's one of those must-buy games.

This game mega took me by surprise. While a limited 'bullet time' power has been explored time and time again by games of many different genres, I don't honestly think I've ever seen it implemented as cleanly and effectively as in Bleed. The game allows you up to three mid-air dashes, which can be performed in any direction and steered to a very precised degree. Normally the high speed and intensity of the game's action makes it difficult to properly utilise this mechanic to avoid the almost bullet-hell like hazards of each level, but that's where the bullet time comes in. Each level is, in addition to being very creative, extremely well suited to testing your ability to find the perfect moment to slow down time and use your air dashes to carefully weave in and out of obstacles, all while trying to deal maximum damage to the enemies in your way with a variety of weapons.
In addition to the well crafted levels, each boss is highly unique and a tonne of fun to fight. You're unlikely to beat any of them on your first try, but none of them ever feel unfair or cheap.
My only complaints about the game are in the nitpicky details. I'm personally not a fan of spritework with coloured outlines, as I think it gives too much of a pillow-shade look to the characters. I can't say anything from the soundtrack sticks out as particularly memorable either. Generally speaking the weapon balance was a little off, with some of the unlockable weapons being downright useless, and most were just generally worse or less universally appropriate than the  default loadout, so you'll unfortunately probably go through most of the game without bothering to switch out.
Overall though I'd absolutely recommend this to anyone who into difficult games that require quick thinking and precise movements and aiming. I've already enjoyed Bleed more than enough for my money's worth after two full playthroughs (first on hard and then on very hard), and I absolutely plan to go back and try and get an S-rank on each boss!

A game that reminds of the great Theme Hospital but sadly is not one - although it is not a bad game in itself.
Big Pharma is a game about drug production by setting up processing lines that change different ingredients into a drug that can be sold with profit. You get a number of machines that can change the drug intensity, upgrade it or remove side affects that come along. Each steps of course comes with a price and it's up to you judge if you want a better drug or make more money on it - sometimes both means the same but not always.
The visual aspect and general user interface are really great. A bit old school but well designed and look.
The processing line design is pretty fun - I must admit. In general it's a puzzle - place more cheaper machines that takes less space or more costly ones that do the job for three but at higher cost. Either way you have to judge space requirement over probable income loss. Depending on the drug complexity the processing lines can be quite long and interesting and putting them up together is the meat of the game. You need to watch for side effects, adjust proper concentration, mix them together to combine certain effects in order to upgrade them. The whole marketing model is quite complex and opponents do put up a fight.
Apart from that you get scientists you can hire in order to discover more complex machines and other enhancements. You also get to hire people to discover other ingredients curing different diseases. They're costly so you need to manage this as well.
There are some issues though - ones that really spoil a lot of the fun. First of while the theme is interesting it causes the names to be hard to remember. This goes especially for ingredient names and diseases treated - I could not remember them whatsoever and had to constantly check by hovering over or visiting cures screen. Fact that processed drugs at each stage look almost the same - apart from the small distinction in colour does not help at all. The machine names are easier to remember but just a little. Also the fact that once you research Creamer there is no point in shipping pills is also off putting.
But the worst offence was a combination of trying to optimize the output combined with competition. The game gives you a packaging machine. This enables storing multiple drugs in a single package, thus the packages contain more but are less frequently occupying the conveyor belt. This lets you output multiple drugs into a single slot. The number of slot is limited and you can use them both for input and output - thus makes sense to have 4 inputs and single output - and is doable. However if your opponent gets a patent on one of the drugs you're producing you are screwed. The forbidden drug will stop the export and halt all four lines to a point in which you have to manually delete and replace the conveyor belt in order to get your other lines working. Really annoying and proves that optimizing this area is pointless.
Overall apart from the problems noted the game is pretty good. Has it's flaws but did enjoy it. Though probably will not get back to it again.

On the downside, starting positions can still be extremely unfair, just like all the previous Civilization games. I can start one game in a large expanse of prime territory, with no adversaries nearby; and I can start another surrounded by aliens, with my expansion blocked by canyons, mountains, and other factions. This can make for very interesting variety, but it can also be very frustrating. Oh, and diplomacy can be just as annoying as other Civilization games.
Overall, the great things about the game offset the bad, at least for my enjoyment. Expansions should make the game even better.

It is the most unique and refreshing MOBA of ...ever. Don't lose me yet — I am calling it a MOBA since it means "Multiplayer Online Battle Arena" and, well, if Bloodline Champions isn't a MOBA, no game is.
It is nothing alike League of Legends or DotA2. There are no minions and no lanes. This right here is the Quake 3 of MOBAs. Rounds take around 1-3 minutes, and a match is 3 rounds.
No levels. No items. No chance dependent skills. All "spells" are skillshots. ALL SPELLS, even melee "autoattacks" are skillshots. Usual classes apply: Tank, Healer, Assassin, Nuker, ADC, etc.

When I first heard of Garden Rescue, I got excited as I love Tower Defence games. However, I was quickly disapointed when I found out Garden Rescue brings no new aspects to the Tower Defence Genre with 90% of its features/ideas/towers etc seeming as though they were stolen from Plants vs Zombies. Hence, I can't really recommend buying and playing this game and I will let you know fully why I can’t via the detailed pros and cons below.
Pros:
♦ Graphics and style of the game is awesome
♦ Sound effects are great
♦ Each level has a unique path
♦ Good number of upgrades for progressing throughout the game (This keeps the game interesting)
♦ Easy Achievements with a little bit of Grinding (Easy game to 100%)
♦ Awesomely detailed book about the Towers, Bugs (Enemies) and Levels
♦ Probably get your money’s worth (I say probably as it's fairly long, though read my con about game length)
♦ Three Star Concept is great
♦ Cheap
Cons:
♦ Repetitive (Gets to a certain point and it's just the same thing over and over again)
♦ Doesn't bring anything new to the Tower Defence Genre
♦ Feels as though the Devs just played Plants vs Zombies and copied most of its key aspects with changing Zombies to Bugs and making the game Path Based (This is evident such as Lawn Mower concept being the same as PvsZ, Plants giving coins is the same as Sunflowers giving Sun in PvsZ, Towers having 3 upgrades which is the same as PvsZ, the first tower you get directly copies the PvsZ PeaShooter, the level where you don't need coins to buy towers and randomly get given a tower is the same as one of PvsZ minigame level. There are many many more examples of how they copied PvsZ but there are too many too list.)
♦ The levels/the rate the enemies come out feels really slow even when you press the 3x speed button (This is really annoying as you sit there with nothing to do just waiting which bored me in some levels)
♦ Variety of Towers could have been better (Too many Ground Towers, not enough Air Towers and the Harden/Defence Tower was useless)
♦ Game offers Tips, however it seems to only have one tip which keeps appearing unless you turn them off (This is annoying as I personally think if there is a tip system there should be more than one tip...)
♦ When the level is paused, upgrade icons don’t go away from certain plants (This is annoying if you pause the game and then upgrade something before unpausing some plants upgrade indicator don't disappear)
♦ No incentive to play on Harder Difficulties (There are three difficulties and no matter which one you use they all feel the same, except there may be slightly more health on the Bugs and there is nothing really unique about each difficulty to make you want to play the game on a Harder or Easier Difficulty)
♦ The last level seems stupid (The Devs seemingly have just spammed bosses into one annoying level making it near impossible to 3 Star compared to any other level in the game which was quite easy to 3 Star)
♦ No Storyline (This is terrible as it gives you even less incentive to play on as there is no aspect of wanting to know what happens next. Also when you finish the game on any difficulty it just shows credits which annoyed me as the last level is ridiculous in difficulty compared to the others)
♦ No replay value (I say this as there is only 30 levels and once you beat them there is no incentive to do them on different difficulties except one achievement and there is no new worlds, minigames or anything unlocked for beating the game to give it more replay value and make you want to keep playing the game)
♦ Could easily find a Tower Defence of this Calibre for free on Miniclip or a Flash Game Website
On a whole there are way more negatives than positives and as the game feels as though the Devs ripped off 80% of the games aspects/content from Plants vs Zombies without bringing anything new to the Tower Defence Genre and also having no replay value whilst feeling like a free flash game from Miniclip means I can’t really recommend for anyone to buy this game even though it is cheap, works and you will get a few grinding hours out of it.  Thus, I also wouldn't recommend this game if you are looking for a Unique Tower Defence that brings something different to the Genre with high replay value as this has none of those aspects as it’s all been done before. Lastly, IMO this game was a boring, slow grind to get to the end just to get 100% of the achievements as you need to 3 star all the levels to get 100%.
*Note: The only reason I’d recommend buying this game would be if you want a quick (3 hours is what it took me… which is quicker than most games), easy game to get 100% of the Achievements to help boost your Steam Profile*
