This is a decent but generic path-based grid-placement tower defense. There are very little PC options, but they aren't really needed to enjoy it. I 3-starred all 30 levels and unlocked all achievements in 9 hours of playtime, and probably a quarter of that was AFK. You start with like 2 towers, and have to unlock the rest by playing through the levels. There is no story at all. Just kill bugs with plants and collect gold that appears out of strawberries.
There is very little tower interaction with each other, although there is one buff tower (which doesn't tell you if it buffs speed, damage, or just makes a glowy animation). There is very little description of what a tower does before you place it, no description of how much benefit you get from the two upgrades each tower has, and no description of how much damage a tower does in raw numbers or DPS.
In my opinion, all of those are very important to make a good tower defense game. As is, its all guesswork. The levels with 3 paths, and it auto gives you towers are basically puzzles you have to start over several times to get right. You don't know the best placement since it doesn't tell you what else you will get or where the next wave comes from. If you don't want to trial-and-error it, then just watch a YouTube video of someone playing the level and match their placement. Useless levels really.
I found the cactus to be the best tower most of the time, since it hits ground and air targets, and each upgrade adds an additional target it can hit. The flame tower and the bomb tower do great damage and shouldn't be overlooked. Placing plenty of slowing towers before your kill zones is recommended.
I recommend it only if you like casual level tower defense games and get it in a bundle or for a cheap price. Don't come in expecting Bloons or Defense Grid quality, but its decent.

SINGLE PLAYER - Homefront's campaign is rather bland and short. I completed it in less than five hours. It's set in a version of the U.S. that's been occupied by North Korea. Though I don't see how that makes Homefron unique. There's no decent attempt in the campaign that explains how North Korea managed to become a superpower capable of invading the U.S. You might as well have been shooting at Russians or the Chinese.
The gameplay is linear. You get to control some gadgets and vehicles for here and there, but you'll end up running and gunning most of the time. There aren't any situations which require you to think. There are no puzzles, dilemmas, skills to master, etc. As long as you know how to point a mouse, you'll be fine. In short, it's your run-of-the-mill modern arcade shooter.
MULTIPLAYER - Here, unlike in the single player mode, you can play as infantry and drive vehicles you didn't have access to in the campaign (Which is kinda odd because the campaign should serve as a tutorial for the multiplayer). This mode features a decent balance of infantry weapons and vehicles for both sides. Good luck finding a full server though.
If you find this on sale, then it could be a good cheap thrill.

First off, let me start by saying that this is one of the best platformers I have ever experienced. Now to the nitty-gritty stuff:
PROS
- Great game mechanic
- Controls are on point
- Unique and new play style make it all the more fun
- Awesome 8-bit (I think) graphics
- Pretty good story
- Terrific jumping and gunning system
- Fast-moving, fluid movement that feels good
- Overall good layout in general
- Soundtrack is amazing
CONS
- Definitely too short
- Does not have enough replayability (the sense of replayability comes from beating each level on one of four difficulties)
- Weapon mechanics are WAY unbalanced (the Dual Pistols are, in most situations, the best)
- Should have had more 'meat' to its bones (as I said, more levels, as well as possibly a more extensive shop and upgrades system)
CONCLUSION
An overall great game. It nails the 8-bit (I think) graphic style and layout. The control style is one of the best and most obscure I have seen. The other character variations and modes are not overly appealing to come back to. Main things to work on is game content, as I completed the initial game in just under three hours.

Years ago, back in early high school, I used to play this game with fellow classmates on the weekends at each other's houses. Years later and a college degree later, I've re-downloaded a game (which was quite heftier than I had remembered) to see what kept the game around for so long.
The graphics are still cute as my memory had served, and the music delightful with each swing. However, the key mapping was awkward and different enough from the norm that it proved a bit difficult at first to remember which key did what. The story's dialouge was heavy, and although sprinkled with jokes, did not hold my interest in the least bit, and I found myself clicking over and over trying to finally get to any of the gameplay. I appreciate the vast amount of options you get with picking a class as well as customizing your cosmetics to truly make your avatar unique- unfortunately, I spent a lot of time just on the class alone, lost as to where to go or even start. It felt like too many options presented all at once, and given the lengthy and chore-heavy of the tutorial quests, I did not fancy the idea of going back to replay these areas over and over again just to find which class suited me, unlike in many other notable MMO's.
When it comes down to the bottom line, this game does not hold up as well as I thought it would have, especially considering that it's still kicking around today. Fun for maybe a little while, but in the long run, time is best served on a game less clumsy.

So, yeah, definitely check out this game and don't be a salty Raigon main. Thanks.

As Steam indicates, I got
for free.  If you can get it for free as well, I could maybe say it's an okay time-killer.  But I cannot recommend paying any amount of money for this game, even at a deep discount.  This game plays like a store-brand version of any number of modern-warfare games that came before it, so I'd recommend playing one of those instead.
For one thing, Steam tells me that I logged 5.0 hours at the time I finished the campaign.  While that sounds short, the actual runtime is actually quite shorter.  I'm currently playing on an 8-year-old gaming laptop, so I dealt with what I imagine were longer-than-usual loading times, and on top of that I needed to restart several checkpoints because various plot-advancing events failed to trigger.  (This game is buggy as all get-out, as an aside.)  So the actual runtime, I would guess, is probably somewhere closer to 4 hours, or even less if you don't suck as bad at shooters as I do.
The overall experience of playing
can more or less be summed up by describing the opening sequence.
It's essentially a remake of the scene in
that takes place from the perspective of the captured politician.  You are taken from your home, handcuffed and put on a bus, and go for a ride down a road where various acts of tyranny are being committed, such as civilians being detained in droves and occasionally being executed by firing squads. Although
escalates the scene rather tastelessly, because the firing squad executes a couple in front of their pre-school-aged child.  The rest of the game, story-wise, pretty much follows that pattern:  pulling ideas and even whole scenes from other games, but lacking any of the nuance or thoughtful execution (no pun intended) that made those games good.

During the late 90’s/early 2000’s Humongous Entertainment released an absolutely fantastic stream of “edutainment” point and click adventures for children. These titles focus on a range of light academics including basic geography, basic to upper elementary level mathematics, logical thinking, critical thinking and puzzle solving, topped off with reinforcement of good manners and polite social etiquette. At the lower end of the age spectrum, they may require some adult supervision and supportive guidance, but there is no better series of games for a child’s first venture into PC gaming.
I played the Haunted Schoolhouse right after finishing the Kelp Seed adventure and I remember not being okay with the whole “Haunted” part. Between the already scary sharks, and then some sort of paranormal activity in an elementary school, I remember that this game really frightened me at first. I think it was almost a year before I went back and actually really enjoyed it. It is by no means inappropriate, but I would recommend some supervision at first until you see how your child reacts to some of the opening scenes and concepts.

DFO is a fast paced 2.5D brawler/RPG which is similar to games like the Simpsons and X-Men arcade games, as well as games like Final Fight or TMNT on the Snes, but with much more polish.  The game has a current total of 42 different character/class combinations, each with their own unique skills and playstlye.  The main focus is the PvE, but there is also a great PvP element which some players choose to focus on exclusively.
You progress like you would through most RPGs: Kill enemies, Complete quests.  As you do so you gain levels, which allow you access to increasingly advanced equipment and abilities.  The current level cap is 86, and you offered at least 1 additional ability every 5 levels, with more advanced powers hitting harder, but requiring more mana consumption and having longer cooldowns.  You are free to distribute the Skill Points as you desire and are given more than enough skill points to max a majority of your skills, adjusting a few skills up or down based on preference and with no penalty for resets.  The game has a focus on equipment value, has 5 armor slots, 3 accessory, 1 weapon, and 1 title, each of which has varying degrees of rarity, which may be further enhanced through reinforcement (The games gold/currency sink), as well as enchantments and amplifications.  You may also use (mostly) cosmetic items to change your appearance while adding a small stat boost on some of the rarer and premium content pieces.
The gameplay takes place in instanced dungeons with map pieces which the players advance through as they choose, clearing one room before being able to advance to the next.  Each instance takes anywhere from 2-5 minutes, however some of the end game "raids" may take longer.  Most of the time you will be able to focus on quests, giving some purpose to your actions and providing you with bonus exp.  Most of the standard game enemies and bosses are fairly easy until you get furter into the game when you need to begin to time your attacks and watch your movement.
The combat is fast paced, and mostly consists of you combing your basic attacks with your standard abilities, or "canceling" your attacks and abilities into each other to create long and satisfying combos.  Each ability is a pleasure to watch (especially higher leveled ones), and the impact is visilbe as you watch enemies life get chunked away as they go flying up or across the screen.  While the higher leveled attacks may do more damage, they also have longer activation times, so you will find yourself using your lower leveled abilities frequently into the late game, but they remain a pleasure to use.
The PvP element of the game works slightly different from the PvE side in that most skills have had their power readjusted, and others have had their hit boxes reduced for balance.  The PvP has it's own ranked system as well, and has a surprisingly deep level of skill to it.  Expect to spend several hours in PvP before you can begin to grasp nuances of it and begin to use the various combos to deal maximum damage.  With some many classes one may think that the PvP would be unbalanced, and while some classes may be more uniquely qualified to deal with other classes and play styles, things are rather balanced.
Premium content for the game includes things such as increased storage, increased exp gain, or premium cosmetic items with slight bonuses that affect gameplay.  Most of the premium content that matters, the cosmetic avatar items and pets, can be bought and sold on the auction house or through personal trade, and usually the price is attainable through some grinding and patience.  The premium content makes things easier, but does not give a large edge in combot for those lacking funds, and you can have all the best premium gear without ever paying a dollar.  There are also constant events occuring which may allow access to some of the premium content.

Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory. Where do I begin?
For a game released in 2004, the graphics are simply fantastic. That's all that needs to be said.
The gameplay is, even by today's standards, in a league of its own. I love how the player is able to affect the course of the story in-game with simple, nifty features such as plenty of NPCs being able to give synopsises of the plot when you grab and interrogate them. Or how about at the beginning of every chapter when the game allows you to choose your load out: stealth for more non-lethal weapons such as the infamous sticky cams, choosing assault gives you heaps of ammo, but fewer non-lethal gizmos, but Redding's reccomendation gives you an even mix of both.
There is a lot of puzzle solving to be done, such as in a certain chapter when you have to use a captured enemy's "electric shadow" (very Sci-Fi) in order to pass through a laser-beam grid without triggering the alarms.
I struggle to think of any bad things about this game... Oh no, I have found one! It's too short! I was expecting the game to be at least three chapters longer than it is. But still, too much of something is too good... or bad... whatever.
Definitely reccomend this game to fans of stealth as this was one of the defining games of the defining franchise of stealth gaming. It's a real pity that the future Splinter Cells just simply weren't as good as the first three games, this being the third.

As long-term paper Magic fan, It pains me to see that this product is the only actual "magical" competitor to Hearthstone on the market.
Every design descision that differentiates "Duels" from from its predecessor - "Magic 2015" is straight up borrowed from the market's most succesful shark.
2 bucks for a 6-card pack for a 60 card deck? really?
No chat? Not even for a 2v2 gamemode? How dumb is that? There is literally NO way to communicate with your ally other than randomly spazzing your mouse over his cards in hopes that he takes the faint highlighting effect as a cue for what you want him to attack with.- Forget strategy!
_____
About "balance"
Amount of copies of certain card you can have in your deck is restricted by the card's RARITY.
Yes that's about the LAZIEST design descision you could possibly make in terms of balancing the cardpool.
"it's ok guys! Better cards are harder to come by and you can have fewer of them, so you would have a fewer chance of drawing imba all the time." - How about you actually try and create a balanced format that is fun to play?
I understand that big vanilla creatures that dont do anything are an important hurdle in new players understanding of power curve, but in my some few hundred hours on record I've never seen a Broodhunter Wurm hit the board across from me.. or Minotaur Abomination.. or Siege Mastodon.. or Canopy Gorger. This is not exactly a critical point though.
So far I've encoutered so many bugged cards that dont work as promised. They are absolutely broken and what little value they had in deckbuilding is being stripped away. And I dont even own half of the cardpool to have seen all the interactions! Who knows whats gonna happen when I start tapping allies! -probably nothing.
e.g. as of may(2016) :
Oh, and don't even get me started on the main phase autoskip. a descision in favor of speeding up the game and teaching new players about instants? oh rly..
_____
A LOT of what makes Magic the truly deep and fun game to dive into is being watered down in the game mechanics aimed at casuals, and what is preserved is being gimped even further.
If you're aiming at casual market with this game, which is what devs obviously do, then there is a problem: with this half-arsed attitude you will always lose to Hearstone.
Dont get me wrong, I generally dont like Hearthstone for what it is, but It will allways win just by the virtue of being a better game.
It's goofy, random, and intrinsicly silly, but it will NEVER trick you or lie to you. People cherish that trust and they leave when the game breaks it.
I don't know If "Duels" is being monitored, overseen and patched by just one dude somewhere in a dusty closet (if that's the case then good for him), but if wizards want to have any kind competitive edge on the market, they need to step up their goddam game!
This platform has the pontential to be so much more than it is now, and it has taken steps in right direction over the past year, but  its legs are crooked and it desperately needs HELP!
I just have to recommend the game. I do this with a guilty conscience, but It's the best we got and we deserve BETTER. If it does not come from above then we just have to push it from bellow.

Hitman: Absolution.
I absolutely love this game. If you have not tried any of the Hitman games, this basically refines and enhances the gameplay given to a whole new level. It's one of the few games I've played where I was able to play over the course of an entire weekend, and I'm still enthrawled to the Contracts, despite finishing the Campaign.
I love Hitman's functionality of stealth. The best feeling you can possibly get from this game is when you completely stealth an entire level without being caught and successfully sneaking either away or closer to your opponents. The functionality of assassinating people is amazing. You can kill your enemies in many creative ways. You can choke, snipe, explode or disintergrate your enemies in more than one way. You can even put sleeping pills in food, and collect evidence to gain an achievement called "Information is Power".
Hitman has quite an intense backstory involving a woman named Diana, a girl named Victoria and an evil jackass called Dexter,
I don't wish to spoil too much, as this is just a review, but, if you choose to read over the text, that's completely up to you.
Hitman has very interesting stories all taking place simultaneously. One revolves around the Agency and how they want to
. There is another group of scoundrels nicknamed "Hope". They are corrupt people who's only desire is to get money. They do not care for anything else, and are involved in with the main story as they try to
. Hitman 47 has the main plot-story, as you play as him. In the beginning, you work for the Agency, trying to
. The story then elaborates from there.
Hitman: Absolution becomes very dull after you finish the campaign, but I only like it more because of my bias look on Hitman games, as I love the stealth mechanics. I've always liked games to that extent. There is two gamemodes in the game, one of which is the campaign, and another gamemode called: "Contracts"
Hitman: Absolution has always been notorious for establishing contracts, which friends can play against each other to establish hits. There are certain conditions for each of the kills, whether you have to wear a certain outfit, or use a certain weapon. There are many things in this gamemode which prove difficulty to you as a player, whether you stealth or decimate everybody.
Do I recommend this?

What entertains and inspires me most is the way that players can choose to complete the objectives. 1. Upon deciding your playstyle, you can simply pull the trigger at the patrols and fight along the way to the target though it's much more violent and will decrease your score. If you are in favor of stealth, then you can knock down someone and take his clothes to disguise yourself. To test your limit, you can even give up disguise and try to approach the target during the patrol's break. 2. You can choose where to finish your task. Whether to kill him in his room, on his way to somewhere or on the spot where he's holding a meeting is up to you. 3. How do you kill him. Shoot him down, poison his meal, shoot the nearby explosives or push him through the window to create an accident.
This game is funniest when we are exploring different ways to play, but once we have played it again and again we would easily get bored. And that's when we should put it down and recall those best moments.

Think of this game as a MOBA, where everyone is already max level, has a full build of items, and are already positioned for a teamfight... This is where a match of BLC begins, and also where the similarities end. Because this game is so focused on the intensity and fast paced action of those teamfights, it goes above and beyond anything you've ever encountered before. Magic bolts flying everywhere, explosions all around you, split second juking and dodging, careful timing, focus, and precision.
Simple enough layout/gameplay that you can pick it up in 20 minutes.
But, a ridiculously high skill cap means you can always do better.
Top down, WASD to move. Each character has 6 basic abilities, 2 special abilties, 1 ultimate.
Every ability is a skillshot. You have to actually aim to hit things. Every time you hit things, you gain energy which can be spent to cast your special abilities for a small amount or your ultimate for a much larger amount.
It's free to play, and I can not recommend it enough. Funcom drove the playerbase into the ground, but they have since been removed, and the players have come back in droves. It only takes a minute for matchmaking to find people for a game now. (Perhaps longer for new players that have no in-game rating yet.)
In-game tournaments every other day (which cater to even low skill players, so everyone can join in!) with great rewards.
As a free to play, there's some things we have to cover:
Q1) How long does it take to grind a new character to play?
Less than any other f2p game I've ever played. Between a large daily coin boost pool, really short match times with high rewards, low cost characters in the shop, and two quests unlocking a character each for free, there's just no comparison. There are 27 characters to choose from, all free to play/try against bots before picking one up in-game.
Q2) How's the real world $ to in-game currency rate?
First, you can unlock every single character (all 27) for $20. So that's insane.
Second, those in-game tournaments reward you with coins for skin unlocks/etc. So that's awesome too. Third, the devs give out free skins/avatars/titles on holidays just for logging in, which is unheard of in f2p games. Otherwise, if you wanted to buy a cosmetic with regular cash, it has about the same going rate as other f2p's out on the market. So, there's lots of freebies and character unlocks are super cheap, but cosmetic items are of usual prices.

Crazy Machines is often overlooked "successor" to Incredible Machines, so to say. No, not officially, but it did delivered fun of same genre during years when there was no similiar game.
Even though it's not modern game, it still should run just fine, albeit not supporting widescreen resolution. it comes with two packs of puzzles (that you can pick in "Change Lab"), each having around 100 puzzles, with New Challenges coming out later and introducing new elements. There are also 3 music that you can choose in options, game repeating only one of them all time. Really, Game Music 3 is the best one, immeditly choose this, great upbeat melody.
No idea how and when New Challenges and two new music tracks came to be, maybe they were patched or came bundled with new version of the game... There is really no info on Internet on them. I only remember playing Russian version which lacked those, with different title screen. Professor, who's head pops randomly to give useless random phrase, was the best there. Biased. And yes, you can disable him in options too.
So yes, to those unfamiliar, each puzzle is about placing available elements on the level, testing and if it doesn't work, then you are off to replacing, either slightly tweaking position or completely changing whole plan. But where Incredible Machines had more of wacky elements, Crazy Machines gives you more of "realistical" set of items, like bucket and magnet. And, importanly, while doing so, it introduces a more advanced physics, more modern, being more complex than in Incredible Machines. And that is unique strong point of this game. Not to mentioning that it's always great to have more games in this genre, well-done ones at least.
You got usual physics, electricity, gravity (in New Challenges) and steam to handle. Great stuff. Setting is quite jolly too.
Yet the game isn't as perfect as I wanted it to be. There are a lot of situation where you have to place object pretty much pixel-perfect. Yes. Move that mouse slowly while holding button. Don't twitch. Test 100 times until it works.
And even then some of the puzzles are so out of the box... Well, no, it sounds like positive thing. What I meant, is that some puzzles have solution that appears like physics exploits. Example: in one of the level you have 3 conveyer belts to place, to somehow deliver a box on top of a platform that is way above. What is solution? Place two converyer belts together so the box will get stuck between them and with enough pixel-perfect placing it will roll around and somehow get shot out onto platform. Work of a genius!
Yes, after this you can never be sure if solution is something sane or not, making you want instead check walkthroughs.
I might go futher and just say that learning curve in this game is simply horrible and difficulty is uneven, not exactly always enjoyable... But I still like this game.
The game also allows you to create your own levels, fully. Using interface that may confuse for first impression. (How to put element into player inventory? Put element into level and then choose it and click on lock icon. Will not appear on level itself after this). But otherwise, you can do as much as normal levels can, setting up task too. Then you can save experiement and uhm, find a friend who playes this game too and maybe wants to try your thing, copying file to his computer. Or you can just set up many explosives to watch physics. Yes, no Steam Workshop support.
So, while Crazy Machines gives a good spin and has it's place in a genre, it has some flawed puzzles that worsen up whole offer and taste. Otherwise, ignoring them, I can recommend it. Just not whole-heartly.
P.S.  Also check out Crazy Machines 1.5 if you like this one,more of same. Quite good from what it appears. Because of the screwy way developers handled that "2-games-as-1" app, no one can review it. HA.

It's not really a moba. It's more of an arena. 2v2/3v3 in an enclosed colosseum, fighting it out for 2 min until one team dies or the circle closes in on you kinda like pubg circle. No exp, leveling or bosses to kill. I think there's a mode for that though, it's in beta and I haven't tried it myself.
(EDIT: Tried battlegrounds mode recently, this beta mode is what you would expect from a moba. Complete objectives around the map for points, once you get 100 points, you get to attack the enemy guardian. Rinse and repeat until it's dead. Queues are much longer than casual or ranked arena though. It generally takes 10-20 min to finish a match, unless each team just insta wipes the enemy group and vice versa each time.)
There's pve/vs ai mode, but it's restricted to 2v2 if you use queue. You would need a premade to access 3v3 ai mode.
Unlocking heroes is a bit grindy though. You only get about 10 coins during vs ai and around 20 vs players per game. Beginner heroes cost 1k, while newer heroes cost 4-6k. Dailies give only 100-200 coins. Most achievements give only lootboxes, and the lootboxes themselves don't help towards getting heroes. Leveling your account/heroes gives some coins, but that is very grindy as well and feels like there's no difference in exp rates no matter which mode you choose.
There's casual and ranked arena. The beta modes are casual only. Queues generally take about 1-3 minutes. 1 to get in, and another 1-2 for the servers to fill the remaining slots. This is while queueing in casual mode as a healer.
Haven't really had any technical issues with it so far. It has multiple servers, so you can just connect to the one closest to you.

With the current state of world politics, it's not hard to see how another world war could break out - and how an occupation of the United States could happen. That's the premise of Homefront, a story set in an American occupied by the united Korea, which had annexed most of Asia. A nice touch is the newspaper articles scattered around the maps which tell this story.
Gameplay-wise, Homefront has little difference from games released in the same time-frame, such as Call of Duty 4. The guns and mechanics are straightforward, aside from an interesting helicopter overwatch mission.
Where the game really shines is through its story. It follows Jackson, an Army pilot, who apparently refused to serve the Koreans. On his way to an internment camp, he is 'head-hunted' by the Resistance, who need a helicopter pilot for a wild scheme to steal Korean jet fuel to supply the US Army holed up in Sausalito, near San Francisco. During his journey, he journeys through a Korean internment camp, hides in a mass grave, and witnesses a faulty napalming.
Believably, the Resistance is always one step of disaster, as tragedy strikes their home base and they try to break out of Montrose, Colorado. Tensions are high and personalities clash. Their scheme is suitably hair-brained, but I felt the game could have made more of the conflicts between the more hot-headed Connor and the calmer Rianna. Similarly, I think they could have made more of Hopper's past - as a Korean-American, he experienced his share of tragedy, being persecuted both by the occupiers and the resentful Americans. However, the wrenching scenes of occupation and conflict are logical settings for the shooting action.
I got this game for free as part of the Humble Sale, so I can't say whether how much the game is worth, given that the main campaign is only around 5 hours long. I think it's worth playing sometime in your life, to experience a thoughtfully crafted image of occupied America.

Nights of Azure 2 is a very rough and an ill implemented game that tries to do way too much while giving the players two time constraints in a very short game that really erodes the overall experience. Given the game's demographic, the characters are decent enough. However, the gameplay has taken a huge hit. I did find some imporvements, such as the lily system's combat portion and the Striker Servans. However, I can't help but feel a lot of the other enjoyable aspects of the combat have not been carried over from the first game. The Servan system especially has been given an upgrade and a downgrade at the same time. Such as the point allocation, which is a step in the right direction but the "reincarnation" feature is a waste of time and could've been replaced with some other more useful mechanic.
As mentioned earlier, the biggest issue with Nights of Azure 2 are its time constraints, the hunt timer being one and the Azure Moon phases being the other. Now the Hunt timer is not that much of a hinderance but the moon phases are really annoying and often punishing, for trying to do the various tasks. Nights of Azure just had the hunt timer and had the moon phase progress with the story which was perfectly fine. Here, the phase progression feels as if it was added for the sake of it. Also the enemy variety of this game ,to be honest, is lacking and the one off bosses are disappointing as well.
So in conclusion, you're better off playing the first game. This game is a shallow, unwieldy successor and is best picked up during an -80% sale.

DFO, a great 2d beat'em up style game. It was released here previously, but nexon stopped hosting it a long time ago. It was brought back over here through the devs and I'm glad for this. I played during the alpha test and enjoyed it, and I will admit it being a bit different from the alpha shook me away, but I came back without a shred of regret.
Positives:
- Neat arcade art style.
- Great beat'em up gameplay.
- Good soundtrack. Has some great ones, and some.. questionable ones; still great.
- Alt friendly.
- Really good cash shop model.
- Balanced. Every class can actually hold their own ground. Yes, some are better than others but its tight enough.

- Tons of events, content added.
Negatives:
- Questline is a bit repetitive.

"Yeah, (I am) the real kind (of spy), not the tuxedo kind. I'm the kind that makes you bleed all over your Andretti unless you give me information."
Chaos Theory is a third-person stealth video game and the third installment in Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell series. It, again, puts you in the boots of NSA (and Third Echelon) special agent Sam Fisher as he undertakes missions around the world to avert the possibility of an all-out war between military superpowers.
The single-player campaign is divided into ten missions with locations ranging from the America's to East Asia. The game was released almost ten years back but it definitely holds well from a visual point of view. Missions usually take place at night (or in the dark) which probably help mask a few of the game's graphical deficiencies.
Chaos Theory has probably some of the best stealth mechanics in any game. A sliding light bar indicates whether Sam would be visible to the enemy or not while a noise bar shows how much noise is being produced as the protagonist moves around. Sam's pace of movement is tunable by scrolling the mouse-wheel, giving players a much greater control over how the character moves. Enemies can be sneaked upon from behind and knocked-out or put in the choke-hold to extract vital information. Apart from moving around in the shadows, the game provides you the option of traversing through vents, zip-lines, hang from ledges and overhead pipes; all the while avoiding enemy encounters.
The game is designed around stealth so players would experience gun fights to be clunky in nature. Apart from the usual arsenal of silenced pistol, sticky cameras. stun grenades and assault rifles, there's a very useful EMI feature that allows you to remotely disable lights and electronics temporarily. It helps a lot in moving around the environment unscathed. Hacking is a fundamental portion of the game. Computers, keypads and security terminals can be hacked, with the mechanic favouring those with quick reaction times. Multi-vision goggles are once again an essential part of gameplay with Sam able to alternate between night-vision, thermal and EMF modes.
The enemy AI is excellent with sentries coming to snoop around if they see open doors or turned-off lights. Enemies can also be distracted by whistling and flinging objects around the environment. Instances of direct combat are extremely rare but if such a scenario does crop up, enemies take cover and periodically change positions to improve their chances of winning gunfights.
The plot was interesting but not something that hasn't be done already or since. The script is well-written and character voice-overs are extremely well done (Michael Ironside ftw!). But I felt character interactions felt a bit too formal and serious. Mission briefs involve relevant characters droning off about mission objectives, although there's some fun banter between Sam and his handlers during missions; but that's few and far between. The game could've done with more cutscenes, in my opinion.
Chaos Theory is a definite recommendation if you're looking for a pure stealth experience. The SP campaign length is around 12-15 hours, subject to one's playing style of course. The game is definitely much much better than the p.o.s that was Splinter Cell: Conviction.

Not quite Project CARS levels of sim, but not arcade either. It's a bit more arcade than Forza, perhaps about Gran Turismo 6 level.
And it's pretty fun. The unique fun factor of this game resides in the fact that the objective is not usually to finish first, but at a decent position. The AI is much more competent and aggressive to compensate for this, meaning that instead of leading, you'll spend the bulk of the game doing "pack racing", negotiating every turn on the track with cars in front and behind you, and even next to you.
Combine this with the finely tuned arcade yet slightly realistic handling and you get all the thrills of competitive racing without too many sacrifices.
It isn't a substitute for a simulator on the level of Project CARS though. And ultimately that's what makes this game a pass: Project CARS is far too good. Unfortunately for this game, I'm just gonna go ahead and recommend that you skip a competent racing in favor of a truly outstanding, spectacular one.

I once would have recommended this game.
A little time away from the game and I come back to players killing my characters in one combo while I just can't seem to damage them, while the basics haven't changed the game has undergone some changes for the worse. Namely: the Gear Up system. By adding equipment with stat boosts two players using the same character are no longer on equal footing. Where before the game was entirely based on skill and tactics now having better equipment can give one player an honestly unfair advantage in what could otherwise be a fair contest. I'm not just condemning equipment entirely though; I'm specifically upset with the equipment that can only be bought with real money, equipment which is obviously better than anything you can unlock with in-game currency. That's right, Archeblade has become Pay-to-Win.
Equipment aside the game has many different characters and play styles, some are easy to pick up and play while others take time and dedication to get those combos down and truly pay off and when you can get into a match of evenly matched players it's honestly quite fun. Unfortunately there are also some pretty serious balance issues that were never solved; a pure melee character stands almost no chance against a sniper who can take half of your health in one shot, then run away and do it again. One character can even come back with full health after having been killed.
With nearly 20 hours of gameplay and earning mvp pretty consistently before, I don't think you can call it inexperience. This game could have really been something.

What a let down this game is.
The career mode has left the idea of creating your own team, aquiring your own cars and teamates out in favour of the 'offer system' which was a fund saving option every season in the original GRID. By doing this you no longer have any personal attachement to the team, the car or your teamate who btw always seem to suck. The Ravenwest team is your constant rivals while leveling up, always one tier above the rest of the AI.
And whats your reward once you've jumped through all the hoops of said leveling? Driving for them of course! The team you've been drilled to loathe is suddenly your employer and youre supposed to feel proud? honored? pfffff.....
The aquiring of cars and making your own livery is still present, but only in online modes.... which is divided between the challenges we know from previous iterations, sadly updated only weekly and only offering a single entry per class making buying a car kinda useless while starting out, since you'll most likely only be able to afford one car, the chances of getting to drive it are slim, since the challenge also needs to be for the right tier of vehicles.
Or you could go for the other online mode - forced matchmaking...or wait no you can't because no one plays that.
Mechanically the games is fine bar the rubberbanding which seems everpresent in all modes and the drifting which is horrible, gone are the linking up of high speed drifts from the original grid in favor of doing snail-paced burnouts while streering, easily doubling the score of the AI. In the race modes the AI are boring robots rarely doing anything out of the ordinary, no spin-outs, crashes or remarkable performances, every race will end with you first, then both Ravenwest drivers, then the rest of the field and lastly your teammate. It got so boring I spent and entire season just trying to run the Ravenwest drivers off the track... all i discovered was that the AI seem to have Scalectrix levels of front end grip.
There are two bright points in the game however - Open wheel classes which have a distinct feel of downforce and good pace, and the managing of tire conditions in the Endurance mode. The latter should have been expanded to all modes and the pit-stops from the old TOCA games should have been brought back and this game would have been more than it is which is an incredible beacon of mediocrity 5/10.

Gameplay
An improvement on the previous Nights of Azure game. The combat has more depth, meaning it’s not all button mashing. Game mechanics such as combos help add some variety during battles and therefore make the battles more interesting.
A lot of people don’t like the time limits on Gust games, however I have always found them to enhance the game by providing focus to the games plot. It not only makes the game more engaging, but it also adds a layer of difficulty that without might render the game boring.
While I enjoy Atelier games, the recent releases are an example of how boring a game can become without a time limit or a main quest line to provide a purpose to continue playing.
The attack combos, party members, breakable objects and time limits, story make this game enjoyable to play.
Sound
The game does not have an English dub, however it doesn’t need one, the Japanese voice acting is superb and there are few lines that are not voiced. The music is excellent which is standard for most Gust games, in my opinion the music in this game is among their best.
Story
The story follows a similar story to the last entry, but successfully manages to feel new and refreshing.
Waifus
Who doesn’t like waifus? The ones in this game are all top tier.

I recommend DFO to anyone to likes to play MMOs, for DFO is relaxing, exciting, and fair to all players, with no serious Pay 2 Win ruining the game.

This game was/is not much different then many other match 3 games except that you use characters to beat up other characters.
It was quite fun and a way to waste a few hours just battling it out.  But then they did a few changes which made it so that if you wanted to progress you had to do whats called grinding (for those that don't know, thats when you have to spend 5 or 6 hours playing just to keep up with others playing).  This made things less fun.
Now for the biggest change, if you have any characters that can heal the team during combat its called false healing.  Basically what happens is that while in a round, they will heal your characters, but soon as its done, any and all damage that was done to your character during a round gets applied to your characters, which means they will more then likely be instantly down and you have to wait somewhere between 3 and 14 hours for them to heal.
So now instead of being able to play for a couple of hours, you're lucky if you get in a couple of rounds that can last about 5 to 10 minutes at most and then you need to wait till the next day (least for those of us with families, work and who require sleep) to play for another 10 minutes and then wait.
They wanted to stop people from using their healing characters in story mode to heal their wounded characters and instead buy heath packs, which cost Hero Points which while they do come in game, they are very rare in game and they expect more people to buy Hero Points so they can buy health pack.  This has basically turned the game into pay 2 win game, well it was before but now its much worse.
The majority of people who play F2P games will never actually put money into free 2 play games.  Once it gets to the point where they are spending more then a few hours playing and not being able to keep up with their friends, they loose interest and leave, and start bad mouthing the game, which causes people not to go play that game, which means the game looses lots of money.
So for now I can not recommend this game.  Maybe if the devs wise up and actually listen to the community and things go back to how they were a couple of months ago, may I will start playing again and maybe even recommend this game, but lots of things have to change.

Steam says I have more than 2000 hours in the game, but the truth is it is mostly running on the background. I'd say 500 hours is much closer to reality.
Here is what you need to know about the game. It is a 3vs3 match where you bring a team of heroes/villains and try to win by making use of their abilities. You use them by spending the required resources (AP) which you get when you match tiles. The characters are divided in 4 tiers (1* - 4*) with only the 3* and very few of the 2* being useful at the moment. Most characters have 3 abilities, but there are some with only 2 because the developers have left them incomplete for months. The abilities can gain levels by buying or winning covers. The stats of the characters and the effectiveness of their abilities are increased as you level them with the use of ISO-8, an in-game currency used solely for leveling characters and buying boosts you can use in matches. The second currency is called HP (Hero Points) and is used to increase the size of your roster and to level abilities without the use of covers.
The good: Fast game / doesn't require too much thinking which makes it ideal for short gaming bursts / you get to use your favorite heroes / very simple rules.
The bad: Several incomplete characters with no plan to finish them in the near future / a turn from F2P to P2P since March 2014 / Inconvenient event end times for Europeans / success depends heavily on playing close the end of an event / several exploits are reported which allow cheaters to roam free in the game / market prices for in-game currency are the worst I have seen in a game.
Advices:
1. Use HP only to buy roster slots. At least until you have 30-35 slots. Never buy tokens (they give random covers). The % to get a specific 3* hero is less than 1% in most cases. You have better results if you level the abilities directly with HP.
2. Never use ISO-8 to buy 1* tokens. You will need it to level your heroes and it will always, ALWAYS be in short supply.
3. Always take part in Lightning Rounds since they are the most efficient source of ISO. Try to get to 100 points.
4. Don't max a 3* hero unless you have a diverse roster with at least 3-4 more heroes with levels 85+. When you do, the levels of the teams you fight will also increase a lot.
Epilogue: I will not tell how to spend your money, but you have to know that the game has made a turn into a more P2P model after March 2014. The changes in late June change how healing works in the game and restricts your ability to play since there is practically no way to heal heroes unless they have an innate regeneration ability. Heroes heal over time, but with most of them taking 2-4 hours to fully heal. healing packs are your only alternative and they cost HP which is relatively rare. The market prices are ridiculously unreasonable. To fully level a 3* hero you will need ~170k ISO which costs ~$300. The game is quite addictive so be warned. I would advice against letting young children play with it. I bet they can find better things to do and you should encourage them to spend their time doing something more creative. So do I recommend this game? After the changes in the last 2-3 months, I do not.

I originally recommended this game, but no longer do. The primary reason is that power creep makes it so that you can put in thousands of hours into the game, but still have a worse roster than someone who put in a fraction of that effort in the last 2-3 months. Unless you are willing to spend at least 6-8+ hours a day into a game like this, and at odd times, I don't recommend it.
Original review below.
===
This is quite a decent puzzle quest (match-3) setup with the additional backdrop of the Marvel universe. The biggest difference between this and a typical puzzle quest is the addition of timer counters, which trigger effects for either side. There is also the addition of standard attack and hp for each character, based on the color matched. This triggering difference leaves you trying to balance the matching of strong attacks with trying to get rid of opponents stronger timed attacks. Strategy wise, often you have to allow certain timed attacks to go off. Some pvp enemies also do not make moves at all, but attack only with timer counters.
Leveling is restricted by a character power level, based on the abilities of your hero and the level of those abilities, raised by an ingenious card system. These ability cards are won through missions, tournaments, and general pvp play. Of course the rarer character ability cards are hard to get and require many hours of investment.
There are 2 main types of currency, Iso-8 or xp (the common currency) for leveling up characters, and Hero points (rare currency) for gaining additional hero spots. Any other use of Hero points is mostly a waste. Honestly, the monetization is a little ridiculous. Iso-8  is not worth buying at all unless you are a pay to achieve kind of person. There is a huge temptation to buy Hero Points when you just need a few more to recruit the next hero.
Character balancing has been decent overall, though many characters are plain useless unless you manage to level them up, or they are temporarily 'iso' boosted for a tournament.
Overall, this is a great time-waster and quite addictive. I can't count the number of times where I was like, just one more game before I go to bed, even after 100 instances like that had already passed. I really have to quit playing this game. After one more round.

Jalopy is a very relaxing game set in the year 1990 about driving a communist-built East German car through the Soviet satellite states, finding and overcoming environmental and mechanical challenges along the way.
It's a Rogue-like, so the main goal is to get as far as you can go with the resources you have, and to try to have more resources at the start than you did last time.
The car in the game is the fictional Laika 601 Deluxe, which is heavily based on the real-world Trabant 601 Deluxe.
It's a classic East German car, and while it doesn't exactly have the best reputation, it has its share of enthusiasts who love it so. It defintely lends to the setting and the experiences in Jalopy.
If you're a classic car enthusiast - this game is for you!
I love this game a lot and have personally found quite an intimate relationship with my Laika - perhaps it'll be the same for you.
If you were thinking about trying out this game, you definitely should!

Another point and click cult classic. This game is more intended for children, as the game is very short, depending what you need to do and where to go.
This time you take a visit to Freddi and Luther's school house. A ghost is haunting the school and stealing kids toys in the process. Who is the ghost and will our fish heroine and silly sidesick capture it?
Just like The Case of the Missing Kelp Seeds, where you need to go and what you need to get is randomized at the start of the game. Need either a life preserver, rope, helmet, cork, a-very-wordy-device, trident, and/or a
pulley.
New characters to meet, with a reoccuring character, Ray the Stingray. Draw something on the school chalkboard, watch silly short clips in the theater, and keep Luther from that fishing hook! Stop and play a mini game of spitting at crabs on a walk wall and watch them fall on Lurther! Watch out for the coconut crab though, he'll bonk you.
You may face some backtracking, but it's possible to minimize it once you know what to do after a few playthroughs. Some of the soundtrack is rather catchy, like the save/load theme and a few track loops in the school.
Just like any H.E. game, there's sillyness to click on in each background scene that kids may find amusing.

As far as I can remember, this is the first time I've reviewed a game on Steam. That's not because I'm new to Steam. It's because this game holds a place in my heart that no game has before or since. And I've played many, many games.
Bloodline Champions is the purest PvP game that has ever been. It is so unique in that sense that there is literally no game out there like it. People will compare it to other games using terms like MOBA, which will invariably conjure images of massive maps with jungles, rivers, monsters and all the things that artificially infuse what we have come to think of as MOBA's with their complexity and depth.
But BLC doesn't need any of that. Its depth comes naturally, as a result of its actual complexity. BLC is what a MOBA should be: an arena in which players do battle--not one in which players level and shop and kill little monsters until they are ready to do battle. There is no avoiding battle in BLC. And when it happens, it's determined entirely by the skill of the player on the keyboard.
There is a lot to say about BLC. Perhaps, the most important thing to say is that it's a shame that one of the worst game publishers in existence got its hands on what you can tell is the work of a passionate development team. But I'm eccstatic to see what appears to be a revival now that Stunlock has taken it back.
In the mean time, if you are reading this and thinking about playing Bloodline Champions, this player couldn't possibly give a more sincere endorsement. If you like PvP, you absolutely must try BLC.

A super short indie pixel plattformer with shooter elements. We follow Wryn, a young pink haired girl who wants to become the greatest hero ever. Doing so, she must first eliminate the top list of the greatest heros of all time, which include a fat purple blob, a robot ball, worms and so on. That is basically the story in this case, nothing more, nothing less. I was kinda let down finding this out, but considering the games overall lenght, it was kinda predictable in the end. Must mean, the game focuses more in terms of gameplay. Well, sorta.
Basically, you use the mouse to aim your guns, the WASD keys to move and space to jump, standard stuff. However, you also have a "bullettime" button on Shift, a very useful tool in this game. The game slows down, also zooms in on the character a bit but still letting you see alot whats going on around you, which is very usefull since the game tends to throw dozens of projectiles at once at you. Wryn also is capable of a "triple dash", which you can perform after jumping and is used for dodging. Combined with her wall jumps (wich work very well in my opinion) this can lead to some pretty tricky maneuvers and helps keeping the game fast paced (even with bullet time, which can be drained very easily).
As for the guns, i found most of them not that usefull to downright completely useless, and usually stuck with the standard dual machine guns and the flame thrower. Because of that, anything that wasn't these two weapons, felt really unsatisfying and unhandy to use.
Difficulty wise this game is ok. Normal is what you expect. In Story mode if you die in a stage, you usually just respawn earlier in the stage, with some Point loss i believe. Wryn isn't really robust but she still can take a few hits, so it's fair in my book if you take the overall gameplay in retrospectiv.
The graphics were my biggest dislike about the game. I just can't stand these sprites. Wryn and her rival look atrocious, enemies and bosses look basic as hell and the overall looks of the levels don't impress me either. As for the level design itself, it's average. They are all fairly short, most of the time containing a mini boss, an element new to the prior stages and (of course) a different theme. For what they are doing they are alright, allthough they had no real depth to it, which i missed highly here.
It is difficult to say how i really felt the entirety of this game. Some part of me enjoyed it, some other part thought it was pretty dull and the most mediocre thing in a long while, lack of story didn't help either.
I guess for that price it is an ok game. Next to the Story mode there is also an Arcade mode, some things to unlock and a boss battle mode, so there should be more time after. If you are fan of Jumpers with shooting elements give it a go. or stick to better alternatives. Like Metal Slug. Yes.

BLC is an awesome game and you should try it, but it used to be more awesome and I'd like to bring that back with your help.
BLC, BLC, where do I start with you?
I played this game from very early on, back when the game was brand spanking new and advertised as the one true PvP arena game where only skill mattered. The one game you could pick up and play without having to spend several weeks of grinding for levels or runes/masteries in order to actually start being competitive. In theory, a team of new players who were just completely at home with the game as soon as they started could beat a top competitive team who had played the game religiously half a year in advance.
And it was glorious.
Of course such a situation rarely happened. Since skill was all that mattered, veteran players were almost always set to win over newcomers, but it was as it should be. Those moments where I as a relatively new player were able to out-manouver players who were obviously better than me are memorable even to this day. The free Bloodline rotation was satisfactory and the fact that you could try them all out in single player vs bots is something I for my life cannot understand why every single F2P online game has done as well. That particular move is a stroke of genious.
Every Bloodline feels and plays differently. The only time it feels bad playing a particular Bloodline is when you're being outperformed by another which leads you to wanting to try that one instead. That is the beauty of the game. Nothing stops you from learning every single Bloodline in comfort and privacy against bots. No fees, no need to purchase the Bloodline. This means that if you were willing to put time and effort into learning the Bloodlines in-and-outs, you could prepare yourself to stand an even better chance when playing against real people. And really, Hard mode bots are way more difficult than many players!
There's practically always been a leveling system. Your level, however, was mostly just a measure of how long you've been playing the game. It had no impact on the game what so ever. What really mattered was your rank, which showed at what skill level you belonged (again, skill was all that mattered as advertised). It's important to note that at this time, it was also advertised that you could obtain most every single thing in the shop, even cosmetic items like skins, weapons and emotes, with the use of Blood Coins as well as Gold Coins, the former being the currency you earn by playing and the latter being the one you purchase with real money. Sure, the Blood Coin prices were discouragingly steep, but it really helped me customizing my one favorite Bloodline (Psychopomp btw) with some cool, non-standard gear and emotes.
The only few items that were only purchasable with Gold Coins at this time was things like the Replay system that only very serious and competitive player had any real use for.
Every single thing with this game, at that time, was geared toward easing newer players into this awesome community and experience. Stunlock knew in their heart that few people would start the process of grinding another game for points, levels, masteries and runes in order to be competitive when they've most likely invested their time heavily in other games. What they did, supplying a theoretically even playing field for new and veteran players alike, was game design ingenuity pure and simple.
FunCom however never had that much faith in the game, and it was horribly undermarketed. This is a story most of us familiar with BLC before Steam know of.
The fact of the matter is that when Stunlock introduced traits, medallions and masteries into the game, they deviated from their very own core design philosophy. When this new system, trait points unlocked by leveling and heavy Blood Coin investments in crystals and medallions hit Live, they lost a capital h Huge part of the loyal playerbase. The game, suddenly, wasn't new player-friendly anymore. Because when you tried to introduce your friends into the game in this state, all they saw was another huge time sink they had to fill in order to even have a chance. Skill was still central to the gameplay, of course, but the entire sight of the traits and nigh-mandatory medallions that you had to fill was daunting and off-putting. Suddenly, BLC seemed to be on the way of becoming every single other PvP game by mimicking the competition, when its one biggest appeal was its differences from them.
"I'd rather just keep playing League, cba BLC grinding", many of my friends said.
Combined with the much smaller player base, the Match Making system were acting strangely. There simply weren't enough players so uneven matches like 3 boneys (lowest grade) vs 2 doubleskullies (grade 5) 1 friggin Arbitrator (grade 16) wasn't an uncommon sight. Thus, even the gameplay suffered.
One would think such an immense community outrage and hit to the entire game's ecosystem would make the developers falling over themselves trying to roll back their newly introduced system. I don't know if FunCom advised them against it or if it was pride messing with them, but the system stayed. Its still there, despite the fact that it single handedly "killed" the game overnight. Well, the release of the Grimrog Bloodline, which was morbidly OP at launch, also played a role of course.
The release from FunCom made me feel hopeful. Maybe they could finally start moving back toward their roots, I thought.
Sure, there are more players now. Probably brought on by the recent media coverage the game's been getting with this step. The level-dependent traits were still there to my disappointment, but I could live with it. I still have my old medallions and gems. I also noted that I have a small size of Blood Coins and a couple of hundred Gold Coins left over. I entered the market place to refresh my mind on what things cost.
What met me there turned me off a lot.
Another core design philosophy had gone down the grave, the one where you were supposed to be able to earn everything with Blood Coins. Every single cosmetic item have had their Blood Coin price removed and were now only obtainable with Gold Coins, i.e. real money.
This may not sound like a big deal to those of you who didn't play the game before it was this way, but it really just gives me the impression that Stunlock is in it for the money and wants to do what everyone else is doing and milk the game before it dies off completely. Sure, I guess the system is fair compared to other games, but it really just feels like they're taking their design decisions without feel for what the game has come to symbolize: a realistic alternative game that you can play alongside others without having to spend a huge amount of time in order to start being competitive.
I had absolutely no trouble recruiting friends to this game before the trait and medallion system. When they were bored of playing other games, they'd say "Hey let's fire up BLC", I'd gladly oblige. They didn't hesitate buying Gold Coins (at that time called FunCom Coins I believe...) because it just felt awesome customizing your favorite Bloodline when at the same time feeling you had an alternative if you didn't want to spend the money. That's the exact kind of business plan we all wanted to support.
Gameplay? Jesus christ, I love
, it's lovely in its simplicity, its "easy to learn, hard to master" way. But if you find that you like this game as much as I do and want to spend more time, please, engage yourself in the community at its subreddit (r/bloodlinechampions) and
. Stunlock Studios are finally in position to make this game
again. Help us make them understand we want that too. Help us make them understand that we want the even playing field between new and veteran players back.

You play an armored, mutant hulk called a "Big Daddy" fighting mutant gangsters in an underwater, post-apocalyptic, diesel-punk city. You collect a number of upgradeable guns and mutant abilities throughout the game. Abilities such as ice, fire, lighting, and bee throwing. Also telekinesis.
There is a basic morality system based on "live and let live" that changes the ending. Most of the bosses throughout the game can be spared. There are also small mutant girls guarded by other armored mutants that you can harvest and murder for extra upgrade points, or spare for less tangible benefits.
Some prominent criticisms of this game is that it does nothing to distinguish itself from the first one, and is therefore a cash grab. I disagree. I think Bioshock 2 is an excellent counterpoint to the first game, from the narrative to the gameplay.
The first game is much like a survival horror, in which the protagonist Jack is essentially a normal guy facing off with superpowered mutants. The second game is much more empowering, as the Big Daddy is much more resilient if less agile. The weapons types, such as the drill and bolt gun, have a much different impact on the gameplay and coincide with certain powers. For instance, I made a build that would freeze enemies solid with the ice power then shatter them with my giant drill in an instant.
Storywise, the first game is about fallen paradise ruined by the flaws of its extreme right-wing objectivist ideology. The second game addresses the follies of extreme left-wing utopianism as the socialist villain seeks to completely obliterate the sense of self along with all of the survivors.
The first game is about a protagonist who SPOILERS believes to be a free individual making his own choices but discovers that he is actually a brain-washed pawn following orders (a meta commentary on in-game objectives), thus illustrating free will as an illusion. END SPOILERS.
The second game features a protagonist that expressly has no free will from the get-go, and must follow orders. In spite of this, no matter how specific the order, the protagonist still finds ways to make his choices his own, whether to spare or kill in-game opponents and mutant girls (a commentary on in-game choice), thus revealing the impossibility of free will as an illusion.
The DLC, Minerva's Den, is the best of any game in my opinion, and continues with these themes. It has layers of twists that add to the depth of the story and contribute to the philosophical points made, as well as adding new weapons and abilities that enhance the gameplay, like lasers and black hole grenades.
Essentially, Bioshock 2 is a must own for fans of the first.

Con Update: Appears to be a big bug during second playthrough that doesn't get rid of the timer. Despite that I was able to get all the lillies done apart from Eleanor, because ♥♥♥♥ that character.
I've never written a review before, but I adored the first game and enjoyed this one. So here goes.
Pros:
- ran perfectly for me, no port issues here
- great music
- enjoyable atmosphere
- easy-to-learn combat
- variety in companions
- time limit gameplay
Cons:
- Limited variety in enemies
- Only six stages
- Short first playthrough
- Tedious sub-quests
- Awful boss battles
- Lacks many qualities the first game had
So, my biggest gripes about this game was the enemy variety and the boss battles. I'll talk about enemy variety shortly. You basically have a few types. Small floating enemies, standard two-legged enemies, bigger two-legged enemies, and harpies. That's it. You'll get variations of those enemies throughout the game, mostly using the same animations even. When you compare that roster to the first game? It's disappointing.
Boss fights were just terrible. One boss fight wasn't even really a fight, all you had to do was click on six mirrors, hit a head that won't even fight back several times, and you're done. I kept thinking "The real fight will surely start now!" but it didn't. One boss who uses a single attack showed up -twice-, one was so buggy it clipped into a wall and died, and another had you stand stationary and waiting for it to throw projectiles so you -might- knock them back at them. The only boss fight I enjoyed was the final one and the fights against individuals.
Compared to the first game I felt there were a lot of qualities missing too. Like how one of the assumedly main characters took a back-seat for the entire main quest line while a secondary ended up getting more screentime instead, which I didn't mind since I preferred that secondary character anyway. I also missed how calm and comfy the first game was, with its pleasant hotel atmosphere, its music, and the altar where you levelled up. That's not to say NoA2 isn't comfy with atmosphere, it can be at times, just a lot less than the first game was.
On that comparison I'd like to add that while a larger roster of female companions is appreciated, I feel it took away the magic that the single one had in the previous title. I felt like there was no true progression with the companions simply because of how many there were.
With the plus side though, the music is just as good as the first one was. The combat was also enjoyable, as well as using companions and how they changed the approach you took to fighting. The limited time with other weapons was somewhat annoying though, and I discovered that a max-evolved pheonix that can turn into a greatsword broke the entire game, as when fully charged with fire that greatsword can three-shot most bosses and one-shot every enemy. Though that made the more tedious parts of the game less so.
The time limit seems to be a point of controversy for most people, but personally I enjoyed it. The limit isn't so brutal that you constantly feel pressured, but more that it encourages you to make the most of your in-game days, it encoruages you to be efficient. I always checked which sub-quest I needed to do, and what zone I needed to do it in before checking which companion also had a quest in that zone. I never missed a single sub-quest in my first playthrough, though it was impossible to max every companion. But thankfully if 100% is your thing, the second playthrough does away with the timer. The in-level timer was barely noticable.
Overall I think that this game lacks the passion the first had. I'm not sure why that is, but certain small details and qualities were just completely absent this time around.
Is it worth the pricetag? No.
Is it worth it for a Gust fan who enjoyed the first game? I'd say yes, if only to support this kind of game for the future and hope that if there is a third installment it gets the love from the development team that the first game had.

The game is still relatively smooth and playable despite the low fps as long as you play the game in fullscreen (windowed mode is all sorts of terrible).
This is a relatively simple action rpg best enjoyed for its art and atmosphere rather than gameplay.  The austere, old-fashioned decorations of the hotel and the Victorian-esque street scenes go nicely with a lot of piano background music and JRPG style rock for the battles.  The enemies are a sort of gothic horror theme and some of your allies/enemies look like bisque dolls in frilly dresses.
Fighting is based on two button combos.  You have a primary weapon and can equip servans that allow you to use other weapons by draining their mana.  Other servans provide skills like breathing fire and/or bypassing map obstacles.  Since you can only equip two at a time (along with a NPC partner), you will have to return to maps many times to fully explore them and find treasures and servans.  The game makes this slightly stressful by having a mission deployment timer that results in game over if you do not find a door and teleport back to base before it ends.  Additionally, you can only deploy a certain number of times per chapter.  Some may find these time pressure mechanics to not be very fun.
This game adds a costume system for the main characters that the first game lacked, including rather exotic swimsuit designs.

Bottom Line: Battlerite isn't without flaws but the game rewards player skill and gives satisfaction of learning the ins and outs of your favorite characters.
Pros:
Character Lineup: Immediately appealing was the cast of characters. Some, such as Jade and Raigon, are simply trope staples for any fighting game genre. Then you have Ezmo, an imp who stole the soul of the warlock that summoned him. Or Thorn, a living, nightmare forest. A varied cast means there's almost guaranteed to be a character you enjoy.
Controls: Game is quick to pick up but very hard to master the combos for your character.
Combat: The game does a fantastic job of forcing you to fight over the center of the map. An orb that spawns in the center heals your team, a valuable resoure in the game, and eventually after 2 minutes a death vortex will start closing in and making the playing field smaller and smaller.
Cons:
Balance: Not far enough into the game but there are certain heroes COUGHraigonCOUGH that I almost always dread fighting. Its not bad enough to not play, but there are a few heroes that feel very inneffective and some that feel that there's no punishment to play them.
Community: So far, the bad has outweighed the good. The game needs more players and berating players for playing poorly in the non-competitive mode is a surefire way to turn off people. "ggez" and similar taunts are common.

,,,if this is designed to be kid-friendly, it features some of the worst difficulty design of any game I've ever seen.
It plays like One Day For Ched for Kids with some incredibly awful weapon physics.
However, if the 'kid-friendly' was meant as a troll & it was meant to be either a hardcore shooter or a inobvious rage game then it worked.
If 'One Day For Ched for Kids' doesn't make sense, good, you may have wasted less of your life than I have; here is that sentiment but in list form.
Positives:
- The environments were fine.
- The sound was annoying but appropriately spoopy.
- The second weapon you get is a skull with spinal cord which fires cannonballs & alternate fires a cluster of jiggly ghost skulls, this is the biggest plus in the game. I was also managing to hit enemies on the other side of walls with this, don't know if that was by design.
Negatives (this one got updated after playing this for another hour...the positives did not):
[FEATURE REMOVED] - Tried to use the 'Watch Intro' button, the first 3 times it played the first 3 seconds & then went back to then menu; the 4th time it played the whole way through. The cutscene was fine, it made an attempt at threading a story although the "Egypt" world boss is shown on top of a castle which is a different level set; that is just me being nitpicky, it is mainly the 4 times to watch it once that makes it a negative.
[PATCHED] - Not that the games has Settings or Options from the ESC menu, but in-game, if you spawn into a level & press ESC (at least in the "Egypt" maze level) all of the skeleton & mummy enemies will get sucked through the walls of the level & mash up against the player. Oddly, not all the enemies get clipped through the level, the wobbly scarabs & the ghosts stayed in place.
This isn't really positive or negative, just never seen it before in any game ever.
[PATCHED] - Maze Mode will (maybe unintentionally) randomly generate a hedgemaze of the 5 times I loaded it, 3 times it didn't have an entrance & the other 2 times it was one corridor, an open field & the house with the candy dish which is the ending trigger. Dreadful.
- Pumpkin Patch (the Bonus Mode) is a sandbox with all the assets of the game scattered around the map & a hedge maze, so you can make your own map I guess.
- Enemies don't have useful audio cues, so you get snuck up on lots.
- You can't look all the way up (I'm assuming going by player shadows that this is because you are an outline of one of the ghosts in Pac-Man, so you can't look up because you don't have a neck) & this makes dealing with flying enemies & enemies firing through the floors above you, an annoying chore.
[PARTIAL FIX] - You get swarmed.
[PARTIAL FIX] - Some enemy types & bosses seem to have nonsense amounts of health & deal too much damage (if this is kid-friendly). I say partial fix because you're often swarmed so it is hard to tell how much damage one-on-one enemies deal, you either get mullered or you take 5-10 damage from an encounter, it is all quite strange, but not like spooky.
- The giant Egypt labyrinth where you collect at least four keys & then have to do first person platforming (where you stick to edges of platforms if you're too close) is an awful experience because labyrinth levels aren't very fun at all.
[UPDATED:
Figured out why I hated this so much the first time (I still hate it but this might help you fix why).
The level is a horrible-to-navigate maze in a game with no minimap, where you have to find keys to open the Scarab doors to progress, but when you touch the key, it automatically opens the Scarab Door, so unless you
A) find it before the key & then B) memorise the directions you take between the locked door & where you eventually find the key, it is then more aimless wandering until you get ambushed by the silent minions of this devious Witch.
If you insist on having players pick up keys; let them open the doors then at least they can stumble across that as a point of navigation.]

[PATCHED] - Weapons have nonsense physics (assuming a Candy Corn Blunderbuss should have conventional weapon physics).
- The level with the elevators up to what I assume is the final boss is actually not a bad design (in theory), in this game though (well, I annotated a bunch of screenshots for why) but it is a combination of the elevators are poorly designed, enemies shoot through the floor & while you can too, because you can't actually look all the way up then you can't actually hit them.
Many of the projectiles wizzing through the floor as you go up the ramps don't actually seem to hit you and do damage, it could be that they are just missing or the intention is that these are just meant as the illusion of traps but it just looks awful because it is ghost cannonballs whipping at you.
Also, this level is just more corridors where the flood of assets get wedged & try & walk all over one another because whatever the attempt at AI pathing, there are too many of them so it looks comical but not in a good way.
In summary, it isn't the worst thing I've played, but that is probably more a commentary on how I spend my time rather than the quality of this game. It suffers from confusing & poor design choice OR worked fine depending on if it's a troll or not. [I've now put in nearly 3 hours in this game & I'm still not sure; the Developers has said there is a patch coming for things brought up in early reviews; don't know if they're talking about me, but I guess I'll wait & see].
