Chaos Theroy is both over rated and severly dated (Coming from someone who grew up with far older titles I think that says something) and if your wondering if you should buy the game you might notice that all the positive reviews say it's great without explaining why. The story is a Call of Duty esque snore and the stealth is simplistic and boring but I must reluctantly say since there's a lot of freedom in how you deal with enemies (Kill or do not kill) or for how you can screw up it's still a video game (Take that for what you will).
The AI springs between aimbot accuracy, sloth like, and just plain blind and or stupid. Unlike the console versions you can actually see whats going on as the PS2 and original Xbox version suffer from pitch blackness gamma syndrome even with the goggles or turning up your TV's brightness settings all the way. The graphics get the job done in regards to the world but the character models are frankly attrocious and suffer from pre next gen Ubisoft graphics with the enemy models looking especially bad (Barely better than Max Payne's) what with their mouths being green. The character models and blurry badly animated CGI make the game look even older than most PS2 games. Hell for 2005 it wasn't even the best stealth game. I think that title goes to Metal Gear Solid 3: Subsistance which was the re release of the 2004 original on weaker hardware that added a free thirdperson camera which is embarrassing considering that this Splinter Cell has better hardware than MGS 3 to work with on the Gamecube and Xbox Original and of course the PC.
The real issue is it's terrible controls and awkward bindings for mouse and keyboard. The console controls were already wonky (And thats coming from someone who's used tank controls, pressure sensitive controls and motion controls.) but here on the PC both options control as if you were drunk. It's controls are harder to understand and get a grip on than any of the Arma titles and yes that extends to Operation Flashpoint/Cold War Assault. You name it and it will probably control better than Chaos Theroy (Middle mouse to aim, shft to jump?). At least you can rebind some of the conrols (The mouse wheel effecting your speed is interesting albiet flawed). If your excuse is "bad controls incentivise sneaking or avoiding combat" than every stealth game prior or afterwards would like to have a word with you.
It's a mediocre third person shooter disguised as a stealth game with that aspect only just barely being above average and with the latter being primarily in focus. It's voice acting (Other than the gaurds), music, SOME of the level design, COOP and lack of Uplay are the only thing that salvages it from being total♥♥♥♥♥♥in my eyes. Even then the COOP is capped at 35 FPS for some bizarre reason and its hard to even get it working. If you like scanning crates and bad spanish accents this is the game for you. If you like stealth try anything else (Might I suggest Hitman: Blood Money or Theif?).
I don't usually do numbered score but I give Splinter Cell: Chaos Theroy a 3/5 or a 4 out of 10.

As far as casual games go, this one is pretty epic in it's time-consuming...ness. I enjoy it quite a bit, but I've always been a fan of puzzle games, not excluding the 'match 3' genre. This one isn't as in-depth as say... Puzzle Quest 2 which is made by a totally different company, but I think there's still enough there if you want something more than Bejewelled. I think the best part is figuring out which heroes/villains work the best together and trying to build up their combos and such.
As far as downsides go, I really don't like the weak AI, the randomness of drops and the money for power aspect. I'll go into each point by point here.
The only real challenge comes from the level of your opponent, which determines how much HP they have and damage they do. When it comes to the actual gameplay, you can easily predict what they're going to do as they have certain priorities. They definitely play worse than a thinking person would. I would like it more if they made better decisions, as frustrating as that could be.
As far as getting loot goes, you have very little control over what you get. Essentially you do different missions, most of which have four rewards. The first time you beat a mission, you're guaranteed one of them. Typically, you'll get ISO (the game's main currency) Hero Coins (the game's premium currency), heroes or random hero tokens, or boosts. Each time you repeat the mission, you'll have a chance to get a reward that you haven't already received or 20 ISO (which is a tiny tiny amount) This does get frustrating after a while, especially if you're trying to get a specific reward. Now, in order to get more characters, you need to either complete certain missions, trade in recruit tokens of varying quality or progress/place well enough in events (there's usually something going on every day). The problem here is with the tokens. Some guarantee a certain quality of hero, but it's still random since if there's a character you want, there's next to no guarantee you'll get them. They break down the odds on their website, but it doesn't really help. But that's not the worst thing.
The worst thing is of course the bane of most free-to-play games. Paying for power. You can buy two things: ISO and Hero coins, the two currencies of the game. ISO is used to level up your characters and buy more low-quality ones. Coins allow you to buy more recruit tokens of higher quality, level up hero powers, (which aside from their actual effects, allow you to raise the character level higher) protect your characters in PvP mode (>:| ) but most importantly, buy more slots for characters. That last one is really frustrating, because you can only increase your character slots with coins, and if you don't want to spend money, you're going to have to inevitably pass up on recruiting certain characters, or get rid of ones you've progressed on in order to get new ones simply because if you don't buy coins, it's a hell of a grind to get more. The worst of the worst is that the coins/ISO are really expensive for your dollar, and I think don't really give you proper value. If you want to make this one of the only games you play it might be acceptable, but if you want to just play casually, I highly recommend not spending the money on it.
Myself, I've put in a fair amount of time, so I begrudgingly purchased some coins to help open up some space for more characters on both my steam account and my iPad. ~sigh~
Anyways, if you can overlook all the shortcomings, it's still a fun puzzle game, and you CAN get by without dropping any of your hard-earned cash on it. I recommend giving it a try if you're into the genre at all, especially considering it IS free.

First off, this is my favorite game of all time. I've had it for a long time in physical format, but due to it's drm it's unplayable on modern systems, so I bought the steam version. I was a bit afraid of how it would run based on some of the reviews that have reported problems, so I was ready to issue a steam refund just in case.
So here's the score: this game is flawless. I've seen some negative reviews and let me address some of them. First of all, all those who say it's unplayable with keyboard and mouse are idiots, no two ways about it. You control your speed via the mouse wheel. It's that simple. Besides, you can customize the controls to your heart's content. Second off, no, it doesn't have checkpoints. And you know why? Because it doesn't need them! It has a quicksave function! I swear, some people...
How about the game itself? It's the best stealth game of all time. Period. You have full feedback of how much noise you make and how much noise is in the environment, how visible you are, you get a lot of tools for dispatching or distracting your enemies, you have nightvision, thermal vision and even "electric" vision that let's you see objects that use electricity (useful when completing some of the objectives). It has a fairly intelligent AI. The game is a bit too easy if you just kill everyone in my opinion but it's damn fun. If you like the suspense of stealth, look no further.
The graphics still hold up to this day in my opinion. Some of the round objects are a bit angular, but it doesn't take me out of the experience, and the textures still look great. There's also a surprising ammount of color that, compared to a lot of modern games, are a breath of fresh air. The sound design is superb and the soundtrack just ups the suspense. The music is low key and dynamic, changing to the gameplay.
Some of the writing is a bit too convoluted for me. Don't get me wrong, it's good, but it's hard to follow, especially for the first time playing. You really have to invest your brain into the story or you'll get lost in it.
All in all, if you even remotely like stealth games don't you dare miss out on this one.

To be fair, this is a nice idea for a game with an okayish execution, but in the end there are just too many negative aspects that made me stop playing this.
I like the atmosphere, the way you have to look after your vehicle and interact with it and like I said, the general idea of the game. It really feels very nostalgic and captures that period of time very well.
But pretty much everything else is done quite poorly. I don't mind the art style and the graphics in general, but there is a huge lack of detail and variety that desturbs the overall impression. Especially the cities are very small, use the same buildings over and over again and don't feel like an actual city. The landscape is very boring, using the exact same roundabouts, exits and gas stations over and over aswell. This made me feel that I'd pretty much seen everything there was to see after my first hour of gameplay.
There are also quite a few german spelling mistakes in the beginning (you start in Berlin and head to Dresden) which is unneccessary and could easily be fixed (f.e. you should be able to add an "ü" wherever it is needed, even though this letter doesn't exist in the english language).
The trailer gave me the impression that Jalopy is more or less open world and you can drive whereever you want and create your own journey. That isn't quite the case. In fact you can usually choose from 3 different routes before you start your trip, twice the same route with different weather and a longer route. Apart from that, all you can do is just drive forward (or backwards again), there isn't much to discover or if there is, it's put right in front of your nose. Also, the trips from town to town are VERY short! An average drive from city to city (without stopping for spare car parts) which is presented as an entire day in game, will take about 4-5 minutes. Ingame time flies by and I was hoping for way longer drives with an interesting countryside.
Another annoying feature is, that whenever your uncle talks (you can't hear a voice, he's just mumbling) you can't interact with your car apart from driving with W, A, S and D. You have to click the left mouse button first to make the text disappear and if he keeps talking, you have to do it again till he stops talking.
The car part and consumable management part is fun in general, but because ingame time flies by so fast you can't drive for more than a couple of minutes without fixing or changing something. I totally get that this is part of the game, but the overall time for everything in this game should take way longer. This is, to me, the biggest issue of Jalopy, because you never get to "just drive" and it doesn't feel like you're on a journey across the Eastern bloc. It rather feels like you're driving your uncle around the block for some grocery shopping.
I also encountered a lot of bugs and glitches, but I try to leave these out of this review because the devs are still actively working on this and its not a finished game as of now.
You might think that because Jalopy is still in Early Access there will be more to come, roadtrips might take longer in the future and there will be more to discover in general. But the current build is 0.94 and as far as I know the devs are only fixing bugs and glitches before leaving Early Access and that's why I'll pass on this one. It's still something special in its own way and kind of a shame it has these many issues.

When I was still new to Steam, I ran across Big Pharma on sale and thought "okay, looks interesting, I'll get it." Paid my money, downloaded my copy, and...well...forgot about it. Then, a day or so ago, I decided to give it a try after all.
I really wish I'd done so earlier.
Okay, so here's the deal. Big Pharma is part business sim, part process puzzle. It's important that you recognize this duality, because unless you like both, you may not enjoy yourself. Pure business sims like Capitalism of days gone by focus on acquisition of materials, production of product, marketing and sales, but they ignore the mechanics of actually making those products; it's a black box where inputs go in and outputs come out. On the flip side, process puzzles like Space Chem (which I truly enjoy) or Factorio place the emphasis on how you're going to make something and naught else. Big Pharma is what you get when you combine those two. Maybe a little heavy on the process side. In BiPh, you're running a pharmaceutical plant (surprise, right?) and you need to make useful products. You'll be adjusting concentrations to activate and deactivate ingredients' properties, purifying compounds, combining ingredients, and basically performing gymnastics to produce a drug that will, for example, treat angina without having your patients firing diarrhea all over the place or something even worse.
The nifty bit is that you can be a ruthless pharmaschmuck who doesn't really care about the product so long as it makes money. If you're content to market a painkiller that causes nightmares, swelling, and anal leakage, you can. But you can also go the three extra miles to make a drug that cures Alzheimer's, is fast-acting, and non-drowsy. It's all down to A) how you want to run the business, and B) how creative you can be in getting your production lines to work. You need to feed your inputs into specific machinery in specific orders to do what you want, and that means that you're also playing a path puzzle game. BiPh is three games in one tidy, creative, attractive package.
Graphics are good, plenty good for the purpose, and even include customization options. Play is as flexible as you want to be, as detailed and difficult as you want it to be. Replay value? You bet; you'll learn something new all the time, mostly better ways to do the same thing. Music is enjoyable. And perhaps most importantly - it's fun.
Plus, they were good enough to include a Freebuild mode, so you can experiment to your heart's content. Major plus in my book.
As for negatives, there are very few, mainly orbiting the sphere of "not-quite-intuitive." There will be times where you set up a complex production line that SHOULD be producing the Wonderdrug Of All Time but is instead turning out what amounts to Kool-Aid. Then you'll find out you had a mixer set backwards and it was combining inputs wrong. And you'll get annoyed and have to purge the line before getting things going again. But some philosophers argue that frustrations are the lessons we learn best. Clearly, these people needed a day job because they had way too much time on their hands. However, as you build up your experience, you'll make these mistakes less and less often, your production lines will become more efficient, and you'll inflict nuclear incontinence on fewer people who take your meds.
The multi-part tutorial is complete and easy to follow. You can also use it repeatedly to reference parts that seem to have gone wrong for you; I did. There's also a nice wiki community supporting BiPh, and the developer seems like an honestly decent sort, the kind of dev you want to support. And as if all this wasn't enough, BiPh was deliberately designed to be moddable! If there's more you can ask for...you might be bordering on getting greedy.
At the end of the day (and beginning and middle), this one has my thumbs pointing up. There's a lot of fun to be had here. Just don't make my mistake - play it as soon as you pick it up. You won't regret it.

Having played the game, this was how I pictured the creation of this game:
Fresh off the success of the the original Race Driver: GRID, Codemasters decided to have a look at the rest of the multi-platform, half-arcade-half-realistic racing games market to see what the competition was like. So they picked up a copy of Need for Speed: Shift - which they stopped playing after half an hour because of how terrible it was, but not before they had a good look at the driving mechanics and the physics engine. Enraged by the fact that 30 minutes of their time was wasted in such a manner, Codemasters decided to make a game that had the same glossy sheen as the Need for Speed franchise, but used its own assets and physics engine, and thus GRID 2 was born.
Okay, so it doesnt really have the same sheen as a Need for Speed game, but it does feel like someone took a Need for Speed game, ripped out the internals and put in brand new and much more functional parts.
Things got off to a bad start when, like the original GRID, the game throws you into a race at an unknown track and asks you to begin driving - with no knowledge of the controls nor the track itself. I found out that WASD was used rather than the more conventional cursor keys as the default driving keys. This made the race not so much challenging as near impossible without immediately changing the controls once the game starts.
Heading off from there, the game is entertaining and is an excellent racing game. There are many more race modes in here than in GRID and compared to SHIFT, and I like the increased customisation options available for the cars.
However, the cars selection feels a bit.... anaemic. There are definitely more cars, just not much variation, especially when you dont include the DLC cars. Vehicle handling also feels rather challenging: it is unbelieveably easy to lose the back end of a car in a corner and either spin out or drift around the corner. The game balances it out by making controlling the drift easy, but this becomes extremely difficult and eventually frustrating when you reach the much faster, higher tier cars, where just a bump in the road causes the front and back end of the car to switch around.
Track selection feels rather weak too. Sure, you get a handful of excellent tracks such as Indy, the Red Bull Ring and Brands Hatch, and there are a good variation of street-based tracks. But its rather sad that tracks featured in the original GRID such as Donnington Park and Le Mans to name a few, were excluded from the game. You can get some more race tracks such as the excellent Bathurst and Spa-Francochamps via DLC, as if to further rub salt in the wound.
The AI appears to drive with the same behaviour as in the original GRID: With extreme tunnel vision. These are drivers who refuse to check their mirrors, refuse to give you space and will move in front or into your car when you are passing by. Speaking of which, your car, like in GRID, feels like its made of styrafoam whereas the opponents feel like they're weighed down with depleted uranium, so any bumps into them will result with your car bouncing off them into the nearest wall while they carry on with no change in their vehicle path.
Overall GRID 2 is still a competent racing game despite all its flaws and people who like driving games with a dash of arcade-style physics will still have a blast with this game. But this doesnt feel like the outstanding sequel which the original GRID deserved.

Bleed is a faced-paced platformer where you become the greatest hero of all time by killing all the current best heroes?? Doesn't really make sense, but i'm not here to question. I will add a TL;DR at the end.
You are Wyrn a girl who dreams to become the greatest hero of all time. To become the greatest hero of all time you must kill the current best heroes to claim your title. The controls were a bit odd and it took me a bit to get used to them.  The feature of being able to slow down time is amazingly fun and you have a decent arsenal to pick between. There are 13 bosses to fight through. The game plays fluently and the triple dash is really helpful when you are in a pinch (along with slowing down time). The game can be completed in a quick amount of time, however it's a very enjoyable and challenging experience. There are a total of 4 levels of difficulty to enjoy (Easy, Normal, Hard, and Very Hard) along with 2 other gamemodes to fight through.
The Graphics are pixelated and really match with the charm of the game. The music is upbeat and allows you to immerse yourself into killing whatever you happen to be fighting at that moment. The whole game gave me a kinda old-school vibe; in a good way.
+ 3 different ways to play and 4 levels of difficulty
+ Multiple characters to choose from (unlocks characters if you beat story on higher difficulties)
+ Interesting combat mechanic
+ Slowing down time
+ Boss fights are different in nature and strategy
+ Good ending
+ Fast-Paced and Challenging
- Short game overall
- Controls are a bit odd and take getting used to
- Local Co-op only (It would be amazing with online co-op but still amazing to play alone!)
I have thoroughly enjoyed playing through bleed. I honestly felt like a badass when I would slow down time dodge multiple bullets, reflect the rest with my katana, then shoot the hell out of the boss ending him. I might have gotten a bit addicted; only a bit! I enjoyed this game and while it was short, it was sweet. I once tried challenge mode only to realize I'm getting butt kicked by 3 bosses at once. Overall a very fun game which I can recommend to almost anyone who likes platformers or becoming Neo from The Matrix.
Bleed is a highly enjoyable fast-paced, pixeled, challenging platformer where you fight your way though all the old heroes to become the greatest hero of all time. You have 4 difficulties to choose from and 13 bosses to defeat. The combat is fun because of the ability to slow down time and the ability to triple dash. The arsenal has an decent amount of weapons to choose from and the increase in challenge when you go on higher difficulties is noticeable. The controls take a bit to get used to and overall the game is short, but highly enjoyable to play through.

This is without doubt one of the worst racing games I've played in past few years. It sells itself as a fairly serious racer, but 30 seconds is enough to demonstrate the absolutely terrible floating physics - quite what they are attempting to simulate I don't know - if it's hovercraft then they've got it spot on.
I had the XBox version and played it for a few hours, and actually managed to get a small amount of enjoyment out of it until about race 3 or 4 when the moronic AI finally become too much. Restarting a race 20 or 30 time just to try and avoid getting punted off by the oblivious AI as they batter their way around the track finally became too much and instead of smashing my Xbox pad I took out my rage on the disc and snapped it in half. That was a few months ago and even seeing the box on the shelf still makes me angry.
Anyway, after some time away from it I thought perhaps I'd give the PC version a go for 2 reasons - 1. I can use a proper wheel and 2. I can get a refund when it inevitably turns out to be terrible. First impressions were not good as it refused to recognize a Driving Force Pro wheel pedals in the default combined layout, and I had to quit and reload 3 times to try and figure out what was up. Setting them to seperate finally got it going.
Rather unsuprisingly 14 minutes from first loading the game I requested a refund. 2 laps of the first career mode race were enough to know that the physics are unbearably terrible - the car seems to rotate around a central pivot, which means from bonnet or nose cam the whole world seems to revolve around a point behind you, leading to a really weird feeling of having to steer too early and then let the slidey car sort of catch up. I thought they'd got over all this central-pivot rubbish that seemed to become apparent in the games after Colin McRae Rally 2.0, but apparently not, their physics system is just as hopeless as ever.  Also, for some reason it kept switching from bumper cam back to bonnet cam during gameplay, a bug that I also found happened on the XBox, and of course it always happens right at the worst moments. I assume even QA couldn't bear to play it for more than 2 minutes in one go to spot this obvious howler.
I bought DIRT Rally a while back too after reading about just how good a sim it is, and again it soon became clear that while sliding around on dirt hides their terrible physics system to certain degree, once you get on tarmac it's just as bad as it is in this game.
I skipped F1 2015 as I was frankly sick of buying the exact same game every year, and I think this is the last straw - any future Codemasters game will not be purchased as every single time I am disappointed.
Despite the positive reviews in certain places, this game is completely destroyed by almost all of its competition and IMHO is not deserving of a 5/10 , let along a 9/10 as it appears to have been awarded by some reviewers.

In general, I like Big Pharma, and have had fun completing some of the various challenges. The initial puzzle solving is interesting, and I enjoy trying to create the perfect drug in the space allotted. I also very much like that it is pauseable real-time, so that I can take as long as I want figuring things out.
However, the game is very similar each play-through, with only minor randomness (the floor layout and the ingredients list are all that change). So once you know what works, it pretty much works every time. The computer opponents are also not so much competitors as a nuisance, as they cannot beat you, but only get in your way. The only thing you are really fighting against is the clock, and your own goals.
So while I think this game is good for people who like puzzle and optimization games, it is not for everyone, I am not sure it is worth the full asking price. So if this looks interesting to you, watch for a good sale and give it a try.

This is a review based on 22 hours of gameplay, $0 spent.
Tutorial is in depth enough to give you a feel of the game before throwing you into matches. It felt organic and seamless.
Two separate in game currencies compliment each other and are used for separate types of items. In 22 hours of play I have earned enough to unlock two or three characters, whilst earning currency for skins/weapons, AND earning silver/gold chests which grant avatars, skins, weapons, poses, etc etc, all just by playing the game.
The rewards system in this game is really well done and it gives you more than enough to work with, and that's rare in a f2p game. I have spent $0 on this game and have felt quite satisfied with my progression. I will be buying the founders pack for $50 to support development.
The community is leaps and bounds better than other MOBAs and PvP based games. I won't say names, but you know what I mean. Everyone (save for a very small number, maybe 5 at most?) has been friendly and helpful. I have not yet played ranked, but my experience in Casual queues is that this community is great and just wants to have fun team fights.
I would strongly recommend this game to anyone who loves teamfighting in MOBAs, but not so much grinding for them.
Furthermore, I have gone through the negative reviews and many of them do not hold water. I'd disregard anything negative anyone's said with less than ten hours play time. It's still a game where you need to work for progression, and that seems to be the biggest complaint among the negative reviews.

I could go into a big shpiel but I'm sure others have and probably better than I could, so I'll keep it short and sweet.
DFO is worth a shot. Absolutely. If you can put up with the loads of mindless dialogue drivel and boring, arbitrary quest-wrangling, the actual gameplay itself in the dungeons is an experience you won't find anywhere else.
Part of what makes the combat system so great is how every single move you learn can be performed with fighting-game style commands (Down, forward, attack. Etc). You can have fifteen skills, only have hotkeys for 4, and still be able to perform any and all of them at the drop of a hat just by remembering the commands. It's so much slicker and cooler than the typical MMO that has you assign EVERY SKILL to a hotkey, often requiring you to occupy your entire number line.
Fighting Game Mechanics are there as well, and you'll have fun playing with the rock-paper-scissors style system of Grabs, Super Armor and Range, where Super Armor beats Range, Range beats Grabs and Grabs beat Super Armor (in gaming terms, Super Armor is typically resistance to flinching when hit. Basically resistance to being interrupted while you're trying to do something. Naturally, Superior Range lets you hit the enemy first. If your attack lacks range, though, you can push through with Super Armor. And if your opponent is using super-armor to power through your attacks you can stop him with a Grab move).
So many different characters with radically different skills and playstyles will ensure you'll start over just to try new classes and subclasses.
Do yourself a favor, try it. JUST ONCE.

TL:DR Pretty bland FPS game though the North Korea occupying the USA setting was an interesting background for the game. The campaign is very short though and the multiplayer wasn't great so I cant really recommend this.
Full Version:
Homefront is a fairly generic FPS game although it does have an interesting setting. The game takes place in an alternate history where North Korea has managed to defeat the US and is occupying parts of the country. You play a pilot who is busted out of captivity by the resistance and then joins them to help fight the Koreans.
The campaign is ok-ish although really short. It has a few memorable moments showing the horrors of the Korean occupation which seems almost surreal in an American backdrop. So it's a shame that most of the campaign feels pretty bland and doesn't really stand out much at all. It feels dated and a bit buggy at times. There are points in the levels where you have to wait for an AI companion to open a door to progress and they'd often just awkwardly walk around or stand there for a few secs before opening the door. At one point they didnt even open the door and I had to reload to the last checkpoint!
I did give the multiplayer a quick try and I was surprised to find that I was quickly able to find a match. (I suspect this may have been due to the game been given away for free on HB and Steam a few weeks ago which is how I got the game). The multiplayer feels a bit like a mix of COD and BF. The one new thing it adds is Battlepoints which are earned by getting kills, capping points etc. You can then spend them on spawning a vehicle or special weapon ammo for example. The multiplayer wasn't that great though and I didnt feel like I wanted to continue playing.
Overall I cant really recommend buying this game unless you can get it really cheap. If the campaign had been a bit longer it might have been worth it but it's too short to justify it. I dont know if the multiplayer will remain very active but it wasn't anything special and theres better FPS multiplayer games out there.

So here is my review of "Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory".
(just imagine and low voiced guy saying Tom Clancy)
TL;DR it's in my top 10 stealth games, get it.
So I'm going to split my review up into 4 sections, gameplay, story, graphics, & how does it compare to the newer games(?).
GAMEPLAY
Tom Clancy's splinter cell CT has problems but also does things that I adore.
Ok, stealth; the stealth in this game is realistic but it gets kinda annoying after a while.
You see, there are 2 monitors attached to your U.I called your "aural monitor" and your "brightness monitor". Now of course your brightness has a big impact on you and your enemies. The bar works like a brightness setting I guess. Point is, the closer you get to light, the farther left (right?) it goes. If you are in full brightness then enemies I believe from anywhere can see you. Now the Aural monitor is the annoying part. The aural monitor watches your speed setting, the faster you go the easier enemies can hear you. Now the scoll wheel on your mouse functions as a speed changer, the closer you get to enemies the lower you scroll your mouse because unlike most of the games, you can't just walk behind a enemy and grab them, you have to gradually get slower until it prompts you to grab them, but this can f**k you over cause it doesn't tell you very much about the monitor. But I must admit, for it's problems I can forgive it, I...LOVE REALISM IN STEALTH GAMES! I am not a big fan of the cartoony stealth like "stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s" or...well you get me. I like realistic stealth games where you are in situations that can mimic real life. This game does that almost perfectly, I guess this game i- I am getting off track. Stealth = 8/10
STORY
Now the story takes you through a bunch of locations ranging from a
The story is quite enjoyable if a bit cliche'ed but it does take you to some nice locations. story = 6/10.
HOW DOES IT COMPARE TO NEWER SPINTER CELLS
I've always found the new spinter cell odd, they changed so much. I felt and think they changed devs or engines, probably both. But I've always thought of conviction and blacklist as different games. They are great themselves it's just if you WANT a STEALTH game then choose this game. The newer ones are more likes AC, if you have someone in your way you kill them, but if you want a "stealth" game then you go for the ones that make you think about your decisions. If I kill this guy will anyone see it? Will I be able to move the body in time? Will anyone hear him drop? Those are the type of stealth games that in my opinion, represent the stealth genre greatly. How does the game fair? 8/10
FINAL THOUGHT
Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory is a great stealth game. If you are a die-hard fan of stealth then you should have this game. Yes the FMV is cheesy but this is a game that was made in 2006, I don't blame it, and you shouldn't either. But for my final thought, this game is a underrated gem of the series, I find it a guilty pleasure, and from the reviews I see this is a very loved game. Pick it up, please, if you don't like it then just refund it.
Tom Clancy's Splinter cell: Chaos Theory (I am saying Tom Clancy too much) get's my final rating of 8/10, a great game! If you enjoyed this review then leave a comment on my profile saying "+rep decent reviewer" it will make me happy <3

As someone who grew up playing M:TG, I was curious to see how they translated it online.
They seem to have done a fairly good job of translating the rules to the computer, but unfortunately they made some design decisions which I found to be large negatives.
Most online card games have a series of continue buttons to click when you finish a phase, or when you have the chance to react to the other players actions. Unfortunately Magic Duels takes the opposite approach. You need to actively pause a timer in order to take an "instant" action. You also have to wait for the timer, you can't fast forward. This decision made playing games feel too long.
If you play an hour and that doesn't bother you, then this might be a good game for you. You can fairly easily earn gold to buy packs and you can play against humans or AI.
Just because I personally don't like the interface doesn't mean it is a bad game. Give it a try and decide for yourself.

A completely unique and incredibly interesting game. You take the role of civilians trapped in a worn torn city attempting to survive. During the day you must upgrade your shelter to ensure it is safe from raiders and able to provide for the inhabitants. At night you venture into the ruin of the city to scavenge for supplies including food, water, building materials, and weaponry.
You can either start with a story mode with three people or build your own story with as many people as you like. At the time of writing I have played a few days of the story mode and a few days of my own story with two civilians in a hideout. Both provide their own challenges but at present I prefer my own story to the one set up by the game.
The game is 2D and black and white, simplistic but very atmospheric. The controls are all mouse based, clicking on icons to perform actions.
Taking the view point of those most affected by war is an interesting twist and a refreshing turn from most of the games currently on sale. Each character has a bio to give a bit of background but you are also free to fill in details yourself as to how each character ended up where they are.
You upgrade the shelter from work tables that can also be upgraded in order to provide more useful items. For example at the beginning you will be able to create basic furniture and cooking appliances, but at the next upgrade you can create herb gardens and boards to block up the holes in the walls.
Scavenging is fairly straightforward, each location will require at least three or four visits to get everything there and have a brief overview of what they contain, meaning you can target what you need. There aren’t many supplies you need making it fairly straightforward to get everything, but the supplies aren’t always in abundance so you can’t create amazing things straight away.
I only have a couple of issues with the game. Firstly, you can only have one story going at any one time, which means you have to focus on one playthrough at a time. I find this detracts slightly as, with games such as these, I would enjoy being able to switch between a different variety of games such as the story, and my own stories but with different types and numbers of characters.
Secondly it doesn’t say when the game saves, which for reference seems to be when you return from or start scavenging. This can lead to annoying moments when you are halfway through a day, quit, and then have to start the day over. A simple message telling you this would stop any confusing.
Finally there is no tutorial. I’m not sure if this is a conscious design, as if to say that if you really were trapped in a war zone you wouldn’t have a tutorial but have to find you own way. If this is the case then fair enough, but again this isn’t explicitly mentioned meaning the first couple of playthroughs are based on trial and error.
Overall this is a great game though, a really interesting take on the war game genre, and hopefully something that will be expanded in the future. 9/10

Bleed is bleeding fantastic. I haven't finished it 100%, there's still a number of unlocks, difficulties, and achieves for me to go for, but after finishing the game on normal, I have to say that it's some of the most fun I've had in quite a while.
So what it is? It's a classic-style action-platformer that plays like a mix of Megaman, Contra, and Gunstar Heroes. You have a number of weapons, ranging from the basic dual pistols and rocket launcher to explosive mines, a laser rifle, and a katana. Each one has it's uses situationally, but the game is plenty playable with whatever setup you prefer. I myself like the pistols for accuracy and the katana for its ability to deflect bullets. There's an incredibly controllable triple-jump, wall jumping, and bullet time to help you dodge the massive amount of ordnance that will be flying around. You'll progress through seven short levels, each with a miniboss and a boss. The levels are derivative, as this game is basically a love letter to its influences, but it does a number of neat things with the design. It operates on a checkpoint system, which is good, because while it's not that bad on normal, but it is approaching Nintendo hard, especially on the harder difficulties. Thanks to the liberal use of checkpoint, each inevitable death ceases to sting all that bad. Like Dark Souls, Bleed is very difficult, but never punishing. Every time you die, you will know why, and that's because you messed up. That's in addition to the absolute badassery you'll unleash. While for most games the triple-jump and bullet-time would be gimmicks, in Bleed they are central to both the combat and platforming and allow you to pull off some seriously awesome moves. Rather than being nastily cheap, Bleed gives you the tools to succeed and encourages you to rise to the challenge.
The story is practically nonexistant, as it was in the old days. It is the year 21XX, and the last century was the time of heroes. However, the heroes have gotten old, there's no new ones, and a cotton-candy-haired girl named Wryn dreams of supplanting them and becoming the greatest hero in the world. There is a twist, if you can call it that, at the end, but ultimately this has a classic-style video game plot to complement it's classic-style gameplay. All it is is a setup to excuse the chaos. If you want depth, look elsewhere.
One last comment. The game has a wonderful atmosphere. While most of the backgrounds resemble old SNES/Genesis backgrounds, the character designs are extremely cutesy, and pink is a prominent color in Wryn's character design. While I understand that this might be offputting for many gamers, the way the designer used it to contrast with the intense action is delightful, what little story there is is hilarious as a result, and the ending is pure saccharine joy. Give it a chance. Bleed may not be complex or terribly unique, but what it is is an absolute blast. Recommended to anyone who can deal with a bit of a challenge.

Z.A.R. is a retro FPS that's been build in what seems to be a similar engine to magic carpet or terminal verlocity. A meteor impact sends sci-fi humanity's galactic AI rogue and it's up to the player in his suit of power armor to retake the planets in the name of humanity! The storyline is interesting although why the earth military would send a single solider to quell a galactic uprising is questionable, and the shooting has it's moments. It also features a "CD" quality soundtrack, whatever that means. The game has a lot of annoying niggles though which definitely hurt the overall gameplay.
-Good enemy variety
-large number of planets to fight across
-features a "watch battle" mode that is essentially a funky screensaver. Very cool
-the fall damage is ridiculous. A standard jump does significant harm
-enemies have unnervingly high accuracy at range (you don't) and often it is preferable to fight at long range
-really needs a crosshair. Why would a mech suit not have some way to aim?
-the stages seem a little "pallet-swichy"
-the game gives you no ammo to start with and no default attack. You are constantly looking for ammo packs, often completely unarmed and you rarely get to feel like a powerful battle mech
-no run button
So despite doing quite a few things right I feel like the down points really hurt the overall gameplay and while this game would have been a breath of fresh air in 1997, that was then and this is now. I wonder if there are any mods for this (no), it could be vastly improved with just a few balance tweaks. C'est la vie.

This is a cool little gaming artifact of the late 1990s. Coming out a year after BioWare's premier game, Shattered Steel, it has numerous similarities—outdoor maps, deforming terrain, a story about AI gone rogue, a rather tank-like feel, etc. But, it is a little more Quake than Mechwarrior, in that it has a 1-through-10 weapon roster, health pickups, and just-slightly-archaic-for-the-time sprite based enemies.
It's hard to say that it's a better game than the average for the time, but it does have a good sense of focus and style, dropping a lot of cruft that began to appear around this time (e.g., overly elaborate mission briefings and loadout screens), and embracing cinematic cutscenes and a throbbing CD-audio soundtrack.
Also, it's a Russian game about a collectivist industrial AI gone wrong, so that's some neat flavor right off the bat.

I enjoy this game a lot, and I do not understand some of the anger it gets from others.  Reading the negative reviews I get the impression that it's biggest sin is that "it wasn't groundbreaking enough".
If you played and enjoyed Civ V, you will find a lot familiar in here in a much more streamlined package.  Hex grid movement, basic diplomatic communications, and a familiar build system with a more intuitive flow to it's interface.  They also have an expanded espionage system from the Brave New World expansion of Civ V, and the Virtues system is a more long term variation of the social policy mechanic.
And why change things too much?  If they did, likely the fan base would have even more outrage.  In the end it was smart to have this basic and solid entry game to see what people wanted more and less of, then focus continued development into the future DLC.  Frankly, that's just the nature of big budget game development these days and Rising Tide is showing that it is likely going to work out well.
What's great:  The build system is smooth and leaves very little learning curve, and gone are the requirements for prerequisite buildings to make other buildings available.  Combat units will auto upgrade as you advance your Virtues, meaning no tracking through lists seeing who's still stuck in the bronze age when everyone else has machine guns.  The alien life forms feel much more intimidating early game than barbarians in Civ V, and mid game can still be a force to consider when making plans.
What needs improvement:  Exploration feels like it's going to need continued work, though they will be getting new content in Rising Tide.  Diplomacy also will be a welcome overhaul in the DLC, as the offer of "favors" from other leaders never felt like something I was able to use effectively in my games.  There are no "luxury goods" like in Civ V, which made diplomatic negotiations more interesting in my opinion, but there may be a new consideration in the new diplomacy system.  I also feel the Orbital layer of the game is under-utilized, and it seems like more could be done there than just the satellite units in future expansions.
As a sci-fi junkie I highly recommend this game.  I'm not a long time Civilization fanatic, but I have respected the series for a long time, so take my opinions as you will.

It's a Russian version of Quake/Doom/Duke nukem, so you know it's going to be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ knockoff. Basically every level is the game, just a giant open area of hills and valleys, whose color changes on some levels. You run around these hills shooting tanks, turrets, and planes, that's it. Enemies are boring and repetitive. It's super ugly and the draw distance is terrible, as you can't see anything in the distance. The map is terrible and unhelpful. The worst part is the mission design. Most levels you are just supposed to kill a certain number of machines. What this ends up being is you kill 16 of the 20 you are supposed to kill, and spend the next 10 min continuously wandering around the same hills looking for the final 4. Because all the enemies are spread about without rhyme or reason it can be very frustrating. Since the map has no enemies on it, and theres no waypoint or marker on your HUD, and every hill and valley looks the EXACT same without any structures or landmarks, you are screwed. This  happened multiple times and feels like lazy design. You use the same 3-4 guns, a rocket launcher, gattling gun, grenade launcher, and annoyingly unhelpful tornado thrower. Enemies take tons of hits to die. Finally after the 5th level of wasting 15 min running around the open area looking unsuccessfully for 1 guy I saw the game for what it is, a lazy Russian POS, like most products from their. It does have destructible environments though. 3/10.

This game requires a HUGE amount of skill. Legitimate skill. You need to know your bloodline and a lot of esoteric information in order to even get by in this game.
I've played since shortly after post-beta and I bought most of the characters I wanted back then, and I maxed out my level and all my stats and have nothing to worry about... but for people joining now, you're going to have to either pony up some cash or play for a long time before you can unlock all the bloodlines you may want to play, the minmaxing medals and stat slots, etc.
This game is PLAY2Win, meaning the more hours you have put into the game the better you'll be at it. The upgrades you get from leveling up make you strictly and objectively better than someone who has just started out, so new players WILL start at a disadvantage.
It's an extremely fun game if you're willing to put in time and effort, but it can be discouraging at times.
I of course strongly recommend it (and I'm always looking for people to play it with) but I also strongly suggest that you understand what you're getting into before you join up. There's not a huge influx of new users daily like other more popular free2play games, so you may very well be a small fish in a very large pond.
It's hard to get into, but once you're into the game it's the most fun and addictive game I could ever recommend to somebody.

The sound is just horrific, with awful hiccups, the voice actors aren't not bad, but not good either, though the guns aren't that bad.
In conclusion, for a game released in the same year with Battlefield 3 and Modern Warfare 3, you don't have any excuses for being that bad.

Bleed is an extremely fun, albeit short, side-scrolling bullet-hell time-manipulation game. It has a great and very distinct art style, very catchy and upbeat music, a funny twist on the standard plot, great control, and a unique and memorable main character. The overall tone is somewhat cutesy, but rather than hindering the game, it gives Bleed a funny and uplifting tone that is oddly in contrast to all the shooting you're doing. I beat the normal game in about an hour and a half on normal difficulty, but there are also options for coop mode (as yet untried), hard mode, and very hard mode. The controls are extremely good, it has customizable options, and it runs very smoothly. It has some interesting weapons that you can unlock by purchasing with points at the in-game store, as well as extra health and time-slowdown energy.
Some people will say the normal mode is extremely hard; don't be fooled, I think people are making it out to be worse than it really is. What kept me playing was the good level design, unique enemies, brevity of the levels, interesting boss battles, and the infinite continues. The game may be difficult (there are some incredibly tough sections, most notably in level 6) but it is incredibly forgiving and very fair. You just have to push yourself through to the next screen and you'll start from there if you die.
I only have two minor gripes with the game. The first is that level 6 begins with an auto-scrolling section with some difficult platforming that the game had never introduced before; I would've preferred a section that introduced the difficult terrain management before the auto-scrolling screen kills you. The other gripe is that level 6 also has a section where you have to try and dodge seemingly infinite bubbles that are constantly in your way; it's a bit like jumping into the ocean and trying to not get wet.
Other than these two sticking points, my only other suggestion for improvement is MORE CUTSCENES! The characters and plot were great, and the main character Wryn's dialogue was very funny and full of personality! She really had spunk, although it was definitely not overdone, and I loved to see that because she felt like a real person. It really felt like the developer made this character effortlessly, so mad props to the dev for a character more memorable than any I've played in a long time, even in big budget games. I wanted to see and hear more of her between each stage, or at least every other stage. The plot is quite funny and the ending was comedically unexpected but satisfying. I only wish it had lasted longer; the main game is unfortunately short. But I hope to see more from this developer, especially a Bleed 2. :)
Bleed is kid-friendly but the level of difficulty may be a bit high. Replay value is somewhat "eh" but I'm sure kids could get a more than a few hours of enjoyment out of it.

I will review all my humble bundle games and see which is worth playing and which is not! Like a lot of people i buy H.B. games as a pack because i want some of the games, but not all. I will play for 5 minutes (or a little bit more) and give you my opinion on it. Sometimes the game will surprise me, sometimes it will be a total disappointment. Just keep in mind this is my opinion only and is not an objective view of the game. You might actually like it!
The review will be constructed into 5 parts:
1. Game description (from what I’ve seen in the time I’ve played).
2. Did i finish the game (YES/NO/Maybe in the future) and why.
3. Pros/Cons.
4. Final thoughts.
5. Rating
So let's begin...
1. Game description:
When I started this game I had expected something like Roller coaster tycoon(what I think a management game should be) but with medical drugs. I was so wrong.
The graphics are on par for a management game. Nothing too special but not bad. Music and sound effects are ok and the gameplay is…well OK too. It’s nothing special and definitely not what I expected, but it’s OK for what it does. However the building part doesn’t matter too much and that’s what killed it for me. It’s a micromanagement decision making game, with a little construction thrown in.
2. Did i finish the game? NO
The fact that the building portion of the game was so small made me uninstall it after the first mission. I don’t think I will be coming back to this one.
3. Pros/Cons.
PROS:
- A pretty good management game
CONS:
- Not a lot of building in it
4. Final thoughts:
Not my style of management game, although a lot of people will enjoy it.
5. Rating
6/10

A completely unique and incredibly interesting game. You take the role of civilians trapped in a worn torn city attempting to survive. During the day you must upgrade your shelter to ensure it is safe from raiders and able to provide for the inhabitants. At night you venture into the ruin of the city to scavenge for supplies including food, water, building materials, and weaponry.
You can either start with a story mode with three people or build your own story with as many people as you like. At the time of writing I have played a few days of the story mode and a few days of my own story with two civilians in a hideout. Both provide their own challenges but at present I prefer my own story to the one set up by the game.
The game is 2D and black and white, simplistic but very atmospheric. The controls are all mouse based, clicking on icons to perform actions.
Taking the view point of those most affected by war is an interesting twist and a refreshing turn from most of the games currently on sale. Each character has a bio to give a bit of background but you are also free to fill in details yourself as to how each character ended up where they are.
You upgrade the shelter from work tables that can also be upgraded in order to provide more useful items. For example at the beginning you will be able to create basic furniture and cooking appliances, but at the next upgrade you can create herb gardens and boards to block up the holes in the walls.
Scavenging is fairly straightforward, each location will require at least three or four visits to get everything there and have a brief overview of what they contain, meaning you can target what you need. There aren’t many supplies you need making it fairly straightforward to get everything, but the supplies aren’t always in abundance so you can’t create amazing things straight away.
I only have a couple of issues with the game. Firstly, you can only have one story going at any one time, which means you have to focus on one playthrough at a time. I find this detracts slightly as, with games such as these, I would enjoy being able to switch between a different variety of games such as the story, and my own stories but with different types and numbers of characters.
Secondly it doesn’t say when the game saves, which for reference seems to be when you return from or start scavenging. This can lead to annoying moments when you are halfway through a day, quit, and then have to start the day over. A simple message telling you this would stop any confusing.
Finally there is no tutorial. I’m not sure if this is a conscious design, as if to say that if you really were trapped in a war zone you wouldn’t have a tutorial but have to find you own way. If this is the case then fair enough, but again this isn’t explicitly mentioned meaning the first couple of playthroughs are based on trial and error.
Overall this is a great game though, a really interesting take on the war game genre, and hopefully something that will be expanded in the future. 9/10

Imagine, in your eyes, what the perfect game would be. Maybe you're thinking of an FPS, or an RPG. If you imagined any of these games, you are very much in the wrong. Let me describe a specific game that you should be thinking of right now. A game where you build, refuel, and drive a dilapidated car on a grand journey through the terrirtory of the former Eastern bloc. That's right; the perfect game you should be thinking of is Jalopy.
Personally, I have never had as much fun as I had in the time that I've owned this masterpiece. It manages to captivate you by immediately introducing you to the Laika 601, which you must repair so it can escort you on your miraculous journey. Almost instantly, you will notice the beautiful, simplistic art style. It's just so different from every other big-name game out there that the feeling is similar to getting a fresh breath of air after being stuck in a Chuck-E-Cheese for half an hour during your son's 8th birthday party that one time.
My second point is the superior gameplay. You must understand that before you purchase this game, you must know everything there is to know about car parts and their functions. Do not even TRY to figure out the intricate mechanisms like the engine or the car battery if you haven't at least built a few cars in the past. As soon as I set foot in the car, I felt like I was somehow PART of it. Like I was just another one of its many parts. I'm sure that I won't be able to even come close to describing how it feels to actually drive the car, so I'm not even going to try. I got Second Life after playing this game, because at the moment that I played it my life was so great I literally wanted a second one.
Finally, to anyone considering buying this product, don't get it when it's on sale; buy it at the full price, as to support the developers for their excellent, hard work.

Lost Grimoires is a little thin as a hidden object or as a casual adventure game, but its non-conventional story with its grey morality can offer quite a few nice moments.
I do not remember many hidden object games where the main title of the first entry is not related to the content itself, but Lost Grimoires makes an exception: there aren’t any books being lost in it, but a kingdom is surely stolen all right.
Ironically, it is still the story that carries the game: we play as an alchemist apprentice who has to unravel the mystery behind the strange behaviours of her king, her master, and a robed figure. Interestingly, they don’t have a simple good or evil role, because everyone is motivated by a set or grey morals; something we rarely, if ever, see in a HOG.
This story must serve as a main motivation to play though, since there isn’t much else in here. The stages look spectacular, but they are often half-empty. There are maybe ten hidden object scenes in total, with even less conventional puzzles. Even the point ‘n’ click parts feel half-hearted. Neither of them is a deal-breaker, but expect a very barebones game when you buy this.

After playing this game for 5+ hours I can confidentally say this review.
At first glance it seemed like a great game, interesting characters and play style, new kind of fighter game popping up. What could go wrong right? Oh so many things little billy, oh so many things can.
This game has SO much damn potential, but right now it's not being utalized. The games balance is a little off but what game hasn't got a balance issue? Sadly this one can't make much room for the amount of balance issues it has right now due to the fact of 14 characters. Which means the other characters are hardly ever seen on the battlefield, why the most played fighters I see are big hammer lady with horns and Mr. Middrift leather outfit elf. You'll see why if you were to ever play this game. They're fairly over powered in their mechanics, Hammer lady swings, no escape for you little billy only death awaits. "Oh perhaps Mr. Middrift leather outfit elf will be easier" No no billy, he touches you with that stun you're doomed. Even if you can catch him off guard, his going to turn invisible and come back at you with heavy damage like the most fabulous truck you've ever seen.
Then we get to match making, loljk there isn't any. I don't mind that, servers are hardly the problem in games to me. Though for this game, it's not too fun on the Australian side. There's atleast 2-3 servers up if you're lucky, and they're either filled, have the hard core players on ready to crush some scrubs for free exp and points or just your friendly 4 person deathmatch server where they hunt you because you're not one of their friends in their group. I can't say much about the American side due to the fact the ping isn't great on that side so I never bothered with their servers.
To the mechanics little billy! The mechanics right now are pretty darn basic, mostly just right and left clicking. And hitting E to block etc etc. They're not that bad on the control side. So that's a plus, though sadly we hit the balance issues, Missfortune with a rifle decides to right click from the map, that's right little billy, she has a rifle and you're in her sights it's game over my friend. Unfortunately like other reviews stated, the right click ranged victory is very true. You won't see the great skill taking combo fighters because why bother? There's an OP fighter that requires so much less effort for top scores.
End of it for me, I wouldn't suggest this to anyone. There's no diversity in what people play, the servers aren't friendly for Australians, balance issues and players could be slightly less toxic. If these issues were tuned a little, I'm sure it'd get to the top rated free to play games, sadly the potential is thrown out the window right now.

Lost Grimoires: Stolen Kingdom is an outstanding hidden object game created by World-Loom, set in a fantasy environment and - in many aspects - is among the best in its category. For those who don't know what a hidden object game is: it's a point and click adventure game of the simplier kind with scenes where we have to find the listed items by clicking on them (there are other various puzzles as well). It's probably the first in the genre which features alchemy as an additional minigame. The game's main strength - along with the alchemy - is the exceptionally well-made puzzles and minigames.
As a young alchemist lady, whose mother died years ago, we return to our home city, where our foster father, who also appears to be our uncle, only referred to as 'the Alchemist', awaits us. The king looks and acts rather strange as of late and there are also large golems patrolling the streets, searching for the so called 'Wardens', who seem to be criminals. Our job will be to investigate what is going on here and what actually happened to our parents.
It's also delightful that many elements of the background story is told interactively through easy minigames, instead of just simple cutscenes. On the other hand a bonus chapter would have been nice to gain a bit more insight about the wardens.
The use of alchemy consists of finding recipes for each magical item along our journey, which we have to copy into our alchemy book and then search for the necessary ingredients. After collecting all of them, we can transmute these components into the desired potion, tool or other magical consumeable item through completing a minigame in which we have to rotate rune circles to arrange the same coloured runes into the given position. As we progress, more complex recipes come with more circles. After having solved these, we receive the concocted item and use it on the obstacle ahead of us. It's truly fun and a refreshing gameplay element.
Where the game truly excels are the minigames: there are actual riddles, yes, text riddles in the game, something that's - sadly - quite unusual in hidden object games. We get a fair handful of these during a childhood flashback/nightmare sequence and I really loved how it was merged with a hidden object scene. All the other puzzles are very diverse as well. Some of them may be a bit easy, but they are very creative.
We also happen to find an amulet along our journey (a legacy from our mother) which helps us revealing hidden places.
As for collectibles we have to keep an eye out for kestrel statuettes (which seem to be the symbol of the wardens).
The hand drawn backgrounds are simply amazing looking, the medieval fantasy city/castle environment almost comes to life. Some characters do not blend in though (mostly because they aren't as detailed as the scenery around them) and some of the character animations during cutscenes are also cheaply implemented (instead of fluid movement only frames of them are shown during the animation). This however doesn't really affect the overall beauty of the game as a whole.
The music is a bit generic, it could have used more scores.
Lost Grimoires: Stolen Kingdom is a great hidden object game and unique in many categories: the riddles, the alchemy, the interesting minigames and so on. It has its minor flaws, but they can be easily overlooked. It's also very family friendly because of the lack of violence
.
I could recommend it to everyone, even to gamers who aren't familiar with this genre. Be careful though: it will set your standards high when it comes to hidden object games.
PROS
+ refreshing alchemy feature with minigames
+ excellent puzzles
+ wide variety of hidden object scenes
+ beautiful scenery
+ interesting story
CONS
- could have used a bonus chapter
- character animations aren't that good
- wrongfully tries to depict magpies as nice birds (they aren't)
RATING
8/10

In 1997, I received a demo disc with an issue of PC Gamer, and on that demo disc was the one-level demo of Z.A.R. The game, even then, struck an impression on me due to its advanced voxel engine and open-concept gameplay. But, every month thereafter I'd look at the various PC game sales sheets in the back of PC Gamer, and I never saw Z.A.R appear there, or ever on store shelves. To my knowledge, it was never released here, and for 18 years I wondered what happened to this game. At least now that curiosity can be put to rest; so after 18 years, how does it stack up?
It's very much a game of its time. It's something akin to Terminal Velocity meets Terra Nova: Strike Force Centauri. You play a soldier airdropped into each level. Each level consists of a terrain type, one or more objectives, and ammunition scattered about sparsely over the play area. Missions range in type from search & destroy, defending a point, or escorting a convoy of transports.
How you go about accomplishing your objectives is completely up to your own approach, but the fact that weapons and ammunition are scarce, means that there has to be a bit of planning in terms of your rationing of supplies. Do you waste those rockets trying to down aircraft bombers that have you targeted? Or do you use your machine gun and save the rockets for an enemy spawn-point? Herein lies half the difficulty of the game, and you're never shortchanged, you're always given just enough to approach and succeed however you desire, but it's not a cakewalk. You'll likely be limping along at the end of each mission...
Which brings us to the other half of the difficulty; there are no health pickups save for very minute energy packs dropped by the enemies you fell. This means that you need to be fast, accurate, and keep moving if you want to survive without taking massive amounts of damage with little way to replenish your health-- because the enemies in this game don't whittle you down; a single rocket can easily knock off 75% of your HP. Sometimes, it's almost punishingly unfair when you spawn into a mission with multiple enemies locking you down, meaning you need to be alert and moving before you're even able to get your bearings. Luckily, you don't lose anything by dying and retrying the mission, as your loadout resets to nothing with every new map anyway.
The maps are a mixed bag. Some maps do inventive, awesome things: One map, for example, has the player assaulting a stronghold situated on an island, and the only way to storm it is over thin ice. However, the island's defenses include grenade launching pods, and as you start to assault across the ice, the grenades begin blasting the ice apart (showing off the game's terrain deformation), making it all the more likely you'll fall through into damaging ice-water. Another map has tides that roll in and out, exposing more land and more enemies that were concealed in the water. Yet another has a trench with supplies inside that slowly pumps full of, then empties of toxic sludge, giving you limited windows to restock your ammunition before it fills up again.
But for every exciting angle, I eventually ended up feeling like too many map scenarios were repeated, with only slight variations on a theme. They all end up boiling down to "spawn, walk across mostly empty terrain, scour for ammo, shoot the bad things and keep the good things alive." Which, you know, taken in context of a game from 1997 isn't all that awful. The game ultimately tries to be something more than just another corridor shooter as was so popular for the time. It joined games like Rebel Moon, Terra Nova, and Terminator: Future Shock in being more about objectives and missions than just about indiscriminately shooting-- and it's not like the variety of mission types was anything close to standard at the time.
But, that criticism is based on judging it from a 1997 standpoint. It's no longer 1997. In terms of games today, it's going to feel sparse and empty. It's not easy to aim when all the objects are sprites despite a fully 3D voxel engine. The physics are slippery and muddy (especially so on the ice levels, but that's intended). The maps wear too thin and end up repeating themselves for the sake of making the game longer; they feel like filler. But beyond all those criticisms, there is fun to be had in Z.A.R. The challenge is engaging and rewarding, skirting by with 10 HP and a single round of ammunition left me with my adrenaline pumping in a way that felt like I was able to pull it off due to my own skill and rationing-- not game mechanics designed to keep me from losing. Playing Z.A.R gave me a sense of overcoming challenges, just on Normal, that I haven't felt from a game like this in a long time.
18 years was worth the wait, despite its flaws, and I'm glad to have played it.

lets us step into her shoes as she returns home at a very inopportune time. Her land is in chaos under the rule of a seemingly mad king. This hidden object game has a very intriguing story accompanied by fun gameplay and beautiful graphics. Using your knowledge of alchemy, you can create many useful potions to progress in the game. Can the apprentice solve the mysterious around her and bring peace to land once more? Only with your help, of course.
Our heroine returns home from school to the master alchemist that raised her after her mother’s death and father’s disappearance. As if timed by fate, her house is broken into by a masked thief searching for a magical amulet. It’s this event that starts the ball rolling as the story quickly develops into political intrigue and family secrets. I won’t spoil how things turn out, I will say that while some parts are predictable it was all very well written and more in depth than most games in this genre. My only issue with the story was the main villain's motives. While this person wasn’t totally evil and believed the ends justified the means, it didn’t explain why they nearly destroyed the entire kingdom to do it.
This title is a hidden object adventure game, it mixes aspects of a point and click game with lots of fun hidden object scenes as well other mini games. Players use their computer mouse to do everything, move across maps, play the games and talk to other characters. You’re given an in-game map that allows you to teleport for quick traveling and, depending on the difficulty you’re on, will show you where an action needs to be performed. You have an inventory to hold items as well as a book to hold your potion recipes, these are found throughout the game. This alchemy aspect is the most unique feature, combining certain items will make a useful potion but to do this you have to perform a mini game each time. The mini game itself is simple, aligning colored orbs correctly but the more complicated the recipe the harder the mini game, however I found myself doing just fine on almost all of them. The hidden object scenes are fun and vary from a worded list of objects to find to seeing what the objects look like and trying to find them in the scene. There are also mini games but these didn’t prove to be difficult at all.
The graphics are great, vibrant colors and beautiful scenery. My only issue is the faces of some of the characters and the animation of these faces when they spoke, sometimes it came off as creepy. All of the hidden object scenes are well done, items are rendered well and not blurry. The game has full voice acting, fans of Artifex Mundi games will find the main character’s voice very familiar, as well as a certain crow that shows up. Most of the actors do a very good job, a few are hit-and-miss but overall everything sounded well done. The music in the game fits the setting and isn’t distracting but it’s also nothing too memorable. I enjoyed it nonetheless.
I applaud
for offering players a pretty solid story with a few twists and turns as well as the new gameplay element of making alchemy potions. Usually in games that involve potion making, I’ve found that it’s a rarely use aspect on the game but here it’s front and center. Veteran hidden object game fans may find this title a bit on the easy side. It’s also a little short with no bonus chapter. The achievements are also relatively easy to gain in one playthrough. But this is still a fun game to play and I look forward to more like this. It also has Steam trading cards if you fancy collecting those along with your achievements. I recommend buying this game, not necessarily on sale, but I feel you will enjoy it if you add it to your library.

The puzzles are presented without instruction or any sort of text; however, the game is very good at introducing new concepts in a way that is immediately obvious, then expands on those concepts to provide further challenges. Later levels will present you with a combination of several different previously-learned mechanics, so you really have to pay attention. A bit of experimentation is sometimes required (and can sometimes be frustrating until you get it), and each of the puzzles gives you a decent sense of accomplishment when you finally figure it out.
Overall it's worth the dollar or so you'd spend on this, so get it if you're looking for a new puzzle game to hold your interest for a while.

I’ve been putting off throwing my two cents into the mix about Beyond Earth for... well basically it’s entire duration on the market. I love it and I will continue to lose hours to it until the next civilization game is released. I will also own all the expansions and DLC. I may even pick up the sound track at some point. Yet for all of that love, I can’t justify this game.

I don’t know that I could point out all the specific elements that lead me to this feeling. Civ:BE is not a bad game at all, in fact it is very well made. However, coming right off the back of Civ:V, with all of its’ DLC polishing it to a mirror finish, Beyond Earth feels like a heavy step back. The game seems to have lost a lot of the depth that it’s predecessor had, which is a very unfair thing to fault it with since the Civ:V it is being compared to had an avalanche of DLC and 2 game changing expansion packs. At the same time, is saying “it’ll be fixed in the DLC” an acceptable justification for a lesser feeling game? I want to say absolutely not, that is exactly the reason the AAA market is so god-awful right now. Instead, here I am, accepting that justification and eagerly anticipating the soon-to-be launch of the first expansion pack.

I can think of two conclusions to draw from my mixed bag of feelings towards Civilization: Beyond Earth. Either a) this franchise gets a pass on the whole DLC outrage; they have delivered in the past and the community knows that the content coming down the line means the base game is only the tip of the iceberg - and it will be worth every penny. Or b) I personally love both Civilization and sci-fi so my rose tinted glasses lets me glance over the arguably lackluster content found in Sid Meier's’ latest turn based strategy. Either way I wholeheartedly recommend this game because I love it and I think there are some awesome things to come.

Bloodline Champions is hands down the best venue for displaying player skill through accuracy, dexterity, intelligence, spatial awareness, teamplay, and knowledge. It'll ask you to execute pitch perfect combos via your abilities, aim them true (everything's a skillshot), weight in the benefits of your situation and adapt on the fly, coordinate with your team down to the second, and most importantly, learn every little detail about every bloodline in order to best counter it. Barring Quake and CS, you won't find a better title to test yourself as a gamer - BLC will flex absolutely every important gaming muscle of your being and give you the grounds to prove your worth.
It should be mentioned that as of the last few days the game is now being fully operated by Stunlock Studios - the actual creators of BLC - which is certainly a step up from its previous publishers who were seemingly running it down the ground with poor marketing and cheesy design implementations. Some time ago the progression system was accelerated, the bloodcoing yield increased, and the cost of bloodlines decreased - meaning you can now more easily acquire things in the game, including the much dreaded amulets and gems to slot. The benefits from leveling and statting up were always very marginal, but were the cause for much ire back in the day, for no good reason. Do try to disregard any people saying that the game is♥♥♥♥♥♥solely because there's a progression system - it is an annoyance at worst and if you're dedicated you won't care for them past setting your own builds.
The playerbase might not be very large, but it's a very dedicated bunch, which is why you'll often run into people with thousands of games and hours under their belts.
