I know what you're thinking so far, don't lie. You think this isn't worth your money, that it is just a cheap spin-off.
You are wrong... wait, no you aren't. It probably is a cheap spin-off, actually...
It might be that, but it is FUN. I was never a fan until I joined the High-Kill servers: Ridiculously fast-paced servers with low gravity and infinite ammo, where every kill is a spawn kill.
It will frustrate you at first, but turn your DPI, Framerate, and Reaction Times up and it is immensely satisfying. Every kill is a YouTube-worthy event, especially in slow motion. I recorded tens of hours and hundreds of gigabytes of footage. Because that's the thing. This game makes you WANT to record. After the first kill, you think "Holy Crap, nobody will ever see that again! How could this happen!" and you promply turn on your screen recorder. However, not recording it makes it that much enjoyable, knowing that every kill is an event that only you will witness.
Anyway, maybe I'm rambling, but maybe this mod is worth your money. Go get it.

Unfortunately, i cannot recommend Lost Grimoires: Stolen Kingdom for one simple reason: voiceovers do not work on Linux systems. (Some users report sound not working at all, but mine all works except for voiceovers.) i had not realized, until starting this game, how important voiceovers are. While everything they say is also printed on the screen, not having voiceovers makes the scenes somehow feel drab and lifeless (despite the excellent graphics).
(Yes, i HAVE tried every workaround which has been posted to-date about the problem. None of them work for me.)
The publisher knows about the sound problem, and has known its cause since at least mid-November, 2016 (an error in how they parse floating-point numbers in XML content), and yet no update is in sight. The recommended solution from the publishers is to change the system's regional settings, system-wide, to UK English. (That workaround doesn't work for me, and even if it did i wouldn't do it because i refuse to use UK English system settings.)
i'll reconsider this review when/if Artifex Mundi pushes an update which fixes the audio. However, i can't remember EVER having seen them push an update to one of their games, neither on Steam nor Android, so i'm not holding my breath for them to do so for this game.

Overall, definitely worth the price, but this game could be so much more with a bit more gameplay depth.

Bleed is a fun little action platformer.
In Bleed you play a highly mobile character who platforms while shooting using the analog stick (or mouse I assume). It's comparable to megaman in that it's a platform game with shooting and bosses, however there are a lot of big differences. In Bleed you are able to slow time. Now this might not be the most unique mechanic to video games in general but here it completely allows the game designers to be creative and make normal play very challenging, encouraging you to make careful use of the slow time mechanic. The game starts to feel extremely difficult until you realize it's designed around this mechanic, and you start to get better at managing your energy and slowing time during difficult sections or certain moves from bosses. The game is also different in that as I mentioned you shoot using any angle you wish, which again leads to enemies being more creative, more mobile, and generally harder to hit, but because you have the freedom to aim wherever you want this becomes all balanced out.
The game itself is flowing with creativity. The levels will surprise you from a moving train to a level that actually rotates while you're moving through it. The levels are designed to be very different and throw you for a loop, hoping for you to slow time to makes things managable. The bosses are also very well done. They have a lot of variety and expect a lot of your attention.
Bleed gives you choices in difficulty as well as some RPG elements in terms of upgrading your character and getting new weapons. In playing on the normal difficulty I was challenged but I was still able to beat the game without getting too frustrated. So when I first started playing this game, I was really concerned about the overall difficulty. The first several puzzles are very straightforward, and don't really involve too much thought. It takes a bit of tinkering to discover what a mechanic means and how it works, but I can at least say they are introduced in a way that allows you to fully understand each before moving on.
The game does get harder though, not by too much, but still, it becomes interesting. I'd say it's worth a buy just to see what the last level is.
Now for some more level-specific commentary:
Overall, a short, cute, puzzle game. The mechanics are a bit simplistic, and are developed very slowly, but they are still developed well. The last few levels of the game were fun in a way I don't think I've seen in any other puzzle game.
If you're looking for a chill not-too-difficult puzzle game, this is perfect for you. If you're like me and were looking for something a bit harder, this is still worth checking out. Think about what the mechanics really do, and how they work together. It could have been made to be a bit harder, but was still very carefully developed.

What are you looking for when looking at this game?
A simulator that has some strategy elements? Check.
A simple logic game that explores, albeit superficially, the market dynamics of drug development? Okay.
A game where the computer can beat you if you aren't paying attention? Done. (We all know games are much easier than they use to be)
You'll be satisfied enough, especially if you get it on-sale. The game touches on aspects of the pharmaceutical industry. No, you can't be as evil as you'd like, but the DLC can allow you to be fairly evil. Someone said something in their review about no price adjustment...you CAN price adjust if you have the DLC and patent your drugs. Just like real life.
There isn't the ethical dilemmas that really exist in real life, but those would be hard to replicate anyway without actually having a more human element to the game. Maybe in the future when AI becomes more relevant in video games you might be able to create an irrational element to it, but as of now it's just a computer buying your product following programming that tells it how to behave.
It's simple enough to be fun and has enough depth to be interesting.
P.S. had to mention that treating a disease is less profitable than curing it. It's economics. Someone said it and their ignorance hurt. On that note, you can create cures and treatments in this game. They don't always affect each other.

Bleed is a fast paced, beautiful little bullet time shooter with an unusual game feel. It took me some time to get used to, however, it has become one of my favourite game experiences I've had in a long time. Basically, you fight through a level of level themed mobs and challenges (sometimes with a mini boss included) and then fight a couple unique boss battles. In the end, it's a very short game, but it has a high replayabillity as you unlock more abillities as you go, allowing you to explore new weapons and capabillites. What also contributes to the replayabillity is the fact that as you up the difficulty on the game, the bosses gain more abillities. Finally, there is a boss arena that you can use to fight any boss, on any difficulty; you can even fight up to 4 bosses and mini bosses at once!
All in all, a good game, but you should probably wait for a sale if you're on a budget.

Even though I’ve given this game a thumbs down, it’s not bad! It’s just a shame compared to the other Hitman games.
In previous games you were let loose and could mix and match ways of finishing a mission, and although there are a few ways of beating levels in Absolution it really does have an idea of how it would like you to do it, and it doesn’t really work any other way. Casing point, there is an omnipresent score system that judges you as you play, now in previous games you would be judged also and given a rating at the end of the mission, but this felt far less intrusive. Whereas the score system in Absolution is like a pushy teacher who tuts and shakes their head as they mark you down for daring to have fun in a Hitman game. The create your own contract part is cool, and lets you have a bit more freedom, but little compared to previous games.
The dreadful psychic AI from Hitman 2 is back for seeing through your disguises rendering them practically useless. Also, there are some completely unrealistic scenarios for NPCs sussing you out. For example, in the second mission you can disguise yourself as a market chef, now in real life loads of market stalls open and close every day so there are constantly going to be new people coming and going. Yet the chefs in this market all know each other and chose to stop serving customers (and getting money) to chase you around the market. It makes sense for private guards to spot you, but not market workers.
The fun and chaotic melee system from Blood Money is replaced with *sigh* quick time events....
Also, they’ve removed the first person element to the game, which I only normally used when in a fire fight, but then that would involve me being able to play the game my way and not their way.
And then there is the ‘instinct’ rubbish, or should I say Spidysense. In previous hitman games you had to work things out for yourself and if you got caught you got caught and had to deal with it. Now you’re a superhero/matrix character who can pick where they want to shoot and have the game do it for them rather than actually doing it yourself. I am doing my best not to use this feature and just play the game through my own skill but sometimes the game just forces you to use it.
Now I’ve heard that the new Hitman game rectifies a lot of the issues of Absolution, and I look forward to playing that after I beat this one. Because even though I rag on it for not being a great Hitman game, it’s not a bad game in its own right, but I’m hoping to get through it quickly to move onto the next game.

Brilliant Shadows follows Ash after a ritual gives her an ambiguous result with far-reaching consequences. Her future, and eventually even her safety, are no longer guaranteed. Who, or what, is she bonded to? What does it mean for her and those around her?
The Good:
* First things first. This game is absolutely gorgeous. It has some of the best art of any visual novel I've played, done in a unique and consistent style that really meshes with the story.
* The worldbuilding happens naturally, over the course of the story, and is very solid.
* Ash's story is easy to get invested in, and it's impossible not to care about her.
* The soundtrack and sound effects are great, and pulled me in even more.
* The game is fully voice-acted, and the casting was very well done. I loved Ash's voice.
* The game gives feedback on choices that makes it easy to tell which ending you're moving toward.
* The game has some good representation. For example, Ash is gay, and it's important to the story without being the primary source of conflict.
* The game rewards multiple playthroughs by having things that are only meaningful with information from late in the game.
The Not-So-Good:
* While some choices have far-reaching consequences, others only change a few lines of dialogue and are quickly forgotten as the story gets back to its mostly-linear path.
* The good ending and the neutral ending are a little too similar.
* There is no CG gallery, which is a shame because of how beautiful the CGs are.
* There's a little bit at the end of the game that helps set up the series but feels very out-of-place in the story of this game.
* The worldbuilding can occasionally be a little fuzzy, especially the paladin/necromancer binary when confronted with later information.
I really loved this game. It wasn't without its issues, but they don't mean much next to all of the things the game did right. I really resonated with Ash, and I'm looking forward to getting more of her story in the sequel.

A very pleasant surprise!
Brilliant Shadows is a stylishly presented visual novel, with its own art style that isn't "just the usual anime". Characters are distinct, sprites are large and detailed, and it all fits together nicely.  It has a diverse cast in terms of race, sexuality, etc, but it doesn't fall into the trap of letting these attributes define the characters either - instead they are simply aspects of the characters which are there.
Characters are voice acted throughout, even minor characters, the writing's extremely readable with some humour, and there're a goodly number of choices built in throughout too.
And all this for a mere £5.  No, it's not perfect, there're the occasional minor typos here and there, or a line where the VA voiced it slightly differently to the written word, but the downsides are minor and there's so much good here that honestly, especially at this price point, it's an absolute steal.
And the good news is that if you DO enjoy this, there's a sequel (and a third on the way) with the same characters that continues their story (but this one works perfectly well as a self contained tale).
Recommended.

Ah yes, the least appreciated BioShock game. Hilariously enough, this game is like many "middle" siblings I know: underrated compared to the other two, and great in its own right.
The way I see it, BioShock Infinite has the best spectacle and sights, BioShock 2007 has the most creepy setting and thought-provoking material, but BioShock 2? It's got the emotional core that BioShock Infinite tries so hard to attain and the gameplay that BioShock 2007 wants to have.
Don't even get me STARTED on Eleanor.
I technically nominated this game twice for the Steam Awards 2017 (thanks Remastered Version that I didn't play!). Wish I could nominate it 3 times. This game made me think long and hard not just about the philosophy in the last game, but also about parenting. Surprisingly, no? Well...
SPOILERS AHEAD, PROCEED WITH CAUTION
Simply put, Eleanor learns how to act through how you treat your enemies (not the Splicers, because who cares about them?) and the Little Sisters. If you're a monster, she's a monster. If you show mercy, she shows mercy. BioShock 2 puts you in the position of a parent, and exceeds in teaching you, the parent, a valuable lesson: if you don't want your kids to be massive A-holes, DON'T be an A-hole yourself.
If you are a fan of the BioShock series and you haven't tried this, try it. Even if you aren't, I still think you should.
Also, if you have some problems running this on Windows 10 or whatever, google for fixes. You won't regret it.

Chaos theory is the best splinter cell game and arguably one of the best stealth games ever created.
The story is somewhat realistic and interesting. Tensions are running high as North Korea is threatening an all out war against America and her allies. You play as Sam Fisher, an ex-SEAL member now a 'cell' (spy) working for the a top secret sub-branch within the National Security Agency (NSA). It's your job to uncover who is behind jeopardising the relationship between the two countries and risking all out war.
The gameplay is the best component of the game. Before each mission you get a briefing with other members of Third Eschalon and their allies telling you the task and situation of the mission. You then get to select your loadout based on 'Stealth' (more stealth equipment like smoke grenades and sticky cameras), 'Assault' (More assault rifle ammo and frag grenades) or 'Reddington' (Mixture of the other two) which affects the types of equipment you will have and how much of each item you carry with you. The three options of equipment speak for themselves on how you want to approach the mission. The equipment you may have include the sileneced assault rifle, silenced pistol, sticky cameras, smoke grenades, stun grenades, frags etc. The objectives in each mission will generally require you to steal, sabotage or eliminate a target. As a 'splinter cell game' stealth gameplay is highly recommended. Besides hiding in the shadows, a new element plays a role in in the gameplay, noise. Creating too much noise (more than the ambient sound in the area which is indicated by a bar on your hud) will now cause foes to detect you which may include gun noises, broken glass and movement. As such, you can control your walking speed (which increases noise as it increases) via the scrolling the mouse wheel. The final element to the gameply is manipulating electronics via your pistol. By aiming your pistol and pressing right mouse button you can turn off an electronic device for a few seconds. The purpose of this is to not destroy the item and hence, alerting the gaurds. You can go all guns blazing in most of the missions, but this is not recommended as it not only ruins the atmosphere of the game, but you  die very quickly in frontal combat. As per usual you can eliminate gaurd using lethal force or non-lethal force. Shooting gaurds is lethal as well as choosing the lethal option when grabing them from behind. Non-lethal involves choosing non-lethal ammo and knocking gaurds out after grabbing them. Another new element to the gampley is the ability to quickly walk up to gaurds and knock them out/kill them, which helps when your about to be spotted at close range.
The level design is excellent. Each level is big and unique, spotting plenty of places places to hide in such as shadows. Furthermore, there are more than one route to reach objectives including vents, doors, tunnels etc. The graphics has also aged well and looks pleasant. Finally the levels are so well designed that you can go through the entire game without killing/knocking out anyone and not being detected either.
The audio is good. Voice actors (especially Sam) do a great job at instilling the emotions of the current situation. Weapon sound are also good as well. Each level has a unique track that is played while stealthed and while being spotted. Each level has a unique soundtrack for the the previous two situations, so you won't get bored from hearing the same tarck over and over again.
If you want one of the best stealth games ever made, chaos theory will not dissapoint you.

Finished one of the stories for
.  As much as I was worried that this game would overwhelm me and leave me feeling sad, there's a deeply human element to it; you care about the inhabitants of your house, you care about their emotions and their needs.  Every small victory feels immense, and while, yes, there are losses, they aren't treated cheaply.
One of the most emotional moments of play was when I broke into someone's house and knelt, peering through a doorway, watching an old husband and wife chatting in front of the fireplace.  They were talking about life before this war, life in other wars, and they had to keep prompting one another for memories.  I decided then that, even though I
needed to find some medicine for one of my people at home, I would not take any of the personal belongings on this property, only roam the periphery looking for garbage to rummage through.
As I stood up from the keyhole, they heard me.  "Bernard, what was that sound?" the wife asked.  He said he would go check it out.
I fled into their basement, hoping to find a place to hide -- except the door down there was barred, unbeknownst to me. Bernard walked down, saw me, and told me to leave.
As I went to click on the ladder behind him, I clicked on Bernard instead.
with the crowbar I had in my hands. Again and again because once I'd started, I couldn't stop. Just before I hit this old, unarmed man for the last time, he held his hands up over his head and begged, "Please don't kill me."
I didn't listen.
In his pockets?  The medicine I needed.
Feeling horrible about myself, I pocketed the medicine and continued to explore the house... and then I startled his wife. "Bernard!" she yelled, "Someone's here!"
She raced away from me.  She found him.  And she screamed, "Oh no!", knelt over his corpse, and
.  She didn't care about me ransacking her house. She was in the basement and I could hear her the whole time.
I restarted my game out of guilt.
Here's the thing: in so many games, the death of 'others' is treated callously.  They don't matter; they're just pixel people who have something the player might need, whether it's experience, treasure, progress towards a quest goal, etc.  The fact that
made me feel empathy and guilt towards those 'others', despite the fact that they had something I needed in order to save one of my own characters, is overwhelmingly cool.
There are so many little details like the above, all of which add up to create an incredible story experience.  There's still enough 'meat' to the mechanics that I've got three papers full of notes here on my desk to help keep myself organised. This is one of those
games.

This game isn't perfect. Far from it. I've run into bugs here and there, but nothing that's been fundamentally game breaking, so far.
On one trip, I had to cut it short because my car ran out of fuel and the gas station wasn't adding fuel to my car when I tried to use the pump, and my gas can wouldn't empty into the fuel tank either. Going back to Uncle's garage seemed to fix the issue. While that's a bit frustrating, it doesn't really take away from what I enjoy about the game.
It's just a nice, relaxing drive. Sometimes you see some cool things along the way, or you get excited finding a box along the side of the road. Sometimes you end up with a flat while you're on the side of a curving mountain road and you accidentally drop your spare tire down the hill and have to run after it.
But at the end of the day, it's a game that allows me to just take a nice, long break from whatever projects I'm working on. I can just focus on the driving and going from point A to point B, without any conflict, or worrying about missing secrets, or forgetting what my quest objectives were from the last time I played.
It's not a great game. Not perfect by far. But I've been enjoying the occasional updates and it's just nice to take a break and enjoy a road trip every now and again.

That was one of the best things about the first grid, it felt like your team. Now its just a sucsession of meaningless contract races and the only progression involved is watching some XP bars go up. Thats literally the progression, no unlocks, no buying cars, no customising, nada. But without a shadow of a doubt mybiggest gripe is the ommisin of pitstops. After damaging my car mid lap, i thought id pit and get some repairs. Spotted the pit lane entrance line, dove towards it, and hit a tyre wall blocking its entry. Really this is sub par for a racing game even if its trying to fit into the "simcade" category.
Now the multiplayer looked a lot more promicing in terms of progression, with a garage you could presumably fill with cars you actually buy, maybe even customise them. However after the stale taste i was left with by my singleplayer experience i didnt do much MPat all. I felt like they had gutted the best bits from SP an then tacked on a worse version to MP.
My advice for a winning grid title would be. Include pitstops, I mean really its a car game. Have a large garage we can use for both single and multiplayer, earning the same currency in both modes. Give us back team customisation, this really connects the player to the game. It makes it feel like its "yours", not a borrowed ride.

MMO Games that are free to play always seem to be a gamble that people have to make. There are ones that are filled with pay to win items, others that are sluggish without them, and then there's this work of art, which practically nails the Free to Play formula to a T. What really got me into this game wasn't the characters, it wasn't the story, it was how well they let you play the game, without spending a dime. Nearly any item you could want is obtainable purely through playing the actual game, and without too much effort on your part, I might add. Inventory and vault expansions are easy to get through just playing the game during certain events that happen quite often in the game. Cosmetic items can be obtained through a currency made for people with no money, and that currency can be obtained through running dungeons that are on your level, hardly rocket science. The in game shop gives no impossibly large advantage to the people who do have money, however. It may help them get started faster, with nice titles with stats, however, just by playing the game for a while, you can get titles that outshine those easily as well. Once more, the item shop is for convenience, but not too much of that. It won't just give you money outright, it'll give you some tools that let you get money, but you need to put in the effort. It might let you enter a hard dungon again, or it might give you an exp boost for a while, either way, these are items you can just get by
! I'm not saying this game is perfect, there are flaws that it has, as all games do, but if you want a MMO to play without money needed to be pumped into it, this game is a perfect candidate.
Note: You
still do research on this game before you start playing, it's an MMO, and like most MMOS, it'll have a bunch of facts that you probably won't know about until you play for a while. I recommend this spreadsheet:
. Omitting the jokish name, it's a pretty good guide that tells you a lot about the game, I wouldn't recommend reading through the whole thing in 1 sitting, but you should look through some of the tabs that pique your interest.

There are three different endings to the game depending on what choices you pick throughout the game, they seem to control the protagonists outlook on life, if she'll turn out good or "evil".

There's a free prequel Embers of Magic on steam that gives a short but well presented idea of what to expect of this VN, even if it's tone is more lighthearted.

This VN doesn't have an auto-play function, apparently due to engine limitation, which almost made me put the prequel aside, I am glad I didn't. In the long run it didn't annoy me too much as every character was voiced in both the prequel and in this VN.

While the premise and setting is interesting enough to get hooked into, the story pretty much becomes a generic fight-the-bad-guys shooter. The variety of weapons and arsenal is big enough to fiddle around for a short singleplayer campaign, but the maps are highly restrictive with many invisible boundaries that cannot be crossed or jumped over, such as the playground path, certain ramps, walls, and in some cases, grass. The destructive environment adds a nice touch, but overall I cannot exactly see any memorable events or replay value in its singleplayer campaign. In addition, major bugs still exist, rendering NPCs stuck and story not being able to progress smoothly.
Overall, the story was playable enough. The inclusion of a collectible mechanic in the game seems weird, but the newspaper articles do contribute enough to the storyline. The sketchy invisible walls do make the game mediocre compared to other shooters out there, however, making the path extremely linear despite the map's relatively large size. The controls are average, though I experience no input lag unlike some other players. The player is only able to interact at certain timings, such as when your friendly teammate has (almost) finished climbing the ladder or when everyone else has jumped down into the tunnel, which then you can press an interact button to do whatever is asked of  you. The dialogue, while to some extent interesting and realistic, can get extremely annoying when trying to fulfill certain missions. Time taken to complete singleplayer: 3.7 hours.

Really several tiers above the average Visual Novel. This was actually one of the first VNs where I cared more about what would happen next then what ending I wanted to get, which I was not expecting at all.
I feel it's probably good to get all the cons out of the way first, because there aren't too many, and they are balanced out well.
First off, the voice acting and diologue sometimes seem a little bit amateurish. It doesn't come up too often, but occasionally you get the idea that these people have not done this before, and aren't too settled in it.
Secondly, there are some times when you really start to feel the exposition heavily. This is mostly when characters are talking about how sexuality is viewed in the world, and they are speaking more towards the reader than what someone would naturally say in the situation.
And finally, there are one or two choices where it's not entirely clear what you are selecting. Nothing too drastic, or that would get you a suprise bad ending, but I did get surprised at what happened from a few choices.
Those issues, however, are pretty few and far between. And never so drastic to break the narrative, which is really uite good.
The plot is first class. Period. This is a well realized world, with a lot of things left unexplained that make it feel more alive. You can tell a lot of thought went in to all of it, and it pays off. The story going on in this world, too, has a couple of good twists, but also the meat to keep you going between them. The twists are also payed off quickly enough that you don't feel like anyone is particularly stupid. And, despite being the first part, it has a fairly satisfying ending, without any cliffhangers stapled on to the end.
The characters are also quite good, and all the mains seem to have greater depth than I normally expect from this type of game. They also deal with some issues that are rarely addressed by any game, which I won't spoil, but really struck me as things that real people deal with more often than is represented.
The art is great. Pretty much perfect. Each character has many expressions that fit whatever is going on at the time and nothing is reapeated enough to seem lazy or anything. It also just looks gorgeous.
And finally, the voice acting. Yes, I mentioned there are some less than great moments, but when it is good, it is really really good. The voice actors definately care about their characters and care about doing well, which is missing from some games with much bigger budgets. Nobody is bored and nobody is phoning it in, and everybody gives the emotional stakes they need to. Also, The mains have very nice voices to hear.
All in all, a great VN, not exactly the Dating sim I had expected, but it fulfilled that need and so much more.
Also, blooper reel at the end, very good!

Homefront doesn't bring much to the table for the FPS genre. It seems like a poor rip off from a Modern Warefare series.
It's not polished, the playing field is litered with invisible walls, bugs and infinite spawning enemies that at times, can be frustrating.
The Guerilla difficulty, the mode I beat the game on first time around in a mere 5 hours, simply handicaps the players ability to take hits, in a game where the regeneration of your health restores faster than Master Chiefs shields recharge, provides only a slight inconvinence, rather than a challenge.
The gun play is static, with the guns containing the most ammo in a magazine preferrable, as weapons seamingly deal the same amount of damage regardless.  There isn't anything exciting here. There is, however, an impressive array of weapons, that do feel pasted straight out of a Call of Duty MW series. But again, the similarities, and the deaths of the enemies, are too poor that I relate you to my previous statement.
The acting is poor at best, and you can't really feel connected to anyone at any time. The story was incredibly predictable but to its credit, is well put together. The opening of the game provides a deep depressive state that feels more like something out of Naughty Dog's The Last of Us series. Although this wears of after you realise the faction that recruits you seems to be more equiped to wage war on the world rather than a revolution.
The game crashed on several occassions for no apparent reasons, I noted several game breaking bugs and also the hit detection was hit and miss.
It wasn't all bad, one of the missions I felt were particularly good. Given the protaganists desired skill set, I was disappointed to only see his skills put to use once it was a shame to have not put more effort here and make it more a USP for the game.
Overall, it wasn't a bad experience. It was incredibly short and easy. With a story that seemed to stall very early on. The gameplay is mediocre at best with some interesting concepts put in. I enjoyed beating the game and almost glad the game didn't drag on.
I would recommend the game, heavily discounted.

A superbly cerebral challenge. While it can be daunting at first, as the game throws machines, ingredients, concentration and catalyst mechanics at you, then pours a layer of supply/demand economics on top of it, this game handily avoids a lot of the pitfalls of more traditional economic management sims & city builders. This is primarily because the ingredients, catalysts and cure upgrades are all randomised. So there is no single "best layout" that works in every map for every challenge. You aren't simply creating 2 farms, 2 mills, 1 bakery, in the tightest formation allowed.
Instead, you spent a lot of your time looking at potential cures, looking at the ingredients that lead to it, and working out whether the end product might be worth trying to create the production line for it. Then it's down to arranging the machines in such a way as to produce the product. Mistakes happen early and often, but you get the hang of it with enough practice.
The research and development arms of the game give a real sense of progression as you open up new options for cures and expansion. Finally, you have to make sure you're not oversaturating the market between your own products and your competitors.
It's loads of fun and every bit of complexity is well placed to make for interesting, challenging decisions.

So, MPQ.. yeah.  It's a game that comes in a lot of stages and as a result is very deceptive about what it is.
For the most part it's like any other Puzzle Quest game.  At the very beginning you'll progress through a story mode, where about half of the fights are against minions (characters that do not match gems).  It takes a while but eventually you'll be fighting against villains that  match and use skills.
After you build up a few of the starting characters you'll start participating in the player vs player and player vs environment events.  In these events you'll compete against other players for ranking (prizes).  An event ends almost every day, so you'll probably end up playing every day to maintain a high score.  How you play will change a lot as you transition from starting characters (one stars) to mid level ones (two stars) and then into high level ones (three and four stars).  Having a roster of three stars allows you to more easily compete in the tournaments.
The game itself is well designed in that it will hit every one of those points that keeps a player playing (events that have a definite ending, a pokemon-esque roster that keeps you intrigued, timers on healing and health packs, and a currency used to level said roster).  Transitioning from one stars into two stars and then two stars into three stars is a fantastic feeling and the gameplay really changes when you do.
However, because of how the game is designed, there are a bunch of flaws.  For one, it's almost never ideal to enter an event until just before it ends due to  bracket placement and rubberbanding (your nodes will score a lot more later in an event than earlier, so you'll catch up to a top rank player very very quickly).  Of course, rubberbanding doesn't exist in all of the PvE maps but it's in most.  As for bracket placement: when you enter an event you're put into a bracket with other players that entered around the same time.  Entering late usually guarantees that the top players of your event will not score as high, making it far easier to place higher (and thus get better rewards).
The biggest problem, though, is with the system called "MMR."  MMR is effectively an invisible score attributed to your account that more or less compromises your win/loss ratio, pitting you against other players with similar MMR.  This sounds like it would balance the game a lot -- and it sort of does -- but in actuallity it makes climbing early stages of brackets much more difficult than it should be, since you'll be fighting similarly leveled rosters for marginal point gains (so you'll be taking tons of damage).
Since I've started playing, the transition into two star rosters was made negligible, as two star covers are given out very, very frequently.  Transitioning into three star rosters was also made easier, but it still takes more than a couple of months to break into them after you've made a strong two star lineup.
While I greatly enjoyed this game while playing, I ended up leaving due to it taking up a significant amount of my time (minimum of an hour a day, sometimes up to 4 or 5) just to stay competitive.  That, alongside of a fairly venomous (if you arent scoring well enough in any event, most alliances will just kick you on the spot and take in a new member: I was threatened three or four times with removal from my alliance over a point total in a PvE event with rubberbanding.  Low and behold I score a ton of points right at the end and place in about the middle of the alliance, this over the course of about two hours compared to the 6 to 8 each other person in my alliance was putting in, but they were still talking about kicking me lol) end game community just pushed me away and made me say "Yeah, I'd rather play other games with my friends than devote time to this."
Anyway, hey, the game is well designed but I'm not so sure the developers really care about it being fun so much as making money out of it.  Your mileage may vary and it takes a significant amount of time to get anywhere, but yeah, I had a really good time with it.  Shame that the community really pushed me out, but whatcha gon' do?

A *very* fun and cute shopkeeper game. If you've played Receatter, then the gameplay style is very similar.
Plotwise, you've taken out a school loan, a portion that needs to be repaid each week. In order to repay your loan, you've opened a shop catering to RPG stereotypes (clerics, warriors, ninjas etc). To stock your shop, you're mainly expected to "run" dungeons and get loot. The actual running of the dungeon is automated, but it's the looting that you control. In order to loot stuff, you need to fit them in your lootbag. Each item has a unique shape, so fitting everything in your lootbag becomes a puzzle. But you can't take your time turning and flipping items to fit in your lootbag, as each dungeon run essentially has a timer. Once the timer runs out, anything you failed to loot gets lost.
Once you think you have enough loot, you can sell them in your shop. You have the option of outfitting your shop with tables and shelves that possess unique bonuses (armor shelves give a bonus to armor price etc), as well as ancillary furniture that can buff prices further, attract more customers to your store, attract certain RPG classes to your store (warriors, mages etc) and so on.
There is also a crafting system. You can craft better items by combining loot with ingredients. This way, you can "value add" to your existing loot if you have sufficient ingredients.
There are a few minor UI / QoL issues that prevent this from being the "perfect" shopkeeper game. Feedback and data are lacking for a shopkeeper game. For example, I can't tell how appealing my store is to certain classes, or what influence does lower prices have. I mean, I know that lower prices will increase the likelihood of being sold, but will it attract more traffic to my store as well?
But these objections are minor. If you enjoyed Receatter, you'll definitely enjoy this game. Strongly recommended!!!

...is a physics-based puzzle game. Help a crazy inventor build wacky contraptions to cause a chain reaction in order to achieve specific goals. This review includes the
and the
DLCs.
The
franchise is the spiritual successor to
where, just like this one, you build devices à la Mouse Trap best explain with an example: Drop the ball which flips a lever, which turns on an engine, which activates a conveyor, which moves a box, which pushes a button, which turns on a toaster, which pops a toast, which hits a switch, which lights a torch, which ignites the rocket you've been trying to launch. You get the idea.
You have a series of Puzzles you must solve by figuring where to put the missing parts in an incomplete contraption. There are also Challenges which gives you a base setting from which you build contraptions of your choosing to achieve the goal. Then, there is the Editor which is a sandbox free play you can assemble contraptions of your own design.
There's a large variety of parts to pick from when building your contraptions, each of which will react to multiple elements and can serve different purposes: a torch can ignite fuses, heat boilers, or even serve as a light source for solar panels, wood planks can serve as shelves or walls, can rotate on axles, or light up on fire, and so forth. This is in addition to the environmental effects such as wind, weather, and even gravity that will affect the results.
Graphics are bright and colorful, each part being distinct and easy to recognize. The user interface is further simplified with quick access to any item description, just hover your mouse over it to get a quick description of the part and a list of elements (fire, electricity, rotation, light, etc.) it can interact with, making the game very accessible.
Developers probaly tried too hard to be original with the parts. I mean, objects such as flying saucers being attracted to planet-looking balloons, or weather machines that launch lightning-bolt-spitting clouds, are quite a departure from the traditional "home-made contraptions" the attraction for this game usually comes from. Even the aesthetics are items built on plywood sheets in a backyard or a brick wall, instead of the basement laboratory theme  people have come to expect and love.
Difficulty has been dropped from past games by a milestone. The 140 Puzzles are way too easy to figure out, you are given the exact amount of part you need to complete it, the background limits the locations you can place them, and there are floating cogs you must collect which serves as additional clues to show you exactly how you should solve it. While the Challenges give you more freedom to solve theme, there's only 30 of them.
The reason people have always come back to such games was to design contraptions of your own, but here, you are limited in the quantity of parts you can put by an arbitrary currency and value-based parts. Furthermore, the goal of self-made contraptions is to design puzzles of your own, choosing which parts players can use to complete it, and what goals the puzzle has, yet there is no way to export and share them with other players, so what's the point?
If you wish to recreate Pee-Wee's Breakfast Machine from
, this isn't the best iteration for it. Still, there are plenty of puzzles to pick your brain to keep you occupied, at least for a time. Veterans might not find their fill, but it's an easy entry point for those who never played these games before, the target audience I am recommending it to.

I like management games like this, so I was excited to play this one when it came up in my queue. Unfortunately, it's simply very tedious and repetitive rather than any kind of fun. It has nice art and good aesthetic, but that won't save mindless and pointless constant click-click-click-click-clicking.
- Every day you set up to sell, you have to rechoose all of the items. There's no automation, no "choose best". When your shop expands, that's a lot of clicking.
- When you select a table space, the list of items you can choose from are not the ones the table uses. So you click on an Weapon table, and it shows you whatever items you had selected last (was it Armor? Misc? All? Who knows!) Which means yet another pointless, poorly designed need to click.
- When you're crafting (especially from a big list) there's no indicator of what you can actually make, so you just have to click down through the entire list to see which ones you can make... over and over and over.
- None of the equip screens (weapon, item, decoration, etc.) actually show you what you currently have, so there's no way to compare. If you want to buy or equip something, you're going back and forth between many different menus, just to see if that wallpaper is better than your current one.
- The shape of the items in the battle screen quickly become tedious to fit together, and the items disappear so fast that it feels more like mashing items into your bag mindless than any actual strategy.
- There's some kind of "hanging out in the park with potential customers" that has no explanation or seeming effect at all on the game
- Reorganizing the shop is hugely tedious because you can't move furniture unless the items are all off of them. WTF?! So you have to click on each item—hoping you clicked on the item and not the table—then remove the item on each space. Do this for every piece of furniture, rearrange.
- Speaking of rearranging, furniture only shows you the aura if you select *and then move it*. If you just select it, nope... no aura. Makes moving even more tedious.
- Once you've played the first part of the game, you've played the whole game. Nothing interesting happens. Oh but you can garden, which means more tedious clicking... ok.
Basically, the developer has a good idea but the game has really obnoxiously poor user experience design. If you like menu simulators and pointless clicking (not even the kind that give you a reward, just clicking in menus) this might be the game for you.

The main reason I am writing a review at this time is to help shed some light on all the misleading reviews.
First off, I bought this game fully expecting bugs and glitches as I play early access/alpha/beta games all the time.
If you don't want to deal with bugs and help with the development process, then please don't buy the game.
Now onto the game.
Will it run?
It's hard to say whether or not the game will work with your machine hardware at this point since there is still a lot of optimization to be done, but I have been able to get the game running on many different hardware configs including: intel i5-4700k, amd 8350, xeon e3-1230, xeon e5-2640, i7-7700k, and even an old intel X5650 for CPUs. For graphics: GTX 660, GTX 960, GTX 1050, and a GTX 1080ti have worked.
All machines were on either DDR3 or DDR4 with speeds ranging from 1300mhz on up.
Screen resolutions are 1080@60hz on the low end and 1440@144hz on the high end.
How are the graphics, bugs, and crashing?
There are bugs. The game crashed on my first time loading. My main menu was flashing with green every other frame. My settings wouldn't stick when clicking apply(use accept instead). Once in game, the graphics looked like poop and there was some graphical lag among other weird smearing and things. After playing with video settings(trying different resolutions, frame rates, fullscreen vs windowed etc...trial and error), I was able to finally get the game to run smoothly and very beautifully. 90% of the time it's smooth and looks just as beautiful or better than Skyrim(for reference).
Is it fun?
I have really enjoyed the game thus far. I would highly recommend playing on a public server(feel free to join mine) or make a server with some friends. The game really seems to be designed around the multiplayer experience and playing by yourself could be much more boring if you play the game without using cheats or modding the rates at which you progress in the game(xp, knowledge, etc).
I'm not sure if the devs are going to change the xp and knowledge gain at some later point for a better balance, but personally would recommend doubling the xp, knowledge, and resource amount you get(most servers already do this).
The spells are fun even if they could use another graphical pass.
Building is a really enjoyable experience that is addicting.
Resource gathering and crafting are pretty fun as well and don't require too much extra tedium.
The loot drops from monsters are a bit underwhelming at this point, but i think it has more to do with a lack of content at this point as most of the stuff you can craft is better than what you would typically find in chests.
There are a few minor crafting glitches where you will have to exit and reopen crafting to get it to work or cancel something you didn't start before you can start crafting what you want.
My biggest complaint is the AI at this point. Sometimes the AI will dodge and run around trying to kill you which is good fun. Other times they will stand there doing nothing, run away, or glitch through a mountain and keep shooting at you.
There are a few minor bugs with tamed creatures as well. For example if you use fast travel then your creatures may never follow you again.
The game is definitely in a playable and fun state, but it sorely needs some polish and a bit more content to really make it stand out as a jewel in the gaming community.

Crazy Machines Elements is a 2011 game from the Crazy Machines series, could be called "Crazy Machines 3". It's a game of Incredible Machines genre, where you have to solve the linear puzzles by placing lacking elements in the contraption. This game also came out for Xbox 360 and PS4. If I am not mistaking, those versions had leaderboards implented, while Steam version doesn't make use of any online features. Even achievements are done in game itself, no Steam ones.
And presentation is really great here. The graphics are really amazing. Well, sure, maybe technical side lacks whatever graphics-crazy people are hyped over nowadays, but with more colrful and nice art style it gives us incredibly atmosphere. Each element appears more of toy-like, jolly for eyes. Thanks to that, you can tell away what contraption is about from the first look, unlike Crazy Machines 2 where you had to focus to tell away what is what. Well, game sure doesn't try to be too realistical, you suck UFOs into vaccum cleaner there after all.
Music playes it safe. Nothing terribly original or memoriable. But it's great and doesn't repeat often, helping you to immerse yourself on thinking over the puzzle.
The game takes place at outdoor placed, like Professor's backyard, where he screws gravity up with his inventions with no care for neighbours. Professor himself finally took care of his hair and rarely appears in the game itself, not even talking to you anymore. Actually, there isn't even hint on intro plot for puzzles anymore. Previous games had little instructions written for each puzzles, like "I need that basketball to 1v1 Einstein". But that's not something people will miss anyway.
Outdoor enviroments not only give you gorgeous scenery, but you also can't place elements just in air. You can place them only on the walls, in whatever way they are placed. The layout of the wall can also give you visual clues to help you. And you will have to appericate that, as there is no hints system in this game. You will have to figure it out on your own and with visual clues. At least it doesn't have cheap puzzles with ridiculous solutions like Crazy Machines 1 does.
Gameplay-wise it's somewhere closer to the first Crazy Machines. If you don't know, Crazy Machines 2 was more focused on building and connecting complex systems of gears and pipes and lasers. Elements reverts gear system back to simplicity of the first title.
Completely removes steam pipes. Less things to do with laser. Perhaps it tries to focus more on physical puzzles, removing every other fluff and "time-wasting" parts. Even dominoes aren't in this game. It does add few more elements and focuses on Elements. Well, or more exactly electricity and fire. And how bolt of electricity can set things on fire. And wind messing your experiements up too.
As said, think of Crazy Machines 1, with slightly different focus. At least I don't miss having to decide if I need small, medium or large gear in CM2.
Oh, and now description of each elements shows you a bunch of icons too, that explains it's special properties, like "can be set on fire, can be tied to rope". If you get stuck, feel free to check each elements. Perhaps you will find out that some element is electricity conductor too.
Oh, and bonus. Instead of providing bonus objective, there are now golden gears placed through the puzzle level. They have to be touched by elements to be picked up, and you should get them all to count puzzle as 100% complete in a proper way. It's developers way of making sure that those who want to fully beat the game have to fully find the most complete solution. But I have to say, in some puzzles I found some elements aren't needed to solve them. No idea.
Didn't go without technical flaws though. While it's not as broken as Crazy Machines 2, it still got some small stuff. Mostly, rare cases of physics bugs. When placement of unrelated to chain reaction element may lead to change in behavior of another object. I also think that in rarely I encountered some slight placement-grid part, where element seemed slightly misplaced on the grid. Could be just me. But sometimes it may be good to restart the puzzle fully, just in case.
The game has three modes to play:
Puzzles - Your classic Crazy Machines puzzles where you have to place given elements to solve the contraption. There are 100 of them, plus 40 from DLCs.
Challenge - Now that's something new to the series. For those who complained about linear puzzles. Instead you have simple goal and then given full list of elements, with some of them locked for sake of challenge. And you are given 2000 or so points that you spend by placing elements of different costs. Game also tracks the amount of elements and time it took you to beat the challenge. The less the better.
There are around 20 challenges, plus 10 from DLCs. They are either easy, designed for sake of getting high score, or quite a tough nut to crack. Lost of placement tweaking around.
I know that consoles has online leaderboard for this mode, so you could see all the creative ways that players solved challenges by. But in Steam version you will not challenge anybody, I am afraid. Just beat the stages.
Not really fan of this mode myself.
Editor - Your usual sandboxish editor that allows you to build contraptions. Some silly fun, I guess. You can build proper puzzles too. But there is no online feature to share your creations. I didn't even find the file where puzzles are saved. So, I am afraid, you may not have fun with community works and not going to awe online friends. Dissapointing.
So, in conclusion, Crazy Machines Elements, while not being true continuation of Crazy Machines 2 ideas, still delivers. Combined with presenation, it's one of the best Incredible-genre games you will find on the Steam. Not to mentioning that it doesn't have technical problems of CM2, nor cheap ridiculous puzzles of CM1. So, all the fun.

This game is ridicilious. If you liked Civ 5 - dont buy it. If you liked Alpha Centauri - also, dont buy it!
I played CIV 2-5 as well as Alpha Centauri and I hoped this would be like Alpha Centauri. But it wasnt. It also wasnt like Civ 5. In fact, it's essentially a Civ 5 Multiplayer Space Mod that takes away everything that is good about Civ 5 and leaves only boredom.
My biggest problem with the game is that it takes forever so that planets are rarely fully colonized, the aliens are annoying and the AI is even more stupid than the Civ 5 AI. Unit customization is a joke and there is little atmosphere.
1. It takes forever to get anywhere here.
Spawn cities like Attila the hun in Civ 5? No way (aliens, content & slow expansion and long building times in general wont allow for that). Even when played on fast pace, the game is increadibly slow paced. A LOT, really A LOT slower than Civ 5, both research-wise and city-expansion wise and building time wise. You go to war with your 4 cities against the enemies 3-5 cities empire and then when you win and capture another city from another faction you're essentially the boss. Because with 8-10 cities vs. their around 5-6 cities (at that point) they will hardly catch up.
2. The aliens seriously inhibit expansion in early game.
You cant spawn cities like crazy like in Civ 5. Now, maybe that is a good thing for some. Maybe you dont want 5 cities by turn 50. But the aliens are annoying in that they are really random and play a huge part in early game (a siege worm can easily randomly destroy all ur army in early game) so that multiplayer matches are not fair (never lost one, but thought I mention it anyway).
Anyway. The thing is, you also cant expand later, at least not until the "early" LATEgame (!). Expansion in midgame is still quite limited. In fact, as pointed out above, in turn 150 on Difficulty hard (Gemini or Soyuz, I dont remember) much or even most of the planet isnt colonized. I dont know what game the game magazines play in all those reviews where there are dozens of cities covering the whole planet, but it must be really REALLY late game. And because I was increadible bored I never really went a lot further than like turn 150 (maybe turn 175 or so).
3. For some reason, the AI on difficulty 4 out of 6 sometimes doesnt expand at all. I saw the "Brasilia" (German, dunno how they are called in English) faction with exactly one city by turn 150. Maybe they had another one somewhere hidden but I dont think so. At turn 150 in Civ 5, pretty much the whole planet is covered in cities. I dont expect it to be the same in BE but one city? Seriously?
4. Unit customization - aehm, yes?
- You can customize your units by choosing from two possible upgrades when developing certain technologies. It's very linear and not interesting at all. You cant really design a completely new unit like in Alpha Centauri.
- In addition to this, experience-based abilities are less interesting than in Civ 5 or any Civ game, for that matter.
- Lastly, no special units for the factions.
= all in all, a worse experience (regarding unit diversity) than any previously played civilization game.
5. Atmosphere
Sometimes you get a bit of it. Sometimes it looks nice, somewhere on the planet. The launch video was great. But that's it. Because of the boring and confusing tech tree, the lacking ability to customize ur units or have them at least as interesting as in Civ 5, the stupid AI and the slow expansion, the game is just boring and if you add in, that the planets are a bit too dark often, you never get a really good atmosphere.
Summary:
I cant recommend this game at all. What annoys me the most is the impossibility of fast expansion and the slow advancement through the boring & confusing tech tree, resulting in endless matches, particularly but not limited to multiplayer. Since I bought this game, I have played a lot more Civ 5 than I played BE.
The VERY LEAST to make this game playable would be an option to make building and research even faster than the current "fast" setting, because for me personally, that just takes too long as compared to Civ 5.
About 20 hours of funny puzzles for a low price (got it in complete pack in discount). It sure is worth the price !!!

As you can see by my playing time, I beat the whole game and in no case I would recommend this game.
Don't get blended by the graphics and buy Crazy Machines 1, Crazy Machines 2, The Incredible Machine or if your kid is just 6 years old Crazy Machines 1.5.
There are 3 terrible terrible mistakes in this game:
1) Inconsistent Physics: Imagine an object is flying on the left side of the screen. It always has the same trajectory, but if you place an element on the bottom right corner, which doesn't interfere with the other object, suddenly the trajectory changes and making it often impossible/very difficult to finish the task.
2) The grid on which you place your elements is way too big, causing a lot of unnecessary trouble. Imagine your idea/plan is absolutely correct, but you cannot execute it, because the laserbeam misses your mirror by 2 length-units, but you can move the mirror in the grid only by 10 length-units, causing the beam to miss your mirror again. This makes a lot of trial&error work necessary, even though it could have been easily avoided. In no other Crazy Machines game this was as annoying as here.
3) And that is the absolute deal-breaker here. You get punished if your solution is more intelligent than the default solution. The rewards are not task-based (the less you use, the better), but instead path-based. This means you have to place objects the way the game thought for you. Because if you don't, the trajectory of objects might be different and you won't be able to collect the cogs in the level. This is such a horrible design choice, I can't imagine why any sane developer would make this.
There is also something other bothering me and that was the "help". By looking at the shape of the background you can instantly see what object has to be placed. For example mirrors belong onto circle-shaped wood and generators on square-shaped wood. This dumbs the game down and no, that's not suitable for very young children, because Crazy Machines 1.5 makes it right. In that game are easier tasks, and more puzzles in between, so the difficulty doesn't rise too fast, but it does not dumb the puzzles down.
Stay away from this game and don't bother playing it. Get the other games I listed in the beginning of the review.

Rapture has always had a heart and a soul, and the sequel continues to be an excellent game, even if the multiplayer is mostly a gimmick, mostly generic, and mostly dead.

God, this game is RIDICULOUSLY well-designed.
It's an abstract, minimalistic puzzle game like no other; it's probably closest to klocki (another clever minimalist puzzle game I'd recommend with unique mechanics by the same developer), but even then it's still very different from its predecessor.
To play PUSH, you must press buttons on 3-dimensional objects, and in a specific sequence or pattern. And at the same time, like with klocki, you must also figure out the mechanics or rules of the button patterns, or the entire pattern resets. This leads to a sort of investigative trial-and-error gameplay that just feels genius when all put together (how do people even design puzzles like this?). Again like klocki, the game starts almost trivially easy and smoothly transitions to more tricky puzzling, especially as the different mechanics combine together.
The whole experience feels like playing through a visual-spacial, mental-rotation, intelligence test. But unlike the IQ tests, the game also feels rewarding and soothing with its abstract visual design, soothing music, and forgiving gameplay that rewards experimentation. It's also very affordable, like $1? If you appreciate simple games with unique gameplay, I would definitely recommend giving this game a try.
(One note though: I would recommend playing through the game by actually trying to understand the rules of each mechanic and pattern. Just like with other finite puzzle games on PC, it is possible to solve each puzzle by randomly guessing, but that kind of playstyle doesn't really reward you for seeing how each button is connected in sequence.)

With the direction this game is currently going in - No, I would not recommend playing MapleStory.
I have been playing MapleStory for years, as such I've chosen to stick by it through good times and bad; but I have to say that I am not happy with Global MapleStory's choices, as of late. It seems that Global MapleStory wants to make itself the superior version of MapleStory, but it has a very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥way of trying to achieve this. So far, pretty much every attempt at being different from the mother version of the game, KMS(Korean MapleStory), has been an annoying step-down from what could have been awesome. For the last few years, GMS has made unneccesary changes to content coming from KMS to make it seem like their version of MapleStory is somehow "different". The problem is, these changes have always been sloppy, and they've continued to hold the game back from being much better.
In my opinion, what GMS should be focusing on is creating completely NEW content that could easily go side-by-side with anything we receive from KMS, rather than making nitpicky changes and removing pieces of content that players have been looking forward to for months.
The main problem with the game is how Pay-To-Win it feels, and it is sad to see that unlike KMS, which has been slowely making attempts to make the game fair for non-paying players, GMS has continued to hold the game back in its Pay-To-Win state. For example, in the Korean MapleStory as part of the "RED" update they added things like an Auction House, allowing players to buy and sell items from other users without needing to purchase a permit with real-money. GMS has opted not to add this to the game, claiming that it had some "problems that needed fixing" but months have passed and we've seen no news on it actually coming for us. Another example of ways that KMS had attempted to walk away from Pay-To-Win (and another example of how GMS simply ignored those changes to continue on their Pay-To-Win path) is the "Maple Mileage" system which allowed you to optain mileage through playing the game, and having the option to pay for Cash Shop (real money) items using Mileage instead! This meant that anybody who played long enough could have the option to EARN Cash Shop items through playing if they chose to do so. Of course, in a decision that surprised no-one, GMS simply did not make any attempts to add this feature to our version of the game.
There are many other features that helped even the playing field with paying players and non-paying players, and I could go on-and-on about what else GMS has decided to skip, but I'll stop there. (If you'd like, you could look up things like Additional Options which added all sorts of randomized stats to your items to help players who weren't quite powerful enough to fight Bosses for their loot. You could also look into how KMS added the ability to buy 'Maple Points' with in-game currency. Maple Points being an alternative to NX, which is what you use to buy things from the real-money 'Cash Shop'.)
I continue playing this game in hopes that one day these things and more will be added to make the game friendlier to non-paying players, but only time will tell if any of these will happen. For now I would stay away from MapleStory, as it continues to give the Free-To-Play genre a bad name.

+ With a different career experience this time ‘round, the more story-focused single-player feels a lot more fleshed out than its predecessor. Feeling like a driving personality rather than a member of a team makes the solo experience much more memorable and charming. Clocking in at around 11 hours, the career mode is easily long enough to satisfy gamers who enjoy a bit of character with their driving experience
+ Again, just like the first game, the handling strikes the perfect balance between simulation and arcade. While I will admit there is a bit more of a learning curve when it comes to oversteering (especially when it comes to drift events), and less customisation when it comes to driving assists, there’s still no denying that the driving is as fun as ever
+ Different to the first game however, this game seems to focus a bit more on street circuits, as a lot of the newly added tracks take place in city streets rather than strictly closed-off racing circuits. This does give the game a slightly more arcade aesthetic than the previous game, but for me it didn’t really detract from the experience at all (though people who prefer simulation games may be put off by this)
+ Compared to its predecessor, the graphics here are a definite step up. Every positive graphical aspect that was in the first game has been touched up and been given even more polish (though the bloom effect is a tad excessive).
- While the game does have a lengthy career, compared to the first game, there is a noticeable lack of variety in the courses. While the game does add a good amount of new tracks, it also reuses quite a lot from the previous game, which does hurt the total amount of different and unique tracks that you can race on
- The same audio problem that existed in the first game is still present here, in terms of the in-game dialogue getting boring and repetitive. If that was an issue for you before, not much has changed unfortunately (though I do prefer the voice actor more so this time around).
• Codemasters decided to remove the in-car view in this entry of the series. Personally, I have never used this view in a driving game, so the absence of this did not phase me at all. However, if you are the sort of person who does play their driving games using that view, then you will be disappointed in this aspect (though there is a community mod that adds an in-car view if you want to check that out first).
“Just like its predecessor,
is another highly enjoyable and fun racing game. While some people may be put off by the game feeling more arcade-like than the first one, for me, it didn’t deter me from playing the game at all. Another great driving experience!”

GAMEPLAY
Basic design is 3-vs-3 team of super heroes where each hero has 2-3 powers and they level up with XP. You do Bejeweled style color matches to build up the powers and activate the power which either affects the board to your favor (like forming defensive shields, invisibility for your character, bleed damage tiles, secret trap tiles, count-down timers that have some affect, and many other tile types that are essentially damage, buffs, debuffs, heals and so on). As time goes on and you win matches you gather both XP (called ISO-8) and character covers (new characters, new powers, or level-ups for existing powers). You build your character, you level them and have fun.
MODES
There are two main Modes:
1) Story - You play a storyline with a lot of different types of teams you fight and this is called the "PvE" side of things in the game.
2) Versus - You play matches against the computer where they other people's teams are computer-controlled.
Both modes very fun.
MICROTRANSACTIONS
Microtransactions do speed up the game for you but are NOT required. You can start out easily and keep playing it and you will easily get good characters reasonably quickly. Alternately, spend $5 to $20 like a normal game and get your boost.
PROs
The game is very well designed.
There is a lot to do and the devs are constantly working to add more and fix the existing,
Many fun events all week long.
Great gameplay that is easy to pick up but the strategy is deep.
All your favorite Marvel superheroes.
It simply is a good addictive game.
YMMV
Microtransactions help you speed things up.
CONs
Currently the only downside is that the PC version and the Mobile version are kept completely separate so if you start on one you are stuck using that version as all your progress is limited to that version. This *needs* fixing but so far nothing. :/
TLDR

In short- super fast paced, pure PvP arena action with a MASSIVE skill ceiling.
They essentially took the standard MOBA format and took out everything that made it bad- RNG (ciritcal hits for example), auto-aim skills (everything from basic attacks to heals are skillshots than can miss), mana (your abilities are only limited by your cooldowns, with the exception of your ultimate), and objectives which slow the game down and take away from the PvP focus. There's no item shop, no "feeding," no pay2win nonsense, it's balanced and perfectly suited for competetive play.
And then they added to it. Each character has autoattacks bound to LMB, basic abilities bound to RMB, Q, E, R, movement ability bound to space, ultimate bound to F, and 2 alternate ability variations which can be triggered with a key combo, meaning that each character has essentially 9 abilities at their disposal. The game also has a great atmosphere, with a tribal theme, well represented through both visuals and audio.
One of the few games that I would say is 10/10. Can't reccomend more. Only downside is the playerbase, but you can always find a game after a couple minutes.

I have to say I completely disagree with what the top reviews are for this game.
First off let me say that it is FREE TO PLAY & not pay to win.
The in game currencies that everyone is raving about are really given to you quite often. I would like to point out that you cant simply pay your way to the ultimate team of characters. Really it is quite smart in that you have to get "covers" that unlock your powers & let you level up from in game rewards. It can be frustrating as hell when you can't get the cover you need to level up but it also means you can just drop $30 on your hero (or villian) & perfect them.
The other side of this is in my experience you are only matched with players who are of a similar skill level to you. You shouldn't be getting nerfed at anytime.
I have only spent real world money on expanding the amount of heroes I can have & I didn't even need to do that, just wanted to have more people. I would say it cost me $8 bucks because I did it a couple of times. It's worth noting though that I was given plenty enough of the game gold for free, I just chose to spend it like an idiot on trying to get rare players!
With that I would like to give out some hints that are really going to save you alot of time.
#Use the in game gold that you get through playing to expand your roster first instead of trying to get rare characters. The more slots you have the more likely you can level up. Also means with mulitple characters you can play with one set while the other heals.
#Pick two (maybe even 2) of the one star heroes at the start (Iron man, Black Widow, Storm, Juggernaught, Venom,) & focus on levelling them up. Cover drops are ultra common & a fully powered level 50 one star player is really powerful, you can beat much higher levels if you use skill. I have got other characters far past level 50 & still throw Storm in against high level players because here powers are so strong.
#Play the daily events. Even if you only have ♥♥♥♥♥♥ characters you can at least get a cover drop from playing only 1 or 2 matches.
#Don't forget when you are starting out that in the daily events you can skip a match if you think you will lose. There is a button in the lower left hand corner
Anyway, obviously I enjoy the game. It's a great time waster (as you can see by my hours) You can choose to trust me or you can choose to trust someone with .2 hours game time.
Good luck!

+ The gameplay is extremely addicting. Basically you are building a lab full of assembly lines that take raw ingredients and converts them into medicine or pills to sell for profit.
+  Visually the game looks great with a very nice clean charming style. Once you build a bunch of machines it can be very entertaining to just sit back and watch your factory essentially print money.
+ A lot of strategy and planning is involved while designing your machines. You will often have to move around or completely change a line to develop an even greater product. Every machine has a different entry and exit point, so you really have to keep in mind how much space you have, and try to make things compact.
+ Surprisingly complex. I found the game to be a tad hard to learn at first, but once you grasp the concept it will feel very rewarding as you learn how to upgrade and mix ingredients to form greater level cures.
+ A LOAD of content. If you plan on beating the game I'm sure you can spend over 40 hours easily as each level is quite time consuming. (which is not a bad thing)
- The tutorials were very lengthly and a bit tedius to get through as they have you read through a bunch of instructions rather than introducing the mechanics in a more fun way. (A narrator could have helped)
- There isn't any information that tells you the supply / demand for each type of drug. Therefor, you do not really have any idea what a new drug will sell for. I'd often find myself spending quite a bit upgrading an assembly line to make a higher tier medication only to find out that the new medication was not selling for much and there's no way I could have known.

Many people seem to dislike Civ:BE - I like it. It may not be a master piece, but it brings some new concepts:
- orbital layer,
- affinity (city and unit customization through affinities, also affects the graphics of towns, units)
- virtues
- tech web
One real improvement is the ranking window, which also shows the reasons
for the diplomatic state towards a specific oponent.
Civ:BE is lacking several stuff, that we enjoyed in previous Civ series:
- leaders do not have a real personallity.
- peoples happiness
- producing specialists
- tourism
computer AI is not very smart:
- it builds a lot of workers, but does not build usefull improvements
- builds orbital, that are not usefull or in locations that don't make sense
- AI does not try to build veteran units or use the units according to their strenght
(the fighting AI in Civ never has been very good - take a look at Open General)
In higher difficulties the AI seems to get a lot of energy  (which acts as kind of money)
and can buy a lot of stuff in the beginning, which seems to be the compensation for the
lack of intelligence. They also seem to get an unfair advantage in virtues.
the UI could also need some improvements:
- when oponents ask for a trade for strategic resources, it might be helpful
to see the current state of your resources.
- the economic overview could offer more information like free trade routes
- the city window could offer to set the focus on producing a certain type
of resource (production, science, culture, energy, food)

Even if the list of flaws might look a bit long, I'm still enjoying the game. I don't think it
is worth to buy for the regular price, but on discount its ok.
