Like maplestory but better... but noone plays it really.
PROS:
-Fun 2-D beat em up style gameplay (like streets of rage or TMNT Turtles in Time) but with a skill slot bar for really cool moves.
-Can change your subclass at any time until lvl 50 (gotta commit sometime)
-Can use any skill as long as you have at least one skill point in it without having to use the skill slot bar. (Theres a combo system that allows things like pressing: UP, DOWN, Z to use a special move instead of equipping it to your skill bar.)
-Cash shop stuff can sometimes be bought with in game gold or you can use the mileage shop.
-Easily the best sprite animation/art I've ever seen. (If you play it an get to behemoth you'll know what I'm talking about. Them eyes tho.)
-Many different classes with unique abilities and skill levels. (The monk subclass for the priest is hella hard to play but its badass too.)
-Doesn't cost a hella lot of money to buy an outfit for a character (lookin at you elsword)
-Story is interesting enough I guess (If you like to read that is.)
-Lots of endgame stuff and raids and challenges.
-The only crafting system I've seen that lets you craft other NPC helpers for dungeons, its great if you can't find a party.
-The only game I've seen that implements a legacy system where you can summon you're other characters to help you in battle. (At lvl 50 you can use any character over lvl 50 or higher and summon them to perform a special move during a dungeon, it has a cooldown and can be used as many times as you want per dungeon.)
-Everyone should be able to run it, it's not graphic heavy but it still looks great.
-They have welcome back gifts for players who haven't played the game in a while that keep giving you stuff everyday you log on for about 15 days. It's nice.
CONS:
-The fatigue bar. (Limits how long you can play a character per day, I wouldn't mind it so much if it was at least infinite on the weekends, but it's not, you can probably manage to do at least 30 dungeons until you can't play that character anymore, but there are some dungeons that don't use fatigue.)
-Finding a party is almost impossible. (They have a quick party feature that noone uses for some reason even though theres great benefits for playing together.)

FAIR WARNING:
-This game can be pretty hard sometimes.

Jalopy is one of those rare games that you initially shrug off thinking, "How is this even a game? You're just driving a terrible, yet likable, car on bad roads." Then one day it came on sale, and I decided to take a chance, after all, it's just a few dollars. I hopped in game, came to terms with an old man's coat, and started my journey into eastern Europe.
A few countries later, all was going well. I was broke, had a trunk full of cheap wine, and was having a good time. The basic mechanics (pun not intended) of the game were fairly easy to get the hang of despite being eaten by a roadside fence in Hungary.
Then it happened. I fell in love with the game.
Not because of its charming, low fidelity graphics or the intricate recreation of a Trabant, but its atmosphere. My god does this game have atmosphere! There is a specific point where all the moving parts of the game moved as one for me. It was the transition between Hungary and Yugoslavia. I don't want to spoil it too much, but if you manage to get to the halfway marker for the first part of the journey, you're in for a treat.
You may have noticed that I haven't mentioned what I think of the story. That's because I think the story isn't too important to the experience of Jalopy. The game to me is about overcoming the hardships of a long journey and seeing gorgeous views along the way.
Should you play it? I can't answer that for you. But what I can tell you is that you can beat the game, unlike many other early access games. There are a few bugs, some of them bad most of them minor. In the 60+ hours I've played at the time of this writing, there are only two major (albeit rare) bugs that require a save reload. The first is the one where you can't pick up objects, and the second is when a fence eats you if you touch it. Other than that, you should be fine.

Pros:
+ Relatively good playtime, with replay value if you're interested in better scoring/alternative paths. I've personally redownloaded this game numerous times, it's just so fun to play and let your mind drift.
+ Responsive controls, visually impressive and entertaining gameplay that is both true to Hitman but also a bit easier to grasp.
+ The story in this one is interesting at the very least, and approaches 47's character in a different way, with his dialogue and personal character fleshed out somewhat more than the last entry.
+ A lot of the dialogue and scenes are very entertaining to listen to/watch.
+ The first game to introduce custom contracts, a feature that can drastically increase your playtime with the game.
Cons:
- As any Hitman fan will mention the second you talk about Absolution, it's not REALLY as true to the Hitman experience. The levels are very linear and storydriven, and the gameplay feels more focused around action rather than clever use of the environment. It's also not very subtle and a bit easier overall. This is where the title is weakest, of course.
- Some maps are weaker than others. It becomes clear, especially later in the game, that several areas were only meant to be played one way. The linearity of the maps becomes more and more noticeable.
- Disguise/instinct system kinda blows in this one, as anyone will tell you. Instinct is a good idea in a way, and the newest Hitman builds on it while removing the dumb bits... but in this one, it's both unnecessary and too easy to abuse. And when it isn't those things, it makes your playthrough annoying and inconvenient.
- Some of the villains are entirely too ridiculous.
Overall:
Should you get this over the newest Hitman? No. The new Hitman is definitely a better experience.
But is it a bad game? No, despite what a lot of the negative reviews say, this game is a blast to play and deserves its spot in the Hitman series. As one of the weaker titles, of course, but even so, I haven't regretted buying this game for a long time.

After 280 hours played, I'm finally done with the game. But at the very least I should be able to give people a very thorough review of the game.
At 280 hours played, the game can't be that bad, right? So why stop now?
The core of the game is still really cool. You build up a roster of Marvel heroes and villians and level them up to build a stronger and stronger team. And the devs support the game relatively well with new events and new heroes so there is always something to do.
Still, they just pushed it too far. This game isn't really a game, it's a second job. I see no way to play this game casually, either you are all in or you are out. Every two weeks there is a new hero, accompanied by a 10 day long PvE event that's a pure battle of attrition to defend a placement in the leaderboards high enough to get the new hero. If you don't? Without the new hero you'll have already lost in the next tournament. The new always gives a insurmountable advantage for the next. There is no way to escape this sweatshop.
And the PvE events are less fun with each iteration. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rubber banding and level scaling makes PvE tournaments an exercise in frustration and disappointment. Have a maxed out Lv141 roster? Enjoy being beaten in placement by Level 50 teams, because their enemies get scaled to level 20 and take 1 minute each while you slog it out against Lv300 enemies with 10k HP each.
And then the PvP tournaments... They used to be great. But then they changed the match making algorithm so that now every fight is a tired slog. And since there is now always an Alliance season running, you HAVE to do well in every single PvP tournament non stop or you are letting down your alliance.
Alliances are another thing... they are great socially. But the pressure they put you under is enourmous. And again, it's all in or all out. Without being in a good alliance, you'll miss 30% of each tournament's reward! You might as well not bother if you aren't in an alliance.
And the time commitment required to stay in the game is 2 hours EVERY SINGLE DAY. And even that is sometimes not enough, with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending times in the middle of the night for EU players which means all your effort is wasted thanks to rubber banding of US players near the end of the tournament while you are sleeping.
Just do yourself a favor and don't get involved in this game. It's a bottomless black hole that you can't escape from.
Why I quit now and not weeks ago? Season 1 just ended and I could finally leave without ♥♥♥♥ing over my alliance. They are great people and they didn't deserve being abandoned halfway through the season.

This is a good game.  I do recommend it, but be warned--it ends suddenly.  The game world has two interlocking systems of magic.  Paladins develop a rosy glow, and their partners, the necromancers, have a pasty look.  (This does interesting things to the wide variety of skin colors on display.)  The main character is a necromancer who expects to be partnered with her lifelong friend and crush, now a paladin, in a graduation ceremony.  But she instead is partnered to a mysterious unknown who may or may not be horribly evil.  The friends, and Prudence the Paladin's new partner, try to discover the truth about Ash's partner, despite opposition from all corners.  You have the option to play as a good version of Ash, the main character, or to turn her evil.  There are also various smaller choices.  Unfortunately, the game does cut off rather quickly, with a lot of last-minute mythology being rapidly introduced.  It does have a complete arc, but it felt as though the game just...stopped.  There is a sequal coming out soon, though.
The art is good, although I'm usually not a fan of the "what happened to my nose-bridge?" style.  Here, though, the pudgier characters are missing their nose-bridges, and the more thin, angular characters have sharper lines, so I'll give it a pass.  The writing is better than average, though not spectacular.  The worldbuilding is interesting, and the magic systems are carefully internally consistent (good, because the plot relies on them), but I did wish for a little more concrete detail.  (The world is that standard fantasy world we all know with only some specified variations.)  Mechanics are par for visual novels.  Some of the voice acting is too high-pitched for my taste, but that is deliberate, and it is well-done.
Overall, I would say give it a try unless you can't stand cliffhangers, in which case I would wait until the next part is released (currently set for April 2017; currently called Pale Spectrum, according to the Kickstarter page).
Note:  I received a key through the Kickstarter backer campaign.  My key cost $3 (USD).

I am usually very careful about which games I buy, and do a lot of research on games before deciding to buy them. My research on Bleed left me on the fence as to whether I should purchase it or not, as it seemed very mediocre. I decided to pick it up when it was on sale. I was pleasantly suprprised within the first few minutes of playing the game, and my experience stayed pleasant throughout this 2D shooter.
There's not much for settings for this game. You can choose to play with a keyboard and mouse or controller, with mouse/right stick used for aiming and the WASD keys/left stick for moving. You can't customize the controls for the gamepad. Only the keyboard controls can be customized, unfortunately. That doesn't matter, however, as the button mapping is done well (assuming you're using a controller with Xinput). Since you'll be using your thumbs to move and shoot, the remaing controls (slow time, switch weapons, and jump/ double jump) are mapped to the shoulder buttons, which works well. You can slow time with an ability, but it uses up a gauge that refills as time passes. Anyway, The only face button that does anything is the start button. The keyboard controls are also done well. It's nice to see some customizable settings that allow for more personalization. They include recticle color (the reticicle only appears if you are using the keyboard and mouse, rather than a controller), HUD position, sound options, and you can even turn off the ability to wall jump, which seems strange to me. Why wouldn't you want to be able to wall jump? Overall these features are a nice touch, and I especially like the ability to change the HUD position.
The game has 7 levels, all of which are action-packed and straightforward; look to other games for exploration or depth. There's not much else to do other than slow time, dodge and shoot, so I can't really say much about that. Each stage is unique and has various elements: on one stage, you'll be on top of a train and have to move to lower cars before the train goes under a tunnel, on another you're inside a dragon, on another you must avoid laser beams that don't hurt you but send enemies after you if you trigger them... You get the Idea. Anyway, there's several mini-bosses in each stage, though I'm not sure if I should call them mini-bosses as they can sometimes be as hard as the stage's end boss. Each stage is extremely fun and unique, and changing the difficulty also changes the stage a bit, rather than just increasing enemy health and damage dealt to you, though it also does those things too.
The game also has a lot of personality and charm. The music is usually upbeat and catchy (and reminds me of Megaman music), the main character expresses her emotions in game over screens and in the title screen, and when the game ends, it tells you to follow your dreams, never give up, all that jazz. It's refreshing to have something like that, rather than a grim-dark, edgy anti-hero using a ridiculous plot as an excuse to make pretentious social commentary. After beating the game, you unlock a couple of new modes. A challenge mode which allows you to fight up to 3 bosses at once, and an arcade mode that requires you to play through the ENTIRE game without dying. Unless I just suck, it would take many hours to become good enough to complete arcade mode on even easy, and I can't imagine doing it on any level of difficulty higher than that.
The game's ending brings me to my next point; the bad things about this game. The first of which is the length, as I beat Bleed in a little over 4 hours on the hard difficulty. While I very much enjoyed my time with the game, I wish it lasted longer. You could argue that the arcade mode raises the time the player can spend playing this game before getting bored, and I agree, but I still wish there was more content, because what little content that does exist is fantastic. The next bad thing about this game is the weapon selection. Now, if you know nothing about this game besides what you've been reading, let me explain. You acquire points at the end of every level, and these points can be spent at a shop to buy weapons, health upgrades, and time gauge upgrades. All of the weapons available for purchase besides one are useless. The default dual pistols are the best weapons in the game, and even the one other weapon that isn't useless, the laser rifle, is only useful against some bosses, though to be fair, it's extremely effective against said bosses. All the other weapons either don't do enough damage, have too short of range, are only useful in rare situations, or a combination of the three. More thought and careful balance should have been put into the weapons, as I've never seriously used any of them besides the default pistols and laser rifle, because the other weapons are simply worse, and a waste of points.
That's all I have to say about the game, really. If you like games of this type, you'll probably love this game, as it's one of the best of it's kind. If you don't like games of this type, you probably won't like this game. If you're on the fence, pick it up.

If you're thinking about buying this game because people say it's like Recettear, I can't recommend it to you. But wait; don't stop reading.
I think it's important to note; I don't find it very similar to Recettear, and I'm not quite sure why that's where everyone goes. The only thing it has in common is that it's an item shop game, as in you collect items to sell in your shop, and you have to pay off a loan -- but that's the only similarity. That could be said for a lot of games, from some Harvest Moon titles, to some expansions on the Sims. That doesn't mean this is a bad game, obviously.
Pixel Shopkeeper is very cute, and endearing. Definitely scratched my money-management itch, that I'm sure everyone here is familiar with. While I'm a little put off my it's repetition (and grating music), I see how often the game is updated, and I'm very excited to play it again when they've added more to it.
To me; this is more like 'You Must Build a Boat'. If you haven't heard of it; it's a pixel-style passive dungeoning game, where you don't control your character in combat, but you play a minigame to move it along, then you sell items you've collected for gold, and use that gold to upgrade yourself, and your boat to forward the game. How is this similar to Pixel Shopkeeper?
Let me just copy/paste what I just said, with a few choice word changes;  it's a pixel-style passive dungeoning game, where you don't control your character in combat, but you play a minigame to collect items, then you sell items you've collected for gold, and use that gold to upgrade yourself, and your shop to forward the game.
If you're thinking about buying this game because people say it's like Recettear, I can't recommend it to you. Recettear has very satisfying combat, interesting characters, an RPG element, a lot of re-playability, better sound, less repetition, and fun controls.
However, if you're thinking about buying this game because you like shopkeeping games, enjoy money management, cute pixel graphics, challenging goals, collect-athons, crafting and general mind-numbing repetition; I can absolutely recommend it to you. It's fun, and I don't regret buying it.

Great, fun, little shop keeper game.
At first, I was turned off by the tetris style way to get items.  But it really grew on me due to the different types of bags to store items in and the special blocks in those bags.  Bigger isn't always better when it comes to items, except when you need gear!
Managing the shop was a lot of fun.  Picking the decorations, picking the items to sell, etc.  It was all great fun.
There is a lot of clicking, but not as bad as cookie clicker or other games like it.  Mostly you click on NPCs and your tables to keep them clean, but that's it.  As someone with old hands that hurt, it didn't aggravate my hands at all.
The loan concept is great.  It keeps you pushing forward, but not too hard.  I had to figure out if I wanted to get more items, level myself up, or spend money on my shop.  It was a good balance I had to manage.  Though, I found once I was done with the loan part of the game it fizzled for me.  There is a story afterwards, but I didn't feel as motivated.
A few negatives - you can't delete save games, it seems.  But you can overwrite them.  There are some minor bugs, but not enough to detract from the gameplay.
Oh, and the dialog is great.  From the main character to the NPCs.  It's basic, but in some ways better than more expensive games I have played.
However, these games are so few and far between, and I consider this one to be a gem and completely worth the price.  I enjoyed the time I spent in it and see myself going back once the game has even more added to it.  I completely recommend it!
Edit:  I tried going back after completing the loan part of the storyline, and just couldn't get into it.  It felt like a grindfest instead of a face paced and natural progression, which did take the fun out of it.  However, I still strongly recommend it, as the price is really worth the entertainment it will provide.

OKAY SO!  I completed the good path, don't care for the neutral, and my friend completed the evil path because she's a toot and I can tell you a LOT about this visual novel.
First off, it's more like a book, less like a visual novel as visual novels tend to have 3-6 endings deciding whats your waifu, this is not one of those visual novels.  In fact, if you hate visual novels but love books, pick this up.  It's basically a book because the writing is REALLY well done.
I'm going to stop rambling and make more readable explanation off the bat.  I hate, HATE visual novels.  They are disgusting anime waifu trash that pits a male protagonist in a room with ten half-naked cutsie girls of various personalities and animal ears... or tanks... or ships.  Whatever floats their boat I guess.  However, this is not one of those stories. Your character first off, is a woman, and though she has a heavy romantic interest with a character, it is just one specific character and not the waifu tray to choose from.
In fact, that's what makes this story so great.  The romance COMPLIMENTS the story, where as most visual novels, the story compliments the romance... or is just kinda shoveled on... looking at you Bird simulator dating... crap.
See, it sparks a tension in the pages you read through.  Deliciously juicy drama but no clear indication of 'will you get the girl or not', in fact, there is this dreadening atmosphere as you FEEL the character's hopes and dreams scatter multiple times but she picks herself up time and time again.  It's a really good heartening experience.
Now let me explain the characters role.
Main character: An interesting and dynamic character.  She FEELS so real, and her attitude can change from spiteful and depressed to straight up malicious depending on your choices.  I have felt her concerns myself in the dating gig so I know how it is.
Love interest:  A character where drama revolves around but she isn't the driving force behind the plot (not directly anyways).  She brings the main character's tension along and is a point of interest, but isn't a mary sue princess that needs saving.
The 'will he betray us' guy:  Okay, sometimes you see a 'plot twist' coming from a mile away.  Sometimes you think 'no it's building up to reveal he was the good guy all along.  It isn't obvious in this one, it just isn't.  Sometimes I'm like OH YEAH HES SO GOOD, and other times I'm like HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥STAB HIM HES SO EVIL!  But I didn't know, I never did until the end segment. I'm not going to spoil whether he is a good guy a bad guy.
The tag along characters: Well, these two people are basically extra spicing to flesh things out.  They fufill their role... they flesh things out, they add more dynamics but they are indeed, tag along.  Don't expect too much from them as they are a basic package.  NOthing too interesting but they add more perspective.  All in all well done characters if, a bit dissapointing.
I'd describe more characters but I feel that it may be too spoilery so let's just say this.  Some characters will be completely meaningless and useless, while others will actually have a lot more involved with the plot than you would first think.  So just play it safe and pay attention to all characters :3
Now, the story itself.  The plot is very interesting.  Once more, I won't describe in detail what it is but I will say the beginning is WAY Too slow and the ending is WAY too abrupt.  That's my only complaint, your first hour will be spent reading the beginning while the next will be speeding by the middle and the end as the plot snowballs down.  The story and even the world itself however, is very facinating and this DOES excuse the speed and pacing.  The beginning had to EXPLAIN the world, show you how it is.  And it doesn't do it in a stupid♥♥♥♥♥naruto way, no... it expects the reader to be actually intelligent and piece things together with solid information.  So that perhaps may be why the beginning is so slow and the ending feel so sudden and fast paced.
TL;DR?
Story 8/10
Pacing 7/10
Romance 9/10
Characters 10/10
World 10/10
IGN 7.8/10.  Too much water

Made me realize how much I underappreciated voice acting in visual novels. It's very well done and really helps the characters come alive. The art is great, sort of Burtonesque instead of the typical anime style, and even the most minor side characters have unique sprites. The UI is a little awkward (I consistently had trouble finding the hotspot for save slots), but the text is large and easily readable.
The story feels very much like an introduction to a series. Most of the plot is focused on developing a small part of the setting, and then an epilogue abruptly shows a window into a larger world. It's also very linear; choices can give you evil points (too many and you get the bad end) and sometimes branch off into an extra scene, but the overall plot stays on the same path, and the good/neutral endings are very similar in both content and tone. Linearity isn't necessarily a weakness, especially since it leaves a clear starting point for the sequel, but saying there's three endings is kind of misleading.
That's a minor complaint, though. Overall,
is one of the best English visual novels I've played, It has a unique setting and compelling characters, and the writing, art, music, and voice acting all come together in a harmonious, beautiful experience. Highly recommended.

From the creators of Klocki and Hook comes another fantastic puzzler.  The concept is extremely simple: Press all the blue buttons to finish the level.  That sounds incredibly simple, but the game introduces different types of buttons which must be pressed in a specific order according to a rule set.  The game does an absolutely fantastic job of teaching you the different rules and gradually building up to ridiculously complex puzzles.  They start with the simplest possible puzzle involving that symbol, and then give you another simple puzzle that requires a deeper understanding of the rule, and so on.  If I have one complaint about the game, it is that they introduce a lot of mechanics that are swiftly dropped and never used again, which is kind of disappointing.  Unlike Klocki, there's no great final puzzle where everything comes together unfortunately.  That being said, the puzzle do get increasingly difficult as the game goes on, and the final puzzles were such brain melters that I think that if you showed the solutions to someone, it would be completely impossible to reverse engineer an understanding of the mechanics.  Overall another very high quality entry in this series of claming puzzlers from Hamsters on Coke games.

PUSH is a very nice minimalistic puzzle game that will provide you with something between one and two hours of playtime. Each of the 60+ levels is about pushing buttons situated on an 3D shape in a particular order. There are no explanations as to what that order could be but each button is marked with a symbol that hints to the solution order.
So you first need to figure out the meaning of the button symbols through trial and error / through logical deduction. Further mechanics include among others panning and rotating particular parts of the 3D shape you are working with, and multilple dimensions with different 3D shapes to work with in a single level.
I'd say that the learning curve is pretty flat in the first 20 levels but after that, puzzles become increasingly complex while still introducing new puzzle mechanics. I had great fun solving the remaining two thirds of the puzzles and they do provide for a satisfactory mental challenge.
Finally, given all the above I do not hesitate to recommend this game to any fan of puzzle games. Go and get it since it is only 1€ (or even lkess if you get it in the bundle).

PUSH is a testimony that you do not need complex game mechanics, an absurd amount of content or even a line of text to have a great time.
With the simple premise of pushing buttons on a sequence (discovering said sequence is the puzzle), it makes you feel immersed from the first puzzle forward.
There isn't really that much that you can talk about mechanic wise without spoiling the discovery process (arguably of the best parts of the game). However, it is safe to say that every puzzle kept things fresh until the very end. And the fact that previously introduced mechanics meet once again in the later puzzles, adds a layer of depth that is missing from several other puzzle games.
I can't really find something bad to say gameplay-wise about the game, other than the fact that some levels were a bit tedious (to name an example, some with the multi-screen portals), but there are only a couple of levels like that, and said mechanics don't ever come back. So the positives definately obliterate the few pet peeves I had.
Yes, the game is short, around the hour worth of length. Yes, it is one of those games that you will likely play only once. But it sticks with you for much longer, it is criminally cheap, the time you play it is very enjoyable, and all in all it'll leave you waiting for the developers to launch their next experience.
PUSH is just that good.

TL;DR: Rose-tinted garbage fire.

It's obvious that this game has not aged well. And because the remastered versions are still unplayable crash-fests, you're stuck with this one. I understand the appeal to this game; I understand why it was such a big hit. But there are too many little things that shouldn't have to be dealt with that caused me to stop playing.
1. Surround sound doesn't work. Forget that the option exists in the menu; it lies. This is a major problem that many more people than just me have tried to fix.
2. FOV is straight up nauseating and fixes don't work. In Bioshock 1 you could at least change the user.ini file to get a wider FOV. If you do that in this game, it will reset back to the default ~70 at every chance it gets. Sure, you can just press the hotkey on the keyboard to change it back, but if you're streaming it to another room (like I am), you're not trying to get run back and forth to your computer every 15 minutes to do so.
3. Controller aiming/movement controls are clunky as heck. This was acceptable in 2010, but not today. I didn't notice the same problems with mouse/keyboard, but that's not how I intended to play this game.

This is a game where you chose a champion or hero with max level directly (no character leveling up required) and battle other opponents in a small map (arena) . Think of some maxed out heroes in DotA doing a battle on a small map.
The huge good difference that this game makes :
All the skills and normal attacks are casted on a line, in a AOE attack zone or directly on a character AND there are no chances to stun or to crowd control something - it either happens if you hit or not if you don't - which makes the game 100% player-skill based and also makes it HARD to master at the same time.
Where the game fails is in the art style chosen for the entire game... In my opinion it isn't very catchy and pleasing to the eye (some kind of dark-tribal-cartoonish slightly unpolished aspect) - I believe this is the game's biggest problem.
It's a good game for people who like to challenge themselves and test their eye-brain-finger coordination and also for people who like a good fair coop game.

After 280 hours played, I'm finally done with the game. But at the very least I should be able to give people a very thorough review of the game.
At 280 hours played, the game can't be that bad, right? So why stop now?
The core of the game is still really cool. You build up a roster of Marvel heroes and villians and level them up to build a stronger and stronger team. And the devs support the game relatively well with new events and new heroes so there is always something to do.
Still, they just pushed it too far. This game isn't really a game, it's a second job. I see no way to play this game casually, either you are all in or you are out. Every two weeks there is a new hero, accompanied by a 10 day long PvE event that's a pure battle of attrition to defend a placement in the leaderboards high enough to get the new hero. If you don't? Without the new hero you'll have already lost in the next tournament. The new always gives a insurmountable advantage for the next. There is no way to escape this sweatshop.
And the PvE events are less fun with each iteration. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rubber banding and level scaling makes PvE tournaments an exercise in frustration and disappointment. Have a maxed out Lv141 roster? Enjoy being beaten in placement by Level 50 teams, because their enemies get scaled to level 20 and take 1 minute each while you slog it out against Lv300 enemies with 10k HP each.
And then the PvP tournaments... They used to be great. But then they changed the match making algorithm so that now every fight is a tired slog. And since there is now always an Alliance season running, you HAVE to do well in every single PvP tournament non stop or you are letting down your alliance.
Alliances are another thing... they are great socially. But the pressure they put you under is enourmous. And again, it's all in or all out. Without being in a good alliance, you'll miss 30% of each tournament's reward! You might as well not bother if you aren't in an alliance.
And the time commitment required to stay in the game is 2 hours EVERY SINGLE DAY. And even that is sometimes not enough, with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending times in the middle of the night for EU players which means all your effort is wasted thanks to rubber banding of US players near the end of the tournament while you are sleeping.
Just do yourself a favor and don't get involved in this game. It's a bottomless black hole that you can't escape from.
Why I quit now and not weeks ago? Season 1 just ended and I could finally leave without ♥♥♥♥ing over my alliance. They are great people and they didn't deserve being abandoned halfway through the season.

This game is surprisingly the most emotional game I have ever played.. although you won't hear any dialogue from your characters, whereas all you have is a short biography that expands over time based on the decisions that you make in order to survive, you surprisingly become very attached to each survivor. You just KNOW that each life is valuable and sacred, and you would do anything to keep surviving in this difficult time.
The game will give you a huge amount of freedom of choice. Do you want to stay civilized and ethical when it comes to trading? Will you respect the territory of other survivors and come in peace, asking to barter for goods? Or will you sneak in at night, killing everyone and looting the place for medication and supplies?
Each survivor reacts differently and there are certain choices that they aren't willing to follow through with. For example, there is one survivor who is an ex soldier and ran away after the conflict of war became too much for him, I traded an axe for some meds because the NPC's dad was very sick... and then I killed both of them with the same axe took all the meds, food and a gun. As a player, I felt horrible. But I needed those supplies. I needed my group to survive. But here's the thing. The next morning, almost all of my survivors wouldn't move. They refused to do the chores like check the water filter, cook food, harvest the garden and board up the windows. Just, no one wanted to do anything because they all felt devastated about what transpired the other night.
And that ex soldier of mine? Had "Broken" as a status ailment.
I cried that night...

Well, I am reviewing this game because I see its potential, most games that have a lot of bugs I drop and move on, but something about this game keeps me interested. I would love to see this game become a lot more popular. Here are some bugs I have encountered and suggestions I have.
-Many monsters especially orcs, undead, imps, and death weavers get stuck on trees when trying to run away, for example, right outside of the starting area I find enemies that are much higher in a level like 15 and above. When I first got my weapon I would try to go into caves where there is orcs level 15 to 20 and usually get instantly demolished, but when I run away they get stuck in the tree. They don't move nor attack, this sometimes happens inside the cave, in camps, and random spawn areas, where they don't move nor attack and you can just walk up and kill them.
-When you go into the taming menu after clicking on the animal I sometimes click escape which opens the options menu and after closing the menu I am able to move around but I am stuck on the animal taming menu still, this is the same for when you click on your magic items like forges and whatnot.
-Sometimes I get stuck between rocks and inside trees and I am unable to escape so I have to force a respawn.
-The game itself stutters and rubber bands when I have it in any graphics setting.
There are probably much more but those are the main issues I have had. Onto some recommendations.
-In the early game, you don't get as many spell slots for your weapon, I would recommend adding the ability to switch between a set of spells, I find it tedious to switch between my spells.
- I have noticed you are not able to have multiple trinkets, I would suggest adding separate trinket slots for the ring, necklace, amulet, and bracelet.
- You should add travelers bags, I know you have your animal storage but on long expeditions, you need all the space you can get.
-The building system could use more refining and the ability to rotate the items at the click of a button.
-My last suggestion, for now, would be to add the ability to refund points after allocating them, sometimes I misclick on the wrong thing.

Bloodline Champions is BY FAR the best pure PvP arena game, possibly ever, and that's not an exaggeration. Biggest thing I have to stress is that while BLC may look like another "Moba" (Dota2/League of Legends), it its essence and spirit it's
closer to fighting games or even fast paced first-person-shooters like Quake or Unreal Tournament. Yes, you've heard that right. That's a very important distinction which a lot of people don't realize. Unlike "Mobas" you don't need to have a huge collection of top tier heroes at your disposal, some of the best players in the game mastered 1 or 2 bloodlines and play them exclusively, similarly to fighting games.
For this reason the game certainly isn't for everyone, there's very little downtime where you can casually stroll back to your lane while considering which item you should buy next, there's no mana so you never run out of things to do in the middle of the battle. You don't level up - you have full arsenal of abilities (that's more than twice as big compared to "Mobas" AND are all skillshots) at your disposal from the first second you enter the arena (with an exception of energy that allows you to cast your ultimate and EX abilities and is gained by hitting your opponents). Reflexes/mind-games/ability to coordinate with your teammates in the matter of seconds is far more important than theorycrafting.
is a skillshot and that applies even to your basic attacks AND heals. That means that it's possible to miss even your basic melee attacks if you don't position yourself correctly or anticipate your opponent's movements. Each bloodline has the basic attack that has no cooldown (in the case of the healers, they also have a ranged healing ability with no CD as well) + 5 other skills + Ultimate + 2 variations of other abilities (called EX abilities which cost energy). That's a lot of stuff to do, at all times.
The amount of control you have over your bloodline is extremely high, your bloodline is controlled by WASD movement, similarly to FPS games - most bloodlines also have multiple ways to dash/jump/knock opponents away and maneuver around the battlefield, leading to a very fluid and fast-paced gameplay. There's also the fact that you can try to actively dodge your opponent's abilities, creating a huge potential for mind-games.
There are a lot of cool skills like:
Very important part is that there's VERY little Hard CC like stuns - you won't be locked out for 3 seconds with no chance to do anything while enemy team focuses you to death. Your teammates can always use their defensive abilities like shields on you as well.
Because every skill is a skillshot, mind-games are extremely important - for example, if you're about to hit your opponent and they use their counterattack, you can cancel your own attack and wait until their counter-attack timer finishes (called trance baiting). If they relied on that counter-attack to survive, they might just die!
Overall, while BLC is certainly not for everyone and has a steep learning curve, once you get over it, there's a lot of fun to be had.

Easily the best Splinter Cell game there is, harking back from a golden age where Ubisoft didn't bog us down with proprietary DRM and shove Season Passes in our faces for $30-$50. Not only is the stealth gameplay pure, simple, and a pleasure to play even to this day, but the game boasts an amazing soundtrack that manages to stay relevant, and classic at the same time. The humorous quips of Sam Fisher never tire, and are always welcome, despite the serious tone the game takes on for the most part, giving Sam that old, characterized charm that you can't find in modern protagonists. Guns are represented faithfully, and many military terms are used correctly, and regularly- as a Tom Clancy game worthy of its title should.

Hitman: Absolution started the way I envisioned the Hitman series but slowly devolved into a frustrating hunt for signature kill methods with numerous checkpoint restarts.  To it's credit, the game gives you many options on how to complete an assassination, but the scoring, skill unlocks, and achievements all compelled me to search out the most insane method of securing the kill.  Disco balls falling on someone, activating scientific equipment at an oppourtune moment, and waiting minutes for a target to eat some poisoned sushi are a few of these signature kills.  Many times, a quick garrote or silenced shot from afar would be much cleaner, but it is not rewarded.  Each successive level feels like it further promotes these unique kill methods.  So I snuck around, assessing the guards and other NPCs until I could find the right path to get to the required spots without being spotted.
A major problem with this is the save system.  There are periodic checkpoints where you can save your disguises, equipment, location, etc., but it does not save your "progress".  So anyone you had pacified before the checkpoint comes back if you reload that checkpoint.  Given the constant sneaking around and the uneasy disguise system, there are alot of times you'll want to reload a checkpoint.  Worse is when you don't find a check point at all and need to perform the same series of steps to get back to where you messed up.  I usually only found one checkpoint per level, at most, and they were generally located along the path that guides you to signature kills.
This was the first of the Hitman games that I've played and overall, I would not recommend it.  I completed the single player aspect game in about 17 hours, but I did not go back to repeat missions.  You can go about on normal difficulty and complete every mission via massive firefight, but that doesn't feel rewarding.  The story is okay, but there are several levels where there is no primary assassination target; you're tasked simply with eluding people or escaping a location.  Those levels are particularly painful.
I did not attempt the multiplayer aspect of the game and cannot speak to the livelihood of the community or the quality of the contract mode.  The game was ambitious with it's design on disguises and NPC behavior, but it ends up feeling just a bit off.

The definitive Splinter Cell game: Chaos Theory ironed out the imperfections present in Splinter Cell and Pandora Tomorrow, whilst also retaining what was good about the first two, to achieve perfection as, not just an entry in the Splinter Cell series but, as stealth-based games go.
While I enjoyed the first Splinter Cell’s storyline, Nikoladze and the Georgian information crisis, I thought Pandora Tomorrow’s (East Timorese rebels) was somewhat lacking. Chaos Theory returns to form though as Sam Fisher must prevent full-scale war erupting on the Korean Peninsula.
Chaos Theory was the point where the series matured and achieved perfection. Michael Ironside must have had a blast recording Sam Fisher’s dialogue for this edition. There are nuggets of pure comedy gold among Sam’s dialogue, such as when he cons a National Guardsman into believing his presence (and knife at his throat) is simply a training exercise, or Grimsdottir’s most recent attempt to set him up on a date.
Aside from the introduction of a knife and the OCP on the pistol there are no new weapons in Sam’s arsenal but there are a number of new non-lethal ways of dealing with your enemies. The OCP is a huge boon, used to temporarily disable electric lighting which not just saves bullets but also helps maintain your stealth as the AI’s powers of perception have improved greatly, especially when spotting broken lights. Sam can also change what arm his SC-20K is resting on, making shooting around left-sided corners without being detected much easier. The ability to choose the contents of your weaponry prior to starting a mission (recommendation, stealth, or assault) is another cool introduction. Players are also marked on their performance at the end of each mission out of 100%, with non-lethal kills, never being detected as an intruder, and the completion of secondary objectives contributing to your final score.
As well as feeling much more authentic than its two predecessors in terms of graphics and lighting, Chaos Theory also saw the first time Sam had a relationship with one of the antagonists, which culminates in a gripping showdown reminiscent of GoldenEye. Overall the dialogue is snappier, the gameplay more fluid, the graphics sharper, which unsurprisingly makes it just as enjoyable to play as it was back in 2005.
A massive 10/10: the best entry of the whole Splinter Cell series.

I have played each of: Civilization, Civilization 2, Civilization: Call to Power, Civilization 3, Civilization 4, Civilization 5, Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri.
I have to say, Beyond Earth has the worst writing by far in this game lineage. Whereas SMAC is about future possibilities, BE is about global warming--how we didn't show enough respect to Earth, how we made a huge mistake, how we didn't regulate enough, how much grief, shame, or guilt we all feel for what we did to Earth, etc, ad nauseum. Everything that isn't about global warming is vacuous "flavor" written not because it's worth reading, but because the formula demands that something be written. The game mechanics in BE are on par with the previous seven games (most similar to Civ 5), but there's a conspicuous absence of a competent mind narrating this game. The writing in SMAC is in a different league--as is the voice acting.
Also, the alien planet is gloomy and cheerless; Civilization 4 looks better than Beyond Earth.
This is also the buggiest game in this lineage. For example, when you scroll around the main map, sometimes tiles aren't loaded as soon as they appear, instead they appear as a black void until you stop scrolling the map and give the game a few seconds to load all the tiles (this happens repeatedly, not just once when tile is first loaded, and it happens on small maps on a high-end PC).
I recommend playing Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri or Civilization 4: Warlords. SMAC has the best writing but is not beautiful; Civ 4 is one of the beautiful ones, and Warlords has the best gameplay among them (better than Beyond the Sword or Civ 5).

I'm having a lot of fun with this game so far. It's a pretty interesting mashup of a couple different genres: of course at the heart of it is the shop management, which has a nice bit of depth to it as it involves outfitting your shop with the tables, shelves, windows and flower pots, and pairing them with specific items you slowly accrue. You've got to know when to invest in a bigger shop, when to attract more customers, or when to subtly increase prices for certain items. This is also paired with elements of crafting, growing crops, and even some small clicker-game elements that don't outstay their welcome (e.g. try clicking the birds).
Complimenting this already interesting management side of things is the way you actually get the items you end up selling: by adventuring. This part of the game is crisply short and to the point; there's no need to worry about hour long dungeons or lengthy battles. Instead there's the refreshing twist that your character does the fighting all on their own, while your job as the player is bag management. This ends up getting into some Tetris-y moments of fitting oddly shaped items together by rotating them around and trying to save as much space as possible, all the while you're on the clock. There's even different shaped bags you can get which provide new and strange challenges as to how you pack away your items (some bags are bigger and square, while others may have strange and challenging shapes while giving you other perks).
And the glue holding these two sides of the entreprenurial endeavour is a time-management mechanic where opening the shop for a day or heading off adventuring will take up days in a precious week. So you've got to balance when you re-stock weapons, when you sell them off, and how you spend your money; you could save it to be ready to pay off increasing payments of a rather large debt, or take the gamble and use that money to level your character up to hit better dunegons and get more pricey loot, or buy new loot bags or other such gear.
While all of that may seem like a lot it actually comes together pretty neatly. After a few minutes I got the hang of the gameplay loop and it's been a blast since then. One thing I'll say is that the inviting, playful appearence of this game masks a pretty intense race against time that tests your skills with a good bit of difficulty. I died while adventuring or failed to make my payments more than a few times. While this was a bit frustrating at the time, it also forced me to delve deeper into the mechanics of the game. I appreciate that the game doesn't seem to want players to be able to spend carelessly or do a sloppy job of balancing adventuring and selling. It's a game that demands your attention and comprehension and rewards you for taking time to examine it and learn from it.
All in all I've been having a blast. I've failed more than a couple times but never unfairly, and the more I've died or missed my precious weekly payments the more I've come to understand all the cogs in motion at once here, and which ones I have to focus on at different times. I'm not there yet, but I aim to be a master shopkeep yet and I think it'll be a lot of fun getting there.

I'm not sure if its a limitation of their tech or my system (GTX780 SLI), but the framerate is very choppy while moving your head.  I believe this is probably due to the framerate of most of their video not matching the 75 hz of the rift, so as you turn your head you are seeing 1 frame of video dragged across up to 3 frames of rift screen refreshes (for 24 hz video)?  This issue certainly needs to be addressed if they plan on releasing comercial VR "films."  Also, I'd suggest a disclaimer recommending that you don't move your head side to side or back and forth while watching, as positional tracking is impossible to support with this tech, and VR sickness is quite nasty.

ArcheBlade is a game that I went into after reading about balance issues pretty much expecting a game with some easy heroes that some pub stomp the competition with, but not TERRIBLY imbalanced if played right. After a couple hours of playing and having a good amount of experience with MOBAs and fighting games of different sorts I would have to agree with the concensus that this game is currently imbalanced to a flaw. My biggest issue is the disparity of useful special abilities. Some have game changing and (depending on the map) breaking abilities, while others should probably just remove their shift key from the keyboard. I feel the heroes themselves are kind of hit and miss as well. Outside of personal playstyle preference some just have way bigger and in-depth ability kits than others. I am not a fan of some characters HAVING to move directionally to perform attacks when this is a game with deadly pitfalls that can be easily jumped into from basic attack animations. To give an example, there are several small platforms that if a sniper were to roost upon, some other characters would be without 50% or more of their kits when trying to flush them out and the only viable option is to leave them...there are literally scenarios that if you are a certain type of character, and an opponent of a different type has a mind to, they can do things that make them inaccessable to you and your only choice is to ignore them and hope that there is someone else that can deal with the situation. Also some characters can't stick to a target for their whole combo if it was it max range or so, while others flow with the combo well enough that as long as you hit one part the rest will follow (unless otherwise interrupted, of course.)
Oh, and you can buy items to improve your characters with cash. You can also purchase them with hefty in-game currency pricetags, but still...someone can hop in with cash to spend and have an actual advantage over longtime players that haven't maxed out that character's gear loadout yet. Never ever a fan of games that sell anything except cosmetics. Shame on the developers for that, make skins appealing if you want money from your free game.
Overall I do see lots of potential for the game with some balance changes, probably largely based around making special abilities more in-line with one another and making some abilities less of a liability in areas of precarious footing. Also remove cash bought upgrades for characters...probably just remove equipment upgrading altogether and just make it cosmetic. For now I give the game a 4/10 for being fairly broken. It wouldn't take a ton to get it another 3 points though.

My very first review, and a fairly extensive one for ArcheBlade™.
These are merely first impressions though, so take it with a grain of salt, I guess?
My time with ArcheBlade, while brief, was very interesting. I remember playing the game during beta, in which I actually quit after about an hour due to the extreme imbalances plaguing the game's characters and such. I recently returned on word of a friend, just to see what all the fuss was about.
What I found was ultimately a game that... ultimately falls
short of expectations. To save you some time, I've compiled a list of pros and cons I've discovered in ArcheBlade.
- Simple, easy to grasp controls.
- Great music
- Decent artstyle
-
- Ridiculous balance issues - See '♥♥♥♥ed Up Combat'
- Free To Play, Pay to Win Model - This is one of the leading reasons noone will care for ArcheAge.
- ♥♥♥♥ED UP COMBAT: Despite simple controls, Combat fails to flow fluidly and instead feels like a disjointed mess when you're trying to quickly react to a threat, or perhaps come up with a simple technique such as attacking and guarding fast right after. Now, I understand that not every game needs to be obsessed with input speeds, else you get games like GunZ /GunZ 2 that pander to ADHD ridden children that hammer their keyboard like their lives depended on it, however there should be advantages to having practiced and built the skill to react accordingly to something... Actually, in ArcheBlade's case, the entire combat system needs an overhaul and some tweaking. Many characters are far too overpowered(Renoah. Succubus, Elrika, Renny), and the Back-Attack damage mechanic should be done away with altogether for now. The advantage a character gets from back damage is far too great.
- What maps offered are good, but there's a lack of them.
- Archaic Online Systems:
. There are no real excuses behind the way the game attempts to facilitate online. For a game with such a simplistic approach to multilplayer online combat, there is a stunning lack of a simple and easy match-making or private game mode. Quite plain and simple, the game needs dedicated main servers and needs to utilize them intelligently.
ArcheBlade's problem seems to be developer funding or complete laziness and incompetence. The P2W model may kill this game due to the potential power creep,  (google it). If that doesn't kill it, the fact that it's giving you stat boosts for paid items is BAD. The game has potential, but it's all just wasted currently.

Zero Point is an experiment, delving into the unknown territory of VR cinema. My relationship with this project is that I originally pre-ordered the movie back in March for ten bucks. Did I get ten dollars worth of material here? Nope, not even close. Am I disappointed? No not really because my original intent was to help these pioneers push out a product that will help us decide what and where this new medium can and should go. I am glad that it happened, I am glad this exists, and I'm glad that Condition One pulled the trigger rather than giving up.
What does it mean for you? For the price, not worth your time or money. It's only 15-20 minutes long. That's a dollar per minute and you're really not going to be coming back to this over and over. There is only one or two scenes in here that were somewhat intriguing but marred by the deficiencies of the recording equipment. If you've tried the Oculus Google Streetview experiment, the 3d is about the same quality that's supported there. The 3d is tacked on having things farther away appearing closer than they should and there's one scene in particular where the scale was significantly smaller than it should have been making the people appearing in it seem like midgets. Sound wise, some scenes have good implementation where others are off by a long shot. I experienced some technical issues immediately trying to start it up, the resolution being very far off for some reason when mirroring my rift with my monitor. Extending it to the rift got the resolution to work out but the movie would show "Optimizing Video Quality" would fade out and then just show a blank screen. After several restarts it finally loaded without any real changing of settings on my part.
The whole thing is just very unpolished and left extremely wanting. If I were to speculate though about the future of this product, I imagine the price will eventually come down quite a ways. Presently it's most likely reliant on making sure that the pre-orders don't feel like they were ripped off as they originally intended for the experience to be worth $10-15. From the way they've behaved the last 6 months I would guess that as they pieced it together, they realized that they were missing the mark by a bit, but couldn't just down the price immediately without incurring the wrath of their early supporters. If they're smart and want their product to actually reach more than just a handful of people, they'll drop the pricing on this as soon as they can down to a few bucks because it's really not worth more than that. Until then, save your dollars, download the demo, and just wait to see how this one plays out.
Again, I want to congratulate Condition One for sticking with it anyway, tackling problems without any kind of standard to follow, and doing their best to deliver the best product possible. Like the first ever motion pictures, the actual quality was much less important than the groundwork they were laying down that generations to come would study and learn from.
*Edit: With the new price change I'm going to go ahead and switch my review status to recommended as I absolutely wish to support the devs and all the work they did for this. That being said, the product is still the same. About the same price as a bag of chips and as far as VR products right now go, this is a decent snack right now.

If this were a perfect would, I would be a millionaire and purchase every single Magic card there is. I love the illustrations, the rules of the game, the lore... everything.
However, seeing as this world is far from perfect and there is no way to keep up with buying cards all the time, this is the closest it can get to doing the real thing.
After finishing the campaigns (I suggest you do that, as that's how you will get booster packs), you can play against the A.I. or join online matches. Of course, winning matches gives you coins (as well as finishing daily quests), which you can then use to buy new boosters.
As with every other game like this one, you can buy cards with real money and that's actually the fastest way to get to the good stuff, but you can still make good progress just by playing daily and finishing quests.
There are still bugs that should be fixed - some of them can be quite annoying at times - but there's no doubt that this game can provide you with hours of pure Magic The Gathering fun.

TL,DR: DO NOT BUY THIS. IT'S NOT A REAL HITMAN GAME AND IS RIDDLED WITH FLAWS THAT MAKE IT UNENJOYABLE. IF YOU CAN REFUND, DO AND BUY A KEBAB INSTEAD!
Oh god, this is a tough one. Hitman. It's a damn awesome series, and this one still has the same mechanics, the same gameplay, the same idea at it's core. But everything around it seems so damn wrong...
First, there's the graphics. Set to Ultra. LOD of Doom. At 5m away, characters have a face straight outta minecraft. Coming somewhat closer, that gets suddenly replaced with an actual face (but still of horrible resolution), with an emotion of an iceblock. Call me crazy, but wasn't 47 supposed to be the cold killer here? He's got more facial animation throughout the whole game than any other character. Then, there's the cutscenes. Rendered in glorious 720p, with letter- or pillarboxing, depending on your taste, they look just as bad as the game. But hey, can't fit a higher resolution on a DVD for the Xbox 360, I suppose. And then there's the actual environment. While closeup it doesn't look bad, basically the next room already isn't much more than a blur. And before anyone asks, that's definitely not an issue of graphical horsepower, a 980 Ti is more than capable to push some proper view distance. I mean it was 2012, we got Far Cry 3, Assassin's Creed 3, Dear Esther, Dishonored, XCOM, I mean, even Borderlands 2 and Spec Ops looked a lot better than this.
But fine, graphics' not everything about this game. What about sound? Voice acting is good, music and mixdown - not so much. Music sets in as sudden as it stops, they mixed some stupid sounds in for tension, and a lot of the voice acting is looped too often.
So what's left is the gameplay. And this is where it gets hard. This game is still the old Hitman. Sure, the AI is pretty stupid most of the time, but it's still fun to sneak through levels, avoiding most of the good guys while taking down the bad guys. What isn't so much fun is the fact, that some parts are basically unplayable in stealth, that they had to add some stupid bullettime-events, and that the levels feel much more linear and cramped than the previous title. Weapon handling, although this most definitely should not be an FPS, is really bad. You might think a professional killer might know how to shoot steadily, but nope - that aiming♥♥♥♥♥♥is all over the place. They also added a♥♥♥♥♥♥lot of collectible stuff that requires you to do the same short missions over and over again, for basically no good. Sorry, that's not how give a game good replayability.
But then, there's the good parts - the story really isn't bad, and it has it's moments where you just get a good series of moves and actions together that make it feel like it should be.
Still - with those hard flaws in the graphics, sound and AI department, and the fact they're trying to convert Hitman into a damn mobile series, I cannot recommend this game. Very much not for 20€, definitely not for 60€.

Splinter Cell Chaos Theory is not a perfect game - but as old as it is, you can find it surprisingly fun to play and fairly easy to get into.
Chaos Theory on is focused mainly on sneaking and getting from point A to D. You will occasionally be lockpicking doors, hacking, hiding bodies, interrogating enemies, etc. Killing isn't a necessity to progress, either. Feel free to speedrun through (most) levels as a pacifist!
There are several video options regarding quality. It supports HDR, Shader Model 3.0, Anisotrophic Filtering, Anti-Aliasing, and such. This includes widescreen-monitor support as well. Unfortunately, Versus Mode is completely different - locked at 30 frames, only supports DirectX 8, no 16:9/16:10 ratio support, various missing or unincluded game options, and overall a huge disadvantage. It is most similiar to Pandora Tomorrow in terms of quality and gameplay elements.
My only problem with the game that remains is the lack of players. The modding community on the other hand is still fairly active. In another note, Gamespy servers have been long since shut down, and much of the fanbase has moved on, especially after Splinter Cell: Blacklist was released in 2013. You will likely notice less than 15 players a day in Versus lobbies, and an even smaller number of players in CO-OP lobbies. I recommend bringing some friends along to ease the stress of waiting and finding more games to join.
The game deserves my overall 9/10 rating. I've never given a game such a high rating, and my expectations have always been rather high for most games. It's worth it. Bear in mind that it isn't perfect, and it still has it's fair share of issues to this day. But it is *the* perfect stealth game.

Brilliant Shadows is a well written and drawn visual novel.  There are a few choices to make, but they seem mainly to give a bit more backstory than have a significant impact on the story itself.  The art is stylized and interesting to look at, which is good, because there isn't a whole lot of it.  Mainly you are looking at the same character models exchanging dialogue with some limited animation.  It is fully voice acted and clearly there has been effort made to have the characters emote when they speak.  The writing is solid, if a little stiff at times, and the voice acting is fine (though I was always aware that the actors were speaking into microphones).
The story is interesting, though it does drag a bit at times.  Apparently this is the first part, as the title suggests, so the ending is not particularly satisfying.  If you enjoy fantasy stories with a bit of romance and mystery this might be a good bet.

I don't usually write reviews, but I feel that there are a lot of unfair and/or misleading reviews left for this game which I would like to address.
-This is an early access game and as such suffers from some bugs and glitches that can negatively impact your in-game experience. I have seen NPC clipping, texture smearing of both terrain and NPC skins, crafting menu glitches that require you to log out and back in, and slightly inconsistent NPC aggro ranges. Try to keep in mind that this is a fairly new game, it is in early access and honestly, for how young it still is, it is in pretty good shape.
-This is a slightly grindy game, but that can be adjusted by simply cranking up the player XP multiplier when creating your game session or server. The amount of resources required to create things (gear, consumables, and buildings) scales well as the complexity of the items increases during the course of you leveling your character. Very rarely have I experienced a problem obtaining the required materials to craft a piece of gear or new structure for my base. The overall level of grind to get to that feeling of being powerful is a little high at first, but evens out as your u become familiar with the way the games world works.
-The powers that are currently available are fun, but will eventually require some rebalancing due to the fact that I can ride a broomstick around and kill pretty much anything I want from relative safety. The different weapons offer some variation in gameplay style and certain powers are only available for specific weapons (which is a nicely executed way of preventing someone from becoming an uber-wizard-god).
-The building system is easily one of the best parts of this game, the mouse controls are very intuitive and there are a lot of choices when building your base. There are multiple types of materials that you can choose from, each offering some benefit over the other (obviously the higher-tier materials are better for their HPs but require A LOT of preparation to obtain). It would be nice to be able to build a structure that hangs underneath an overhanging rock formation, but that is really the only negative thing I can say about this part of the game.
-A lot of users complain about crashing and overall performance issues. I run this game at the lowest possible visual settings because my laptop is from 2014, and I have only had it crash three times, all of which happened within the first two hours of me opening the game. I am not saying that it is perfect, but I wouldn't take performance issues into consideration when trying to decide on buying this game, just be smart and know your computers limits. If you are having crash-issues, try lowering  view distance or turn down the shadows at least until the game gets some more stability/optimization updates.
-Some people are having community issues and write negative reviews based on that. This is not a valid complaint to have about any game that has a PvP aspect. What people do in games is not governed by the developers, but their is a responsibility on the devs part to make their intentions known to the players as far as the type of gamer interaction they are attempting to foster in their games. With Citadel, there is an incentive to attack another players base which is pretty much standard in any base-building game, on any platform. The best way to play this game is with a friend or group of friends, multiple players can tackle harder obstacles earlier, which enables the players to level up faster. Furthermore, multiple players, working together can build a much bigger, much better base more efficiently. Having said that, I have logged some solo hours and enjoyed flying around, killing monsters, and exploring the map on my own.

I hope that this review has been helpful and informative. I am enjoying this game very much and I am looking forward to seeing better reviews and continuing support from the devs and the community to help this game live up to its great potential. If you are still cautious, put it on your wishlist and wait for a sale!

I'm generally a fan of a good, fast-paced platformer.  I really, really wanted to like Bleed, but that anticipation was crushed in less than 30 minutes of play time.  The challenge of this game owes a lot to the awkward control scheme.  The game relies on you making use of its double (triple?) jump mechanics and bullet time ability, both of which are default mapped to shoulder buttons.  You can change the mappings, but since it's a directional shooter (left stick moves, right stick shoots) the default mapping is really the only one that makes sense.  It sounds like the controls should work, but more often than not I found myself jumping in the opposite direction than intended.  By the time I got to the first boss, I was already more than frustrated with the controls.  After dying at least 5 times to the first boss, I gave up.  I can't recommend this one at all...there are far better platformers, even at this low price point.

Know what you are buying before actually buying it.
It's important to see this short film more as a tech demo to show what film in VR can be capable of.
It's a short, roughly 20 minute or so documentary that really just serves to show a lot of neat different scenarios captured on film to immerse you into the experience.
The film is primarily just some guys in the industry talking about how big VR can become and its incredible possibilities while several different scenarios and scenes are gone through during the short running time. There isn't really any connection at all to the different scenes you are put into throughout the documentary, however if that doesn't bother you then enjoy the ride! If anything, their random nature is to help prove the point that the guys are saying about how many endless possibilites there are for VR to have.
Some scenes stand out more than others, and honestly some of them can be truly fascinating. One scene in particular made me feel incredibly present in the setting, and really pretty uncomfortable (in a good way, haha!).
All-in-all, if you're going to buy it then just make sure to know beforehand that this is more like a tech demo for what film in VR can be, and that this ultimately proves that there is a very bright and exciting future ahead for that. If you go into this with that knowledge I really believe you'll find this to be a great, enjoyable, and fascinating experience. There is some really great material in this short film, and even with its slightly pricey tag, I'd recommend it to VR users looking for a really neat and new experience.

Probably the best entry in the series, even compared to the newer games.
Story is excellent, with a number of twists and turns. The options to stealth or kill one's way through are actually present; unlike SOME games, with the right set-up I can get through 95% of SC:CT without killing anyone. If I do, whether on accident or on purpose, then I at least have the option of hiding the body or running away. Takedowns are similar, and the environment kills are nothing short of fantastic!
Speaking of - its environments still look gorgeous even on modern systems - even if the character models are less-so. And the sound design and soundtrack? Absolutely brilliant; a perfect mix of background noise and high-tension BGM makes me almost crap myself if I accidentally blow my cover and the alarms start going off.
The only downsides are that it may be difficult to run on some newer systems, and... well, not to spoil anything, but the last level was somewhat of a disappointment, as it turns into nothing short of a bloodbath, despite all my efforts to prevent that from happening. As well, it may be problematic to get used to the controls (it took me a few hours of play before I got them down), but once you do it becomes less of an issue.
Overall, for anyone interested in a true stealth game and not just a short break from running and gunning, this is a must-have.

I've only played for 3 hours and 40 minutes at the time of this review but I'm having a blast with this game so far! The art style is simplistic and the music can get a little repetetive but the gameplay is very addictive. You can pick from multiple difficulties which is always nice for challenge runs and such. A lot of customization in your shop, from the stands, down to details like wallpaper and roof types (each with bonuses)
The core of the gameplay is split into managing your shop, in which you stock up your shelves, plant seeds in your garden and then away you go. There's a few things you can do while customers come and go, including clicking people to urge them to visit the shop, watering your plants, clicking birds and tumble weeds to get random drops of bits of gold, getting quests from NPC's in whic you supply and item and they later return with some great rewards. You can also train to level up your character, craft items to sell or equip and buy supplies from the merchant.
The second major gameplay area are in the dungeons. The character moves along attacking themselves, but the player has a pretty interesting job. As enemies die they drop items which you must quickly slot into your bag. There's a ton of different bags with unique shapes and unique features (certain tiles that warp an item to your shop or sell an item directly etc). It's almost like tetris in terms of trying to fit as many items as you can in. You also need to keep an eye on your character's health and use potions when you need to. Different dungeons have different quirks such as some where items placed in your bad will fall to the bottom ala tetris, while others may have obstacles such as rain falling on random bag tiles making you work around them until they disappear.
Sure the game may sound simple but it certainly has that old-school addictive feel. The multiple parts of the game with completely different play styles keeps things interesting and there seems to be more and more that unlock over time. I've recently unlocked the ability to buy another shop on an island as well as take NPC's to a park to raise their relationship level and get some extra rewards. I'm always looking forward to see what features will unlock next!
The developer listens to the community and makes changes and additions based on feedback which is always a huge plus. They even have a survey for new features built into the game i nthe form of an NPC who occasionally will ask which feature you would prefer from a couple of selections. A unique and interesting way of voting for new features and I love it!
Can't wait to play more of this and to see wha tthe future holds.

There’s a lot going on in Pixel Shopkeeper, in fact, you’ll probably be a lot busier running a shop than you’d be if you were just adventuring all the time.
And unlike most fantasy games, the evil forces in Pixel Shopkeeper are truly evil, with their legends being based in reality. I speak, of course, of the dreaded student loan debt.
And just like real life, if you miss a payment for your student loan, you die and have to restart back to when you graduated.
But that’s okay, cause it’s pretty fun running a shop, gathering all the ingredients, and doing everything you can to milk those adventures of all their gold.
The developers seem very dedicated to working on the game after release, and the game even includes a survey taking NPC who comes by the shop every now and then and gives you a multiple-choice question on what new features you’d like to see in the game.
Balancing your loot-gathering skills, and how well you run your shop can be challenging at times, and just one missed payment means starting over, but all in all it's a fun experience, and one I recommend.
