An excellent showcase for first-gen VR filmmaking. I had the DK2 in extended mode, with my solo monitor set as primary, launched Zero Day from Steam (not in VR mode) and it just worked, perfectly. The short film (~15min) is sort of a compilation of various demo footage, most in 360* 60fps, all of it in stereoscopic 3D. Some of the footage is better than others, and around a third of the footage is either 180* or normal footage projected onto a curved display. The opening and closing segments feature a fully rendered cinema where you are transported to and from your seat, through the IMAX-like screen, and into space. Yes, it's awesome. With the latest Oculus runtime and firmware installed, I noticed very little judder, but some judder and screen tearing is normal during the 360* footage, due to the work-in-progress nature of the techniques used to stitch together so many camera views.
I'm all for supporting premium VR content at this stage, since it will allow developers and filmmakers to developed new tools and processes to keep pushing things further. The price may seem hefty for a short film, but this is good stuff, and a lot of resources went into putting it together. It's also by FAR the easiest way to showcase a number of great things VR can be used for. From epic nature footage to sightseeing, a wedding, and a shape ship, there's something that would appeal to anyone who you might want to demo a Rift to.

The majority of people who do not recommend the game are Civ V fans angry at the games new mechanics, also claiming that many features have been dumbed down or is otherwise stupid.
But I'm going to be honest here, this is because the game has not yet reached its full potential; remeber what Civ V was before Gods and Kings and Brave New World? with the addition of Rising Tide soon it is going to be likely soon that it, and along with other DLCs will make the game likely better than the other Civ games.
Beyond Earth also takes into account a new problem that Civ V didn't have to deal with before: Competitors; with new, more technical games such as Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis IV people are now departing from the Civ games to favour a more complex, procedural and immersive experience. Beyond Earth solves this problem by removing itself from that niche, making it more of a "build a colony on a new world" style game than the now-contested "build humanity from the stone age" game. It is definitely worth noting as well that the hex system definitely fits the colony sci-fi style much better than the ye olde knights style of Civ V
To conclude, I wouldn't suggest buying this game YET, but I'd definitely suggest playing it with the soon-to-arrive Rising Tide expansion to give a truly unique experience that its older iterations can only dream of.

A real good and fresh shopkeeper game. Definetly the best since recettear.
The bad stuff first. It needs works in almost every aspect. The gameplay loop, interface, balance, controls and much quality of live stuff. Further many mechanics are not very clear or it fails to explain them properly. As the tycoon genre is about optimizing and min/maxing that is certainly harder then it should be here. My biggest problem is that I can't play it for longer sessions as there are to many tedious tasks and they get more the larger your shop gets. There's no way to automate even the most simple tasks. I want to play, I have things I really want to archive but after an in-game week I just have to quit because the thought of filling my whole shop again feels like work. I don't think I ever had this problem with another game.
But the developer shows great ambition to improve the game. And the basis for that is really quite good. The puzzle element is nice, maybe one problem is it's rather stressfull than challenging. There's much to unlock and constructing the store is the best part. Most of the furnishings are shelves or passive bonuses and I'd like to see more things changing up the gameplay though. The progression feels good and there's always a goal and it has surprises and new gameplay elements that open up later on. Again most of those are not fleshed out or explained enough, but it shows a certain understanding of the genre.
To be honest it probably should have been an early access release, but if you like shopkeeping games take it - we don't get that much and this is our best bet at the moment.

Archeblade: Not as Bad as You Expected, Yet Not as Bad as You Hoped.
(Verbose: You might have, like me, given this game a try because it looks comedically awful. While the character design is, including a mech-dwarf named "Dic the Megaton" and a black dude who started a money-cult and could only be more offensive if he used gratuitious slang, the rest of the game isn't THAT bad.
That said, it IS bad. Balance is a bit weird, where some characters are actually fairly balanced (Sewon, the black guy I mentioned earlier, is actually interesting to play, and there's a lich who is fun without being too broken as well), others are almost hilariously broken (an archer who is equally deadly in close and far ranges, a dual-wielding pistol character who can kill you literally from across the map without warning). Matches are simple deathmatch variants that drone on for far too long. Cosmetic items and weapons are limited, which I could forgive since this game is quite new, but the best items are locked behind the paid currency, meaning this game toes that "Pay-2-Win" mentality.
That said, you might have fun downloading this with a few friends, stomping around as the Megaton Dic, and laughing at it all. But, honestly, there's probably far more valuable uses of your time. Like Gunz 2: The Duel, this is yet another F2P game I expected to be a total joke, yet walked away disappointed by the fact that it seems like, on some level, this very well could have been a decent game.)

Bloodline Champions is a unique moba in my eyes to be one of the only games of the genre to fulfill the MOBA term. The game is centred around two or three champions on each opposing team with one main goal; to defeat the enemy team. There are no objectives or items in the game so you don't have to worry about last hitting or farming for a lategame composition, you are the champion you play and nothing more.
There are a few things you can add onto your account to help you ingame such as masteries, gems to socket into your medallions which can buff, damage or even protect. The game is very fast-paced and skill based almost every skill in the game is a skillshot played through an isometric camera. The game has four main roles of Tanks, Healers, Melee and Ranged. There's a lot of champions and each have strengths and weaknesses, there are tournaments as well as PvP seasons for you, the game is very satisfying however the only real problem with the game is the lack of updates from the developers and the rapidly decreasing playerbase.

Do I recommend Homefront?
no.
The idea of this game is a great one, I’m always down for alternate history (even though this is set in the future) but you see my point. You play as a pilot who joins a resistance force, who fight off Korean forces that have invaded many years prior, the ideas that this game brings to the table are good in theory but don’t hold well at all.
The characters are shallow, cringy and at their worst, annoying, not only their dialogue, but the ways they were implemented into the game. For instance, if you want to walk through a door that an NPC has opened, you MUST wait for that and all of the other NPCs to enter before you do. This forces the player to wait and gets annoying fast. Also in combat, you constantly get stuck on characters because of their large hitbox, and they constantly walk in front of you when you are shooting. Along with this, there are moments where the characters go through some "deep" emotional scene, but because of how little you care about the characters, the messages that they are trying to tell don't come out very well, because you can’t get invested at all.
My main problem is how restrictive everything is, how you MUST do this, or how you HAVE to do that. I think the more choice a developer puts in their game, shows how much they really values the experience the player is going to have. It shows that they are giving up a piece of their narrative to better suit the players experience, this game does none of that, everything you experience in this game is shoved down your throat, forcing you to eat it. I’m all down for linear games, but if you restrict my movement and make me do things I don't particularly care about, I wouldn't want to play your game anymore.
And it leads to just that. I have only played two hours of this game, and I don’t want to play anymore. Bear in mind, I try to play games at their highest difficulties to get the best possible challenge out of them, but that challenge that I love experiencing isn't here, I have no reason to finish the game, I don't care for its characters or mechanics, I would rather play something like Deus Ex or operation flashpoint, but in the meantime, I will not recommend this game, and I will wait to play Homefront Revolution in the near future, to see if any of my criticisms have been corrected.
If the Price lowers in a sale and you pick it up for almost nothing, then I recommend giving it a go then to see how you feel, if not, then stay clear. This is a game I really tried to enjoy, but I just couldn't.
Thank you for reading.

Half-Life 2: Deathmatch is a multiplayer first-person shooter video game developed by Valve Corporation. Released on Steam on November 30, 2004, it uses many of the assets from Half-Life 2 and its Source engine. That being said, this game was an after thought, Valve has never really cared about this game or its fan base. With the exception of Counter-Strike this game is/was one of the most exploited, buggy, and hacked multiplayer games on the Source Engine. With every new update it got worse and worse. Now all negative thoughts aside the game did have one of the best advanced movement mechanics of any game I've ever played, again with another exception of HL2DM Pro Mod/AG2. As of the time of writting there are less than 300 servers and only a dozen or so cater to vetran players like myself. I've worked in the modding scene and level design for this game for several years to try and bring a new player base to this game but that only goes so far. This entire game needs to be reworked from the ground up starting with netcode. Sad to say if someone asked me today what I thought of it I would have to say it is bad, look elsewhere for a better arena shooter like Toxikk or Quake.

Hitman Absolution suffers from the same thing that held back Thief 2014 and Splinter Cell Blacklist in that it's a good stealth game in itself but pales horribly in comparison to its predecessors. That being said it is indeed a solid and fun stealth-action game with a nicely directed story held back by really goofy characters and lack of innovation. The gameplay here is definitely tailored for a more linear experience rather than an open-ended puzzle structure like Blood Money. The gameplay mechanics differ from that of Blood Money in that disguises are easier to omit here due to the obvious paths developed due to the more linear level design. What's also frustrating is the limitation of the disguises themselves which lose effect once you get too close to an enemy of the same dressing or run out of focus, a resource meter that acts as a sixth sense mode. People have pointed out often enough that it makes no sense for every cop to recognize you once you wear their uniform. That being said it's also in place to accommodate the design of the environments. Playing through easy mode essentially gives insight into how easy the game would be had the disguises functioned as the did in previous Hitman games with Absolution's level design. Another gripe would be performance, the game drops considerable frames in larger and more detailed environments on hardware that should be plenty more than enough to accommodate this game's visuals. It could just be my system but some have reported that a certain update has impaired performance. Another gripe, and this is just a nit pick, but there's a vignette that is always present during levels which I absolutely hate. The contracts mode is a neat idea but as usual the linear and restrictive level design can't accommodate something with such a small scale design. Most challenges present in the game are made for masochists who enjoy hardcore challenges instead of levels with genuine care and creativity put into them.That being said there is some enjoyment to be found in this mode.
Overall, this is a solid stealth-action game for those looking for this type of game. For Hitman fans such as myself, it isn't the next big creative chapter in the series but it's an enjoyable experience nevertheless.

Hitman Absolution may not be a "true" Hitman game, since it lacks the big, open sandbox areas, but it's still a good stealth game nonetheless, prefering the use of several smaller, more linear and contained areas. You're supposed to try to complete the areas as clean as possible, with the help of disguises that are nerfed. They're still helpful sometimes, but don't function in the same way as past titles. If you need to use combat, it's functional but too generic. There's a mechanic that let’s you freeze time and pick your targets before executing them, which is cool but wastes many of your instinct, which gives you hints. But it depends on the difficulty you choose. I suggest a full playthrough on normal for enjoying the game first. And then, if you liked it, try to play it again on higher difficulty settings, or try to complete a lot of the optional challenges that this game has for each chapter. The game also has a well written story and voice acting, more personal to 47. The graphics and music are OK, but i didn't really enjoyed the overall scenery of the entire game. It's too dark and lacks some variety. It's a long game with lots of replayability, but for that you need to enjoy it. I liked it, but was a bit disappointed by it. If you enjoy stealth games, get it on sale. It also includes the Sniper Challenge prologue, which is a separated title and a fun, little time waster.

Having burned a lot of hours on this game, I would love to give it a positive review. The gameplay is decent and the character balance is fairly good so long as one learns how their skills synergize with each other. The plot is nothing special, but it's better than the atrocity Marvel sold to us as the Dark Reign crossover event. It dragged to hell and just wasn't very good.
So why am I refusing to recommend it? No, it isn't because of Pay 2 Win. Yes, the game suffers from that severely; people willing to burn hundreds of dollars on this game will quickly find themselves way above other players, with most high-ranking players having obviously bought their way to victory via cover upgrades and hero packs. But in the end, there can still be a satisfaction of working your way up to that level and doing a good job with what you can earn for free.
The problem is the AI, which has been horrendous ever since the original Puzzle Quest and hasn't been improved in the slightest. You see, the thing with Puzzle Quest games is that their grids are not generated on the fly. Rather, each column has gems pre-generated for a good 20 drops in advance. The AI knows that; it is given full information to which gems are going to drop next, meaning it can set up combos by abusing information the player has no way of accessing.
The result is that if you play this game, you should get used to losing not because you did bad, but because the AI made one move which escalated into 10-30 successful combinations, overloaded its resource pool and allowed it to spam you to death in one move. There was a time when I legitmately sat there for 30 seconds, doing nothing but watching as gems drop onto the field and immediately successfuly match themselves because of one enemy move.
I could forgive Pay 2 Win, but I will never forgive artificial difficulty achieved via a cheating AI. As such, I cannot possibly recommend this game to anyone.

The game looks good by 2012 standards. It neither fails nor exceeds reasonable expectations for a game of this caliber in the visuals department. Audio however seemed off at times. I was baffled by how nearby conversations or environmental effects would be muffled or muted. A good gaming headset didn't help either.
Otherwise I encountered no bugs, exploits or crashes. The game is undeniably resource intensive but still runs fine. Probably even more so now in 2017, I presume. For some reason the interface and menus felt entirely like a console port to me, in the bad way that cross platform ports tend to do.
Story in
games never seems to do much in terms of advancing the overall series to someplace new. This one holds true to that tradition; the story and timeline is fairly standalone and self contained in view of the whole. It's also cliche considering how closely some elements of it resemble other games and films in the action espionage genre, but it's nonetheless well done and enjoyable.
On the Easy and Normal difficulty settings (Enhanced) you can pretty much figure out what to do just by snooping around, and the harder parts of the mission can be brute forced, either by combat or heavy reliance on the Instinct resource (Ctrl is your friend). The three higher difficulties (Professional) are Hard, Expert & Purist. These contribute a difficulty bonus to your score.
Beware that they also provide significantly less hints, checkpoints and resources while adding more enemies with faster reactions! You can check your score breakdown mid-mission. It's fun to compare your performance to other player scores and redo missions differently to try and earn more points. That replayability is enhanced a bit by custom contracts (including player made ones).
At higher difficulties,
successfully captures the unique brand of fun that its predecessors offered! It's so rewarding to find ways of creatively, stealthily eliminating the opposition through observation, planning and finally precise timing and execution. Opportunities for this style of gameplay are abundant in the campaign, just waiting to be found (along with some subtle humor and easter eggs).
The

Nope!  This game is offensively too broken to justify spending even $5 on if you intend to be chasing any sort of game progression or steam achievements.
Sure, the racenet site is pretty terrible, does a poor job of barely handling the minimal functionality required to support the features for which it is needed.  Sure, the AI and other humans are often out of sync between gamers in the same multiplayer game.  Sure, you will usually find multiplayer lobby empty unless you switch your Steam download location to somewhere in the EU.  That's all relatively trivial next to the known save game corruption bug that's wiped out my progress twice within 6 months.
Twice now, the game has rendered my save data corrupt.  Both times, this was after normal quitting of the game through the exit option in the menu.  This is apparently not uncommon, and has happened with a number of others.  None of the online racenet progress is actually stored online in any way that can be recovered.  Nor, for some reason, is the Steam cloud being leveraged to recover one's lost progress.
Some gamers have recommended  disabling Steam Cloud support for the game, citing repeated failures by codemasters to handle it properly in other games.  Further, it's been recommended that users go through the hassle of digging into their C:\Program Files(x86)\Steam\Userdata\<steamuserid>\255220 to save backups regularly.
After the first time it happened to me, I disabled Steam cloud support, and made a copy of the 255220 userdata folder on occasion.  I eventually got comfortable and a bit lazy, and had not backed up for some time, at which point it occurred again.
Hundreds of online races, purchases, upgrades, and funds lost.  Hundreds of career races and progress lost.  No way to complete the missing achievements without first redoing all the lost effort to get back to where you were before your save game data was corrupted.
I honestly think this game could be good if the publisher could be bothered to fix the handful of bugs plaguing it.   It appears the developer has no intention of fixing any bugs in the game at this point.  Though one could argue hours of fun racing did occur, resetting users' progress when they are halfway through the achievements... repeatedly... is absolutely not an acceptable situation.
Most active developers update their games with bugfixes as the need arises.  Codemasters apparently feels this game is complete, bugs and all, and is focused on putting their efforts into releasing new paid-for content instead of fixing the glitches.
I could say save yourself the money, but honestly, save yourself the wasted time chasing achievements, and save yourself the frustration and anger at a developer who took your money and doesn't seem to care that the game is broken.

The best Splinter Cell game to date.  I'm a huge fan of stealth games.  Chaos Theory came out near the end of what I like to call the Golden Age of Stealth games and it still holds up today, for the most part.  Story wise the game is lacking, which is one of the reasons I would rank Choas Theory under games like Metal Gear Solid 3.  The graphics aren't great even for a game that came out in 2005.  Enemy AI is decent for the most part, but their imposibly quick reaction time to spotting you can be frustrating.  Somtimes if you bump into an enemy or are somehow spotted they will
start firing, as in no animation of them turning around or rasing their gun, just immediatly firing.  Apart from that the AI is decent. Mechanincally it's a phenomenal stealth game worthy of the genere.  There are light and sound indicators telling you how visibil you are or how much noise your making, it even tells you the noice level at which the enemy will hear you.  Unlike recent releases in the franchise, Chaos Theory isn't a game you can approach with guns blazing.  You actually have to use stealth.  You can't fire from the hip and you have to pull your gun out every time you want to fire which decreases your movement speed significantly.  The PC version runs fine on modern systems, I had very few problems, and the game supports 1920x1080 without having to mod the game(old titles tend to be hit or miss with resolution support).  If you have a high refresh rate monitor like I do you should know that the game is locked at 100 FPS.  Keyboard and Mouse work fine, but it doesn't have controller support like most title now do, so you'll have to figit with it if you want to use a controller.
Story Score: 6/10
Rest of the Game Score: 9/10

Do you like handmurder? This games does, especially if you try to master it!
An action-platformer that strangely unites the best of Megaman X and, I'd argue, a teensy bit of Devil May Cry, this game captures the best of both with its dashing, harsh combo counter (you gotta be mad good to stay at S-ranking), and nifty boss designs. Each level is thematically different, with bosses suited to each, and hazards similarly well suited for the environments you encounter, and every last bit of each is (if you ask me) intended to rip away at your health and combo ranking, making it a fantastic game if you like high-speed action and a high skill barrier to master it.
The art style and music are also really enjoyable, unless you're tired of the retro stylings a little, but even if you are, I'd recommend this on the basis of its gameplay alone, as that it makes it stand out from the loads of other somewhat slower, more methodical puzzle platformers or sidescrolling roguelikes. The story isn't much to talk about, though, as it's the basic hero's quest to overcome past heroes and be the new best hero of the world, with pretty frequent acknowledgment of you as a player if you die often.
In short, if you want a good, solid action platformer similar to old Contra games or Megaman X games, you can't go wrong here.

The level design tries to give more options. While the game still is highly linear there are multiple paths to the same objective giving a bit more sense of freedom and choice. The side objective in every mission also add to the replayability.
There is also coop mode which is quite fun, while far from perfect and multiplayer versus mod which I never had chance to try.
Overall a really good package.

*Those of you who try to bash me over the fact its an "Early Access" game, seriously would you rather I give every game 10/10 praise just because? Read or don't, your choice*
NOTE: The amount of time spent is correct (at the time of writing this review, 2.5 hrs), so no, I am not done. Just giving my thoughts on the so far. This is NOT by any means a "I'm done" review, just a so far review.
No joke, this game is HARD! Find food? PRIMARY! Find Meds? PRIMARY! Find Bandages? PRIMARY!
Have a knife & you see enemies? DO NOT RUSH, you are far more likely to die if you rush in.
Build Beds so your guys can heal from sickness, some wounds, and your guys will ALWAYS get tired after every scavenge mission. Build Stove to cook food (you can eat raw, but i doubt thats a good idea). Upgrade your stuff to unlock better build & upgrade options.
Watch Totalbiscuit's "WTF is.." of this, and if you're still unsure, check GT Reviews. This game is dark, cold, psychological, mostly a sneaking type game like Thief, some ways feels like Castlevania (minus the monsters), and reminds me heavily of the Scattered Colony flash game (very similar, except you can't pick what you get in that game, this one you can).
Trust me, its very easy to die in this game if you're not careful. If you can make a shovel, bring it with you on scavenge missions (it will help if you need to clear the way or need to defend yourself). Trader will always show up at your door, read the item descriptions to gauge their worth to your survival - and don't ONLY get components while out there on missions, you can't trade that (which is dumb - devs, seriously, what is more important? surviving or building?) and if you find diamonds grab them (really good trade items even tho i don't see why anyone would value that over guns, food, meds, and bandages).
Personally, I wish I could just say "Maybe Recommended" since I haven't played enough. For now I'm recommending.
I'll update after I beat the game multiple times (multiple stories in the game including a Make Your Own) or until I get seriously frustrated with it.
Buy if you LOVE challenging games.
If you get frustrated easily in games that give you little in the way of starting off, then don't buy it.
This game is NOT for everybody. If you do get it, don't take it lightly cause if you do, you lose very quickly.

Buy this game. Just do it. Hands down one of the best games I've ever played and I've played a lot of games.
First of, the atmosphere is just amazing. Gunfire echoes in the background and shells explode somewhere far away (thankfully). There is always a sense of insecurity and dread. Do we have enough food? Do we have enough water? Enough ammo? Medicine? These questions usually come up in survival games but where most games (IMO) only ask these questions during the first half of the game This War of Mine keeps asking you again and again and again. It keeps throwing new challenges at you and if you ever start feeling like "okay, I think we got this" it makes damn sure to pull you down to earth again.
Then there are the choices. Some are easy, some are hard and some are just borderline impossible. Do you help your neighbours when there house is shelled? Do you give away your last bandage to help someone in need? Do you kill an innocent to stay alive?
This visual novel is one of the best I have ever played. Not only do the MCs tell a compelling story through Maple Syrup, but they bring the Canadian Dream to heart.

Maplestory is a game I have been playing for quite a while (I think 7-8 years) and I still love it! Many people's complaints are that the game is "too easy" or "easier" than how it was previously, and it's true, it is easier, but the big problem I see with their complaint, is that the game will still take hours of your time to max a character. It was only recently that level 250s appeared, and that took them months to go from 200-250. I realize this game is a lot of grinding, but the same can be said for a lot of other MMORPGs on the internet. The music in this game is amazing and deserves a listen to, especially in places like Henesys. The gameplay, while being very grind heavy, is fun and fast paced! You've got a wide variety of characters each with their own set of skills (5 different sets: 1st Job, 2nd Job, 3rd Job, 4th Job, and Hyper Skills with the exception of Evan, Dual Blader, and any others that have more than 4 Job Advancements), and while some are overpowered, this game isn't a competition unless you make it a competition! Another complaint people have is that there are several "Pay-to-Win" concepts in the Cash Shop such as EXP boosts, Money Bags, and ways to make your equipment better, but once again, it's NOT a competition. There may be some PvP side areas, but if you don't want to go against somebody with overpowered equipment, just don't go to the Battle Square! All the things people complain about are easily fixed on our ends! If it annoys you that people decide to be all high and mighty about their high level characters, ignore them! It doesn't matter! This game isn't a competition, it's simply a game for messing about on your own or with friends. People argue that people rarely do Party Quests anymore, which is true, I can't argue against that, but Party Quests are not required by any means, they are just a fun way of getting EXP. My biggest complaint with the way Maplestory is, however, the fact that a higher level cannot train a lower level like we used to. If there is too big of a difference between your level and the person you are training/being trained by, or maybe between the lower level and monster's level (20-30 levels I believe) then you will not get ANY EXP from their kills, meaning if you want to play with your friend's higher level character, there won't be much point because they'll be the ones getting experience. My main point is that almost everything people complain about is how much more powerful certain classes are, or how powerful people can make equipment by paying, or how much money people can get by paying, but the fact of the matter is, this game is only a competition for those that want to make it a competition. This game isn't meant for you to challenge a random stranger to a hunt, but rather to challenge your friends to a hunt. Overall, Maplestory is a great game as long as you remember that it's not a competition, and if you're the type who can't stand people being better than you at a game, or can't stand it not being a competition, than I can't help you.

or those of you who are having CTD issues, follow these instructions.
1) Right click on Bioshock 2 in your Steam library.
2) Select "Properties"
3) Select "Set Launch Options"
4) Paste "-dx9" without the quotation marks, hit "Ok" and then "Close."
5) Relaunch the game.
Credits to Master Bates for finding this fix. It seems that Bioshock 2 crashes when attempting to run some sort of element of DirectX 9 that is incompatable with newer hardware.
If you still experience CTD issues, try this fix by Pheabus2K19
1. Find "Bioshock2SP.ini" under C:\Users\YourName\AppData\Roaming\Bioshock2Steam\, make a backup if necessary;
2. Open the .ini in notepad,and search for "TextureStreamingMemoryLimit", the default number is 256, which is too low, try set it higher as suggested below:
512MB VRAM = 400
1GB VRAM = 600
2GB VRAM = 800
3GB VRAM = 1000
For example, if my GPU had 2GBs of VRAM, I would set TextureStreamingMemoryLimit=800;
3. Save and run Bioshock 2

Grid 2 had me hooked from start to finish. You start out as a nobody in some random race and get noticed by a billionare due to your driving skills. You become the material to promote a new world series - WSR (World Series Racing). Your fame grows, you get contacted by sponsors who want you to take part in various events, you take on more difficult opponents all across the globe and eventually participate in the WSR Grand Finals over a set of races.
It's mad action from start to finish.
The graphics are fantastic and the car physics are exceptional. You notice a vast difference from driving a FWD car compared to a RWD or an AWD. Each car handles differently and you really need to be on your toes if you want to master it.
The game isn't without faults, however. The most prominent among them being the difficulty level. I consider myself a fairly competent player when it comes to racing games; I was playing on Medium from the start and almost the entire game through. Near the end I had to switch to Easy because the AI was just too fast. No matter what you did, they would always catch up. They would overtake you and then you were screwed.
Playing on Easy felt too easy and playing on Medium felt like Hard and sometimes Very Hard. It wasn't an enjoyable experience. I don't mind it being difficult, but it should also be fair. It reminds me a lot about the first Need for Speed: Underground game where in the last five races or so the "Catch up" was horrendously broken. No matter how good you drove, the AI would always catch up and overtake you and you had no hope of beating them. Only by downgrading the engine in your car would everything work the way it should.
While this game portrays the cars and their handling exceptionally well, some cars are just way too finicky. Cars that are normally glued to the road when it comes to handling in real life are suddenly all over the place here. I don't expect a true representation but when other cars in this game are near identical as their real life counterparts, I do expect some kind of resemblance.
The tracks are well made but it's only a select few you race on near the end. Some variety would've been nice. That goes the same for the class of cars you're allowed to choose from. Somewhere in the middle of the game you have plenty of choices in what class and what type of car you want to drive, near the end it is only two classes and a select few cars. I would've liked a better selection.
I haven't tried online racing so I'm not going to touch on that aspect.
All in all, GRID 2 is a great game that offers plenty of action and challenge.
FInal Verdict: 7/10. It's a great game but the difficulty level is kind of messed up and lowers the score a bit.

This is not a simulation racing game, but it is a good racing game to keep coming back to.
Originally, when the game was released, there was a lot of discussion about the interior camera and the fact it was not fully rendered. In fact, for as long as I have played simulation racing games, this has been a major concern. With this game, I don't see it as a necessity, as it plays well the way it is. There is certainly a "weekend race" asthetic they are going for... and they are the best who have done it yet. I personally don't think that anyone has done it quite right yet, but this is not bad.
As far as the driving goes, it really feels the most like driving a go-kart than it does driving a car. You drive the car from the rear wheels, wanting the car to rotate off throttle. On throttle, you feel like you are driving off the right or left rear tire. In transistion, the cars yaw incredibly quick, which feels more like karting than GT/production car handling.
With controls, I use a Fanatec setup. I attempted to get it working with the sim, which it would. However, I could never get the correct feel for the cars at all. Even with the ability to change the degrees of rotation on the wheel, the cars just felt incorrect. However, once I fired up the XBOX360 controller, the cars felt correct. This just proves the game was designed with the controller, and not the wheel, in mind. I am sure there is a way to look up and change values for the game to make the wheel feel good, but that is not what I am looking for. I am looking for a control solution, out of the box, that works well. The controller is what works.
With the career, I get the same problem I do with all racers of this generation -- career burnout. It is just an endless series of races that really never feels like progression. Completing races to check the boxes in the career is the GRID championship. Also, the championship forces you to drive racing disciplines you many not enjoy. This just never felt particularly engaging.
I will eventually beat the career mode, but this is definitely just a "when I have time" game. Between iRacing and a myriad of other simulation raing games, this sits a distant, yet respectable, 4th or 5th. However, when I have time and I need a break, GRID Autosport is always a solid and consistent racing experience with a controller.

Big Pharma is a strategy/puzzle game and an assembly line simulator, in which you’re tasked with manufacturing and selling pharmaceuticals. You are creating drugs by altering the concentrations up or down each step requiring a machine with a line in and out. The raw materials and finished drug need an exit from the game. You research new materials and upgrades to your operation and apply for patents before your competitors do. Each material has a density from 0 to 20. Effects and side-effects apply to a segment of the density scale. The game is sufficiently complex without the expansion, which adds setting prices for meds and real competition.
Verdict:
The game is complex and surprisingly fun to play. The expansion is too complex IMO and not much fun since it’s too hard. It’s worth a buy, but save yourself a lot of grief and stick with the vanilla version.

One of the greatest stealth games ever created. It's in the Holy Trinity of stealth games, along with Thief 2 and Hitman Blood Money.
Gameplay: There's a light and dark stealth system, which means that staying in the dark is crucial to sneaking by. Some of the tensest moments are spent hiding in the dark while a guy with a huge gun is so close you can see his nosehairs. You can always see how visible you are and how much noise you are making in the HUD, which provides a lot of convienence. You can also use sounds in the enviorment to mask sounds you are making, like thunder. I recall one moment where you have to open a loud door in front of a sleeping guard, and if you don't open it while he's snoring, he'll wake up. You can also interrogate guards you've grabbed, and it leads to a lot of hilarious and memorable moments. The gadgets from Pandora Tomorrow make a return (the previous game in the series) while adding some new additions to Fisher's arsenal. The gameplay overall is tense and satisfying, and makes you feel like a badass spy.
Graphics: The lighting system is brilliant, and looks better than most modern games. The character models, however, are lack luster. I remember one specific guard who's gums were light green. And Sam himself, when he's not wearing mask, has a consistent cross-eyed dumb look on his face. The textures are fine, not really anything special. It looks fine, overall.
Sound: When the absolutely kickass music isn't playing, there's atmospheric sounds and really sets the mood. The sound design of effects like footsteps rivals even the Thief games. The enemies have very stereotypical accents, and it's done for laughs. The music starting to play when an enemy is suspicous and is looking for you really kicks up the tension.
The sound design overall, is fantastic.
Level Design: There's usually at least one alternate way to get into an area (although it heavily relies on pipes and crawl spaces.) It's non-linear and sprawling (excluding the first level) and is fun to explore. The level design is great (while not anywhere near the masterful level design of the Thief games.)
Conclusion: Buy this game. If you're looking to get into stealth games, this is the game. One of the greatest games I've ever played.
And I don't know why the enemies can't see the 3 suns on top of Fisher's head, shut up.

Bleed is a twin stick (best played with mouse and keyboard), pseudo-bullet-hell 2D platformer with some of the smoothest, most fast-paced, and most gratifying combat I've ever seen. You play as Wryn, a pink haired videogame heroine wannabe on a quest to dodge, dash, jump, and shoot herself towards the title of Gretest Hero of All Time. At her disposal she has an arsenal of weapons, a triple jump, and the ability to slow down time. You think you've seen bullet-time done right? You've seen nothing until you've tried this game! I cannot describe with words how incredibly satisfying it feels to air-dash your way, in slow motion, through the one small gap in a wall of bullets (very hard-mode) while maintaining your combo-meter for maximum damage.
But let's not be completely biased here. Many players will probably be upset by the fact that this is a really short game. Like a
short game. To make your way through the seven levels on normal will take you about an hour. To get through hard might be another hour or so and after that the same goes for very hard. There are ofcourse some extras like arcade and challenge mode but the main bulk of the game is easily beaten in an evening.
The weapon unlocks also seem pretty useless, I stuck with the starting weapons through most of my playthrough on both normal and hard as I saw almost no reason to switch weapons during any stage or boss fight.
That said tho, this is a really, really fun game and I will probably end up spending more hours just replaying this than in most $20+ games I've bought.
Pick this up if you're:
A fan of fast-paced, skill based combat.
An old-school gamer with too little time for those 40+ hour AAA titles
A speedrunner. This game is the perfect speedrunning game.
You just want to relax and have som fun for an evening.
Don't pick this up if you:
Are on a budget and/or want a high Time/$ ratio
Hate pink
Want to miss out on a great time

Still the best game in the serie.
It was made when AAA stealth games were actually challenging, and punished you hard for going full rambo.
The plot isn't really memorable, it's your average action movie scenario involving really bad guys and your witty american hero saving the day. Nonetheless, Sam Fisher is a character you'll find easy to like, and can make you crack a smile.
When it comes to gameplay, it's kinda frightnening to notice how rigid it is, how the game got old. It gives you everything you would expect for a good stealth game, a lot of possibilities, some alternate routes, and a heavy dose of "waiting in the shadows hoping for that guy not to see you".
Graphics-wise, it's holding up. When the game came out, it was one of the most beautiful thing I had laid my eyes on, it really blew me. It was on par with all the AAA games that came out at this time, maybe better.
Soundtrack was composed by Amon Tobin. Yep, Amon Tobin. As a result, Chaos Theory has an atmosphere no other Splinter Cell game has, and god, they wish they had it. It's a real pleasure to lurk in the dark, your knife ready to stab Generic soldier#54 with a stressful, sometimes a bit creepy, note from the wonderful soundtrack.
And co-op has to be the best co-op experience I ever had on any game. It's challenging, it requires communication, and you can climb inside a vent by touching your partner in places you wouldn't even have thought about in the first place.

Ever wanted to finish school and begin the start of a new life... with a ton of debt. Well I haven't either and that is why we have this pretty fun game.
Its graphics are, as the title of the game states, pixelated. 8-bit. Nothing wrong with that and always a very refreshing look that never really tire the eyes.
The music is very upbeat and makes the game lively.
But the real question here is: How is the gameplay? Well first, imagine you are playing a good old retro rpg and stumble upon a shopkeep. Where do they get their items? How is their lifestyle like? Why do they sell things?
Well now you are a shopkeeper, fresh out of school and in a ton of debt. How do you get stuff to sell in your shop? Well, work for it.
This game implements a type of battle concept. Theres a side scroller on the top with your character fighting monsters. As you kill a monster, it drops items. Simple enough, but the tricky part here is you have to pick up the items and place them in your bag before it disappears. Depeding on your bag layout, you have to befit the items into the bag, similar to tetris. This concept is very unique and it makes you become quick on your fingers to gather the most amount of items in the most efficient way possible. While all of this is happening, your character has its own health and attacking stats. If your character "dies," then you do not gain the items. If you win, the battle finishes, you gather your items that you collected and then comes the more "relaxed" part of the game.
Shopkeeping is the next challenge in this game, you have set up tables, all in which has their own attributes and advantages. You place your collected items and you put them out to sale. But that is not the part where you can just leave the game running in the background. Next you have to attract upcoming wanderers and the likes, and occassionally you will come across npc's that have a star above them, that indicates that they are special npc's and can give you tips, free items, and teach you new abilities (In which I will explain briefly later). There are also aspects like keeping your tables clean, have them upgraded to gain more profit, and if you have picky customers, they simply won't buy it because of how dirty the tables are.
The goal of the game is to rack up enough money to pay off your rent ever other week or so, and the price will raise, requiring you to find ways to raise the amount of money you get per day. If you fail to do so, you simply just, well... die.
The "abilities" stated earlier include crafting recipes, remodeling, and several more, but those will then help, up your income from of the items being sold or raise more interest in future customers.
The environment whilst you are going about your day selling stuff are interactive from birds to tumbleweeds. They can give you stuff like gold or items, or even the chance of taking gold away.
There are a lot more stuff that I wish I could cover, like the level system, stats, dungeons, farming, etc.
Overall this game was very enjoyable, and has much much more than what I put here and I look forward to continue playing this game and seeing what more it can give.

Hello Close friends and strangers of the interwebs. I'm going to be reviewing ArcheBlade, a game that was officially released on Friday. ArcheBlade is a 3D multiplayer fighting game that primarily uses simple combos to perform powerful and extravagant moves. Let's get to it.
The game has some fairly common mechanics. Each character has a different combination of amour and health. Once your amour has been destroyed, your character begins taking damages to the health. Health can be regenerated by specific abilities and items found on most maps. Amour, however, cannot.
The combos and what they do vary from various characters. There are some common ones, but the amount of damage varies. Some of the more complicated abilities use what is the equivalent of stamina. Stamina regenerates quickly.
The final piece of the combat is the rage abilities. Most characters have 2, requiring different amounts of rage. Rage is generated by causing damages on another opponent.
In ArcheBlade, there are six different game modes.
The thing that really sells the game (so to speak) is the variation between characters. There are 12 different characters altogether, but they plan to add more. These characters are all very balanced in a combat but I found myself drawn to one specific character while I was trying them all out in training. I strongly recommend trying out all the characters before choosing one, as it will cost the in game currency to purchase one.
Currently the game only has six game modes. They are described below.
Undersiege: This is a 3v3 mode in which you earn points for kills. The teams play up to a score of 30. The players continue to spawn until the score has been reached.
Netherdale: This map is a capture mode where up to 14 players are allowed, 7 per team. The aim is to capture the pylons scattered throughout the map. When a pylon is in your team’s possession, it will gradually earn you points. However, when a pylon is in the enemie’s possession, it will gradually earn them points. The first team to 2000 points wins.
Nagas Pit: This is a free for all game mode in which up to 8 players are allowed to join. Once a player reaches a score of 70, the game ends
Steam Canal: This is a 4v4 mode; the round does not end until all the characters on one team have been defeated and the first team to win 4 rounds wins the match.
Night Undersiege: This mode is a 3v3 consisting of 4 rounds. One team wins the round as soon as all opponents have been defeated.
Altar of War: This mode can be a 2v2 or a 3v3 of 4 rounds. One team defeats the other and wins.
As you can see, some of the game modes are very similar.
The graphics and the position of the camera both remind me of the free game "Smite." It's clear that the camera angle is designed to make the combat as fast paced as possible.
I have to make a special mention to something that every fighting game implements, that ArcheBlade did very well. Voluptuous women wearing tight clothing that is few and far between on their figure.
Okay, Let's recap
Strong mechanics
12 characters
6 game modes
Good Graphics
Embellished women
Free
It's a 8.5/10 From me

I have no idea if Steam will say at all if I've played Maplestory but I promise you all I have put a lot of time into this game and absolutely loved every minute. Unfortunately Maplestory just became completely uninteresting since I've tried to relive it. And it makes me really sad. Maplestory originally had the classes we all see in every MMO (no matter how hard other MMO's try to make it different) and of course also like every MMO it started off simple. One big difference of course was the fact that it was a 2D sidescrolling MMOPRG and it's done so beautifully. You can make different faces at people depending on how you feel which was really fun before the cliche "lol" and "lmao" texts we all now universally know. Getting weapons was also a little more unique since most MMO's just milk weapons. Now a lot of MMORPG's have bows with unlimited arrows and guns with unlimited bullets. Maplestory made you buy arrows and throwing stars/shuriken if you wanted to be a ranged class. And Mesos (Maplestory currency) was hard to come by at low levels making it even more challenging since you had to actually ask for money from time to time.
When I originally loved this amazing piece of gaming art you had to use a taxi to get to different cities (which you still do at least) and use flying boats to get to different continents. This was a huge deal because it allowed you to just settle down for a short time and actually talk to people; and listen to music along the way. Now this is not the case. There were no overpowered and annoyingly voice acted 'Hero' classes that literally kill everything in their paths with ease. You really had to work to get more powerful back then and you also needed to manually know what your stats needed to be for your class. Maplestory added more powerful classes over time but they were never 'Hero' status. Yes they got more powerful due to their unique skills compared to the default classes; however you still needed to start off as a default class and work your way into the more unique class you selected and leveling was still just as hard for you as the rest.
The music is still the same Maplestory anime music I know and love. I just wish it could be heard with the game I knew and loved. For all you new players out there reading this review it'll mean close to nothing probably. To shorten what I just said: Maplestory used to be a surprisingly vast game filled with lots of social opportunity and hours upon hours of questing and leveling. It's a shell of its former self now. This does not mean I say it's a bad game. It's still good and worth the try. But unfortunately you have missed the golden age that was Maplestory. It's all milked down and I can't recommend it in its state now. What used to take a couple weeks to a month takes less than a day now. Bosses that originally required a full team can easily be defeated solo and the monsters that were originally intimidating and powerful are powerless. The challenge is gone. I will miss you Maplestory.

Have a knife & you see enemies? DO NOT RUSH, you are far more likely to die if you rush in.
Build Beds so your guys can heal from sickness, some wounds, and your guys will ALWAYS get tired after every scavenge mission. Build Stove to cook food (you can eat raw, but i doubt thats a good idea). Upgrade your stuff to unlock better build & upgrade options.
Watch Totalbiscuit's "WTF is.." of this, and if you're still unsure, check GT Reviews. This game is dark, cold, psychological, mostly a sneaking type game like Thief, some ways feels like Castlevania (minus the monsters), and reminds me heavily of the Scattered Colony flash game (very similar, except you can't pick what you get in that game, this one you can).
Trust me, its very easy to die in this game if you're not careful. If you can make a shovel, bring it with you on scavenge missions (it will help if you need to clear the way or need to defend yourself). Trader will always show up at your door, read the item descriptions to gauge their worth to your survival - and don't ONLY get components while out there on missions, you can't trade that (which is dumb - devs, seriously, what is more important? surviving or building?) and if you find diamonds grab them (really good trade items even tho i don't see why anyone would value that over guns, food, meds, and bandages).

Yes or no? I think Dungeons 2 is barely a yes but falls short. I want to give a yes but there are problems. Dungeons 2 is a supposed parody of the Dungeonkeeper series. However, it is only partially similar to Dungeonkeeper. Everything in Dungeons 2 is like a parody. From the story, to the gameplay, to the design. Dungeons 2 is a real-time strategy (RTS) game that looks like Dungeonkeeper. Dungeons 2 has a joke story, parodies characters from other games/novels and doesn't seem to have anything original to add. All of that simply reeks of laziness and in-your-face attitude. Parodies might be enjoyable if you don't try to blatantly ripoff other people i.e. an in-game joke, but Dungeons 2 is an entire parody based off Warcraft 3, A Game of Thrones, Dungeonkeeper, Lord of the Rings and God of War. It's not fair to other developers who take the effort not to copy. Kalypso may think that it's funny and is engrossed with making big bucks.
Gameplay-wise, it's RTS, not Dungeon Keeper. Your aim is to build up your base in the underground map, grow your foces and send your minions into the Overworld to complete objectives. There are 2 different control schemes which are very confusing and depends on whether you are looking at Overworld or Underworld.
Overworld, RTS style where you group units using CTRL and right click move. You can micro-manage your units to attack specific targets. Spellcasting is limited to friendly spells and you can't use certain spells like Lightning. This is odd as lightning normally strikes from the sky, in the open.
Underworld, you have a hand that can pick up minions. You cannot micro-manage your units here. You can only pick up them, drop them or slap them. All spells can be cast in Underworld.
Conclusion, Dungeons 2 is actually a no that can turn into a yes, if Kalypso Entertainment can improve the game greatly. It has to choose how it wants to play. Do you want RTS or Dungeonkeeper? Don't do both, please.

Minimap is bad. 2 control systems that work differently above and below.

Snot, Goblin, Naga, Orc and Troll. It's too few. I think 7 would be just nice and you get to pick and choose which 7 you want.
3. Bugs/Glitches
a. Models fly across the screen when you pick them up in the dungeon
4. Inelegant and Confusing Teching/Research
Do you want to upgrade a Troll to a Troll Juggernaut? It's not Troll (Level 1) -> Rockthrower (Level 2) -> Troll Juggernaut (Level 3). It's Troll (L1) either Rockthrower (L2a)  or Troll Juggernaut (L2b). L2b only appears when you upgrade your dungeon to L3. Imagine the confusion when you have to do it manually.
Then they create a demonic evil which is a purple version of the Absolute Evil and that one upgrades L1-> L2-> L3.
5. Inelegant Room Building
Every single room has to have add-on structures built onto them. E.g. Brewry need 2x3 for a kettle. Can you just auto build the kettle when you make a 2x3? The only elegant one is the Treasury which doesn't need any kind of special spacing and has no add-ons.
6. Can't See Beyond 4 Research/Builds
If you queue 4 research, you will only see 3.
7. Attack move is the F key
Why the F key? Why can't you just use A?
8. Parodies and Tropes
A Game of Thrones, Warcraft 3, Lord of the Rings, God of War. Creating a parody is one thing but this is quite overboard.
9. No sign that you are Attacking Buildings
Attacking units will flash a red circle. Attacking buildings is just a guess that you are attacking it.
10. Minimap on the Bottom Left and Right
The bottom left is supposed to be Overworld and bottom right is Underworld. It is so hard and confusing to look at 2 maps on opposite sides of the screen.
11. 4 Resources, Possibly Too Much Junk
Gold, mana, beer, crates. Way too many things to pick up. The mana bubbles and crates are major problems. The crate model is way bigger than gold and really easy to accidentally pick up. Why do you even need to create so much junk?
12. Compulsory Trap Placement Space
Why does the spinning trap have to have 3x3 grid to work? Why couldn't you just use spinning blades on a rotating pole? It takes up 1 square but you have to have 8 empty spaces around it to place it down. This is so annoying.
13. No Possessing Your Minions
That was really fun in Dungeonkeeper.
14. Reloading of Traps/Doors
You have to have crates, lot of crates to reload your traps.
15. Similar Race Different Skin
The Horde and the Demons have very similar same base mechanics. The only difference is that you rearranged how the units upgrade. One does training, one does sacrifice. It would have been better to combine them into one, just like Dungeonkeeper.

Out of all the racing sims available, and I have all of them, this one is still the best.  Projects Cars looks better, Asseto Corsa has better physics, IRacing has the leagues and community, RFactor2 and its "subsidiaries" have loads of realism,  Forza has countless cars, etc., etc., but this game is very well-rounded in all of those aspects despite not mastering any of them.  IMO, the damage model is simulated extremely well and can be comparable to Dirt Rally.  I've seen some wrecks that really blew my mind and many of them were without my direct involvement and rather the end result of the Ai simply pushing their machines beyond their limits.  I'm glad there is a rewind feature for those moments.  And the Ai are incredible.  Other than iRacing, I don't play against online players.  Simply too many factors can work against me.  So, I rely on really good Ai behaviour and you get it here.  I can't begin to describe how well of a job Codemasters has done in programming the Ai.  They're not too hard and not to easy, not overbearing or sloppy/wreckless.  The best Ai I have ever raced against.  Awesome.
There are many good racing sims out there, but this one is a must-have.

Dungeons 2, despite being the follow up from the first Dungeon game, works very different in mechanics. Dungeons 2 goes more back to the classic strategy game. You still build an underground dungeon, but now you actually get to control your army and often need to take it above ground to fight the allied forces on their own territory.  Neither do you 'control' your lord and he just sits chained on his throne.
The game is way easier to pick up because of that. No more complicated ways to get energy by making complicated dungeons and you can satisfy your bloodlust right away to your hearts content while your minions happily doing the gathering.
The story is filled with silly references to give you some good shuckles. It's a very light story which is hard to take serious filled with references to other games. Personally I found it quite entertaining.
The combat is a bit messy. Your army like to run out like brainless individuals, not caring whether their ally is under attack or million miles apart and it makes it quite hard to succesfull target a specific unit in a heat of a real battle.
All in all, I'd advice this game to anyone who enjoys the slapstick humor and references. It's, in my opinion, the best thing of the whole game. If you're more into serious organized and well balanced gameplay and combat. Then you might want to pass on this one.

This is considered my favorite game of all time, and to make sure I have your attention now I'll tell you why :
-Awesome storyline
-Chaos theory has the best multiplayer of any splinter cell
-There are co-op missions that me and my cousin spent countless hours on (unfortunately the PC port doesn't have it... for some dumb reason).
-The gameplay is amazing as there is never one way to get through a scenario
-The graphics are still relevant to today's high tech world
Now the detailed explanation.
The
is epic. Why is it epic? Splinter cell series has always been known to have a crazy or sort of conspiracy storyline, chaos theory delivers a lot more than that. Two lead programmers that cracked Philippe Masse's kernals from the first splinter cell have enhanced his algorithms and now could be used for any electronic warfare, be it military or economic. One of these programmers is discovered dead early in the game, and the other one on the loose... the story just begins to exponentially get better from there.
The multiplayer was my favorite in this game as it gave me everything I wanted. I want to play online ... okay go ahead. I want to play with my friend on the same screen or at my house and he at his... fine go ahead. Want to play competitively as a spy? Fine. Want to play as a guard and take down spies with a first person view.... heck the devs cared so much they did this too. When someone really gives an effort to really allow any sort of play when it comes to multiplayer, it's greatly appreciated.
I would say the
of this game is arguably the best type out there. The physics/engine in this one is what would one expect from a third game of the series. I would argue that still to this day even though there are other Splinter Cell's out there, this one still has the best game engine. The soft body touches, the noise system, throwing of objects to make noise, ability to whistle, use the SC-20K it's sniping/assault attachment or it's launcher attachments, the grenade types (frag, flash, smoke), the three different goggle settings (heat, night vision, ECM), ability to either knock out or kill an opponent... there's quite a bit of things to mention. I like the fact you are given a choice of going through vents or alternate ways to avoid conflict or can go through conflict, or one by one slowly "put to sleep and hide the bodies" conflict. The greatest improvement though compared to the first splinter cell is that there is flexibility in the proximity system. When one is close to the enemy, they don't ultimately see/feel you just because they walked past you going through a doorway. This game is fantastic in how you are able to knock someone out or kill someone before they can react. This was a major breakthrough in the series.

In short, this really does feel like a reskinned version of the previous titles, but it still does offer some fun play and interesting new concepts in Civ.
The landscape, troops, natives, and improvements are some new art, but the aliens are basically just reskinned barbarians under the graphics.
I think they missed the mark there, where they could have had entirely new and foreign races, rather than just different types of humanity. In addition to the human races, they should have had aliens opposed to humans, and others accepting of humans, that are also colonizing. They could have had established ones with just outposts that don't seek to expand. And hostile expansive types of aliens. But they just keep the aliens under the limitations of the barbarians in previous games. I just feel it was a missed opportunity.
There are new and interesting things to be found in the tech tree. And affinity is an interesting concept in that chosing to become accepting of the aliens, opposed to them, or dominating them, allows for interesting alterations to the types of troops you can have. This helps encourage new play-throughs to experience the different types of troops.
I really wish more had been done with the Wonders though. I loved in the old Civ where a cut scene would happen showing you just how wonderful the wonders are once completed. In this game I feel more like they're just another building. One that only one city can get, but that don't really have a great affect on the overall outcome of the game.
Just seems a shame since rather than having the old wonders of earth, they could have had imaginative new designs to show you in a cut scene with interesting affects on your overall game. For the most part, if you miss the wonder, there's tons of other quests or buildings that can cover what you lost from not building the wonder. So they're really just not that wonderful :/
But all in all it is a fairly fresh take on the Civ games, and I do recommend it for those that like Civ. Plus, where developers fail in your oppinion, you can often turn to the mods.
--And that last comment reminded me of something to mention. I have quite a few mods for this game now. If you also use mods, keep in mind that each time you start the game, you need to activate the mods or else when you try to load your saved, modded game, the game just crashes to windows. Annoying :P

Im going to try and sum up this game all that I can in as little as possible starting from the top and most important- Specs.
This game's minimum rig specs are not as specified. You will need a bit more. However, even with more than specified, you will lag. Graphics will not render properly or at all at some points. Spells will be cast, and continue to float there indefinitely. Mobs will flicker and float into the sky. You think something is in front of you? Guess again, it decided to render 300m behind you. You want to avoid a fire ball? You will! It'll still hit you 100m away from impact. Generally, I believe this is development side's fault. This game needs heavy optimization, which wont come because the Dev is too focused on more content. Cant build a house without a foundation and you cant get drapes without windows.
The next most important is the lack of content. The main purpose of this game is to Craft like a sweatshop slave or aimlessly kill anything and everything. When I mean everything, I mean even end game enemies that are 50 levels higher than you. There are no quests. Really, there is no goal to this game. You play just to grind, build, and grief (if on a pvp server). There is no reason to gather and store supplies. Nothing is valuable since it can be gathered almost immediately. Which means there is no real economy in this game since nobody needs anything.
Last but not least: The bugs. The bugs are pretty comical. You will laugh when you see a Giant die and then float into the sky. You will get angry when you see your dragon disappear under the map. And you will cry when you see your own home become, "Abandoned" even when claimed with a throne. A LOT of the bugs in this game are not typical for a game that has a price tag. They are borderline sloppy to the point of wondering if the devs even cared to finish their game. Some bugs were so apparent that they could have been caught in less than an hour of playing through the game. Just by that observation, I dont even think the Devs played their own game. (Not displaying item count in chests correctly when there is a counter, for example)

Ive kept tabs on a handful of players (Who I have befriended) and they have shared with me how they are leveling or how they got to 60. The level 60s on my server are the only players that have played non-stop. One is a game developer (Who plays games specifically to test numbers and push stats) and the other has no life commitments. This is by far the BEST experience I had with any digital version of Magic, no contest here (compared to 2013 and 2014 edition).
Where Magic 2013 and 2014 were severely restrictive and felt like video games just using MtG cards and mechanics, "Magic Duels" feels like the full experience.
This review from the perspective of somebody who's not into competitive aspect of the game, plays very casually and mostly with AI just to enjoy game mechanics, fantastic art and fiddling with cards.
The game's great asset is a friendliness towards new players as it comes with a really wonderful (and even partially voiced) tutorial that explains not only game basics, but also more advances mechanics as they appear in the game.
A special "wizard" helps new players with constructing their first deck, but it becomes useless pretty quick as you get familiar with the game and want full control while building your deck.
Now it's time for elephant in the room - the implementation of F2P system. In this case, it's the best possible scenario: you pay only for the cards - but it's not mandatory. You can earn ingame gold (required to buy boosters) by playing through campaign, by winning battles againts AI or other players or by completing daily Quests.
You can really enjoy it as a true "free" game, without making any investment, and actually play the game for the thrill of getting new cards ("what's in the new pack?"). And still, even with less than optimal deck, you still have a chance with online opponents, because you will be matched based on your rank.
Pros:
+ complete freedom in deck building (the biggest change to the old editions, which allowed only to unlock some cards and customize pre-defined deck)
+ F2P model works well - you can invest to get the cards quicker, but there is a lot to enjoy even without ANY investment. If you commit to invest, you only pay for the cards - it's as fair as CCG can be. No game features are locked behind the paywall and no artificial restrictions (you don't have to pay for additional "deck slots" and stuff like that)
+ good (and often challenging) campaign
+ ability to play against randomized AI
+ beautiful artwork
+ clean, well-designed interface
+ very good tutorial
Cons:
- rare occurances of game instability and connectivity problems
- ingame pop-up's

[Edit: The gamebreaking bug have been fixed] - If you keep playing after you have 500.000 gold. It will open a cutscene that keeps crashing the game.
- The hired manager makes no sense. He earns you money without selling anything. Also you cannot go adventuring, and have a manager/managers work in the store, at the same time. It is one or the other.
- Notifications pop up i the middle of the screen, making it impossible to interact with people, while it is up.
- Not really a bug. But the only way to get ingredients for crafting, is donations from townspeople, The ocassional chest, if you get lucky, instead of collecting them on adventures. I feel like it should be the other way around. You find ingredients, then use them to craft the gear for sell.
[Edit: There is now a Easy mode, if you don't wish to go trough this. So it is no longer a big issue] - The first part of the game is a terrible mess of trying to pay back a loan in time, and reloading again and again. Not sure if i feel it is to hard. But it surely was a pain.
- The autosave saves just before you need to pay back the loan, and if you can't, you lose. So if you dont have a backup manual save, you are fked.
[Edit: This was fixed, you can now build the house a lot bigger!] - The house can only be upgraded to around double the size, but the lot you have it on is huge. This makes the game very grindy, since you cannot make money faster, lategame.
- You have to CONSTANTLY click the tables to clean them. This is probably the biggest annoyance in the game. There are so many other things you need to pay attention to during a sale day. And having to constantly having to click the tables, multiple time, to clean them, makes my heart bleed (At least the shelfes never get dirty. Phew).
- It is missing some story elements in the end, that i know the dev is working on at the moment.
As it is. I just can't recommend it.
I DO feel however, with some patchwork, and more storytelling from the very helpful Developer, this will become a great game.

And as such i can not recommend this game. At the time of writing i have 5 hours played. It feels like 50. I wanted to quit after the first hour but persevered. It did not get better. Its tedious, monotonous, repetitive. Only 1 person can scavenge one location per night, regardless of how much time you spend there. The quantities and variety of materials involved are such that the actual gameplay is just tedious, frustrating inventory management. The only replayability comes from the fact that since there is actually no guidance or tutorial at all, the only way to learn your options is by your mistakes.
It is, when all is said and done, an interactive story, as some "games" are. Ive been gaming for 35 years. It has no real game mechanics and when you seperate the actual gameplay from the thought-provoking scenario theres really not much there. If you want an experience similar to watching Schindler's List, the you may enjoy it. If you want an actual game then you probably wont.
4/10

*Those of you who try to bash me over the fact its an "Early Access" game, seriously would you rather I give every game 10/10 praise just because? Read or don't, your choice*
NOTE: The amount of time spent is correct (at the time of writing this review, 2.5 hrs), so no, I am not done. Just giving my thoughts on the so far. This is NOT by any means a "I'm done" review, just a so far review.
No joke, this game is HARD! Find food? PRIMARY! Find Meds? PRIMARY! Find Bandages? PRIMARY!
Have a knife & you see enemies? DO NOT RUSH, you are far more likely to die if you rush in.
Build Beds so your guys can heal from sickness, some wounds, and your guys will ALWAYS get tired after every scavenge mission. Build Stove to cook food (you can eat raw, but i doubt thats a good idea). Upgrade your stuff to unlock better build & upgrade options.
Watch Totalbiscuit's "WTF is.." of this, and if you're still unsure, check GT Reviews. This game is dark, cold, psychological, mostly a sneaking type game like Thief, some ways feels like Castlevania (minus the monsters), and reminds me heavily of the Scattered Colony flash game (very similar, except you can't pick what you get in that game, this one you can).
Trust me, its very easy to die in this game if you're not careful. If you can make a shovel, bring it with you on scavenge missions (it will help if you need to clear the way or need to defend yourself). Trader will always show up at your door, read the item descriptions to gauge their worth to your survival - and don't ONLY get components while out there on missions, you can't trade that (which is dumb - devs, seriously, what is more important? surviving or building?) and if you find diamonds grab them (really good trade items even tho i don't see why anyone would value that over guns, food, meds, and bandages).
Personally, I wish I could just say "Maybe Recommended" since I haven't played enough. For now I'm recommending.
I'll update after I beat the game multiple times (multiple stories in the game including a Make Your Own) or until I get seriously frustrated with it.
Buy if you LOVE challenging games.
If you get frustrated easily in games that give you little in the way of starting off, then don't buy it.
This game is NOT for everybody. If you do get it, don't take it lightly cause if you do, you lose very quickly.

For a game touting how much it wants to be a fighting game, it sure show an utter lack of knowing what makes a good fighter, good.
Every hit staggers, no matter how light of a tap it is, or even if it's a distance attack, which means as long as your being attacked you have no options.
You can infinitely combo someone if your competant enough with a character, but for best results two on one ensures you can always juggle someone to death
There is no sort of counter system, you either are throwing up a guard or being staggered when you are being hit, and you either wait for someone to bail you out or the attacker to stop, there isn't anything in the way of causing people to cancel out or dodge (Unless your playing a specific character who has a quick dodge ability which is mainly for long range/stealth characters).
Netcode is atrocious, even on servers you have low latency with you'll see people who just seem to bounce around in mid combat.
Character abilities are mainly built around the idea of being quick powerups of some sort to quickly give you some sort of favorable edge, but they aren't instant which would make them much more useful, as they feel like they are built around the idea of being "popped" quickly, but they have animation priority, and the moment you are hit it cancels it out.
One character in particular seems to rule any sort of combat in this, by virtue of their normal attack being an AoE that surrounds them entirely, the animation constantly moves the character about while using this attack making them incredibly hard to hit if you have some sort of way of getting in past their attack without being staggered, meaning any sort of melee character is immediately at their mercy due to the combination of flaws in the combat system.
Overall, it all amounts to something saying it wants to be something it's not, mainly for not clearly understanding what the hell makes what it wants to be what it is.

First of, the atmosphere is just amazing. Gunfire echoes in the background and shells explode somewhere far away (thankfully). There is always a sense of insecurity and dread. Do we have enough food? Do we have enough water? Enough ammo? Medicine? These questions usually come up in survival games but where most games (IMO) only ask these questions during the first half of the game This War of Mine keeps asking you again and again and again. It keeps throwing new challenges at you and if you ever start feeling like "okay, I think we got this" it makes damn sure to pull you down to earth again.
Then there are the choices. Some are easy, some are hard and some are just borderline impossible. Do you help your neighbours when there house is shelled? Do you give away your last bandage to help someone in need? Do you kill an innocent to stay alive?
