Big Pharma could be characterized as a procedural logic puzzle game with several random-ish elements.
But that sounded a bit boring, so I'd rather call it a "living puzzle".
Basically you got your factory gadgets, which need to face certain directions, and you connect them to each other with conveyor belts. Then you input drug ingredients from wall sockets and upgrade them along the production line. You can rotate the gadgets, but not mirror them. After you decide your production line is long enough and your drug is done, it must be processed into a pill, a cream etc. and sent back into a wall socket - then you can begin selling it!
It's not a simple as it sounds, in fact I think this game is quite challenging, at least with the DLC add-on. Some people said that the base game is a bit easy, but I only played with the DLC. Every factory gadget has a processing cost when stuff moves through it. So you have to ensure your drug is cheap to make by optimizing the amount of gadgets. You can make your drug stronger and boost your sales by getting rid of side-effects or adding positive effects and boosters from other ingredients, but there are many specific logical rules in place which ensure that you will mostly have a hard time doing so.
After playing a while I have to say I like this game. Somehow it balances the line between being both addictive and frustrating at the same time. The game is quite well made and balanced gameplay-wise, and I've yet to see any bugs in the game which is also a very good sign.

Three months ago when I started this game, I loved playing it. I truly enjoy three-match puzzles and this also introduced me better to the Marvel universe. There are regular events with witty dialogue and the more I played, the more I felt rewarded.
Then I had two characters leveled to 85 (the current max level at the time for Thor and Storm) and that's when hell was unleashed. Oh dear.
Even though there is PVP in the game, you never play against an actual person. Instead their three characters are controlled by the computer. And since the computer is dreadful at this game, the only way the computer can win is by having victory magically handed to them. Every single day I see the exact same cheating tactics and that is what makes me angry about the gameplay. The opponents gets everything they need for their abilities magically apearing on the top row, they get deadly cascades of nodes dropping endlessly and I have seen them clear one row only to have it replaced completely with nodes of a color they need.
I finally had enough of this game. I don't enjoy playing a game where victory is handed to the opponent, when there obviously was no nodes to ensure their victory when I ended my turn.
One year after writing the review originally, I decided to see if things have changed for the better. Some things are better, while others have the exact problems as last year.
- Many new heroes. Easier to collect some heroes that were concidered "rare" last time I was playing.
- Updated abilities for older characters, making some of them better to use.
- City nodes are replaced with team-up nodes. You have three team up cards (which can be given to you by your alliance and found randomly) that can be used with team up points. These are far better than the city nodes and have actually helped me win some games.
- A daily quest which gives you a chance to get rare heroes or plenty of resources.
Anytime I try to play anything that isn't 50 levels below me, the cheating AI will kill my team with no effort. They get cascades (nodes endlessly falling and matching), you move one node and they get a perfect 4 or 5 on their next turn and they color starve you, to force you to play "bad" while they get what they need through the toprow.
Anytime you loose, the game gives you horrible advice how to win. Let's analyze why this doesn't work anymore:
Reality: The AI's will clear your nodes within a few turns. The first time I put down Invisible Womans bubble that shields a character from all damage, it was cleared instantly by the computer getting a cascade.
Reality: The game deliberately forces you to only move certain nodes, which forces your weakest characters to the front.
Reality: You have to kill whichever character has a cascading ability or the least amount of point to charge their ability. One of the most difficult opponents in the game is Juggernaut, because he combines both of these. His 2 abilities cost very little (6 points). One cascades, the other deals a little damage to himself and a lot to you. So he cascades, deals damage to you, cascades, deal damage to you. The sad thing is? Juggernaut is one of the weakest characters you can recruit on your team, being only a 1 star character. But for AI events, he is buffed up and kills you easily.
Reality: Either the AI are teamed up with another AI that gives them free points or they simply cascades and get the points they need from the toprow.
Reality: The game forces you to only move certain nodes. Whenever 2-star Storm is on my team, I only need 11 blue nodes to charge her ability. There is very rarely a single blue node when she is on my team. Most of the time, you are only allowed to collect pink nodes, which is one of the weakest colors in the game. And then watch the AI get the colors they needed through the toprow.
- Enemy AI usually have few colors to collect, which makes it easy for them to make a lot of damage in little time. Ninjas and thugs usually have abilities that cost 4 mana, they get free mana because they aren't allowed to move nodes and the countdowns are just 2-3 times long. Unless you are really lucky, it's very difficult to clear those nodes in time. Because you rarely have anything to match them with.
- The "match node helper" will regularly point out a bad move while ignoring a 4-5 match.
- Because cascades happen so regularly, you need to waste health packs often. You never know if your character will survive with only half of their life.
There's no strategy in this game. You win if you are lucky. Even though technically my characters are 50 levels above the other team and should massacre them.  I feel dumbed down when I play, because I always look for a good move and still loose because my characters can't match colors they need.

I received this game as a free download with the purchase of new computer hardware.  With that said, it is an adequate racing game with many of the bells and whistles that one might come to expect.  However, playing it many a time in solo career mode as well as the split screen co-op mode, both my co-op partner and I had to point out multiple times that the game leaves something to be desired.
[[[LOTS OF CARS!]]]
Kind of.  They all behave the same way in my eyes.  Don't get me started on these "drift-tuned cars", I can't figure that nonsense out for the life of me.*  But of course, having the trademark performance cars and Indycars and the like are all fine fun.  Then we have Supercars and Hypercars.  More on that later.
*=Probably just terribad.  Co-op partner always flipped me over and f*cked me sideways when she consistently beat me at the "drift" races.
[[[PHYSICS!]]]
I don't know about this one.  Maybe it's because my ~80 hours logged is primarily devoted to the co-op mode, I likely don't have a reliable opinion.  But there were times when my partner's car slid, literally from left to right, as if being yanked by a piston on a conveyor belt.  Of course, when that didn't happen, our reckless driving often jettisoned our very expensive Hypercars hilariously into the air.  Otherwise, we would be skidding across the track at hairpin turns.  TO BE CLEAR, this is not the fault of the game or the engine; this is user experience in the CO-OP mode.
Beyond those elements, I have little to offer for review.  Other reviews would more adequately describe the AI and the Career mode.  As I said, most of my experience is in split screen co op, and so my opinion may be wholly unreliable.  And again, I received this game for free.  Would I recommend buying this game for $39.99?  No; maybe if it was under $10.  Only under the circumstance in which the user could come upon this game at a low price point, or for free, do I recommend it.

Insincere attempts to be a nostalgic throwback to classic FPS games of the PS1 era, but it ultimately crumbles under the weight of terrible design choices, shotty gameplay and a host of bugs & glitches. In just under 2 hours of total play time (at least 20 minutes of it spent restarting levels and the game itself), I was victim to key items not spawning, cutscenes either cutting to black or knocking me to the desktop, and save files reverting progress. The horrible graphics wouldn't be an issue if the game ran smoothly, but sadly, this is not the case. Insincere often has severe frame rate drops even if only 1 or 2 enemies are on the screen. AI is either superhuman (enemies with 100% accuracy mow through you from across the map) or mind numbingly stupid (they will walk away while you shoot them), with no inbetween. There is some kind of story here (clones, AI constructs, and mutations ), but it is so poorly explained through its jittery cutscenes and awful dialogue, that you will have little to no interest by the time you reach the conclusion.
It makes me sad. Insincere initially reminded me of a game like Armorines, Turok, or System Shock. It starts off silly with a goofy scientific premise that has the heart to go somewhere. Sadly though, the game just feels unfinished and abandoned, as if the developer got bored and just threw it on Steam to die. There is a shell of a fantastic game here, but as it stands, Insincere is best avoided.

I am not a man that has played much in the way of visual novels. I think I may have played a grand total of 1. That being said I have read many a book and have a craving for good solid story.
From the very start of this one, we see a well done style that looks like a painter has just left the easel to dry and it catches the eye. I even praise the colors used that really draw the eyes and help make the characters simply LOOK unforgettable.
The story setting has enough of it's own lore that I want more, and not even just from the main characters. There were several smaller mentions of things that I would love to see explored in other ways, even as small as a short story or something of that nature.
The main character goes through a few points where it is difficult to like her, however, during these points her actions and mannerisms really sell what she is going through and seemed like very human responses. Being honest I think I only felt that way due to her being upset with a character I found very charming!
The relationships felt real and there were a few times I expected the story to focus on some of the negative emotions of a character for longer than needed and I was pleasantly surprised that the development felt organic.
The ending leaves alot of questions, but its very clear (the title..I mean..) that this is but one part and that we can expect to see more. It doesn't leave on a cliffhanger so much as a hope for the future of the characters.
If you like visual novels, I gotta say to give this one a try, worth your time and money. Looking forward to part two!

While it is a classical FPS with a nice story idea, there are too many issues to really enjoy this game:
- Interact-Key is "Enter" which means you need to move one hand away from your regular controls to interact with stuff
- Sound effects are sparce and weren't placed in the 3D environment properly. On headphones this means I heard an enemy snarl on my right ear only when it was right in front of me. I can't hear my gunshots or if I actually hit the enemy. But I do hear that I'm hurt.
- The attack distance of the melee-Enemies you encounter right from the start seems off. It feels like they have arms longer than rendered and can attack you from a distance way too far away. This is only a minor thing though, since it just affects the difficulty of the game
- I stopped playing on the fourth level or so, because an enemy pushed me through the wall into the void, effectively killing me.
- After I died, I had to restart entirely, because the game does not save automatically for you. Not even upon reloading new levels. I know this was rather common back in the day, but being used to modern game mechanics it is something that should be indicated to new players.
To sum it up:
- Bad controls
- Misleading sound rendering
- Strange melee distances
- Clipping errors lead to insta-death
- No Auto-Save

The game is simple, upkeep your shop by traveling out for items to sell. When you're automatically killing enemies, you have a mini Tetris-like minigame with different obstacles to hurdle. Each stage is harder, so you have to upgrade your shopkeeper through constant upgrades. Along with your shop too.
But it's more than simple, since the world is very vast with many items! Perhaps simple pales in comparison to the game. You can have relationships with merchants, ninjas, warriors, fighters, clerics, mage, archers, blacksmiths, etc. These relationships means more customers that buy your stuff! They will turn into loyal customers.
The music is good, but can be repetitive at long hours. This was made through Unity, so I'm throughly impressed.
If you bought the game;
Important to know!:
-Remember that when Green Herbs drop during stage runs, you can heal yourself. Sustain yourself.
-Check the calender regularly.
-There is no load function unfortunately.
-Speaking of loading, save your game! I had to restart a few times because I done goofed.
-Don't expand too quickly. You'll know what I mean.
-Invest small things and save up! Make small goals like redoing the roof, new tables, and new decorations for bonuses!
-Equip the newest items as soon as possible on yourself. It'll make you clear stages easier.
-When you sell your wares, click everything! Click the birds, your dirty tables, the people (especially the people with stars over their head when they pass by your shop!), and the little dust thingies!
-Each stage run counts as a day! Don't spam lower dungeons unless you need base items for crafting!
-Save your game!

I'll list the reasons why I didn't like this game, take it witha grain of salt though after 30 minutes of playing I was so over it and unimpressed I just uninstalled it. 1) It seemed crazy to me to have a fighting game without proper game pad support, worse yet is half arsing it. You can play with an Xbox controller, but you need a mouse for menus and all tutorials only show keyboard commands.
2) Characters attack in the direction the player model is facing, not the direction of the camera or the movement direction of the player. So if an enemy is coming toward you from the right you need to aim the camera at him press forward to reorient your character and then attack. That's crazy. I could see how that might be easier with a mouse and keyboard, but like I said I was hoping for smarter DMC type controls or even maybe Arkham type controls.
2b) It seemed like quite a few characters were designed simply not to attack strictly in the direction you are facing. Which only makes point number 2 worse.
3) Community is aggressive and unfriendly. I think this is an important consideration when a game is multiplayer only and probably won't be wide spread in it's adoption. It might not be worth it. Also I should point out that this is why I uninstalled and didn'y bother to put in more time.

5) [BONUS POINT] Still don't understand why every female in a fighting game must wear almost nothing, that might just be a hangover I'm having from my christian days but it is a pet peeve.

Halfway along a 420km journey, uncle and I ran out of fuel. We hadn't passed a gas station on the first half of the journey so we figured the best option would be for me to grab the empty gas can from the trunk, walk up the road and look for somewhere to fill it.
I left uncle in the car and started walking.
The sun went down. It began to rain. I think I heard wolves.
But I didn't find a single gas station along the route. I didn't find any abandoned vehicles to raid. And so half an hour later I squelched into the destination city and located the gas station, not at all looking forward to the return journey.
After filling the gas can I headed to the payment counter and reached for my wallet... which I'd left on the dashboard of my car.
The game's still in early access with a variety of bugs but being able to tell stories like the above are one of the reasons why I love games.

A rather okay game. An interesting idea and a complex idea. The good: it has some real science behind it, though obviously not even near 100% correct. But for the point of the game, you can ignore it. The challenges are in fact challenges. It's not an easy game. You'll have to plan a bit.  I enjoyed parts of it but you can't play too long or you'll burn out. I wish I could better explain it.
Good:
>You'll have fun many times
>It's not easy, it's a challenge so you'll be entertained
>Good music
>Careful planning is rewarded
>Addictive
Bad:
>The beginning of each challenge is near identical as you have to restart learning the same techniques; but the parts that change are the ingredients. Based on luck. If lucky, it's easy. If not, prepare your♥♥♥♥♥♥
>Some things seem utterly random , such as which side effect is on each ingredient
>Some effects contradict themselves
>You will be in debt a lot. No idea how people hit the 600$ daily when I can do at best 200$ when being careful (this is on EASY by the way). I constantly was close to meeting an objective, just waiting for a new loan
>Competition nearly never does anything BUT when they do, they do in fact screw you over
>Something is off with the economics. I have a superior product (cure and sales rating), no side effects and it ISN'T dominating the market... when the only other one is a weaker, side effect ridden competition drug. How???
Neutral:
>There's a learning curve so take time to learn.
>The tutorials aren't too easy to follow, so pay attention
That's about it. It's a game that you play a challenge and once done, you take a break. Come back the next day.
Advice: Beat the tutorial. Free build is nice to test out things (a good idea, especially about combining ingredients), but is utterly boring to play in. Custom build might be better if you want to practice techniques for challenges. It gives you the ability to learn how to properly research, search for ingredients, deal with money, etc, WITHOUT being restricted.
So again: Free build if you wanna quickly try out how to combine things or how equipment works. But use custom build to practice for challenges. The challenges can be very hard and very easy. This game is one of my best recent purchases. I got this at 66% off, but 21 hours in, I can definitely say it is worth full price.
I completed the tutorials in about 90 minutes, and it has taken me a further 20 hours to beat all the beginner levels to Master standard.
I've just moved up to Intermediate level, and discovered that there are a whole load of new machines and research topics, plus more cures, ingredients, side-effects, and ways to combine them together! I wasn't expecting such a leap in complexity, and I still have not checked out the Advanced levels yet! I've also noticed, that many of the achievements seem interesting, and might be worth pursuing in their own right.
Before purchasing. I read some of the negative reviews, which mentioned the randomness of the game, and repetitive nature of the gameplay. Sure, some of it is repetitive; when starting a new level, you have to build up your factory and income, but the randomness is a good thing - in different games, different ingredients lead to different cures and side-effects, and you have to combine them in different combinations. You have to think - you can't just keep repeating the same cures you developed in previous games. In my view, that's a very good thing!
There are so many aspects of this game, and it is much deeper than I expected. I've yet to unlock and discover all the elements of the game, but already I can see the potential for creating super drugs which cure multiple illnesses at once, and could potentially be worth thousands of dollars. That kind of drug won't be easy to create, but is definitely doable if you make the right combinations.
Do yourself a favour, and just buy it!

VN's aren't my usual forte. In fact, I'd probably not pay attention to this game were it not for a YT vid showcasing it in my feed. But it instantly caught my attention with really polished production values for that kind of game- the artwork is detailed, pleasant to eye with good mix of earthy and vibrant tones and manages to vary enough to make it look like it's not all taking place in one white hallroom. The character artwork is animate and expressive (again, within the limitations of the medium- the horseriding sequence really could've used a separate character model) and the style fits the setting of the story.
The other thing I have noticed is the voice acting. That is, to my knowledge, a rarity in VN's, and most characters seem to be cast well. A few minor issues with delivery here and there, but nothing glaring. My one real issue would be sound volume- I assume the reason is that the VA's were recording in different studios, but some of the lines sound clear and crisp, while some sound muted or muffled. Still..it's fully acted and the three main characters are very easy on the ear (Hector's performance in delivering the deadpan lines was perfect).
Music is very good, and I'd gladly use it as a background for pen and paper RPG session.
Now, as to the story itself, it's decent. The writing isn't Hugo-winning, but it got me invested into what seemed at first to be a simple  coming of age story. The characters are all easy to like, the plot flows fairly fast and without major stuttering, and it even manages to build good suspense, and there wasn't a single moment where I cringed...a feat that not all mainstream dev studios manage. The writers were well aware of the trappings of the genre, and delivered a solid story (not without some plotholes) within it. Solid enough that I definetely want the next chapter.
I would also love for the world to be more populated. The Mountain seems to be existing in a desolate void. We know there's the kingdom, and in the last few minutes of the story we get rushed attempt as establishing the world, but still, a rough sketch of the world as known by the characters would be great.
One minor thing that was slightly grating: Dear writer,we get it. People of all genders, sexes and walks of life have the right to love and should not be prejudiced against. Pretty sure no one who disagrees with that notion will be playing this game, so...spare us the heavy-handed "only a primitive would" lines next time, it's preaching to the choir.
Despite minor flaws, I'd still recommend the game if you want to read something nice, romance-themed and in fantasy setting. The visuals and soundwork are high quality, and the story solid if not breaking any new grounds. I'd liken the experience to Old Kingdom trilogy in terms of tone, or one of Gaiman's earlier novels, like the Stardust.

The storyline in this game is the worst I've seen in a pretty long time, it starts out really well, but goes further and further downhill as the game goes on.   At the beginning the protagonist and her true love's relationship is set up very nicely, they're best friends since childhood and now that they're adults they're set to complete their magical bonding ritual which will be the beginning of their lives together.  It's great stuff, you're definitely invested in their relationship.  But something goes wrong, leaving your main character bonded to an alien (who you don't even really meet until near the end of the game) and your true love bonded to a super annoying dude.  Of course that's all OK, since, you would assume, True Love will overcome even the power of magic, and it'll lead to a great and happy ending, or so you would expect.  The problem is, at least in this game, True Love doesn't overcome the bonds of magic, you'll spend the entire game trying to overcome it, but you'll fail at every turn, all your choices essentially lead to the same depressing result.   Eventually your character is simply alone and miserable, and as a conclusion to this terrible story, the only two other lesbian characters in the game are revealed to be bad guys, and your character has to kill them.  But wait, after everything's been terrible and depressing the entire game, at the very end you meet the alien you're bonded to, and, since your character is going to be extremely attracted to it no matter what it looks like because of the power of the magic of the pairing ritual, it's a good thing that it at least appears to be female.  The end.  Of course, the Title suggests that it is 'Part One' so perhaps in the next game your character will be able to finally break the bonds of the 'pairing ritual', get away from the alien and get your true love away from the super annoying dude, and finally live Happily Ever After, but there's no happily ever anything in this Part One, so I'd suggest waiting to see if things get better in the next one before playing this one.

Been playing this game a long time now, and i wouldn't normally bother reviewing games. But this one seems to cop a bit of flak and i can't for the life of me figure out why.
This is a proper race driver game. It's not a full simulation sure but its damn close. It's a brutal game at the best of times.. almost strategic.. If you don't brake at the right time/take the wrong line around a corner/too much throttle and you can lose it all and i ADORE that in a game.
Having said that i love the flashback ability and how you only get a few of them to use. They really come in handy and will have you sit there and ponder how you could have done better/alternative stradegies. It does not kill the experience and the game is far far away from being too easy. AI is absolutely brutal and its scary as hell when you are winning and you can hear their engines behind you closing in.
Speaking of scary stuff.. How about barreling down an F1 track and having your front tyre blow (in cockpit view). Or that moment you realize you've not remembered x corner correctly and you see wall. OR even better.. When the AI stuffs up ( and they do.. and its spectacular) as they go flying over the top of you. Or spin out right in your intended race line.
The other thing i adore about this game is the Mini coopers/classics races.. All of the cars have a very real feel to them. If you're in a mini.. it feels tiny and nippy and they are SO MUCH FUN to drive. And most of the mini races do nothing for your points so they are there just to have fun with.
Other realistic features i like:
The game feels genuinely stressful to play if you're trying to play serious. A real race driver would be stressed out.
The noises.. the whole game feels chaotic like a racetrack would, You hear the car at work, If someone smashes into you and you lose a window.. everything outside gets louder etc.. The opponents being right behind you is scary stuff.
The feel of the cars..you easpecially feel when you have damaged something quite badly and it feels like it should.. If you break your suspension you hear all the bumping around and it feels harder to control. Lighter cars feel light, F1 cars feel really damn quick and make you think about EVERY MOVE.
The only way to play this game is with full damage on. Id also recommend playing it with at least a 360 controller.. I don't have the time or money to buy a full wheel/pedal set but i imagine that would be an even sweeter experience.
I could go on forever about this one. I tip my hats to the devs.. My favourite car game to date.

Stealth is all about patience. And this game is one big test of your tactical skills and patience. In my opinion, the best in the series, and in the genre, Splinter Cell Chaos Theory towers over all stealth games, the only other game that managed to get near the perfection of this game was indie hit, Mark of The Ninja, but let's talk about Chaos Theory.
Sam Fisher, a splinter cell agent, a one man special ops agent, is tasked by the his agency to find the missing agent on an island, he finds him, and the whole web of conspiracies and plans to start a new world war uncover. The story is excellent, about informational warfare, thin line between war and peace, and the extent a man must go to prevent something sinister. Story is really good, like a good spy-thriller movie.
Gameplay is upgraded from the previous games, more complex, but in the same time, more rewarding. Your main thought that should guide you throughout the game is "SNEAK". You will die of one shot, so think and be patient. There's a new lighting system in the game, showing you, out of 4 levels of lighting, whether enemy can see you or not. A sound system shows the sound you're making by walking, and the sound of the ambient (TVs, radios...), this allows you to walk faster, or shoot the guy, not risking getting caught. Graphics are beautiful, especially seen in the boat mission, the lighting effects on the old walls of boat really gives you the emersion you need.
All in all, stealth fans, get this. It is an old game, but it is a game that passed the test of time, and is one of the more complex and best stealth games out there. A must have.

Personally I love all of the Sid Meirer's Civ games,it seems like this one is only getting hate though just cause people don't seem to like change,etc.
Now for the actual review.
One it's pretty much like any other civ game out there just this one is more futuristic and you are no longer on earth,so you won't be starting in an acient age or anything like that. So if you're looking for stuff like that,then don't buy this game if you're hoping it's like all the other civ games to a hundred percent,while it isn't. You got your aliens,which are like the barbarians,you can destroy their nests and if you're lucky you can actually domesticate the aliens and use them in your army! It's pretty cool and the aliens are worthy allies if you're able to domesticate a few of em,they're technically like pets. Along the side you don't have your warmongering Ghandi and personally I am kinda happy for that,though if you want to anger an AI and turn them in a warmongering annoying bambling idiot,just condemn them publicly and then they will become hostile along with being always angry at you,until you settle a deal with them later if they'll even accept it. Though they shall get annoying after a while of every 10 turns of saying your army is on the weak side and you should watch your back.
So other than that,you got your virtues as well,where one helps you with your armies,another helps with food,etc then science and culture. It's pretty interesting in my opinion despite it being like the other games just with different values to it.  You got your science tree as well,you got a ttoooonnn of stuff to choose from,everything benefits you no matter what almost.
So back on to the aliens,I said they were just like pets right? Well there is one alien I truly hate,it's a huge worm that moves around the map that seems near impossible to kill at the start as he is just completly op. He can wipe out your entire army with only one smack almost for ground units.

BioShock 2 wants you to believe that there was another major character in Rapture: Sofia Lamb. She is very prominent/important, and many characters - even ones from the first game - will be mentioning her in audio logs that you'll find as you explore more of Rapture. It's funny then, that no one ever mentioned her in the first game. I get that they invented her for the sequel, but having her be a major personality supposedly before the crap hit the fan in Rapture goes far beyond my suspension of disbelief. That's just the tip of the iceberg of my problems with BioShock 2, though.
This sequel has you go through Rapture again; parts you never visited in the first game. However, in my opinion, the places you visit here are mostly less interesting than the places you visited in the first game. It felt to me like they wanted more money, so they had us go back to rapture again, even though they'd already shown us the best they had to offer in terms of locations.
There are a few new enemy types, but nothing that really excited me, and new guns as well. You play as a Big Daddy...but a rather intelligent one who is a prototype and somewhat clunkily written into the game. I rarely felt like a Big Daddy; even less so than at the end of the first BioShock when you get your "upgrades" close to the game's conclusion. Only the drill and walking on the ocean floor ever gave me that sensation. The new weapons felt much like the location situation: not as good as the original, at least in my opinion.
Also, the ocean floor I mentioned briefly a moment ago, wasn't a fun or interesting place to visit. It's what lies between some of the places you visit, instead of cool hallways and interior architecture. Less cool structural design is not a plus for me, so walking along a rocky ocean floor when I could be in art deco hallways is a bit of a let-down. The ocean floor thing should have been very brief and very rare, in my opinion; certainly less than what ended up in the game.
Since we've been to Rapture before, we know most of the answers to the big mysteries, and there's no longer the sense of wonder that I had exploring Rapture in the first BioShock. Enemies and human depravity isn't going to freak me out after I saw most everything Rapture had to offer on the first go-around in the preceding game.
The Plasmids make a return, though you can wield a gun at the same time now, instead of having to switch between them. Of course, the Big Daddy you play as can use Plasmids when no others can't...just more writing to make the playable character able to do everything the character in the first game could and then some, without having any respect for believability of the narrative beyond what some folks' suspension of disbelief might permit.
I and other players have had their save games randomly get corrupt. If a save corrupts, it may cost you an entire level's worth of progress in a game with pretty big levels, or more than that if you're unlucky or weren't expecting corruption by keeping a bunch of different saves, potentially resulting in having to start the entire game over.
I didn't find myself caring about the new characters in BioShock 2; not the way I did about everyone in the first game. I felt they were better written and more interesting. I haven't played in a while, or I would likely have more criticisms fresh on my mind. I would honestly just recommend skipping BioShock 2 completely. The first game has great narrative and gameplay, and BioShock Infinite has a really good story as well. BioShock 2 does not come up in Infinite, so you're A-OK if you skip it!

A masterpiece which cannot disappoint, for anyone who likes the first game. A positive note is that compared to Bioshock, Bioschock 2 has less weird, creepy and scary moments - which makes the game feel more like a classic action shooter, along with a few other elements (such as you being a powerful Big Daddy rather than some desperate man).
Some people like the survival/horror element, I didn't, so in this sense I enjoyed Bioshock 2 a lot more. It feels a lot less dark and appalling, it gives you a continuous sensation of hope and light. Each step you take you feel closer to the salvation of the other protagonist, and possibly yours too?
Game-time is sufficient enough. It took me 20 hours with a semi-leisurely pace, for a story driven SP shooter it is quite a lot, and from my experience other titles released in that period have a story-mode 50% shorter: Halo 3, Republic Commando.

Big Pharma is a game developed by Twice Circled and published by Positech Games, the same people behind Gratuitous Space Battles' series, Gratuitous Tank Battles and the Democracy series
Big Pharma throws you into the medicinal making business where you run a pharmacuetical company distributing drugs that help people whilst also making big green dollar bills. The game is both a management simulation game and also surprisingly a bit of a puzzle game
To create a drug you first have to find the suitable ingredients, each ingredient comes with a cure, a side effect and sometimes a booster (these are usually found in other ingredients and not the same one). Through that you then can make you're drug by processing it through machinery that can mix and match to evenly balance both the cure and the side effects

This isn't really a tycoon game, which it may look like from the screenshots. No, this is a production optimization game in the same vein as Factorio, where space and time are your limiting resources, and your goal is to build complex production lines as efficiently as possible. And that doesn't always mean using the biggest machines: speed of production and floor space sometimes seem to require the smaller machines, while more effective (or bigger-money!) cures, or profitability concerns, may require the less time-efficient but more step-efficient larger machines.
So, if you think you'll enjoy laying out machines and tweaking your layouts for the best outcome, this is for you.

The game that the publisher, Nexon America, bailed on and the original creators, Neople, picked up and improved it by an infinite-fold.
My hours don't reflect the amount of hours I've actually spent into this game before, during, and after the Nexon fiasco. I have reached max levels on a few characters and I have casually played other characters for my own personal benefit. I have played the Chinese variation of the game when Nexon America closed the doors on this game and people thought it was gone for good. My experience is all over the place when it comes to this game and I'm glad this game has provided me entertainment for the years it was here, even when it was a cash-grab from Nexon America.
Pros:
Neople was kind enough to eliminate the cash-grab that Nexon America placed over the game, where you have to buy potions to increase your stamina bar or gear for additional stats. Sure, there is maybe some elements still left in the game, but it's quite miniscule compared to Nexon's standards.
Unlike how Nexon America did with their content (releasing every year with barely any events in-between), Neople has consistently kept the game refreshed with events and new content since they have brought it back to English-speaking customers. They even encourage members to join their Facebook and other social media communities to continue with offline events for further engagement with the community. Obviously, Neople has their priorities set out for this game.
This is an issue that Neople has addressed from the first day of Beta in the English DFO launch. They have zero-tolerance for this and they plan to consistently monitor the game and tickets for it. Ever since I've played on the Neople servers, I have seen a major decrease in this type of behavior and if these people are around, then you won't see their character for long as someone has likely reported them.
Cons:
Maybe it's just me, but there isn't much out there going for the community-wise when it comes to recruiting for guilds or groups. Out of the times I have played this game, I would get burnt out after a few days of playing and end up not picking it back up for a few weeks or months because of it. This is a true concern for me and it places some doubt about the recruitmenet methods there are in the game. Maybe I'm not looking in the right places, but even as a newbie--this could be quite concerning.
I can forgive Neople on the translation sometimes, since most of the work is coming out of Korea and the English translation isn't the best at times. In fact, Neople actually encourage people to submit tickets or post on the forums to help correct translation issues in the game, especially with new patches. I do believe Neople should invest their money into a translation team in North America and have them dedicated to translate the patch from Korean to English, correct grammatical mistakes from the translation, and build it around the character's personality.
Big iffy on me sometimes. There has been some bugs in the game that have been game-breaking (like the Cash Shop bug) that would consist around for a while. This might be one of the biggest issues I would say be my problem with Neople; however, it isn't as bad as Nexon would leave the problem stranded and it would be solved in the next content update. (Unless it was a cash shop bug, then Nexon would all over that because they need $$$.) As a person who has deal with Nexon's♥♥♥♥♥♥with numerous of their games, I have the patience to wait out issues, especially with a team that's dedicated to resolving this game's problem.

When I first started the game I honestly didn't like it at all. For the first several missions until I got to the Hotel I just had a bad taste in my mouth because I went straight from all the old Hitman games to this one and it didn't compare in a lot of ways.
There was no first person, the AI seemed a bit too paranoid and psychic, etc.
But after awhile I started to like it. The gameplay was fun, it was polished in a lot of ways, but yeah it wasn't Blood Money.
Its a good game. It may not be the best Hitman game but it definitely has tons of things that I prefer over Blood Money and the older ones in general.
Agent 47 is supposed to be a genetically engineered clone who is a super badass. This game highlights that much better than any of the older games do. The throwing mechanics are better, being able to instantly drag someone after you garrot them is nice, the amount of places you can hide bodies is great, a lot of stealth aspects are improved over the old ones.
But the negatives still shine through for me but it didn't stop me from enjoying the game.
I hear Hitman 2016 is better and I will play that eventually but here's where I think all the Hitman games should just have as a general. Firstly in the old Hitman games when someone saw you there wasn't a little typical AAA bar fill up I hate that its nonsense and in the old Hitman games it wasn't there they generally in most areas if you messed up detected you instantly. Now you can somewhat replicate that by playing at a higher difficulty but the higher difficulties in this game are massively broken because of another problem. The disguise system.
The Disguise system in Blood Money in my opinion was the best. It may have been "easier" but it made more sense. Just because something is easy doesn't mean its bad. You don't have to make something uncessarily hard when it doesn't fit in the series. Most people realisticly don't question the people around them that much. If you're a police officer and you just see a non chalant police officer you'll likely just assume he's from a different district or department or a new guy.
Same goes for lower jobs even more like a gardner or something like that. You wouldn't suddenly be like "Oh wtf there's a Gardner i've never seen before he must be le magic hitman guy I better go tell on him" That's nonsense and the higher difficulties allow them to psychicly spot you through your disguise like 15 feet away. It doesn't make any sense.
Disguises generally shouldn't be see through unless you do something extremely out of character such as holding something you're not supposed to be holding, being somewhere you shouldn't be, dragging a body, being a different race of the person you're in a disguise of (Such as in Asia or a Hispanic country), etc
They need a classic blood money disguise system for all the games. It may be easier and have its own flaws but its more immersive and makes sense.

6/10.
The game starts out good, the voice acting is great and the art is sufficient.
While the setting is unique the game has a lot of similarities to bad fanfiction, (the primary characters are significantly more powerful than any other character in the game doing things that seem 'impossible' to other characters in the setting, they fall prey to 'special snowflake' syndrome, (ash doesn't know who her pairing is for most the game, merely that they are mysterious and extremely powerful, she is capable of ressurecting plants something noone else can do, as well as inexplicably being capable of casting spells and magics that others can't, handily defeating foes that would have killed her otherwise. Prude is a princess, and is the object of half the primary casts affections. Hek is stronger than the Heads of the school, and has powers that essentially have 'mary sue' written all over it. SPOILERS, DO NOT READ PAST THIS POINT: Ash's pairing partner turns out to be a changeling/elf thing, and not only does it handily solve the final confrontation, but it also saves their lives thruoghout the entire game, demonstrating overwhelming power and skill for no reason, this character, (as we have seen it so far) is just a straight up mary sue, she has no real negative characteristics, being an extremely power magical creature, when she meets her ash seemingly just decides that she is over prude, dismissing what had up until that point been a major plotpoint) to further reinforce this similarity to fanfiction is the 'pairing' itself, which anyone with a passing familiarity with the Harry Potter fandom will probably recognize as a extremely cliche trope of that genre, it's essentially just soul-bounding or veela mates or whatever other flavor they choose to call it that week, with the pairing making both parties stronger, as well as somehow magically determining that they are 'destined for eachother' or some bullcrap like that. This makes the overall story feel weaker, at least for me, but since it is the central conceit of the story I will overlook it.
You may have noticed that the (horribly rambly) paragraph above is very critical, yet this is a positive review, and there is a reason for that: Hek. Hek single handedly makes this game, his characterization is amazing, and while the rest of the plot is a load of BS Hektor is interesting enough to keep you playing.
Overall it's story is nothing special, it's plot being a collection of cliches that have been overused so often that there is no way to take them seriously anymore, but it's still interesting enuogh to pick up. (maybe wait for a sale though).

Refreshing, unique, and captivating.
A little background about myself - I'm not a big visual novel 'buff', the most experience I have in such games would be the Phoenix Wright games on handheld, but after watching a youtube video of the game, I was immediately drawn to the story presented, and after doing a little bit more research, promptly purchased the title and completed my own playthrough several times to get the different endings, and little changes in plot based on choices.
Given that I've just explained I'm not big into visual novels as a gamer, I still enjoy a good story, and this title definitely has a good story. Presenting a very different world from the norm in most media, with Necromancy not necessarily being evil but instead another school of magic that's balanced out by Light magic, the game does a good job presenting the basic principles of the world at a good pace, and the player also gets the opportunity to learn more about the world if the right choices are made.
I learned that the voice acting in the game (FULLY voice acted) was actually a stretch goal of it's kickstarter, and I have to say it helped breath life to the characters, and it was quite refreshing to hear new and different talent in an industry that sometimes feels only a handful of voice actors are always given work. (I hear voice actors like Jennifer Hale and Steve Blum across a LOT of titles, across different mediums, and while definitely great voice actors, it's once again so refreshing hearing new talent).  While the writing can also stand on it's own, the acting definitely helps you understand what kind of personality each character exhibits, and makes them that much more memorable. I have been playing Cvilization for almost 25 years already. I was addicted to CIV I as a kid, played CIV II A LOT when I was in college, then Civilization Call to Power which was also pretty good. I did play CIV III a bit, but went quickly on to CIV IV which I played for years and years and years, with all official expansions, and installed and played A LOT of community mods, some of which were absolutely fantastic (thinking of Fall from Heaven II and Caveman2Cosmos and sooooo many others). I played CIV IV Colonization and throughly enjoyed it as well in its relative simplicity.
The Civilization series altogether are the games I played the most in my life. Every new version that would come out was better than the previous, more complex, more accurate, more fun.
Then came this trend of the past few years to simplify games, make them more mobile oriented, more mass consumable by people who play for 20 minutes then buy the next game.
This trend is extremely noticeable in CIV V and also on CIVBE. Even the expansions of these games only bring back concepts that were included in previous versions of CIV, sometimes even on the basic "vanilla" ones. There is almost nothing new in these two games with few exceptions (like the tech tree in CIVBE, which is still only tiny when compared to CIV IV with Caveman2Cosmos mod)
I bought CIV V Complete and played some hours, then didn't even bother and only tried CIVBE during a free weekend, and I say with my decades of experience with Civilization: go play CIV IV, install all mods, try them. Then you will never even want to look at the newer versions again.
Call me old fashioned... but I do wish Civilization would go back to its roots of being among the most accurate and complex games around. Sid Meier lost it along the way. What a pity....................................

Сложнаяя игрушка на выживание.Каждую игру вы начинаете в разрушеном доме имея 3(4) перса.Вам нужно "расчистить" ваш дом и найти ресурсы(разбирать завалы,открывть шкафы и т.д.).После вам понадобится верстак для того что бы сделать некоторые начальные вещи(кровать,печка,лопата и т.д.).После первого дня у вас открывается некоторое ночное меню здесь вы можете распределить что будет делать каждый ваш перс всего 4 действия.
1)"добывать"-вы должны вабрать любую локацию для добычи ресурсов ваш перс идёт туда и ищет там ресурсы.При добычче вы можете видеть маленькие красные круги- это звуки кого либо будь это военный,бомж или же просто крыса.
2)"охранять"-ваш персонаж защищает ваш дом от грабежей используя при этом оружие(если оно есть).При защите могут ранить охранника.Иногда 1 человек не может справится и нужно оставлять по 2.
3)"спать"-ваш перс остаётся спать на холодном полу и под утро появляются параметры "плохо спал" и "устал"
4)"спать в кровати"-ваш прс спит в кроватьи если он конечно же имеется он хорошо высыпается залечивает раны и отдыхает.

This game is just genuinely some nice simple fun. As you can probably see next to my name I have invested some good hours into the game, and I still feel like coming back and playing more and more.
The simplicity of the game is something that makes this game enjoyable, where you only need to watch the durability of each of the seven things in under your bonnet, how much fuel you have, and whether you’ll need to replace your tires or not.
But the complexity of the environment is what keeps bringing me back, as not only are you able to select from three different randomly generated paths to get from point A to B, to C, to D, to E, to F, you can take the same or completely different path back in the opposite direction, where each path weather it looks the same or totally different could have some great rewards to improve your car, or goods for you to sell and make a profit from, where by you can make your car better or look even cooler.
But I do understand some people don’t like this type of game, where there is a lot of nothing happening if you have an unlucky drop rate when you’re traveling from A to B, or how constantly repairing or replacing something is boring. But the layering of things to do and think about in this game give it so much depth, so if your slightly inclined to have a look at this game I can whole heartedly say it is worth it.
Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve been inspired to go on a road trip myself and take a venture to the coast, I hope you enjoy this game as much as I have.

Pros

Cons
- AI is still♥♥♥♥♥♥ some cars are almost impossible to beat while the rest try to slow you down
- Drifting sucks
- Your car becomes unstable at high speeds. CPU can cruise the tight corners easily.
- NO RACING LINE
- Inconsistent difficulty
- Grip cars feel useless
Race Driver Grid was a fantastic game, but in terms of driving it felt quite similar to the Need for Speed series. It feels more arcadey than realistic. Grid 2 on the other hand did a better job of making the game feel real. You can't just hit the pedal and force your car to turn. You have to find the right moment to brake and accelerate. The game feels much better in terms of circuit racing or sprints. You actually have to fight all the way to get to the number 1 spot. In Grid 1 it was quite easy to get to 1st.
There are lots of cars as well, and they are classified as one of the three : Balanced, Drift or Grip. In my entire playtime I don't think I have ever used a Grip car for a race, unless I had no choice and the game forced me to use it. You're going to have to drift a lot in Grid 2, and some grip cars suck at drifting.
Speaking of drifting, it sucks in this game. Grid 1 absolutely nailed drifting. It was perfect. Now drifting here is a 30 second track and no customizations. Plain horrible. It tried to go Japanese since most drift races are on mountain passes.
The game still has no racing line, which can become crucial in those difficult tracks for the Vehicle Challenges on the higher tiers. There were 3 difficult challenges where the racing line would have helped significantly. The Jaguar at Hong Kong, the Benz at Okutama and the Pagani Huayra challenge. Cars also become unstable at high speeds while other cars can just stick to the ground and not slide. I've seen this several times already. I forcefully rammed a CPU car and took a 10 second lead, but he was able to catch up and beat me on the last corner. I've seen his style and even with the car he should not be able to just accelerate through corners at that speed. Don't be surprised if you see the CPUs blast through chicanes at 250km/hr without slowing down.
It's a good game, but I can't recommended it. A lot of race types just suck and the circuit races and sprints are the only fun ones.

This was part of my Astronomic Bundle marathon.
Really risky gamble at it!  I loved the game despite numerous flaws that I best start upon,
- ENTER is used to open doors and pull switches on and while caught by the action we would asume something might jump on us while having one or the other hand midway of their usual position.
- Sadly it crashed at almost each 4 levels.  Fortunately, saving a lot is helpful there.
- Reloading a game is a bit long and sometimes at scene changes we get damage and we always return with the lead pipe as weapon.  Nothing to really hate the gameplay, but it kinda not reassure us about the stability of the game.
- The voice acting got a bit chopped in the cutscene and I'm happy it rolled in chopped slow-motion to read what was stuttered before about 4 sentences later.  It however didn't happened systematially but froze my game about twice!
- I got cornered by mobs from behind that hinderd my character to move or shoot!
- Some of the ennemies just looks like your ally... (Maybe it is a plot twist)
The goods,
- The developper of Astronomic Games specialise in story heavy and tactic heavy RPG and that was what got attempted here on an engine that is NOT made to be cooperative for that type of use (Read above also how just cooperative is the engine in short.) and really shown a lot of hardwork to just get his vision trough.
- For the very little we can use of the voiced charaters in a shooter environement, we got very nicely around them and intrigued to continue the game. (At the exeption that it took me two floors to realize the AI wasn't talking to me when I heard a guard or two warn me someone was close!)
- I got trapped in a logic map near the end trying to grenade every wall apart... So in about 3 floors you get to puzzle your way a bit and same with 3 or 4 tactical traps.
- I would had LOVED to bring back all enrolled bots with my charater because well... :D
Some things to think about if this is first chapter,
When the story ends as not really an end, there are still loose ends around.  Was really the AI helping the guy?  How/why did he made such a mess?  If in the end we have the answer of what he might be, why wasn<t he be more honnest with himself?  What really served all that secrecy purpose with the AI?  Why monsters?  What is that facility all about anyway?
So I know it is hard to dose a shooter as a RPG but when finishing a chapter before introducing new elements especially when it is unsure folks will return back, please... No loose ends!
It is a very good game in a bundle to spend, waste half a day on it!  Sorry Matt, but I would get this in a bundle only and, if possible in its very own bundle beause so many questions!  (This could had been so much fun in a Mass Effet/FallOut 3 engine! Just grabbing stuff getting notes menus and options... You know.)

Alright before I go over anything I’d say a 8/10 for this one. Although it provides a good story and gameplay its down side is that it’s extremely buggy I mean I could’ve probably beaten the game sooner if it was not for the bugs.  But that even said the game is also surprisingly short when I mean short I grinded a lot and when I mean a lot I mean every time I get close to leaving an area or when I enter an area. And the game only lasted 15 hours with the bugs included. Imagine if I played on easy I’d probably beat it in ten.
While what it lacks in time it makes for in tension it’s probably one of the most tense bioshock games but it really lacks in difficulty. I mean you don’t really have much of a struggle until the very end. But what bioshock 2 lacks in difficulty and the constant bugs it makes up for in unique mechanics. This game has way more unique mechanics then the previous ones and the sequel infinite. I am not going to spoil it because I am not rude like that if you want to be spoiled look in the negative review section.  But if your here to see if bioshock 2 is what they say it is that it is criminally under hyped I’d say I don’t know.
I am bent whether to throw the game in the trash or put it on a shelf. It has a good story it is fun but it’s pretty much a poor clone of its predecessor. I mean bioshock the original is my all time favorite game but bioshock 2 can’t hold a candle to it. Honestly the only thing the game has going for it is story and you playing as a big daddy that’s not a spoiler that’s in the description and screenshots. But if that’s enough to make you love the game a hud and a drill really? Kind of lazy of the devs it’s probably because bioshock strove to be way ahead of its time and instead showed its issue from the start. When you think of big daddy you think of an unstoppable force but instead your more like a little daddy if anything.
You have roughly the same starting health and eve as bioshock 1 and the only big daddy move you get is drill dash and that’s late game. The drill actually is a disappointment on its self as it’s like the wrench but it has ammo to it and practically useless when out of fuel. I mean I know you can upgrade it but even fully upgraded it feels weak and pretty much useless. I only used it late game because ammo was becoming increasingly scarce and it’s a fair alternative even though I feel the wrench was more effective. I mean clearly they had good intentions but they probably lacked the funds to do anything more and playing it you can clearly see they focused more on story and lore but in so you can see that the game was kind of rushed.
But the devs did see the error of bioshock 2 and incorporated much of its story to bioshock infinite believe it or not those that have beaten this game and infinite can see the similarities and it’s safe to assume that they did do a little bit of recycling. While this conversation can go on forever I nowhere hate the game I just prefer the original. If I had to pick I’d say the best is bioshock and the 2nd best is bioshock 2. While I love bioshock 2 I’d never say its worth it just because of the stress of going into the game files and deleting save files late game due to constant save corruption and also you must apply a fix from some steam guides to fix it so it does not constantly crash.
Just a recap, get it at your own risk it’s worth it if you’re a fan of the series but not the one you should start with. Constant bugs flood the game and the game is a little rushed and also a pc port from console.

I'm not too sure for what reasons the ratings are as bad as they are.  Perhaps prior to me getting the game a few days ago, it wasn't in the state it is now, that's the only reason I can think of.  Citadel is a great game and I have a minimal amount of complaints.
Pros: The map is expansive and every bit is interesting.
Rather than losing  everything when you die, you keep all the things that you have equipped.
Building is very easy, though some controls for rotation would make it easier.
A very pretty game visually.
The soundtrack is long and soothing enough that I never feel like "Ugh, listening to this again."
The high fantasy setting is, to my knowledge, unique to Citadel when it comes to these sorts of survival games.
Cons: The AI could use some work.  I encounter quite a few times when the AI either chases me across the map, or I jump on top of a rock and now they'll never be able to touch me.
It's easy to get stuck in a group of rocks.  If you don't have a broom or a mount near you, you're going to be forced to hit that respawn button.
It could be optimized better.  I run the game on medium-low settings since I dn't have the best of the ebst computers, but there are many times I still have trouble breaching 30 fps.  The game still seems smooth and all and I could probably lower the graphics for better performance, but it's such a good looking game, I'd rather not.
Low amount of players.  This is my biggest issue with the game.  There's not many people that play, meaning most of your interaction in the game will either be with friends that you play with, or no one at all.  This will probably be addressed better once the game leaves early access, but for now it leaves some to be desired.  I had never even heard of this game before a friend purchased it for me, and in my opinion it's definitely a game worth being heard.
Overall, I would recommend this game, but not necessarily right now.  If you're satisfied with how the game is now, which I personally am, then it's a good purchase that will earn you plenty of fun time, but having friends that play it can make it even more so.  The reason I might not necessarily recommend it right now is the lack of players.  I know, telling people not to play because there's not many players isn't a good way to solve that problem, but if you're wanting to play because you like the idea of servers full of 50 people playing, you're going to be disappointed at this point in time.  If you're fine with not playing with so many people, go for it!  The more people that get this game the better!

Ok, so the game in it's current state is borderline unplayable. Please feel free to read reviews below or swing by the subreddit to get the full picture, but in two words - it's full of gamebreaking bugs, and suffers from some recent stupid gameplay design decisions from the developers and very poor community management.
BUT.
It's still Magic: the Gathering - the absolute best and genre-defining CCG in the world, with 20+ years of history, gorgeous art, great lore, infinitely deep gameplay and huge and awesome global community. And this game, despite being a horrendous mess of bad code and design, still gets it's job done, which is - to introduce new (!) people to the wonderful Magic: the Gathering franchise.
The tutorial is very well built, and explains rather complex game mechanics in a step-by-step fashion. The game also explains main deckbuiling principles (card synergies, manabase etc) and provides a build-me-a-deck engine for new players to use. There is a single player campaign that introduces some of the core characters of the game universe. 1vs1 multiplayer, which is the way the original CCG is meant to be played works fine, although you'll probably need to unlock some more cards to stay competitive past first several ranks. So for that, the game gets a thumbs up from me.
Unfortunately for the rest of us - those looking for a "lighter" version of Magic to spend an hour or two after work, with no time, will, or money to invest into paper version of MTG - well, we can only hope Wizards of the Coast will change the developers team sometime. And hire some goddamn testers, maybe?

This is a pretty cool concept. I initially was interested in this game by the unique concept and was captivated by it. After playing it for a few hours the concept starts to lose it's initial appeal and you're left with the actual gameplay which to be honest is pretty good. The gameplay is fun and fairly well put together and balanced. I will say that much like any team based game the players can ruin games for you and make it a hell however that doesn't make the game itself bad.
My only real problems with the game are the difficulty to buy a new bloodline and the grade system. The grade system seems to be pretty unique but not in a good way. Unlike a typical mmr system that most competitive games have this game has a grade system which gives you a grade based on how well you played ranging from 1-25. This would be fine except for starters it doesn't really explain how it gives you a grade very well and it took a bit of research to get a general idea how it worked. From my research I believe it gives you a grade based on your maximum achieved scores which is a pretty lame way to do it rather than using an average. The other problem is that it takes a fair amount of time to farm up enough to buy a new bloodline but I guess that isn't really that bad so I won't say don't play because of that. The player base is also a little low so sometimes finding games can be a bit of a hassle but that can easily be changed.
They do a lot of tournaments that any team can qualify for simply by signing up which I think is a fantastic idea and more games should implement this. The tournaments reward the winners with certain prizes that let them get special reqards. The tournaments also range in skill level so that you aren't playing with a grade 2 and a grade 25 in the same game, they try and even it out so that you can play in tournaments with people of your own skill level. They also have a ranked system so that you can achieve certain ranks for the season and get little rewards for that as well.
All in all this is a good game for killing some time and certainly worth a look. Check it out and I hope this review helped you!

Overall, I had fun with the game. Nothing exposes your inner evil than becoming a pharmaceutical executive. The gameplay is not too complex, mostly based around creating production lines increasing and decreasing concentration or adding new ingredients to reach the higher tier drugs or to add special effects. Building machinery is similar to tetris: rotate the fixed input and output points until the shortest connection between them is possible or they take up the least amount of place.
Few issues:
- Most maps are badly designed, as a result of the tetris-like elements. Buildings are oddly shaped, full of narrow passages and corridors that make placing fixed sized and shaped machines frustrating or requiring a lot of moving around. I would personally prefer a more Prison Architect style gameplay where I can freely design buildings to suit my needs.
- Just as real medical research, I assume, production lines involve certain amount of rial and error. Some machines remove some effects, but so far I found no explanation for that. The mixers lack labeling on input, so the first mix is a trial and error in determining what will be the base and what the additive.
- The upgrade system is uninspiring. Purely decrease the operating cost of a machine by x amount of money. No tech to increase speed, improve supply, or anything more meaningful. A deeper, more diverse research system would be nice.
- The AI does weird things. I developed Drug A. Cornered the market to 90%. The AI developed Drug B, a less effective version of Drug A. Got the 10%. So far so good. But over time, based on its less effective drug, with a higher price tag and a lower sales rating, it managed to muscle me out of the whole market with no rational explanation.
- The patent system is ridiculous and broken, just like in real life I guess. I have been selling a drug I developed ahead of the competitors for 10 years. Then the AI slaps a patent on it, and retroactively pulls mine off the market. That would be like me patenting apples and hitting all fruit farmers with a cease and desist letter which there is no recourse for. It is an unfair, broken and gimmicky system that should not be in the game in its current form. Drugs already on the market should not be subject to the system, it should be an option once you developed a new drug.
In conclusion, I do not regret my purchase. The game is fun albeit simplistic and sometimes a bit rough around the edges. It is still an entertaining management game. With some additional elements a sequel to it could be a really good game.

Very fun, and not very pay-to-win like all the reviews say.
The PvE story roughly follows the Dark Reign comics, with Norman Osborn, the Green Goblin, creating the subtlely-named Dark Avengers, of which Bullseye is the best by far, in order to do something for someone, I don't know. He is opposed by Iron Man, Black Widow, Storm, Hawkeye, Wolverine, and Thor. It ends with a fairly high level boss fight, which can be easily beaten with stuns or heal abuse because it's a three-on-one curbstomp.
After that, you can go through weekly events against other players to earn more ISO-8, which is your experience, or Hero Points, which can get you more slots for more characters. Most of these events have restrictions or characters that get bonuses in stats, encouraging you to use them in your team and keep the characters you're not as interested in.
I haven't seen the pay-to-win much in my time of playing. Even if you buy ISO-8 and Hero Points, you're still going to have to keep up against people who have more experience with their characters than you and can set up teams with better gem coverage. And even if you get a full party of rare characters, they don't all work together as well as the lower level characters, and many of the three star characters have weaknesses to their powers, such as Iron Man Model 40's Recharge, which provides gems to use on other attacks, but stuns Iron Man for two turns.
Overall, I enjoy this a good bit, and recommend it to others.

If you take a pinch of Stanley Parable, a dash of Dungeon Keeper II and a hint of Warcraft III and mix it together you get something like Dungeons 2: a casual dungeon management/strategy game inspired by Dungeon Keeper II, an utterly sarcastic commentator like in Stanley Parable and an overworld RTS-like game that has the feeling of that of Warcraft III.
I picked this game up at a Humblr Bundle and had fairly low expectations, but surprisingly the game does well in giving you that strategy feeling of managing a dungeon with evil creatures, but obviously trying to avoid directly copying Bullfrog's success. But not all equally successful unfortunately. In Dungeons 2 creatures need to be 'purchased', including your little helpers and the amount of total creatures you can have is bound to "population points".
The fact there is a limit isn't too bad, but since it's shared with your helpers, named "Little Snots", it's a bit of a balancing act between the creatures you need for research, defence/offence and the helpers. While in Dungeon Keeper II the helpers's tasks only consist of capturing ground/rooms (not needed in this game), digging, carrying gold and dragging unconsious creatures to their lair to recover and setting up traps and doors. In Dungeons 2 they are also required to provide the beer (which replaces the chickens from Dungeon Keeper II).
So sometimes when you are on a planning spree and dig out new rooms, series of traps, etc., with the little amount of helpers you have they might be too busy with that (they ALWAYS prioritise digging above anything else), that none are making beer and your creatures are left without. This feels kinda frustrating.
Later in the campaign you are given the training room to "upgrade" a creature into a different one but doing so requires additional population points. Which feels frustratingly limiting again, despite the game's easy difficulty. And the choice of creatures is fairly little. While Duungeon Keeper II had a whole range, Dungeons 2 you can count on the fingers of one hand (not counting the upgraded variations). Same goes for interesting rooms: Dungeons 2 has less (no prison, and so no room to convert enemies or get info from).
The picking up and dropping of creatures feels a bit less snappy and intuitive than I'm familiar with from Dungeon Keeper II, the spells that are given to you half of them I don't find really useful and so mana feels fairly useless other than upgrading a few things like population points.
It's fun to have an overworld where you can send your creatures to, destroy a few camps to make them stop spawning enemies, but other than that very little is done with it and I feel that so much more could have done with it (valuable resources, creatures, research, occupy strategic points, etc.).
So all-in-all, the game has quite a few flaws that still makes me rather go back to Dungeon Keeper II and pick it up again  (go get it and play it if you haven't!): too small amount of different creatures, limiting total of creatures,  mana not done enough things with, less interesting rooms, overall too easy.
On the other hand, and this is why I'd still recommend it, this is a game you can easily relax and zone out with. Little to no stress whatsoever, and very little challenges. You generally have plenty of time to build your dungeon, set up your defences and take your time to trigger the next phase in a campaign map. Together with an utterly sarcastic commentator that keeps passive-aggressively reminding that "the Ultimate Evil should do something very important, but shows no signs of doing anything about it".
The funny comments from the commentator and relaxing gameplay made it, despite the flaws, a fun 25 hours of playtime playing the campaign for me!

In my top 10 games of all time. The only complaint I have is that it was way too short.
General:
+ Difficulty is really, really easy at "easy" pretty easy at "normal", and then gets really hard from there. "Hard" and "Very hard" are actually really challanging. Basically, for any skill level.
- GAME WAS WAY TOO SHORT. I wish there were about 10x more levels and bosses.
Story:
- Not really existant, but doesn't get in the way. The story might as well not be there.
+ Story doesn't get in the way. The point of the games isn't for the story
Atmosphere/Art/Music:
* Atmosphere varies by level, but has an overall cartoonish feel to it. Not "in your face" pixel art, and overall has a nice aesthetic.
* Music was mid tier
Mechanics:
+ The best platformer/shooter mechanics I've ever seen.
+ You get a tripple dash, where you can dash in any direction three times. Insanely fun, and you just want to dash around the screen, shooting things. If you get good at it, you can combine the dashes so you can dodge and couter attack, or to get behind an enemy you would normally think you can't get over. Might take some practice, but you can do things like, tripple jump + wall jump + jump up + right dash + jump up, all withought hitting the ground. Since this game is a bullet hell, it feels amazing when you dash around 10 bullets at once
+ Interesting weapons. You get to select two weapons, which you can switch out. The default weapon, dual pistos, is basically a machine gun, and can get you though most of the game, but buying different weapons adds a challange or an advantage, depending on the level. Adds a great dynamic to the game
+ Bullet time: Great tool to get you though tough situations. Has a reasonable cooldown, so you can't spam it but it isn't an "ult" move. Combine bullet time and the tripple dash, and you feel like a super hero
+ Bosses: Not creative, but good. When I say not creative, I mean the bosses really remind me of kirby or super meat boy bosses. They all have patterns, and they cycle through moves. Each boss is very different, and each presented a different challange. Not as fun as the platforming part imo, but still alot of fun
tl;dr: If you wan't a game that's just alot of fun to play, this is it.

The epitome of the entire Splinter Cell franchise, Chaos Theory marks the high-point of the stealth genre(except maybe losing out to Thief in that regard). Unlike most games involving guns, the most important skill in Splinter Cell is situational awareness, as opposed to the usual reflex-aiming; this is because Sam Fisher is a man, not a stormtrooper strung out on stimulants. Multiple methods of entry and escape from a room or area are usually avaliable, but many of these paths are guarded by some form of deterrant. Cameras are usually hidden in shadow or difficult to see areas, and guards can (and do) change routes. All of these things means that the game tends to promote a cautious advance rather than a blitz. Not a good experience if bloodlust is prevalant.
TL;DR the game rewards you for being cautious, aware, and using your brain to take the path less traveled by.
