An excellent visual novel. As a backer from their kickstarter campaign, I had high hopes after sampling Ithaqua Labs' prior work, Jacob's Island, and after finishing my first playthrough of Brilliant Shadows, I am delighted with this game. Suffice to say my expectations were exceeded.
If you have never played a visual novel style game before, or even if you have and maybe didn't take to it very much, I think Brilliant Shadows is a great starting/re-entry point to visual novels in general.
It is very well presented and well written. Characters are believable and relatable. You start to feel for their predicaments with surprising ease, and the story sucks you right in.
Playtime for a single playthrough took upwards of 3 hours for me, which is fairly good for a visual novel game. As it is not a so-called "kinetic" novel (one with a single story and no branching paths) there are thankfully multiple paths that can be taken, and multiple endings to receive, so this will increase play time considerably. Even assuming you use the skip feature on subsequent playthroughs, getting all the endings is likely to take at least 5 hours or so I would guess. Playing through it normally, probably more like 8 or 9.
I was graced with Ending #1 upon my first completion, and it was quite a satisfying one. Despite the "Part One..." in the game's subtitle, while it is clear there is more to come in future games, this first part doesn't exactly leave you hanging either. It felt like a satisfying place to end the first "book" if you will, and since there are multiple paths in the story to take, I look forward to seeing the significance of the other available routes and endings in subsequent replays of Brilliant Shadows.
Without spoiling anything, I'll just say the final moments of Ending 1 and the epilogue were quite touching, thanks to a very creative surprise twist.
All spoken dialog lines in the game have actual voicework, and it was well executed. The voices took me a bit to get used to at first, but that sensation quickly faded.
Usually adding voices to visual novels is a bit of a gamble. The quality usually ends up polarized from what I have seen, but those fears are unfounded in this case. Everyone did a great job with their delivery of the lines, none of them seemed unnatural or like they were a poor fit to their characters. It all just worked out quite well, and I hope to hear more from this talented cast in future Ithaqua Labs games.
Artwork was incredible. There's really no beating around the bush there. Characters, background scenery, UI flourishes, CG scenes, animations....all of it gorgeous and very fitting to bringing the world to life. Just excellent.
The music score was pleasing as well. It felt fitting to various scenes. While I didn't get the feeling that it stood out as incredibly memorable per se, it also didn't need to be. The important point for me to drive home is that it wasn't distracting. It didn't feel out of place. It's a good solid score for evoking and complementing the scene-appropriate emotions, and I really have nothing bad to say about it.
I highly recommend Brilliant Shadows. It has all of the things a great visual novel should, and I'm eagerly (but patiently)  awaiting Part Two of the Book of Gray Magic (and part three? four? .... alright I'll stop being greedy.)

One of the most intense games I have ever played in my life.
During moments of your gaming in life you experience tonnes of breath-taking, heartstopping and adrenalinic moments which are temporary. These can be from when you sit together with three other friends, taking over B spot on Battlefield 4 while you get surrounded by 2-3 Squads, leaving you to face them 20/3. Moments like these you can feel your heart pumping, your sweat chilling and your eyes focus like they were on freaking crack.
Or take for example if you played Smite, or any other moba - You spend ages to level up and then to gear your character just so that you can join your teammates in team-fights. The fights in these games can vary heavily - some can be instant pubstomps ending up with you killing your enemy rather quickly, whereas others can take some time and some planning. But then there's also those twitch-moments you have in mobas - you know, those rare moments where everything stands still. You are inches away from dying, your mind is blank and you simply are not sure what to do. The enemy is weak, all at low health but plently of mana.
You are the only one alive in your team and you've got plenty of both mana and health - so you choose to do the greedy thing of charging in - ending up with you being put in one of the stickiest situations that you can be in. Enemy after enemy pounces you and you can feel your heart race as well as you see the impending doom that has fallen upon you. Should you escape to base with barely any health left? Or should you press on and get several kills and turn the tide of the battle? Before you even make a decision you see several ulties, abilities and auto-attacks headed your way - you're simply ♥♥♥♥ed... or that's how the situation would be. There's that odd rare moment when during panic and stressful situations your brain enters a complete clear mode. Call it Zen, call it ♥♥♥♥ing super-saiyan, call it binge-eating ben and jerries and get a crack-like sugar-rush on a Sunday evening, your whole body gets heated but - your mind is clear - you quickly devise a tactic in your head and avoid the first ultimate, then you dive in for the kill just to be interrupted by the second ultimate - which you avoid as well. You enter a focused bloodlust where you will kill the enemy team - not plan to, but will.
We have all felt something like this... however these moments rarely come during these games. It's always one or the other. You either pubstomp or get pubstomped.
That is ... unless you're playing Bloodline Champions.
Every moment, every action, every movement, counts to the thrill in BLC. The moments where time freezes and your blood rushes is every second in Bloodline Champions 2 minute games. With instant-tactics and synergetic gameplay, as a Bloodline Champion you must make sure to know what your teammate thinks as well as they know what you think, because there's rarely any room for vocal tactics. The game is fast-paced and if you're damaged - there's nowhere to run. You were put in the ring to fight to death, not to cower back at your base. When you lose a game in Bloodline Champions then it's not as merciful as the other games, where if you respawn you cozy up in your little Base, you get to live to see the cheers. No, here the winner is the one who isn't lying in a pool of his own blood. The winner is the one who survived - For even when the timer runs out, sudden death approaches, allowing no peace - only victory.
cray-review aside - let's discuss this on a more serious note.
The game is a little relentless against beginners mostly due to the fact that it has a low playerbase. When a new player wishes to play a game then they're usually pinned against players who know how to play already. As for the pubstomping, it can occur in Bloodline Champions as well - Just that when you get a proper fight, it's awesome and it happens quite often. Especially once you get the gist of the game - then it happens almost all the time. You know those blood-rush fights that I wrote of a bit higher up on the review? Yeah they happen really frequently.. you just have to have the patience to learn the game. This could mean to learn every character, which there are 21 of I believe, but once you learn a few you begin to notice a familiar pattern within a lot of the characters. Some of them have similiar abilities - but that have different effects basically.
TL;DR - good game. Play it.

The Hitman franchise has always been the odd one out in modern gaming. While mainline franchises in stealth died a horrible rebooted death or got less and less about stealth. Hitman always stood as a solid game about sneaky murder while other games feebly tried to make stealth sections. Yet a game series this long runnung isn't without a bizarre game and Absolution is that red-headed step child. It's a hard turn off the Stealth Freeway into the small town of "WeDon'tEvenKnowsville".
The Story is probably the most batshit in the history of the franchise which is saying something, and to fully explain the madness I have to spoil the game. Following Blood Money, Diana goes rogue and 47 is forced to go and kill her. However 47 finds out the Agency has decided to make more super-soldier clones, this time it's a little gorl named Victoria. Finding this out, 47 goes rogue trying to defend the girl from the Agency. At the same time, and this actually happens in game, a South Dakotan arms dealer named Blake Dexter decides to trap 47 and steal Victoria. So you have a massive spy agency, a arms dealer with the power to control an entire county of the state and 47. It makes little sense, has you stuck in 2 cities and means you have to watch a boatload of cutscenes keeping you from killing everything that moves.
The Gameplay is the biggest shift from previous games and it's a double edged sword. You know how in the last two games there was this weird list feeling to movement between running and walking? Now we have much more flowing movement that doesn't feel like you're constantly wading through invisible oatmeal. Systems like flinging weapons at enemies, making distractions and more are streamlined in comparison to the earlier games. At the same time it doesn't really make stealth particularly hard, given the "Instinct" system which allows you to breeze through guards and figure out all the little trick spots for those fun enviroment kills.
And the graphics...well it's a Hitman game so they're pretty meh. Basic lighting and overall textures are good but once you get to faces you enter some freaky♥♥♥♥♥♥ The cutscenes get worse when they get close to the models given the game's weird love of sweat effects that make it feel like every character is shrink-wrapped. It gets worse with water effects.
All in all, Absolution is a good game at its core with a lot of issues wrapped around it. The story is like a bad B-movie with hammy acting and more crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥than a asylum bathroom. The graphics are a mix between very good and a group of marionettes sitting in a bar talking about "limp" people. And yet despite that the gameplay is very solid, and I can see why it was lifted and then dropped into the newer Hitman game with little to no major changes. So if you're willing to put up with the wrong Hitman voice, slightly terrifying graphics and a story that makes Tommy Wiseau sound like Stephen Spielburg, then this game is for you.

Quick gameplay rundown: Watch cutscene, start mission, (slowly) follow (annoyingly slow) NPCs while they talk about something you don't care about, two of them will go to either side of a door while still discussing something you don't care about, one of them kicks the door open, go through door (sometimes there is an invisible wall in the doorway for some reason not letting you go through for a full several seconds after it's kicked open), shoot a bunch of enemies, watch NPCs talk after the battle (sometimes watch an NPC you don't care about be killed), finish mission, THEN DO IT ALL OVER AGAIN. This is every mission, no variation with the exception of several moments throughout the entirety of the game. None of the characters, including the player character, have their story fleshed out which means you feel no connection to anyone in this game, so if they were to die in any way you won't care. When a stranger dies, you have a brief feeling of sadness, or "that is terrible", but they are ultimately strangers and you just can't care a whole lot, it's not humanly possible. Basically what I'm saying is that the story is terrible, and a FPS cliche if I ever saw one. The gameplay is just, OKAY, and the graphical quality is half decent. If I had paid money for this game, I would be pretty upset.

Dungeon Fighter Online is an old-style beat-em-up arcade game but in the form of an MMORPG. I really wish I could give this game a Positive review as I really enjoyed it the first few hours of playing, even if I felt overwhelmed at times.
UPs:
- The game gets frequent events that feel rewarding.
- It feels retro, so people who played arcade beat-em-up games would definitely feel the nostalgia.
- A lot of characters to pick up from which every single one has 2 or more advancements.
- "Shiny" skills!!!
- Pretty cool story videos as you progress through it.
Downs:
- Really clunky controls at moments responsiveness felt awkward.
- Gameplay can easily become repetitive. Even though you get 12 skill slots, at first it's really fun but then you find an optimal combo and you repeat it.
- PvP is terrible and imbalanced.
- The crafting system (Not the Professions.) while unique it was pretty disappointing and you rarely use it.
- I checked the item shop and was pretty happy when I saw that Avatars don't have stats, until I found some other Avatar items with stat boosts and they are untradeble nor can they be gifted. While I will not scream pay-to-win, it made me feel displeased.
Neutral:
- Fatigue System. I cannot really understand why this system is getting all the hate? You get bombarded with premium contracts and fatigue potions at the start and later on in the game you can afford fatigue potions and those contracts for simple gold.
I know a lot of people love the game and will probably defend it, there is nothing wrong with that. But considering the gaming experience I got from the game, I just cannot recommend it.

I only have about 6 hours in the game thus far so this will be more of a first impressions review, i'll add to it later.
First off, this is more of an open world RPG then a survival game. There is no food/water meter, no sickness or sanity etc.
Personally i find this refreshing, let's be honest, after the first few hours of a survival game food/drink are never an issue anyway, just another chore to do. Plus it's nice to be able to go to the bathroom or talk to my wife for 5 min and not come back to a dead char because i starved to death inside my base.
This game is like if Skyrim and Ark had a baby. It feels and plays like a coop, multiplayer RPG.
Base building is nice and though i don't have them yet, there seems to be a decent amount of styles.
The crafting is solid and pretty intuative.
Combat kinda feels like Skyrim. Find a good spot, spam your spells till it starts running at you, back up/dodge while attacking till one of you is dead. Which isn't to say it's easy, most things will kill you in a few hits, at least early on.
The AI is lackluster, but hell, even large studios have trouble with this, it's a known issue and should improve over time.
While i have experienced a few bugs, i've yet to find anything game breaking or rage quit worthy.
In general it's a solid game, At the very minimum it's got the bones to be a great game! It's very playable and i'm thoroughly enjoying myself atm. There is end game content arriving at the end of this moth and i'm sure they will only continue to improve and flesh out the game.
On a side note, i wouldn't put to much stock in the negative reviews. If you actually read them, most are one line throwaways that are probably part of a review bomb. The rest are complaining about bugs... it's an EA game.
The only legitimate negatives i've read complain about server populations.
1: this will improve as the game gets better and word of mouth spreads.
2: this really only matters on pvp servers.
Personally, i hate crowded servers in a game like this. All the good base spots are taken and you have to compete for resources. I prefer to play on a private server, or on a low pop one with a few friends
TLDR:
Solid, stable, fun game even in it's current form. It'll only get better

Again it's very late to write the review of this game - as it was release for quite a long back.
Still, I am compelled to write the same cause of the game itself. As usual I will be dividing my review in parts. So without any further adieu lets jump into the business here -
Story: The plot is, as with any other "Splinter Cell" title, is self-untangling. At the beginning player will have a very limited knowledge about the entire plot and that is revealed as the game is progressed. The plot itself may not appeal to the average FPS people, who are looking for Aim-n-Shoot kinda play through. But if you invest enough time and senses into the game - the plot is very apt and con-sized.
Gameplay: The best part of any "Splinter Cell" title. Yes, though its not an open world environment, still there are more than 1 ways to complete most of the missions. The player will be given ample scope and time and equipments to complete each of the missions as the way they see fit. Players can vary their tactics - they can go complete "Stealth" and not raise a SINGLE!! alarm to complete mission or they can take a bit more direct approach to solve mattes - using bullets, that is.
The tools are great and fun to use as well - be it a sticky camera or optical fiber or Lock Pic they can make the players life a lot less painful.
Graphics: Now, when we talk about in game graphics - we usually bring out some of the big names of the business but very easily forget about "Splinter Cell" titles. Even for an old game like Chaos Theory, trust me, the graphics is great. The shadows and the ambient glow from the street/table/wall lamps are just too good. But the best part of all of them are the different vision mode of Sam Fisher's goggles. To me, the "Night Vision" is one of the best rendered "night mode" across all the game titles.
AI: The AI is a strong point in this game - specially how they react to a whisper or when they see a body. Some of the guards are as ignorant as ever yet some of they are very suspicious (even of their own breathing). AI bots take some predefined paths or some random one - specially after they are being alerted. Even an open door or torn curtain can raise there suspicion. Be very careful to watch your light and ambient noise meter all the time - and don't hesitate to grab one if needed.
All in all I am really enjoying the game and I would surely recommend anyone who is looking a different breed of the FPS genre.

The name oif this application is misleading in that it does not and cannot "synthesize" sounds as an actual chiptune synth can [ see:
].
Want a music "toy" that can play samples of sounds that sound like old console games and / or write "songs" like the "trackers" of the 90's but with less tracks?
Buy this.
Want a musical instrument that will work with your Digital Audio Workstation [DAW]?
Don't buy this. Rytmik is programmed with the UNITY 3d engine and it is not capable of being used as a DAW plug-in nor MIDI synth.  This is not a synthesizer. It is a very limited audio loop player. You cannot use it with a MIDI conmtroller nor can you actually "play it except via a QWERTY keyboard.
Want to be able to expand your sounds and export your "songs"?
You can buy sound upgrades and export capabilities by buying the "Ultimate" add-on and additional sound packs but if you want to use your own your own samples you are out of luck. All of the configuration and sounds are stored in UNITY native compressed file format. The application does not allow you to import or save your own sound banks.
If you want a real chiptune tracker app try OpenMPT
which can do the things that this app cannot.

The first thing that I believe should be pointed out is that the near entirety of this game was made by one person, with a few others for quality assurance, sound design, etc. While I can appreciate the amount of work it would take for an individual to make a game such as this, I am at first impressed, but then I remember Cave Story, a game made by another individual. Cave Story's composition displays immense amounts of experience and understanding of the craft that Bleed does not. Cave Story, in its original form, is also available to play free of charge, a privilege that Bleed does not, to my knowledge, provide. This is quite ironic to me, since Cave Story feels like a retail-quality game while Bleed feels like a high schooler's B-grade final project.
After playing Bleed, I had no clue whatsoever as to why I had it in my wishlist for as long as I did. On the surface, the game looks bland at best. The background art is a few steps above being on the level of placeholders, the main character looks like something an artist in their very early stages of artistic development would draw in their math notebook, and the enemies look like thirty-second doodles with copious amounts of tweening in place of animation. All of these assets are presented in a style popular amongst indie platformers, which is somewhat inspired, if indirectly, by Cave Story, i.e. drawn in a digital paint program, then shrunk down and blown back up again. Despite this, all enemies explode in a high-resolution blood splatter, which is akin to taking a sledgehammer to the game's artstyle. Even if the game's developer was going for simplicity, they failed to take into consideration that simplicity functions best when based on rules of art that this game does not regard.
The general style of the game as a whole seems to be more directly inspired by Hotline Miami, as both are "retro-styled" games with violent gunplay and twin-stick controls. However, Bleed is more than content with throwing a side-scrolling shooter or two (Megaman X and Super Metroid come to mind) into the stew. This leads to the player having to juggle free, any-directional aiming and platforming, making for a mediocre experience in both regards. One remarkably stupid part of the platforming side is the main character's means of vertical movement. The player is given a quadruple-jump, which combines the directional functionality of Cave Story's Jetpack 2.0 with some of Super Metroid's Space Jump's maneuverability. This is much less fun than it may seem on paper. While the Jetpack 2.0 restricts movement to four directions, and the Space Jump only allows the player one direction that can be adjusted slightly, the quad-jump in Bleed can be used in any of eight directions. The variety of orientations are very hard to justify, as diagonal movement is mostly unneccessary and the momentum from the horizontal jump isn't enough to be helpful.
A further ingredient in Bleed's cookbook is Max Payne's bullet time mechanic. While admittedly the most fun part of the game is dodging enemies and shots in slow motion, the novelty wears off as no other mechanics take advantage of it, making it go stale quickly. However, it seems to be almost required in a few situations, the scenario with the helicopter in the game's first level coming to mind. The shots are practically impossible to dodge, since the level is designed with very little cover from the helicopter's highly accurate shots. This leaves the player hiding in very small crevies waiting for their bullet time to recharge.
The game's balance is almost as laughable as its presentation. Levels are harbingers of torment despite having checkpoints in between every room. Meanwhile, bosses can be faced with comparatively little effort. One of the game's many plagiarized elements, the style meter, brings this to mind, as reaching a rank above a D only occurs once in a blue moon during levels, while it's to be expected to go as high as an A in bosses.
Overall, Bleed feels like a love letter to everything wrong with indie games. The entire experience is bland, the music is forgettable, the art is embarassing, and the gameplay is a chore. Perhaps, wth experience, the developer can one day produce something great, since it is evident that this is a very early attempt at a fully-fledged video game.

Ghostbusters
by
Harold Ramis
and
Dan Aykroyd
Final Shooting Script
Last revised October 7, 1983
FADE IN
EXT. NEW YORK PUBLIC LIBRARY -- DAY
The sun shines brightly on the classic facade of the main library at Fifth
Avenue and 42nd Street.  In the adjacent park area, pretty hustlers and
drug peddlers go about their business.
FRONT STEPS
A few people lounge on the steps flanked by the familiar stone lions.
INT. MAIN READING ROOM -- DAY
People are dotted throughout the room sitting at the long oak tables
polished by decades of use.  Reading lamps with green glass shades cast a
golden glow on the tables.  The patina of age is everywhere.  It is very
quiet.
LIBRARIAN
A slightly stout, studious looking girl in her late twenties circulates
quietly among the tables picking up books and putting them on her cart.
Everything seems completely normal and peaceful.
POV
A single eerie musical note signals the presence of something strange
looking down on the Librarian from a vantage point high above the room.
It follows the Librarian as she pushes her cart around the corner.
INT. WORK AREA
The Librarian is alone in a back room sorting books for reshelving.
Behind her is the card catalogue.  One of the books attracts her interest
and she starts leafing through it.
THE CARD CATALOGUE
Another eerie note is heard as one of the drawers silently slides open
behind the Librarian and hundreds of index cards start popping out.  The
Librarian continues reading completely oblivious to this strange
phenomenon.
She gets up and moves past another row of cabinets.  Two more drawers
quietly slide open, and thousands of file cards start shooting out of the
open drawers just behind her, but the Librarian still doesn't notice.
THE STACKS
The Librarian works her way through rows and rows of old iron shelves
containing many thousands of volumes stacked from floor to ceiling.  As
she puts the books back in their proper places, she slowly gets the
feeling that she's being watched.  She continues her task but suddenly
hears a scratching noise and stops.
LIBRARIAN
(puzzled)
Hello?  Is anybody there?
A ROW OF BOOKS
As the Librarian walks down the aisle, books start shooting off the shelf
behind her.  She turns suddenly and sees the fallen books.
THE LIBRARIAN
Frightened now, she walks slowly to the end of the aisle and tentatively
peeks around the corner.  Seeing no one, she starts to scratch her head
and suddenly a dozen books fly off the shelf right in front of her and
fall to the floor.
LIBRARIAN
(frightened)
All right!  Who's there?  Lyle? Is that you?
Very slowly now, her heart pounding, the Librarian tiptoes to the other
end of the aisle.  She gets to the corner and starts to peek around it,
afraid to look but unable to resist.
INT. THE NEXT AISLE -- DAY
The Librarian comes slowly around the end of the stacks and gets her first
look at the thing that's been watching her.  Her eyes go very wide and her
mouth opens in horror. She screams.

Full disclosure: I know the creators of Brilliant Shadows , but if I did not enjoy the game I would have just avoided posting a review. I played through the game in the beta stages which is why my time played is so low, but the game was complete for all intents and purposes.
I have never really been into visual novels at all, but I really liked the premise of this one. The art is excellent and the writing is on point, all of the characters feel fully fleshed out and well developed. The novel has a combination of action, humor, and romance. I have never been much in the form of romance anything but it is well done. The real draw for me are: 1) The world is rich and clearly designed with a larger story arc in mind (which I am greatly looking forward to), 2) The fantastic art style with fully detailed sprites, varied backgrounds and wonderful CGs.Each character is fully voiced and there are multiple endings making the product feel really polished.  There are a ton of little elements that show the love and care that went into the game, one of my favorite is the blooper reel at the end.
100% would recommend to fans of visual novels and would heavily suggest that people like me who have never played one consider starting with this one. Mox is also confirmed for best character.
TL;DR Good starting point for people like me who have not read any VNs before and extremely well put together so fans of VNs will most certainly enjoy this.

Even if you’re not a huge visual novel fan (I’m certainly not), pick this up.

Big Pharma is an interesting game. You run a pharmasuitical company, who's goal is to simply make products to cure what ails your customers. You research new tools, machines, and send forth expeditions to the far corners of the globe in search of strange components.
I strongly suggest Big Pharma if you enjoy any of the following: automation, strange scenarios, medicine, or building a global medicine empire. This game is a strange sort of fun, and I find it oddly relaxing to play when stressed out. Combining different materials into one super drug is oddly satisfying, and selling products that may have flaws isn't a horrible thing to do. Even the oddest combination of cures can be an effective medicine, like depression and heart attack meds as one pill or cream. It sells well, but may cause irritated skin.
Big Pharma is a strange game, but a great game overall. Give it a try, and see how well you can manage a pharmasuitical business.

While I can't say anything bad about Hitman: Absolution as a game, I have a really mixed feelings about it being part of Hitman franchise. It does lack a little bit of difficult level compared to Codename 47, it doesn't have missions so exciting as in Silent Assassin, the atmosphere of game is weird and can't say it's similar to Contracts and the most important, the gameplay, is really few steps back compared to the one in Blood Money. Sure, the graphics looks really fancy, but's that only best thing while I compare this game to the previous Hitman games. I'm giving this one a thumb up anyway. Why? Like I just said, the graphics: it's beatiful and the executions are really fest for the eyes in this game. There are also many interesting stuff to do and it doesn't mean only replaying the story all the time and collecting bunch of stuff: The Contracts! It's fun to play on contracts made by friends or some random people, it's fun to upgrade your weapons with earned cash and finally, it's really fun to take a part in a contract competitions. While the whole scoring system is a really turn-off for me in story mode, it works fantastic in Contracts mode. Also, achievements: easy to unlock most of them, but really hard to 100% it. Might be double the fun if you are fun of it.

Overall, a great Marvel-themed match-three puzzle-game, which lacks decent storyline and implies way too much microtransactions.
The gameplay is simple: you control a squad of three Marvel superheroes of your choice (the more you play, the more heroes you'll be having in your roster). By matching colored gems, you gather resources which you use to cast heroes' abilities and to kill your enemy's team. You can level-up your heroes by using Iso-8 that you earn in battles. Abilities are also upgradable - it takes a new card to upgrade an ability.
Game is very addictive, even though it's the "play to win" type: the more money you're investing, the faster you progress and the better heroes you own. In general, you must spend Hero Points (which is REALLY hard to get in game, if you're not willing to purchase it) for everything: new slots for new heroes in roster; new hero cards (the good ones); upgrading abilities if you don't have the needed card; health packs for wounded heroes (if you're not willing to wait 2-3 hours for him/her to regenerate, or waiting ~30 minutes for a new health pack to appear).
I think I'd rate it 7.5 out of 10, just because I'm not a huge fan of microtransactions.
PS As for now, I've played 40+ hours and didn't donate a dollar. Not because I don't like the game, but because I don't like being forced to do that.

Pros
- Good plot/story line
- Easy to get in to, still challenging
- Sweet graphics, nice foliage and trees
- One of the better livery/decal systems I've seen
- Drifting is easy/fun
- Special events like overtake are really fun and a nice change of pace
- Road/coastal/highway courses add a nice variety

Cons
- User interface is clunky at times, loses my settings, making it frustrating to use the game
- No tuning options/suspension tweaking except in multiplayer
- Fewer cars and choices for cars than in some other games
Some people complain that there is no cockpit view. While this is true, it's also something I don't mind as there is bonnet and bumper cam, which effectively do pretty close to the same thing.
Overview
This is a drifer's dream game. The handling is true to each car's unique tendencies but various effects have been put in place so you don't slide out as much as you would in real life. I quite enjoy the handling, it feels very responsive in general and I love the ease with which I can slam a Camaro into a drift at full speed and still recover. Probably not realistic, but tons of fun pulling massive drifts with ease, and I like that the feeling of each car still represents the general feel of that car in real life.
The custom game setup doesn't remember any of the choices I've made and it's easy to wipe out my selections and have to start over or not realize I'm not in the right race until I get to a track I didn't expect. Having to constantly swipe through tons of tracks to find the one I want every time is annoying. I like that there are lots of tracks, I don't like that the UI doesn't' remember the one I was on and doesn't have a better way to search for the tracks. This last bit is something that should change, but I put up with it because the game itself is so fun.
I've heard people complain that there aren't enough tracks but I have been plenty sastisfied with the variety of tracks. I'm sure if you play a game for long enough, any game can become boring, but people who like football don't think football is boring just because it's played on the same type of field each time. I don't think racing is boring just because I'm racing the same track. With a different car, it's practically a new course to learn anyway, and lap times can probably always be improved. So far, I'm quite satisfied with the variety of tracks in this game.
That brings me to the cars. There are plenty of cars, but not as many as in some other titles, for sure. I don't feel particularly lacking in car varieties, but it does seem like the car choice is a bit limited, even after unlocking lots of cars via the challenges. Overall, I don't find this to be that bad, but I would have liked more car varieties.

Seriously, if you like Mega-Man, with the insanely difficult levels and tons of replayability, this is definitely your type of game. This game has a short story, but it doesn't hinder this extremely great game, especially with the arcade mode, which allows you to play until you die, and it uploads your score.
The graphics are amazing. Everything is colorful and vibrant. The performance is glorious. No matter how much was going on, at no point whatsoever did my frame rate drop down severely to a point where it hindered my gameplay even slightly, both on a strong pc and a measly laptop. The levels are difficult and require many runs through them in order to get the layout down in your mind, and the sheer amount of stuff happening is sure to keep you on edge at all times. The control scheme is absolutely comfortable and fits this game perfectly. Only problem I have is that switching items via scroll, which is my preference, needs a sensitivity adjuster, for uber-sensitive scrollers.
There are some problems with the game, which sometimes hinder the gameplay. Sometimes, I lose exactly where the mouse is, due to it no having a border or just blending in with the background, which happens a lot, causing me to die a ton. Also, the game is a bit too short for my liking, so I think the developers should make a few new levels for the game. However, the replayability of this should occupy you for a long while, especially with the different difficulties. Completing all 7 levels of this game on normal took me about 2 hours, which felt much longer.
Also...
Although slow motion wouldn't be able to be done, open levels with free for all or killing bosses would be phenomenal. If you are one of the developers, PLEASE make multiplayer levels like this. It would add so much more depth to the game, and add many, many hours of gameplay to it.
Anyways, BUY THIS! It is definitely worth your time and money, and it was a fun time for me. Definitely immersive, colorful, beautiful, performs like a beast, and has tons of replayability, however can get ever-so-slightly better with multiplayer and a few tweaks. 9.8/10

Jalopy is a gem. I score it a solid 8/10. It had a fair share of bugs, forcing me to restart the game a few times. This is annoying as it moves your car back to the most recent checkpoint. For a game that's been out as long as this, there shouldn't be game-breaking bugs occuring with this frequency. Without bugs I would give Jalopy a 9/10.
Gem is not a word I throw around lightly, but it's the most appropriate term for this game.
In Jalopy you find yourself in the company of your aged uncle. He proposes a trip across the country from Germany in order to reach Turkey. Your means of travel? An old Laika 601, and all of the special problems that come with it.
The game could use a more complex maintainence system. After a while it boils down to just applying your engine repair item to the various parts. You may have to make decisions as to what to repair, and when, but I wish there was more troubleshooting involved. When you open the hood, it's immediately apparent what's wrong. That's not how a real car works, and video games have their limitations, but I feel it could be reworked into something better.
The story driven segment of the game is a decent length, took me about six hours to finished comfortably. The game doesn't end there though, you can drive around forever if you like.
The game has all kinds of small charming things. To open the engine bay, you have to pull a level in the cabin. To drive, you have to start the engine by turning the keys and releasing the parking break. When you get out of your car for roadside repairs, it's a good idea to put the hazards on. When it rains, throw your wipers on. When it's dark, put your lights on. There's other things in the game world you can interact with to promote immersion, such as lightswitches and doors. Really small, but immersive things that I loved.
Over time, you watch yourself develop into a skilled motorist and preventative mechanic. You collect upgrades for your trusty Laika, stop forgetting to turn your car off, and devise the optimal way to organize your trunk space. You feel confident in your fuel and vehicle condition to explore off-road paths, and discover the special things they may hold.
You find yourself immersed in this journey, carefully maintaining your car and checking tires at every stop. You mix and match parts to figure out how you like to drive. You find yourself as a motorist with a destination, as the character of this game. It sneaks up on you in such a special way, that it's not an experience to rob yourself of.
It's a fun little game, and more than meets the eye. At it's current price, I say Jalopy is a definite purchase.

I do recommend this game if you expect the same as previous Sid Meier's game releases.
If you expect something new, you'll be in for a disappointing déjà vu.
I have been a huge fan of previous versions of Sid Meier's Civilization: I loved Alpha Centauri.
Now, many years later, I bought Civilization: Beyond Earth.
At the beginning, it was all fun. The graphics looked good; I liked the music a lot. But after some turns (about 100 or so) I realized there was NOTHING NEW about this game. For me it is a HUGE DEJA VU of Alpha Centauri.
After being such a succesful game programmer, I really expected Sid Meier and Firaxis to turn up with something NEW; something innovative; something we hadn't seen before. I didn't expect this cheap program recycling. Because that is what it is, disguised in some modern graphics and sleeker design.
- The aliens are boring. They're more of an obstacle on the road you just need to get rid of.
- The landscape isn't very "beyond Earth". Except for some exotic resources, boring alien insects and fish and a greenish fog, I don't see anything "beyond".
- What's with the resource pods? What the hell? Is that all the game designers could come up with for this "beyond Earth" world?!?! How boring and unimaginative! What about some alien technologies hidden in artifacts? Or strange ruins of civilizations long since disappeared? Nooooo: resource pods, abandoned outposts and bones. That's very, very "beyond"...
- I got HUGELY irritated by the stupid, moronic, illogical and backwards "diplomacy" in the single player game. The diplomatic behaviour of the other faction's "AI" is erratic at the very least. Wars are declared, condemnations are spoken for NO apparant reason but some random algorithm. The "forgiveness" in the diplomatic area when it comes to covert ops is extremely one-sided and highly undervalued compared to the "AI's" blatant and ongoing incursions despite made promises or demands. It is highly unbalanced, illogical and stupid. There is nothing "I" in the AI...
This will probably be the last time I ever spend money on a Sid Meier's recycled game. It's Siphilization Beyond Boring.

That was all written before its official release, since then its had a lot of tweaks including gear added and some balancing. Now for my own thoughts as well
Archeblade isn't perfect yet, and trust me they know it that being said in a genre choked to death by wanna be Dotas and LoLs this game stands out as the evolution of the genre almost. Its not easy despite its simplicity, and sure the graphics aren't top of the line but really its indie and ya learn to forgive this in exchange for a good game gonna list what I feel are the positives, neutral and negative aspects now.
Positives:
Devs listen to the community, they comment on post and talk about what they are doing with the community.
Action based combat, screw skills...its boring and done if I want that I have two great games that nothing will surpass in size
Cast of characters. Its small but diverse at the same time with long range, melee, tanks, dps, mixed range, stealth, caster types all in there. Will it grow, yes they have already said as much. You can make pots: Yup Pots, you want them they have them and they do various things

cash shop: its not pay to win, its not micro transactions, nor is it bank breaking (most an item cost is like $6 that I saw most are less than $5)

If you want easy hit games where you don't have to do anything yeah this isn't for you. Why is this in the Neg given how elitist I normally am? It limits the game and player base always something indie games struggle in. Yes its more competitive but that's a double edged sword sadly
Servers are meh: They aren't the best, again something you expect with indie but in an action game it can ruin a match if lag messes it up badly enough. Its it terrible all the time? No you won't notice most matches and you learn to compensate normally but its there

Bleed is a 2D dual stick shooting platformer with an interesting mechanic that slows down time for a brief moment. You play as Wryn, who can jump wryth the left thumb stick, shoot in any direction with the wryght thumbstick, change between two wrypeans, slow time with the left rigger and jump with the wryght trigger. When she jumps, she can aim jump two or three more times in mid air. So you can jump to the left, then aim her to launch herself right, while shooting left, then air jump up all without hitting the ground. She can even jump off walls, but it seems more like a visual aide than a mechanic. The game has a fast pace. There are speedy bullets, bosses and hazards raining down, the slow time mechanic becomes an easy way to deal with it all.
Wryn is out to become the #1 hero! So she's got a hit list to kill all the other heroes and work her way to the top of the list! By top I mean bottom! The #1 hero gets revealed at the bottom of the list. These heroes are all bosses. After each death she'll comment things like, "Don't worry its just a game, I'll be back in a sec," "Do you have an older brother that can play this part, maybe?" Bleed hits you over the head that its a game, such as hoping you can achieve your dreams for helping her achieve hers.
You go through the game unlocking all seven levels to play. Each level has a completely different theme. A dark mansion, an underground cavern, inside of a dragon and so on. Different levels have different elements, such as getting trapped in a giant apple and forced to get through the top to the bottom of the screen before the apple drops to the next screen. Others like having to evade sensors or time jumps to avoid lasers that warm up and fire.  The bosses are giant and diverse. Everything from bosses that split when shot, to a girl with a giant pink kitten car to mechanical orbs that shield themselves. The bosses are where most of the lives get lost. You need to make use of the slow time to survive and drain their health meters. Every boss has a wide array of attacks. The patterns seem random, which is great. Every level has more than one boss and I can tell a lot of work went into them.
There is a good variety of enemies. They change from level to level and fit the theme of each level without being reskins. Cats hopping around, soldiers that ride trains and get hit by tunnels, worms that burro then leap to shoot at you. The levels are fun and there are frequent checkpoints each time you leave an area. Its a nice quick game without much challenge. Its the dual stick, and dual triggers that make it tough at first. It gets a lot easier.
When you select a level, you chose one of four difficulties, so you can always go back and play harder difficulties. Between the levels, you can visit the store to buy extra weapons. The default dual pistols are good enough and killing everything with a quick stream of bullets. The default rocket launcher does more damage, but has a slower shooting speed. There is also a revolver, homing missiles, a flame thrower and a short range shotgun to buy. While you only need two weapons if not just one, you can pause the game to equip 2 others. Why equip them when the two bumpers work well enough?
Bleed isn't a one hit death game. You have plenty of energy, but there is no way to get more energy. Your slow time bar will regenerate over time depending on the character. Both can even get upgraded in the store, as well as the regeneration speed.
With all that said, the game is an hour long at least on normal (medium) difficulty. There are extras like arcade mode, that is more like a YOLO where you only get once life and need to complete the game from start to finish. I always thought an arcade would give you three lives. You can unlock different characters to play as. Finally there's a boss attack challenge mode that can put three bosses on your screen at once. Its all just extra fluff. $5 is the right price for it.

I am a great lover of online card games, Magic, and the limited format.  I was hoping this game could scratch all of those itches at the same time.  This game tries so hard to be good, but how poorly made it is makes it genuinely hard to enjoy.
Some issues I've had during gameplay:
If finding an opponent is taking too long, there is no way to back out of the loading screen, you are stuck there until they find you one.

If your opponent disconnects while the game is still being set up:
You will have to play an AI
Your rank will still be affected by the results of the match
You will not be able to choose whether or not to take mulligans (in a ranked play no less)
The software automatically changes phases for you, and there is no way to turn this off. If it thinks you have nothing else to cast/do, on to the next phase.  The system that determines when you're changing phases has no sense of nuanced play, and will sometimes just completely screw you.
There isn't a functional system for manual mana tapping, and if you don't constantly second guess the auto tapping, it too will screw you.
This game has combat animations.  That means that every single block and every single minion that goes face get their own animation. Every. Single. One.  This can be toggled off, but when you play an opponent whose animations aren't off (which are surprisingly common), you still have to just sit there and wait for them to watch them all, no matter what.  If you have won the game, you will still have to sit and wait for your opponent to watch every single animation before the game will end
The packs are only 6 card packs, which even makes acquiring playsets of commons or uncommonns a chore.
The quests are sometimes very cumbersome, and will often require building a specialized deck specifically to fulfil it.
This game would be so much fun if so much about it wasn't just absolutely atrocious. If you're going to play card games online, there are other free games out there that are not only more polished, but just genuinely better.

Should let you know that this is a first impressions review, so it will be a recollection of the first hour or so of the game that I experienced. If you want a more in-depth review, you will have to look somewhere else.
Opening up the game: The main menu was very smooth, it was quite nice because usually such games have their main menus work at powerpoint presentation levels. I selected to play by myself, and I quite liked seeing that the game has a number of options to tailor yourself a comfortable experience. Maybe not as many options as I would have liked to see, but still a satisfying amount. However, I was not expecting what would come next...
Starting the game proper: Loading screens. First it was a five minute black screen, then a proper loading screen that took about... Two or three minutes to load up properly. But no problem, I have some games that take a good amount of time to load as well and they run smoothly, certainly this is it, right? Nope, not really. Of course when I started up the game, the textures looked of a poorer quality, despite the default settings being high, and it ran poorly. (Even though when I lowered the settings down, the game ran poorly. Probably need more than 8 gigabytes of ram, but it's still not a pleasant experience). So, making my character out of the limited few options I had, I got constructed in some kind of lava altar, and I set out to see the world. At this moment I am probably having the game running for roughly 10 minutes now.
From 10 to 30 minutes: Most of it was exploring the different kind of menus and exploration, and I have to admit, the User Interface is quite pleasantly made. The categories are neatly listed out from top to bottom in a column to the left, and there is no clutter to really speak of. On first glance, despite the noteably low textures on my character, the world did looked good enough, and the music, while generic fantasy music, was still enjoyable to listen to. So I wandered around and noticed that there are... No enemies to speak of. I looked on the map and saw a bunch of symbols, some blue, some red, and an enemy camp not that far. "I will go there", I thought to myself, and upon my arrival I meet sprites, level 6 against my level 2 self. With confidence I went up to them to take a look at their models, and then they obliterate me. Well that wasn't pleasant, I guess I will go hunt some wildlife.
30-50 minutes: Okay, so I am walking around the world, it's night time and there is... Nothing for me to fight. And it can't be said "Spawn Area protection" because this is also a lengthy walk away from any of the safe zones. So far only enemies I encountered were sprites, Orcs and fall damage. Which sounds pretty terrible considering that if a sandbox/survival game has no enemies in the open world to speak of, apart from designated camps and caves, then it just feels like a dull experience. So, I go in to a cave and take a look inside, find a bunch of Orcs standing around. Attacking them I see that the Orcs do... Nothing. In fact I go up to them and punch them, and they don't take damage nor do they react, so all I could do is kill them with magic. Not only is the open world empty, but this one cave (Cave of Jordan or how it was called) has Orcs that stand around and do nothing. What kind of game is this?
50-60 minutes: Well, it looks like it's daytime finally and... What is that? A bear? Rabbits jumping around, and there is even a wolf in the distance attacking an elk? Do you want to tell me that when it's night time, creatures are no longer around, but during the day you find them around? Well that is just a disappointment.
In short: It took around 60 minutes for me to get the game rolling with monsters in the open world, but even then it took too long. With the AI on certain parts working about as well as a drugged ox and there being a distinct sense of "Poor texturing", the game running very poorly and the main menu being deceptively smooth (I had such high hopes from the main menu), I have to say that this was a very poorly spent hour on my end, an hour I could have spent playing another game.
My conclusion of this first impression? Game's not that good, it feels like a disappointing round of sex, where it starts off romantically, only to end with you being in bed while your partner drives off to a store to get themselves Snickers, while not bringing you anything back.
I give it a red thumb.

If you're looking for a review you're at the wrong place, but heres a receipe for spaghetti!
Step 1: Get Your Supplies
Before you can start making your spaghetti you will need to first get the proper supplies and materials. To make this spaghetti you will need:
a box of spaghetti
a jar of marinara sauce
1-2 pounds of ground beef or Italian sausage
two large pots, one for boiling the pasta and the other for making the sauce
serving untensils
salt
water
You can use as much meat as you want, really - but anywhere from 1-2 pounds per large jar of sauce should work out best. I tend to use 1 pound of meat nearly every time.
Step 2: Cooking the Meat + Get the Water Boiling
Before you start, fill up a large pot with water and add a handful of salt. Put it on the stove and turn it to high so it'll start boiling!
Next you will need to cook the of meat. Take all of the meat out of its container and set it all in a large pan, then put the pan on the stove and set the stove to medium.
After that you will need to break the meat into smaller pieces. When the meat is in small pieces you will then need to start flipping the meat and make sure it gets brown all-around and cooked thoroughly. The cooking should take approximately 10-15 minutes. When all of the meat is brown and cooked you can add in the sauce.
Step 3: Mixing in the Sauce
Next you will need to mix your marinara sauce with your cooked meat. Take your jar of marinara sauce and pour all of it on the cooked meat and then stir it all around until it is all blended together. Then turn the heat down to low and let it simmer while you cook the pasta.
Step 4: Cooking the Spaghetti
Once the water has come up to a boil, you can throw the spaghetti in. Typically it should cook within 7-11 minutes - just follow the time on the box!
Make sure to stir every couple minutes to keep it from sticking.
Depending on your timing, you can either strain the spaghetti and set it aside, or you can put it right into the sauce.
Step 5: Serving Your Spaghetti
You can do this in a lot of ways but I prefer mixing the noodles in the pan with the sauce. I use tongs to drain the noodles and place them in the sauce, and then put in a couple spoons of pasta water. Stir it all together really well - the pasta water coats all the noodles and lets the sauce stick more.
You can also put plain spaghetti on individual plates and spoon the sauce over top. Whatever works for you.
Top with cheese and enjoy!

1 – GENERAL
Hitman Absolution it's a stealth action third person shooter where strategy still plays a major role in your gameplay.
As usual 47 is the main character in this game. The story is well set together. Most of the main characters are well built, but there's a lot of sideckicks in the plot that are simply forgettable. I understand their purpose in the game, but for me that's a fact, I do not know why and from where they got into the story.
Graphics are very good and detailed for a game with 5 years. It has aged very well.
Sound is very well put together, and it makes the game a joy to play. It helps a lot with immersion.
2 – GAMEPLAY
Stealth plays a major role in this game, but as usual, for me, being stealthy means that I am able to hide the pile of bodies that usually leave behind. This doesn't means that the game is very hard, just that I am very impatient. Well, on the contrary the game usually offers more than one solution to the problem that we face at any given time, but even so most of the fans of the series say that this game is very linear... I think I have to play the others, since I could always see different choices that I could make.
When we got all stuff right, we feel like a ninja, and that's very rewarding. The feeling of a clean kill, no suspicion to be made is impressive and addictive, and that make want to progress so I can meet my next challenge and see how I would perform. There's no difficulty curve whatsoever. I've found some of the last missions surprisingly easy, and some of the middle ones incredibly hard. But that doesn't mean nothing.
If we join all this with the well written plot, we can imagine that the replay value is huge!
On top of that the game also offers a major sandbox, the contracts. In that mode you can play contracts made by other players, create your own or even invite friends to play your contracts and try to beat them. It's a very interesting mode!
3 – CONCLUSION
Absolution was my only game of the Hitman franchise and I've liked it a lot. It took me about 12h to get through the campaign, but at some point I have lowered the difficulty. This game worths the asked price, but try to get it in a sale and enjoy!

I'm a long-time fan of the Race Driver series and played every single one of them.
The classic Race Driver games (especially RD2 and RD3) were absolutely superb games.
Then came the first GRID and just added to it. It was a great game with decent cars, decent simcade handling, good racetracks (especially those Japan Docks).
GRID 2 was a disaster. To anyone who knows Codemasters and the Race Driver franchise it's obvious that they just lost track of their heritage on this one. It didn't have a monetary system.
The handling was changed to something that can only be described as super-arcade. The sponsor system was terrible too - supremely dumbed-down. And the AI was irritating. Generally just a bad bad Codemasters racing game.
I told myself I'd never pre-order again, then came GRID Autosport.
Which I didn't pre-order and bought on sale.
BUT
It's a good game. Not GRID 1 good, but it's eons ahead of GRID 2. The single player mode isn't quite where GRID 1 had gotten it so right, with a lack of a monetary system and no ownership of cars. You cannot choose the car you want to use to compete in events with and the sponsorship and team progress has been surpremely changed to a very limited and very basic layout. If I were to review this game on SP alone it would still be NOT RECOMMENDED.
The multiplayer, however, is where the game really proves itself. Earn money, earn xp and build your garage. Track your stats on RaceNet. Create or join racing clubs. Race vs friends, strangers or just AI. It really has a nice balance to it. There are community challenges to keep you interested and leaderboards to work against. Generally GRID Autosport is well rounded with handling only marginally below that of GRID 1.
GRID Autosport proves that Codemasters have not comepletely lost their touch with racing games.

Blade Runner meets DooM? Kind of, a magnificent cyberpunk setting with an arsenal to use against machines without thinking too much and a story that doesn't give much justice to the game's setting.
Major Fletcher is part of a private police force that hunts rebelling machines attacking the futuristic, decaying city of Bezoar (yes, Bezoar... XD). By looking for those responsible for the attacks you will discover more than you were looking for.
Yes, the beginning sounds good, but story develops in a predictable way. You can definitely expect what wil happen and where this is going. What you're not expecting is how abruptly the game ends without a reason and an excessive opening for a sequel or whatever. (I didn't pplay any DLC, so I'm not sure if the story goes on there).
Story is clearly the game's weakest point but don't get to a conclusion too fast, because the cyberpunk setting is incredible.
There's nothing to say, Wild Hog definitely know what they're doing, you definitely have that familiar feeling looking around the streets, advertises, cars, skylines. Feels a lot like Blade Runner of course. Yet that's not the only thing they did, levels have been built with good care for details, but the best you can see is in open areas where landscapes or warehouses will grant you beautiful sights and lighting.
You will hardly notice loading times because they've been clever enough to show story sequences and dialogues through comic screens. Again a clever move but not constant as there will be some loading screens without any comic. Not a great loss, though.
I can't say it sticks into your mind but the usual trick of being almost silent or going slow during exploration while going Rock/heavy metal during shootings does the trick. Too bad there isn't a particular theme or tune that catches your attention.
It's a very simple FPS. Very straightforward, shoot everything that moves, pull the trigger to open the door or passage and go ahead. The game is very guided and the player moves through a very strict path, there are no alternatives or cuts and this might be a bit annoying.
There are only 2 weapons, firearms and energy based. By killing enemies and finding secret (well hidden) bonuses you gain experience tu buy upgrades for your character or both your weapons, and this way you can unlock new fire modes ranging from the classic shotgun, rocket launcher and granade launcher for firearms, to energy mortar, railgun or special energy fire modes. I've found the energy weapons to be the most fun and visually pleasant to use.
Story is pretty simple and predictable and the end interrupts everything leaving a strong sense of insatisfaction. The Rail scheme of all maps doesn't help as well and this is a bad loss for the game because it's aesthetically good to see and fun to play.
It's good and Fun. But Never can find any rooms.

Hacking minigame is massively improved by mere merit of being really short and snazzy.
The artstyle is still absolutely breathtaking, but enemy variety and AI are still kinda meh (better than in BS1, though).
The story is somewhat of a retread of BS1, but takes a different thematic angle by dealing mostly with extreme collectivism instead of objectivism as the main antagonists philosophy/ideology of choice and also focusing on a more intimate Father-Daughter relationship as part of the core narrative.
Doesn't have the "would you kindly" "super-smart" meta-narrative twist about player agency and choice in videogames the first game had, but instead takes a position of "even pre-designed choices can have meaning and emotional depth if there are consequences for your choices."
Whether you think this makes the game less interesting or more emotionally deep and satisfying (I'm part of the latter group) is up to you.
The portions of gameplay where you have to protect a Little Sister while she harvests ADAM from some corpses can feel a little samey and repetitive, but this is alleviated slightly by your ever-expanding arsenal of guns and plasmids with legitimate options for crowd control and trapsetting.
Plus, you get the whole Minerva's Den DLC for free with this thing, which is just even better than the main game and basically the single best piece of Bioshock content, both mechanically as well as narratively.
For being the "black sheep" of the series by being the only one NOT made by Irrational Games, it sure manages to be the best out of the bunch. Recommended.

TLDR: Very tough call to up or down arrow this one, but in the end it doesn't quite make the cut - overworld RTS controls a bit too clunky, dungeon keeping not as good as competitor game.
I put off trying Dungeons 2 for a long time, because many moons ago I bought Dungeons 1 in a shop (that's how long ago) and it was truly terrible.  But, like everyone who is old enough to have played Dungeon Keeper 2 in their youth, my life is really just a spiritual quest to find a dungeon-keeping, destruction of all that is good and cute semi-RTS game that copies it without quite feeling like a copy so that i can play it forevermore and be fulfilled. So, every few years, I brace myself for disappointment and buy a dungeon-keeper-alike - and so we have Dungeons 2. It's basically two games somewhat connected to each other so i'll take them one by one;
Overworld Invasion RTS
Section TLDR - level variety OK - graphics OK - story/narration Pretty Good - controls Sub-par.
So. once you've built up your little minions of evil a bit, it's time to send them out in to the world for the actual mission - these all take the same format, rescue some extra minions of evil, use their particular skills to kill a big minion of good or occasionally a rival minion of evil.  Maps tend to be somewhat linear, but not game-breakingly so if you've only got through half the campaign anyway.
Graphically, it looks a bit like warcraft 3  - i suspect this is a deliberate attempt to play on the nostalgia aspect that led people like me to buy the game in the first place - which is fine for a not taking itself too seriously type game.
There's the traditional sarcastic hint giving narrator who has some decent lines, but annoyingly, you do have to deliberately fail sometimes to hear the best ones.
Control is where it falls down rather, your minions have skills, in most cases they only have one skill for one target - e.g. the only thing the goblin assassin can do to a door is unlock it, the only thing the Naga queen can do to an ally minion is heal it. So why, when i've selected a minion and right clicked a target it can only do one thing to - why doesn't it just do it? Why do I have to specifically click the little skill button (with a dodgy response time) or remember a metric♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of keybinds?
Overall - worth playing long enough to hear a couple of classic narrator putdowns, but no further.
Underworld Dungeon-keeping
Section TLDR - nearly there, but too samey and not enough minion variety.
Explore, mine gold, build rooms, attract minions, slap them and laugh maniacally, murder the occasional band of heroes that wander foolishly in...  Sounds perfect right? And for a while it seems like it is. Sure, there's the point where you realise that there are only 5 basic types of minion. Sure, there's when you realise that trap placement is a bit cumbersome and destroyed traps get replaced whether you wanted them or not. But these are minor things right? It's still like i'm playing Dungeon Keeper right? But sadly it isn't, and for one real reason only. There's never the sense of relaxation and joy of just playing with your dungeon. Of levelling your little dudes in peace so you can unleash a storming horde on the enemy.  Every level is the same sort of rush to get enough to go and do the mission - and it's that variety of approach that is missing. That variety of approach that I hadn't even realised that Dungeon Keeper did so well, until i played Dungeons 2 and it didn't.
So thank you Dungeons 2, for making me realise once more just how good Dungeon Keeper 2 was.
On a side note, another game War For The Overworld does a better job of the dungeon keeping element, so if you aren't looking for the RTS element go look at that instead.

I really wanted to give this game a thumbs up, but as a fan of the original Dungeon Keeper series I just can't do it. This game is a huge step backwards for the genre.
After 27 hours (taking my time) completingly the painfully simple, albeit somewhat humurous, campaign I moved on to the skirimish in hopes of finding some real gameplay value. Sadly, it wasn't there.
The construction of your dungeon, upgrades, and managing of your monsters (both in and out of combat) is mindnumbingly simple. It is completely linear in that the only real options you have is how you build traps (which quickly become so overpowered that even that is pointless) and how many of each unit you have in your army (also rather pointless as combat consists of just throwing your army at the enemy.)
Half of the spells should be basic control mechanics (such as telling your army to attack a location) and the others are minor buffs or basic damage spells.
There is some slight strategy necessary to beat levels on harder difficulty (such as building a labyrinth of traps), but again it's so linear that it doesn't feel as if it really matters.
I got this game on sale for $5, spent 27 hours on it and had a relatively fun time, but that's about all it's worth. Again, I would give the game a thumbs up just for that if I hadn't had higher hopes for a real Dungeon Keeper like game.

While I'm not at all opposed to the idea of remaking Dungeon Keeper and I'm completely okay with Kevan Brighting stepping in to replace Richard Ridings, the game itself just doesn't do it for me. This feels like Dungeon Keeper, ages 0-3, and not even because of the graphics that much, but gameplay.
Next to none complex mechanics, army size is miniscule even at the later levels, you summon (=buy) units yourself, hell, there is even no such thing as claiming territory - it's all yours by default. You could ask, "wait, if all land is mine, how does the Keeper vs Keeper skirmish work?" Well get this - there is none. You're the only Evil in these lands, and your only enemies are Heroes. Who don't have bases underground, no, they just spawn at the Gates every now and then. These Gates are always visible to you, they are indestructible, and they always have a highway straight into your dungeon. Trying to expand your dungeon only to dig into a Hero outpost? Nope. Cutting off a Hero supply route by destroying their bridge over lava? Never heard of it. Stealth fortress attacks by digging at the weak point and jumping the Lord of the Land? Nuh-uh, not in this game. And don't even get me started on the travesty that is "overworld mode", they could've done so much more with that Warcraft wannabe.
DK managed to stay interesting even on the levels where there were no enemies at all (My Pet Dungeon ones), because actually keeping and running the dungeon, catering to creature needs and boosting their happiness rating, was a fun game on its own, but here everything is so needlessly simplified and dumbed down, so that bit is lost as well.
While WftO went in the opposite direction and became all hardcore zerg rush sim, here it feels like a complete slog even to complete one level, with only the Narrator helping to fight off the boredom with his comments. I would recommend this game as a sort-of "The Keeper Parable" for TSP fans who want to try a new genre, but hardcore DK fans? Well, maybe you can use this to introduce your kid to DK series, idk.
PS. I had very high hopes for Dungeons 3, because of how big an improvement Dungeons 2 was over Dungeons, and at first it seemed like they were heading in the right direction, but it's more of the same. Oh well, thanks for more brilliant narration, I guess.

Dungeon Fighter Online is similar to classic 2D side-scrolling arcade hack and slash games, such as Golden Axe or Double Dragon. Players will traverse 2D screens while fighting hordes of monsters. There are a number of social aspects to Dungeon Fighter Online, including Guilds, PvP Arenas, Party Play, and Mentorship.
First off, I love side scrollers. I love beat em' ups. I love games like Golden Axe or Double Dragon.  So any game with all of that combined automatically appeals to me. That being said however, this game is so much more then that, and if you love this genre, and MMORPG's themselves, you should support this. This game is free-to-play in every sense of the word. Everything you need can be obtained through gameplay and grinding aside from cosmetics and rare costumes. The artwork in this game is absolutely stunning and beautifully crafted, a good reference for this would be the opening introductiosn to each character class in the game, and let me tell you, there are alot.
That's another thing, the variety in this game is insane! There are fourteen diverse classes that do, in fact, all feel diverse and creative. Each have their own special weapons, masteries, skills, appearences, backstories, etc, and its fun seeing and playing all of them. My only real complaint with them as well as the game itself is the limited customization. Don't expect everything you equip to your character to show up on them in-game, for the most part they remain the same as they begin and the armor merely provides increased stats or buffs. Same as some of the weapons, but that's a very small complaint in a game thats otherwise a truly hidden gem amongst the steaming pile of pay-to-win and cash grabbing garbage that is the majority of steam's FTP titles.
All in all. DFO is Beat em' up MMORPG that features your standard guilds, pvp, and co-op social interactions. It has a few minor kinks holding it back from being truly perfect such as limited customization or repitiveness in combat after so long, but with beautiful artwork, diverse classes, fun and stylish combat, and addicting management, this game is truly a gem amongst all the others like it. If you've ever been a fan of this genre or are a fan and would like to see more TRUE FTP titles on the steam market, then support and play the ever living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game. You won't regret it, or maybe you will, entirely depends on you.
In the end, guys, I give this game a 9/10.

Big Pharma is a combination of tycoon sim, Tetris, and puzzle game.
The tycoon sim part is basic; you try to make sure your profits are higher than your expenses, you take out a loan if you're low on cash, you supply more of the drugs that are high in demand, and so on. The simple business management aspect suits the game well.
The Tetris part comes from the unique shape of the machines you place in your factory lines and the limited space in which you have to use. In the early game your available space is small, in the late game your factory lines are complex and long, and in both cases maximizing the use of space for optimal output is important.
The puzzle part is the meatiest: drug ingredients have components (with negative or positive effects) which can be removed, upgraded, or swapped around using one of your machines. These all have active ranges that vary, and it takes a bit of mental arithmetic to find the sweet spots to create the drug of your choice.
When creating drugs, all three parts of the game come into play, making Big Pharma a game with depth and replayability. The campaign missions start you off in an empty factory, which makes gameplay fairly repetitive (though getting randomly generated ingredients and starting ingredients mitigates this somewhat). If you don't mind starting from the beginning for every campaign mission and you're a fan of business sims and casual puzzle games, this could be a good fit.

Bleed is an absolutely refreshing indie platform shooter that presents a female protagonist with up to 12 or so different unlockable guns in seven very fun and diverse levels.  The controls are a bit odd at first, as jumping is defaulted to a trigger, but this frees up your thumb the ability to run, aim, and jump simultaneously--seldom heard of.  What makes Blleed even more unique is its time-slowing ability, sort of like a Prince of Persia sand of time thing, but meter-based instead of amount of times used.  With this ability in hand and many achievements and upgrades to discover, Bleed may be worth well more than the retail price depending on when you stop playing (a run through of all levels on easy is less than an hour, but attempting arcade mode (no deaths) on very hard could take many many hours to practice for).  All in all it makes for a very pleasant kamikazee-esque style blended with cute story/graphics and a lot of fun.

It's bad. Not even salvageable with friends along the ride. The game is pretty much only fun for the first 50 turns before it becomes unceasing tedium.
First, Cities. If you build every single defensive structure in a city, it's literally impossible to take. No joke. The AI doesn't do this, so you can stomp all over them.
Next, health. Health is this game's "Happiness" and it's virtually impossible to keep up. but it doesnt matter, since it doesn't do jack. I once had -50 healthiness and I was still able to defeat all AI in a game without being stopped.
Next, aliens. Aliens are actually slightly threatening early game, especially the seige worms, but once you get the alien repelling building, you don't really need to worry about them anymore.
Next, AI. Their personality and abilities rival a cardboard box. They don't do anything to you.
Next, Sattelites. They're slightly okay, until you get the orbital laser that essentially kills everything in a few hits.
Next, Affinity. It seems slightly good at first, until you realize how ridiculously unfair it is. When you get enough affinity points to select the next unit upgrade, it upgrades all the existing units free of charge. This is a huge problem since these upgraded units make can easily curbstomp any unit a level below them with no effort, meaning that if you decided to focus your research on something besides affinity points, you're screwed. Just imagine if in civ 5, all of your opponents warriors upgraded into longswordsmen free of charge just because they researched the tech.
Next, victory. Every single one of them except domination and promised land is pathetically easy to get. There's contact victory: Build a tower and wait 20 turns, you win. Supremacy:build a gate and send 1000 military strength through a gate and you win. Harmony: build a mind flower and you win. Notice a pattern? It's just build a structure and wait. Since you're cities are virtually indestructible.
