Rather than asking for twitch reflexes and an emphasis on mass murder, Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory asks the player to be
.
This is not a game where the locales are merely canvases to spill blood - every inch of ever level is laden with multiple ways to progress through the mission. Shadows, vents, windows, pipes and balconies which can be hung off of... not only are you given a wide array of ways to avoid enemy detection, but these assets can be used to silently (and stylishly) take out enemies.
Not only does the environment give an incredible amount of replay-friendly playstyle options, but it also reeks of atmosphere and immersion in a way that I've never seen in a video game since. Not only are the dark, glistening graphics and ambient sounds well-done, but the moody soundtrack by Amon Tobin serves as the syrupy glaze to the atmospheric pancake. Meanwhile, the level design has a realistic feel to it, as though every hallway that you enter could be a real place.
Overall, Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory is a gameplay masterpeice and a technical marvel that still impresses today, over ten years after its release. Almost every aspect has such a great level of polish that, despite the game's relatively niche genre, I reccomend this game to everyone who has ever picked up a game controller.

For those of you who are having CTD issues, follow these instructions.
1) Right click on Bioshock 2 in your Steam library.
2) Select "Properties"
3) Select "Set Launch Options"
4) Paste "-dx9" without the quotation marks, hit "Ok" and then "Close."
5) Relaunch the game.
Credits to Master Bates for finding this fix. It seems that Bioshock 2 crashes when attempting to run some sort of element of DirectX 9 that is incompatable with newer hardware.
If you still experience CTD issues, try this fix by Pheabus2K19
1. Find "Bioshock2SP.ini" under C:\Users\YourName\AppData\Roaming\Bioshock2Steam\, make a backup if necessary;
2. Open the .ini in notepad,and search for "TextureStreamingMemoryLimit", the default number is 256, which is too low, try set it higher as suggested below:
512MB VRAM = 400
1GB VRAM = 600
2GB VRAM = 800
3GB VRAM = 1000
For example, if my GPU had 2GBs of VRAM, I would set TextureStreamingMemoryLimit=800;
3. Save and run Bioshock 2

maplestory's been my weird on-again-off-again girlfriend since 2006, and while it's still very possible for the game to be "saved," so to speak, i don't see it happening, at least not while their current business model remains hyper-profitable, one which totally kills the free-to-play player.  when your maplestory experience first starts out, it might seem pretty promising,  because it's a very aesthetically charming game.  the visuals and sound are probably the best redeeming feature of the game, and for good reason; a lot of effort goes into the presentation of the game.  the detailed level designs are very reminiscent of old school platformer games, the music is very vibrant and upbeat, the backgrounds and scenery have a lot of detail and depth to them and while there's not much of a story to go along with all of this, it does a nice enough job of sucking you into the MASSIVE world that you'll likely end up exploring a lot of it just to see as much as you can possibly see.
unfortunately, the charm is only skin deep, and the different systems in the game have been simplified so much since the game's initial release.  when you first make a character, you're led through a pretty pointless tutorial that explains different game mechanics until level 10, when you're released into the maple world, where your life for the next 100 levels is killing monsters and possibly questing, if you can handle doing what basically amounts to the same quests over and over again for not much more reward than xp.  at level 30, you go through your second job advancement a la certain final fantasy games, at 60 you have your third advancement and at 100 you have your 4th.  after level 100, endgame content consists of quest chains that culminate in a boss fight you can repeat every so often for drops, and grinding levels in your downtime.  the level cap is 250, and content tends to get a little more bare as your level gets higher.  there's a pvp mode, but it's not very balanced or fun.  there's some party quests and expeditions you can do, which are basically like instanced dungeons and raids respectively, but don't expect to get an invite to a party for any of the main end game content, because none of your gear is upgraded.  and that's where the nail in the coffin comes in, the one thing that everything i've said so far combined doesn't even match up to: the godawful potential system.
this is where nexon takes a♥♥♥♥♥♥all over the free to play player.  they added a system to the game a few years back called the potential system, which basically adds extra lines of stats to an item a la diablo.  you can add potential to an item by using a potential scroll on it, or you can find potential on an item you'll pick up from a monster every now and then.  an item's potential is divided into four tiers: rare, epic, unique, and legendary, and an item can have three potential lines at most.  so let's say you have a level 140 piece of equipment you want to put potential on.  you use the scroll, and it comes out rare, the lowest rarity, and the stats are total garbage.  that's a bummer, but you can use a cash shop item that costs $1.30 USD to reset the potential, and at a very low chance increasing the tier of the item's potential by one.  a STR/DEX/INT/LUK +% line on a level 140 piece of equipment can increase that stat by 4% if it's rare.  epic, 8%.  unique, 12%.  legendary, 16%.  and that's only one line.  it's not uncommon to see high ranked players buying hundreds of miracle cubes (the aforementioned cash shop item) to give an item insane stats like +40% STR.  the economy is already insanely broken otherwise, and some of the most valuable items in the game can be created $1.30 at a time.
all of this combined with the fact that nexon has absolutely never listened to its playerbase, the cruddy community, completely one-dimensional character growth and skill trees, and boss fights that only require you to be able to deal x amount of damage while tanking y amount of damage, it doesn't take too long before the game turns into a chore, and the only thing that's gonna change that is if nexon decides to sacrifice the extreme profitability of maplestory for game balance, but it'll never happen.  but at least it's pretty~

Some of the recent comments here are truly incredible and one has to wonder if the writers even played this or are sleepwalking in a drug-induced haze. Citadel Forged with Fire is a beautiful game. I am still new to this game, but my experience has been overwhelmining positive - and that's for an EA game.
My first impression during the first few hours was of a gorgeous world. Beautiful graphics and music to get me in the wizardly mood. Then I got mauled to death in the first 10 minutes by a dire wolf - and that kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. So next time i was more careful and started buliidng my humble shack on a rock outcrop. The moon came out and as I was walking up the hill to my growing wood castle, the moon light shone thorugh a window and onto the floor - and it blew me away. That was special for me and i was hooked. I'm only at level 8 and am more into building and crafting and love the building system here. It's simple to use and from what i see on the server i am on, there are some gigantic, massive castles built by other players on mountains. Amazing stuff.
I am getting close to level 10 where I can then fly on a broomstick - which is why i got this in the first place - i want to be like Harry Potter.
Positives:
1) The optimization, at least for me, is really good. Decent frame rates and I experienced very little lag at all. So the devs must have made some big improvements since it came out last summer. That was a big compaint when it launched.
2) Beautiful graphics and art. The world of Ignus is rendered with an good eye for detail with plenty of odd mythical creatures and animals roaming around. I think its especially beautiful at night.
3) The building system is the best feature and allows you to build incredibly creative massive castles and structures. Really what ever you can imagine. The harvesting Extract spell works well to save on the grind of gathering building supplies and i like that you earn XP as you gather resources.
4) Flight on broomsticks through the trees and valleys of Ignus - that looks amazing and fun.
5) The devs at Blue isle seem very responsive and have been issuing large and small pacthes and updates almost every week since this came out. The biggest one is out soon and is a content expansion with three end game bosses.
Negatives
1) Server populations are really low, which is a real pity as this should have a lot more players  - it's that good. I think the community will grow as the devs add more content and keep making improvements.
2) More work is needed on the AI of some critters and creatures here. Some don't respond very well and others just don't quit attacking you. Still needs work.
3) No real end game or major bosses, but they have announced that is coming soon.
Overall, for the money, Citadel is a solid EA game that is a work in progress, but one I am really enjoying playing. If you love magic spells in a beautiful world where you can be like Harry and zip around on a broomstick, then check out Citadel. Trust me on this one, its only going to get a lot better.

Hitman Absolution is my first Hitman game (not counting the 10 minutes in blood money) and I was really curious if it was able to make me play more of the hitman series.
It has an interesting story and the cutscenes are well done and realistic. They are however a bit of lesser quality in terms of facial animations and graphics. The game itself looks much better than the cutscenes. Next to this, all of the different NPC's you'll come across have small conversations/fights which are funny to hear.
Hitman Absolution has great graphics and some interesting locations. From a house full of hippies, to a slaughterhouse, and from chinatown to a courtroom. All of the locations are designed really good and look awesome. Stealth mechanics work great as well. Exploring the levels, learning the movement of every npc and so on. Hitman gives you loads of options and ways to complete each level. Which route do you take? Do you go stealth, guns blazing or do you disguise yourself as one of them? Do you go slowly and check out every corner, kill every person and collect everything, or do you take the fastes route? However, I did hear older Hitman games have more of a sandbox twist to them and Absolution is a bit more linear. Besides this the missions may get a bit repetitive, most of the time you're hiding from cops, guards or whatever, while trying to kill someone or getting towards the end of the level. It would be fun if they gave you a few more missions where nobody is looking for you, and you have a target to kill, or a trap to setup or something like that.
While playing you'll get plus or minus points for certain actions you take. And although this is an interesting system it kinda bothered me at times. Why do i get minus points for killing an guard for example? Yea, you can get points from it aswell by giving the person a headshot or dumping their body in a crate or something, but that seems like an unnecessary task.
Another big mechanic in the Hitman games, is the disguise system. Basically you can kill someone and than disguise yourself as one of them. Now this is a great system and is really interesting. For example: this gives you the option to discover parts of the level before actually doing something. However if you ask me the system has 2 major flaws. First of all, let's say you dress yourself as a guard. Other guards can then find you "suspicious". the problem is, they find you suspicious way to often. Even if you're wearing a mask and stand on the other side of the room they'll find you suspicious. Second of all is something which is logical, but unbalanced at times. Let's say the guards discover you and are hunting for you, you can just simply kill someone or walk up to a body or whatever and dress up as something else, and if the guards dont see you doing it, you'll be perfectly fine.
Do i recommend this game? Yea! Despite the flaws it has, it's still alot of fun to discover the various levels Hitman: Absolution has to offer. And thanks to the many options every level gives you to complete it, and all the collectables such as outfits, weapons, evidence etc, the game has alot of replayability.

Oh HLD:DM, how I've missed you so.
This was the first online multiplayer game I ever played, and ultimately the reason I favored PC gaming as a kid when everyone else my age had no idea what it even was. I remember when I was just a chubby wee lad back in 2004 playing this game with his dad on his crappy PC, pulling all-nighters, hosting his own server and trying to find any persnickety little reason to ban/kick people, getting banned from servers for my squeaky voice, and spending hours upon hours in Source SDK making coop and obstacle course maps. It was great fun. I was afraid that the game would be dead after coming back to check on it after so many years. Fortunately, it's not, but it is reaching its death throes.
There's still a reasonable amount of people who play (around 200 at peak I think), it's just saddening to see that there's not as many as there used to be, naturally. Most of the servers have relatively high ping, and many of the amazing servers we all remember like Joe Scoma's coop server and Singe's server for VERY unique and well made custom maps are no longer in existence. However, I still managed to find some of the maps I used to play way back in the day like dm_airstrike (literally the first map I ever played), dm_wtc_singe, and dm_steamlab and they just brought me back.
HL2:DM, I love you.

I tried this and then wandered away to play other games for a few months.  Coming back to it now, I realise it is actually pretty solid.  It will take a long time to upgrade everything for the achievements and I can understand why people don't put the time in but I am really enjoying this.
Some of the weapons are a real hoot.  Basically, I am finding so far that the best strategy to build up plasma, which you use to buy the better stuff, is to buy 9 ammo refills and 9 base repair kits, which are both cheap and use your secondary currency, the cogs along with one upgrade for a base for the lightning gun then keep using the ammo refills on that base.
Plenty of the various weapons and boosters drop from the sky.  They are a lot of fun - there's a black hole generator, an armageddon smart bomb, a little guy that resuscitates a destroyed base, homing missiles, a laser gun which can knock a few out with one hit and many more.
If you pay too much attention to some of the reviews you would think this is a flat experience.  It really is not.  I have been gaming a long time and this really is a fun game.
What I should add that I realise I didn't mention is that this is effectively a campaign game. This is a game for those that love replaying a mission segment over and over until you get it right. This is the way of Hitman, in general, but because the devs figured out that they can spawn loads of enemies for each mission, the replays involve snaking your way through nearly every mission until you just get frustrated and have to start killing to keep from being bored. The use of "instinct" feels like cheating and often doesn't do much in the way of helping. Some of the missions are fun, but overall, it gets too repetitive and replaying the same sequences over and over just isn't much fun.

In
, you take the role of a CEO of a pharmaceutical company, and you have to take your fledgling company from minor painkiller pusher to mega-corporate cancer killer.
At the start of the game, you are dumped into an empty factory lot where you will be able to start building production machines and start manufacturing some cures. Each segment of the factory will have an input point where you can choose to pull through certain ingredients which may or may not have positive attributes. Running these ingredients through a careful setup of specific machines will either emphasise or dissipate the base positive or negative effects of your ingredients. Once you’re happy with the result, throw what you have into a pill machine and pipe it out through one of your output points where it will be given a name and shipped off into the world to be sold.
You can also put scientists hard at work to research some brand new machines and ingredients, or simply improve existing ones. This is a nice way to improve the quality of your production lines and keep a consistent, stable way of producing reliable cures and boost profits the legitimate way.
The
DLC helps to give you more control on the money side of things, and instead of just selling a cure for a set price throughout you can hike the cost of a drug when you know the demand is high and people are in desperate need of it; something as simple as a paracetamol may be in high demand after a tragedy somewhere in the world, and you can use it as an opportunity to charge a fortune for it. You can also undercut a competitor to gain your own company more money at the expense of theirs, adding new ways to play
and causing you to be savvy off the production floor as well.
does feel unique, as it’s rare to get an economic/sim game that was built from the design level up to be a morality play on human greed.
People who enjoy business sims, and want to engage with something that requires planning without overzealous micromangement may find
to be the cure.
- Unique morality play in a sim game
- Addictive gameplay
- Adds a new personal approach to playing
- Perks system

- Once you’ve played around with the features it loses appeal

Surprisingly good game. Put way more hours into this than I thought I ever would and I keep on playing. It keeps you engaged, when you work a problem out like compacting a production line into the smallest space possible in a cramped factory you legit feel good about it. Then your heart sinks when the market for that product falls out. Luckily you can save money, look for another ingredient that needs to be processed in a similar manner and with minimal effort crank out another drug. Or instead of selling the machinery at a loss you could re-use machinery different configurations or manufacturing lines to make a completely new process for another ingredient. Another thing, ingredients are randomized. This means you cannot make the same thing the same way. Ever. Each time you load a new level you have to think on the fly, formulate what conentrations you want, and if it's worth processing an ingredient enough to remove side effects. Sometimes side effects disappear with almost no effort, other times it's too cost prohibitive to even try unelss you want to make a drug at a profit-loss.
What furthers the gameplay is competition. There are AI that can do exactly what you do in the game. All the dirty tricks and good recipes. They might not be as good as a human right out of the gate, you are typically the first to release a product, but each personality of AI can specialize in certain things. The CEO fellow goes around putting patents on easily made drugs like a prick, the nerdy looking old man makes very high-level drugs typically quicker than I would, sometimes an AI will make enough of a product that it drops market demand so you won't be on top in that market. This helps keep the game very fresh at all times, you don't know which AI you are facing and they can give you a run for your money at times.

As a guy who's played Conviction first, I have to say I'm actually having more fun playing this game more. While I still feel like the controls could've been better, something I also feel about Double Agent, I enjoy the game immensely. The most obvious reason for the game is the story, which isn't "US vs. Russia". From what I can gather, it's North Korea.
Chaos Theory is also easily the best game in the series, according to the dozens of reviews by new fans and Splinter Cell veterans alike. I certainly would agree; stealth is paramount in any situation. Sam's suit comes with a variety of items to help you know when you're hidden, or when you've screwed the pooch. Light sensors to let you know when you're visible, sound detectors to let you know how slow you need to move to keep quiet. An option I'm familiar with because of Double Agent is the OPSAT, which is a real-time objectives and map menu, meaning you'll need to hide to use it effectively. Hacking is way more interesting than Double Agent, and shooting, when done right, feels like an accomplishment.
Graphics wise, character models in game show visible age and are acceptable if you remember it's from 2005. Environments though show great lighting and attention to detail. I did get a feeling of being in the locations Sam visited. And again, for a game in 2005, it looks just as good as some games from this decade.
Sound is phenomanal, with a soundtrack by Amon Tobin and layered for different events in gameplay so it never feels stale. Sam Fisher is voiced by Michael Ironside; not the new guy who everyone hates for some ridiculous reason. Seriously guys, move on. In fact the voice acting and the script writing are good too; minus the enemy/foreign character voices. While Sam and his pals are witty and relatable, enemies tend to have such bad and stereotyped accents. And let's not forget the character "Long Dan". Turning on native voices solves this, but there's no subtitle option to let you know what's being said, so it's more for immersion after beating the game.
So yes, I'm joining the bandwagon. But at least it's a good one; Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory is easily one of the best stealth games I've played. And it's one that really deserves it.

Eh, i'm not entirely sure what i think of this game, while i like what the devs were going for and the building mechanics and some of the ideas are great, there are too many flaws in this title for me to reccomend it as of now.
Firstly, the game released much too early, it should have been released many months after it was. This is because many areas of the game are unfinished and extremely unpolished. For example, the PVE is almost non existant becuase half the time the AI does not function at all and when it does it's some of the most basic AI imaginable, the orcs or any ground dwelling creatures will simply run after you and cast a spell, if you go on a building they can't follow you (this may have been fixed) and to add insult to injury they are just complete bullet sponges.
Secondly, the progression is also ridiculously slow and unsatisfying. The levels up to 20 or 30 (sorry i can't remember, i haven't played for some time) are fine, you earn cool magic items to unlock and craft and it feels decently rewarding, but after these levels progression slows to a halt. Even if you go and grind XP by zapping the high level bullet sponges in a cave, you gain the stuff exctruciatingly slowly and you unlock very little per level up to level 60.
I see many people on here complain about the state of PVP, but i never really got the chance to engage in any so i can't really comment on it.
Another thing to add is that the dungeons or caves are just silly. You go through them fighting the sub-par AI until you get to a loot box, you think "sweet, i'm ready for the good stuff" but when you open it all you recieve are some crafting materials and "legendary" robes or whatever which are much worse than the items you can craft. There should have been some unique, truly legendary items scattered around the map in random places that groups would fight each other for.
Moving on, the bugs were horrendous. I'm not sure how many are fixed now but at the time I was playing the bugs were just ridiculous. Sometimes your mount would dissapear for no reason when the server restarted (I hear this is fixed) or maybe the "bosses" would be completely stationary when you attacked them, there were many others but these are the ones I remember most vividly. Many of these are probably patched now, but it just goes to show that the game should have released much later than it did.
Penultimately, the player base is dead. This is by far the main reason I don't reccomend this game. After the dissapointing PVE encounters and broken PVP, along with the leveling being so slow, most people left the game, including myself. I looked at some stats on one of those steam player base websites and it said that Citadel Forged With Fire peaked at 100 players in 24 hours. That screams dead player base to me.
Lastly, I almost don't want to downvote this game becuase it showed real promise and the building mechanics are great. Some really fantastic ideas went into this title and the music and atmosphere is well done. From my review you can see that I haven't said any base mechanics are bad, just broken and in need of tweaking, I did enjoy this game when I was playing it and some encounters with other people will be remembered by me and my friends for quite some time, but the issue is the lack of playerbase. If more content is added and the bugs are patched and the AI is improved and most importantly, the playerbase makes a return somehow, I would definitely get back into playing this game.
If you enjoy building and have a huge group of friends to populate a sever, i say buy this game. If you're looking for a polished PVE and PVP expireince, you'll have to wait until the players come back and the AI is revamped.

This is a terrific sequel to a classic game. The story is amazing and the relationship between Eleanor and her "father" is immersive and believable despite the ridiculous circumstances. This is to BioShock as Half-Life 2 was to Half-Life. It is better in some respects but worse in some others and still historic fun for the ages.
The gameplay is the same awesome BioShock gameplay you would expect after playing the original. One major change is that you can wield plasmids at the same time as your regular weaponry which leads to some complicated and frustrating combat for me. I find myself getting confused with which button to press in the heat of battle and occasionally screw up and change the ammo type when I meant to switch plasmids etc. Of course, that is more of my problem than the game's but I still miss the original BioShock's layout of having either one or the other out at one time.
The level design is every bit as awesome as its predecessor. The game isn't quite as long but still much longer than modern FPS titles out there and with Minerva's Den you get at least a good 16 hours of fun from it all.
The best part of this game though is the fact that you can change the ending based on your choices in game. You could do that in the first BioShock based on what you did with the little sisters but with this one you also have several characters that you can choose to execute when you finally meet them. This gives you, I believe, 4 endings rather than just two.
The audio in this original version is still as frustrating as the original BioShock and the 30fps physics problem is ever present as well but these are more reasons to consider the remastered version of the game.

Abstract
Citadel: Forged with Fire is just like any other EA game these days: a lot of promise, no delivery. Depsite being an EA game, we should still feel a genuine sense of progression in any game--whether through plot or achievements. CFF gives us nothing but a bare-boned sandbox game. You spend hours accumulating resources just to build a structure. That's it. If you want a game that acts more like a temporary novelty than anything else, buy it. You'll have fun for a few minutes, then you'll be asking yourself: what the hell do I do now?
Gameplay - 1/5
The combat feels very clumsy and the movement, forced--as if walking through syrup. It slows down the game immensely and doesn't make you feel like you're naturally in this living world. There are mostly creatures here and there, as well as few blood orcs, but down the line they provide no challenge whatsoever. They're simply there to offer the player *some* kind of challenge, but fail in every aspect.
World Building - 3/5
Average. No better nor worse than any other sandbox MMO with world-building elements. You start off with wood and eventually get to stone/metal buildings. As to the question of whether there's a point in building structures? No. Absolutely not. If it was a SINGLE SERVER, OPEN-WORLD MMO, yes, it would be worth it. But what we're essentially given are servers with 3/100 people in each.
Servers/Community - 0/5
The servers are unstable. You get 1 character per server, and it's usually made by another player. Said player can slow down XP/gathering rates or speed them up. At some point, you question whether spending hours on a 'normal' server is worth it, when you can get the same results within a faster-rate up server. By choosing a slow/normal gathering/XP rate, you only lose something, not gain anything. And what you lose is time: something far more precious than an EA game. The worst thing about the servers, however, is that there is no way of knowing where your characters are. You have to scroll through hundreds of servers and HOPE you remember which served you spent 2 hours on.
Overall Rating: 2/5
CFF had a promising pitch, but delivered a disastrous shadow of what it advertised. The only EA game I've bought that I haven't regretted was PlayerUnknown's Battleground. Why? Because the developers are consistently working on their game, and a single game consists of 100 players--all adding their skill, their experience, or their sheer stupidity in a single session. CFF doesn't give you the chance to experience a genuine multiplayer game.
Just play it.

There are so many things that I LOVE about this game, that I likely will not be able to list them all.
Let me preface this by saying DO NOT LET THE GRAPHICS SCARE YOU AWAY. This game plays wonderfully and has so much to offer, and the graphics serve to lend to its arcade beat-em-up feel.
PROS:
- Tons of characters, most of which have four different class paths. No matter your playstyle, there is a class for you. To top it all off, there are PLENTY of character slots for you to experiment and find classes you like.
- Relatively inexpensive costume shop. You can get nearly a full costume set (same set or mix-and-match) for roughly $10. There are also free costumes available that you can purchase with "Mileage Points" which are earned by clearing dungeons. They start out timed, but you can make them permanent with an item ALSO purchasable with mileage points.
- Free skill reset. Don't like your skill setup? Reset it. Free of charge.
- Class change until level 50. Don't like the class you picked? Change it. You can do this as many times as you like, and it doesn't cost real money. In fact, the first switch is free of charge! Subsequent switches cost a chunk of in-game currency (gold).
- This game requires skill. While some classes are easier to use than others, skillful play is definitely required to some degree. You can put skills onto hotkeys, but you can also use key inputs. Moreover, you get better as you play, even without realizing it, and growing in skill feels REALLY good. Especially if you taught yourself the combos.
- Events aren't paywalled. Unlike some MMOs that require you to crack open your wallet to fully participate in some events, DFO events are almost always 100% free and VERY rewarding.
- Bustling, friendly community. If you're in the right channel for your level, there is no shortage of players. The game feels alive and very busy. On top of that, I've had nothing but good experiences with other players. Yes, a bitter unpleasant player passes through every so often, but this game has had the most positive community I've seen in a long time, with minimal shoutbox drama to boot.
- Virtually grind-free. Aside from grinding at endgame to get sweet gear, level progression is pretty well organized. Following the story quests and picking up any subquests you find will easily prepare you for whatever dungeon comes next.
- Devs that care. Unlike the unbelievable trashfire shill that previously managed this game (Nexon), Neople listens to the community. They enjoy feedback and make a point of banning bots and gold sellers ASAP.
CONS:
- Character balance. Some classes are simply stronger than others. While I firmly believe that there's no such thing as a "bad class" (just good and bad ways to play it), Female slayer takes high precedence over her male counterpart. Some classes are better suited for dungeons than PvP (witch and summoner IMMEDIATELY come to mind). As a Summoner main, I suffer in ANYTHING that isn't solo play, and end up feeling pretty useless to a party. But I have a pretty solo playstyle, so that isn't too much of an issue (for me).
- Everything else in cash shop is somewhat steep. Pets, account stuff (inventory/storage expansion, and costumes with stats are significantly more costly.
- Parties can be hard to find. Despite the large active community, parties are pretty scarce unless you're grinding for gear. Almost nobody uses Quick party, so you either have to make your own, or join one that someone has already made.
- Random bans. I personally have never had an issue with this, but from what I've seen and heard from some other players, Neople can sometimes have a twitchy ban-hammer finger. Thankfully, appeals are usually heard, and bans are rectified.
NEUTRAL:
- Stamina. It's pretty much standard with most dungeon-focused MMORPGs, but I've never had any issues with it. If I run out of stamina on one character, I go play another one. Or spend my time doing something actually productive.
- Story. Not bad. Not amazing. Animated scenes look cool, even if there aren't many.
- Same class, different gender, DIFFERENT PLAYSTYLE. I cannot stress this enough. The gender you pick can make or break the way you play the class. Male Mage is entirely different than Female Mage. Male Nen Master is attack-focused, Female Nen Master is support-focused. Female Brawler is close-combat, Male Brawler is ranged. Male Mechanic works better with the explosive robot-focused skills, Female Mechanic has the better G-Series skill buffs. The list goes on, but there's too much to cover, so I suggest searching Google for further info.
Overall, 8.5/10. A great game all around.

Quick Summary: Dungeons 2 is a real time strategy game that plays extremely similarly to the old Dungeon Keeper games, putting you in charge of a dungeon full of monsters fending off the forces of Good. You can fill your dungeon with traps and locked doors to hold the heroes back, but mainly you’re going to be dropping monsters on their heads to get rid of them. Just like Dungeon Keeper, the highlight of Dungeons 2 is the narration and humor in storytelling, which in this game is mostly parodies of Game of Thrones, Lord of the Rings, and Warcraft.
In Dungeons 2 you are the Ultimate Evil, some sort of dark lord with all the minions of “the Horde” behind you (orcs, trolls, goblins, etc.) except that you’ve been defeated by an Alliance of goody goodies and now sit in your dungeon as a malevolent spirit (like Sauron in Lord of the Rings). Your ultimate goal is to avenge yourself on the Alliance and crush King’s Ending, their capital city.
Instead of directly attacking your enemies, you issue commands as the Hand of Evil (your mouse cursor), picking up and dropping your minions, and pointing out tasks for your workers to do (like dig new rooms or build/destroy). If you’ve played the awesome Dungeon Keeper games you will pick things up very quickly because the gameplay is in many ways almost identical. However here are some of the major differences:
There’s no “possession” where you take direct control of a minion (first person perspective). It’s all top-down real time strategy in Dungeons 2.
Each level has 2 “maps,” a dungeon (under your control) and an “overworld” that you need to invade in order to conquer the good guys. Enemies spawn from camps/cities in the overworld, and invade your dungeon through portals that cannot be destroyed or walled off. This means that unlike Dungeon Keeper, you can’t seal up your base and just train your monsters until you’re strong enough to let the heroes in to be crushed. The enemies in Dungeons 2 spawn in waves and attack you in short intervals.
It’s harder to “level up” your monsters in Dungeons 2. You need to put some effort into building up your base to the point where you can actually train your minions. Otherwise you can only level up your creatures through combat. Once you’ve improved your dungeon enough, you will gain the option of building a training room to passively improve your monsters. In Dungeon Keeper, the training room is available nearly from the start.
You get to pick what monsters enter your dungeon. In Dungeon Keeper, you build rooms, and certain types of rooms will attract certain monsters. In Dungeons 2 you have complete control of your army’s composition. You need to mix things up because each task can only be done by a specific creature type (for example only goblins can work the workshop, but they suck in combat).
The workshop and the spell rooms both need to build up resources before they can start “researching” anything. This means it takes longer in Dungeons 2 to get your base up and running.
There is a lot more money available in Dungeons 2. Every level has rich gold veins for you to mine that last for a long time. It would take a great deal of effort to actually run out of money during a mission.
Dungeons 2 was offered free a while ago, so you might already own it and just need to decide whether or not to play it. You SHOULD play the game if:
+You enjoyed Dungeon Keeper. This game has modern graphics and a wacky story campaign. Note that Dungeons 2 is actually very easy to beat as long as you don’t make stupid mistakes (like not summoning any fighting creatures until after you get invaded).
+You’re looking for a long game. It takes 16+ hours to complete Dungeons 2 because you start each level almost from scratch, and need to research a bunch of stuff before you can start building the good stuff. You’ll be fending off hero raiding parties all along the way.
+You like “patient” games where you slowly and carefully build your base, then amass an army to overrun your opponents. There’s no zerg rushing here.
You should NOT play Dungeons 2 if:
-You’re looking for a fast game. Every level in Dungeons 2 is slow and steady (maybe an hour each). You can expect a lot of this time to be just waiting for your minions to do their jobs (dig, train, or research). The game has multiplayer as well, but because of how long it takes to build bases, I would expect a match to take a couple hours between competent opponents.
-You don’t like to micromanage your armies. Most of your units in the game will lollygag around not doing anything unless you give them a task. It also takes them a long time to march across your dungeon, even when they’re doing what they’re supposed to do. For example your goblins are working in the workshop and decide to grab a beer, so they slowly walk across the dungeon to the brewery, then slowly walk back. You can’t turn up the game speed, but you can pick up the goblins and drop them in the brewery, then pick them up again afterwards and drop them back in the workshop.
-You’re looking for a lot of variety. Each level has basically the same structure. Start with almost nothing, begin digging out rooms and researching, summon combat creatures right before you’re invaded, start filling/upgrading your population cap, and finally invade the overworld to conquer the good guys. The population cap is pretty annoying to be honest (start with a max of 15, and most of those will be workers).
Overall Dungeons 2 is a lot of fun if you’re patient and like to design/manage your own cities. You have very little control in combat so don’t expect to be outmaneuvering/ganking your enemies like in Dota 2. Your monsters will do their own thing, and you just make sure they’re positioned right. Or you can lay down the fireballs and lightning to help them out if you’re being invaded (most offensive spells can only be cast inside areas under your control, like your dungeon). The game has some DLC, one of which is a full campaign. I haven’t played it myself but I am told that the difficulty in the new campaign is significantly higher. Admittedly the base game is probably too easy.

In a nutshell, Beyond Earth overpromises, but ultimately grossly underachieves.
A game that can't seem to make up its mind whether it is intended as "Civ in space" in the sense that the game is little more than an existing game with a fresh coat of paint applied in a hurry (Which it basically is at this point), or a spiritual sequel to Alpha Centauri (Which it definitely is not)

HARD RESET REDUX
Genre: FPS
Publisher: Gambitious Digital Entertainment
Developer: Flying Wild Hog
Systems: PC (Steam), PS4, XBONE
THE BASICS:
Hard Reset: Redux is an improved, updated, and expanded remake of 2011's single-player dystopian-cyberpunk FPS, Hard Reset. You have three main weapons: A futuristic katana for melee attacks (non-upgradeable); an assault rifle which can be equipped with rockets, grenades, and mines; and a plasma rifle that can be upgraded with X-Ray scopes, electric mortars, stasis fields, and more varieties of dishing out blazing electric death. Both guns feature their own bevy of alternate attack modes, each with their own Alt-fire modes, as well as other upgrades such as scopes. The weapons are upgraded with the points you accumulate during gameplay, both by killing enemies and by picking up yellow upgrade pods. These points are also used to upgrade your character's shields and the like, so choose wisely.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
You're an Agent who has been called in to investigate a bombed-out area of Bezoar City, which has been taken over by the Machines that just wiped out all of the locals. You are in humanity's last holdout against the Machines' otherwise total domination of the planet. The story, in general, is conveyed primarily through two means: Conversations between your character and his allies back at the base via codec transmission, and intentionally rough-looking comic-book style cutscenes in between levels, all complete with voiceovers and optional subs. At the end of each level – some with boss fights, some without – the game pops up a tally screen, showing your kills, deaths, secrets discovered, time taken – all that good stuff.
CONTROLS:
Standard WASD, which should be familiar to any FPS veteran. Also reportedly works well with an XBONE controller. A recent patch opened up more control possibilities, as well as a graphical boost. The environment is littered with blue electrical devices which will let off debilitating arcs of electricity when damaged, as well as red containers of things that go BOOM reeeeal good ;) Several of the latter will allow you to easily blow up walls to allow you access to secret areas, and both are sometimes needed simply to unlock the path forward, as you'll often need to follow power lines (a la Borderlands) in order to find the right fusebox to blow up in order to bypass a barrier.
GRAPHICS:
Dark, gritty, cyberpunk-y. Takes a great deal of obvious inspiration from the likes of Neuromancer, Blade Runner, Shadowrun, and the like – which isn't bad company to be in. Fires and wrecks dot the landscape; glowing neon advertisements for shops, ♥♥♥♥♥ bars, and much, much more are omnipresent – and, for the most part, can be destroyed if you like. The game even encourages you to do this, by making random environmental destruction part of your post-level tally. The feeling of having been dropped into a bombed out warzone (which is exactly where you are) is conveyed quite well. The recent patch also fixed some slowdown issues which had previously been caused by the use of SSAO – the game now once more uses a “baked” AO/SSAO hybrid approach.
OVERALL:
You could do a hell of a lot worse! Satisfying combat, good pacing, plenty of secrets to find, in-depth upgrade system, and great atmosphere. Knowing what weapon type to use against what enemy helps – some will fall more quickly to an onslaught of plasma bolts or electricity (better yet, both at once), while others are more vulnerable to conventional ammo – or just a well-placed rocket between the eyes.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Win 7 or later, 2.5GHz P4/Athlon 64, 2GB RAM, DX9.0c, 512MB NVIDIA 8800GS/Radeon HD3870

First of all, this is a solid, well designed game that I would recommend to anyone interested in educational RTS style play that doesn't involve shooting things.  Its real strength comes from realistic approach to balanced resource management (expand too slow or too quickly and you die).  There is plenty of challenge build into the game play which will probably keep anyone intrigued by potential Mars colonization glued to the screen for hours.
Having said that, the game does need some polish.  I haven't encountered any major bugs, but I felt that camera rotation and individual colonist management could be made more intuitive.  The tech tree and achievement system are adequate but seem a bit disconnected from the game play.  I found graphics to be more than sufficient since I don't believe more visual realism would add anything to this type of game.  Finally, I think that this game could focus a bit more on Mars exploration that promotes fantasy and curiosity elements of play.  In other words, less grind, more unexpected discoveries and surprises with larger maps.
Overall, this a great start and I look forward to future updates.

It’s really sad to see how many negative reviews this game has… I don’t think it’s a fair assessment of the current situation. I've got already 100+ hours in the game and still a lot to do!
I would say, don't be afraid of the mixed reviews - it seems that an early access launch was really rough, and therefore it influenced the current rating, but the dev team has done a great job of squashing the bugs that earned this game so many negative reviews early on.
Anyway, I would like to lay out some pros and cons of this game, so at least you can have a better picture what to expect from this title.
** PROS **
1. The world is truly beautiful, shall I say - almost magical in feeling. It gives you a sense of immersion and the atmosphere is very chilling... Varied biomes - starting from swamps, moving over the forests, plains and ending in the high mountains. I love a very clear map/navigation system - it shows all the tags of visited places (quite similar to Skyrim approach).
2. This is obviously totally open world survival game, so you can go anywhere and do whatever you want.
3. You can tame most of the creatures in the game! You can make an ad-hoc army from wolves while adventuring if you fancy. For a long term companion use scrolls which are extending the loyalty of the creature. You can tame horses, tree-men, dragons, demons, and what not :) Taming is much easier and not as time consuming like in other similar games.
4. Flying! Yes, you can fly in this game not just on a mount but also on a broomstick or just simply with a flying potion. Obviously you can still go back to more “traditional” way of flying - on a back of your very own dragon!
5. Build your house wherever you want. You can build a majestic wizard tower in hard to reach places, or maybe you fancy a more impressive castle - your imagination is your limit. The building system is really good! I would even risk and say, that it is one of the best in comparison to other similar games. The pieces you are building with, they fit together very well, and let you build really complicated shapes as well (e.g. curved walls, etc.). Variety of materials and different furniture packs additionally spicing things up.
6. I really like crafting system, which has a bit of RNG in it, but it gives you a sense of polishing your perfect armor or weapon. RNG is not bad, because if let's say armor pieces have the statistics you don't want, you can put them into deconstructor and regain most of the valuable resources and re-craft!
7. Magic! This is after all a WIZARD GAME! There are 4 different types of weapons which dictate what kind of spell you can slot: Wands, Staves, Gauntlets and Melee. I really like this approach, with some reservations though, about which I will mention in CONS section. You can swap two weapons in-battle so that gives you 4 different spells you can use during the fight. In terms of abilities themselves, some of them are projectiles, some semi aoe, instant dots, channeled beams - the variety is really outstanding. You can easily choose the specific skill to match your preferred type of strategy.
8. Knowledge system - I also like how you improve your abilities. There are 60 levels in the game (so far). Every level you get knowledge points, which in turn they can be invested in different "trees". You can’t max everything out so you need to work with others, or reset your skills from time to time with a potion.
9. Developers are active in the Steam community - they inform what is in the pipeline, reply on any reported bugs - they just listen to the community. Thumbs up.
** MIXED **
1. No proper end game yet, however there’s a lot of caves and mini dungeons scattered around the world, so the sense of the adventure is there, nevertheless what is missing, is a reward that would excite you. I know though that very recently devs announced a content drop that will give us new dungeons with a proper challenge vs reward - looking forward to it!
2. AI of the creatures… It’s rather bad, you can see that they are trying to avoid your projectiles, they are strafing, but at the same time sometimes they can just stuck and becoming sitting ducks.
3. Sound -  while music is really great in the game (however we need more tracks), the sound is not great. For instance, I hate very abrupt and non-climatic explosion of fireball (kind of a shot gun sound). Also some of the sounds are too loud or are being triggered at the wrong time. There’s a lot of improvement needed in this area.
4. Optimisation - while not bad anymore, it still needs more work. Especially for bigger buildings / constructions the game can be really sluggish, even on a good PC spec.
** CONS **
1. Learning new spells - I like how currently spells are divided between different types of weapons (with a couple branches independent of the weapon). However, how you acquire them is very… shallow for a "wizard sim" type of game. For me this is the biggest complain.
I would love to see the system where you need to study spells (mini games maybe?), during the study let's say you discovered that there is a way to increase effectiveness of fireball but you need to get a really rare ingredient, or control a specific place of power in the word, etc. As a magic user, a player should feel a sense of progression in his or her arcane study. There are no magic experiments - they could add a bit of flavour to the game - e.g. the more dangerous the experiment is, when failed, would give a player some debuffs for a while, but if done right, would give nice bonuses to study new spells, etc. Obviously spell crafting from Oblivion would be my dream come true :) (but no overpowered combinations, please).
2. PvP needs some kind of ''in-world struggle system'' - maybe capturing the resources or places of power? At the moment the only incentive of PvP is raiding the bases and stealing resources - not very innovative.
3. Still long loading times when you first log into the game.
4. No support for economy between players. Maybe addition of marketplace mechanic, where players could visit a town market to buy missing resources from other players’.
5. Animation system - recently much improved, there’s still a lot of room for improvement - e.g. swimming animation which looks a bit silly at the moment.
6. No story driven content. I personally don’t want traditional quests in the game though… What would be great to have, is some kind of procedural generated events that are happening in the world. What would be even better, if these events would influence the world somehow...
7. Game definitely needs more players, hopefully content-drops at some point will lure some population back.
8. Minor bugs
** CONCLUSION **
Really great game! I have easily already got my money's worth for the price tag. Very immersive game, very believable world, amazing building system, sense of progression (but not fully there yet) and when fully fledged dungeons will be added with an upcoming content drop - it will be a really nicely done game.
On the other hand, if you expect more story driven content - this is not a game for you. You need to organise yourself and decide what to do in this vast and diverse world.

This was really hard for me to rate because Absolution is like a turning point for this franchise. Absolution introduced a lot of new mechanics that opened almost infinite possibilities in approaching the missions and how they can be completed. This makes assassinations much more realistic, and immersive in a sense.
However, Hitman abandoned its ranking/rate system that defined the franchise. So the game is now after efficiency and pure completion. The difference with Absolution and the other Hitman games:
- I can play the same mission more than 10-20 times to get a Silent Assassin rating, and probably 10-20 attempts more to get the same rating in Professional. Then probably 20 more attempts attempting to perform all these in a speed-run environment.  But with the new system, I don't feel the need nor the incentive to re-do these missions after having completed them for achievements. All we get is a vague top score system that acts like a leaderboard (open-ended with no conclusive meaning whatsoever)
Change and innovation isn't always good especially when you change the identity that defined your franchise over the past 4 games.

I see so many people giving this game a thumb up. And i don't entirely disagree...but i don't agree either.
The game plays and feels much easier compared to the previous Hitman titles, and also seems to be "dumbed down" in order to be less frustrating for everybody. That means you get to play in rather small areas, against fairly stupid AI, and most of the times you don't even need to try really hard in order to kill someone or get past a door/entrance. The solution or the suit needed is highlighted in front of your eyes.
Visually, the game still looks pretty good, the colours are quite vivid, and maybe the lighting is exaggerated at times (some light effects and flare effects are funny).
The characters are nicely designed and each of them gets a good background, and the voice over work is good, too (aside of the italian one being odd at times, for some characters).
Overall i liked this game, but i expected quite a bit more plot depth, the story itself isn't really complicate and maybe i would have liked another short chapter at the end telling me what happened to Victoria.

If you played the♥♥♥♥♥♥out from DK2 and you still want something similar, then purchase the game.
It definitely has it's own highlights; narrator is good, graphics is also cool (it is coming from someone who hates this kind of style), story is also decent on it's own way.
However, the gameplay is fundamentally broken. First and foremost it's easy. Too easy. So unless you go full retard and start mindlessly fighting it poses no challenge whatsoever.
Secondmost, the gameplay is slow. I mean SLOOOOOOOOOOWWWW
.. meaning that you need gold, lots of gold to research and upgrade things. Rooms, traps, you name it. Now, in Dungeon Keeper you had to be smart to acquire the gold. Smart with dungeon layout, smart with resource management, smart with traps, smart with protecting your dungeon. Here? All you have to do is to wait. Because of the population cap (which takes gold to raise and some mana as well, but mainly gold is the bottleneck), you cannot afford to have many imps (workers, minions, whatever). Gold veins is not a problem, those are dime by the dozen, you just need to be patient enough till those little midgets mine enough gold so you can progress. And when imps haul gold, they slow down, just to make things even more painfully slow.
There are other problems as well with the game. In DK you got all the options and freedom; how to build the dungeon, what to do with enemy heroes (convert them, transform them to skeletons or vampires), how to secure gold veins and so on. Here all maps are the same. Mine some gold, hire one goblin for traps/boxes and some orcs for muscle, maybe a naga or two. Then perhaps dig around a bit to get some additional units, but mainly wait until you have enough gold to build/upgrade stuff.
Perhaps I will get more unit types later in the game, even room types, but to be frank after ~5 maps I just got bored. Utterly bored.

I love puzzle games, but I'm not afraid to admit when they get to be too much for me. SpaceChem is a perennial favorite of mine that I burned out on way before the end, for example. Big Pharma shares certain similarities with SpaceChem, but with a layer of corporate management on top of the mind-bending puzzles. It's an interesting combination, and also a very exhausting one.
You get to be the CEO of a pharmaceutical company, which turns out to be a lot more interior design and number-crunching than the vlogging and buying Wu-Tang albums that I expected. Starting with a small empty room, you import ingredients through hatches in the walls, run them through a gauntlet of machines, and funnel the resulting pills, creams, and tinctures back out for a profit. Each ingredient has positive and negative effects that are activated at different concentrations, so your machines can raise, lower, and rescramble concentrations to make effective medicines.
Cramming all the necessary machines and connecting conveyor belts into the space you have is your primary concern. You can research and unlock more efficient machines but you're trading space efficiency for higher running costs, which must be weighed against the profit of the drug. These values in turn fluctuate with the cost of ingredients, the market demand for that cure, and any competitor companies in that market. This is the management layer I spoke of and while you can do well enough ignoring price fluctuations, more difficult scenarios and the Master-level goals require you to retool your operation based on the market, especially once patents come into play and companies start locking each other out of producing specific cures.
This additional layer of complexity may be unwelcome to those just trying to wrap their brains about their assembly lines. Cures can be upgraded to more valuable remedies by hitting specific concentrations with specific machines. This sometimes requires catalysts mixed in with special machines, which might also require re-arranging your chemical's traits with yet another machine. All of these processes must then be crammed into limited space, and layout mistakes can be costly to undo. An efficient, profitable line is incredibly gratifying to put together, but it can be a difficult road to get there.
You'll have over three dozen scenarios to choose from, with goals ranging from make X dollars over Y years to deliver Z quantity of a specific drug. Regardless of your goals, the means will be similar, building assembly lines for simple drugs while you research the ingredients and tools to make more complex ones, and refactoring everything when you start to run out of space. New machines, upgrades, and rules may come into play in later scenarios, but never to particularly dramatic effect. It's one of those games where you really have to love the core gameplay loop because it's not going to deviate much from scenario to scenario.
The presentation is perfect for a puzzle game, with clear, colorful, cartoony shapes and pleasing animations for all your machines. I want to give special recognition to the sound effects, which reach Blizzard-levels of polish for how perfect and gratifying they are to hear. Machines make delightful buzzes and clanks, belts whirr along happily, and even the buttons have rich bleeps and bloops to them. It's an excellent concept assembled and presented as well as anyone could expect, so the only question is how long you'll care to stick with it. There's not a lot of variety to building lines or running your company, but if you want to build Rube Goldbergian conveyors and tax your brain in turning a profit, you'll find no end of content to keep you happy.

EDIT: The developer sent out an email to backers telling us that there has been a significant overhaul of the game and asking that we give it another shot, so I've done so. According to the update, there's improved graphics, a UI overhaul, and a greatly improved research tree. It's been so long since I played that I cannot comment on how improved things are over the original, but I'm still not able to recommend the game.
In this version, you still send out colonists and wait for things to happen. But it's still plagued with a series of strange design decisions that make it difficult to play. For example, the camera is attached to whichever colonist you're currently directing. You can rotate the camera, but that's about it. This makes it incredibly difficult to send your colonists to do things far from their current position. The developer also improved interacting with modules, which is nice, but I still have to send my colonist out in the atmosphere if I want to move them from one module to another. What's the purpose of connecting tunnels if the astronauts don't even use them. Lastly, the sound levels are far too low and in game sounds are drowned out by the music. I could probably fix that with the settings, but I didn't feel compelled to look.
At this point, I'm still confident that this is not a game for me. I still wanted to like it, which is why I backed it, but I cannot recommend it to anyone without another major overhaul.

This is a review of the Redux version in particular.
Overall, the game is alright, the weapons (or rather weapon modes) are fun to use, the visuals are quite nice, the soundtrack is average with some great tracks. However, I can't really say it's anything more than just "Okay" due to a few issues.
The enemies are very bullet spongey, it's somewhat improved in the Redux version, but it can be very tedious taking down some of the enemies as a result. It's very annoying especially when the most bullet spongey enemies spawn so soon after the last ones.
The redux version appears to have made the game much easier. This is due to the addition of the Shadow Warrior (Flying Wild Hog also developed that, the redux is infact clearly a port of Hard Reset to the updated Road Hog Engine which Shadow Warrior uses) style dodging mechanic. This makes avoiding enemies much easier to the point you can avoid most attacks by dodging around the battle area. Insane difficulty as a result felt very much like Normal - Hard instead. It's fun don't get me wrong, but it does make it feel too easy almost.
Story is nothing to write home about. Generic cyberpunk Bladerunner/GitS kind of stuff with a dash of Terminator. Plot seemed somewhat hard to follow as well. Cutscenes are animated comic book kind of things. They look rather crude and honestly they aren't that interesting.
And lastly, the Redux version is barely any different from the original Hard Reset. You get a new energy sword weapon (also straight out of Shadow Warrior, the hand pose is also identical as well as the animations) and a few new enemies (I think...?), but aside from a new engine and a weapon, it's barely any different.
So if you already have Hard Reset, maybe skip this one. If not, I would definitely buy it.
I dunno if you will want to play it more than once though. Shadow Warrior surpasses Hard Reset in virtually every way.

This game, is at best, a mediocre time waster that doesn't fill either of the shoes its awkwardly tried to put on. It tries to claim its a fighting game, and it tries to claim that its a arena style pvp game. Theres a semblence of both here, but they both fall horrendously short so we'll hit the easiest to explain first.
As a PVP game, ala Unreal Tournament 2004, Chivalry: Medieval Warfare, TF2, etc. This game just can't hold up, its horrendously balanced with incredibly small rooms (the largest I saw was 10 people), and no semblence of match making. It was rare I saw a room that wasn't either full, or completely empty, with most rooms being the latter and in truth I found myself spending more time looking for a room to play in than the length of the games themselves.
As a Fighting Game...this game is just attrocious. Again we return to the fact that this game is horrendously balanced, and while most games can't be truly balanced, this game is ridiculously bad when it comes to that. The already rather small amount of characters falls into two categories and nothing but: Absolutely Worthless and Utterly Amazing.
A fast moving character can completely wreck a slower character by just moving around them and punching them into oblivion.To put this into perspective, I am a relatively poor fighting game player, I can win online matches in games like Persona 4 in Mayonaka Arena and Blaz Blue only by choosing a single character and practicing that character ad nauseam until I have every combo in their repetoire down pat. In Arche Blade, I was able to crush any slower character in one on one combat, and sometimes in two on one combat, with little to no issue my very first game. It wasn't a challenge, and I'm not bragging, its the sheer fact that these slower characters just can not keep up with a faster character like Renny.
The second major part of a fighting game, the character selection, is abysmally poor in this game. The collection of available fighters is incredibly small, with one character (Renny) repeated with only a slight change to her kit between the two. On top of this fact, some of these characters are obviously lifted from far superior games. I'll point out the two I noticed, and I'm sure theres others. The first one was the already mentioned Renny, a character who uses her fists and teleports around... huh that sounds oddly familiar to Makoto Nanaya from Blazblue. Oh well, I'll try Elika out.....wait shes spinning around firing two guns and blasting in every direction so she fills the area around her with bullets.... why am I playing a mediocre version of Noel. Her muzzle blast colors are even the same color as Noels.
Then finally, the thing that makes this game NOT a fighting game....everything collapses down to two buttons right and left mouse button. And every single combo, all 10 of them, is fulfilled by mashing down on those two buttons. You know how I said each character has 10 combos? Its the same 10 combos for every character, just with a different outcome. Theres no change in what buttons you push to do various moves, theres no special combos for each character, everything just falls down to mashing two buttons and hoping for the best while ocassionally pressing shift to use your "special movement" such as teleporting, flying, sprinting (yes only one character can sprint), and jumping backwards. You can't have a fighting game without special moves, without combos, and without any semblance of mastery.
Theres a feeling of elation for me in a fighting game when, after getting my butt kicked by every player who comes my way for the first week, start turning it around and winning matches and holding my own in the ones I lose. Theres a feeling of accomplishment, that makes me want to keep playing and get better...theres none of that here. I finished in the top 3 of my first match, I don't feel accomplished, all I did was run around with Renny and mash my left mouse button while ocassionally pressing shift and my right mouse button. In any GOOD fighting game, in any GOOD pvp game I should have been the bottom of my scoreboard with my character weeping in the corner if all I did was run around and mash a button with no thought to what I was doing.  Just avoid this game, if you want a fighting game go get Blazblue, or Injustice, or Persona 4 in Mayonaka Arena, or anything....spend your money on that so you dont waste your time on this.

Take to the red planet with this gem.
This game drops 4 astronauts on the red planet in one of 4 (for the moment) regions. Order your people to gather resources, investigate anomalies or other points of interest, extend and maintain your facility and order new people and / or resources from Earth.
The interface is simple but effective, don't crowd the screen or intrude with the way of the actual chores / jobs you need to perform. The way the developers chose to build / extend your base leaves much to be desired, as you can only order the construction of a new module and then just assign an astronaut to perform the construction, but you don't get to decide where and how, or even have multiple astronauts speed up the process. This is all fine since it isn't about building a base on Mars, and with the statistics for the astronauts present, which range from temperature, oxygen, general health and radiation, as well as the environmental problems you'll have to cope with, such as landslides, dust storms and the increase in solar radiation during daytime, you will have your work cut out for you.
And therein lies the problem that at least I have with this game; It feels a lot like work and there is too much on rails for a game like this. The developers have seemingly tried to compensate by using rendering methods that appear to do a whole lot in terms of making the game choppy and laggy at times, but when you just look at some of the models and effects from say dust storms and such it really doesn't justify such a load on the GPU compared with better graphics and smoother gameplay in other similar projects.
On the other hand, there is not a single catagory this game falls in as it really is a simulator of building and maintaining a base on Mars, with all the reasonable problems you could imagine we would face.
Definately interesting, not sure if a lot of people will enjoy this game given the limited freedom though.

PeriAreion is as flawed as can be. The outdated and ugly graphics are easily forgiven since it's not a game that relies on them. They're perfectly serviceable in fact, everything's easy to identify and that's all you really need. The animations are stiff and awkward, but you know what your little colonists are doing outside the base at a glance. There's no base interior, which I'm thankful for, and the UI for controlling colonists within the base is decent enough.
The problems with the game all arise from a feeling that the developer didn't quite know what they were doing. You can tell they studied and researched what's required to colonize Mars, but I find it hard to believe they did the same regarding game design. The control scheme belongs in a 90s game; you can only ever select one colonist at a time and your camera is stuck on that colonist. You can't move the camera around, only just spin it around your unit. This means that if you want to send your little guy over a hill, you first need to send him to the hill side, then on top of the hill, then over it. You have to hold their hand the entire way. There's no easy way to send them back to base either, making managing more than one at a time a pain. Not hard, just annoying and sluggish.
The game also comes with one of the worst tutorials I've seen. It's functional, entirely functional, but it teaches you next to nothing. Camera controls; sure. How to left click and right click, how to sort through your little dudes, how to enter and exit the main module, how to give them jobs inside of it. Done. It didn't tell me how to get ice though and, in half an hour or so, my colonists all died from dehydration.
Before that the base was a mess anyway. I had to find out that bases needed maintenance only when one of my colonists got CO2 poisoning. At first I thought it must've been a life support issue. I built a tech module which was supposed to give electricity and life support to the whole base, but it changed nothing. It was only when I flipped through the manual that I learned that you need to build a Geology module to do maintenance. At this point, the CO2 poisoning had gotten much worse with that colonist and developed into a broken arm. A few moments in a freshly built medbay would surely have saved her, but I had run out of sulfate at that point, so no go.
The sad thing is this game has plenty of cool ideas. Colonize Mars? Dude, yes! Managing a small team of colonists, building a base that'll grow big enough to receive even more. Doing research, exploring on foot and in a rover, surviving the harsh environment. All of this sounds fantastic. There's just not a game to go with it. I hate to say it, but I can't recommend this game to anyone. It's set at $15 USD right now, but I don't think I'd even suggest you check it out if it was free. Sorry. :(

An eye-opening game!
I've thought of colonizing Mars as something we may do, later on, somehow. I'm sure they'll figure out how to do it.
After playing this game, now I can see that colonizing Mars really is something that we can do. I feel like I can join in on the discussion on colonizing Mars, or at least listen and understand more of what people are saying; understand what's needed, and what the concerns are. I feel like I understand the kind of life the colonists will have, on Mars. After playing this game, my whole view of Mars has changed: it's another place; not all that different from Earth, but without any oxygen, which is kind of a problem. For the first time, I could imagine myself on the surface of Mars, and felt like I could feel what colonists might really experience there. I'm really glad I played this game.
From a gameplay perspective: colonizing Mars, is a lot different than playing Sim City. There are different challenges than in other games in this genre. Decisions are much more critical. If you go short on a resource you need: you could easily die. In other games, you can often go short on a resource for a while, and be fine. Not here. When I started losing power without realizing it at first, it lead to a very tense few moments as I struggled to overcome the problem. Then all my colonists died, when I could not fix the problem fast enough. It's something that could really happen on Mars. You have to search for the future problem and fix it before it can become an emergancy, deciding what is and what isn't going to become a majour problem is what really makes this game.
It's an easy game to pick up, too. I played without the tutorial, and felt comfortable, fast. I think almost anyone could play this game, and it's truely a great experience for everyone to have. I'm glad I played this game, and I think you will be, too. :)

This game is far from being Magic. The response times are a sketchy at best, and the game does not know what to do with a stack. (Example: Opponent declared an attack, and before blockers I sacrificed my Black Cat to make him discard his only card, and in response he cast it as an instant to kill another one of my creatures. There was no timer for his instant to respond to. I just lost my creature and the rest of the stack resolved.)
This game also does a VERY poor job of laying out the different phases. When a player passes priority to end a phase the other player(s) will always have a chance to respond. (Example: When an opponent passes his main phase you have the chance to make an action, whether it is kill a creature before it starts attacking or making the opponent lose cards in hand. Not in this game it seems.) The phases also do not account for thinking out a strategy. If you have lands or instants in your hand and you have already laid down a land then the turn will end on you. It will skip your main/second phase and go straight to the end phase. I had an instant to draw cards and it was my end step before I could draw the cards and play any permants that came up. There is also no mention of untap, upkeep, or draw phases which should also has their own end phase responses.
I feel like the developers have no idea how to play magic and have only looked at some brief youtube videos of mtg. Overall I would not recommend this game to any one. Especially new players as this game will give them bad habbits and a poor base idea of mtg.

Also, you gotta understand that is an early access game and its in progress. Many changes will be done and a lot of them have already made it in the game, I hope that my review helped you and your decision on buying the game. Look, I'm not all that coordinated anymore. I get that. It happens with old age. We fall down. We drop things. We lose our dentures. I want to die sleeping peacefully, not like the other screaming passengers in my car. But if I'm awake, there's one thing I can still do well and that's drive.
If real cars had physics like this, no one would be able to stay on the road and I've raced vehicles before. These ice skates with axles handle horribly. They don't turn or brake worth a darn. Tapping on the brakes will send the car suddenly careening off 90 degrees in some random direction. It would be easier to drive a pinball than these tings. Bumping another car - even if you hit their back quarter panel on a turn - will send your car careening off wildly while their car isn't impacted at all. I guess Newton's Second Law does not exist in the GRID2 universe.
The most important things about any racing game are the driving and physics. GRID2 seems to have forgotten both. Perhaps it is different with a wheel, but with a gamepad I find it unplayable. It smacks of a poor console port and you can do better for your money. This game isn't worth your time or your dollars.
