Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory is an amazing game and instantly worth a recommend if you are a fan of the stealth genre or just like the series and haven't gotten into the 3rd instalment for some reason. It's worthy of its Steam-tag "Best in the series". I have debated with myself about it, but I would add this game to one of my favourite games of all-time. No, I am not a huge stealth enthusiast. Also being a legacy title, it doesn't have any UPlay integration at all!
A good stealth game is dependant on solid mechanics and unlike later instalments of Splinter Cell. Chaos Theory and its predecessors are mostly stealth driven games.  Sam Fisher is given 3 settings in his trademark 3-scope goggles (Night-Vision, Heat-Vision and an EEV mode which highlights electronic equipment),  an EMP function on his handgun and of course a knife.  The game also features  sound and light bars in the HUD to show how silent and hidden you are which is a nice touch. With these tools, some environmental manipulation and the solid controls it's possible to get through entire missions without being detected or firing a bullet. Infact in the 1st mission I got through with only firing 2 on normal difficulty.
Controls are excellent here on the PC with a keyboard & mouse. With the controls already premapped sensibly and are all rebindable.  A notable control mechanic is how you can alter Fisher's walking/sneaking speed via the scroll wheel of the mouse which is a really nice touch. The game does have a good tutorial which teaches you how to work with these efficiently.
The plot is worthy of the Tom Clancy name and is immensely detailed. I didn't understand it as a child in 2005 and I still only have a relative understanding of it now with some help from the Wiki and knowledge from previous playthroughs. It follows on from the previous 2 installments and takes you all around the world. That's the idea of the plot without mentioning spoilers.
Visuals are from the Unreal Engine 2.5 and are pretty solid. The game is from 2005, so it's safe to say that the visuals are antiquated. The lighting plays a key role in the game as it can be the difference between having bullets hurled at Fisher. The textures are antiquated for the most part, but that's to be expected. Still it doesn't look too bad for a 2005 game.
Soundtrack was composed by both Amon Tobin and the well-know Jesper Kyd. The OST is amazing and each tune has a unique vibe that sets the scene whether it be ambient whilst Sam Fisher is sneaking around or frantic when enemies are firing at you due to your carelessness. It was also apparently featured on the UK motoring TV show Top Gear which says quite a bit and my favourite tracks from El Cargo (the 2nd mission) have been part of my personal music library for quite some time.
So all in all give it a try. At its current price of £9.99 ($9.99/9.99€), it's not a bad deal for stealth enthusasts. Though it has been reduced by Ubisoft to at least 75% making it cost around £2.50, I would it's worth getting for most gamers.

I'm having fun. On the surface, it's a simple colour matching game. Easy, right? Anyone can do it. As a Hard Core Casual gamer, I really appreciate that. No timer, no hand eye coordination and instant decision making required. Yeay!
It's also "Free to play" or supposed to be. Don't believe it! It's addictive. Like... like... shopping for a shopaholic. I'm a shopaholic. Having said that, I'm well aware of my gaming budget limitations. So i've spent enough on this game to buy a PS4 or so my friend tells me. I don't really care since there are no games on a PS4 that I can actually play and my PS3 works just fine. The games on my Playstation watchlist are all coming out on PS3 anyway. So, my game budget can handle this. I just wish Steam would stop blocking me, all the time. I'm nowhere near $2000.00 in 24 hours.
Anyway, back to the game... Past the surface there are strategies and tactics that make the battles interesting. Different enemies change the feel and style of play required to win and so it keeps being fun. It's very grindy if your gaming budget or Steam doesn't allow you to buy what you need to level up your characters. BUT if you're not a PVP ♥♥♥♥♥ it doesn't really matter. Take your time, wind down after work with a game or two and eventually in a few... errr... years... ^_~ you'll get there eventually. I've only been playing for a few weeks, but I've paid for my character levels in cash. You get a present everyday you do play a game or two and if you care to play in the PVP arena, the rewards are more consistant than in the PVE games where the reward randomiser can give you the minimum reward heaps before surrendering the good stuff. It seems to be getting better, but that might just be my imagination. I didn't collect any data to compare last week's drops to this week's.
The only downside at the moment is that the PVE content seems very limited. There's a Prologue which I have completed, though not obtained all the rewards and no sign of "Chapter 1". There are PVE Events, but because they are of limited time... go on holidays without your computer and you miss them.  If your team isn't at a sufficiently high level, you may only be able to complete the first few fights before the opponents get too hard to fight. Then you're stuck grinding those same few fights, your team can manage, to get enough points to reap the rewards on offer in the time that the Event is on for.
There's even PVP Events - lots more of these, with Lightning Rounds and Tournaments you have to pay to play in.  I'm not much of a PVP player and once the teams I have to fight get too hard as my ranking climbs, I lose interest until I can level up my characters to get a chance at winning again. BUT by then the PVP Event, is over. Hmmm....
I'm much more interested in Chapter 1 and the continuation of the Story started in the Prologue. Don't tell me they continued the story in past Events, cause I wasn't there to play them and when do they become Chapter 1?
That's the MAJOR downside of this game. There doesn't seem to be anything beyond the Prologue.
So you ask yourself why I'm recommending this game?
Because I'm having FUN!
Read a few other reviews and the forums and there are all kinds of grumbles about its inadequacies. BUT when all is said and done, it is a FUN game. It is an easy game to pick up and play, and once you get started, the character and power combinations become intriguing. It gets addictive simply because someone like me whats to collect them all and see how well, or not, they work together.
I might wish for more permanent content... maybe there will be. I can only hope. In the mean time I'll be having fun with what is there.

The short version:
DON'T! Just don't.. I did.. And I regret it..
Uglier than Civ V, WAY fewer options than in Civ V and very linear too!
For what you get, the price is ridiculous!
The less short version:
I played Civ V with all the updates and I love it! Incredibly addictive, and the 243 hours I spend on it, was during a few months only.. Then I see this Civ-in-space-game.. And I love space games.. Around 60% would recommend it then, it cost 40€ and I thought: "What the hell.. Why not?" well.. let me tell you..
I've spend 42 hours in Beyond Earth, won 5 rounds and lost 2.. And god ****** but I am disappointed... You can't change the victory conditions or the number of AI, and there are only 8 factions.
You can use spies to steal money and tech, which is a good thing, but if you are caught, you rarely get an option to stop or face consequences, everyone just starts to hate you. You could just not use spies then, you think.. Well yeah, but it is also incredibly overpowered! You can get 2-900 energy (which is the new gold), a lot of tech, (which boosts your technology), several military units or other even more overpowered stuff..
The graphics are really disappointing! It seems far uglier than Civ 5, which is a little confusing to me.. Why wouldn't they make it look better?! In all fairness the game gives you the choice between normal graphics and the AMD mantle version, which is apparantly something incredibly pretty.. Which I can't use.. Even though my computer has a 2gb graphiccard, 16 gb ram, 3,5 ghz quad core and so forth, but apparantly I'm lacking something everyone else seems to have.....
Bandits has been replaced with roaming alien lifeforms, which are not aggressive until you move in on their turf.. Mostly at least.. And apparantly water everywhere is their turf.
The religion has disappeared, which isn't a loss really, but have been replaced with 3 different idelogies, somewhat like Civ 5, but with the distinction, that you get points in either or all of them, but can only win the game if you chose one of them. One hates aliens, on loves aliens, the last is sort of in between.
The resources has had a facelift ofcourse, and are now very confusing.. Tubers, Chitin "fruit" and other stuff which gives some kind of bonusses I'm sure.. But I really can't see where I'm supposed to monitor them... At all..
The units has also had a facelift, and they sound cool enough, but there are only 7 units plus 4 from which ever ideology you choose. The units gets up to 4 upgrades as you preogress in the chosen ideology, the starters being puny and the end being overpowered.. Units you already have gets upgraded automaticly, with cost of maintenance and so forth following.
I may be a criticizing turd, who knows nothing about computer games, but I was really disappointed in this game.. Compared to Civ 5, its seems like less than an expansion.. Oh, and did I mention.. Its only 6 gb big... Which somewhat indicates a game with too little content.

The main issue with this game is a matter of expectation. Many negative reviews were written by people who bought Beyond Earth at $50, at which price the expectations outweigh the reality. This game is not a revolutionary addition to the Civ franchise; it is a high-quality, space-based DLC for Civ 5. The combat mechanics, diplomacy, and overall "feel" of the game are virtually identical to Civ 5. In that respect, Beyond Earth is very similar to the Final Frontier mod in Civ 4 Beyond the Sword. Both games do not deviate far from their parent platforms, and they both introduce new ideas to the series. The only difference is that one is $50, and the other is free.
Of course, Beyond Earth is different from Civ 5, chiefly in the artwork, which is great. Even in design, though, Beyond Earth has a hard time escaping the clutches of Civ 5. Sure, the units look completely different, but the same 12 man formation for infantry is present in Beyond Earth. Even the menus are identical to Civ 5, with sleek, futuristic text being the only change.
However, in the areas where Beyond Earth really needs to be different, it succeeds big time. The affinity system is great, and it lends much needed variety to the game. Also, the tech web gives a new perspective on research, forcing a player to choose one technology at the expense of another. These two features give the game replayability, something needed in any good Civ game.
I bought this game when it was on sale for $20, and I'm very satisfied. At $20, it's about the same price as a Civ 5 DLC, which is what Beyond Earth is, essentially. I'm perfectly willing to buy another Civ 5 DLC.
Conclusion: Buy it on sale.

It's one of those games that you start over and over and over and over trying to make it better next time. Only to realize that, well, you won't. The theme of the game is, basically, building a pipeline from a start to a finish point with some machines in between to "produce" your pharaceuticals. The tricky part is that every type of machine has a defined input point and a defined output point, which means that if you have to put like 5 of them behind each other, you will invariably end up either in a circle or in a really bad design.
Solving this is, basically, the game.
Is it still fun? Surprisingly, yes it is. The graphics is cute enough to make it fun to watch that machine do its magic, and the liberty you have to make decisions is just enough to give you something to ponder. Should you scrap that low profit production line and hope that you can squeeze in the much larger one that gets you better profit? Do you have room to use three cheaper machines than one expensive one? Should you hire more scientists to make production cheaper in the long run, even though they're expensive to hire and maintain?
Is it good enough to warrant the price tag? I'd say yes, but I wouldn't pay more than that.

I've had Big Pharma for a while now; I bought it when it wasn't on steam (A few months before the release) and have gotten a pretty solid idea on the game.
Graphics: Simple 2nd Dimensional, isometric camera view. All the machines have nice animations, and the customization of your building, albeit basic with flooring and wall paper, add a bit of hominess and individuality to your lines.
Sound: Not much to say. The music is nice and the sound effects are good, but far from breaking any records.
Gameplay: Big Pharma is a building game, a puzzle game, and a business management game. You pick "play" and you are presented with a wide varity of missions. These range from "produce X amount of treatment for X" to "Make a profit of X dollars." What is great is that you are able to approach this however you want; the game doesn't force you to follow specific paths. You get to build whatever manufacturing lines you'd like to produce medications. It gives a feeling of freedom, compared to other games where they hold your hand and demand you do things in a certain order, and more or less penalize you for differentiating. Each effect requires a bevy of actions first. To get treatment for X, first you must set the concentration to the right values with machines like the evaporator and ioniser. You may need to combine it with a catalyst effect- Which comes with other symptoms too, so you have to figure out what to do with the biproduct too. Along with keeping a functioning line running, you need to keep a mind for space conservation- each exspansion of your building takes money, and they aren't too roomy. Along with making sure your lines work and you have enough space, you need to keep an eye on your competitors; developed a wondercure for a very exspensive symptom? Soon, the AI competitors will rush to roll out those medications and steal some of your profits. Multi-tasking is a critical part of the game, and if you will have a bad time if you're only good at focusing one thing at a time. Another great feature is the hands-on tutorial. It lays down the foundation you need to understand the game and get a business running, but is entirely skippable if you chose.
Overall, Big Pharma is a great game if you're into the business management economic simulator genre of games.

I actually purchased a bundle I had originally passed on because I decided I really wanted to give Bleed a try.
If you like artsy action platformers, score attacks/speed runs, and fun, challenging gameplay, then you will enjoy this one.
The aesthetics are great - the detail in the retro-style character models and environemnt is well-done. The slow-motion and dash effects are very nice, and executing an efficient speed run can look quite pleasing. The music and sounds are appropriate for the theme, but I personally found the bit-style music annoying after a time, and resorted to using my own music.
The controls are fairly easy to learn, however, you will have to take a look at the control scheme to figure out the key bindings. I strongly suggest using a controller if possible, as the feedback will feel much smoother and more responsive; however, a keyboard + mouse combo is still viable. The learning curve is minimal to moderate, however, experience with bullet dodging will benefit you greatly.
The gameplay is pretty fun - your typical side-scrolling progress until you reach the boss. You are rewarded with money after each completed level and can use this to purchase new weapons and upgrades for your health and slow-motion bars. There is an arcade mode that ramps up the difficulty, and the game supports 2-player coop. An arena (challenge) mode allows you to test your skills against up to 3 bosses, and you can select which ones you'd like to fight (after beating them in the story first).
The boss fights are good - each boss comes with a unique attack pattern that mixes things up enough to keep things challenging. Each level is not too long, however, achieving a perfect (S-rank) score requires speed, timing, and precision. For achievement junkies, you will spend a few hours on this game if you wish to get 100% completion.
Overall, the game is very fun, and any platforming lovers should definitely give this a try.
Recommend.

what I would consider a puzzle. It's more like...a meditation with some light puzzle elements. And it's not hard to grasp. "Assets" such as trees and mountains are represented by the sequences of 2-3 colored triangles along the left side of the screen. Clicking a color sequence the first time unlocks the corresponding Asset. Placing an Asset on a tile costs "Awe". The pair of colored triangles at the top represent a sequence which earns you Awe. Awe is represented as white diamonds. To claim your Awe, mouse over the diamonds after they appear. You must place enough Assets of each type to fill its meter, as well as at least one Illumination asset to complete a world. (You can, of course, place more.) It's really very simple to learn, and very soothing. There is also room for creativity in where you place how many of each Asset. Great way to relax!

To be quite honest, the last side-scrolling platformer I ever played was when I last broke out Megaman X3.  I've had Bleed for a couple months now, and to be very honest, it has that same particular flavor and fun.
The backstory is very simple- our heroine, Wryn, wants to be the best Hero ever, so she decides the best way to show that she's better than the heroes currently enshrined in the Hall of Heroes is to hunt them all down and destroy them, wearing a cute smile upon her face.  To be honest, Wryn is a refreshing change from all the big, overly-muscled guys who usually catch this role- not to mention the story that she's just doing this because she wants to prove that she can be a better hero  than all those who came before her.  That's all- just to prove that she's better then they are.
The heroes you go after are a mix of different patterns, and each boss battle is a different experience.  What worked on th first boss won't work on the next one.  You'll be jumping and learning patterns and generally having a great time.
The weapons are a lot of fun, as well, but I managed to make it through just by using the starting pistols and the rocket launcher.   To be honest, though, everyone has their own playstyles, and it might be that they suited my play-styles.  You'll find your own style of play, so buy and upgrade them all and see what suits you!
The graphics are actually well-done for what they are- you don't need supremely-sharp graphics to make a fun game- the cartoon-like graphics actually enhance the game, and even if you and Wryn can't make it through the level, she'll always be there with words of encouragement to get you to keep on trying.
In short- buy this game!

An excellent side scrolling shooter with a taste of A.R.E.S. Controls are solid even with keyboard and mouse (I still prefer a controller). Unfortunately, the game is a tad short, but well worth the adventure.

Overview
I have played for over 30 hours without mods or cheats and do not own the expansion pack. So far I have managed to progress to Intermediate level in the scenarios. From my experience this game is what a sim management should be.  With a bit of twisted humour thrown into the mix seen in classics such as Theme Hospital, Big Pharma is beautifully made and very entertaining with a lot of replayability.
Interface and graphics
The main menu looks like a mobile port but don't be fooled! The simplistic buttons and side menus in the main game add to the overall functionality of the game. There are options to change the resolution, sound and graphic quality in the game. The graphics are in the cartoon style. I personally prefer this because cartoon style graphics will age much slower than the more realistically styled games, if at all.
Gameplay
There are 3 game modes for you to play - Free Play, Custom Game and Scenario. Free Play is the sandbox level where every machine and research branch is already unlocked and you have no money. Custom Game is where you set your own criteria to win the game. All of the goals/criteria in the game are number based and it would be nice to have a little more variety in how you win like being the most or least ethical competitor in game (but this might be in the expansion). Other than that the gameplay is solid. There is a lot of scope for replayability. There are 3 ranks in each game: standard, expert and master. The higher up the rank, either you have to do more within the standard time limit, or you have a shorter amount of time to complete your criteria. It's not just about what the game tells you to do as I find that I set myself personal goals long after I have finished my game criteria on a certain level.
A few funny bugs
I have experienced some world events that were not logical at certain times. An example of this is the 'mild winter' event that popped up in May. I was also stuck on the 'Keep calm and carry on' scenario for a bit because none of the raw ingredients that were available to be explored in the game had the certain enzyme that I needed to be able to upgrade my drug to an anti-anxiety treatment. I made sure to explore all of the available areas.
My verdict
This is a great game. It gets really addictive so don't pick this game up if you want to be productive. A solid 10.

It was pretty easy to bounce off Bioshock 2 when I first purchased it. It lacked the presentation of the original, the weapons were needlessly involved with the addition of ammo types, and the emphasis on traps and defense of Little Sister made sections of it almost seem like a tower defense game at times, which is not a genre I really enjoy.

Take the basic framework and art design, then hand it over wholesale to an small indie team, and you'd probably get something similar to Minerva's Den. At this point, on a Steam sale, the complete Bioshock 2 is worth it for this add on all by itself.

200+ hours played.
The only aspect of the game that actually held interest was the base building and the risk of those structures to PvP.  You needed to build in obscure corners, build defenses, be clever about how you arranged your structures, etc.
The serve list to actual player population is hugely off.  There are hundreds of servers and most only have 3-4 players (instead of 30-40) each.  It's exceedingly rare to even encounter actual players on most servers.  Those once-in-a-blue-moon servers that actually have 20-30 players (usually the result of a group of people who know each other already), the servers start to struggle to handle them performance-wise.
On PvP servers that are actually populated, I found that every one of them (approx 7 differenct servers over the time I played) quickly developed one overwelming "gang" that dominated the server with no chance to compete against them.  Griefing newer players was extremely common.
The PvP was laughably imbalanced to the effect of One-Shot kills and a near-impossibility to actually have a fight or employ any tactics/strategy... Higher levels stomp on you, and if you are similar level, whomever gets the first hits in generally won without challenge.
The PvE aspects of monster killing for exp and items is, unfortunately, a joke.  It's not challenging or interesting, the AI is painfully poor, and even low-level players can take out the most difficult creatures with little risk.  Killing these creatures over and over and over became a grind-fest for experience and materials needed for Base-raiding.
However in order to raid a base, you need to kill these creatures for "Siege Spells" materials.  From a balance perspective, this means the higher level characters that have been around for a while have huge stockpiles of those materials and can level a base seemingly at-will.  Lower level characters can't even knock out a simple wooden shack.  Those higher level characters who have plenty of materials have no REASON to raid a base in the first place.
The actual base-building mechanics are well-designed, but the gathering of basic building materials (wood/stone) is so monotonously repetative, for not good reason (the materials are plentiful and numerous).  For this reason the vast majority of custom servers employ increases to gathering and carrying weight in an attempt to make this less of a chore... but doing so messes with rarity balance elsewhere.
The item crafting system isn't horrible, but it's very repetative with very little variability.  To acquire "magic" gear, it's simply a matter of repetatively crafting the same gear over and over until you get it.  The materials are easily obtained for any craft with very little challange... it's more a chore than anything.
Ultimately;  if you enjoy base building for the shear creativity aspect of it, and have some friends to play and colaborate with, the game can be enjoyable from a PvE perspective.  PvP however, and serious balance issues coupled with fundamental system design problems, makes the game more frustrating than enjoyable. What this game does well can be found implemented better-still elsewhere.

While I enjoyed my time with GRID 2 (playing the campaign to completion), I can't in good conscience recommend it as a good example of a racing game.
The odds in the game are pretty much stacked against you every which-way. If an opponent touches you your car will, nine times out of ten, spin out and you lose a ridiculous amount of ground. However, if YOU touch an opponent, you'll still receive the brunt of the damage and time lost. The AI relies wholly on rubber-banding too - drive badly, they will be more forgiving, drive well, and they'll go toe to toe with you. The gamemodes are generally enjoyable. The problem is how the game creates progression late-game. Instead of new tracks, the game simply extends old ones, or, by season 5, makes you do the same 6 mile course three times over. This wears thin quickly, and the endgame feels more like a grind than an edge-of-your-seat world championship.
The game looks nice, the tracks are nice - hell, the cars are nice (if you're prepared to drop upwards of $5 to use the good ones). But when the actual gameplay is as infuriating as GRID 2 is, it really isn't worth your time/money - particularly at full price. I happpened across my copy in a Humble Bundle, and I'd be wary of paying any more than the $4 I shelled out for that bundle on this game alone.

Hitman: Absolution is a great stealth game, but a good Hitman game. It strayed from the formula established by the previous games and became a story driven 3rd person stealth shooter. This doesn't make it a bad game, but I can understand why fans who have been playing this since the beginning were dissappointed, and why newcomers (like me at the time) were sucked into the Hitman universe. This was my first Hitman game, and to it's credit it did what it was supposed to: be an enjoyable stealth game while introducing the player to a franchise of older, greater games. After going back and playing the other Hitman games, I will say Blood Money is my favorite, but I probably never would have played it had I not started with this one, so props to Absolution for that. As far as story goes, it's the best in the series but only because this game makes story it's focus. The other games make gameplay their focus. The story here is good, with good acting, characters, and a decent story overall. David Bateson as 47 is perfect casting and he shines in this game. The gameplay here is good but different. In the older games, you start on a map with some targets to assassinate and multiple ways of doing so. Here, you get standard 3rd person stealth gameplay. Sometimes you have targets, sometimes just guards and thugs. Thankfully Absolution executes this well so at least it's enjoyable. Absolution also introduces Contracts Mode, where players can go on maps and create their own assassination contracts for others to compete in. This was a great addition and has added many hours of replayability to the game. You can tell that some of the filler levels were designed for this, since some npc's have more personalities to them, but it works great and was a lot of fun. If I had reviewed this game a few years ago, I would have said that this is a good place to start. However, now that HITMAN 2016 is out, I'd say you should start there, since it has modern graphics and classic gameplay. So, if you are a fan of the older games, get this knowing that it's different but good. If you are new to the series, also get this, but know that there are other, better games in the franchise.

I have been playing this for awhile on PC and android. I am by no means an expert, but I think I can bring a more reasonable spin on things. I think one thing people kind of gloss over, is that the game is not final.
My overall impression of the game is positive. It is a fun low-commitment game. By that I mean the more you approach it casually from a time and money perspective, the more you will like it. Yes, this game is pay-to-win, but if you do that then there really is no reason to play this game. The game is entirely about improving your characters. It is not about PVE or PVP(more on that later). Yes, there are annoying cockblocks that preventprogression, so then do not do so. Consider it an appetizer for your main course, whatever game you are really playing. This is the kind of game you play when you are about ready to go to bed, or that moment right after you turn on your pc or tablet. I would say this game works better as a mobile game, quick and dirty gaming, but the UI is much better in the PC version.
Pros:
-Graphics and effects are nice. The artstyle in particular is noteworthy, if this was a comic series I would pick it up.
-The game is in beta, so the developers are still improving the game. For example, attacks and effects used to happen much more slowly, but now they are instantaneous. The UI in the android version used to be truly terrible, but they have added little changes that make it less tedious to track abilities and AP. There is hope for improvement, and I doubt development costs for improvements for such a simple game are so large that change will never come.
-If you are a Marvel fan, I am sorry to say this, but this is probably the best comic book game available to you. This is no Arkham City, but fun can still be had here.
-The core gameplay is fun and easy to get into. Once you know what you are doing, it is fast and strangely satisfying. That is, before the inevitable wall, but we went over that already.
Cons:
-The fact that it is pay-2-win is not the issue, the fact that "PVP" is forced on you is. Pay 2 win is only an issue in PVP games, for singleplayer games who really cares, and that is how I want to play this. What I mean by this is that PVE offers a very limited means of upgrading your characters. You will never get enough ISO, HP or character covers to upgrade your best toons by PVE alone, it is more practice for PVP with forgetabble storylines. You will get plenty of low level character covers here to upgrade, but the daily rewards will start overwhelming you to the point where you are forced to "compete".
-PVP is not really PVP. Like most mobile PVP games, you are really just fighting representations of other players characters. So, not only are you forced to PVP, it is not even real PVP. Oh, so who are you really fighting? An extremely sketchy AI. The AI is so sketchy in PVP and events it is hilarious. Cascade after cascade awaits you. This is to counter the fact that there is no true skill matchmaking, you will find your level 15 toons up against level 40 toons, uh no thanks. You can skip these guys, in fact you as the attacker have every advantage. You pick the team, you get to use upgrades, and you get to skip. That is probably why the AI cheats so much. Oh, and apparently your team is whatever team you last used, which is never explained to you.
-Nothing is explained to you. You probably read a lot of the above thinking what is this person talking about. This is what the game does, it only explains a very basic notion of the game. You kind of have to learn from your mistakes as you go. They never explain important things like the limited amount of points available to upgrade a toon, imagine if you paid to max out a character and found out you put too many points in the wrong talent, I bet you would be pretty upset since you would have to start from scratch.
-A lot of this game is just luck. Upgrades, prizes, even combat can often come down to good old RNG. If you are like me, I hate RNG with a passion. You have no control over the colors of the gems in this game, but I am sure the AI you will face does. In fact, count on it. Just make sure you have a team that can utilize the colors of the spectrum.
You see a lot of cons there, I often want to quit, but then something happens to pull me back in. This game is a continuous carrot-on-a-stick game, which is not surprising given that it is free. I think at minimum you will definitely need to drop some money for character slots, it is very hard to get around that. You will want to quit often, but then they will give you a free 3 star card and you will say, "maybe another chance". But, like I said earlier, a little perspective helps a lot. Do not try and "beat" this game, and you will enjoy it. It is a good time killer, not a time filler.

You know the game you're playing is something special when you show up to a border crossing in car with two flat tires, smoke rolling out of the front end and a trunk full of booze, pills and cigarettes... and you end up getting hassled about the roll of yarn that you forgot was stuck all the way back in the corner.
In a way this game feels a little like a first-person Oregon Trail, as you have to make a lot of decisions about what to bring, what route is best to take, whether you want to push on and see if you can make it to the next town or go home and fix up your car, and so on. Do you shut your car off to save fuel when you get out to check that box you found, or do you leave it running because you know the ignition coil is shot? Do you ditch the load of coffee you have to make room for those bottles of wine, not knowing if you can even take them across the border? Do you spend the money for a better engine, or just hope you'll find a route with a junkyard that has one for free? These are the kind of things you'll have to consider, among many others.

I really don't know what it is that people hate about this game.
Yes, it is a FREEMIUM (Free to play, pay to win) game.  That in and of itself automatically generates an understandable level of hatred from the internet.  The fact that if I let my little brother play this game unattended, and I can come back to my credit card being charged for tons and tons of hero points, is a bad, bad thing.  BUT...
I don't let anyone else touch my Steam account.  That means that if there are any microtransactions, they are my own doing.  So if I don't want to pay to play, I simply don't.
As of now, I have played this game for 9.9 hours and I haven't paid a dime into it.  Compare that to a Harry Potter console game that costs $60 and has less than that amount of play time and one can say I've definitely gotten a great deal.  Not to mention this isn't a Harry Potter game, which is a plus.
However, this game is a GRIND.  No, you will not be able to just plow through it, even if you make the right decisions every time.  You will need to power-up your characters to progress, and this includes re-playing levels to get all of the rewards.  Re-playing levels runs the risk of only receiving, what is it... 40 ISO points (Actually it's 20 ISO-8 points after further review)? This is a miniscule amount of in-game points, but they really add up over time, especially when matched with the actual rewards between 100-500 ISO points.
But I've enjoyed many games that are grinds.  Hell, I used to pay $15/mo to play WoW, which is just one, huge grind.  All of the old Working Designs RPGs were grinds, but they were a blast.  If you can put up with grinding to get to the top, you shouldn't have a problem here.
The storyline in this game isn't that great, but it is worthy of comic books.  It's really meh.  The whole Osborne "Dark Reign" storyline is after my time anyways (I stopped reading comics during X-Men's Fatal Attractions, and only recently have I been catching up).  But the game is fun.  It's an altered Puzzle Quest that is free to play.
In fact, I enjoy it so much that I just might buy some Hero Points after I beat the game; simply to support the devs.
This game just doesn't deserve all the hate it gets.

Buggy game.
Imagine you have a really efficient system, and a nice long machine, connecting each part to another in perfect harmony. You then add a machine that slows down the process slightly, and although you're limited by space, you see a small opportunity to add in another machine to help increase profits.
You spend the last of your money getting everything in place, then connect it all with belts. Suddenly, everything but your new addition grinds to a halt, as it turns out one of the belts in the new T-junction you've created is trying to move in the opposite direction.
You scratch your head, thinking "but there's an input and an output... why can't it see which way to go? Everntually, you contact the developer, who says "It's literally impossible to fix this"... You then realise that the developer simply doesn't know how to fix this bug, and therefore calls it a feature, telling people not to use T-Junctions, even though they limit the space provided, and encourage you to connect machines together and utlise space as best as possible.
It's a nice game, and certainly a time sink, but whomever designed the belts system needs to go back and do them again. Especially as they're the most used object in the game.
It's not going to happen though... as the developer refuses to admit there's a problem, despite the number of people arguing their point.
For that reason alone, it's not recommended. You'll find yourselves more frustrated than entertained.

If you're a fan of the Civilization series, I wouldn't recommend this game. It is a simplified, relatively boring derivative of the Civilization series. It neither offers a breath of fresh air to the Civ veteran nor an exciting and interesting game to the newcomer.
Beyond Earth offers the slow-paced gameplay of Civilization but without the complexity and nuance. It ditches or simplifies many things that made Civilization more interesting: religion, a variety of military units and veterancy upgrades, a variety of civilizations and starting bonuses, diplomacy and trade, and great people. It tweaks cultural policies, gold (energy), and happiness (health) to make them slightly different, but makes no fundamental changes to these. The only truly new addition to gameplay -- quests -- quickly gets repetitive.
War/combat would be far more interesting if all civilizations and affinities didn't have essentially equivalent units with different graphics, and if the power of all these supposedly futuristic units didn't feel more limited than the ancient weapons from Civ V. Unfortunately, most games devolve into a military match, as in Civilization. This is in part due to the fact that most victory types involve some degree of military involvement. All victory types are no more than some combination of building an expensive improvement and building up your military. There is also no significant difference between the alien mechanic and the old barbarian mechanic.
The orbital unit mechanic is underwhelming. There might have been some neat ideas, but in practice, you can only deploy your orbital units if there are no enemy orbital units nearby. The only way to remove the enemy orbital unit is to melee attack it with one of your artillery units, which will magically float up into orbit to attack, even though it is barely able to move two tiles along the ground...
The differences between affinities seem better suited to a real-time game than a slow, ponderous turn-based game like Civ. You'll typically "pick" the affinity for the victory that you want or for the strategic resources you have nearby. The high-end units for each affinity, despite ostensibly being different, don't make you change your tactics to use them. It is much like Supreme Commander in this regard, except without the fast pace and epic feel. It comes down to mostly a color choice, really.
Despite being about exploring other worlds beyond Earth, every choice of planet has exactly the same terrain and aliens, which seems like a real missed opportunity. If the game creators wanted to open up the Civilization universe, planets of different types would have gone a long way.
Bottom line: Beyond Earth disappointed and bored me.

As a fan of games like Spacechem, the old Mysts and 7th Guest, TIS-100 even and pretty much any other that requires heavy thinking, I really don't get why there are "so many" (22% as of now) bad reviews about this game.
Big Pharma is not as hard on your brain as some of these games I mentioned above but it does require a fair amount of thought and planning, specially at the begining when you're not used to it, and the hardest levels are also pretty challenging.
Put simply (if you're not in the mood for reading everything): the game is good, it keeps you entertained and focused for plenty of time.
People writing bad reviews mostly claim that:
1 - The game gets repetitive/boring - I disagree. Well, ok, every game gets repetitive - even life itself does - and Big Pharma is no exception. Still, you always get a rewarding sense of accomplishment when you see your production lines running efficiently, your drugs selling more than your competitors (and for a higher price) and when you get good trial reviews because you're a good man and ran the extra mile to make them patient-friendly. Also, every level has a different objective, and you can get a standard, expert or master "score" on each, depending on how fast (usually) you achieved your objective, and that keeps you on your toe every time, avoiding any mistakes to get your "master" rank in every level. You do, indeed, start every single level with the same formula (slight variations, but the same routine), but I find the game is still fun after 20+ hours playing it, mainly because achieving the master rank in the toughest levels is a good challenge.
2 - The "managing aspect" isn't a big part of the game - Again, I disagree. You absolutely need the money aspect, and it fits the game perfectly in my opinion. You must keep your drugs (and their sales rating, if you have the DLC, which I recommend) profitable, your income on the green, to be able to keep going. You must beat your competitors (and fast) or they'll end up showering you with patents and taking a huge share of the market, diminishing your sales. You gotta be careful with the loans you get so their interest don't end up eating all of of your profits, and also balance how many explorers/scientists you have - and what they are currently working on - to keep enough cash flowing in and your company, again, ahead of the competition. In my opinion, the management aspect works perfectly with the puzzle/logistic facet of Big Pharma. It's a double-fun experience, specially if you're the type of person who enjoys both things.
I think that covers most of the "thumbs down" this game has received.
***
About the DLC:
If you liked the base game, you'll like the DLC. It adds some neat new features (check the DLC's steam page for specifics.)
***
On a serious note / Something special about this game:
There's a very interesting and particular side to Big Pharma: it opens your eyes for how the REAL "Big Pharma Industry" works, or at the very least it makes you think about it.
In this game, you can leave side-effects on drugs on purpose (and regulate their, as well as the cure's, strenght as you will) to keep demand for some of your other drugs (those that treat such side effects) up high. You can patent your drugs to get a temporary monopoly of a market's share and raise your prices up to the sky. With the DLC, you can run trials on your drugs and deliberately disqualify the bad results to trick the consumers and raise  your sales. You... see where I'm going with this.
After playing this game, one must wonder: "Dude... this can totally be done for real. Maybe real companies do this kind of stuff." Then you keep thinking about it and... "Why wouldn't they? Well... maybe they have principles, and goodness in their heart. Maybe they want to help people." But wait... we're talking about some of the (if not THE) richest people in the world, people you never heard about, people whose names no one knows. People who torture lab animals on a daily basis, who tested prototype-drugs on jew prisoners during Hitler's Reich. People who profit from the suffering of the sick and weakened, and make a living extorting the dying. People who steal an old guy's economies dry under false promises of an unlikely cure (**Google "cancer" here**).
Finally, you'll find yourself concluding: "Man... screw polititians, mexican cartels, weapon dealers and african warlords. Big Pharma - that's the real nemesis of mankind."
I just read that Johnson & Johnson was just condemned to pay and indemnification of 55 million dolars to a woman because one of their talc powders gave her cancer. The doctors had to remove her ovary, and it was literally lined with talc. And that's a second (at least) for them because, months ago, they had to pay 72 million to another woman for the same reason.
If this example and reason alone aren't enough for you, Google "Big Pharma" or any company's specific name (Johnson & Jhonson, Pfizer, etc.) and read for yourself.
What I know is I'm never taking any medicine again unless it's strictly necessary (AKA I'm in heavy, constant pain). If you keep thinking about all this stuff, it's easy to see how far these companies can/could/do go to take your money (like an infinite chain of side-effects and their temporary-with-more-side-effects treatments). Seriously, we are on the "genetic mapping age", how hard can it be for trillionaires (the Big Pharma industry generates a trillion dolars per year) to cut off side effects and balance a drug's components if they want to? Damn, even I can do it, according to Big Pharma (the game).
***
Conclusion:
Big Pharma is a very nice game. It gives you a sense of reward every time you score a "master" on the tough levels and that's the raw thing every game aims for. If you like puzzle/management games, I'd say this one should keep the average guy entertained for 30-40 hours, maybe more (it took me 70 hours just to get "Master" on all the levels in "Advanced" and beyond). That's good value for your money, and this is the kind of game that you start playing at 6pm, play for one or two hours straight, quit, and realizes it's already 11pm.
If you're concerned about the negative reviews (I always and seriously take them into account myself), maybe you can wait for a sale, but I really don't think you'll regret your purchase at full price, as long as you understand what the game is like (the screenshots alone can give you a fair idea) and feel you are going to enjoy it - the game's execution itself is great, that is not going to disappoint you.
EDIT: btw, I never got a single bug or crash whatsoever.
EDIT 2: ok, now the game has crashed once, after 45 hours or so.
EDIT 3: I just found out that this game was made by ONE dude, alone. That always baffles me (Terraria was also made by a single guy, if I'm not mistaken). I, myself, can barely get dressed on my own, so... congratulations Tim, amazing job.

Big Pharma is a management/strategy/puzzle game where you have to build and manage a medicine company. You can say it’s a business simulation puzzle tycoon. You build, research, develop new medicine all the while trying to maximize profits. There is one part of the game that focuses on the production aspect of the medicines, in this part you have to concentrate on researching new medicine/cures and try to improve your medicine overall. The second part of the game is the economics of your company. You basically have to earn profit and try to improve medicine.
The graphics are simple yet beautiful looking. The colors are very bright and eye-catching. It almost sort of has that cartoon look. There’s not many options in the graphics menu other than resolution adjustment.
The music in the game is okay, you won’t get bored from it but it’s nothing to write home about as well. The announcer voice can sometimes become annoying though. Other than that most of the sounds work as they should and not bad at all.
The majority of the game is based on missions, where you start out with $50000 and you have a task. For example the first mission has you earn a certain amount of revenue in 10 years. Most of the missions are like that and as you keep doing missions the next batch of missions gets harder and harder. There’s a lot of missions and even free mode where you can just play without having to worry about anything. There will be a rival company which also influences your company when they introduce new drugs etc.
There’s also a puzzle element of fitting your medicine making machinery in a limited space, so figuring that out can be a lot of fun. You can choose from 8 different characters when you start a game. There are perks when you start a new game. E.G a perk where refunding equipment gives you 100% money back instead of regular 50%. You can choose 2 perks, at the beginning there’s only 4 perks unlocked but you can unlock more as you do missions and do the objectives the said perk requires. It’s a very strategic game where everything you do has an effect eventually so you must make your decisions well thought out. Game can be pretty complicated so if you like serious management games, this game is for you.
The DLC “Marketing and Malpractice” adds a whole bunch of add-ons to the game such as marketing tools where you can adjust your prices of your drugs as per the demand/demand, you basic economics. This basically changes they way the game works with your competitors as you can undercut their prices. You can give “gifts” and other such to doctors to increase sales. The DLC in my opinion makes the game much more interesting and gives it that new perspective of playing.
Big Pharma is an excellent time waster and a very good business/tycoon/simulator/puzzle game. Though prepare to spend plenty of time learning the ins and outs of the game as it can get very complicated. All in all it’s a fun title and the DLC is pretty nice as well.

Bleed is a short-and-sweet difficult platformer reminiscent of other video games and will occasionally reference them. The story goes that you and the main protagonist Wryn have to kill all 6 great heroes in the hall of fame who have hidden themselves from the rest of the world in order to join their ranks, and reveal them for who they really are. The game is pure enjoyment, and in my opinion is what a Matrix game should be, even if it has nothing to do with that franchise. Wryn can do three directional dashes while in the air, making her extremely mobile, if a little hard to control. You use the mouse to aim her weapons and can even go into bullet time (see why I compared it to the Matrix).  Wryn is probaby the best main protagonist in an indie game. She is just so adorable! The only real issue is the control. While you can get used to it, it can cause a lot of death, especially on stage 6. However, once you start making some serious money in a few years, you can just get caught up in designing the perfect drug for each disease and then creating the production layout for it in tight factory spaces.
Some reviewers have mentioned that drug designing is a simple matter of increasing or decreasing the concentration but I think that those players have not yet discovered other aspects of drug designing which really compel you to look at all the possibilties and then create that Viagra-like drug that will change the world!
The best part, perhaps, is that all these complexities offer value to those players who wish to indulge in them. If you just want to keep it simple, you can easily make enough money by just producing simple generic drugs.

Awe is a color tile game that revolves around populating a 3-Dimensional shape with various objects, or as the game calls them: Assets. In order to purchase these Assets you must have "Awe", which is collected by clicking on tiles in the order the game tells you. Once you have placed so many of each Asset, and you place the final Asset down, you win the level.
The game is pretty straight forward, and there isn't much more depth to it than that. It also doesn't really explain much and I almost didn't play the game at all because of it. You just kind of have to click randomly around until you figure out what to do.
I'm not too sure this game qualifies as "Puzzle", because there isn't really much problem solving involved. The game can unfortunately almost be boiled down to a "Match The Color" activity. I feel like this might be fun for a young demographic, but in its current state it's not really even relaxing. It feels rather tedious and there are certain mechanics that make it infuritating at times. For example, you have to wait for the 3D object to rotate all the way around in order to get the colored tiles you want, which adds a rather unnecessary waiting mechanic.
To be fair though, Awe is $0.99 USD, so for what it has I think its passable, but not worth picking up unless you really don't have anything else to do.

Oh how I've missed dfo. ♥ It's still just as great as it was before.
Edit:
Okay, now that I'm over the initial shellshock from the return of this game, let me just say to those of you who played dfo when it was with Nexon, it's back and better than ever.
Pros:
•Fast-paced dungeon runs
•Amazing particles and effects keep you coming back for more
•Events to help you level your characters are almost always happening
•A plethora of classes and sub-classes to try
•Rare+ Drop rate is fairly high
•Free Auction House is still a thing ♥
Cons:
•It's still just as grindy as it was before
•The grinding is still very monotonous as you will be playing different versions of the same dungeon numerous times
•Without consumables, the exp does slow down considerably at higher levels, but not enough to make you quit the game
•The PvP is still very unbalanced
•Boring story (pro: you can skip it all cutscenes)
The game still offers hours of scouring dungeons and beating up all sorts of mobs. With plenty of itemized events that will help jump start a new character, it's easy to get into the swing of DFO even if you're a newcomer. A lot of people complained about how easy it is to level now, but isn't that what these types of games are for? I mean, honestly, who wants 100+ hours of basic dungeon runs just to reach awakening? No one, that's who.
Anyway, you can expect carnage in both PvE with different dimensional maps and dungeons as well as PvP with modes like 1 on 1, Elimination, Team Matches, and Free-For-All. Although it doesn't really take a ton of skill to win in PvP (it's a mixture of your build, level, and hitboxes if you ask me), I still feel like dfo lacks the proper matchmaking that would make it more enjoyable. However, just like most mmos, you'd want to wait until level cap until PvP anyway.
If storytelling plays an integral role in your choice of MMO, dfo may not be for you. This is moreso for those arcade beat-em-up types that love to put the smackdown on a group of mobs and melting away several health bars on bosses.
After years of not seeing dfo, I'd recommend it more now than I would have before.

The most fundamental problems with this game are:
1) While Free To Play doesn't always equal Pay To Win etc, the main problem with this title is that they give you a heap of extra random characters (and in fact specific ones too!) as rewards, but you can't keep them without paying money... and the rewards have a time limit.  You are able to win some of the precious purchasable tokens as rewards, but nowhere near enough to keep up with the characters you receive.
2) While the game lets you play on a variety of places, and in fact makes you sign up with a random external system... there are no in game links to the external system, and they seem to have removed the ability for this Steam version to properly synch with the other devices. I believe some people can and have done this, but either it's been removed from this version, or if you didn't immediately agree then your one opportuniy to do this is never repeated.
3) Lack of in-game support.  Sure - everyone who has played PQ or even anything like it knows the basics.  And there is a tutorial mode which is ridiculously hand-holding, but... later when you want to look up stupid technical things, it is quite difficult to navigate.
4) Everything suddenly gets tied to PvP, which causes everything to be heavily Pay to Win.  There's not enough story of appropriate level to keep people playing on a PvE level... so you either fork out cash to level, or you ... stop playing?
Problem: I love superheroes.  I love Puzzle Quest.  This... is... almost? ish? what people should expect from a free-to-play game that works on phones and tablets (at least these days) but I have objections to games that make you stop playing them as a game mechanic... especially on a PC.  Sorry - it's a stupid design.

Don't expect long playing sessions because of the helath regeneration system, but the deafault heal time plus 5 regenerating health packs usually allow you to play three-four games every two hours or so. I've been holding off on my review, but given the current state of things I wanted to just say some things in defense of this game.  Before I get to that, I'd like to simply admit that the game certainly has faults and really has no end game to speak of right now.  Plenty of piddly little bugs, some even experience some game breaking issues, though I for one have never experienced these.  The servers definitely need to be upgraded to handle the structures once / if more players join up, and the AI / pathing needs to be entirely reworked.
That all said, this game only recently came out on steam and there is plenty of time for that stuff to be addressed.  What's in game right now is an enjoyable world to explore and build in, if not a bit small thanks to flight.  The building mechanics are on point and with a few tweaks, I feel that combat could actually be pretty enjoyable.  I for one enjoy the slow leveling on offical servers, but private servers mean you can bypass this at a whim if you just want to be all powerful and build all the things.
I hear people complain about the devs but honestly I think they've been very open with communications, which has got to be difficult for such a small company.  I've enjoyed the dev streams when they have them and occassionaly speaking with them on the forums and in the discord.  They're an active group of devs who push out patches every week (for better or for worse) and while these patches could definitely stand to go through some more community feedback prior to dropping, BIS has been pretty good about adjusting their changes back down in accordance with our feedback.
The game has great potential but will probably take some time to get there.  If you're expecting to drop your money and be thrilled with the game this year, it's probably best to just hold onto your cash.  If you want a more relaxing experience and the joy of patch notes each week, the game is well worth its price tag.  The Halloween update is coming and while full of silly stuff I'm fairly excited for it, along with the possibility of stronger monsters at night.  I know things seem dark right now but I've been involved with other games from much bigger developers that took quite some time to iron out, with some just dropping off the face of the planet after years of work.
I just hate seeing all the hate because it's still so early and to just call it because things aren't going exactly the way we want just....sucks.

Big Pharma is an enjoyable business simulation, puzzle hybrid with many different scenarios and starting conditions that widely vary. A single playthrough will only take between 2-10 hours, but each run is a new experience with a different combination of competitors, starting ingredients and ingredient traits [side effects + catalysts + cures].
Pros
Replayable (that's an understatement)
Decent soundtrack
Relatively short playthroughs
Many different scenarios
Competitive AI
Problem-solving
Perceivable Cons (What I also like about Big Pharma!)
All machines are puzzle pieces with unique parameters
All floors have finite space with a limited # of sockets (few import/export slots & little floor space)
Crossing belts is not simple
Only 8 categories of cures/diseases
A limited # of ingredients
This is not necessarily a tycoon-styled game, but if you like solving puzzles, then you may enjoy Big Pharma. If you hate puzzles, then find something else. Big Pharma is definitely a problem solving, puzzle game. That's the core feature!

Beyond Earth is a good example of what's wrong with modern game development.
These days you buy a "core game" for full retail price and then pay more for DLC to add on all the things that would have been incorporated into the retail version of the game in the old days. The higher prices wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for multiplayer. Multiplayer game mechanics and single player game mechanics are utterly different, particularly for strategy games, and since MP is where the money is you end up with single player experience getting shorted. Beyond Earth doesn't have even half of the personality of Alpha Centauri because why would they bother with depth and richness when you're expected to play against other people? As an integral game component other people suck. They're belligerent and foul mouthed, they cheat and drop connection if things don't go their way, and that's what modern games make their core mechanic. If you have a group of friends who game then you can have a good time with this, if not it is not and will never be worth your time or money.
You pay a lot more for a lot less.

Bullet time is far from an original concept in video games, quite a few times it is a token shoe-horned in element as a result of a developer running out of ideas. The best examples of bullet time in video games is when it is core part of the the game's elements. In this sense Bleed really uses the bullet time well with it being a bullet hell shoot and having a triple dash ability making the tiniest gap in the projectiles an escape route. The levels a really well designed making a good difficulty curve, this however brings me the flaw of the game which is the length. I kid you not when I say there are seven levels in total and each one is quite short (6-10 mins), there is increased difficulty, arcade mode and alternate character that try to extend the length but the game remains short. There are a few other problems with the game like the fact that the upgrade systems is largely useless the soundtrack while nice is really short and repeats a lot. I guess at five dollars you get what you pay for but still a bit steep for the length for the game so try to get it on sale.

I've played Magic: the Gathering consistently for almost two years so I think I have decent experience to write a review.
Magic Duels has a lot of ups and a lot of downs, it plays out very well and I have had alot of fun with it, yet one bug really ruins it, the bug skips your main phase if you have an instant in your hand and nothing else to play and working your hand around this bug is much harder than it sounds, it also cancels out any activated abilities that you could have activated had you not had that instant in hand. Outside of that, I don't really see any problems with the game, only a few improvements that I would like to include:
-Make deck buliding easier, the deck building in it's current state has almost no advanced searching, you can't look up cards by set or more importantly by keyword. These are all available on the Gatherer so I don't understand why they can't be made available in game. The layout could use improving too, at the moment it's very cluttered and fiddly to use.
-Make grinding slightly easier, it takes 150 coins to get a booster which equals about 5 wins, I think everyone woud appreciate it if you got 5-10 coins on a loss aswell to help with the grind.
-Trading, it would be fantastic if trading was available, it would approve gameplay significantly by allowing people to make the decks that they really want to while developing the community.
Overall it's a fun game and I hope the devs. listen to my feedback because with a few fixes this could be a great game, if you don't want to buy it now I'd stay optimistic and keep an eye on reviews.

1. Free to play implementation is mostly well done. It should be a long and hard process to get cards for free. The one thing I would have preferred is an option to buy from a selection of premade decks for the cost of completing a few story modes. I feel this would be more tempting to new players as they will want to add to their initial deck or get new ones, but not be as disheartening as having to cobble a deck from the odd assortment of story awarded cards and whatever you can get from boosters right away. Yes you can buy cards but you also need to stoke the fire for people to want them. Think of it as a free sample at the deli counter in the grocery store. You want to hand out something that gets people fired up so they want to drop their cash.
2. Despite warnings of bugs I have not encountered any yet. I'm sure I'll find one eventually but for now the play has been mostly smooth.
3. Buying cards in the store, then going to my collection and immediately being prompted to go to the store is a bit aggravating. It's a minor annoyance but it's one of those things that makes me shake my head. More specifically I know it fuels gamer rage over companies being soulless cash generators and little more. If I were talking to marketing I would talk about the hidden costs of these little things that tend to mount up and turn players off.
4. Placement of the skip attack/confirm attack buttons boggles me. Sometimes I get carried away and want to slaughter my opponent so much that I forget that when the attack phase starts, the skip attack button is above the attack with all, and then the confirm attack button appears where the skip attack button is. This is just poor design as button placement should be consistent with intended actions.
5. Daily quests are mostly good. Although one of my first ones is to play a bunch of cards with alternative casting costs, of which I have next to none. Most of the others have been either easy or were fun to make a deck for.
6. The one major problem I do have is that the RNG for drawing cards is insane. In real life it is unlikely you will draw three hands in a row of all spells. Realistically there are few if any players who want to play if they draw less than three mana sources. Many people concede outright in real life or after a couple of turns of not drawing any and watching an opponent draw plenty. Likewise mana flood can also be an issue, but less so. For folks like me who are aware of the possibilities this is less frustrating, for others it can be a depressing matter to restart a duel against an AI or have to concede against a real player for something that cannot be helped (unless your deck is way out of tune). Again it may behoove the developers to allow more non-penalty mulligans at least for hands with 0 or 1 land. A little love also wouldn't hurt for those times your opening draw has all of your copies of one spell. While some folks may like a freebie win against a hobbled opponent; I believe many of us would be perfectly happy to give those up for a little more even-ness.
My overall impression is positive. I would give it a 7/10 for folks who like magic or other card games. The story mode helps get you started with coins and while I feel that process needs some improvement; it is done in a manner that at least prevents takes the game from what would be an unplayable to state to one of mild enjoyment.
Just, no.

I wasn't sure what to expect, but liked the aesthetic.
Turns out it's a nice, sedate-paced memory/puzzle/pattern game, which lacks hand-holding but the discovery of how it works is part of the joy.
If you like the idea of having to pay attention and think about how you could possibly match the required colours, when they just don't exist on your weird polygon planet (yet), give it a try. You can pick it up for a few minutes, since it auto-saves when you exit to the main menu, or spand an hour or so getting a few planets completed. None of the achievements require excessive skill, patience or lateral thinking, but at the same time it's not just a case of "play game, get 100%"
I feel like listing tips about how to lock colours, what seasons do, LR and RL reading directions... but I've had a rewarding experience working it all out so I'll just say there's more depth, planning, and occasional surprises that you'd get in a Simon (pattern copying) game, and whilst some reviews complain about the interface etc. I think it's mostly just fine.

故事背景：主角以杀人的罪名入狱却没有相关的记忆，在监狱中被重点看守，除了一个带红帽子的男人没有人可以和他说话，还经常被全身麻醉检查身♂体，唯一的朋友是一只常被狱警欺负的警犬，主角想越狱弄清事情的真相，久而久之他发现监狱的后门没有任何守卫。后来的某一天，红帽子告诉他那只狗死了，主角一怒之下决定越狱！打晕了红帽子，换上了他的衣服。（这就是视频中主角的装束来历）

等等

I don't know about this one honestly. The game's cheap and I got it on sale, but even at a low price the game didn't really feel worth it. The game looks nice and the music's not awful for what it is, but that's about where my praise for the game ends. The game's menus are very lackluster and the game lacks any sort of tutorial or explanation, and for the sort of game it is makes it very frustrating as it’s not an intuitive experience. The entire game boils down to Simon Says and the additions they add to the game make the game less fun. (The solutions are now hidden and flash on and off, a “seasons” mode is introduced that requires matches to be done at specific times or you have to wait another rotation, ect), and those are poorly explained (there’s a single message explaining that you can “hold” specific colors in seasons mode, but even this confused me at first), and there’s no create-a-level/endless feature once you get past the maps included in the game.
While the presentation was good, it lacked much substance at all and just became frustrating to complete, which is a shame because I really wanted to enjoy a puzzle/god game like Populus.

In general, I like the game and the idea behind it. Basically this is a FPS/action-type puzzle game. You can switch between a human, a dog and an eagle. They have different capabilities and skills. There are several levels of maze where you need to break through using your talented brains. It's actually quite interesting and fascinating to solve those puzzles. It took me some time but I felt really great once they were solved. However, you might find it a bit difficult to control in the beginning. I do recommend the author should consider adding a bit more information in terms of controlling the characters and general stuffs like picking things up or rotating things. Other than that, I think it's quite an interesting game and well worth the money for an Indie game.

I don't really understand the reason for the mixed reviews on this. I'm new to Citadel, but I've played Ark, Conan, 7 Days, and tons of others, and this isnt any worse than those. I'm not deep in to the game yet, but I thought I'd post my initial impressions anyway.
Pros:
Beautiful world.
Building Mechanics - Really like building on this, more than any other I think.
The levelling system - At least at the beginning, it really makes some difficult choices on what to unlock first, and spurs you on to get the next level for something else.
Flying! I didn't like the broomstick at first - Mana guzzling is something of an understatement. However, it's easy to make and store mana potions and for such a powerful early mount, it makes sense to have such a cost.
I've not done any taming or anything like that yet, but I'm itching to get my hands on some of those dragons I've seen in the pictures.
The combat so far is good - better than most. You can choose an axe, staff, gauntlet or wand, or you can have a mixture of the two. You can assign spells you unlock to these weapons and the enemies don't just stand there to take the punch either, they're darting around you, in and out, as any player might.
Its early access, there are bound to be some bugs and crashes - I've been lucky, I havent found one yet.
Cons:
As I said, I haven't done any taming yet, but from what I can gather, the tames you do aren't permanent. Basic tame lasts for 30 mins - that sucks! BUT you can make scrolls that increase the time, up to 2 weeks I think. Thinking about it in that perspective, I guess thats equal to the Ark timers so not much of a con really.
People. I'm a PvE player, always have been and always will be. I tend to stick to myself as well, rather than joining other people and forming alliances. Having said that... the biggest con to this game at this point in time is the lack of players. I've been lucky to find a server with more than 5 people on at once. This is terrible - but I blame the reviews mostly for that.
- Watch a gameplay video! Read up about it, not just peoples opinions but about the game itself, and then decide. If you like any of those other games I mentioned, I dont think there is any reason why you wouldnt like this. Take a chance.
Loading time. It does take quite some time to load. If any of you have played Ark on a server with mods, you know what I mean. It's not QUITE as bad as that, but it does take some time to load up at first.
PvE servers aren't completely PvE. I really didn't like this at first, but the more I think about it, the more it grows on me. From what I can gather, you can't be attacked and killed by other players - but your base CAN be raided. This, for me, combines the best feature of PvP into PvE. I dont like fighting other players - but placing traps, finding ways to hide my treasure, it lends some more depth to the game for when your base is built. I like it. I dont completely understand it all yet, I don't know if, for example, you'd be able to defend your base or just have to stand there watching..
That's about it. Longer than I meant it to be, but thats my two cents. Citadel is definitely worth a look if you like the games I mentioned above.

I played DFO back when it was under Nexon, so I'm not completely new to the game.

But but, its back!
If you enjoy old school beat em ups and very little P2W elements, you found your game.
Since it's a big "complaint" I'll address the fatigue system first. For every dungeon you start it costs you three FP (with exceptions). Then each room is one point. Now premium and premium plus allow more, but you will do alot of dungeons before it completely runs out. It also doesn't hurt since it encourges you to play multiple characters. Each character has it's own pool of FP so you will have a few "mains" to mess around with (which you should, because this gives account or "family" wide bonuses for multiple leveled characters).
You are handed FP potions that restore from 30 to 100+ fatigue points through events, buying some using ingame "mileage points" that you gain from clearing dungeons or through buying cash shop items. So if you really want to grind on one character for a long time, you are given the option. Long story short, the FP system isn't much of a hinderence.
There are events constantly running to help you level up and get decent gear, but most of the time you will be smashing your way through each stage, doing cool looking, screen clearing attacks. I reccommend looking up youtube videos of each class to see how they look at higher levels of play. There isn't a wrong choice*, you will be swapping between at least three to four characters and it took a few hours to burn through my FP on my main. Having alts will help you level up more alts in the future since they can assist you in your dungeons.
*(disclaimer: We are getting raids later on and yes, some classes perform way better than others in that content. Does not mean your class isn't good/useful, just makes raid runs quicker and more efficient. This applies to top tier content only. Neople is constantly changing the balance of each class for the raids, so you could top tier one month and trash the next. YMMV. So you are better off choosing a class/classes you enjoy.)
