you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Oh my, this game was quite long...23 hours for the campaign and the expansion (without any skirmishes or scenarios).
Dungeons 2 does A LOT of things right compared to its predecessor, but it also still has some glaring flaws. More on that later. Basically every mission has you expanding your dungeon, doing research, recruiting units and sending them to the overworld where they fight like in an RTS. Which is funny, because there's a game called "war for the overworld" and that has nothing to do with fighting on said overworld :D
The core gameplay works surprisingly well, but also, unsurprisingly, both dungeon building as well as the RTS component aren't as good as in their big role models (Dungeon Keeper and probably Warcraft III). Building a dungeon is way easier than in War for the Overworld (WftO) for example and fighting within the dungeon also works very well. Contrary to Dungeon Keeper (DK) and WftO though you will not be fighting any rival dungeon lords or alliance bastions in your dungeons -  at least not in the campaigns. Your dungeon will regularly be invaded by armies though, which you have to repell with your troops, spells and traps. Annoyingly, traps can be easily disabled if you don't pay attention and become completely worthless. Moreover, ordering your units to attack the enemy costs mana and you need to have the relevant spell researched. Otherwise you have to just pick up the desired units and drop them in front of the enemy (which in itself is difficult, since you only have small thumbnails in the creature list as well as their obscure names, but not which tier they are)...that is tedious. On the other hand, using the "rally" spell means ALL units will drop what they're doing and rush to meet the enemy (and more often than not their death). It would have been great to be able to create warbands like in WftO, so that your weaker "production units" can continue working.
What I mean by that is that Dungeons 2 has 3 unit tiers. You start at level 1 and have to manually upgrade each unit twice to get the highest tier (which isn't even the best in every instance...for example, you don't want to replace all your healers with more specialized units, so you have to be careful what and when you upgrade). Anyway, weaker units die very quickly, but you may want to keep some around to keep your production going, while the rest of your army fights the enemy off. Speaking of production: It was perhaps not the smartest idea to a) have your actual workers count towards your army cap (a separate cap would have been fine), since you do need a lot of them in the beginning to excavate, build, mine and produce, but having to rely on fighting units to keep your dungeon production going is just annoying. It's also going to cause some weird "build paths" that are just unnatural.
The rest of the game plays out on the overworld, where you can take direct command of your units...at least in theory. The goals are pretty much always the same: destroy this or kill that, but the campaigns have enough diversity to not get too boring. Sometimes you have to invade a rival dungeon, which gets messy, because you're in a dungeon, but you're also still in the overworld...but there's no minimap for it!!!! Speaking of campaigns: the "Game of Winter" DLC is probably the only one you want to buy, the others are just unvoiced scenarios that string together into "mini campaigns" so to speak. Not really worth the asking price imho, but Game of Winter has a complete 8 mission long campaign and introduces a third faction: the undead.
This brings the game to three distinct factions. All play basically the same, but have different units and traps. The undead are, in the beginning at least, the weakest however. At least in my opinion. They do not get access to a healer at tier 2 like the other 2 factions and their units do not really regenerate hit points. The other factions have healing chambers which quickly heal units up after a fight. The only real "advantage" the undead have is that their units will instead revive if they die anywhere, including the overworld. The other 2 factions have to invest more heavily into research to get to that point and even then it's a very slow process. With the undead you "only" need to research a grave yard and build enough graves and you can revive your army within 2 minutes or so. The other factions also have to drag their "dead" to the healing chambers for them to revive, which is impossible during a fight, since your workers will just run away. The undead shine later in the game with powerful ranged units and devastating aoe abilites like blizzard or bat swarm (which turns the bloodsuckers from being not used at all too absolutely overpowered).
Sadly, the AI is just terrible and your units will simply die in droves in the dungeon and require a lot of micro on the overworld. Collision and pathfinding is also a bit of an issue, with units just mindlessly walking into each other, instead of letting other units through...
Dungeons 2 offers a very funny campaign and a good expansion for a pretty low price now. I'd say it's worth it, but maybe you're just not a fan of the silly humour. Check that out beforehand, because I think that's what a lot of the enjoyment may come from. And please, devs, for the love of all that is evil implement a persistent upgrade system like in WftO in your next Dungeons game...to have to research the same stuff over and over again in the campaign is just tedious, especially since the game is SO slow to get going.

I have never played the first Dungeons game, but I have played and beaten Dungeon Keeper 2 many times and as of writing this review, I have beaten the entire campaign of Dungeons 2, so I feel comfortable writing this review.
- Excellent Aesthetic
The game looks great. I don't really need to elaborate much on this, because you can see this for yourself with screenshots and videos. All I can say is that the animations look good, the transformation of lands that you claim in the Overworld are cool to watch and overall the game is very polished aesthetically.
- The Narrator and Humor
The same man from the Stanley Parable (something I only realized after he made a reference to it), you can expect a lot of humor from him and this game is definitely a more tongue-in-cheek successor to the original Dungeon Keeper series. While I think the humor can be a bit of a downside (what are "Little Snots"? The name isn't horrible, but it isn't great, either), it's also plenty refreshing. The narrator will spend most of the game prodding you when you're being lazy and commenting humorously on the events of the game. I'm willing to bet they spent a fair amount of their budget on him alone and it shows.
Expect him to make many pop-culture references to the Lord of the Rings, Supernatural, Warcraft and so on. This game is a bit of a parody, but stands on its own two feet, as well.
- The Gameplay
There are plenty of cons that I'll get to in a minute in terms of gameplay, but if you've ever played Dungeon Keeper 2, you can expect this to play quite similarly. There are technically two groups you can play in this game, but at first you'll start off with the Horde, who are very well balanced, I feel, and the easiest to play as. The others I won't spoil, but while they are fun and quite powerful after upgrading, they are very imbalanced and easily toppled if you don't prepare plenty of traps early on and build up your forces. The more time you spend building your dungeon and playing about, the more likely it is they will be obliterated.
The Horde doesn't have this problem, however. As long as you recruit plenty of Orcs and provide a Hospital (earned in later missions), you'll be fairly safe. Later in the game it will help to also focus on traps, but unlike the second faction you can play as, you won't be in any immediate danger if you just avoid taking huge risks like digging out obvious spider nests underground or antagonizing the Overworld faction too much (called The Alliance).
Now I'd like to talk about a few cons of the game. Specifically, I'd like to state that while it's a very close Dungeon Keeper game, it is a bit lacking. Not enough that I'd say "don't get this game" because it's totally worth getting, at least the base game, which I've enjoyed immensely. What's lacking, though, is a sense of progress. You recruit a lot of factions, but the game feels like it cuts off to encourage you to buy the DLC. There's a third faction that they clearly sectioned off behind DLC and your character, "The Ultimate Evil" never fully recovers his form. [[[REDACTED]]] It's a fun dungeon-building/RTS game (the RTS part comes in when you toss your minions out into the Overworld, where you control them to destroy the Alliance buildings and forces).
I'll summarize as quickly as possible in a TL;DR.
Pros:
- Great Dungeon-building, plenty of units and upgrades to keep things fresh.
- Enjoyable humor, excellent narrator (from the Stanley Parable).
Cons:
- Felt a little (and I stress the word "little" as much as I can) cut off and intentionally unfinished. You get a resolution to one problem, but it's clear the DLC is where the rest of the game is finished.
- Second controllable faction is unbalanced and can be hard to start off as. I hear the third faction in the DLC is even harder, but I haven't purchased that yet (though I very likely will).
I recommend this game. Absolutely. Even without the resolution to the story that I wanted, it had a decent one and I really enjoyed playing it. I say that even after playing one of the levels as the second faction and getting obliterated early on because of its imbalanced start, so I'm praising the game even while I'm frustrated by it. That should give you an idea of how much I enjoyed it.
I don't know if I'd recommend it at full price, but $15-20 on sale? Yeah, sure. Definitely worth that. I'm eager to try out the DLC when I can get it. Hopefully it isn't as frustrating as I've heard and offers a finale to the story that is really needed.

Robots have attacked your Blade Runner dystopian city, go explode all the robots, the end. A nice relaxing FPS campaign with story on rails, to escape for 10 hours, when strolling through once on normal. Perfect for those who grew up on the likes of Quake.
Redux version looks and moves pretty good, considering it was originally released in 2011, the first title from this small Polish developer. There's a substantial quantity of map areas to progress though, all playing out reassuringly as you'd expect, with ambush after ambush, never having too long to get bored or lost. Models can be a little angular, of course, and there's plenty of invisible walls, with low barriers totally unjumpable in general (the way things always used to be, heh).
But the double tap dash makes strafing feel nippy and fun, as you play bull fighter with charging metal Gorilla thingies. While the boss battles are nice and big and obvious for the most part. Although, saying this, I totally failed to figure out what I was supposed to do for the first phase of the giant statue fight, having to YouTube it. Also, the final battle had some trouble too, with *too many* handy EMP barrels accumulating, going off and borking proceedings. While I'm griping: there were a few places where I got unfairly insta-jibbed - a set piece Gorilla charging down a corridor kept clipping me, and a lift did me in towards the end  when trying to get a currency pick-up, right after a big fight (I had to redo a couple times).
There are effectively 11 different weapons, separated as 5 different modes between 2 gun platforms. Plus a sword that might be Darth Vader's windscreen wiper (pretty cool and effective). The CLN and NRG guns that you start off with only have one mode each initially, with another 4 on each being unlocked and upgraded entirely at the discretion of how you choose to spend your accumulated credits (which you pick up from hiding spots and are spontaneously awarded for killing stuff too). The weakest point of the action was trying to remember, in the heat of battle, how to dial up the particular weapon mode I wanted. After the 'cyber-katana' had been aquaired, using 'Q' to toggle weapons has a third (disruptive) stop, so then it has to be F1-F3 keys to directly pick weapon, and a number key 1-5  for the specific mode (mouse wheel being too slow for that). Selection was a skill I eventually started to get the hang of, with time and familiarity.
There was decent variety between the weapon modes. CLN (traditional weapons): machine gun, shot gun, grenade launcher, (guided) rockets, mines. NRG (electrical stuff): 'plasma' rapid fire, 'blaster' short range AOE lightening (looks cool), 'mortar' AOE grenade, 'rail gun' and finally 'smart gun' are kind of weird, in that they let you shoot straight through any scenery, and also see enemy skeletons through any scenery... (Although this doesn't always let you hide from their fire entirely.) The options let you play in the style you prefer, but also string together a few combinations: e.g. stunning a big enemy with your shotgun's secondary fire (upgrade), so that it'll sit there and take a rocket straight to it's face (where-as some of them will actually dodge these deftly, at times). Or gravity genade a bunch of grunts together to be blown up by a regular greande, or whatever...
Hard Reset seems to try telling some kind of story via it's animated comic strips that are slotted in between sections (so every ~30-50 minutes of play). But this mostly consists of our protagonist dropping the "F***!" bomb relentlessly, which is apparently the main source of humour (aside from the pushy, talking sales terminals, heh). There's always someone popping up an occasional spoken exchange via the HUD during play too, so you never feel totally alone. There are various sci-fi notions and phrases flopped out, but it's never really of any major consequence and often fails to relate to what you're actually doing in a meaningful way. Which is generally: go push this button to open this, killing the stuff on the way there and back, etc. Although, right at the start, it does feel briefly atmospheric, like you're being attacked by makeshift little kill-bots, improvised from power tools by this invading AI, or whatever.
Anyway, no need to worry too much about anything, just dodge and shoot all the baddies! Then there's plenty of scope to ratchet up the difficulty, if a challenge is your thing, and a ludicrous number of achievements too (140 odd). Enjoy!

I picked up bleed in the canada day sale a while back, and it sat in my backlog for quite a while.  Just a few days ago I decided to play it, and was quite amazed at what I found.  Bleed is a platformer shooter that also has some bullet hell mechanics.
The game is about Wryn, a girl who is trying to kill all the heroes in her time period to become the best hero ever.  There isn't much else to the story, but the game doesn't need it.
The gamepad controls for this game are great.  I used the Xbox 360 pad and after a while of practice it was quite easy to control Wryn.  It plays like a twinstick shooter, one pad to move the other to shoot.  The right trigger is for jumping which you can move in any direction with the stick. Unfortunately I did try the keyboard and mouse controls and found it lacking.  The keyboard can't compete with a pad, if the developer made it so the mouse controled Wryn's movements it would have been viable but since the arrow keys control it's unusable.  Gamepad is definetely recommended.
The game does play great though. It is a platforming shooter and the shooting is quite great.  There are 12 weapons to choose from that you can change during the level.  Some of them shoot great others are harder to shoot but have more power.  One of the main mechanics of bleed is slowing down time, which you use to dodge projectiles and move around precise areas.  When I started playing the game I ignored the slowdown as I found it not worth it, but really you learn later how important it is, and with a little bit of practice you should be able easily use it.
The music for this game is 8-bit and I feel they do fit the levels and the bosses. Each level has different music but each boss has the same music.  I enjoyed the 8-bit music but after a while they do get old.
Bleed is quite short but for the kind of game it is, this works well. In about 2 hours you can complete the campaign on normal, and after that there are two higher difficulties that require a lot more work.  Achievement wise, most of them require just a lot of time and understanding of game mechanics, and enemy patterns.  There is a guide for all of the secret achivements because I honestly didn't understand them, they are harder to do then understand though.  As for the last bunch of achievements the ones that require you to beat the arcade at certain difficulty levels are really tough.  You have to beat the entire game with one life, it will take a lot of practice and a lot of restarting to get them, but they are possible.
Overall I'd say Bleed is a great game.  The controls are good and the mechanics are original.  It will take you between 2-20 hours depending on how many achivements you go for, and at 5$ it's amazing.  If you do not have a gamepad though, I can't really recommend it.

I can't really recomment this game because you get so little from the cool concept i initially had in mind (having a shitbox and driving it through a world). The game itself is fun for no more than 4 hours when you get to do basically everything you can in the game.
Personally, I think this concept of a game would fit better in an open world scenario with a huge map.
The game also fails to show you the real pain of dealing with a dilapidated old car because all the mechanics are dumbed down to a bare minimum: there are a couple of parts that do a specific thing, they have a durability system and they are very predictable when they break making the whole idea of fixing your car very easy to deal with when you get the hang of the game. There are no oil leaks, no engine overheating, no spontaneous breakdowns that define old cars, basically the relaibility of the cars is extremely simplified to a durability system.
The driving becomes extremely boring after a couple of hours as it sufferes also from extreme simplification (no gear shifting) and you only have to keep pressing the up key with minor use of steering.
The environment is repetitive, boring, empty and lacks npcs, events, roads to explore. Everytime you enter a country you are forced to choose a route that is more or less a straight empty highway road (when you get closer to turkey you get a minor change of scenery, but that doesn't save the fact the world is so empty). You barely get to see cars on the road, you can count all the npc's in a country on two hands, the cities are empty, lifeless.
The concept of the game is very cool, but the implementation suffers greatly from dumbing down everything possible, from the car parts that break down, to the driving and trading system that is mostly fueled by random roadside locked boxes with items. You get the impression you have quite a choice for customizing your car, but you quickly realize only the last three items from each tier are worth and they also have minor differences between them.
So, if you are expecting an car adventure exploring different roads and experiecing life with a old car, you should look elsewhere as this game can't really offer that feeling.

Awe is, supposedly, a god game, but comes across as more of a meditative musical experience. You move from planet to planet, trying to maximize your "awe" in order to create foliage (green), landscapes (orange), ore (yellow), satellites (gray), and a wonder that serves as a sort of crown on to be placed on each finished planet. In order to unlock each of the various panel colors, you must press them in different orders (blue, green, green). This is more or less difficult by where on the planet you've placed your creations, as well as by the speed at which each planet spins. As you play more melodies, you earn more awe, and step-by-step get closer to crowning each planet. Once you've made a preset number of each colored tiles, the planet is considered complete and you move on to the next.
There's no real challenge to the game, but it's very pretty and relaxing. Worth the one dollar it's going for in store.

Have you ever been playing Half-Life 2 and wished you could shoot Rebels instead of Combine? (I know I did.) Well now you can thanks to the online-only Half-Life 2 Death Match. Released all the way back in 2004 for the PC, it only recently come to Mac courtesy of Valve's Steam service.
I actually don't like Half-Life 2 as much as Half-Life 1. I recognize it as a great game, just one that doesn't appeal to me. I like the story, the characters and setting. But there is one thing I can't stand: The combat. Something about it just feels really stilted and awkward. I could never quite be sure why, I just knew I didn't like it. So I was a little hesitant to pick up HL2 Death Match, but what did I find? It's not only good - it's ridiculously fun. Placing the game in a fast paced frag-fest somehow transformed it from being unplayable, to immensely enjoyable.
The premise here is simple: Get on a team or a Free For All (FFA) Map and start shooting. There's no multiple game types, complicated maps or weapons. But the game's simplicity is also in its favor. It's easy to learn and jump right into and have a good time without having a learning curve. Unless of course you are completely new to shooters online, you will be having fun right away.
Maps are diverse without being confusing. There are a number of larger outdoor settings in which to get around or several indoor settings where hallways are narrow confines that define the combat arena. One map has a control room which launches a missile after a few minutes that kills everyone outside. Once you hit the button an alarm goes off and everyone scrambles to get inside as the blast doors close. It's thrilling to slip under them just as they shut, but then you are locked indoors for a minute with everyone else trying to survive until the doors open again.
Half-Life 2's excellent physics are on full display here as crates and objects break, glass shatters, and the ragdoll of your dead enemy crumbles oh-so satisfyingly to the ground after a shotgun blast to the head. Explosions of any kind also cause hilarious results, with bodies flying through the air, and bouncing off walls due to a well placed grenade or rocket blast.
If you haven't played HL2, then the weapon load-out is also simple, but unique enough to keep things interesting. Everyone starts with a melee weapon, a pistol, a submachine gun and two grenades. So when you spawn you aren't helpless. In standard death match fashion, better weapons, ammo, armor and health are strewn about the maps for you to pickup. Learning the spawn locations of the superior weaponry will certainly help you get a leg up over the competition. My personal favorites are the shotgun, and the crossbow which serves as the game's sniper weapon. You also get an energy machine gun, and laser-mines which can be set on walls or the ground for the unsuspecting passer-by.
I found the rocket-launcher to be a little unwieldy as it's laser-guided only, so you can't just shoot and forget. If you move your aimer, the rocket follows. This works for and against you, I found. Suffice to say if you see a red laser dot near you or on a teammate, get out or the next thing you see will be your limp body flying through the air.
Most guns also have an alternate fire. The shotgun can fire two shells at once, the submachine gun can pickup grenades for an underhand launcher, and the energy gun can also get an insta-kill ball of plasma that fries your opponents into little bits. But most unique of all is that everyone also starts with a Gravity Gun which allows you to push or pickup objects and then shoot them at other players. Almost anything you pickup serves as an instant death, whether it's a crate, table, shovel or toilet you launch. High-use gravity gun matches are humorous as all manner of objects fly around the map in an attempt to crush the opposing team or players.
The game is of course built on Valve's own Source engine, and despite being a little dated the game still looks great. It's not going to win any awards these days, but it's still visually pleasing and it certainly doesn't detract from the experience. Since it doesn't have the fanciest eye-candy around, the game should easily run on just about any computer, unless you have one that is more than several years old. I encountered the occasional odd spawning glitch, or visual bug but it was rare, and the game was smooth and never crashed.
Sound also remains minimal with no music. What you will be hearing is the patter of footsteps, the constant chatter of gunfire, muffled explosions or the sound of dying. I personally like to put on some iTunes to blast away to, but the minimalistic approach to sound doesn't take away from the gameplay at all. What is there stands out sharply and clearly with no interference and allows you to easily identify what is going on. Voice chat is also present, which is easy to use with the press of a button, and is crisp and clear.
At only $5, and a few cents when on sale, Half-Life 2 Death Match is a no-brainer. Whether you are a Half-Life fan to begin with, or just a fan of online shooters, the game is simple, outrageous fun. It's easy to jump into, but remains entertaining even after hours of play. The player-base is great, and there's always several matches available to hop into for Team play or FFA. Buy it and start launching toilets and barrels at your friends today.

So I began my journey, a lonely wanderer seeking my soul out in the wastes of ex-Soviet bloc states with only a little more money in my pocket than the entirety of which my destination probably spent on their transportation budget in the last year.
But, hark, a rail station in the distance. Overwhelmed by curiosity, I pull off to the side of the road, killing the engine and shutting off my headlights. In the pouring rain, I eagerly partake of the bounty of cigarettes and coffee held in poorly-guarded boxes, and load down the boot of my trusty Laika with the commodoties. I continue on my way.
The road bridge is out, so I am forced to lumber my ill-suited wheels over the rugged and poorly-maintained railroad tracks over the metal bridge a couple kilometers back down the road, and a frontage road brings me to an old general store and gas station. I decide to top off my half-empty tank (or, is it half-full?) and go to pay my bill and sell my ill-gotten gains to the attendant.
After about 3 or 4 trips from trunk to shopkeep, laden with tobacco and ground beans, she pipes up.

The lever creaks and a satisfying 'click' signals my despair. A fountain of paper-wrapped nicotine and murky black coffee beans geysers out of the storefront.

Battlerite is one of the most surprising games I've ever played. Originally introduced to back in early 2017, I never got a chance to play it until it went F2P. I'm going to say that I was surprised at how fun it was to play, how balanced it was, how enjoyable the characters were, and how quick it was to learn.
Many call Battlerite a "MOBA." Battlerite is to a MOBA as Overwatch is to a MOBA FPS in that, they sit just outside of that genre. Battlerite is all about elimination combat. You pick a champ and go either into a 3v3 or 2v2, depending on your preference. Your goal is to eliminate the other team while also claiming the orb in the middle of the arena for a health and energy advantage. If you were to compare this to a MOBA, than it's all about the teamfights and nothing more.
The champions in this game are all varied and likeable in their own aspects. While each are put into a melee, ranged, or support catergory, they all tend to have very diverse kits and play differently. One support may be heavily focused on healing while another is more centered around debuffing. It makes each champ vastly diverse form others who accompany a similar role. I'd also like to add that supports in Battlerite have amazing kits that don't feel recycled from one another.
Fun and getiing better :)

Game consists of 20 missions and in those missions you usually have to kill some targets. Every mission has rating points. If you kill an enemy that is not a target you will get negative points. However if you hide the body you will get your points back, so back to like it was. If an enemy spots you, and it doesn't take a long for an enemy to spots you, you will lose a lot of points, and he can alert other enemies. It's all up to you how do you want to play, but my guess is that everyone plays this game silently, so if enemy notices you, you can restart checkpoint. It also depends on which difficulty do you play. I usually play games on the hardest, but I've played this game on normal, since above normal you don't get hints, also enemies will spot you easier and there are more enemies. Game wasn't easy on normal either. You can use a lot of disguises in this game to decieve your enemies, however if you for example use cop's uniform every other cop will in a matter of seconds notice that you're not a real cop, since somehow they all know each other. You can use those instict hints to decieve enemies in those situations, but it all depends on how high is your instinct bar at that moment, and you can fill up your instinct bar by getting those ranked points(killing enemies and then hiding them, finding clues etc.). Completing main necessary objectives in this game gives you a lot of ranking points(main source of those ranking points). You can distract your enemies by throwing some objects, you can drag dead bodies, you can throw those bodies over the ledge, or hide them in closets, containers etc., or just leave them there, but that way you're risking of enemies finding the bodies in those situations. Agent 47's signature weapons are his guns, Silverballers, and his fiber wire. I mostly used only fiber wire and Silverguns in only necessary situations. You can kill your main enemies on few different ways usually. Poison their food, drop something on them etc. It's different in every mission.

First, the graphics are really ugly. The artistic direction aim to be "realistic" but lacks either the budget or the technology (Crysis released four years before, and looked better). Or maybe the talent?
Now the story is beyond ridiculous. Like in the first crysis, the main enemy is North Korea. But here, they invade the USA. Except that they did not have any alien archeology findings or decades to advance their "evil" agenda. No, it's just good old North Korea who invades the world. I mean, really? What will the next be ? Switzerland? Somalia? At least, Somalia government would easily be overthrown by an evil corporation or something. It's like they just did the game to make pro American propaganda. I mean, who's the more likely to invade the other, the USA or North Korea? Who is it that already tried to invade the other? Who is it that blockaded the other for decades, resulting in a lethal famine, killing more than 10% of the population? Who is it that lived less than a decade of peace in its entire history, and was nearly always the attacker? Not counting false flag wars, of course
Then the game. At the start, you get a very improbably grim look at Korean occupation. Soldiers everywhere (like if Korea had about as many soldiers as USA had people) in a town, where they needlessly brutalize and kill people, like if every North Korean was a psycho. A bit later, you get a fight scene with plenty of soldiers firing on you. You where just taken out of your home, so, no armor whatsoever, but you can sustain something like ten second of automatic weapon fire before going down. Well, to sum it all, immersion is impossible.

The easiest way to review Dungeons 2 is to say that it is clearly trying to mimic the style, gameplay, and humor of the Dungeon Keeper series by Bullfrog Productions, and succeeds admirably. If you've ever wanted DK3, you'll feel like you finally got your wish playing this game.
The original Dungeon Keeper series placed you in the role of the villain, building a mighty underground fortress populated by foul creatures ready to destroy any foolhardy "heroes" that came calling. It was a humorous and engaging take on RTS. Dungeons 2 starts there, and adds on an "overworld" element; your minions can leave your dungeon, and when they do are controlled like a traditional RTS game. The narrator (voiced by the amazing Kevan Brighting) is great from beginning to end, and there are other bits of humor throughout the game, such as the spell and upgrade descriptions or the names of the Naga that fight for you.
The campaign was enjoyable, and there are plenty of maps available for skirmish or multiplayer, if you want more after you've completed it. The one annoyance I had with the game were the couple of missions that placed you in charge of another faction; they seemed tacked on as an afterthought, and felt like they should have either been a second campaign entirely or simply removed.
Full disclosure: I did receive this for free as part of a Humble Bundle giveaway. That said, I'm looking forward to buying Dungeons 3.

Bloodline Champions is a unique, fast paced, action packed arena game that will get your heart pumping every single match. Unlike a traditional MOBA that requires you to farm NPC's and level up to make your Hero/Champion more powerful, there is nothing of the sort in this game. It is just 100% Player vs. Player action, from start to finish. Anyone looking for a nice change of pace from the traditional MOBA setting should try this game. Especially if what you love is fighting other players, rather than the boring and reptitiveness that is the "laning phase".

This game is the spearhead for the next wave of independent fighters.
Punch Planet charms players with it's own vibrant, minimalistic, retro, sci-fi-punk aesthetic that doesn't exist in competitive fighters today. It also echoes that of Steven Universe (the character Tyara seems to be a nod to the Gems...and WW respectively)
This art style also typically lends itself to catchy, cool, retro, synthesized beats which the soundtrack perfectly captures. (makes for great fighting music)
The game has a memorable roster so far (only 4)
all with their own unique fighting styles that very much live up to their dream function, with their personality beautifully expressed through their fighting style and battle cries a la street fighter. I can't wait to see the others.
The battle system feels like home! (I speak for myself)
The focus cancel mechanic borrowed from SF4 is amazing, and is what allows you to be creative with how you play, except in this game, you can cancel any normal move, and special move by tapping the same single button you last pressed. this mechanic has it's own meter bar that you must manage.
The parry mechanic becomes intuitive, and easy once you get the hang of it. in experienced battles, the parry will make you think twice about doing a lot of things, which makes for exciting gameplay. and the universal overhead/hop is a nice touch (maybe a nod to 3rd strike?)
If you're a competitive fighter looking for a new playground, Punch Planet won't disappoint.
Remember the game is a work in progress.
With that being said, it's this promising in it's alpha state, and i can't wait to see the final product. I believe in this project.

So I went into this game completely blind, and I've gotta say, overall I'm impressed.
Archeblade is a Free To Play, online Third Person Brawler. With a character system similar to League Of Legends (minus the free rotation system), and gameplay which I imagine is a dumbed-down version of the niche title, Anarchy Reigns (although honestly I've never played it, but I imagine it's similar; so take this with twelve metric tons of salt).
The game starts you off with enough "currency" to buy up to two different characters. As all characters are priced the same, you can pick the two you like (I'd reccomend picking two characters that are distinct from one another though so you can get used to a variety of different playstyles).
After playing the (optional) tutorial as a character named Valle - some form of blonde Valkyrie wielding a giant hammer - I was given a free 7 Gems (paid currency; hardly enough to get you anything). I then noticed a Training mode on the main menu. This mode allowed me to try any character I want against a couple of static bots. Useful for figuring out combos, both listed and unlisted (and by unlisted I just mean attacks that recover quick enough to be chained) and how a character feels in general.
My first match was a Free-For-All match, in which I had chosen Elika, a gun-toting, tan, dark elf lady with a bountiful chest, lucious legs and a
. She's kinda ugly, but I can see the appeal. She mows down her foes using a series of kicks and gun-fu; VERY reminicent of Bayonetta.
The game is very quick to pick up provided you're observant and already used to similar third-person brawlers (i.e., Dynasty Warriors experience will transfer a little bit here). Characters control using 6 buttons (not including WASD), for:
<> A light attack - Standard; leads into a combo of some sorts
<> A heavy attack - Can be any number of things; for Elika, it's a forward sliding kick that is followed up with a backwards dash and two gunshots, for Valle it's a series of 360-degree hammer spins. Can also be comboed with light attacks for unique moves.
<> A special move - Default keybinding is shift; again, this can be any number of things. For Elika it was a backstep, for Valle it was a forward dash. Costs stamina.
<> Jumping - Characters can use their light or heavy attacks while in mid-air.
<> Power Charge - Holding the ALT Key will change the properties of some moves in exchange for stamina usage. Some moves become capable of breaking guard, others do more damage, some even gain "super armor", which prevents the character from flinching (similar to it's usage in fighting games, but not exact)
<> Skill Buttons - Every character has two skills which cost RP gauge segements to use (RP being gained on-hit and being hit)
[/list]
The controls are quite intuitive, in my opinion, and responsive too (all my actions are done with purpose; I rarely misclick ).
Talking outside my first match or two, I've come to the conclusion that the characters are fairly balanced for the most part, with no characters outright dominating the field (however, there are cheap characters - looking at you, Renoah and Hyde). One issue I have though is that the characters all appear to be balanced for duels, rather than teamfights. This leads to some AoE buffs becoming stupidly strong when stacked (for example, Valle's regeneration), or duplicates of the same character in a fight becoming too strong as they can cover for eachother's weaknesses).
There is also an issue with juggling, as once you are knocked up in the air, successive hits from any source will keep you up there. This means that if you're laid into by multiple enemies at once, and they get past your guard, it's likely you'll die unless you have an ability that actively prevents it, such as DanMei's temporary invlunerability, or Renny's teleport. In duels though, juggling is much harder to pull off, and can only be done effectively with a few characters (others are just better set using their other comboes).
There are also some issues with hitboxes and animations. My best example would have to be DanMei, whose light attacks are far lunging. However, due to his large size and his melee attack's lunge, it is needlessly hard to hit targets that are at point blank as you can easily overshoot.
After poppin' some caps in foo's heads with my gun-fu, I came close to the top of the scoreboard on my first match. Unfortunately, I earned a meager amount of meceta (money) for my win (I earned around 70; characters cost 1400 each, and items can range from 800 to over 5000).
To sum this game up:
Third-person Brawler
Good outside of teamfights - Only decent in them
Considerably long unless you focus all your money on kitting out a single character. Pricing and meceta gain rates need adjusting. However, upon leveling up you get an extra 200 meceta, so that can speed you along a bit, especially at the earlier levels.
Moderate - Very low if you have decent prior experience with third-person brawlers.
Boobs, butts, thighs, abbs. Many of the character designs are quite sexualized. If you're the kind of person who legitimately believes that "trigger words" are a thing in written text, or tells people to check a privilege of some sorts. This game might not be for you.

Big Pharma is a very refreshing take on factory building that offers genuine satisfaction for coming up with the best production line you can think of.  Where similar games get by overloading with content and chaos--more things to build, higher volume, etc, Big Pharma rewards for elegant solutions.  It isn't about how much you produce.  It's about how you produce it.
For simplicity's sake, I will contrast Big Pharma with Factorio, which I also got a lot of enjoyment from.  Factorio is about managing resources and logistics--incredibly large numbers of exceedingly simple tasks that combine to create hectic situations.  The entire game (Factorio) can be summed up as deciding what you want to make, then ensuring the right buildings are getting the right amounts of all requisite materials in a massive and complicated chain involving dozens of buildings.  All gameplay revolves around that.
Big Pharma is absolutely nothing like that; rather, it is about design and decision making.  Where Factorio gets complicated, Big Pharma is merely complex.  In Big Pharma, you can make whatever sort of cure you like.  Expensive or cheap, whether you earn or lose money is determined by *how* you chose to make the product and whether it was a wise choice to make it at all considering demand, competition, and your current capabilities.  You can make crazy wonder drugs and lose money with a hasty production line a la Factorio, or you can put some thought into it and make millions.  The same applies to the cheap drugs.  Maybe you even allow a minor, negative side effect in the product to ensure economic viability.  It's up to you to determine what the right move is, and when you make that right move, you get genuine satisfaction out of it that games like Factorio are simply incapable of matching.
I am not saying that Big Pharma is better than Factorio.  I got a lot more time out of Factorio than I did from Big Pharma.  But I do believe the time I spent with Big Pharma was more enjoyable and satisfying, which is quite fitting.  Production in Factorio is all about volume, and production in Big Pharma is all about quality and substance.  This mirrors my gameplay experience with the two games quite nicely.

Big Pharma requires you to fit a number of tetris-shaped machines in as little space as possible in order to make drugs for profit. I'd love to say there was more to the game than that, but sadly there really isn't. All the challenges are basically the same, which makes the game very repetitive and it gets boring very, very fast. SImply not worth the price. You can get mobile games for free that are much more worthwhile and will give you many more hours of entertainment.
I bought this in early access (and got the Steam version for free, but never played it on Steam) and expected a lot more to be added to the game, but was then surprised when the release date was announced, constantly thinking "that has to be a mistake, it's not remotely done." But no, Tim considered it done and it was released. Sorry, Tim, but you made a bad game.
The good part:
- Figuring out how to turn ingredients into drugs using as few machines as possible is fun, at first.
- Trying to create crazy drugs by combining different cures that aren't normally combined can be fun, at first.
- Watching all the machines work is fun, for a while.
- You can name all your drugs whatever you want, which is also compeltely pointless because there's no multiplayer so there's no one to laugh at the names you use.
But then comes all the bad (and the list is only short because there's so little to the game):
You have AI opponents who for the most part only seem to be there as decoration. They're no real challenge and even with the patents it's not a problem to beat them because you can just make another drug that's slightly different. You never feel cornered or like you have to rush. The only challenge remains beating the timer if you care at all about scoring gold on everything (which in itself doesn't earn you anything whatsoever other than a golden line on the scenario selection screen).
Once you beat the first scenario you know how to beat the rest of the game. The only thing that changes is how fast you have to make your money and what drugs you can make. Nothing else changes.
Tim (the developer) has a background in simple mobile games and it shows in Big Pharma: It lacks depth, it lacks complexity, and everything is over-simplified to the point where you have no control over any of the things that would have made the game remotely interesting. I wasn't the only one who asked for a more complex economy, but Tim felt it wasn't needed. Unfortuntely having no control over the economy means it doesn't really matter what you do because prices fluctuate at random. It also means that half the info screens don't matter because you can't do much at all to affect your economy anyway.
Tim's idea that "scoring gold on a mission can be incredibly motivating" doesn't fly when the game is so incredibly boring to play and has no real content. You simply have nothing to do, ever, other than plopping down the machines, connecting them with belts, and trying not to lose count of whether you needed two or three machines to get the right concentration.
Meanwhile you scream for more to do and bang your head against the wall to express your frustration for yet another incomplete game that was released with no plans for more content.

The game describes itself as relaxing take on the god game genre, and even looks like one. The gameplay however has nothing to do with a god game. It is basically the 'Simon says' segment from Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes with just enough extra mechanics to make it a 99 cents standalone game.
You are given a combinations of colors, and need to press the same colors in the right order on a spinning shape (planet).  This way you earn currency (awe) and unlock new colors (biomes). Pressing the wrong color in a combination does not punish you, but just makes you restart the combination. With the currency you buy the new colors to place on the shape, so you can complete more of the given combinations which require these colors. You complete a level when you have added enough patches of each color and have unlocked and bought an item that does nothing for your current shape.
After the first couple of levels the combinations are not just given, but you need to figure them out. Sometimes they are backwards, flashing or both. This slowly gets a little harder each level but never requires much thinking. If all else fails you can just keep pressing colors until you get a combination right or at least part of it to understand the combination.
Later a timer (seasons) is added which changes some of the colors on the shape, making the game just a little bit harder.
There are 5 chapters (solar systems you can name) with 5 levels (planets you can name) each. Plus the Christmas and Halloween chapters, also 5 levels each. This makes a total of 35 levels, and since later levels are mostly spend waiting for the correct color to pass on the spinning shape this means you can take up to several hours to complete the game.
My biggest problem with the game is how it is advertised and what it actually offers. The store page promises puzzles, discoveries and a spiritual experience among other things. "The player is a god in a yet-to-be-shaped universe" it says. Unfortunately the reality is that I am just clicking colors in order, and this not why I bought this game. It may be relaxing and fun for others, but I think there is just not enough fun lements to keep you playing if you are not an achievement hunter like me.  The nice presentation can’t hide or fix that…

It is certainly an older game, and in some parts it shows, but generally the lighting and textures look great. It's also a great stealth game, though. In fact, it's probably the next best thing to a Co-op stealth game you can find out there, and this was made in 2005! The Co-op is different from the singleplayer. It features it's own story that you and a friend (or complete stranger you met online) follow and the maps are full of areas/tasks that can only be completed with both players. It's satisfying when everything goes smoothly and you can high five the other player (in your imagination).
The AI isn't particularly bright, but that sometimes is because the area they are guarding isn't particularly bright either. This gives you the advantage unless you let them stub their toe on your balls while you crouch in the pitch dark hallway feeling all cool and stealthy. If you're smart, you can press up against the wall like a shadow. They can hear you if you move too fast and get suspicious of things like dead bodies for example, unlike in Assassin's Creed where the guards are like, "Hey, what happend here? Did anyone see the killer? We'll find him eventually!" Then they go on their mary way waiting for you to kill them. Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory does it right, because the enemies get anxious and stay anxious.
When that happens, the in-game music changes to a faster, super spy tempo and sets the mood. But they aren't really your enemies unless they are in your way. You can knock them out or kill them, depending on the mission intel. Sometimes, killing means you lose, so instead of choosing your battles, try your best to avoid them all together, because they have more guns than you that go ratatatatat.
TL;DR - It's a good game from a forgotten time. 9/10

Though not lead by the same team that made Bioshock 1, Bioshock 2 somehow surpasses its predecsessor in many aspects. Little annoyances from Bioshock have been fixed, and core pieces of the gameplay have been expanded upon to deliever a more fufilling overall experience. Things like the Hack Gun, which allows for long distance hacking, and the much needed duel wielding of plasmids and primaries smooth out kinks and polish the Bioshock formula to a shine.
The little sister/big daddy system from the original has also been expanded, and the gameplay and story integration really hits a peak here. You are the big daddy now, and these little girls are yours to protect. No other game has been able to match the sheer burst of primal anger you get when the sound of that child crying for help echoes through the room.
Pitty the poor fool who dared to lay a hand on Your little sister.
Not spoiling anything here, the story is quite heartfelt: Your role as a big daddy delivers some crucial context to the lives of these hulking protectors, and the relationship they have with both the little ones and the city as a whole. You'll come out of the experience (assuming you didnt harvest the girls like a complete monster) feeling, for lack of better words, like a dad. A proud one at that.
Though not anything really new in relation to the first game, Bioshock 2 delivers what I personally believe to be Bioshock at its smoothest and most polished. Worth every penny.
tldr: Its Good, You're a Dad Now. Congratulations.

After nearly 900 hours playing the game, I'm uninstalling it today.
I did enjoy my time in the game for a (long) while, and I feel I have had my money's worth from it, but am now unwilling to give it any more time, for reasons as follows;
Although I have played many early access games, and I understand the nature of early access games, what I cannot tolerate is a heavy handed approach from developers who can't see the faults with their project and treat their customers unfairly, in any way.
When the game, after the last few patches, became too unstable to enjoy any more, I started to post on the forums here, about both my specific problems, and my suggested remedies on how some of the issues might be addressed.
At no time was I rude. Being British I have no need to be rude to get a point across, I can be scruplessly accurate instead in my native language. The two developers I had reply to my threads both responded quickly, a point in their favour, but likewise both their replies weren't really to do directly with the points being raised, so ultimately useless.
For me, the game is broken now, I am unable to play for more than a few minutes at a time without some UE4 exception fault or another happening and crashing out the game.  I asked in one thread for help or at least advice on how I might remedy the problems introduced with their last 3-4 patches, and got none.
In the other thread, I identified for them how seriously underpowered their game servers are, leading to a terribly sub-par experience on the only European pvp server left with ANY population left worthy of the word. All the others having 0, 1, or occasionally 2 people left playing. The second developer tried to refute this, but didn't offer any quantifiable data to back up his insistance that things were fine, when they are quite obviously not.
When lightly pressed for some kind of specifics as to the actual specifications and supposed requirements of a server for this game, I was left ignored.
In the end, my comment to him was exactly this " Steam numbers down 90% in last month. GG Denis." This was making the final point that if everything was fine as he espoused, then people wouldn't be leaving the game faster than rats during a building burning.
This comment got me banned from their forums for being "unnecessarily rude".
This game is broken in its current form. The developers, such as they are, seem unable to fix it, and unwilling to acknowledge how broken it is.
There is no end-game past leveling to lvl60. There is no meaningful pvp left, just offline ninja-raiding. This has turned the end-game into a tower defense game instead, but to build anythig that can survive in your absence overnight against even 1 or 2 determined players is ultimately self-defeating as the servers they use can't handle their sub-standard, laughably optimised, buggy coding.  If you build something that can survive such a ninja-raid, then the game breaks.
GG Denis.

This War of Mine does a really good job of replicating those frustrations while still being fun and light hearted enough to be teachable. By this I don't mean fun the sense of "Yay I am in a warzone". No. I mean that this game is to War what fire drills are to real house fires. When you loose you will feel it in your bones to a degree you would not in any other game with violence. When you win you'll feel hallow, regretful, bitter, but self satisfied all the same. Man is a beast and you beat Mother Nature. Where this game succeeds is that it tries to be a game of real life simulation (Sims with guns perhaps) but instead it turns out to be the most realistic Horror game you will ever play. When combined with very good graphics, very good story telling, strategy problems that actually matter, as well as dilemas that go beyond what anyone would ever experience in the above situations, you will be not just more thankful of what you have in your real life after playing but more concious of what you have to loose if ever a Hurricane Katrina, Greek Style Nation wide Bankruptcy, or San Fransico like Earthquake situation ever occurs and you are not prepared. Between this, the Walking Dead, and the daily news I'm not yet a prepper but definately more concious of life and its risks.

You start with an open area and have to build production lines for medicine. You start with a vent on the wall to import raw ingredients, pass it through several processing machines to refine and produce the medicine, then end with a vent on the wall to export the completed product. There are a variety of machines and you'll have to make decisions on how to make your medicine. There are tradeoffs in space, manufacturing speed, profit, and quality of medicine based on which and how many machines you use. Also, there is a research system in place that requires you to invest money to eventually unlock more ingredients, machines, and other bonuses,

There are a couple UI changes I would have liked:

Dungeons 2 is a dungeon management meets real-time strategy game. You are the Ultimate Evil who tries to rid the world of those pesky goody-two-shoes like elves, dwarves and “heroes” who live on the surface and regularly invade your dungeon to steal your gold. You fight back with your evil horde consisting of orcs, goblins, trolls and snake-like nagas which you first have to train and slap into proper shape while trying to keep them
drunk and entertained, and mining gold to pay for it all.
Sounds familiar? Then you are an old fart, most likely, because the original Dungeon Keeper Dungeons 2 is based on came out in 1997!  You can still play it; DK was re-published in 2011 by
. DK and the equally brilliant Startopia (available on Steam) were games that for a lot of people, and certainly for me, started a live-long love of management/god games but very few games managed to strike the same balance of humour, love of detail and well-balanced game mechanics.
Dungeons 2 holds up really well as a DK clone and it adds another level, quite literally, because now you can also carry the fight to the surface and defeat these tree huggers once and for all in a campaign and several skirmish maps. On the skirmish maps, you can play either as horde or as demons with slightly different mechanics, which adds replayability.


The dungeon management works basically the same as in Dungeon Keeper. You have to dig for gold, maintain traps, conduct research and upgrade your troupes while defending against waves of invaders. Since you have only a limited number of population points, you have to balance your need for simple workers and your different fighting units. Fighting in the dungeon consists of simply dropping your units on top of the enemy, they do the rest automatically.
To beat a map you need to evilify the surface, i.e. defeat those hippies and replace their sickly sweet architecture bit by bit through wholesome graveyards, tentacles and freshly glowing green lakes. Fighting requires a bit more effort on your part, here. You can highlight individual units, groups*, or all of them at once and tell them where to go, whom or what to attack, and if they should use their special abilities.
I found that working with two or three groups of tanks/melee fighters, ranged units and possibly units with special abilities worked best. Ranged units are usually relatively weak in melee combat, by ordering them to stand back a bit they are way more effective.
*
The
consists of
that you have to beat to win, loosely connected by a story told by a narrator. He also gives you tips during the game, tells you what to do and not to do, and berates you if you don’t listen to him. I found him pretty amusing but if he talks too much for your taste you can adjust how much he says in the settings.
I would have liked the campaign to be a little bit longer and maybe a bit more difficult. Since the first few maps double as tutorial, they are relatively easy and quick. E.g. you can’t upgrade your dungeon, so you are stuck with basic units and a relatively low max population. There are a few extra tasks during the campaign maps that make them slightly more diverse than the skirmish maps, though.
The
of the base game are considerably harder than the campaign. You can play as both horde and demons, and individual maps can take quite a while to beat since you usually have to upgrade your dungeon to max to win. You can adjust the difficulty and you can start with a higher dungeon level if you want to shorten the playtime a bit.
I had a lot of fun with the skirmish maps, although they could have been a bit more diverse. Some of them are relatively similar to each other, and there isn’t any narration, either, which could have provided some unique flavour to them.
This is where Dungeons 2 really shines. There are so many great details, e.g. your evil hand makes the sign of the horns when you don’t move it around for a while, orcs do push ups when you don’t move your troupes on the surface, your minions wave at you when your hand hovers over them. It’s almost a shame you don’t have a lot of time to simply look around. There are lots of funny little details to discover, it’s obvious that a lot of love went into this game.
Purists probably won’t like the fighting on the surface but, in my opinion, it provides a nice change of pace when you want it and it adds another layer of difficulty. If you liked the original, generally like the genre, or want to get more proficient at multi-tasking you can’t go wrong with Dungeons 2. It has a lot of replay value and if you ever get bored with the base game, there are two DLCs with three skirmish maps each available as well as one DLC with a completely new narrated campaign and two new playable factions (A Game of Winter).

I despised this game when I bought it. I felt ripped off and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on. But I waited until my blood cooled and the bile went down in my throat.
So here I am now playing the game with a sort of grim determination. I have put forth the effort I believe required to honestly judge it for what it is. And what it is is what I thought it was at the beginning.  This game is a lazy, redundant milking of a cash cow.
You want pros and cons? Sure, why not:
Pros
It is the newest Civilization game
It is easy to learn (since it is just Civ 5 with different icons)
It has never slept with Peggy
Cons
It is the newest Civilization game
It plays exactly like Civ 5
It would probably be less painful if it had slept with Peggy
But to be truly honest... This game has a completely "yawn" storyline. Hell! That was wrong even calling it a storyline. It hides it's downfalls by trying to create intrigue from a "backstory" or half-baked attempts at futuristic technologies. So I won't bother you with trying make a failed attempt at finding pros and will just give you the cons.
- A total lack of story
- the "different" sponsors are identical other than one single "bonus"
- The techs are the laziest attempt I have ever seen in any Firaxis game ever. They just colonized another friggiing planet and they still have to discover how to make a dang laboratory?
- The units are a joke. You start out with a group of five guys in space suits? Later they have sprites that are just ridiculous. Titan units that are larger than the friggin cities. But then again that would mean you are ignoring that the explorer unit is larger than some cities.
- The tech trees and the "virtues" are direct, and once again, lazy copies of Civ 5.
- You have an ability to randomize planets that does NOTHING more than change the name of the world. (An obvious placement of an ability intended to be charged for later in DLC.)
- The AI is a complete joke. (Just like Civ 5) Higher levels just cheat buff the hell out of your opponents. I once had an island to myself for 10 turns. An AI landed on my island and I declared war. Within 5 turns the AI had built 4 military units (including an alien unit) and his city had grown to 4 population.
So in conclusion let me repeat... this game is a lazy, unfinished piece of crap. This franchise is dead folks. It has become a way for a corporate conclave to make money off of our memory of a great man's great works. SId Meier is somewhere right now checking his bank account and feeling ashamed at what he has allowed his work to become.
DO NOT buy this game. Use your money on warm ice cream. It will be as satisfying.

X The one negative thing I have to say about the game is that I wish there were more of it. And that's hardly a complaint, because the creators are working to put in all kinds of features: An Arcade and Story mode, more stages, and the 4 additional characters I mentioned before.
I'm writing this review for completely selfish reasons, I WANT this game to succeed, because the bigger it gets, the more possible content I can wring out of it, and the longer I can play it!

I'm not a connoisseur of this genre, but I do like the Space Empires franchise as well as Star Craft (which is RTS not TBS, but not too distantly related). Space Empires was my main frame of references for judging this game. The two games are quite similar.
It's not as customizable as Space Empires, but you have enough options to give your faction your own personal touches. In fact, based on playing SE, I can tell you that it gets tedious designing every single ship and then having to redesign them when you level up, so any more customization could just bog the game down.
For a strategy game, the run time isn't bad, depending on your settings. You can knock out a game in a few hours if you have a small world and not a lot of factions. I've found diplomacy works better in this game than other strategy games I've played, and things like a peace treaty tend to hold up. Going to war with a country won't forever ruin relations with them.
The one thing I dislike about strategy games is the combat mechanics. It's very ridged. Everything comes down to the unit's stats, and unlike say a first person shooter, you can't win an engagement by skill alone, you can never have an underdog win. If you have a unit with lower stats than the attacking unit, you lose. But that’s true of most strategy games.
I'm not a connoisseur of this genre, but I do like the Space Empires franchise as well as Star Craft (which is RTS not TBS, but not too distantly related). Space Empires was my main frame of references for judging this game. The two games are quite similar.
It's not as customizable as Space Empires, but you have enough options to give your faction your own personal touches. In fact, based on playing SE, I can tell you that it gets tedious designing every single ship and then having to redesign them when you level up, so any more customization could just bog the game down.
For a strategy game, the run time isn't bad, depending on your settings. You can knock out a game in a few hours if you have a small world and not a lot of factions. I've found diplomacy works better in this game than other strategy games I've played, and things like a peace treaty tend to hold up. Going to war with a country won't forever ruin relations with them.
The one thing I dislike about strategy games is the combat mechanics. It's very ridged. Everything comes down to the unit's stats, and unlike say a first person shooter, you can't win an engagement by skill alone, you can never have an underdog win. If you have a unit with lower stats than the attacking unit, you lose. But that’s true of most strategy games.

This game is Marvel vs. Capcom meets Bejeweled. Its a match 3 game with 3v3 combat. There are 6 colored jewels and environmental tiles. Match 3 of a color to acquire AP of said color. Your Heros use the AP for special abilities. The strategy in this game comes from setting up a team of 3 with synergistic abilities. You want to be able to utilize all 6 colors and you dont want one hero out too long or they will take too much damage.
DIfferent types of challenges require different strategies. Some PC villians use tiles with count down timers. You have to eliminate or delay those tiles with your abilities or take massive cascades of damage. Other times you have to acquire certain colors to keep them away from villians in a turn based game play. You can use AP as you acquire it or save it to combine multiple abilities in board clearing strategies that will allow you to play above your character level.
Overall this game has a depth that is surprising and exceeds its genre. Start free to play and then decide if its worth investing.

Greetings.
I don't specialize in writing reviews, I don't have that many hours in, so it's just a human moment / perspective from a regular gamer. A little bit to describe my playstyle: it ranges from primitive shooters to sophisticated strategies, though I do have a thing for city building / production line management games (starts with Caesar III, then onto Anno and Zeus/Pharaoh/Caesar IV, Simcity, Skylines, etc).
What do I have to say about the game? It's extremely catchy. System requirements are low, price's not that high (especially if you manage to grab it during a sale like I did); the game really does remind you of Theme Hospital quite a bit. Hell, when I first saw it in my "featured" tab, I thought this was a remake of the series. You know, the kind when you can't exactly sell a game under its old name due to some legal issues, so this potentially looked like an Indie rework of some Theme Hospital fans. The similarity ends right there, Big Pharma has way more depth to it. I'm just going through the first stage of the tutorial but I can already see a lot of -interesting- complexities. Having said that, the game is really easy to learn. It's not a Hearts of Iron or Victoria by Paradox that you'll spend two weeks learning with constant hit-n'-miss play sessions resulting in frustration before you understand what every little button does and every tiny switch stands for.
All in all, Big Pharma is exactly defined by its tags. An indie (the dev seems to respond in the hub), puzzle (gets you thinking, that's a check for a fact), strategy-management (Theme Hospital- / Tycoon Deluxe-style) with a theme that makes sense (simulation).
Let's see if it manages to keep me busy long enough, I'll edit it then. <:

One of the best (if not the best) stealth games ever made
This is it. If you want the most in-depth Splinter Cell experience offering everything the stealth genre has to offer and more, look no further. Chaos Theory is Splinter Cell at its prime, taking the stealth genre to new heights with all of its features.
As Sam Fischer, you must navigate your way through enemy territory to uncover plans, eliminate targets, and do all you can to put a stop to a diabolical terrorist plan that could mean World War 3 if the villains succeed. Story-wise, this is about what you would expect from a Splinter Cell game and it can be pretty intriguing to say the least. The single player is a decent length, featuring 10 levels at high security areas that for me took roughly 13+ hours to complete.
Let's get this out of the way. The game was released in 2005, so of course the visuals are dated. The characters' eyes are kind of big and googly, backgrounds can look very bland, etc. But if you can look at and appreciate the textures and details for what they were at the time, you will overlook the graphics and concentrate on what really matters (and this can be said about many old games).
The dialogue is thrilling Tom Clancy as usual. You receive orders from Lambert as usual as well as chatter from your other Third Echelon members. What really shines here are the many, many jokes, sarcastic remarks, and gripping words Sam uses in various instances. Not only does he retort with witty responses over the radio back to Lambert as he did in SC1 and Pandora Tomorrow, but also during the vast amount of interrogations he has with enemies should you choose to put the choke hold on them. I really got a kick out of Sam's exchanges with foes in his grasp; enemy: "What's going on?" Sam: "Are you supposed to be here? Identify yourself" or "I'm the landlord and Zerkhezi forgot to pay his rent. Any idea where he is?" Just like the stealth options, these responses seem limitless and different for each enemy that I interrogated (and there are many basic enemies you can interrogate in each of the 10 levels).
Here is what truly makes this game soar: the GAMEPLAY! Game developers could learn (or relearn, as some seem to have forgotten) several concepts of how to approach an action-packed spy tale while getting rid of the cliches and mundane, run-of-the-mill gameplay mechanics of today (Assassin Creed's "kill guy from hay bale, leap out, run to next instant kill point, repeat" comes to mind here). Chaos Theory gives the player a multitude of options: Open door? Open door stealthily? Bash door open? Pick lock? Break lock? Optic cable? Many doors have all of these options for whatever you are feeling at the time. DIstracting guards: Pick up and throw object? Whistle? Blast light with EMP from pistol? Or take the old way and just shoot out the light? There are also several routes to the objective(s) and you can spend several playthroughs going through the level, perhaps through the vents here and taking out the guard there or maybe climbing up the pole and onto the balcony this time to snag the intel and avoid the first floor cameras. The point is that the choices are so many and you are constantly hammered with scenarios in which you can do it all again and again. It is all up to you and how you want to play the game. This type of game most likely inspired the varied choices of stealth games like Dishonored and Mark of the Ninja because it plays much the same way. It's perfect!
One minor flaw is that the AI can be sort of annoying in some areas, especially the Seoul level later on when the fighting breaks out. It can be difficult to maneuver around these guys which, at the drop of a hat, can instantly recognize you and fire upon you before you even know you were spotted. However this is typically not the case, as most of the game takes place in areas with relative amounts of darkness to use to sneak by the unsuspecting guards.
All in all, this was a wonderful gaming experience and perfect for any Splinter Cell fan as well as gamers that enjoy true stealth (not the stripped-down stealth games we seem to be having today).
