The gameplay's fine. You get experience points to make your gun do different things, and you shoot the robots, and it's whatever.
If you like story in your games, this one is completely asinine. You play a Corporate Cop in a cyperpunk city who has swear words and tryhard bitterness instead of a personality. When he isn't confused, he is complaining. At no point is it clear exactly what's going on, or what you're trying to do - even though it is not presented as a mystery - and at some point even the setting itself becomes unclear, not because of any plot-twist mindscrewery, but because it seems like the writers can't decide.
It's said that you're all personalities in a data matrix or whatever, but you're at war with machines with people struggling on the outskirts of the city. Then cyborg zombies start appearing and literally no one remarks on this as shocking or unusual, or even as a known phenominan. Just when it starts to seem like you're definitely in a real world whose technology is being hacked by a robots, a public monument statue comes to life and gains ballistic weaponry because of a virus.
You're implied to be some experimental messiah, and then they just sort of forget about that. It's stated outright that the Corporation isn't part of some conspiracy with the robots, but then they start trying to kill you because you don't report in after someone tells you you're cyber jesus. Then you (apparently?) complete your goal of... plugging into a construction robot(?), when you immediately fail in a cutscene, get dumped into a garbage bin, meet some people on the outside of the city after fighting through trash for three levels, and the game just ends with nothing apparently accomplished.
Half the game is told in blurry comic-book cinematics with some attempt at the messy art style of the Metal Gear Solid comics, and the hero stays silent during gameplay; then the comics stop happening, and the hero learns how to talk during gameplay. I thought this would help the story have more context, but it just gave him more opportunities to complain.
I don't know if it's a localization problem or what, but whenever this game isn't confusing, it's embarrassing.
Two of the three bosses are kinda rad though, even if they're not that interesting to fight. If you like neat skyboxes, this has some.

This isn't a turnoff by any means. If anything, it adds to the abundant charm already present, but admittedly I'm biased; I've driven the odd shitbox or two in my day.

Fun game for a few hours; however, once you learn the basics there is very little to this game. The whole premise is that you fix a beat up old Laika 601, and then try to drive to Turkey. That's it. When you get there, there is no 'end game'. You just hit 'return to home' and start over. It took me about 4 hours to get to Turkey on my first play through.
Along your journey from point A to point B you will find boxes along the roads which contain commodities such as wine, cigs, more cigs, hot dogs, etc. The price for these is rather random, you can literally save/load your game until you see prices you like. Which tells you this is not a working economy, but rather just random luck on what you get and when. You can sell the items you pick up which help you afford things such as fuel, repair kits, new tires, car upgrades and motel stays.
The core game loop is sound yet mundane with nothing to mix it up:
-Fix up car until it works
-Pick new route
-Drive route
-Stay in motel
-Start over
Let's talk about pros and cons
PROS:
-Fixing up your own little car is fun!
-You learn a little bit about engines
-Game aesthetics are very pleasing
-It's just gosh darn fun to drive a car you work on!!
-Lots of car upgrades
CONS
-Extremely repetitive core gameplay loop
-Buggy terrain generation and clipping issues. I've fallen throught he world, and so has my car
-Uncle, a core part of the gameplay, is broken
-Some generated routes have the same 1-2 roads over and over, making you think its groundhogs day.
-Currently no end game
-Save scumming / game reloading for easy money
-Only 4 tracks in the in-game radio
-Barely any traffic in-game, even on max. I went from home base to Turkey, and saw 2 cars.
In it's current state I cannot recommend this game. It needs a lot of feature work and polishing before it is worthy of the price it commands. This has the potential to be a REAL GEM! It has been in early access for almost a year now, with not much changing in terms of feature-sets. I am getting worried this will be another 'dead' game we have invested in.

Bioshock 2 is an amazing game. Hell, the whole Bioshock Series is amazing. Even though Bioshock 2's story is the weakest, the combat is the strongest.
Bioshock 2's combat is 10 times more different than it's brother, Bioshock. You can use your Plasmid and Melee/Gun at the same time, and because of that, they made the game much more intense, yet much more fun. Since you are a Big Daddy, the way to get Adam is much more different than before. You actually need to find the Adam yourself, along it the Little Sister, and when she's getting the Adam, you have to protect her (Simular to the part where you need to protect the Little Sister while she is getting Adam in Bioshock.) which gets quite intense. Then you can chose to Harvest or Rescue, to get even more Adam. But saving all the Little Sisters in a level will summon the Big Sister, and she's not easy.

-Magic Duels
So, I've been playing this for a while now. I've been a fan of M:tG for years, so there are going to be a few different points I'll be covering in this little review, coming from both a game play stand point, to how the game is transferred from physical cards, to a digital version.
So to start off, the gameplay is a little tricky at times. Especially for people who are new to Magic.
The tutorial, which grants you gold to purchase cards with at a later point, seems to cover as much as it can, but at the same time, it is a little monotonous. I've never encountered a game before where I had to click "Do not show this again" when tips popped up on the screen. I suppose I'm used to games where once a tip shows up, and you click out of it, you don't have to concern yourself with it popping back up every time an event occurs.
Other than the slight issue with the tips, the gameplay is fairly well explained, from receiving your first hand, using mulligans, to laying lands, playing creatures, going over creature abilities, how to use them, and even going so far as to guiding you in regards to a red arrow that pops up over cards that the game suggests you should play.
The downfall however, is unless you're playing Versus mode against another player, the game continues to try and baby you through the campaign. Cards you have in your hand, often have that red arrow over them as the game is trying to get you to play them.
Campaigns to me, especially in a competitive card game, are generally ways to get you more familiar with different card types, colors, strategies and the like. But with this 'suggested card' arrow popping up, it really feels like there's little to no freedom. Of course, you can ignore the arrow and play your own cards, but there's just something nagging in the back of your mind, wondering if something is going to go wrong because you didn't play a suggested card.
It seemed a little uncertain to me, playing throught he campaign, as to if the enemy AI was scripted to react to said cards or not.
Once the campaigns are completed, you have a nice little chunk of gold to purchase your first starter pack with, and that's something that I do enjoy about this game, is the ability to play without paying. Of course this is your stereotypical 'pay-to-win' game where you can drop a bunch of money into it, and attain all kinds of cards. But if you're willing to work for it, it can be quite rewarding.
My only issue with it being that in order to get money, you have to win against someone in a random versus match, and that the winner only receives 30 gold, and the loser receives nothing.
This is very demotivating. Especially if someone can't afford to pay for cards.
Imagine this :
You finished the tutorial, finally. You go to the store, get your starter pack, and open up some decent cards. With these cards, and the starter cards you unlocked from the tutorial, you decide to go and build yourself a sweet little deck.
Once satisfied, you head into Versus mode with your head held high with determination and confidence in your deck and your knowledge in playing this game.
You get your♥♥♥♥♥♥stomped.
Okay. Maybe that was a fluke. You can't win them all, right?
Next game. Wait. What kind of card is that? How come I don't have any of these awesome cards that this person has? Okay, well I guess I just have to endure it and keep playing.
Twenty matches in, you've lost 16 matches, and won 4. For all of your playing, you've accumulated 120 gold. Not even enough to buy a single booster pack, which totals in at 150 gold.
I think that a person should get at least a minimum amound of gold, even for losing. That way, at least with all the losses, you can still afford to update your deck every once in a blue moon. But with the way they have things laid out, (And of course I understand, they need to make a profit off of this game somehow) it just seems that  the game punishes you for doing poorly, and barely rewards you for a win. Why not make a limit to how much gold you can get a day from Versus? Maybe a 300 daily gold limit for wins and losses combined? Maybe it's 50 gold for a win, and 5 for a loss. It's not a lot, but at least it's something, and you'll have more people motivated to play the game in order to get better when they can't slap their wallet on the screen just to get more cards.
I don't know, that's just me I guess.
The earning system is really the biggest issue to me in this game. It's a struggle to preservere when you don't have good cards like people you're put up against. Of course there's a lot of strategy to playing said cards, but at the same time, not everyone is going to understand that when they first pick up this game if they're new to Magic.
The game itself, the story line in the campaigns, the characters, the deck customization, the box customization, the play itself, are great. I'm horribly addicted to this game, even though I'm one of those guys who can't afford to throw money at my monitor.  This is, in my opinion, a great Magic game.
Things I might change however, would certainly be the earning system.
I am hoping that they come out with more updates/expansions for this. The fact that there is a limited amount of cards means that there's going to be limited amount of things to work towards. Sure the game play is fun and all, but building a collection is also part of the fun.
If you've made it to this part of my rather winded review, then I sincerely thank you for your attention. If you are into magic, give this game a try. It's a little dodgy getting into it, and understanding how the interface works, but after the tutorial, you'll be making people rage with blue control decks, or red speed decks, or grave digger black decks.
Thanks for your time.
-Zagru

This game may appear cheap at first, but it is actually freaking awesome. It is essentially an online-2d-brawler with a heavy focus on loot and fast advancement. There is a plethora of classes available and every type pf playstyle can be found in this game. It is fun, fluid and just works well. Plus it is free, so there is no reason to not try it out! Fights against other players, countless dungeons and a lot of freedom also incuded. Plus a great soundtrack, tons of events and a great publisher!

PRO
- A good mixture of Skyrim, Survival (like Rust, Ark) and Harry Potter.
- You can freely build whatever you want.
- Good progression system for you character (you can increase stats and learn crafting stuff, spells and other).
- Taming (up to 4 creatures) with mounting them and leveling.
- Active developers, patches are arriving on weekly basis and it seems like they are listening (mostly). You can even follow their trello board.
- You get experience for literally everything: Hunting, crafting, gathering, exploring and so on. It is very rewarding.
- Talking about exploring, the world is very beautiful and it makes a lot fun to explore caves, mountains and whatever. The view distance is also one of the biggest I've seem so far in a open world RPG. You often say to yourself "wow what is this??" while you get eaten by a big Balrog walking around burning.
- Group play with experience share and building rights. Good for coop play, I had tons of funny times playing with friends.
CON
- Low playerbase, if you have a friend it makes a lot fun, but playing solo is boring.
- Bugs. Well it is in early access, so bugs are a given. So far I haven't encountered game breaking bugs, just a few minor ones.
- Endcontent is kinda limited for now. After reaching max level and exploring the complete map, it is kinda boring. So take your time and don't rush things.
- Just a few spells so far. You have a lot items for building and crafting, but just a few spells to be a fleshed out mage. The spells so far are good, but a mage needs a lot more.
Seriously this game is gorgeous and makes so much fun. Yes it has issues and bugs which sometimes are a letdown. And it misses features needed for endgame gameplay. But if you like sandbox games which includes the world and atmosphere like Skyrim did, this is your game.
Servers are kinda dead right now, so pick up a friend or two and dive into the world.

The game tells the story of a former US Marine Helicopter Pilot Robert Jacobs and his fight for the Freedom of America along with three of his comrades in a North Korean occupied Colorado and California. The might and power of the once-great US military is gone with the EMP and the 'norks' and laying punishment on everyone they see. It's up to you to drive them back out of the Land Of The Free.
The idea is alright, no more of the 'Here gun kill Taliban pls' cliche, the fight comes to you now.
The game sometimes makes you feel what the occupied America is feeling: seeing two koreans mow down two parents, for their toddler run to them screaming is kind of heartbreaking, seeing Nork helicopters and bombers destroying neighbourhoods for YOUR acts on THEIR camps makes you feel like the bad guy.
It also has a really fun flying level, the flying itself is quite satisfying.
All the guns are very mediocre. They all sound the same, barely have recoil, if you pick two of the same, they have separate ammo pools, but they all do what they have to- kill the enemy. What I found alright, was the small ammo pool, makes you go for the headshots and switch guns often.
The characters are 'eh'. I didn't really care about them.
The levels are 'eh'. It's somewhat cool to see burned-down suburbs and destroyed schools, but they could really use more color.
It's very glitchy and buggy. You'll sometimes find level progression not triggering, crucial enemy fighters you need to kill don't spawn and those that do spawn, sometimes mow you down through solid cover, sometimes with only 1 shot or sometimes with a quick bursts that is impossible to evade.
From what I hear the multiplayer is both buggy and dead, so I wasn't even going to poke that horse with a stick.

DFO is a very nostalgic game for me because back in the year 2008 when I was in elementary school. My best friend reccomended me this game because I played Maplestory, which is also a Nexon game. When I first boot it up, I was so excited to play it because it's something new to try out, though I did not play much because my most favorite game back then was Maplestory as mentioned earlier. I did get on and off DFO at times because the grinding seems to be too tiring for me. My highest and most prized character was a male ranger level 36 and I always felt over powered when I run dungeons using him. A few years forward to 2014, DFO got shut down when I was really into it , playing my necomancer with a many avatar items. I felt betrayed by Nexon and I wish I had known so that I didn't spend money on DFO (though Nexon did issue a refund for players who spent NX in a certain time span). I was so devastated that I turned to Rusty Hearts (another mmo that has the same style of gameplay as DFO but got shut down) to fill the void (that void also ended when Rusty Hearts server shut down too). But about a year or so, Neople announced that they were holding a closed or open beta to DFO and I immediately downloaded the game and played again and now, the game is fully opened again with major changes that makes me felt that I was playing a whole different game, which is okay, but I do wish that the difficulty of DFO had stay because it's no fun when there isn't a plethora of sub quests, harder dungeons, and people actively looking for a party to play. However, this isn't the worst thing because one of my most favorite game came back, new and refreshed. If anyone new to DFO and happen to read this (which is a tiny chance) do try it and don't judge it negatively after 5 hours or because of fatigue system because DFO encourages you to play multiple character.
TL;DR: DFO is my most favorite game that I started in 2008 and many things have happened to it like server closure but now it's back and you should try it and don't judge it too quickly because of minor things like fatigue system.

I only played this while it was free for a weekend so I didn't actually get that long to play it. I only got through one playthrough, but I was left with enough experience to make up my mind.
I have been a massive fan of Civilization for a long time. Ever since we got Civilization 3 complete edition on the PC back in God know's when, me and my family had so much fun destroying civilizations with the might of our empire. Since then, I moved onto Civ 5 complete and I found my love rekindled. It's easily accessible modding scene and design make it probably the most polished and excellent Civilization games, but as for me it was most certainly the perfect Civilization game.
Naturally, when Civilization: Beyond Earth was announced, I was excited. It looked cool, it sounded cool. But when I got my hands on it, I was disappointed.
Let's begin with what is easily
Beyond Earth has less units, but instead you would upgrade units through the unlocking of affinity points. I thought this was a cool idea, and as I developed my affinity further and further, I got excited to see my puny human soldiers transform into machine of war and destruction. Even better was when I unlocked the most power affinity unit, which for harmony was the Titan. Seeing your units improve over time and tech was awesome instead of having to upgrade them to waste more of that precious gold. This both works in it's favour and against it depending on how you see it.
Depending on what you wanted, say a specific unit type or bonus, you could unlock a certain affinity. Each affinity had it's own play style. Harmony for me, was based around using the planet to your advantage. Healing in Miasma, using aliens as weapons, merging humans with aliens and so forth. It's a cool concept, and one that I would love to see affect Civ 5 in terms of political structure perhaps, but more prominent than the culture tree in Civ 5. (Don't get confused, there is still a cultural system available in Beyond Earth).
Progession feels great. As you begin you are helpless colonists but in time, you learn to take the planet for your own and in time come to rule as you rightfully should. Technology allows you to take advantage of the alien planet and improve on pre-existing Earth technologies.
It's still a Civilization game. Some people are harsh on this one for not being as good as the others. Quite frankly they're right, this isn't as good as V by a stretch but they're harsh. It still has the classic Civilization formula of 4X turn base strategy and it's as fun as ever. The reason for the harsh judging is because this, the newest game in the series, does more to take away from the experience Civ V gave you.
Quest's! Quests are awesome, they give you bonuses for things that you do such as destroying outposts or just making decisions on what a building should do. Take for example there was this outpost (a dumbed down city state essentially), as part of the decision I made I had to destroy it. Now, I honestly never got around to it because it was worth more to be alive but eh, whatever. When you build a new building after a few turns it asks you to choose it's direction giving buffs such as +1 production or +1 science. It's a cool feature.
There's too much to say, but at the same time they're just not worth mentioning.
Now let's continue into
Civilization 5 is better. Simply is. Civilization Beyond Earth feels like an overpriced re-skin of the game. Civilization Beyond Earth replaces grass for alien grass. Instead of some resources such as sheep you get things like chitin. Instead of iron, you get titanium, instead of uranium you get floatstone or xenogas. In terms of map layout, the most original thing is miasma. When you're in the gas, it hurts it you each turns but it changes along with technology. It looks cool in the beginning but then everything just get's boring and you realize there isn't much character to the world. Instead of ruins you have artifacts from aliens or previous space expeditions. There are no more great people, instead you have quest bonuses which don't really compare. The few (less than 12) civilizations don't even have special units or buildings. There is no advisor counsel, which makes me sad as I would very often turn to them for advice in my playthroughs on Civ 5.
The aliens are cool! ....For a time. When I spent 10 turns building an explorer, my first unit, I sent it to explore. I passed many aliens hoping they wouldn't attack me, sometimes they did and sometimes they didn't depending on their feeling towards me. But they're more of a nuisance than anything in the end. They're like barbarians but more unpredictable. I would prefer aliens to barbarians, but in the end neither matter.
It's more repetitive. Civilization 5 has a massive roster of civilizations ranging from the most famous and prominent to more rare and extincted Civilizations. The choices you have in this game are much fewer, you have the Spacemerican's, Spaczillians, Spacsians, Spindians, Spafricans, Space Russians, Spacetraillians and that's about it. There isn't much variety and no civilization has anything really unique, they all function the same apart from different starting resources such as +1 science in the beginning or +1 culture, so on. A starter unit such as a free worker or free explorer are about as much difference you'll get. Affinity is what makes it more replayable as you can choose supremacy, harmony or purity. These are the 3 things that'll set your playthrough apart, but I was not in a rush to start on a new affinity as they weren't interesting enough for me to want to play them all. Quite frankly, I had a sigh of relief when I was finished my playthrough for the sake of this review.
The tech web sucks! I get to choose where my technologies go, that's awesome, I like it but the way it is in it's current state, quite frankly it just sucks. I dreaded going into it as I navigated each stupid technology in order to find where I needed to go technologically. It took me often 5 minutes or longer just to find what I wanted to do next.
Lastly, it doesn't feel finished. It feels like the developers wanted to make this game and release it and then release how it's meant to be played with expansions. It'll probably happen. But as of now, with 1 expansion released, it is not worth it. Civilization V is better and I'd recommend waiting this one to be cheaper than €10 or free on a weekend for a play if you're a fan of Civilization. But even so, you're not missing out on much.
Civilization: Beyond Earth tries to be a breathe of fresh air in an already long running series, but it just leaves you wanting to come back to Civilization V. Maybe this is what they wanted. But as for the game, it isn't good enough to warrant it's price, maybe at €10 now or €20 with expansions if they're any good (have yet to be released as of now). It's still a good Civilization game, and maybe it would have come out better in a market without the already near-perfect Civilization 5, but instead we get a lower quality Civilization. It could've been so much better.

Hitman Absolution, the 5th main series Hitman game released, and it looks beautiful, even on today's lower end hardware on low settings. So, how is it? I think it's pretty good.
Taking a huge step away from the previous games in the series, Absolution has completely reworked the stealth system for the game. Unlike Blood Money, which I felt was made a little too easy with it's detection mechanics, Absolution has a new mechanic where you are quickly noticed by enemies and NPCs who wear the same uniform as you, or if you enter an area you aren't supposed to be. This is visibly telegraphed by a yellow meter that fills up, which can be negated by quickly ducking out of sight, leaving the restricted area, or by making use of 2 new stealth mechanics, namely "Instinct" and "Hiding in Plain Sight"
Hiding in Plain Sight is a new mechanic where players can do costume specific actions such as reading menus as a civilian, mopping as a janitor, reading about the Lord as a henchman, or sniffing doughnuts as a police officer. These actions allow the player to stand still in open areas without nearby NPCs seeing them, and often prompts them to say funny lines if it's used to hide from someone who has seen though your costume. (which, to my knowledge, is the only way to fool people who have seen through your costume)
Now let's talk about the other new mechanic: Instinct. By holding down the CTRL key or the Right Bumper, players can slow time slightly and look around for highlighted weapons, hiding spots, and enemies. While in this sudo detective vision mode, not only can players see enemy pathing via fire trails on the floor, but if te player is dressed as that enemy, they can hide from them in exchange for some of their instinct meter. But that's not all!
Players also use Instinct to slow time to a crawl, and line up multiple shots to be executed in a cutscene like manner, very useful for cleaning up after yourself if you've been seen by a lot of enemies. You can earn more on lower difficulties by doing anything to gain points, such as scoring headshots, hiding bodies, and completing objectives.
Now let's talk about some of the not so great things in this game. For starters, Absolution as a system where the player can take cover against walls and furniture. This has lead to very square centric level design, as well as giving way to a new gameplay style: cover shooting. Now I don't advise you to try this method for highscores, or even really on higher difficulties, but let me tell ya, the occasional sudden, intense cover shootout really broke up the frustration of the tight, tense stealth; and on Hard, I always felt like I was in serious danger in a cover shootout. I found the cover shooting surprisingly satisfying, between creping up and flanking hostile enemies, and sections where they give me a sniper rile and a nice long stretch of enemies wandering around to carefully and strategic pick off enemies without them seeing each other die. Another complaint people have about this game is that it pushes you down a hallway, making you play how it wants you to. andwhile I agree to some existent that the game is more linier than previous games in the series, I never really felt like I didn't have any options.
Let's address another complaint, the online mode that some people call "Tacked on", Contracts Mode. This is a game mode where you can go back into almost an level in the game, starting with an unlicked costume and weapon of your choice, you replay the section of the level, pick out target from any npc marked on the radar, kill them however you'd like, then exit the level. This generates a challenge that you can then post into a big pool of everyone's levels. And the interesting thing about this feature, is that the servers are still up! Today on March 10th, 2017, I uploaded a new (relatively difficult) contract, and 9 other players played it within the hour, a few beating my own score.

When I first saw the unveiling of Hitman: Absolution, I was optimistic to see our favorite nefarious assassin make it to the current generation of gaming. What I was not optimistic for was the Hollywood cast, or the introduction of “magic pockets” (that is, the ability to carry a sniper rifle in your coat pocket). In the faux pas words of Max Scoville, who interviewed IO Interactive staff after a preview of the game, my worries were “assured.”
It is true that Absolution retains its stealth ethic (and arguably with as much rigor as Silent Assassin), but it is greatly downplayed by an obnoxious point system ever present in the upper left corner. Every misstep you perform is noted here, and it cannot be disabled unless you play on purist. I assume that this is the IO’s snide reply to those who complained about mystery witnesses at the end of the level in previous games.

Speaking of AI; it has improved to some extent, there are no longer telepathic NPCs who know who you are just by hearing a guard lift up a radio without saying any words in it. At one point, I was amazed how the AI suspected I was behind them when I reloaded my gun, or when I knocked out a guard and his radio made some interference. But it is still not perfect. Unless you make noise, guards never look behind themselves, even when you throw something right in front of them from 5 feet away. I found this AI was most comparable to Silent Assassin since I still remember being shot in St. Petersburg for running.
The story in itself is one to question. Although it lines together with the conclusion of Blood Money rather well, it goes into a whole other direction with the inclusion of a plot device, a 14-year-old genetically modified girl given superhuman abilities with an isotope in her necklace. A dying request by one of 47’s former employers is to protect her prized innocence, and seek out and kill those who wish to do her harm. The initial casting of William Mapother and recasting of David Bateson has 47 speak more lines in this game than arguably any of his previous titles. Yet 47 doesn’t babble, his newly founded areas of dialogue include briefing the player, found about via pressing the F1 key when on a level.
Regarding level design, the developers have largely abandoned that “open world” feel for a more linear theme. The open world concept is still alive in some levels such as the Chinese New Year and Hope missions but is by no means to the same extent as Blood Money was: a lot more consistent. I do admit, though, that they were far more generous in sheer number with 20 levels.
Graphically speaking, the visuals are stylistic, but too many filters and post-processing get applied in the name of artistic direction. It was almost reminiscent of Battlefield 3 in a way, knowing that the visuals already looked just fine 5 filters ago. Luckily, you can turn off the bloom in the settings, with goes a lot further than what it claims to do.
The depth of field is incredibly flawed, however. Even at the highest setting, you have a severely myopic camera that will unexpectedly blur out even the most important things in your field of view. It is especially bad when 47 is coming out of a dark tunnel in a mission to enter Dexter’s Industries, but perhaps it is intentional. If so, it was not a good decision to include it within the game.
With the absence of Jesper Kyd, the sound design is left extremely sporadic and often random. The music will often cease or begin without any cue, and the action music, when 47 is discovered, and when NPCs turn hostile, is uninteresting and bland compared to the orchestral/electronica mix we’ve come to know and love.

In conclusion, Absolution is probably one of the most polarizing titles in the Hitman series since its conception in 2000. Now approaching its adolescence, it has lost most of its innocence and changed its state of mind to fit in with the crowd. That means no more map, no more first person point of view, and no more “stop and smell the roses” missions. Is it a good thing? I’m not so sure at the moment. Usually, when a game gets a mixed rating the critic suggests that only true fans pick up this title, but I suggest the exact opposite. If you’re new to this series, playing this first can give you a taste of the gameplay so you can work backward to the core of the series and see what the true aim of the series was. That is what I believe Absolution, after 6 years in development, seems to be lacking.

Big Pharma is a great little game in which you get to play as the big pharmaceutical companies, create drugs, sell them and build up reputation.
The game is in essens a puzzle game with some light management thrown in for good measure. Most of the gameplay is creating drug chains that optimizes drugs (for profit or usefulness) and then to sell them. Which is really a really satisfying puzzle game. All of the machines that create drugs have a different shape and size and in order to fit them all in you either need to plan out what you'll need ahead of time, because moving production lines after they are completed is really difficult, alternatively you can buy smaller more effective machines, however those will crank up the production cost for the drug, directly affecting your bottom line.
The game is great in that you can create really weird drugs that may or may not actually work, but after all it's all about making money and not drugs right? You will need to decide wheater you value space efficiency vs price, what research should you prioretize. All the while trying to stay ahead of the competition which have just patented your new drug formula rendering the giganormous production line you just created, worthless...
It's a great little zen game where once in a while you sit back and just wait for your drugs' ratings go up or down, accumulate money etc. Contemplating weather or not it's the right time to expand, what you should expand into, is it worth optimizing that one cure so that its drug rating goes up...
There's almost always something to do, at least in the beginning and then the game zens out after a while.
One bad thing about the game however is that when you get to a sort of "critical mass" you basically cannot lose, except  for deadlines. There's not really too many challenges after the initial ones, because when you manage to get enough drugs to sell, you will start making tons of money and the game really turns into a fine tuning game. I'm not saying it isn't  fun at that point, but it really doesn't require as much baby sitting.
On the other hand that might be exactly what you're looking for as you can then sit and maybe catch up on a series, Youtube etc.
All in all, it's a nice little game, especially if you can get it in a sale, great if you need something to stimulate that gamer part of the brain as you catch up on videos or whatever. I for one can't just sit and do one thing at a time, so this is a great game for me. :)

The hit detection is worse than Alice in Wonderland for the SNES. You have to be dead center, as though this were a FPS, but there's no sight reticle or anything to suggest that. The animations mean nothing. Even the AoE attacks only hit what's directly in front of you. When you attack, you are forced to move forward, even on ranged characters, and you're locked in the animation for quite a long time. On melee characters, this will usually put you behind your enemy to attack the air rather than hitting him.
The jumping is stiffer than Bubsy 3D for the PS1. You cannot change your path once in the air, which more often than not leads you to your death. Even the original Super Mario Bros. had fluid jumping controls. There's no excuse.
This game has the worst melee combat I've ever experienced. Your weapon will phase through the enemy without damaging him unless you're facing him dead center, even with spin-attacks. Melee characters are riddled with useless moves that send you past the enemy and/or face away from him, like Karate Champ for the NES, but because the camera is fixed on the direction you're facing, you have to painstakingly turn it back around. There is no collision between characters; you just walk right through each other, which makes melee even more frustrating because you can't avoid going through your enemy and attacking the air behind him. You have only two choices in this game: flail away at someone in the hopes of stun-locking him, or choose a ranged character and spam. On that note, once someone start's flailing away and hits you, you're basically dead. There's no way to break out of a stun lock. The blocking is useless as it offers you no chance for counter-attack, and you can't block immediately after being hit. There is an animation to go into block, which delays it.

IF YOU WANT TO PLAY HARD RESET JUST BUY THE ORIGINAL ONE
I've played the Hard Reset demo ages ago but never played the whole game, until recently I've found out about this remaster edition and, since they were both on sale, I've bought em both so I could get the discount on the Redux one.
At the beginning it was fine, funny fast brainless FPS just as expected. but something was off: I remembered the demo to be quite challenging, while the Redux was pretty easy. I've played for 4/5 hours without dieying a single time on hard difficulty, so I've cheched some forum.
Turns out THE REDUX VERSION IS COMPLETELY BROKEN: I'm not sure if it was intended by developers, but the new dash mechanic basically gives you the possibility to dash continuosly and dodge everything without basically any cooldown and NO STAMINA BAR DEPLETION, while the original Hard Reset just let you sprint with a fast depleting stamina bar!
The problem is that the difficulty of the game is calibrated on the "dashless" version, so the dash will break the game challenge completely allowing you to doge most enemies way too easily.
THE SWORD: coupled with the dash there is the new sword. Same cons here, the original game wasn't developed with the sword in mind, so it feels horrible to use and the fact that it gets in the way every time you cycle weapon is SUPER annoying, also I'm quite sure you are forced to pick it up to progress the game.
THE GRAPHICS: if you wanted to play the game because of the improved graphic, you will be deluded. The quality is basically identical, most changes are just particles.
In the Redux there is an option for over resolution (nothing you can't do anyway on the old version with NVIDIA control panel for example) , but the only available option for AA feels blurry for many people (FXAA).
THE GOOD: thank to the revamped engine the game runs much more smoothly, if you have an high end system it won't matter but it might be a good thing for old pc or laptops.
So, as I said in the beginning, the original game is nice and the graphics hold up very well (actuallt the atmosphere looks beautiful imho), so just buy that. If you really want to give the developers more money you are free to buy both, but you can definitely skip playing the redux.

The popularly accepted theory that Jazz stemmed from a simple combination of African rhythms and European harmony is in need of a little revision. Both African and European rhythms were employed. African music supplied the strong underlying beat (absent in most European music), the use of polyrhythms, and the idea of playing the melody separate from or above the beat. European music provided formal dance rhythms. Combined, these rhythms give Jazz its' characteristic swing. Likewise, the harmonies and musical ideas of both continents are present, the blue notes derived from the pentatonic scale, "call and response" and unconventional instrumental timbres of African music together with "conventional" harmonies and, most important, the formal structure of European music. The multiplicity of ethnic, cultural and musical conditions needed to spawn Jazz was thus unique to the United States, and specifically to New Orleans. The necessary philosophical impetus for Jazz, i.e. , democracy and freedom of individual expression supported by group interaction, are also American institutions.

Citadel: Forged with Fire is a fantasy RPG sandbox from Blue Isle Studios and Virtual Basement. The official trailer is here:
In Citadel, you play a new apprentice magic user, waking inside a fiery magic circle within a ruined stronghold: one of the safe zones of the fantasy world of Ignus. You begin the game with literally nothing but your tattered clothes: no weapons, no spells, no abilities, and no instructions, save for the few brief tutorial-like snippets carved into the rocks scattered about the safe zones.
You quickly find that interacting with the world around you -- picking up items, crafting, building, and fighting -- provides you with experience, and before long you've gained a few levels, chosen your preferred weapon type (glove, wand, staff, or melee), and crafted your first weapon, learned some crafting recipes, and maybe even started to build your first home. Perhaps Ignus isn't so big and scary after all.
Hold on. Is that a giant? Run!
Citadel uses Unreal Engine 4 and, as you might expect for a game made with this engine, some of the graphics are superb. Trees and other flora look wonderful and are placed in a lifelike manner. Heavily forested areas give way to small clearings, and grassy plains dotted with boulders lead into steep hills. The terrain is variable and appropriate to the setting with plenty of realism. Building and crafting models and textures, too, are very nice, though necessarily 3D-tile-based.
Most creatures you encounter are well modelled, too, with high-resolution textures and significant variation in size and shape. It's often disappointing, though, when you see them move. Many of the animations seem to have very low frame counts and end up looking quite crude and wooden. This carries through to the player character graphics, too; these are probably the biggest let down to the visuals, with very few character generation choices, poorly modelled and animated characters, and terrible animation blending. Though you can change between first- and third-person view, at this stage I'd recommend you don't; the character animations are laughable.
Special effects are excellent, with powerful fireballs, undulating light rays, and the like. Water looks mostly very pretty with gentle wave animations, but reflections and shadows often don't look right at all. There's a large viewing distance, but noticeable pop-in at different stages for different objects, making things look a bit weird at times.
The interface is a bit fiddly, but consistent and functional. There are plenty of detail options; being Unreal, it gives my video card fan a work out regardless.
There's not much music in Citadel. The title theme is typical of the genre, but it's well produced and appropriate. In-game music isn't really music; it's more like a gentle sort of repetitive ambient trilling. It sounds much better than I've described it, really, and it prevents the game from feeling lonely.
Sound effects are good, with big explosions and other magical effects, typical tool-like crafting sounds, and good aural feedback when building and placing items. Creature sounds are good, too, but more variation in character sounds wouldn't go astray; usually you see you're being attacked due to the screen effects before you notice the rather lacklustre "Oof."
There is no speech.
Citadel is a fantasy world sandbox. You start with nothing, grind a few levels to learn some abilities and recipes for crafting and building, and then you do what you want to do; there are no set goals, no quests, and, from what I've seen, no storyline, or at least not yet. If you don't like setting your own goals and making your own way, then Citadel isn't the game for you.
Living in Ignus is all about gathering resources. Certain plants and magic crystals can be used to make health and mana potions. Other plants can be turned into cloth, which can be made stronger with a tailoring bench. Wood and stone can be used to make weapons, as well as to build a house to keep you safe from wandering creatures and give you somewhere to craft other things. Other resources can be taken from dead creatures or extracted from the world.
As you play you gain levels, and as you gain levels you earn both character points to spend on your four basic characteristics (mana, health, damage, and carrying capacity) and knowledge points to unlock spells and recipes for crafting and building. You gain experience for gathering resources, crafting, building, and fighting, so the more you do all of these things the faster you gain levels, and access to more and better things. You choose entirely where to focus your knowledge and thus how to spend your time in the game.
Combat, though it can be fun, is more limited than most action RPGs. You have two quick slots, one accessory slot, a few armour slots, and two alternate weapon slots, each of which can only have up to two spells equipped, bound to the left and right mouse buttons. So while there are quite a few cool spells and options, you're practically limited to using a very small number of them at any one time. Taming wild animals and giving them silly names does help, though.
The base building in the game is simply fabulous. Once you get the hang of the interface and learn what needs support and what doesn't, your resource-gathering abilities and your imagination really do seem to be the limit. So far I've made a more traditional mansion and a sprawling, multi-level, warren-like monstrosity on the shore of a natural healing pool, but I'm only barely touching the surface. As you gain knowledge points you can unlock more and better building materials, as well as dynamic lighting options and an array of decorative objects, too, should you wish to pretty things up a bit. The developers recently held a marble building competition and some of the entries were spectacular, all built with the in-game interface.
Citadel is designed to be multi player, but you can also set up a private server using the free server software, or even set up a custom game from the main game menu and play on a single PC if it has enough grunt. If you want to play by yourself or with friends, a private server is definitely safest, but I should also say that I haven't seen any griefers on the two official servers on which I've been playing. That said, the servers in my region are not exactly teeming with players at the moment, and from other reviews it sounds like there have been griefer problems in the past.
As you'd expect from an Early Access game of Citadel's scope, the game is still a bit buggy, but the developers release regular and emergency patches: one of each in the last week alone. There are still issues with windows staying open when they shouldn't (ProTip: try interacting with the object again to re-enable and then close them), some graphical issues, and I've had one big crash when I accidentally tried to pacify a cave rock. The pet AI is pretty terrible, too; pets often ignore combat entirely or get stuck on objects. I'm sure there are more issues, too, but I haven't encountered anything game breaking yet.
Pros:
+ World graphics
+ Building
+ HUGE world
Cons:
- Character and creature animations
- Very grindy
- Pet AI
Don't be put off by the griefer-related negative reviews. Citadel: Forged with Fire is an impressive game. The world is well realised and the terrain and flora graphics in particular look absolutely lovely. The lack of contextual information can leave new players wondering what to do and grinding is necessarily a big part of the game, but for anyone interested in creating their own fun in a huge magical fantasy sandbox, Citadel: Forged with Fire should hold many hours of enjoyment.

Intensely serious and dramatic, built on top of a game whose mechanics are very simple and mostly adequate. Taken as a pure game, it's nothing fancy, and arguably resembles a mobile game in just how simple it is to play. But with its rich sound and stark visuals, it really deserves to be played on a full monitor. Like many indie games, it doesn't set out to be a fun and addicting game, but rather to create an experience and make you feel "there". It does this very well, with a sense of overarching dread and impending doom made worse by every little mistake. You never quite have enough food, or if you do, enough medicine, or supplies, whatever. No playthrough will ever be perfect and you'll be left to decide just what you can afford to sacrifice.
Combat is something you're generally supposed to avoid, though that's no excuse for how awkward is actually is. Seeing as the game autosaves whenever you do much of anything, you may end up losing a survivor to the strange mechanics, which is a frustrating experience. Other than that though, this is a bleak and depressing survival sim that's nonetheless very enjoyable to play even though it left me feeling pretty devastated. Most importantly, it portrays a situation that's all too real in the world, and is very good at inspiring empathy in the player that may well translate to real life. That the only DLC is a donation directly to children affected by war just reinforces the solid intentions of the developers.

I've played this game on the Xbox 360 years ago, got it for free a few days ago.
TL;DR: Homefront is a bit of a gem, I'm glad to see it still has a player base, because it deserves it. It's sequel did the setting a diservice, but the original is still as good as it ever was. It has quirks, and the singleplayer is nothing special, but the multiplayer is unique and still kicking. It's worth 15 bucks if you can get it for that, but any higher and I'd be leery.
The singleplayer is somewhat bland and forgettable. The story can inject bits of life though. The first mission has a very... Unsettling, opener. Anyone who's played it and was paying attention will know what I'm talking about. One that made me feel a bit ill even though I knew it was going to happen after having played it years ago. One of the most memorable moments in gaming for me, and I mean that in a sense that it's very gripping. Unfortunately the game slowly loses momentum after that. 7 missions, though some are quite long, is not enough for me to get invested in these characters. Especially when your allies get stuck on something or take forever to open a door for you.
Now, on to what you're here for, the multiplayer. It's damn good, even years later. Homefront is the first, if not one of the first, of games to impliment a system of purchase points earned in a battle. These points are earned by killing foes, completeing objectives, and killing enemies who are on killstreaks. You use these points to buy bulletproof vests, rocket launchers, drones, and vehicles. It works really well, though it makes using vehicles a dangerous game, since launchers are quite common. The gunplay is... Odd. It's hard to explain, because it's not bad, but there's no other game like it. It's kind of like playing with your mousepad replaced with a tray of bearing grease. Aiming is kind of sticky, but smooth at the same time. You have to play it to see what I mean, but it's not something that is a negative, just a quirk.
The maps are well designed, with large map open maps, and small urban maps, all of which promote all kinds of gameplay at the same time. No weapon is useless on any map, which is something quite impressive.
Reminds me of Dungeon Keeper. Funny narrator on the campaigns.

Greetings Again!  Today I’m going to be talking about Dungeons 2 the sequel to well…dungeons…yup.  Anyway, I wasn’t secretive by my distaste of the original as it ended up feeling more like a tycoon game instead of a dungeon builder.  But!  I can say with great glee that this game is significantly better in almost every way possible.
Get out of my dungeon:  The most significant improvement right off the bat is the trashing of this ‘let the adventurers in your dungeon to be happy and steal souls stuff’.  The previous game created an environment where you basically gave the invaders what they wanted but had to chase them down before they left.  This game is much more about building a dungeon and going to the surface and killing everything; admittedly not always the most intricate missions but fun none the less.   This alone would make this game enjoyable by comparison but the game goes further.
Stop Cluttering:  Gimmicks are removed and so are spawn points; you are left with more of an evil genius style game where you mine gold, carve out space and build rooms with the ultimate goal of moving to the surface to destroy everything in your path.  The different monsters (or demons) are unique to each other and even are unique in many ways between the two factions.  I would have liked to see a third one (undead) as the story kind of hinted to it).  Instead of a theme park you are left with an underground base building game with a touch of RTS for good measure.
Stupid Penguins:  There are a few small problems; the most annoying for me is the finite amount of resources.   I am not a fan of timed games in this genre artificial or direct and this game has one for every mission.  Ultimately there is a finite amount of gold on the map and your monsters need paid about every 5 minutes.  Though it never happened during the campaign I did feel rushed on a mission or two as I enjoy exploring the map and training my monsters which ends up taking longer than more aggressive players.  There were also a few annoyances like dumping monsters into the exit can be annoying to line it up exactly (why not just have a larger exit hit-box) and clicking the top monsters can sometimes be difficult as the menu’s appearance covers a bit of the pickup icon.  It also would have been nice to just drop them on the map entrances instead; especially when you have multiple locations to spawn from and they don’t line up on both maps.  Finally, it would be nice to have maps for the mini dungeons like my dungeon or world maps.
I think you all see where this is going.  I enjoyed this game; love dungeon building games and this one had a bit of RTS mixed in and wasn’t done poorly.  So, overall, yes you should get this game.  I would even if it wasn’t on sale.  I would like to see more story and campaigns as the skirmish maps (even the DLC ones) only last me so long!  I hope you all enjoy as I did.

I played this game quite a bit in pre-Steam alpha - I recommend this game only to those who enjoy puzzle games, I'd say it's worth it if you can get it on sale for 10 bucks or less.
If you are looking for a tycoon/management game, this is not it.
------
I was originally intrigued because it reminded me a bit of Theme Hospital, which - like most Bullfrog games, I loved - but this doesn't play like a tycoon game, or a management game. It's more of a puzzle game.
Think Tetris where you have to research the different pieces.
This game cries out for a sandbox mode... where you can build a room, build an import, layout your machinery, then build an export - use the funds to research/innovate/explore etc - enlarge your factory, add more production lines, make more money, stay ahead of the competition.
Instead you get numerous scenarios in which you have to gain an arbitrary amount of money and/or create a specific type of medicine by a certain date and/or before the competiton.
The game itself is that you fit your production line into a predetermined amount of space. The ingredients must be researched and require various amounts of machines (which must also be researched) to get them into medically effective states. Your work out the logistics to make it all fit. Rinse, repeat.
Personally, I dislike scenario games like this; any game where I'm asked to spend time building something only to leave it all behind and start again from scratch level after level, wears thin on me rather quickly.
That said, the game is extremely well made in terms of quality, the UI has been streamlined and overall it's very solid. This dev knows what they're doing, and I look forward to more of their work.

Decided to play this instead of the remaster just because 1) It's a smaller download. 2) It's likely more stable. Bioshock 2 looks great even without the remaster anyways. I don't know why people have a problem with two's story, I think it is just as exciting and mysterious as the original. There is lots of good changes from the first game, especially in combat. Combat feels different, but more fluid in this game. I could care less about the protector trials DLC because of the boring little sister harvesting I mentioned earlier. I don't care for the multiplayer either because the whole principle of being an unstoppable genetic monster on the battlefield doesn't translate too well when playing with other people (and is likely why it was cut from the remaster). However, the Minerva's Den DLC is a is up there with one of the best expansion to the game in my book. It deals with an all new, separate story set in Rapture. It features new enemies, plasmids, and characters, and is overall a really well put together DLC. My only gripe with the whole game, is the parts where you let the sisters harvest the Adam, because in my opinion it slows down the pace of the game, and makes returning to the harvesting pace a little annoying after playing the game regularly. I may play the remaster someday, as I only had a few problems with the first one remastered, but looking at the reviews for the second remastered, I think it may be too unstable. You get both when you buy the game anyways though, so it doesn't really matter. This game is another classic FPS set in an original, interesting setting. It is not a game I would recommend missing. (But play the first though.)

Awe. It's an emotion one expresses at something that's hard to describe. That's actually a pretty accurate description for this little... thing. It's very cheap. So cheap that you'd be forgiven for thinking it was knocked together off the back of Unity Personal, and it probably was. However unlike most of those sad little products, this one is a diamond in a sea of very brown and stinky sewage. It's not particularly difficult, it's not particularly mechanically challenging, it's not going to blow you away with graphics.
... but it is going to chill you
.
You start simply enough, with a slowly spinning planet, a mellow ambient track, and a set of coloured triangles you're supposed to hit. Create those combinations and you're rewarded with new assets to plop down, fill the coloured circles representing those assets and you'll get to move on to the next planet. Slowly and gently you'll end up moving towards more complex reactions requiring three steps, then four, and the chains will become obscured, so you'll have to explore the planet, testing the colours to see what reacts with what.
It becomes a mellow puzzle, without ever becoming overly challenging, and always offering you the chance to start again. It gives you a very gentle, exploratory, and relaxing experience where nothing you do is really wrong, and you have the chance to create planet designs of your own style, with each planet looking significantly different by virtue of the puzzle layouts from the last.
Married to this is a gentle, swirling ambient soundscape that never invades, never presses down on you, and will put you at ease with the game, clicking on the planet surfaces and dropping assets will result in soft chimes, and it's quite easy to set up melodic harmonies quite by accident when you're creating reactions. You wind up smiling as you're working your way through the planet as you hear these gentle, encouraging chimes as the planets become more and more colourful.
Considering the price point? This is a no brainer to recommend to people who are interested in relaxing puzzlers. It's not going to stretch the gray matter, but if you need something that's going to help you wind down after a hard day of gaming? This is the gaming equivalent of a glass of red wine.

Originally it was a moderately entertaining F2P game that was still enjoyable without spending much real money on. The in game economy was always horribly broken. The 100 to 1 Hero Point ratio was not bad, but what it bought you was ridiculous. For an example unlocking one level of a skill in a three star(Rare) character is 1250 HP. Or $12.50. They want $12.50 to unlock one level of one skill of which there are 13 per character. Or around $150 if you want to completely unlock one character.
Fine, I was happy to play alound with the covers I could get through tournament rewards and the daily drops. Then came along the latest patch. Instead of fixing the rampant cheating or other various broken portions of the game, they decide to nerf some of the better characters that are relatively easy for the free players to get. No Devs, they weren't overpowered, they were accessible and most of the other accessible characters suck. Again, nerfing happens, most devs have still yet to realize it's better to balance up than down, but any relatively experienced gamer is used to that. But they also decided to start charging HP for the +3AP to all boost. They're now charging the equivalent of $1 for a stack of three boosts that will last maybe 10 to 15 minutes of game time and is very necessary for the casual players. The devs basically too a look at the game stats, saw what the casual players used most, and either made them less effective or started charging for them.
I had intended on buying $15 or so worth of HP to support the game and buy some roster slots, but I am definitely glad I waited and they will now never see a dime from me.

I got the game for free, so… I guess that’s cool.
“Thanks, Humble Bundle”.
I decided to give it a second chance given that the first time I played the game years ago, I found it a bit underwhelming, repetitive, and tedious to complete.
It just wasn’t that fun, or enjoyable, nor entertaining, so I wanted to see if, now, I could enjoy, or see different things in that game that I never seen before.
Sadly, things have remained the same.
Thing about Homefront is that the game has a great concept, and the ideas that it tries to deal with are interesting, and genuinely creative within its given context.
The problem comes from the execution of those ideas.
Gameplay wise the gunplay feels great, but sadly, you have to be secluded to only a couple of weapons, that don’t really change that much, unless you’re in scripted sequences in which maybe you need to use a sniper rifle, just to provide an example.
Eventually it gets old, and the other problem it’s the characters, the way some moments in the story are just handled, at one point you’re in a situation in which you and your group have to be hidden from the enemies, and all of the sudden, one of your group members sees something that “shocks” him, and out of nowhere starts shooting.
It is deliberately created as a moment that’s supposed to be meaningful, and powerful, but because of the way it’s presented, and because of the way the poor voice acting goes hand in hand with the terrible timing, both in relation to the nature of that particular situation in which you’re in, as well as in the subsequent consequences that affect how you play the rest of that mission, it comes out as a dumb, an absurd moment, completely redundant, that end up making that particular character that was supposed to, in a way, embody the whole idea of the resistance that its trying to repeal the North Korean regime, into a being that annoyingly makes mistakes that you have to fix, literally, by just completing sequences that become annoying knowing within the context of the illusion the game tries to create, could have been avoided.
I really have problems commenting on anything other than isn’t negative.
There really isn’t much more than the gunplay, which is the reason I think it has become a game praised by its multiplayer.
Problem is the game principally tried to be a single player focused experience.
The campaign follows up a basic formula, you get into a sequence in which the game tries to present the world around you, the way things have changed, and the idea that the resistance it’s trying to create.
Then it throws you into a situation in which you have to get into gunfights, that last for the most part in the game.
Only to then be thrown to a sequence in which you usually witness something merciless and brutal, within, sort of, like an unskippable cutscene, in which you can only move the camera around.
And that’s it.
Then there’s the fact that this game came out in that era of games that were still trying to “profit” from Call of Duty’s popularity by replicating, literally, some gameplay elements, as if somehow just by repeating the same game over, and over again every game would have sold the same way…
Don’t mention Call of Duty as the example of a game that does that, that game has earned that, by being that, people like Call of Duty, people that like it will keep buying it as long as it stays the same, but that can’t be extended to other games, because the “formula” or the experience of that game, is already “owned” by the game it created it.

Intensely serious and dramatic, built on top of a game whose mechanics are very simple and mostly adequate. Taken as a pure game, it's nothing fancy, and arguably resembles a mobile game in just how simple it is to play. But with its rich sound and stark visuals, it really deserves to be played on a full monitor. Like many indie games, it doesn't set out to be a fun and addicting game, but rather to create an experience and make you feel "there". It does this very well, with a sense of overarching dread and impending doom made worse by every little mistake. You never quite have enough food, or if you do, enough medicine, or supplies, whatever. No playthrough will ever be perfect and you'll be left to decide just what you can afford to sacrifice.
Combat is something you're generally supposed to avoid, though that's no excuse for how awkward is actually is. Seeing as the game autosaves whenever you do much of anything, you may end up losing a survivor to the strange mechanics, which is a frustrating experience. Other than that though, this is a bleak and depressing survival sim that's nonetheless very enjoyable to play even though it left me feeling pretty devastated. Most importantly, it portrays a situation that's all too real in the world, and is very good at inspiring empathy in the player that may well translate to real life. That the only DLC is a donation directly to children affected by war just reinforces the solid intentions of the developers.

I've held off on writing for a while but i figured now it’s time to finally write it. I know i do not have a ton of hours, but i’ve been with this game since launch day.
This review comes from the perspective of playing the game, and hosting a private server for the game. My server; Avalon - was up an hour after the game launched, and to this day as i’m writing the review it is still up. So to say i’m generally invested in this game is an understatement.
- i’ll try to elaborate on each.
The devs said in their live stream they have no plans to add to the size of the map. Really disappointing because the map is fairly small.
The monsters in the game aren’t that great. You can range them down before they even get to you. Adding to that, there’s only like a total of 15 mobs in the game right now.
The only objective of this game is to level and build; and leveling is only a means of unlocking new items to craft/build. And building in incredibly easy, as resources are abundant. Once you build yourself a nice base, there’s really nothing else to do. There’s no deep or intricate production/craft chains.
I think the dev team is great; they seem passionate about the game and want it to succeed. They’re very personal with the community (discord) and sometimes they release 2-3 updates a week. But the updates are shallow and the current updates lack a proper direction.
Each week they release an update; but the updates they release don’t add that much gameplay. They added marble structures. Most players will come back; build for 1-2 hours and then leave. They added a few creatures; most players will come back, try out the new creature and leave.
There no point to pvp besides to player kill. There’s zero competition for resources, zero reasons to engage someone. Which breathes a way bigger issue; griefing. Veteran players will simply kill newbies for the sake of killing them, because they have nothing else to do. The devs said they plan on adding a rank system for pvp, this is just going to encourage more griefing.
For raiding it’s the same thing; there’s no point too it besides wanting to wipe out someone’s base.
The game for some reasons lacks basic features that a game should have before hitting EA. You can’t delete your character, you can’t make a new (second) character, there’s no local chat, chat commands like /r don’t work, settings constantly reset. I just think by now these things should have been addressed.
It feels like they release an optimization patch each week; and it seems like half of them don’t do much. At the start of a new server you’ll load in within a minute and be at a stable 60 fps at max settings. Come back in a week you’ll take a lot longer to load in, and you’re fps bounces between 35-40.
I know structures built causes this sort of thing; but there are a ton of other games out there that resemble citadel that don’t have this issue. Even as a server admin this becomes annoying. For some reason when servers are up for 3-4 hours they start to lag and a restart of the server usually resolves it. Eventually restarts take 10 minutes because the game world takes so long to load.
And this leads me to another issue; the servers. I wish the dev team would consolidate servers, and rent their own hardware to host. They currently have servers hosted by g-portal - for anyone who has hosted a server in the past, hearing the name g-portal should tell you everything you need to know about their service.
I find it really weird that the official servers are hosted on game-servers with worse hardware than private servers.
I have 3 months left on my server host (paid for 5 months) and after that i’ll be moving on. I supported the game for a while, but after the past few updates i don’t see a proper direction. I didn’t want to write a negative review; but this may be the only way to get feedback noticed it seems. Despite constantly leaving feedback on the discord.
Add some objectives, give players things to do besides build - because building really has no purpose in this game other than crafting stations. There’s no point to pvp besides PK. Make some arenas, add towns and npcs, make currency a thing. Resources are too abundant.

In theory, this is idea was clever! Moving into the endgame of a Dungeon Keeper-like management game has never been satisfying, so replacing it with an RTS battle might’ve been a good payoff--thematically appropriate too, as it connects the idea of an underground evil corrupting a totally different surface. The central idea of Dungeons 2 is a good one. As a personification of Ultimate Evil, you’re playing a Dungeon Keeper-like strategy game belowground — indirectly controlling your creatures to build rooms for efficiency, sending little imps out to find caves and gold, managing entertainment for bored creatures —all this stuff works. When you’ve got a decent little army, you send them above the ground, where it’s a conventional real-time strategy game in the Warcraft vein: direct control over troops, right-click to move and attack, and so on.
And it feels like playing Warcraft...the first one, from 1994. There’s no major strategic element--you just find enemies and smash them. Nor is there’s a significant tactical component. Things like attack-while-moving, or formations? Not present. A few units have skills, like upgraded orcs who can buff nearby units with a Battle Cry, But you’ll have to wrestle with the interface to get to them. There are hotkeys for the special skills, it turns out, but Dungeons 2 never makes this clear.
Obfuscation of important information, or poor explanation, is a consistent problem throughout Dungeons 2. It tells you what you need to do (often, and annoyingly, during the campaign) but rarely how you might go about doing it using the confusing interface. For example, on one campaign map, you have a mission to build an arena and train a unit with it. I did this, and consistently dropped my units on the new fighting pit. He or she would sit there, whack the training dummy for a while, gaining experience...and the narrator would continue to tell me I needed to train units. It turned out that by “train,” Dungeons 2 meant a much more specific use of the Arena: I had to drop the unit onto the pit, then click on the Arena and select a unit upgrade. That would get the narrator off my back… half an hour later. That was simply the most egregious example — far too much of my time was spent trying to figure out how to navigate three or more levels of maps, or why, despite clicking the “attack” button that appeared over an enemy trap, my troops were simply standing there and letting it kill them.

See what it feels like to be Martin Shkreli, in this pharmaceutical company management sim, ... well maybe not. In Big Pharma you do manage a pharmaceutical company but it's more of a puzzle game with management elements.
Big part of the gameplay is placing various machines that increase or decrease concentration of ingredients or mix them up and finally turn them into pills or creams or syringes. All these machines have different input and output locations and often sizes, you also need to add conveyor belts and with limited amount of space and doors through which ingredients can enter and leave your factory creating a new drug becomes, well a puzzle. Besides planning your factory you'll send explorers in search of new ingredients and researchers to invent new types of machines or improve existing ones.
You can play in free mode or one of many challenges. What is really smart and should be adopted in other games is that the challenges get progressively more complex. And I don't mean that the competition gets tougher or you are hit with arbitrary debuffs. The game actually limits your research tree and ingredient list to only present you with simple choices. Then as you progress you are given more and more options. It's a really nice game that hits that improvement itch, you've created a cure for bad breath and now you can improve it and cure sore throat. Coming up with more and more complex recipes for more advanced cures is extremely satisfying.
I highly recommend it my 10h with Big Pharma felt like a breeze and I'm looking forward to many more.

Generally, the graphics are truly wonderful and pleasing to the eye. There weren't any moments while playing where something hurt my eyes. The cars look nice, as well, and the livery options have a large variety of choice. The racing environments are very well detailed and surprisingly open/expansive. Not only that, but one of my favorite graphical features is the fact that it is not always the same time of day from one race to another.
The controls are a bit different of a story. The controls (mostly steering) seem a bit more sensitive than they should be. Not only that, but I can't seem to be able to locate any sort of option for changing steering sensitivity, if there is one.
Another problem I have with this game when compared to the first is probably one of the most prominent features of the GRID series: flashbacks. In all honesty, a flashback system, in my eyes, is pretty interesting. It gives a chance for redemption if you've made a mistake. Unfortunately, this feature has been changed, and it feels as if it's an attempt by a knock-off game to implement this mechanic. For one, you cannot navigate through the flashback to find the exact spot you messed up. It has become pressing a button and hoping you hit it again in the right place to fix a mistake you made, if that makes any sense.
Another problem is the artificial intelligence. The artificial intelligence of the other racers seems somewhat independent of the player. It kind of takes out the feel of the game as a true racing career simulator. Although, this isn't the worst thing ever.
A personal issue I have with this game is the apparent lack of any voice other than your manager (I think). The voice acting for this character, though, was cast well, and the role really adds some realism to the game.
Here's an issue I have with this game that I haven't seen a lot of other reviewers address. Sound. First off, the man who speaks to you during races talks FAR too little in order for the game to feel like you're really in a racing simulator. At times, it begins to feel like the lines he says are recycled over and over again. Another issue that I would also say gets neglected in the reviews is the music. The music just seems so unfitting for a game like GRID 2, especially when the music for the original GRID fit so well. Not only that, but oh boy... THERE ARE WAY TOO MANY HIGH-PITCHED SOUNDS IN THE MUSIC. I often find myself wanting to take my headphones off because of how high-pitched some of these sounds are.
Now, there seem to be a large amount of city-based courses in the early parts of the game. This is fine and all, but when you have players whose computers are lagged by all of the detail of cities, it kind of spoils the gameplay.
Overall, I enjoy it (after having crashed into a tree on the first race...). Decent sequel. I had a lot of enjoyment from the first, and this game feels pretty familiar. Despite that, the original GRID, as other reviews have stated, is far superior on most aspects. I still would recommend this game just for fun.
Just as a fair warning before you play this game, racing games don't really work too well when the control scheme is keyboard based. If you're going to play Grid 2, I STRONGLY recommend some sort of controller with a USB.
