I don't know why this game gets so much flak. People complain about lot's of things because it gets compared to Civ 5 too much. A lot of people seem to be mad becaues it doesn't have some of the same features, and others complain that it has too many.  What I have to say to that is, it's not Civ 5. It is part of the Civilization series so a lot is going to be the same. Also, most of this review will be the improvements from Civ 5.
Pros:
After playing hours of civ 5, this game is flipping amazing. The first thing I noticed was there were lots of beginning choices  so you can basically choose your play style. Another thing, I was worried this game wouldn't be as immersive because they're not real civs. WRONG! I loved being able to colonize the world, and the intro movie got me really pumped for it. The next thing I noticed was the diplomacy starts at the beginning, getting rid of having to find everyone. This was nice, because what I didn't like about Civ 5 is that after starting many games, it gets boring doing the early game crap. Also the diplomacy added favors, which was needed very much in Civ 5.
Probably my favorite new feature was the intrigue. It was AMAZING! I loved how you could actually control you agents more then just "steal tech" and "stage coup". The system was really fun. Also the quests made things interesting, and the quest decisions made it even more emersive.
Finally, the Affinity sytem was really interesting, and was something that never came out of Civ 5.
Cons:
It isn't as big as Civ. Yet. It is bigger then Vanilla Civ 5, though Civ 5 with expanions is bigger. Hopefully the Beyond Earth expansions will fix that.
Not as many kinds of units as Civ 5. That's said, until you realize nearly all the units in civ 5 are just variations of a base unit.
Not as much diversity in the civilizations (companies). This is probably my least favorite part of the game, the companies aren't all that different, and there aren't unique units or anything.
Conclusion: The game is amazing now, but has flaws. With DLC it will probably be even better.

I'm very conflicted on this. The game has good music and graphics. The happiness system is actually well-balanced. The mini-quest system adds some interest. Gameplay is really quite boring though. Some letdowns:
* I would say that the AI is really, really bad. Terrible diplomacy skills and absolutely awful unit management in a war.
* The biggest map size still feels small and cramped.
* No more than 8 civs per map.
* I want slow-tech games to be about slow tech, not slow-everything else. With the marathon (or w/e it's called) speed, road building is slow as well.
* Techs are just boring. Descriptions are good and fancful, but just boring techs overall. Remember those 0-travel cost railroads in earlier Civ? Well, in this game we have roads and magrail. Boring, boring, boring. It just feels like a re-skinned Civilization. They really seemed to try with the O.K. terrain improvements.
* Crashes sometimes for no reason after long play. (memory leaks)
Overall, it just seems like this game was designed by a committee.

Remains one of the best stealth games ever made, and still one of the best games of all time really. Easily the best in the Splinter Cell series, this is in my top 5 favorite games ever. Every element this game aims for, it achieves perfectly. The graphics are amazing for the time, the gameplay is fantastic and requires patience and skill, and the map design actually allows some exploration but keeps things focused. It's pretty laughable at times when it drops dates "this is 2008... the future!" but as a game it works unbelievably well. It's the most balanced when it comes to combat vs stealth, in that it's very realistic in how it handles it. If someone catches you off guard, they can kill you pretty much instantly, but the same goes for all the enemies.
Playing the newer installments, it's sad how simple they've become. It's not a simple "it's new so it sucks thing", this one is better than the older installments. It has just the right balance of skill requirement vs being accessible and holds up the best. You have to manage how well you're lit up or how loud you are compared to the environment masking your footsteps, but it's easy to do and incredibly rewarding once you master it. Some games like the Hitman series or the newer Splinter Cell installments don't really do the stealth elements well enough to really get into it, but this game achieves it perfectly. You do need to stay hidden but it's fun and worth it to get that badass feeling of coming out of the shadows with your knife, or whistling to get a guards attention and snap his neck from a pipe above as he nears you. Co-op missions are decent if you have a friend to play it with, but the story mode is the main focus as it should be. The soundtrack, dark visuals, and excellent stealth gameplay are just amazing. If you're into stealth games especially, I recommend this. It isn't an action shooter.

Awe sees you take the role of a god to slowly build up planets filling them with both natural and artificial assets until you build the last structure and move to the next one: you do so by spending "awe" a resource created by matching sequences shown on screen by clicking on the planet's different coloured tiles, the same matches will also unlock new assets, and thus colours for the sequence.
The game comes out a casual puzzle-ish title that starts easy and relaxing but, as new areas are unlocked, adds enough new mechanics (hidden colours, seasons that bring in new coloured tiles for a limited time) to keep things fresh and slowly ramp up the challenge.
-the 3d graphics are simple but are quite charming to look at
-good variety of assets for each planet ranges from the usual trees, mountains and caves to broken bottles, tires and wrenches
-minimalistic soundtrack works well
-the gameplay slowly introduces new ideas and manages to stay interesting while not being too challenging once you get the hang of it: it's pretty relaxing without ever becoming dull
-good amount of content and thus length, 25 planets to solve took me almost 5 hours at a leisurely pace
-some tutorial are pretty vague and/ or in a somewhat cryptic English, this means certain mechanics ( e.g. how repeating a match to unlock an asset also brings a bit of awe, how every asset can lock down season tiles used to unlock it etc..) are not explained properly and could leave you stuck on a level: thankfully the Discussion area has most of the info to help you
-before you get the hang of how to put assets to make subsequent matches easier and/ or to lock down season tiles in the most useful areas you'd end up waiting for the correct season to appear AND the season tiles to be on the right face of the planet, if this doesn't happen you might have to wait a minute or two to finally get the match you need and this can get a bit dull at times
I must say I was quite impressed by Awe, the first planets were quite easy and I was afraid things might get boring but once seasons, longer matches and hidden sequences were introduced the game became a pretty fun brain teaser capable to keep me occupied while never becoming frustrating. The art style and music are pretty simple but do their job  and I really appreciated how each area had its own theme thanks to different tiles and assets.
For a buck Awe offers some nice and easy-to-learn gameplay backed up by a good amount of content: I heartily recommend it , especially to people that want something uncomplicated and/ or suitable for the whole family, I found it perfect for the early morning/ late night hours when I wanted something to play but was too tired or occupied to fire up complex games.

I came to this game not knowing anything about Magic: The Gathering, and being the kind of person utterly uninterested in multiplayer games. I had dabbled in Hearthstone, but found it boring.
Now, about 250 hours in, I'm a confirmed Magic fan, and look forward to playing about half an hour to an hour a day. I've built lots of decks, and spent no money.
I would recommend this to anyone with a vague interest in trading card games. There is quite a high level of complexity, but that makes it very strategically rich. I remember a light bulb moment when someone beat me in such an interesting way, I suddenly looked at all the crads again, realising that with various combos you can do almost anything. This has lead to many memorable games, sudden reversals, and tense losses.
This game isn't a perfect version of MtG - some of the best cards aren't there, occasionally 'streamlining' means that cards like Elder Deep Fiend lose their application, and most importantly of all, without a best of 3 approach, you can sometimes lose purely for mana reasons, which you can do nothing about (although they give you an extra, 'free' mulligan to make this less likely). There are also a few bugs, the latest being a botched AI when it comes to vehicles. But bugs do fixed every time they release a new set of cards (about every 3 months).
Still, even given that, this is a fun game, which is more than generous with coins. You should be earning at least a booster pack a day, even just by playing a few rounds.
One thing to note, if you start playing the multiplayer when a new set of cards come in, everyone has just had their rank reset, so you'll often have your behind handed to you. But even losing can be fun, and you're always earning coins, so soon you'll be able to get that deck set up that allows you to take your sweet, sweet revenge.

Marvel Puzzle Quest: Dark Reign

Marvel Puzzle Quest is the newest game in the Puzzle Quest line of games. This series has seen a lot of iterations and copycats over the years, with none being nearly as successful as the original title. This latest is an officially licensed Marvel title with the Puzzle Quest formula. It has the added benefit of being entirely free-to-play. You may of course purchase bonuses like any other free title, but these purchases are not required to play the full game. Is this latest attempt at a Puzzle Quest success worth a look, or should you just let it speed by and fade into the distance? Keep reading, perhaps I can help you decide.

To begin with, the Marvel universe has been utilized pretty well here. You have a team of three characters, each with three possible powers to be used. Typically you begin with one of these powers and you must find comic covers of the character to unlock or upgrade said powers. This also allows you to level up your character a little bit more each time. It’s a system that constantly keeps you feeling like you’re making some kind of progress and it works very well. Winning battles and missions grants you rewards, randomized from a pool of up to four for each story mission, giving you reasons to play missions again and again until you’ve received every reward available. It’s structured remarkably well for any game, let alone a free-to-play title. It’s a nice change of pace to see a free game with a lot of effort put into it. The content level is more than a lot of full priced games have, and the developers deserve some credit for it.

The presentation is decent. Each character is represented by a comic book cover from any number of different Marvel universes, and has a full 3D model as well as a 2D comic profile. Everything is vibrant and colorful and stands out very well in a sea of photo-realistic browns and grays of more recent games. The music is a bit generic, but it’s suitable for a superhero game. There are lots of highs and thumping bass tracks to drive the combat forward. It can certainly get repetitive, but that’s what the volume slider in the options menu is for. Overall, it doesn’t detract from the experience any and fits in well enough that some may not really notice it.
On to the meat of things; the gameplay! I’m pleased to say that the gameplay of Marvel Puzzle Quest is, well, fantastic to be perfectly honest with you. It is a very well implemented use of the Puzzle Quest formula with enough difference and excitement to stand well on its own feet. Each color is representative of one member of your team, and has an icon to indicate which member that is. Wolverine, for example, is represented by scratch marks across the gems, while Storm has lightning bolts. Each icon makes sense and stands out well, making it easy to determine who will be attacking. Collecting gems allows you to use character powers, which can drastically change the way a fight is going. More powerful abilities take more preparation time and cause severe damage, while less powerful abilities can be used more often but do less damage or have fewer utility effects attached. There is a story mode separated into four separate mission groups, which will last you a good number of hours to complete. There are also daily and weekly missions and a PVP mode to keep you playing as long as your interest remains. Each of these modes offers its own rewards and characters, and as a result each also adds a huge amount of content to the game.

As for the dreaded free-to-play purchased content that inevitably unbalances these games? Well…it is present, but it’s not nearly as bad as other games often are. You can purchase the two currencies present in the game in bulk quantities, and use those currencies to recruit more and rarer characters or power up your existing heroes. It does unbalance the multiplayer somewhat if you let it, but it’s not so bad that it ruins the game entirely in that department. In order to counter the unbalancing, you just have to search a bit harder for an opponent on the same level as you. It can definitely be a pain in the backside from time to time but it isn’t something that ruins the overall experience and shouldn’t keep you from giving the game a shot.
Marvel Puzzle Quest: Dark Reign has far more content and playability than a free game should ever reasonably be expected to contain. If you let it, this game will suck you in and keep you playing into the wee hours of the morning without even realizing it. There are far worse ways you could be spending your free time. Don’t let the price tag fool you; this is one game that doesn’t skimp on the content just because it’s free of charge. Give it a shot and you might be pleasantly surprised.

As most would probably agree, this isn't really what one would consider a God-Game like Black & White, From Dust or Populous. It's more of a relaxing, simplistic terraforming puzzle game. Essentially, you have a planet of varying dimension and size that rotates very slowly. By clicking on the color of the ground, you match it with the combinations on the left of the screen to unlock more terraforming features (for example a forest or a mountain). Placing a mountain or a forest requires the ingame resource, AWE, which you stockpile by matching additional color types. For example, I've unlocked forest by clicking brown land types and blue land types but I don't have enough Awe to place it. Now I must gather awe by clicking brown, brown, blue, blue etc etc. It's all very simple and surprisingly addictive and with the incredibly mellow music playing in the background, you will easily slide into this game feeling relaxed and unpressured. Keep in mind, you don't want to terraform all the spaces on a planet until you unlock all of the terraforming features... otherwise, you'll have to start over.
Summed up, this game is totally worth a dollar just for the peaceful experience alone. Definitely recommended.

Not technically a god game, more zen-like puzzle involving planets and 'terraforming' at a low poly level.
Start off by naming a solar system, each has 5 moons circling a sun. Objective is to fill worlds by placing coloured tiles containing different biomes. New tiles are discovered by highlighting in the correct order and completion of each level comes from maxing out specific groups. Progress further and planets change from rounded objects to more complex shapes and order of tiles becomes much more difficult as well. Colours flash rather then stay lit so it turns into a game of  concentration/memory.
Runs on unity, screen resolutions of 4k+ are supported and controls were all mouse driven. Not sure how many planets Awe contains but for some casual puzzling with a relaxing soundtrack it's hard to go wrong for the price. Cheers.

While I understand the need to get new players into the game, I feel you are undervaluing a platform to allow people to play MTG from anywhere in the world with one another. The limited scope of the game and simplistic watering down of the rules I feel only cripples the very thing you are setting out to do. There is a huge market for this game but time and again all I hear from YouTubers is "This game would be great if ____". The lack of attention to detail is troubling as well, even from a game development standpoint. It has been riddled with bugs since launch and the dev team seems to take ages to respond to anything.
A final complaint I have, why remove cards? I understand (though barely) the need for a limited release of the sets, as not to hurt paper magic sales, but if you have already added cards in, why remove them? It feels like I am being robbed of something I payed for. There are a few cards I can reference but most notably the gates and gatecreeper vines. I can find no explaination online about this either.
All in all, while the skeleton of Magic is here, there is no substance, and I cannot in good faith recommend this game to anyone until the devs fix the appaling bugs and perhaps respond to community feedback.

Ok, so I am casual player and have now spent a fair bit of time playing this game. I can see that there are mixed reviews for this game which I can sort of understand as the game is not perfect and is still being developed. The developers are quite active and often respond to posts on the forums and I get the feeling they are listening to our feedback, which is always a good start. The developers have also provided a chart of the things they working, what coming next and things they would like to introduce at some point. This is great when engaging with the community.
So first off when you get in the game the graphics are great and the world environment is nice with two prominent biomes (forest/mountains and snow/frozen areas). The interface has recently been given a face lift and very easy to use and navigate with the building commands and the spell etc nicely set out and easy to understand.
The game on the whole runs really well and smooth. Although occasionally you do get patches introduced which may mess this up. But these often get resolved fairly quickly (not always quick enough for some though!). The building in the game is nice and easy. Essentially there is a hidden grid system so when building everything will join up nicely. Indeed all elements of your base need to be connected in some way to claim ownership (by placing a throne).
There is plenty to do if you like building and making grand cities. PVE wise, there is a limited about to do. There are various caves you can explore which are usually filled with mobs to take on. The AI of these mobs is not so great at the moment and still needs to be worked on. There is talk about having world bosses in the future for large group encounters which will be nice. PVE still gets the usual griefing where people build in caves or block areas off. The devs are working on this to keep things fun and content accessible. If you have probs though there are a few servers to chose from.
As far as PVP goes, this is quite fun. They made changes recently which makes this aspect of the game a lot harder, as people found their bases got destroyed to easily. Now its more of break in and grab the loot situation unless your determined to take a base out and willing to spend a lot of time and resources (assuming people hide their thrones well). Whilst this makes raiding harder it actually improves the experience a little, as a lot of raiding probably occurs when people are off line. You can use turrets and shield to beef your base up more which are effective if done right. Together with harder raiding, you can sleep knowing that if you built with pvp in mind you base should be ok. If you do get hit, then your loot may be all gone (depending how you hide it) and your base will be their still. Repair and reinforce and restock. For the raider though, while off line raiding some say is the cowards way, it gives you more time to try and break in, like a puzzle, looking for the quickest route in using the least siege spells to make it worth it. Often people build a base like a maze so you need to try and work out the best way to go when confronted with 3 doors for instance. So I actually find the pvp side of things good. A nice balance between effort of raiding and defence.
I have not done much pvp against other players when roaming around. People either just fly away on their broom or are just friendly....(prob attack you in the night instead :D). I have taken plenty of peoples dragons out when they forage too far away and then I take whatever loot it had on it hehehe
I would say at the moment the pvp servers are best to play on as you can pretty do the RPG PvE stuff on their with an added element of potential conflict with others.
So at the time of writing this review, there are a couple of bugs work out. There is a decay system to remove buildings of inactive players. But this seems to be affecting active players at present with random wall panels and or floors going missing. This will be fixed soon I am sure. There is also an issue with the severs it seem with low fps and things loading up in game. Again this is not normally an issue so I am sure it will be sorted next patch.
So in conclusion, this is a well polished game, particularly for an Early Access. The game is really fun to play and although it has limited content, there is still plenty to do. It will take you a while to reach level 60 but things will unlock along the way to keep you interested. I am not level 60 yet and I have been playing nearly 300 hours!!! mind you I haven't been power levelling.
So I would say get the game, try it out as you will get plenty of game play for only a few quid! Come join the official Basilisk server :)

Absolutelly one of the most surprising game of the year for me, although strictly survival games are not my cup of tea.
The game is all about living through a war trapped in a desolated town full of snipers, other survivors and militia. It§s not much of a fighting game, as one might suggest according it§s title, but more of a strategy one.
You start with three random people, where each has some kind of perk like good cook, handyman or sneaky person and of course a lot of bad habbits like smoking, drinking, etc. Each day and night for that matter, you have to get resources (food, medicine, wood...) and make sure you take care of your shelter. You have to keep people fed, rested, keep the sad and bad mood out of the doors and especially, do everything there is to gather more resources and stay alive while making so.
The more days you keep people alive, the more and harder choices are put in front of You. People start visiting you in your shelter nad offering trade, requesting help or asking to stay with you even. Will you take the poor man in and increase your chance for survival as more people are needed to guard the house and risk, you won§t find enough food or water, or turn him away?
Each night, you can send out one person to scavenge for materials and food the other buildings around shelter. Some are empty and only blocked door or pieces of collapsed wall block your way to treasures as simple as can of meat, other times you may find milia, medics, or just people like you trying to survive.
This game will let you think about the war in absolutely different context than Medal of Honor or Call of Duty sort of games. Here, you are no hero to charge to the front lines, no supersoldier to take out the enemy. Here, your enemy is cold, fear and shortage of food and people to trust.
Subtle music is very much increasing the overall gloom and is well placed and doesn't become a chore. Inventory is simple and functional while character actions are dictated by various icons around the map, which is always like X-COMs HQ style.
Game is certainly difficult to master and I guess very few managed to succeed for the first time. Anyway after the first playthough, playable characters are unlocked step by step as you play more and more games. There is also a custom game, which lets you set up your own challenge with the right group of people.
And let me emphasize the DLC. This is the first DLC that actually matters. For as low as 1€ you are donating money to charity and in exchange you get a piece of art, even though in a digital form. Who needs five new batman suits for twice the money. I challenge other developers to bring more of these.

The game can be useful only as a time killer.
Dungeons 2 is closer to DK1-2 than its predecessors. Unfortunately, gameplay is simplified almost to a point where it feels like a tablet clicker. Excessive use of references and primitive jokes (mostly about Warcraft 3 and Game of Thrones, although there are refs to LotR, God of War and a dozen of other universes) cannot mask the shallowness. To say that campaign playstyle is linear is to compliment the game, which is further worsened by constant kicks of the narrator urging you to walk the corridor plot.
Given some writers' love it could become a pleasant parody game. Unfortunately, now it is not. Jokes aren't required to be shallow in order to be fun.
+ Consistent and quite likeable visual design. Don't expect it to have any grimness of DK though.
+ Strives to be a DK follower. A rare case.
+ At long last, surface combat
+ Two stylish races to choose from (three, if you have the Winter DLC)
+ Effective and interesting traps
- Usability is severely lacking in some places. There's no speed slider, picking several creatures one after another (or gold, or anything) quickly becomes torture - the game is rather inresponsive. The same inresponsiveness when digging or placing rooms/traps. It simply doesn't highlight things and catch mouse clicks good enough.
- Horribly slow workers. Even more so when they are carrying something. Even with all the upgrades. You will find yourself carrying gold instead of them more often than you think.
- Exploration is almost nonexistent, both on surface and underground. Unlike DK2, there are little to none interesting places or secrets on the map. At most, you will find some small constant buff to apply to one of your warriors.
- Combat is extremely simplified and mechanistic. There are unit vs unit priorities but following them requires tons of micromanaging. You will most probably ignore them and stick to microing just to keep your troops alive. The same with combat abilities - you will rarely have time to use them. Your units have no understanding of formations, so placing ranged at the back and tanks at the front (and rotating tanks) is something you will be doing with frustrating frequency (Something Warcraft 3 always tried to do for you).
- Magic is mostly useless. The last one or two "ultimate" spells are useful when the enemy will be mass-rushing you. Evac spell has some usefullness (if you have time to cast it). Direct damage spells are too weak.
- Resources on the map are limited. If you ran out of them before you complete the objective, you fail. Unlike you, the enemy has no real economics, so you can't damage it (although he has little chance to damage yours - workers will mostly flee, and rooms/traps are indestructible).
- Surface raid is "grab some soldiers, kill everything on sight, repeat". There is literally nothing on the surface except enemy units and spawner buildings. Automatic conversion of territory is fun at first, but quickly gets boring, and its only function is providing visibility (aside from visuals). No useful things, no interactable things, no neutral things. You can't even select enemy "buildings" - they are just destructible decorations, nothing more.
- The plot is a lie. The game has it, but even War of the Overworld's one is deeper. Jokes are good as spices but make up for a poor meal.

Grid has and continues to be less of a simulation fans racing game for the sake of being more of an arcade racing game. And it does what it does as well if not better than it ever has before in Grid:Autosport. That being said, there is precious little telemetry and car customization and you're given little to no selection for what you'll be driving from one race to the next. And I hate that, I'm a sim-racing fan more than anything else. But I've enjoyed my time in Grid:Autosport for sure. You won't find bespoke graphical / mechanical car customization and selection in Grid, but  you will find lots of solid arcade (think ridge racer) fun.
The HD textures (while perhaps one of my favorite optional free DLC offerings from devs of any game) causes what appears to be memory-leak crashes for me but the game is pretty enough in high-res mode for me to be fine without it. As for other visuals, I feel much more like I'm racing in particular cars than I have in other games, hatchbacks typically have some weighty body-roll thats ideal to pre-load going into a corner, and high-strung sports cars feel like their "twitch" is pushing your head around like it owes this game money.
I have a few minor problems with the audio, but they're minor and can be completely overlooked unless you really care to hear them. The team radio announcer is a little bland most of the time and a bit uninformative. But I like the idea of having radio-comms to coordinate car condition and situational performance. I'd especially like it if more games swapped out some selectable or even voice activated voice checks for the typical HUD items that tend to litter most racing games.
Split screen!!! Thank you! I wish more games tried a little harder to put/keep this in their PC games. I like online gaming, but few things are as satisfying as sitting next to the person you're stomping into a dirty mudhole on the track =)
I really like the idea of a youtube button during replays for uploading them to youtube. A wonderful addition to a very pretty and exciting racing experience. And it has been pretty user-friendly (as far as reply controls go) for me to capture some decent footage for machinima things I do in my spare time. But the manually selectable camera angles are limited to the same ones you have access to during the race. So that could have maybe been better. Note* - the automated cinematic camera angles are on a loop, so if you're trying to get footage, it's easy to accidentally repeat the same exact camera angles over multiple takes.
I've had zero problems using my cheapo (but heaven-sent) logitech gamepad with analog triggers with no in-game setup at all. Right outta the gate everything worked flawlessly. There's a lot to be said for that.
I can't speak for the online play yet. But if I get around to giving it a shot I'll sure update my review accordingly.

Got this for a fiver, and for that price it's excellent. I played one of the earlier Hitman games back in the day, can't remember which, and I like the concept. Absolution has a good idea and nice graphics, but it has a couple of serious drawbacks:
First of all the controls. There's like 12 different functions in the game, and for some reason there needs to be a separate key assigned to each. Once you've played the game for a dozen hours or so, you'll start to get the hang of the controls, but they never cease to feel clunky and unwieldy. Get prepared for a lot of "oops, I pressed the wrong button!" in tight spots, which results in you more or less failing the mission. Not cool.
The second, and perhaps more significant problem, or rather issue, with the game design is that completing the missions unnoticed is insanely difficult, even on the "normal" difficulty. At the same time the character can take hits like a tank, so you're actually better off not even trying to be sneaky, and instead just going in guns blazing. More than once I tried to complete a level "in style" half a dozen times, taking out guards with precision strikes and stealing disguises and sneaking from cover to cover etc, only to get noticed by one of the brazillion guards and have the whole mission go to hell. Then I just went in there, shot everyone and finished the mission in 3 minutes. That's just rubbish. The game should reward the sneaky approach, but instead trying to be sneaky is most of the time just a massively frustrating and futile effort, you get discovered sooner or later and then you have to shoot everyone on the map to finish level, so why even bother? Yeah yeah you get more points if you manage to finish the level without killing everyone, but who cares? I certainly don't. I haven't tried the harder difficulties, but apparently the higher the difficulty, the more difficult it is to stay unnoticed so ramping up the difficulty is clearly not the answer.
If you can get the game cheap and you like the concept, go for it. I can't recommend paying the full price, though, and that's why the thumb down. :(

Harrowing with a heart of gold, TWoM puts gives you leadership over a group of desperate refugees attempting to survive in a foreign city under military siege and occupation. Gameplay revolves around resource management hybridized with a strange, yet engaging 2D point-and-click adventure style. The environments and art, while naturally a bit glum to say the least, are rendered with a striking and beautiful attention to detail. The same is to be said for the writing, with most decisions plucking away at those morally-grounded heartstrings of yours as you navigate the shattered lives of a crumbling city's inhabitants. Get what you need to survive by scavenging the ruins, trading with other groups of survivors or surrender your humanity and turn to banditry and violence - but remember an abrupt and unwelcome fate can find you no matter what side of the line you stand on. Do the ends justify the means, or will one compromise just lead to another?
Oh yeah, about that "heart of gold" bit - TWoM supports War Child, a charity helping children that have been displaced or otherwise had their lives impacted by armed conflict. So you get to help kids and play this rad, engaging and unique game all at once. Cool stuff. So, buy it, play it, feel good. Simple!

I don't like puzzle games. That's my story and I'm sticking to it. I bought this game because it's a business management simulator. Thing is, the business management part is only half of it, if that. The restf is very much a puzzle game, but not one that requires you to go so in depth with your puzzle solving thinking that you end up with a migraine.
When playing Big Pharma, you'll notice that most of your time is spent, with the game paused, trying to fit equipment into spaces that make it work well with other equipment, within the constraints of the sometimes awkwardly shaped space provided. Sometimes you'll find yourself thinking "Geez, they must have made this chain of machines incompatible with this dumb building on purpose", while at other times you'll think "Wow, this fits so perfectly here, without wasting any space at all, that I must be doing something right!" Odds are pretty good that the reality is somewhere in the middle, where there wasn't much thought put into it at all aside from using the shapes of the buildings to throttle the difficulty. You will be annoyed at the lack of space, irritated with the AI for seeming to be able to patent something just as you're ramping up to produce it, but overall, you will get a sense of strange euphoria, seeing your machinations chug along, making you lots of money -- and it is pretty darn easy to make lots of money in this game. That part isn't hard. The difficulty definitely comes from making the pieces fit in a way that accomplishes your goals, effeciently and on timie, without blocking you from making the next line.
This is a great game to play with the background music turned off and your favorite tunes playing instead. That's not to say that the background music is bad. It's just mediocre, and mostly pointless.
The graphics look exactly like they should for a game such as this -- good enough. They're not realistic but they're not so cartoony as to be a distraction from the puzzle aspects.
There is no story or campaign or anything. The closest you get is the "challenges" screen, which is the first thing you see when you click "New Game", and offers various scenarios with challenges attached. There is a tutorial which is both easy to use and fairly comprehensive, though you'll probably have to Google some of the higher tier equipment to see how they work. The information is not hard to find, though, so that's not really a downside.
Overall, Big Pharma is a pretty good game. The simplicity will draw you in and keep you hooked even well past the point where you're tired of doing the same things over and over again and, really, that's its biggest rub -- redundancy. From the moment you play the first game in the "Beginner" column to the moment you put it away, you're doing pretty much the same thing over and over again. Think about it as an assembly line simulation tied in with some simplified business management concepts and you've got a good idea of what Big Pharma is all about.
You're simply placing machines in a way that will be as efficient as you can make them. Everything else is just details. Is that a bad thing? In this case, I don't think it is. To me, the repitition gave me a sense of comfort, knowing that, at the beginning of every scenario, I had at least some *idea* of what I was doing. The first level drugs are extremely easy to make, and they get you off the ground pretty quickly, though you are forced to get more complicated since you'll oversaturate the market with them if you just make those. It was when the idea of starting fresh became significantly more appealing than continuing to try and get Master Level of accomplishment at a scenario that I realized it was probably time to play something else. However, that was 80 hours in, which is not a bad return for a game that costs $25 when it's not on sale! I'll probably go back to it at some point, too.
